plans.foundation: Two foundation options included: 4x6 treated wood skids (20'-0", qty 4, on gravel) with a framed floor, or a concrete slab
plans.floor_framing: 2x6 floor joists at 16" o.c. (16 @ 16'-0") with 2x6 rim joists (2 @ 20'-0"), 3/4" full-face T&G OSB sheathing (10 sheets), Simpson A23 clips (16). Floor load rated 50 psf, "the same floor load rating used in building homes."
plans.wall_framing: 2x4 studs at 16" o.c. with a double top plate, "just like a home is framed" (74 studs @ 8'-0", 2x4 plates 16'/20', 2x6 headers)
plans.overall_height: Not stated on the plan page. iCreatables' own "Gambrel Shed Heights" section drawing for the 16'-wide gambrel shows 17'-11" total (1'-1 1/2" floor/skid assembly + 16'-9 1/2" from the floor to the ridge) when built on 4x6 wood rails with a framed floor; the site notes a slab build is "about 12" lower".
plans.roof: Gambrel / multi-pitch barn roof over a full 16' clear span; site-built plywood-gusseted 2x6 gambrel trusses (26 upper + 26 lower top chords, 11 collar ties), 7/16" OSB deck, 12" front/back and 6" side overhangs, 25-yr asphalt shingles or metal. Lower/upper slopes shown as 12/7 and 7/12 on the vendor heights drawing; page recommends a local structural engineer size the members and connections.
plans.siding: Textured plywood siding (26 sheets 4'x8'x1/2") with 1-1/2" battens at 12" o.c. (board-and-batten look); "You may add or substitute other sidings such as cedar shingles or horizontal lap siding." Trim is 1x3 and 1x6 wood, Masonite or cement board.
plans.doors: Double doors making a 6'-0" x 6'-8" opening (6068) on the 16' end wall, plus a 3'-0" x 6'-8" (3068) door on a long wall per the floor plan and materials list. Build your own with the included door plans or buy factory pre-hung units.
plans.windows: 5 windows, 2626 size (2'-6" x 2'-6") — "a standard window size that can be ordered from any window company. You may add other windows on the other walls if desired." Plus two 12" x 18" gable vents on the materials list.
plans.loft: Storage loft under the gambrel: "Storage loft - The multi pitched roof adds 300 sf. of useable loft area inside the shed." Floor plan shows a partial "Loft line above". The free materials list's loft section lists only 6 sheets of 3/4" T&G OSB (≈192 sf of loft decking) and no loft joists, so loft extent/framing sizes come only with the purchased plans. Loft headroom is not stated; the vendor's 16'-wide gambrel section shows a 2x4 collar tie with roughly 6'-3" of clear height in the upper area (dimension read off the drawing, not text).
plans.skill_level: Not stated per-plan; vendor FAQ says the plans are "designed for homeowners to build their own sheds," show cut lengths and board placement, come with a How To Build A Shed manual, and are meant to suit "both an old pro or a first time framer." Realistically an intermediate DIY project: 16' gambrel truss assembly, loft framing and 17'-11" ridge height.
plans.permit_notes: Plans are not engineer-stamped. Vendor FAQ: "Do the plans have engineering? No, the plans do not come with an engineers stamp"; plans "have implemented elements from the 'prescriptive codes' in the IRC" and "are used regularly to apply for and get building permits," but local snow/wind/seismic requirements may require review and a stamp by an engineer licensed in your state. For this plan specifically the page tells you to have a local structural engineer size the roof framing. Roof snow load: "The roof load varies depending on your regional weather conditions. Check with your local building department or truss plant." At 320 sq ft this shed is well over the common 120/200 sq ft permit-exemption thresholds, so a permit is likely.

plans.summary: A $59.99 emailed PDF plan set (SKU shed16x20-GB, $65.99 for mailed prints) for a 16' x 20' / 320 sq ft board-and-batten gambrel barn shed with a storage loft, built on either 4x6 treated skids with a 2x6 framed floor or a concrete slab. Framing is house-style: 2x4 walls at 16" o.c. with a double top plate, 8'-1" walls, 2x6 floor joists at 16" o.c. under 3/4" T&G OSB, and site-built plywood-gusseted 2x6 gambrel trusses that clear-span the full 16' width with 2x4 collar ties. Openings are a 6'-0" x 6'-8" double door on the 16' end wall, a 3068 side door and five 2'-6" x 2'-6" windows; roofing is 25-year asphalt shingles (about 570 sq ft / 6 squares) or metal. The full itemized materials list is a free PDF download on the page, but the page explicitly recommends having a local structural engineer size and specify the roof framing members and connections, and the plans carry no engineer's stamp.
pros: Free, fully itemized materials list downloadable before purchase (26 siding sheets, 74 studs, 16 floor joists, truss chord counts, even nail weights) — you can price the whole build at a lumberyard before spending $59.99

House-grade framing spec rather than shed-grade: 2x4 studs at 16" o.c. with double top plate, 2x6 floor joists at 16" o.c., 3/4" T&G OSB deck, 50 psf floor rating, Simpson A23 clips and H2.5 ties called out
Both a skid/framed-floor and a concrete-slab foundation are included, so it suits a level yard pad or a poured slab without redrawing anything
Real usable loft from the gambrel shape — the site claims 300 sq ft of loft area over the 320 sq ft footprint, plus 8'-1" walls give full standing height below
Door plans are included, so you can build the 6068 double doors instead of buying pre-hung units (a meaningful cost saving on a barn this size)
Openings use off-the-shelf sizes (2626 windows, 3068 and 6068 doors), so no custom orders

Instant PDF delivery printable at home on 8-1/2" x 11" paper, at known scales (1/4" plans, 1/2" section, 3/4" details), with a free How-To-Build-A-Shed manual and a matching how-to video for framing the gambrel truss
Deep size ladder in the same design (12x16 up to 16x24, and 14x20/14x24), so you can scale the footprint without switching vendors or styles
cons: The plan itself punts on the structure of its biggest element: "The roof on the 16x20 gambrel shed is large enough that we recommend that the owner and builder consult a local structural engineer to size and specify the framing members and connections. The plans do include a guideline for the rafter construction." That means the 16' clear-span gambrel truss may need engineering (extra cost) before you cut anything.

No engineer's stamp at all — vendor FAQ: "the plans do not come with an engineers stamp" — so high-snow, high-wind (Florida/coastal) or seismic jurisdictions will need a locally licensed engineer to review, calc and stamp them.
At 320 sq ft this is far above the usual 120-200 sq ft permit exemption, so expect a permit, setback review and possibly a footing/anchoring detail the plan doesn't provide.

Loft data is thin and internally inconsistent: the page advertises "300 sf. of useable loft area" but the free materials list's loft section shows only 6 sheets of 3/4" T&G OSB (~192 sq ft) and lists no loft joists, so loft extent, joist size and headroom are unknown until you buy.

Tall build: the vendor's own heights drawing puts the 16'-wide gambrel at 17'-11" to the ridge on skids — that means scaffolding/ladder work at height for sheathing and shingles, and it can trip height limits in some residential zoning codes.
Roof/truss spacing is never stated in text; you have to infer ~13 trusses over the 20' length from the materials list quantities.

Gambrel trusses are site-assembled from 2x6 chords with 7/16" OSB gussets — 13 of them to build accurately on a jig, plus lifting them 8' onto the walls, which is the hardest part of the project and hard to do solo.
No refunds of any kind once purchased (electronic product), so you are relying on the free example sheets and free materials list to judge the set.
The published spec omits things a 320 sq ft build usually needs: no ramp, no anchoring/tie-down details mentioned, no insulation or electrical, and the loft has no stair/ladder spec on the page.

Price is injected by JavaScript via a Shopify Buy Button, so the page can look priceless if scripts are blocked; the site's edge cache also served a completely different product page (the 16x20 Modern Studio shed) for this URL on one of our fetches.

cost_estimate.confidence: MEDIUM-HIGH on the total, HIGH on the method. Why: (1) Quantities are effectively certain — they come from iCreatables' own free materials-list PDF, already verified byte-for-byte in a prior pass, so no quantity is invented. (2) About 89-91% of the dollar value rests on real, dated retailer prices I fetched and parsed myself, and I show the source and snapshot date for every one. (3) The strongest reason for confidence is independent convergence: a completely separate benchmark — Sutherlands' own live 2026 shed material packages at $17.31-$23.55/sq ft, including a gambrel-with-loft at $21.27/sq ft — implies $5,539-$7,536 for 320 sq ft, and my bottom-up bill came out at $5,753-$7,612. Two individual lines also matched across independent retailers to within 0.3% (T1-11 siding $44.78 vs $44.92; 4x6 treated $78.88 vs $78.99). It would be hard for both methods to be wrong in the same direction by much. What holds it back from HIGH: four lines (~6-9% of value) are honest estimates rather than quotes; the five windows carry a ~$720 spread because neither priced product is exactly the specified 2626; Menards prices come from Wayback snapshots dated Jan-May 2026 with two fastener lines from 2025, and FRED WPU0811 shows softwood lumber already +6.3% above the April level those snapshots reflect; and it is a Midwest price picture that will not transfer to high-cost regions. Anyone about to spend this money should treat the range as a well-anchored planning figure and still take the vendor's part-numbered list to two local yards for a firm bid — which is exactly what iCreatables designed that numbering system for.
excludes: CONCRETE — the plan's alternate slab foundation is entirely unpriced. A 16x20 4" slab is roughly 4 cu yd plus rebar/mesh/forms and would add well over $1,000 delivered.
GRAVEL — the materials list literally says 'F5 Gravel' with no quantity, so it cannot be priced. A skid pad needs roughly 3-5 tons of compacted base.
Site work: excavation, grading, leveling, sod removal, drainage, spoil haul-off.
PERMITS and fees. At 320 sq ft this shed is far above the usual 120-200 sq ft exemption, so a permit is likely.

STRUCTURAL ENGINEERING — and this one is not optional-feeling: the plan page itself says to have a local structural engineer size and specify the 16' clear-span gambrel truss members and connections, and the plans carry no engineer's stamp. Budget a real engineering fee.
LABOR — the entire number assumes you swing every hammer yourself. Contract framing/roofing labor on a 320 sq ft building would typically exceed the materials cost.
TOOLS, and specifically the ones this build forces: staging/scaffolding and tall ladders for a 17'-11" ridge, plus a truss assembly jig for 13 site-built gambrel trusses.
DELIVERY / lumber-yard haul fees. 26 siding sheets, 42 sheets of OSB, 58 2x6x8s and four 20' treated 4x6 timbers will not fit in a pickup.
SALES TAX (shown separately above, not in the headline total).
ANCHORING / TIE-DOWN hardware for the skid foundation — the plan publishes no anchoring detail at all.

LOFT FRAMING LUMBER AND LOFT ACCESS — a genuine gap in the vendor's own free list, not just in my pricing: the loft section lists only 6 sheets of 3/4" T&G OSB and NO loft joists, and there is no stair or ladder spec. Loft joists for ~192 sq ft could add $200-400.
PAINT, primer and stain. Textured plywood siding must be finished; 320 sq ft of shed needs roughly 8-10 gallons of body paint plus primer.
INSULATION, vapor barrier, interior wall/ceiling finish — none are in the plan.
ELECTRICAL: service, conduit, panel, wiring, receptacles, lighting.
House wrap / weather-resistive barrier behind the siding (not on the plan's list).
Gutters and downspouts.
A RAMP — not on the plan's list, and a 320 sq ft shed with a 6' double door almost certainly wants one.
Shelving, workbenches, loft railing, or any interior fit-out.
The $59.99 plan set itself.
Waste/overage beyond the one extra shingle bundle in the high column. Real jobs typically run 5-10% over on cut lumber.

plans.summary: Shedking's 16x20 barn is a 320 sq ft site-built gambrel with an unusually livable loft: 7'5" of headroom over the loft floor, 2x12 loft joists at 24" o.c., and a real 3'+ wide interior stairway with a framed landing instead of a ladder. Framing is heavier than typical shed plans — treated 2x8 floor joists 16" o.c. on five 4x6 skids with concrete pier anchors (slab optional), 2x6 walls 16" o.c. at 8' interior height, lap siding over 7/16" sheathing, and builder-built 2x6 gambrel trusses 24" o.c. under shingles, to an overall height of 18' 5-5/8". The $29.95 instant PDF download includes 34 pages of blueprints, a separate barn building guide, a full materials list, free cupola plans, designer email support, and a 90-day money-back guarantee. Designer John Shank is candid that the truss plans carry no load limits and that you should buy engineered 16' trusses and hire a local structural engineer if your building department wants a stamp.
pros: The complete materials list is published as a free public PDF (no purchase needed), so you can price the entire build before spending a dime — quantities down to nail counts, hangers and Simpson TWB bracing

Loft is genuinely usable rather than a crawl space: 7'5" headroom, 2x12x16 joists, 3/4" plywood floor, and a full-width (over 3') stairway with a proper landing detail — vendor even suggests a bedroom up there
Structurally beefier than most hobby shed plans: 2x6 walls at 16" o.c., 8' interior wall height, double top plates, wall bracing straps, H2.5 hurricane ties at every truss/joist bearing
Very cheap for a 320 sq ft lofted building ($29.95) with a 90-day money-back guarantee and direct email support from the designer
Foundation is DIY-friendly (treated skids + concrete pier anchors and blocking) with a documented concrete-slab option if your jurisdiction or use case demands it
Honest about permitting: tells you up front to get a permit, that truss plans lack load limits, and that stamped calcs are not included — no false 'permit ready' claim
Extras that reduce cost/risk: separate barn building guide, free cupola plans, and an AR viewer on the page to preview the building in your yard
cons: 16' clear-span gambrel trusses are site-built from 2x6s with plywood gussets and come with no engineering; the designer himself recommends ordering engineered 16' trusses for permit approval, which adds real cost and deviates from the plan's truss detail

No engineer's stamp or structural calculations are provided — a 320 sq ft two-level building will trip permit thresholds almost everywhere and often stamped-plan requirements, meaning an extra fee to a local structural engineer

Loft joists at 24" o.c. spanning 16' are sized for storage-ish loads; if you intend sleeping/office/gym use, verify the live load with an engineer, and expect some bounce with 3/4" sheathing at 24" spacing
Door spec is inconsistent between sources: the page says pre-hung 5' wide double doors while the free materials list orders a 6' wide double door — confirm the rough opening before framing the header
Only five 4x6 skids under a 320 sq ft lofted structure; in frost-prone or soft-soil sites you will need proper piers/footings or the slab option, which changes the floor system and cost
No stated build time and no dollar cost estimate anywhere — the materials sheet has quantities but no prices, so budgeting is on you

Digital-only, no printed/mailed set; the on-page price only renders via a JavaScript Shopify Buy button (the HTML has no price), and shedking.net was unreachable by direct fetch from this host, so the record leans on the Wayback snapshot plus the vendor's Shopify catalog
Plans are one-size-as-drawn: 2x6 walls, lap siding and a specific window/door set; substituting metal siding, a roll-up door or a different roof covering is left to you

excludes: Foundation of any kind: concrete slab (the page offers it as an option), gravel pad, concrete piers/footings and the pier anchors the plan calls for, rebar, form lumber, sonotubes. A 16x20 4in slab is roughly 4 cu yd = $900-1,600 delivered in 2026, and gravel/excavation is extra.
Labor. This is a materials bill only. The plan involves 9 site-built 16ft-clear-span gambrel trusses, 2x12 loft framing, a full stair with landing, and 18ft 5-5/8in of working height.
Delivery. A 320 sq ft framing package is 3-4 tons and will not fit in a pickup; yard delivery is typically $75-250 per trip.

Tools and rentals: circular saw, framing nailer + compressor, roofing nailer, air hose, scaffolding or ladders (an 18ft-plus gambrel effectively requires scaffold rental), truss lifting help, safety gear.

Permit fees and plan review. Shedking's designer explicitly says he recommends a permit and that his truss drawings carry NO load limits or engineering, so a structural engineer's stamp may be required on top - typically $300-1,500 depending on jurisdiction.

Engineered trusses. The designer recommends buying engineered 16ft trusses from a truss plant rather than building them, for permit purposes. That would replace the 2x6x8/2x6x10/gusset/plate/nail lines here (roughly $700 of material) with a factory truss package - budget $2,000-3,500 for 11 gambrel trusses delivered.
Paint, primer, caulk, sealant, flashing tape, house-wrap tape. LP SmartSide comes primed but not finished; 768 sq ft of siding plus trim is 2 coats over ~900 sq ft.
Insulation, vapor barrier, interior wall/ceiling finish, interior paint, interior floor covering. The bill sheathes the loft floor and main floor in bare OSB/plywood.
Electrical: service feed, trenching, conduit, panel/subpanel, wire, boxes, receptacles, switches, fixtures, and the electrical permit.
Stair handrail, guardrail and loft edge rail - a full-size stair over 3ft wide plus a loft opening will need them for a permit, and the materials list contains none.
Gutters and downspouts, cupola material (free cupola plans are included with the plan but no materials are listed for it), ramp or steps up to the door threshold.
The $29.95 plan purchase itself, and sales tax on everything above.

plans.name: Free 16x20 Pole Barn Plans (2-part: frame + roof/doors)
plans.http_status: 403 on direct curl (Cloudflare bot-block); 200 via Wayback (web.archive.org/web/2026id_/) for both PART 1 and PART 2
plans.style: pole-barn (post-frame gable shelter/barn, open-plan, double doors on the 16 ft front gable end)
plans.price: Free (both web articles); optional 24-page PDF of the same plan is $5 on Gumroad (howtospecialist.gumroad.com/l/LKhrr, "16x20 Pole Barn Plans", schema.org "price":5.0 USD)
plans.format: On-page article split across two free step-by-step pages (PART 1 frame/siding, PART 2 roof + doors), each with ~10-14 numbered 3D SketchUp-style diagrams; optional paid instant PDF download (24 pages, 1.23 MB) via Gumroad
plans.page_count: Web version: 2 articles (no page count). Paid PDF: Gumroad lists "Length: 24 pages", "Size: 1.23 MB"
plans.summary: A genuinely free, two-part DIY post-frame ("pole barn") plan for a 16x20 ft / 320 sq ft open shelter with a gable roof and a pair of double doors on the front. Construction is 17 pressure-treated 4x4 posts set 3 ft deep in 10-12 in diameter concrete-filled holes, a 2x10 skirt board at the base, 2x4 girts for the T1-11 siding, and 11 site-built 2x6 trusses with 1/2 in plywood gussets and 2x4 webs at 24 in on center, sheathed in 3/4 in plywood and finished with tar paper plus asphalt shingles. There is no floor and no slab detail — it is a shelter over grade. PART 2 publishes its complete cut list and shopping list free on the page; PART 1's cut/shopping lists are now behind an "UNLOCK PREMIUM PLANS" upsell on the live page, but are fully preserved in the site's 2018 Wayback snapshot (captured below).
plans.foundation: Post-in-ground: 17 pressure-treated 4x4 posts set in concrete in holes dug 3 ft deep and 10-12 in in diameter ("Dig 3′ into the ground, about 10-12″ in diameter and then fit the pressure treated posts into place"), plumbed and temporarily braced until the concrete cures; layout with string, batter boards, the 3-4-5 rule and equal diagonals. A 2x10 skirt/splash beam closes the base of the walls. No slab, no perimeter footing, no skid option; post depth explicitly deferred to local code.
plans.floor_framing: None — no floor is framed or specified in either part; the building is a shelter over bare grade, so a gravel or concrete floor is entirely on the builder.
plans.wall_framing: Post-frame: 4x4 posts (cut 134″, 141 1/2″ and 166″ long) in concrete, a 2x10 skirt/base beam ("Attach a 2×10 beam to the base of the walls, so you seal the pole barn properly"), then horizontal 2x4 girts screwed to the posts with 3 1/2″ screws as backing for the siding. No studs, no top-plate detail beyond rafter ties, no diagonal/knee bracing shown.
plans.wall_height: ~101 1/4 in (8 ft 5 in) to the eave, per the dimensioned render of this same design on MyOutdoorPlans; HowToSpecialist never publishes a wall or eave height (its PART 2 elevation only dimensions the 103 in x 96 in door opening).
plans.roof: Gable, with 11 site-built trusses at 24″ on center secured to the top plates with rafter ties. Truss: 2x6 chords (2 rafters at 120″, bottom chord 192″ = the full 16 ft span), 2x4 webs (22 pieces at 23 3/4″, 11 at 50 1/4″), and 1/2″ plywood gussets over the joints fastened with 1 1/4″ screws. Deck is 3/4″ plywood screwed with 1 5/8″ screws every 8″. 2x6 overhangs front and back. Covered with roofing felt (2″ minimum overlap, stapled) then asphalt shingles. Pitch is NEVER stated in the text — the 50 1/4″ king post over the 192″ bottom chord implies roughly 6/12, but that is an inference, not published.
plans.siding: T1-11 (T1-11/T-111 plywood siding), 48″x96″ sheets: 16 sheets on the walls in PART 1, plus gable-end panels and 2 sheets used for the doors in PART 2. Installed with edges flush, no gaps, 6-8d nails every 8″ along the framing.
plans.windows: None — no windows appear in the plans, cut lists, diagrams, or hardware list. No vents or louvers either.
plans.doors: One pair of double doors centered on the front (16 ft gable) wall. Each door is built from a 4'x8' T1-11 sheet on a 2x4 frame (2 pieces at 89″, 2 at 48″, 1 at 29″ per pair listing), assembled with glue and 2″ screws. Opening is trimmed with 2x4 jambs (2 pieces at 96″, 1 at 103″), so roughly an 8 ft x 8 ft opening. Hung on hinges with a latch and handle ("latch & hinges" is the only hardware spec).
plans.loft: none — no loft, no ceiling joists usable as a loft (the truss bottom chords are only 2x6 spanning 16 ft, which is not a storage deck), no headroom figure given.
plans.overall_height: ~161 1/4 in (13 ft 5 in) at the ridge, per the dimensioned render of this same design on MyOutdoorPlans (not published by HowToSpecialist)
plans.skill_level: not stated as a level; the page only claims "This pole barn is easy to build". Realistically intermediate: 17 hand-dug 3 ft post holes set plumb in concrete, angle-cut rafters on a miter saw, and 11 site-assembled trusses to lift onto 8 ft posts.
plans.build_time: Page states "Time: One Day" on each of the two parts (i.e. 2 days total). This is not credible for a 320 sq ft post-frame building — see cons.
plans.est_material_cost: Not stated by HowToSpecialist; the MyOutdoorPlans printing of the same design claims "between $5,000 and $8,000" — unsupported, since the publisher's own FAQ says no cost estimate is included in any plan
plans.permit_notes: No permit, engineering, snow-load or wind-load information. The only code reference in either part is about footing depth: "Make sure you check out the local building codes, so you see the proper depth you have to set the posts in concrete. In most cases 3′ will be enough for the footings." No stamped drawings, no lumber species/grade, no fastening schedule for the truss gussets beyond "1 1/4″ screws". At 320 sq ft this building is over the permit-exempt threshold in most US jurisdictions, and the site-built unengineered trusses are the likely sticking point with a plans examiner.

includes: PART 1 web page: step-by-step written instructions for posts, layout, 2x10 skirt, 2x4 girts and T1-11 siding, with ~10 labeled 3D diagrams

PART 2 web page: rafters/truss assembly, plywood gussets, truss setting at 24" OC, gable panels, overhangs, roof sheathing, felt + shingles, door jambs and double-door build, with ~14 labeled 3D diagrams
PART 2 full cut list (components A-I) and full shopping list, free on the page
Tool list (miter saw, jigsaw, drill, chalk line, tape, spirit level, pencil, safety gloves/glasses)
PART 1 cut + shopping lists — gated behind the premium upsell on the live page (present in the 2018 Wayback snapshot)

Optional $5 Gumroad PDF: "1 PDF file with full plans, full cut and shopping lists" — step by step diagrams, step by step instructions, full cut list, full shopping list, full tool list, 24 pages, imperial measurements
pros: Actually free and actually complete as a build sequence — two illustrated articles carry you from post layout to hung doors, with ~24 numbered 3D diagrams total.
Cheapest possible way to get 320 sq ft under roof: post-frame means no slab, no perimeter footing, no floor joists, no rim/skid beams. The entire foundation is 17 holes and some concrete.
PART 2's cut list and shopping list are published in full for free, so you can price the whole roof/door package (31x 2x6-10', 11x 2x6-16', 13 sheets of 3/4" ply, etc.) before committing.
Everything is commodity lumber — 4x4, 2x4, 2x6, 2x10, T1-11, plywood — no engineered beams, no LVL, no special order, no crane and no truss lead time.
Trusses are site-built on the ground from 2x6 with plywood gussets, so two people can assemble and lift all 11 without equipment.
Roughly 8 ft x 8 ft double doors on the front make this genuinely useful for a tractor, trailer, boat or ride-on mower rather than just shelving.
Dimensions are explicitly meant to be adjusted ("you can easily adjust all the dimensions to suit your needs"), and the same author publishes a 16x24 sibling if you want more length.
$5 / 24-page PDF is a cheap way to get the paywalled PART 1 cut list plus an offline printable copy.
cons: Bait-and-switch on PART 1: the frame/siding cut and shopping lists that used to be free are now replaced by "UNLOCK PREMIUM PLANS FOR CUT & SHOPPING LISTS". You either pay $5 or dig them out of an old Wayback snapshot, so the live free page alone will not let you buy materials for the walls.

The trusses are NOT engineered or stamped: 2x6 chords with 1/2" plywood gussets and 2x4 webs spanning a full 16 ft at 24" OC, with no lumber species or grade, no snow/wind load rating, and no gusset nailing/screwing schedule beyond "1 1/4" screws". For a 320 sq ft permitted structure many building departments will reject this outright and require stamped trusses or an engineer's letter — budget for that.

4x4 posts are light for a 320 sq ft post-frame building. Commercial pole barns this size typically use 6x6 or laminated 3-ply columns. No post spacing dimension, uplift connection, or diagonal knee bracing is shown anywhere, and lateral stability depends entirely on the buried posts plus siding.

3/4" roof sheathing over 24" OC trusses is heavy and expensive overkill — 7/16" or 1/2" is standard. Those 13 sheets of 3/4" plywood are one of the biggest line items and the easiest place to overspend.
No floor at all, and no slab or gravel-pad guidance. If you want a usable floor for a workshop rather than a shelter, that whole scope is on you.
No windows, no ventilation/soffit venting spec, no insulation, no electrical, and no gable/ridge vent — this is a shell, not a habitable or conditioned space.

"Time: One Day" per part is fantasy. Hand-digging and concreting 17 holes 3 ft deep, plumbing 17 posts, and assembling 11 trusses is realistically several weekends for two people, plus concrete cure time.

Material list has visible errors: the roofing line reads "400 sq ft of tar paper, 400 sq ft of tar paper" (the second one is obviously meant to be shingles), and the overhang entry "7 pieces – 2 1/4″ long" of 2x6 makes no sense. Re-take off quantities yourself before ordering.
Roof pitch, wall height, eave height and overall height are never stated in either article, so you cannot check clearances or verify shingle-pitch minimums without scaling the diagrams.
Setting posts in direct ground contact in concrete is the failure-prone detail long term (rot at grade); no post protection, gravel base, barrier sleeve or dry-set bracket alternative is offered.

plans.name: 16x20 Gable Shed - Free DIY Plans (Part 1 + Part 2)
plans.http_status: 403 on direct curl (Cloudflare bot block); 200 via Wayback snapshot of both Part 1 and Part 2 (https://web.archive.org/web/2026id_/...). Gumroad product page fetched directly, 200.
plans.style: gable
plans.price: Free (full step-by-step article + cut lists on Part 1 and Part 2); optional premium PDF "16x20 Gable Shed Plans" = $11.99 on Gumroad
plans.format: On-page article in two parts (Part 1 = floor/walls/trusses, Part 2 = siding/overhangs/roofing/doors) with 3D SketchUp-style diagrams; optional instant PDF download via Gumroad ($11.99)
plans.page_count: not stated
plans.summary: A free, two-part step-by-step build for a 320 sq ft gable storage shed / workshop: 2x6 skid-and-joist floor on eight 10 ft 4x4 skids, 2x4 walls at 16" on center with 92 3/4" studs, eleven site-built 16 ft trusses (2x6 rafters + 2x4 webs + 1/2" plywood gussets) at 24" on center, 5/8" T1-11 siding, 3/4" plywood roof deck and asphalt shingles. It has double front doors made from the front-wall siding cutout in a ~100" wide x 80" jambed opening, a side man door, and two windows in one side wall. The published dimension diagram gives a 192" x 240" floor, 218 1/2" x 264 3/4" including overhangs, ~107 3/4" to the eave and 158 1/4" to the ridge, with rafters cut at 25 degrees. Per-part cut lists are free on the page; the consolidated shopping list, cut-layout diagrams, a front ramp and planter boxes are behind the $11.99 Gumroad PDF.
plans.foundation: Skid spacing IS published in the free Part 1 page. The embedded diagram https://myoutdoorplans.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/Floor-skids.jpg dimensions 4 rows of skids spaced 59 1/4" apart (three 59 1/4" labels), each row made of two 120" 4x4s laid end to end (two "120"" labels) running the 20 ft length. Only the pier/footing/anchor details are genuinely absent.
plans.floor_framing: Half right, and misleading as written. The cut-list omission is real (only 4 pcs of 20 ft 2x6 are listed, no interior joists), but the free page's floor-frame diagram fully dimensions the joists: 2x6 joists 189" long at 14 1/2" clear = 16" on center (~17 joists) with 13 3/4" at each end, plus a 307 1/4" squaring diagonal on a 240" x 189" frame.
plans.wall_framing: 2x4 studs at 16" on center, 92 3/4" studs, double top plate inset 3 1/2" at each end, double end studs with 1/2" plywood spacers at the corners; doubled 2x4 headers with a 1/2" plywood spacer over the window openings; a double 2x6 header, 99" long, with 1/2" plywood spacer over the double front door. Fastened with 3 1/2" screws (or 16d nails at the header).
plans.wall_height: 92 3/4" studs (about 8 ft wall); dimension diagram shows 107 3/4" from grade to the top of the side wall/eave (includes skids, 2x6 floor frame and plates)
plans.overall_height: 158 1/4" to the ridge per the published dimension diagram (about 13 ft 2 in.)
plans.roof: Gable roof from eleven site-built trusses at 24" on center spanning 16 ft: 2x6 rafters (119 1/4") with a 25-degree cut at one end (about a 5.6:12 slope), 2x6 bottom chord 192", 2x4 webs (23 7/8" and 50 5/8"), 1/2" plywood gussets on both faces except the outer face of the end trusses. Trusses assembled flat on a jig and set with rafter ties + 1 1/2" structural screws. 2x6 framed overhangs front and back (119 1/8" rafters + 8 1/2" blocking), 3/4" plywood roof sheathing, 1x8 roof trims/fascia, tar paper underlayment, drip edge, and asphalt shingles - 500 sq ft of roofing called out.
plans.siding: 5/8" T1-11 siding: 16 full 4'x8' sheets plus 4'x16", 4'x29 1/2" and 4'x52" pieces, nailed with 8d nails every 8". Door panels are cut out of the siding and reused as the door skins. No housewrap, building paper or separate wall sheathing layer is specified.
plans.doors: Each front-door leaf is explicitly dimensioned on the free Part 2 page as 48" wide x 73" tall, with a 41" middle rail and two 34 3/4" panel fields. Two leaves = exactly 96" = the 96" framed opening.
plans.windows: The 39" (2 pieces) are the man-door header, not a window part (36" opening + 1 1/2" bearing each side = 39"). The window parts are 48" (4 jacks), 35" (8 = 2 headers + 2 sills per window), 27" (6 below-sill cripples) and 10 3/4" (10 above-header cripples).
plans.loft: none - no loft, attic floor or storage platform is described. The trusses are webbed (2x4 webs at 23 7/8" and 50 5/8") at 24" on center, so the roof volume is not usable for overhead storage without redesign.
plans.skill_level: Moderate DIY: the page says the 2-4 week timeline assumes "moderate DIY skills and good weather". Requires miter saw, circular saw, pocket-hole jig, truss assembly on a jig, and a helper for lifting 16 ft trusses.
plans.build_time: Page states 2-4 weeks of part-time work for a DIYer ("Hiring professionals ... in under a week"). The sidebar "Time" box on both parts says "One week", and the boilerplate paragraph claims "you could get the job done in about a day" - the three figures contradict each other; treat 2-4 weeks as the realistic one.
plans.est_material_cost: $5,500 to $8,000 for materials, "depending on your location and material choices"; permits, site prep and finishes extra; professional labor would add $3,000-$5,000
plans.permit_notes: The article tells you to obtain permits before starting ("Follow detailed plans and ensure you've obtained the necessary permits before beginning") and the Gumroad listing disclaims liability: "It is your responsibility to make adjustments to the plans, to comply with your local building codes." No engineer stamp, no snow/wind load rating, no state-approved drawing set. At 320 sq ft this exceeds the common 100-200 sq ft permit exemption in most US jurisdictions, so expect a permit review of a 16 ft site-built plywood-gusset truss with no stamp.
plans.materials_list_available: free-on-page (per-part cut & shopping lists, keyed A-R, published in full on Part 1 and Part 2) with the consolidated buy-list gated-behind-upsell ("UNLOCK SHOPPING LIST" links to the $11.99 Gumroad PDF)
plans.refund_policy: Gumroad listing states "No refunds allowed" for the $11.99 premium PDF; the on-page plans are free so no refund applies
includes: Part 1 free article: site prep, 2x6 floor frame, 4x4 skids, 3/4in plywood decking, all four wall frames, header assembly, truss layout and truss installation - with 3D diagrams for each step
Part 2 free article: T1-11 siding, framed overhangs, plywood roof deck, 1x8 trims, tar paper + drip edge + asphalt shingles, double front doors, side door, window trims, finishing

Free Cut & Shopping List keyed A through R (A floor frame, B skids, C floor, D/E side walls, F front wall, G back wall, H siding, I trusses, J overhangs, K roof sheets, L roof trims, M roofing, N/P jambs, O door frame, R door)
Free dimensioned 3D exterior view (192in x 240in floor, 218 1/2in x 264 3/4in with overhangs, 107 3/4in eave, 158 1/4in ridge)
Tools list and time estimate

PAID $11.99 Gumroad PDF adds: cut diagrams, parts lists, full cut & shopping lists, cut-layout diagrams for minimal waste, tools/time/cost estimate, plus how to build the front ramp and planter boxes (imperial units, personal use only)
pros: Genuinely free and genuinely complete: a full 320 sq ft shed, start to shingles and doors, with per-step 3D diagrams and a part-by-part cut list - most free plans this size stop at a teaser
Publishes a dimensioned exterior view (floor 192x240, with overhangs 218 1/2 x 264 3/4, eave 107 3/4, ridge 158 1/4) so you can check setbacks and height limits before spending a dollar
No engineered/ordered components: the eleven 16 ft trusses are built on the ground on a jig from 2x6 rafters, 2x4 webs and 1/2in plywood gussets, so no truss supplier, crane or delivery is needed
Doors are cut out of the T1-11 siding and re-skinned onto 2x4 pocket-hole frames - saves buying a pre-hung double door and guarantees the siding pattern lines up
Skid-on-gravel foundation means no concrete pour, so the build can start the same weekend and stays movable/less permit-provoking than a slab

8 ft walls with a 25-degree gable and 2 ft-ish overhangs give a workshop-usable interior with real eave protection, plus two windows and a separate man door so you are not opening the big doors for daily access
Cheap, low-risk upsell: $11.99 buys cut-layout diagrams (waste minimization on ~30 sheets of plywood/siding), plus ramp and planter box plans
Sibling plans from the same author exist in 16x20 lean-to and 16x24 run-in versions if the gable is not the right roof
cons: The 16 ft trusses are plywood-gusseted site-built trusses with no engineering: no stamp, no snow or wind load rating, no gusset nailing schedule beyond '1 5/8in screws spaced evenly'. In snow country or any permitted jurisdiction you will likely have to buy engineered trusses or pay for a stamp, which changes the material list

Foundation is under-specified for a 320 sq ft building: eight 10 ft 4x4 skids with no published spacing dimension, no gravel pad depth, no pier/footing option drawn, and no hold-down/uplift anchoring - the text just says gravel, concrete or blocks 'would take your project to pro level'

Floor framing is the weakest part of the free cut list: only 2x6 lumber at 20 ft (2 pieces, listed twice, apparently a typo) is itemized. The interior joists and their spacing are not in the list, so you cannot price or verify the floor from the page - you have to read it off the diagram or buy the PDF

3/4in plywood is specified for BOTH the floor (12 sheets) and the roof (16 sheets) - a very heavy and expensive roof deck; 7/16in OSB is normal, and this choice is a meaningful chunk of the $5,500-$8,000 material estimate

Wall sheathing is only 5/8in T1-11 with no housewrap, no building paper and no let-in or metal bracing detail; there is no insulation, vapor barrier, electrical, or roof/soffit ventilation guidance anywhere in the free build
The plan is split across two URLs and the consolidated shopping list (what to actually buy at the lumberyard) is paywalled - so the free version requires you to total ~56 cut-list lines yourself
No loft or overhead storage: the webbed trusses at 24in on center make the roof space unusable, so all 320 sq ft is single-level floor area
Footprint with overhangs is 18 ft 2 1/2 in. x 22 ft 0 3/4 in., noticeably bigger than 16x20 - easy to trip a side-yard setback if you site it off the nominal dimensions
Time estimates on the page contradict each other (2-4 weeks part-time vs. a sidebar 'One week' vs. boilerplate 'about a day'), which undercuts confidence in the other estimates
$11.99 Gumroad PDF is sold with 'No refunds allowed', and the plans are explicitly personal-use-only with a liability disclaimer
Direct access is Cloudflare-gated for scripted fetches (403), so archiving the page locally requires the Wayback Machine; the site is also ad-heavy on mobile

EVERYTHING ELSE CHECKED OUT — this is an unusually accurate extraction. Confirmed verbatim/numerically:

Gumroad product "16x20 Gable Shed Plans" embeds price_cents:1199 in its page JSON, i.e. $11.99 exactly as reported. price_usd 0 is right for the free article. refund_policy JSON: {"title":"No refunds allowed","fine_print":null,"updated_at":"2025-04-16"} — the record's quote is exact. GEOMETRY: the dimension diagram (16x20-gable-shed-dimensions.jpg, fetched directly, 1255x906) reads exactly 192", 240", 218 1/2", 264 3/4", 107 3/4", 158 1/4" — every one of the record's numbers is right, including "about 13 ft 2 in." (158.25" = 13' 2 1/4"). sqft arithmetic is right: 192" x 240" = 16 x 20 = 320 sq ft exactly. Roof pitch: Gumroad description states outright "Roof angle is 25 degrees", the text says "Use a miter saw to make a 25 degree cut to one end of the rafters", and tan(25 deg) x 12 = 5.59, so "about a 5.6:12 slope" is correct. It is also independently consistent with the diagram: (158 1/4 - 107 3/4) / (96 + 13 1/4) = 50.5/109.25 = 0.462 -> 24.8 deg.

CUT LISTS: I dumped every <li> from both parts. All quantities the record cites match: A 2x6 20 ft x2 (listed twice), B 4x4 10 ft x8, C 3/4" ply 4'x8' 8 + 4 = 12, D 92 3/4" x18, E 48"/39"/35"/27"/10 3/4" = 4/2/8/6/10, F 2x6 99" x2, G 92 3/4" x13, I 192" x11 + 119 1/4" x22 + 23 7/8" x22 + 50 5/8" x22, H 5/8" T1-11 16 sheets + 4'x16"/29 1/2"/52", J 119 1/8" x8 + 8 1/2" x36, K 3/4" ply, L 1x8 trims, M 500 sq ft tar paper + shingles, N 80"/43", O 36"/29"/73", P 80"/103", R 73"/48"/41". Keys run A-R with Q absent, so "keyed A-R" is fair. Note the site's own C line is a duplicate ("4'x8' – 8 pieces" then "4'x8' – 4 pieces") — the record reads it faithfully rather than inventing.

QUOTES: I grepped all of them with whitespace/curly-quote normalisation. Every single one is present: "moderate DIY skills and good weather", "in under a week", "One week" (Time box on BOTH parts), "you could get the job done in about a day" (both parts), "depending on your location and material choices", "laying a solid foundation, such as gravel, concrete, or blocks", "a concrete slab or blocks will take your project to pro level", "Follow detailed plans and ensure you've obtained the necessary permits before beginning", "secure them to the frame with appropriate techniques, as described in the manufacturer's instructions", "UNLOCK SHOPPING LIST", "No refunds allowed", plus $5,500 / $8,000 / $3,000 / $5,000. The build_time field's flagging of three contradictory figures (2-4 weeks / One week / about a day) is genuinely what the page does.

16" OC CONFIRMED THREE WAYS: text "secure the studs with 3 1/2" screws, spacing them 16" on center"; G BACK WALL 13 studs over 192" (12 x 16 = 192); Plain-side-wall-frame.jpg dimensioned 233" long, 92 3/4" studs, 14 1/2" clear spacing, 11 3/4" at ends, double top plate "3 1/2"" inset each end and "1/2"" spacers — all exactly as the record describes.

PREMIUM UPSELL: Part 2 says verbatim "In the PREMIUM PLANS I show you how to build the planter boxes and the front ramp. In addition, the PREMIUM PLANS come with CUT LAYOUT Diagrams" — the record's gating claim is right. The ramp is visible (purple) in the dimension render, consistent with it being premium-only.

ENGINEERING SANITY (check 6): the record does NOT overclaim, and the plan is actually sound here. Skids run the 20 ft direction in 4 rows at 59 1/4" o.c.; the 2x6 joists run the 189" direction across them, so max unsupported joist span is ~59 1/4" (~5 ft) — perfectly fine for a 2x6, no 15 ft unsupported span problem. The 2x6/2x4 plywood-gusset truss spans 16 ft at 24" o.c. with no ceiling storage rating, so the record's "loft: none ... roof volume is not usable for overhead storage without redesign" is a fair and correctly cautious read. Two internal inconsistencies belong to the SOURCE, not the extraction: (a) 12 sheets of 3/4" floor ply for a 320 sq ft floor that needs 10; (b) M calls out 500 sq ft of roofing where the actual two slopes are ~438 sq ft. cost_estimate.confidence: MEDIUM-HIGH on the unit prices, MEDIUM on the total. High confidence on prices: 26 of 28 lines come from two live, directly-fetchable retailer catalogs (Sutherlands, snapshot-dated on-page 'as of Mon, Sep 7, 2026'; Dunn Lumber, fetched 2026-09-08), every SKU number and URL is recorded, and I re-scraped all of them a second time with a stricter parser after catching the first one pulling prices out of a 'Compare with Similar Items' carousel - so no price here is a mis-scrape of a neighbouring product. The two independent yards agree closely where they overlap (3/4in plywood $41.88 Dunn vs $42.99 Sutherlands), and FRED WPU081 corroborates the elevated level. Lower confidence on the total, for three reasons: (1) the plan publishes a cut list, not a shopping list, so the board/sheet counts are my cut plan and could vary a few percent; (2) three material groups (floor joists, truss gussets, all connectors and hinges) are absent from the published list and I supplied the quantities, which is about $500-$650 of the total; (3) there is no big-box price anywhere in it, so the low-high spread reflects grade and regional-yard choice rather than retailer channel. Treat $4,800-$6,900 as the materials bill and expect $5,500-$8,000 all-in once tax, delivery and a gravel pad are added - and note it is NOT a project budget: no foundation, permits, paint, tools or labor are in the number.
excludes: Sales tax - zero tax in the number. At 7-9% that is another $340-$620.
Delivery. A 1,900 board-foot, ~50-sheet order will not fit in a pickup. Yard delivery is typically $75-$250 per drop in this market, and none of it is in the total.

Foundation of any kind below the skids: gravel pad, crushed rock, landscape fabric, concrete blocks/piers/footings, ground anchors or tie-downs. The plan only says 'gravel, concrete or blocks' with no depth, spacing or quantity, so there is nothing to price. A 320 sq ft compacted gravel pad is commonly $400-$1,200 delivered.

Permits, plan review, engineering. At 320 sq ft this building exceeds the usual 100-200 sq ft exemption, and the 16ft site-built plywood-gusset trusses carry no stamp and no snow/wind rating, so a permitted jurisdiction may force engineered trusses - which would replace the 11 truss chord + 30 rafter + 44 web lines above with a truss package.
Labor. The plan's own page suggests $3,000-$5,000 for professional labor.
All tools: miter saw, circular saw, pocket-hole jig, drill/impact, ladders, truss jig, nailer or compressor, safety gear.
Housewrap, building paper, or any separate wall sheathing layer. The plan puts 5/8in T1-11 straight on the studs with nothing behind it.
Paint, primer, stain or sealer. T1-11 must be finished or it will fail; 640 sq ft of wall plus 8 trim boards is roughly 5-8 gallons.
Insulation, vapor barrier, interior wall/ceiling finish, interior floor covering.
Electrical: service feed, trenching, conduit, panel/subpanel, receptacles, lighting, switches.
Roof and soffit ventilation, ridge vent, gable vents, and any soffit/vented soffit material - none is specified anywhere in the free build.
Gutters and downspouts.
Front ramp and planter boxes (those are behind the $11.99 Gumroad PDF and are not in the free cut list).
Ice-and-water shield / valley membrane, hip-and-ridge cap shingles, pipe boots and step flashing.
Any shrinkage/damage/miscut contingency beyond the modest waste already built into the board and sheet counts.

plans.summary: A free, fully-published 3-part plan for a 320 sq ft gable storage shed / workshop on 4x4 skids: 8 ft walls, 2x4 studs at 24 in. OC, T1-11 siding, two 36x36 in. windows in one 20 ft side wall, and double doors centered in the 16 ft gable end. The roof is eleven site-built 2x6 trusses at 24 in. OC with 1/2 in. plywood gussets, clear-spanning the 16 ft width so the interior has no posts. Each part page publishes a lettered cut list plus a lumber shopping list and tool list with no email gate, which makes it unusually good source data for a real build. Main caveats: cut-list items A and B misprint the two longest members - the 5 skids and the 2 outer rim joists must be 240 in. (20 ft), not the 192 in. printed, as the dimensioned floor and skid drawings, the shopping list, the sheathing and siding counts and the 11-truss layout all confirm; the trusses are not engineered or stamped; and pitch is published only as a 30-degree angle, with no overall height or load rating given.
plans.foundation: On-grade skid foundation: 5 pieces of 4x4 at 240 in. (20 ft) long running the length of the building - cut-list item A misprints them as 192 in., while the shopping list correctly buys 5 pieces at 20 ft - set on a leveled, compacted gravel bed and spaced across the 16 ft width so the 189 in. joists bear on all five. The drawn clear spacings (45 3/4 + 43 3/4 + 43 1/2 + 43 3/4 in., plus 5 x 3 1/2 in. of skid = 194 1/4 in.) overrun the 192 in. floor width by 2 1/4 in., so the spacing has to be trimmed on site. Floor frame is toenailed or rafter-tied down to the skids. No slab, piers or frost footings, and no anchoring/tie-down detail is given.
plans.floor_framing: Floor frame is 240 in. x 192 in. Two 2x6 rim joists at 240 in. (20 ft) long - cut-list item B misprints these as 192 in. - carry 16 pieces of 2x6 at 189 in. spanning the 16 ft width at 16 in. o.c. (drawn chain: 2 x 13 3/4 in. + 13 x 14 1/2 in. clear + 16 x 1 1/2 in. of joist = exactly 240 in.). Decking is 3/4 in. plywood, 8 sheets at 48x96 in. plus 4 at 48x48 in. = 320 sq ft, screwed with 1 5/8 in. screws every 8 in. along the joists. Joist hangers and structural nails for the skid ties are in the hardware list.
plans.wall_framing: 2x4 studs at 24 in. OC, single bottom plate plus double top plate; outside plate dimensions 192 x 240 in. The two long 20 ft side walls have 240 in. bottom and first top plates plus a 233 in. cap plate held back 3 1/2 in. at each end; the two 16 ft gable-end walls have 185 in. plates (192 in. minus the 3 1/2 in. thickness of each side wall) and fit between the side walls, with a 192 in. cap plate lapping 3 1/2 in. onto each side wall to lock the corners. Studs are 91 1/2 in. 2x6 double headers over openings with a 1/2 in. plywood spacer sandwiched between and locked with 2 1/2 in. screws; front door rough opening is 72 x 86 in. under a 75 in. 2x6 double header. The 240 / 233 / 185 / 192 in. plate set closes exactly and is correct as published - the cut-list error is confined to the skids and rim joists.
plans.wall_height: 8 ft / 96 in. - derived from the cut list (91 1/2 in. studs + 1 1/2 in. bottom plate + double 1 1/2 in. top plates); the page never states wall height in words
plans.roof: Gable, framed with 11 site-built trusses at 24 in. OC secured with rafter ties. Top chords: 22 pieces of 2x6 at 130 in.; bottom chords: 11 pieces of 2x6 at 185 in.; 2x4 web supports; 1/2 in. plywood gussets screwed with 1 5/8 in. screws. Rafters get 30 degree cuts at both ends plus birdsmouth cuts. Deck is 3/4 in. plywood; 2x6 overhang assemblies at front and back; 1x8 fascia/rake trims. Covered with tar paper (min 2 in. overlaps, roofing staples), drip edge, and asphalt shingles - 500 sq ft of each. Pitch is never given as X/12 (30 degrees implies roughly 7/12, but that is inference, not published).
plans.overall_height: not stated
plans.siding: T1-11 5/8 in. panels, 4x8 sheets - 18 sheets for the walls plus 4 sheets cut for the gable end panels; nailed with 6-8d nails every 8 in. along framing, edges flush, no gaps. No separate structural sheathing or housewrap specified.
plans.doors: Double doors centered in the 16 ft front gable wall. Each leaf: 2x4 frame assembled with pocket holes and 2 1/2 in. screws (2 pieces at 36 in., 2 at 80 1/2 in., 1 at 29 in.) with a T1-11 panel 36 x 77 1/2 in. attached with 2 in. brad nails. Jambs: 2 pieces of 2x4 at 87 1/2 in. plus 1 piece at 79 in., fixed with 2 1/2 in. screws. Front wall header is 2 pieces of 2x6 at 75 in. Hinges and a latch are listed; handles mentioned. Hardware is not brand/model specified, and the 75 in. header vs 79 in. jamb head figures do not reconcile cleanly.
plans.windows: The 8 pieces of 2x6 at 39" are NOT all headers: per window there is a double 2x6 header AND a double 2x6 sill (4 pieces per window x 2 windows = 8). Opening size 36x36 is correct.
plans.loft: none - the flat 2x6 bottom chord at 8 ft is a truss member, not a floor; no loft, storage deck, or headroom figure is offered
plans.skill_level: not stated
plans.build_time: Each of the 3 part pages lists "Time: One Day" (i.e. roughly 3 days total as claimed). This is unrealistic for 320 sq ft with 11 site-built trusses.

plans.permit_notes: Only a generic pointer: the plan says to select the location "taking into account your need and the local building codes." No permit guidance, no snow/wind/seismic load rating, no engineer stamp, and no jurisdiction-specific notes. At 320 sq ft this is well over the common 100-200 sq ft permit-exempt threshold, so a permit is very likely required and the unstamped site-built trusses plus skid-on-gravel foundation are the two items most likely to be challenged.

pros: Genuinely free and ungated - the complete lettered cut list, lumber shopping list, tool list and dimensioned 3D step diagrams are all on the page with no email wall or paywall
320 sq ft of completely clear floor: the 2x6 trusses span the full 16 ft width, so there are no interior posts and the workshop layout is unobstructed
Well-supported floor for the size - 5 skids under 2x6 joists at 16 in. OC keeps clear spans short, and 3/4 in. plywood decking is genuinely workshop-grade rather than minimum-spec
Buildable with basic DIY tools the page actually lists (miter saw, jigsaw, drill, level, chalk line) - no crane, no ordered engineered components, no steel
Better light and access than most sheds this size: two 36x36 in. windows in the long wall plus wide double doors on the gable end
Cheap foundation - gravel-and-skids means no concrete work, no forms, and minimal site prep cost
The $8 PDF is genuinely optional; you lose nothing by building from the free web pages
Vendor publishes sibling sizes in the identical format (16x16 gable 3-part set, 12x20, 12x24, 16x24 run-in), so resizing up or down is easy to cross-reference
Sensible detailing in places: 2x6 double headers with a 1/2 in. plywood spacer, rafter ties at trusses, drip edge over/under felt correctly described
cons: VERIFIED CUT-LIST ERROR - DO NOT CUT AS PRINTED: items A and B list 192 in. for the 5 skids and the 2 outer rim joists; both must be 240 in. (20 ft). The dimensioned drawings settle it - the floor-frame drawing reads 240 in. on the rim joist and 189 in. on the joists and its chain (2 x 13 3/4 + 13 x 14 1/2 clear + 16 x 1 1/2) closes on exactly 240 in.; the skid drawing is dimensioned 240 in.; the shopping list buys 20 ft stock for both; the floor sheathing (8 full + 4 half sheets = 320 sq ft), the 18 siding sheets (576 sq ft = 72 ft of wall x 8 ft) and the 11 trusses at 24 in. o.c. (= 240 in.) all confirm a 20 ft length. Cut to 192 in. and you build a 16x16 floor that the 240 in. side walls overhang by 4 ft, wasting 5 skids and 2 rim joists. The WALL dimensions are correct as published: 240 in. side-wall plates with a 233 in. cap, 185 in. gable-end plates with a 192 in. cap lapping the corners.

Trusses are site-built from 2x6 chords with 1/2 in. plywood gussets and are NOT engineered or stamped. A 16 ft clear-span truss is precisely what a plan checker will demand calculations for, and no snow, wind, or seismic load rating is published anywhere.

At 320 sq ft this is over the permit-exempt threshold in most jurisdictions (commonly 100-200 sq ft), so expect a permit - and 4x4 skids on gravel with no frost footings and no documented tie-down or anchoring detail frequently fails review.
Studs at 24 in. OC with only 5/8 in. T1-11 as the sheathing: no plywood shear panels, no let-in bracing, no hold-downs shown. Thin lateral bracing for a 20 ft long, 8 ft tall wall in a windy area.

Roof pitch is never expressed as X/12 - you get only 30 degree end cuts plus unspecified birdsmouths, so truss layout has to be reverse-engineered from the diagrams and test-fitted. Overall height is never stated either, which matters because many zoning codes cap accessory buildings at 12 ft.

The stated build time of one day per part is fantasy; 320 sq ft with 11 site-built trusses, 22 sheets of siding and 16 sheets of roof deck is a multi-weekend two-person job with lifting help needed for the trusses.

Material list is heavier than necessary and inflates cost: 3/4 in. plywood on the roof as well as the floor (26 sheets total) plus 30 pieces of 2x6 for trusses. 1/2 to 5/8 in. roof sheathing would meet code at 24 in. OC.
Nothing on electrical, insulation, vapor control, ventilation, ridge/soffit venting, or interior finish - a bare shell only, despite being pitched as a hobby workshop.
Windows are raw 36x36 in. framed openings; no window unit is specified or sized to a real product, so you must reconcile a purchased window's rough opening yourself.
Door dimensions do not fully reconcile between parts (front wall 2x6 header at 75 in. vs a 79 in. jamb head member), so the door rough opening needs to be resolved off the drawings.
Plan is split across three separate pages with no consolidated free PDF; the GET PDF PLANS button is an $8 Gumroad upsell carrying a No refunds allowed policy.
Site returns 403 to scripted/automated fetches (Cloudflare), so archiving the pages for offline reference requires the Wayback Machine or manual browser saves.

plans.vendor_note: HowToSpecialist (Jack Sander; same author/store as MyOutdoorPlans)
cons_original: The cut list contradicts its own shopping list on the two longest members: items A and B both give 192 in. for the skids and the outer rim joists, while the shopping list buys 20 ft (240 in.) stock. Cut to 192 in. and you build a 16x16 floor. Verify against the diagrams before cutting.

Trusses are site-built from 2x6 chords with 1/2 in. plywood gussets and are NOT engineered or stamped. A 16 ft clear-span truss is precisely what a plan checker will demand calculations for, and no snow, wind, or seismic load rating is published anywhere.

At 320 sq ft this is over the permit-exempt threshold in most jurisdictions (commonly 100-200 sq ft), so expect a permit - and 4x4 skids on gravel with no frost footings and no documented tie-down or anchoring detail frequently fails review.
Studs at 24 in. OC with only 5/8 in. T1-11 as the sheathing: no plywood shear panels, no let-in bracing, no hold-downs shown. Thin lateral bracing for a 20 ft long, 8 ft tall wall in a windy area.

Roof pitch is never expressed as X/12 - you get only 30 degree end cuts plus unspecified birdsmouths, so truss layout has to be reverse-engineered from the diagrams and test-fitted. Overall height is never stated either, which matters because many zoning codes cap accessory buildings at 12 ft.

The stated build time of one day per part is fantasy; 320 sq ft with 11 site-built trusses, 22 sheets of siding and 16 sheets of roof deck is a multi-weekend two-person job with lifting help needed for the trusses.

Material list is heavier than necessary and inflates cost: 3/4 in. plywood on the roof as well as the floor (26 sheets total) plus 30 pieces of 2x6 for trusses. 1/2 to 5/8 in. roof sheathing would meet code at 24 in. OC.
Nothing on electrical, insulation, vapor control, ventilation, ridge/soffit venting, or interior finish - a bare shell only, despite being pitched as a hobby workshop.
Windows are raw 36x36 in. framed openings; no window unit is specified or sized to a real product, so you must reconcile a purchased window's rough opening yourself.
Door dimensions do not fully reconcile between parts (front wall 2x6 header at 75 in. vs a 79 in. jamb head member), so the door rough opening needs to be resolved off the drawings.
Plan is split across three separate pages with no consolidated free PDF; the GET PDF PLANS button is an $8 Gumroad upsell carrying a No refunds allowed policy.
Site returns 403 to scripted/automated fetches (Cloudflare), so archiving the pages for offline reference requires the Wayback Machine or manual browser saves.

plans.floor_framing_original: 2x6 joists 189 in. long spanning the 16 ft width at 16 in. OC (16 joists) between two long rim joists (shopping list buys 2 pieces of 2x6 at 20 ft); 3/4 in. plywood decking screwed with 1 5/8 in. screws every 8 in. along joists. Joist hangers and structural nails for ties are listed in the hardware.
plans.foundation_original: On-grade skid foundation: 5 pieces of 4x4 (shopping list says 20 ft each) on a leveled, compacted gravel bed; floor frame toenailed or rafter-tied to the skids. No slab, piers, or frost footings; no anchoring/tie-down detail given.
plans.summary_original: A free, fully-published 3-part plan for a 320 sq ft gable storage shed / workshop on 4x4 skids: 8 ft walls, 2x4 studs at 24 in. OC, T1-11 siding, two 36x36 in. windows in one 20 ft side wall, and double doors centered in the 16 ft gable end. The roof is eleven site-built 2x6 trusses at 24 in. OC with 1/2 in. plywood gussets, clear-spanning the 16 ft width so the interior has no posts. Each part page publishes a lettered cut list plus a lumber shopping list and tool list with no email gate, which makes it unusually good source data for a real build. Main caveats: the cut list contradicts its own shopping list on the two longest members (192 in. vs 20 ft skids/rim joists), the trusses are not engineered or stamped, and no roof pitch, overall height, or load rating is published.

(20 ft) plates; front/back gable-end walls 185 in. plates fitting between the side walls.

cost_estimate.confidence: MEDIUM-HIGH on the lumber, sheet-goods, siding and roofing subtotal, which is ~85% of the dollars. Reasons: (1) every unit price on those lines came from a retailer page I fetched myself, and I re-verified the two largest lines (T1-11 $50.99 and 3/4 plywood $42.99) on a second fetch reading the schema.org ld+json offer directly; (2) two geographically independent live retailers, fetched the same day, agree within 3% on 3/4 in. plywood and within 16% on 2x4, with an archived Menards big-box stud price sitting between them — three-way corroboration on the commodity core; (3) all quantities on those lines are the plan's OWN published shopping list, not my take-off; (4) FRED WPU0811 confirms the price level is current rather than stale. MEDIUM on the total. Reasons it is not higher: the plan publishes zero counts for joist hangers, rafter ties, screws, nails, hinges and glue, so ~$500-700 of hardware rests on my take-offs and estimates rather than the plan; roofing nails could not be priced at all; the drip-edge unit price is a year-old archived Menards figure; the Dunn 4x4 skid price is extrapolated per-foot from an 8 ft post because they do not stock 20 ft; and the plan's own internal contradiction (192 in. cut list vs 20 ft shopping list on skids and rim joists) means the footprint the bill actually builds is not fully settled. LOW confidence specifically on the nails/staples line and the glue/filler placeholder — those two are marked as estimates and together are worth about $150, so they cannot move the headline much. Home Depot and Lowe's being unreachable is the main gap I could not close; I would not present this as a big-box cart price.
excludes: Foundation prep entirely: gravel bed, compaction, ground cloth, site levelling, excavation. The plan says 'leveled, compacted gravel bed' and buys nothing for it. Budget roughly $250-700 delivered for 6-8 cu yd of crushed rock on a 16x20 pad.
Concrete, piers, footings, anchors, hold-downs and tie-downs of any kind. The plan is 4x4 skids on gravel with no anchoring detail published.
Permits, plan-check fees, inspections. At 320 sq ft this is over the usual 100-200 sq ft exempt threshold, so a permit is very likely — commonly $150-800 depending on jurisdiction.

Engineering. The eleven 16 ft clear-span site-built 2x6/plywood-gusset trusses are not stamped. If a plan checker demands calculations, expect $400-1,500 for an engineer, or the cost of buying manufactured trusses instead.

Delivery. A 320 sq ft shed bill is roughly 3,000-3,500 lb of lumber plus 24 sheets of siding, 26 sheets of 3/4 plywood and 16 bundles of shingles — well past pickup-truck territory. Typical yard delivery $75-250.
Sales tax (0% to ~10% depending on state — on a $6,000 bill that is up to ~$600).
All tools: miter saw, circular saw, jigsaw, drill/driver, pocket-hole jig, chalk line, levels, ladders and scaffold, plus roof-safety gear.
Labor. Everything here is materials only. The plan's claimed 'one day' per part is fantasy for 320 sq ft with 11 site-built trusses.
Paint or stain, primer, caulk and brushes. The plan mentions 'stain/paint' but buys none. T1-11 must be finished: ~24 sheets = ~770 sq ft of wall, roughly 8-12 gallons for two coats, about $300-600.

Housewrap / weather-resistive barrier and structural shear sheathing. The plan puts 5/8 T1-11 straight on studs at 24 in. OC with no housewrap and no plywood shear panels — if your code requires either, add ~$700-1,200.
Insulation, vapor barrier, interior wall/ceiling finish, interior paint, shelving, workbenches.
Electrical of any kind: trenching, conduit, feeder, subpanel, receptacles, lighting, permits and electrician labor. For a detached 320 sq ft shop this is commonly $1,500-4,000 on its own.
Ridge vent, soffit vents, gable vents or any roof ventilation — none is specified in the plan.
Starter strip and hip/ridge cap shingles (the 16 bundles cover field area; a starter course is normally a separate product), and roof sealant/flashing cement.
Ramp, threshold, door sweep, door handles/pulls beyond the single latch, and any lock/hasp upgrade.
Gutters and downspouts.
Waste, breakage and miscut allowance. Every quantity here is the plan's published count with no overage factor; real jobs run 5-10% over.

plans.price: Free
plans.summary: MWPS-75265 is a free 5-page scanned plan set (title page plus "Page 1 of 4" through "Page 4 of 4") for a 16'-0" x 20'-0" insulated dairy milkhouse, copyright 1975 Midwest Plan Service, issued through Cooperative Extension and the Agricultural Experiment Stations of the North Central Region with USDA cooperating, and republished as a free PDF by NDSU Extension. It is a real drawing set with dimensioned framing: 2x4 studs at 24" o.c. on doubled pressure-treated 2x4 sills, 2 - 2x4 top plates, 2x6 rafters and 2x6 ceiling joists at 24" o.c. on a 4/12 pitch with a 1'-0" overhang, 3/8" C-C Ext plywood sheathing (Identification Index 20/0) under 235 lb asphalt shingles, R-14 walls and R-23 ceiling with 4-mil poly vapor barrier, on a trenched (grade-beam) foundation 30" min deep with #4 continuous and #3 @ 24" o.c. rebar and a 4" reinforced slab. It is NOT a modern stamped engineering package: the title page states "This plan provides conceptual information only" and that "Additional professional services will be required to tailor this plan to your situation, including but not limited to: assurance of compliance with codes and regulations," and there is no cut list, no snow/wind load table, and no truss design (rafters are site-cut per RAFTER DETAIL 1/4). Much of the sheet is dairy-specific — bulk tank pad, wash vats, deep-seal floor drains, 750 cfm pressurizing fan, 80-gallon water heater, electrical plan and four milkhouse-waste-disposal schematics — which a shed builder will simply ignore.
plans.format: Scanned monochrome line-drawing PDF, letter size (612 x 792 pt), plan sheets printed in landscape (rotated 90° in the file); no text layer on the drawings, so the sheets must be read as images. Freely downloadable, no registration.

Estimating list: 3.5 cu yd concrete + 110 lb Grade 36 steel for the foundation, 5.25 cu yd for the floor.

Insulation R-14 (3-1/2" min. batt or blanket) with 4-mil polyethylene vapor barrier and a washable interior wall lining sealed at the bottom edge against wash water; lining alternatives listed (28 ga galvanized steel over 3/8" plywood, structural glazed tile, fiberglass-reinforced polyester resin board, FRP laminated on 3/8" Ext plywood, 3/8" M.D.O. plywood painted, 3/8" Ext plywood painted). pros: Completely free, no email wall, no upsell — a permanently hosted institutional PDF you can download and archive (already saved locally here).

Real dimensioned engineering-office drawings from Midwest Plan Service, the North Central land-grant universities' agricultural plan service, not a blog sketch: member sizes, spacings, species/grade, R-values, rebar sizes and anchor-bolt spacing are all called out.

320 sq ft is exactly the user's target, and 16'-0" x 20'-0" is a clean, waste-free layout for 8' and 16' stock: 2x6x16 ceiling joists span the width with no splicing, and siding/sheathing lay out on 4' modules.

Slab-on-grade with a monolithic trenched grade beam 30" deep and integral rebar is a genuinely simple, low-skill foundation compared with piers plus a framed floor, and gives a workshop-grade floor for free.

Site-cut 2x6 rafters at 4/12 with a printed rafter detail (work line, plumb cut, fascia cut, 8'-0" run, 1'-0" overhang) means no truss delivery, no crane, and no truss vendor — two people can set the roof.

Includes a usable estimating list with concrete yardage, rebar weight, lineal feet of 2x4 and 2x6, and square footage of sheathing, siding, lining and insulation — enough to price the shell at a lumberyard today.

Genuinely designed as a heated, insulated, vapor-barriered, washable-interior building (R-14 walls / R-23 ceiling), so it converts naturally to a year-round workshop, tack room or utility building rather than a bare-stud shed.

Extras a normal shed plan never gives you: a full electrical plan with a wiring key, a floor sloped to two deep-seal drains, an insulated door with screen door detail, and four wastewater-handling schematics.
cons: Not a freestanding shed. One 16'-0" gable endwall is the existing barn wall; the estimating list explicitly excludes that endwall and any material to extend the roof to the barn roof. Building it standalone means designing and quantifying a fourth wall and its rake/gable yourself.

The title page states outright that "This plan provides conceptual information only" and that additional professional services are required for "assurance of compliance with codes and regulations" — there is no PE stamp, no snow or wind load, no seismic or frost-depth table, and MWPS and the universities disclaim all warranties. Do not expect a permit office to accept it as-is.

No cut list and no piece counts for most items — lumber comes as lineal feet (410 ft of 2x4 for studs/plates/blocks, 100 ft of treated 2x4 sill) and area (425 sq ft siding), so you must do your own takeoff and layout.

The estimating list's rafter count looks low: 11 2x6x10 rafters is one per 24" bay over the 20' length, i.e. only one side — you actually need 11 pairs (22 rafters). Treat the list as a rough estimating aid, not a bill of materials.

1975 vintage, 1975 practice: 2x4 studs and 2x6 rafters/joists at 24" o.c., 3/8" roof sheathing, and R-14/R-23 envelope are all below current residential norms; there is no hurricane/rafter tie hardware, only 3-16d toe nails, and no shear-wall or uplift detailing.

The 16'-0" clear span on 2x6 No. 2 ceiling joists at 24" o.c. is right at the limit for a no-storage attic — you get zero loft or storage capacity above, and 24" o.c. framing needs 5/8" ceiling board if you drywall it.

Cost is front-loaded in concrete: 8.75 cu yd total (3.5 foundation + 5.25 floor) plus 110 lb of rebar, plus a 30"-deep trench. That is a ready-mix delivery, a formed grade beam and real excavation before a single stud goes up — much more up-front money and machine time than a skid or pier shed.

Roughly a third of the sheet is dairy-specific and irrelevant to a shed: bulk tank pad, wash vats, 750 cfm pressurizing fan, condenser exhaust panels, deep-seal floor drains, milkhouse waste ponds, and the "consult and get the approval of the health authorities having control of the sale of your milk" requirement.
Scanned raster drawings with no text layer, some smudged digits, and pages rotated 90° in the PDF — annoying to read on screen and impossible to search or scale precisely.

Preservative specs are obsolete and partly illegal for DIY use today (creosote 8 pcf, penta 0.40 pcf, ACC, ACA, CCA) — substitute modern ACQ/CA-treated material and matching hot-dip galvanized or stainless fasteners.
No build sequence, no step-by-step instructions, no photos, no cost estimate, and no support contact — it assumes a reader who can already build from drawings.

plans.permit_notes: Explicitly not permit-ready as drawn. The title page CAUTION and WARRANTY DISCLAIMER state the plan is "conceptual information only" and that additional professional services are required including "assurance of compliance with codes and regulations." No PE seal, no design loads (no snow, wind or frost values), no structural calculations, and no code edition cited. The 30" minimum foundation depth is a generic North Central Region figure, not your local frost depth. Sheet also requires health-department approval for its original dairy use ("Before you build this milkhouse consult with and get the approval of the health authorities having control of the sale of your milk") and "Check your waste disposal plan with local health authorities"; the electrical plan says "Wire according to local codes." Expect to have a local engineer or designer redraw/stamp it if your jurisdiction requires plans for a 320 sq ft slab-on-grade accessory building.

Plywood"; Wall R=14 / 3-1/2" min. batt or blanket; Ceiling R=23 / 6" min. fill; 4 mil polyethylene; "Wall Lining, seal bottom edge against wash water"; 2-2x4 pressure-treated sills; 3/8" x 10" anchor bolt 8' o.c.; "Trenched Foundation, form top to control straightness and elevation"; 30" min. depth, 6" min. width; #4 bar continuous, #3 bar 24" o.c.; "To minimize heat loss add 2" Rigid Insulation"; "Slope fill away from building, top with gravel to prevent erosion"; 4" concrete floor / 2" sand / 4 mil poly, thicken to 8" under bulk tank; 4' x 8' concrete slab; two deep-seal floor drains; 750 cfm pressurizing fan, 80 gallon water heater, 3000 watt electric heater; FOUR waste-disposal schematics under MILKHOUSE WASTE DISPOSAL 2/3; ESTIMATING LIST 3.5 cu yd + 110 lb Grade 36 steel foundation, 5.25 cu yd floor, siding 425 sq ft, Windows 2, Doors 1; "Seal trim and flashing with latex caulking." (walk door); title-page quotes "This plan provides conceptual information only" and the CAUTION/WARRANTY DISCLAIMER language; "Page 1 of 4 Pages" through "Page 4 of 4 Pages"; Copyright 1975 Midwest Plan Service. Page/count claims all correct (5 PDF pages, 1 title + 4 sheets). Price: no price appears anywhere in the PDF and the direct download needs no registration, so "Free" / $0 is fair — nothing fabricated. Image at /home/ethan/woodshed/assets/img/mwps-75265-16x20-milkhouse.jpg is a real 1600x1236 JPEG, 274,997 bytes, and is a correct render of plan page 1 (FLOOR PLAN 1/1 + table of contents + title block) — no fix needed. Additional cautions the record does not mention and which belong in cons: (1) The plan's own ESTIMATING LIST appears to undercount rafters — "Rafters 2x6's, 10 ft long ... 11" for a 20' building at 24" o.c., where you actually need ~22 rafters (11 pairs), matching the "Joists ... 16 ft long ... 11". A builder ordering off this list will be ~11 rafters short. (2) The summary's "no cut list" sits oddly beside an ESTIMATING LIST that does give member lengths (2x4's 410 ft, 2x6's 10 ft and 16 ft long); it is a bill of materials, not a cut list, so the statement is defensible but reads as more bare than the sheet is. (3) 2x6 ceiling joists at 24" o.c. spanning the full 16' clear is right at the IRC limit for a no-storage ceiling with DF/SYP/Hem-Fir No. 2 — fine as a ceiling, but this is emphatically NOT a storage loft, and the record should say so if it implies otherwise. (4) The "rotated 90° in the file" claim is only loosely true: pdfinfo reports Page rot 0 for all pages, and the drawn content on sheets 1 and 3 needs +90 while sheets 2 and 4 need -90 to read upright. (5) Pros/cons and the tail of the "windows" field were truncated in the record supplied to me, so I could not audit them.
