cost_estimate.caveats:
SHORT ANSWER: buying this FREE plan and building it to spec at a Midwest lumber yard in September 2026 costs roughly $4,300-$6,600 in materials above grade, or $13.47-$20.72 per sq ft on 320 sq ft. Add ~$1,900-$2,600 for concrete + rebar and you are at roughly $6,200-$9,200 all-in on materials — still well under half the $11,000-$15,000 kit price, and the kit does not include a slab either.

WHAT LOW vs HIGH MEANS HERE. Both ends are REAL 2026 prices from the same retailer, Sutherlands, a Midwest yard with ~49 stores. LOW = the cheapest store's price on the value-grade option (SPF/SYP #2, 7/16 OSB, 11/32 T1-11, 3-tab shingles, blown cellulose). HIGH = an expensive store's price on the upgraded option (#2 Douglas Fir, 15/32 CDX plywood, 19/32 T1-11, architectural shingles, primed-panel lining, R-30 batts). I could NOT get a single 2026 big-box unit price — Home Depot, Lowe's, Menards and McCoy's all block requests and the Wayback Machine has no Home Depot product capture after 2023-09-25 and no Lowe's product captures at all. So the high column is NOT a big-box number. Directional evidence that big-box is dearer: Home Depot's 2x4x8 Prime Whitewood Stud was $7.98 in a 2023-09-25 archive versus $3.98-$4.29 at Sutherlands today, and FRED WPU0811 softwood-lumber PPI is up ~15% since then. Treat $6,600 as a yard ceiling; a Home-Depot-only build of the same bill would plausibly land higher. Also note the store-to-store spread inside Sutherlands runs past my high on several lines (19/32 T1-11 up to $59.99/sheet, the R-13 23\" bag up to $149.89) — an unlucky store adds several hundred dollars.

IS THE SPEC HEAVIER? Not structurally — it is LIGHTER than a modern shed plan. 2x4 studs at 24\" o.c. (not 16\"), 3/8\" roof sheathing (not 7/16\"/1/2\"), site-cut 2x6 rafters, no hurricane ties, no snow/wind table, no truss design. What makes it expensive is the INTERIOR: this is a dairy milkhouse, so it carries R-14 walls, R-23 ceiling, a 4-mil vapor barrier, a washable wall lining and a finished ceiling. Those five items plus the screen door, floor drains and removable panels are $1,466-$2,506 of the total — over a third. Strip them and build the same shell freestanding, unlined and uninsulated and you get $2,843-$4,124, i.e. $8.89-$12.89 per sq ft. That is the number most shed builders actually want.

THE PLAN IS ONLY THREE WALLS. This is the single biggest gotcha and it is easy to miss. The 16 ft gable endwall at the top of FLOOR PLAN 1/1 is labeled \"BARN\" and the estimating list states in plain text \"List does not include one endwall (existing barn wall) or material to extend roof to existing barn roof.\" My headline total therefore = the plan's own list ($3,779-$5,830) PLUS a fourth-endwall adder I built myself ($530-$800). If you actually have a barn to butt against, use the lower figure.

THE RAFTER COUNT IN THE PLAN IS WRONG (or at best ambiguous). The estimating list reads \"Rafters: 2x6's, 10 ft long ....... 11\" and \"Joists: 2x6's, 16 ft long ....... 11\". Eleven joists is exactly right for 24\" o.c. across a 20 ft building. But eleven rafter positions need TWO rafters each, one per slope — 22 pieces. I priced 22. If you order off the printed list you will be 11 rafters short (about $80-$145). The ridge board (2x6 x 20 ft), the felt underlayment and the drip edge are also missing from the estimating list entirely; I added all three.

CEILING JOIST SPAN IS AT THE LIMIT. A 2x6 at 24\" o.c. spanning the full 16 ft is right at the edge of modern IRC ceiling-joist tables for an uninhabitable attic with no storage. It is not obviously illegal, but it has essentially no margin, and if you ever put anything on that ceiling it fails. The plan's own title page says it \"provides conceptual information only\" and that professional services will be required including \"assurance of compliance with codes and regulations.\" Get it checked before you buy 2x6es.

SPEC SUBSTITUTIONS I MADE, ALL FLAGGED. (1) 3/8\" C-C Ext plywood with medium-density overlay (MDO) is effectively a special-order product now — no fetchable retailer stocks it — so siding is priced as APA T1-11 and the lining/ceiling as 15/32 CDX (low) or a 3/8\" B-grade primed panel (high). (2) 3/8\" C-C Ext 20/0 roof sheathing no longer exists in the trade; 7/16 OSB and 15/32 CDX both exceed it. (3) The plan's windows are site-built from 22\" x 24\" double-strength glass, which nobody prices online — I substituted small vinyl units at $114-$120 each, which OVERSTATES this line; building them per the plan is much cheaper. (4) The plan's deep-seal dairy floor drains are priced as $11 PVC drains, which UNDERSTATES them.

TWO LINES ARE NOT REAL PRICES, hence priced=PARTIAL: the 3/8\" x 10\" anchor bolts ($35-$50) and the quarter-round/glazing trim lot ($20-$30). Both are explicitly marked ESTIMATE in their source field. Together they are under 2% of the total. The removable-panel lot and the fourth-wall rake roof extension are derived/estimated from real unit prices. Everything else is a retailer-quoted 2026 figure.

TIMING RISK. FRED WPU0811 shows softwood lumber at 300.6 in July 2026, up from 250.1 in December 2025 — a ~20% run-up in seven months, and the highest reading in the series since the 2021-22 spike. These prices are a snapshot on a rising market; re-quote before you order.

HIGH on the takeoff: it comes from the plan's own printed ESTIMATING LIST on page 3, not from my own framing calc. LOWER on three things: (1) single-retailer basis — I could not obtain any 2026 Home Depot/Lowe's/Menards price because they all block and Wayback has no 2026 captures, so the high column is a yard ceiling rather than a big-box ceiling; (2) three spec substitutions were unavoidable (MDO plywood, 3/8\" 20/0 sheathing and double-strength window glass are not sold in any fetchable catalog), and the window substitution in particular overstates that line by maybe $150; (3) the plan itself is internally inconsistent (rafter count, missing ridge/felt/drip edge, one endwall omitted), so any total requires judgment calls that I have documented rather than hidden. Concrete is genuinely unpriced and is excluded.

plans.summary: This 3D Warehouse listing is a free, fully modeled SketchUp file of shedking.net's 16x20 gambrel barn shed — not a drawing set. You can spin it in the browser, drop it in your yard with the AR button, or download the geometry (.glb and .usdz download anonymously; the .skp versions returned HTTP 401 without a Trimble sign-in), and it is detailed enough to be useful: 638,011 polygons, 45 materials, 55 layers, saved from SketchUp 2025 with 2019/2020/2021/2024 back-versions offered. The actual buildable documents live on the linked page https://www.shedking.net/16x20-barn-shed-plans.html: 34 pages of blueprints plus a 79-page barn building guide, free cupola plans and email support for $29.95 instant PDF download, with a stated 90-day money-back guarantee. Usefully, shedking publishes the full 7-page materials list as a free PDF with no purchase (captured locally), which is where every framing spec below comes from — the 3D Warehouse page itself publishes no dimensions beyond the title.
includes: Free downloadable 3D model of the finished shed: SketchUp .skp saved in 2019, 2020, 2021 and 2024 versions (sign-in required), plus public .glb (8.3 MB), .usdz (7.2 MB), Collada .dae zip and TrimBim exports
In-browser 3D orbit viewer and an AR button to place the 16x20 barn in your own yard before building

pros: Free and zero-risk way to evaluate a 16x20 gambrel barn before spending money — you can walk around the model and use AR to check it against your actual yard and setbacks
The linked vendor gives away the complete 7-page materials list PDF and a 79-page barn building guide without buying anything, so you can price the lumber package before committing

Framing is generously sized for a 320 sq ft building: 2x6 walls at 16" o.c., 2x8 treated floor joists at 16" o.c. over five 4x6 skids, and 2x12 loft joists at 24" o.c. — the loft is a real floor, not a shelf
Huge usable loft: 7' 5" headroom above the finished loft floor with a 3'+ wide stairway, which is what makes this workable as a shop-plus-storage or shed-house shell
Gambrel trusses are site-built from 2x6s with plywood gussets and no long clear-span beam, so no crane and no engineered lumber purchase is required
Only 320 sq ft of floor but 16' clear width inside — no interior posts, unlike many big-shed designs
Foundation is flexible: concrete pier anchors with support blocking are drawn, and the plans also allow a concrete slab floor
$29.95 for the real plan set is cheap relative to 16x20-class plans, and it includes email support from the author
cons: This 3D Warehouse page is a marketing model, NOT a plan set — no dimensions, cut list or details are published on it. Downloading the model does not get you buildable drawings; treat the free item as a visualizer only
The .skp downloads returned 401 for an anonymous request; you need a free Trimble/SketchUp account (or use the public .glb/.usdz) to get the geometry

Trusses are customer-built and the author explicitly warns: "I do include truss plans with the blueprints but they will not show load limits etc." — he recommends buying engineered 16' trusses instead if you need a permit

No engineering calculations and no engineer's stamp: "If your building department requires an engineers stamp ... you will have to submit the plans to a local structural engineer. I do not provide those calculations with my plans." That is a real cost adder in snow-load or high-wind jurisdictions
At 320 sq ft with an 18' 5-5/8" ridge and a habitable-height loft, this is over the permit-exempt threshold nearly everywhere and will read as a two-level structure to plan reviewers

The plan page and the materials list disagree on door width — page says "Pre-hung 5' wide double doors", the materials list says "6' Wide Double Doors" — verify the rough opening before framing the front wall
Materials list quantities are only as good as your local sheet/stick lengths, and it omits foundation concrete, stair handrail, paint, gutters, electrical and insulation entirely

Real-world difficulty is above beginner despite the sales copy: 30+ site-built gambrel trusses, 2x12 loft joists on hangers, a full stairway with 6 stringers, and lifting 16' plates/trusses means you need at least one helper

plans.summary: A genuinely free, fully-dimensioned 16x20 (320 sq ft) gambrel/barn shed published as three step-by-step articles: PART 1 floor + wall framing + siding, PART 2 gambrel roof, PART 3 double doors + trim. Structure is 2x8 floor joists 16" o.c. on five 4x4 skids over compacted gravel, 8 ft 2x4 walls at 16" o.c., T1-11 siding, and 16 site-built gambrel trusses at 16" o.c. made from four 76 1/2" 2x6 rafters with 22.5-degree cuts and 1/2" plywood gussets. Every part publishes a full cut list and a shopping list for free, and the author's own cost/time estimate is "$3,000 to $5,000 in materials" and "3 to 4 weekends if you're working solo". The big caveats: the trusses have no bottom chord or collar tie and are not engineered, the advertised loft is only a one-sentence suggestion with zero loft framing or headroom given, and at least two shopping-list quantities are demonstrably wrong.
plans.format: On-page article (3 linked parts) with SketchUp-style diagrams and inline cut/shopping lists; readable and printable free. Optional paid PDF download of the same plan sold separately on Gumroad. No free PDF is offered.

plans.foundation: On-grade skid foundation, no concrete: five 4x4 skids 240" long running the 20 ft direction, set on a prepared bed — "Select the right location for the shed and then remove the vegetation layer. Compact a thick layer of gravel and make sure the surface is level." Skids are fastened to the floor frame with metal rafter ties. The skid diagram dimensions the layout as 8" inset from each 16 ft edge with four 39 5/8" clear spaces between skids. No footing depth, frost-depth, pier, or tie-down/anchor detail is given; a commenter asking "I want to place this shed on pier blocks, how many blocks should I use?" received no published answer. (PART 3 does list an "anchor kit" in materials without specifying it.)

Decking is 3/4" plywood (8 sheets 48"x96" + 4 pieces 48"x48"), fastened with 1 5/8" screws every 8". Note the 189" joists are NOT free-spanning 15'9" — they bear on the five lengthwise 4x4 skids, so the actual clear span is only about 39 5/8", which is why 2x8 at 16" o.c. works here.

plans.wall_height: 8 ft. Page text: "This is a large barn shed with 8′ tall walls"; studs are 91 1/2" + 4 1/2" of plates = 96". The dimensions diagram labels the sidewall 104" (measured including the floor frame and skid).
plans.overall_height: 205" (about 17 ft 1 in) per the published dimensions diagram. Note the author gave a looser figure in the comments — asked "What is the overall height of this?" he replied "About 16′". The same diagram gives the roof plan as 202" wide x 261 1/2" long.
plans.roof: Gambrel (barn) roof, 16 site-built trusses at 16" on center. Each truss = four 2x6 rafters 76 1/2" long with "22.5 degrees cuts to both ends", joined by three 1/2" plywood gussets (one at the peak, one at each knee; gusset dimensioned 24" wide x 5"/5 1/4" tall) screwed on with 1 5/8" screws. Trusses are secured to the top plates with metal rafter ties. IMPORTANT: the truss drawing shows no bottom chord, ceiling joist, or collar tie — it is an open gambrel arch relying on the knee gussets. Separate 2x6 overhang assemblies with 2x4 blocking at the front and back ("You can adjust the size of the overhangs to suit your needs"). Sheathing is 3/4" plywood; then tar paper and asphalt shingles, 550 sq ft of each; 1x8 fascia/trim mitered at 67.5 degrees. No rise/run pitch ratio, no snow/wind design load, and no engineer stamp are stated. (Geometrically the 22.5-degree cuts and the 205"/202" envelope imply a ~67.5-degree lower slope and ~22.5-degree upper slope, i.e. roughly 29:12 over 5:12 — this is derived, not published.)
plans.siding: That instruction is given only for the side walls; the front/back walls use a different, contradictory rule.
plans.doors: One double (two-leaf) door centered in a 16 ft gambrel end wall. The dimensions diagram labels the opening 72" wide x 79 1/4" tall. Opening is lined with 2x4 jambs (2 pieces 79 1/4", 1 piece 79") screwed off with 3 1/2" screws every 8". Each leaf is a 2x4 pocket-screwed frame (2 pieces 36", 2 pieces 72 1/4", 1 piece 29") faced with a 36"x79 1/4" T1-11 panel — cleverly reusing the sheathing cut-out: "The door panels are the pieces that you cut out for the door openings." Hardware is builder-supplied and unspecified: materials list just says "hinges", and the text says "Install a latch to lock the doors into place tightly." No threshold, weatherstrip, or ramp detail.
plans.windows: Two 30"x30" windows in one 20 ft side wall — "you need to frame a 30″x30″ window to the 2 section frames, so you let enough light inside the barn shed", and the dimensions diagram labels them 30" x 30". The windows are purchased units, not built: "Fit the PVC windows to the sides of the barn shed." Framed with doubled 2x6 33" headers (1/2" ply sandwich), 31 1/2" cripples and 30" sills, then 1x4 trim. The opposite side wall, front and back are blank. No glazing spec, egress, or window make/model given.
plans.loft: Effectively none as drawn. PART 2 offers only a one-line suggestion: "If you need even more storage space, you can create a loft to the top of the storage shed." There is no loft in any diagram, no loft joist/decking cut list, no headroom dimension, and no access: asked "is there a plan for stairs?" the author answered "No", and a buyer asking "wondering if there is a floor plan for making a loft" got no published reply. Because the gambrel trusses have no bottom chord, adding a loft means adding framing (and a tie) that the plan does not provide. The page does show reader-submitted photos captioned "DIY 16x20 Gambrel Shed with Loft", so builders have added one themselves.
plans.skill_level: Not rated on the page. Realistically intermediate-to-advanced DIY: you must cut and gang-assemble 16 gambrel trusses at 22.5 degrees, build 20 ft walls in two sections and marry them plumb, and safely lift 16 trusses onto 8 ft walls (a 2-3 person job). The listed tools are basic — "Hammer, Tape measure, Framing square, Level / Miter saw, Drill machinery, Screwdriver, Sander" — no table saw, nail gun, or crane assumed.
plans.build_time: The tabbed "Time" estimates are per part: "One week" for PART 1 (floor/walls), "One week" for PART 2 (roof), "One day" for PART 3 (doors/trim). The article body gives a realistic weekend-warrior figure: "plan on dedicating about 3 to 4 weekends if you're working solo, or a bit less if you've got some helping hands."
plans.est_material_cost: "around $3,000 to $5,000 in materials, depending on your choices for siding, roofing, and finishes" (stated on the page; no date given for the estimate)
plans.permit_notes: Only a generic disclaimer, repeated in each part: "Make sure you check the local codes and make adjustments to the plans, if required." There are no design loads, no snow/wind ratings, no span tables, no engineer or architect stamp, and no permit-submittal drawing set. Notably, a reader wrote "Where I'm at we need 2 x 6 framing for snow load and I was wanting to build a 16 x 24 gambrel shed. Is there any major changes I should know about?" and the author replied only "No, same techniques to be used." EDITORIAL (not from the page): at 320 sq ft this is well above the typical 100-200 sq ft permit-exempt threshold in most US jurisdictions, so a permit is likely required and this free drawing set will probably not satisfy a plans examiner on its own — budget for a local engineer's review or stamped trusses.

pros: Genuinely free and complete — all three parts publish full lettered cut lists AND shopping lists on-page, so you can price and build the whole 320 sq ft shed without buying anything. The $9.99 Gumroad PDF is convenience only, not gated content.
Fully dimensioned: a published dimension drawing gives 192" x 240" plan, 205" overall height, 104" sidewall, 72" x 79 1/4" door opening and 30" x 30" windows — you rarely get this from free plans.

The gambrel roof buys a lot of usable volume for the footprint: 205" overall height over 8 ft walls means real standing room in the upper zone, which is why this shape is the right pick if you eventually want a loft.

Skid-on-gravel foundation means no concrete pour, no forms, and no curing wait — much cheaper and faster than a slab, and in many jurisdictions a skid building is easier to classify as movable/temporary.

The floor is genuinely stout and the span is honest: five 4x4 skids at 39 5/8" reduce the 2x8 joists to a ~40" clear span, so the deck will feel solid under a riding mower or workbench and will not bounce.

Wide double door (72" clear) on the 16 ft end swallows mowers, ATVs and sheet goods; the leaves reuse the T1-11 cut out of the wall sheathing, which saves a sheet and keeps the door grain matching the wall.

Smart construction sequencing for one person: the 20 ft walls are built as two ground-assembled sections and then joined, so you never have to lift a full 20 ft wall. Screw-based assembly means no nail gun or compressor required.
Cheap, fast tool list and cheap materials palette (2x4/2x6, T1-11, asphalt shingles) — no exotic hardware, no engineered lumber, no custom millwork.
Well-socialised design: three linked parts, ~25 assembly diagrams, reader-built photo galleries and an author who answers comments; the paid PDF carries a 4.7/5 rating from 6 buyers.
Author publishes his own honest cost and schedule estimates ($3,000-$5,000 materials, 3-4 weekends solo), which is more than most free-plan sites will commit to.

Easy to stretch: the same author confirmed the techniques scale, and a builder asking about extending to 28 ft or going to 16x24 was told to use the same methods — the two-section wall approach makes lengthening straightforward.
cons: The gambrel trusses have NO bottom chord, ceiling joist, or collar tie — the drawing shows only four 2x6 rafters and three plywood gussets. An untied gambrel arch pushes outward on the 16 ft walls at the knee, and nothing in the plan resists that thrust beyond the gussets and the sheathing. This is the single biggest thing to have reviewed locally.

Nothing is engineered or stamped: no design snow or wind load, no span tables, no truss calculations. At 320 sq ft you are almost certainly over the permit-exempt size in most US jurisdictions, so expect a plans examiner to reject a free web drawing set — budget for local engineering or shop-built stamped trusses.

The 'loft' is marketing, not a plan. It is one sentence in PART 2 with zero loft joists, decking, headroom dimension, or access in any cut list, and the author explicitly answered 'No' when asked for stair plans. If the loft is why you picked a gambrel, you are designing that part yourself — and you must add the tie the trusses lack.

Verified quantity error in the PART 1 shopping list: it says '3 pieces of 4×4 lumber – 20′', but cut list A calls for 5 skids at 240" and the skid diagram dimensions 5 skids (8" + four 39 5/8" spaces + 8" = 192"). Buy 5, not 3.

Likely second quantity error: the PART 2 shopping list allows only one 4'x8' sheet of 1/2" plywood, but 16 trusses x 3 gussets (24" x ~5") is roughly 41 sq ft before you cut the plywood sandwiches for the door and window headers. One 32 sq ft sheet is not enough.

3/4" plywood is specified for BOTH the floor (10 sheets) and the roof (22 sheets) — 32 sheets of 3/4" ply. Roof sheathing that thick is far heavier and pricier than the usual 7/16"-1/2" OSB, and it is a major cost driver and a real overhead-lifting hazard on a 205"-tall gambrel.

Almost no eave overhang: the diagram's 202" roof width over a 192" wall width leaves only about 5" of projection per side, with no soffit detail. T1-11 walls will get rain-washed, and T1-11 is the least durable common siding — plan on diligent painting and a drip edge.

No moisture or ventilation detail anywhere: no housewrap/WRB behind the siding, no ridge/gable/soffit vents, no vapour control. A sealed 320 sq ft gambrel with a big untied roof cavity will sweat and cook; you are adding venting yourself.

Skid foundation with no anchoring or frost detail — no footing depth, no pier option, no hold-down straps. PART 3 lists an unspecified 'anchor kit'. A 16x20 gambrel is a large sail; wind uplift and tie-down are not addressed, and the commenter who asked how to lay it on pier blocks was never answered.

Roof pitch is never published as rise/run — only '22.5 degrees cuts'. You have to derive the slopes from geometry, which makes ordering shingles, flashing, or a matching dormer harder, and makes cross-checking against a code table awkward.

Author's answers to structural questions are thin: asked about needing 2x6 framing for snow load he replied only 'No, same techniques to be used', which is not a substitute for a load check in a snow-country build.

Windows are 30"x30" rough framing only — you buy PVC units, and no size tolerance, flashing, sill pan, or trim overlap detail is given. Only two windows, both in one side wall, so the interior is dim for workshop use.

Everything is screw-fastened by hand across a very large building (76+ 2x4s, 32 sheets of 3/4" ply, 550 sq ft of shingles). Realistically this is more than the '3 to 4 weekends' the page claims unless you have help and a nailer.

Free format is web-only — printing is awkward (a commenter: 'I am having difficulty printing this plan'), the author's answer was to read the FAQ, and the tidy printable version costs $9.99. The PART 2 and PART 3 archived pages also show broken '[tabs tab1=...]' shortcodes, so the materials tabs render as raw text.

No larger sibling plan: the author's related barn/gambrel plans are 10x12 and 12x16, both well under 200 sq ft. There is no 16x24 or 20x20 gambrel to step up to — you would be scaling this one yourself.

plans.wall_framing_original: 2x4 studs at 16" on center, 91 1/2" studs with a single bottom plate and a double top plate, giving "8′ tall walls". Each 20 ft side wall is built as two sub-frames on the ground and then joined ("assemble the plain side wall, by joining the two section together tightly"), with a continuous 240" 2x4 cap plate tying the sections. Double studs at both ends of every wall frame. Headers are doubled 2x6 with a 1/2" plywood sandwich: 75" over the double door, 33" at the windows ("Use 2×6 lumber for the headers. Sandwhich a piece of 1/2″ plywood between the two 2×6 pieces"). Assembly is screwed, not nailed — 3 1/2" screws into studs and through bottom plates into the floor, 2 1/2" screws joining sections.
plans.siding_original: T1-11 sheet siding, called out as 5/8" T1-11 in the roof-part shopping list. Walls: 14 sheets 48"x96" plus 4 pieces 48"x91 3/4". Gambrel end panels above the walls: 4 pieces 48"x81 5/8" plus 4 pieces 48"x101 1/2", over 2x4 supports pocket-screwed to the end trusses. Fastened with 6d nails every 8"; "Align the sheets to the top edge of the double plates and leave no gaps between them." Trim is 1x4 (8 pieces 96", 4 pieces 30", 4 pieces 37") at corners and around openings, plus 1x8 roof trims. Finish is paint or stain after filling and sanding — no housewrap, rainscreen, or WRB is mentioned behind the siding.

VERIFIED CORRECT (checked character-by-character against the Wayback snapshot of all three parts plus three downloaded diagrams):

PRICE — record is right and the $9.99 is NOT invented. The page publishes no price; it only says "If you want to get PREMIUM PLANS for this project, in a PDF format, please press GET PDF PLANS button bellow." That button links to https://myoutdoorplans.gumroad.com/l/oXcaF, whose HTML contains `"priceCurrency":"USD" … "price":9.99` under `<title>16x20 Gambrel Shed Plans</title>`. No .pdf hrefs anywhere on the page, so "No free PDF is offered" is correct. price_usd 0 is right for the on-page plan set. (Aside: an older comment "Do you have premium plans for this 16×20 gambrel?" → "Not at the moment." is now stale.)

FOOTPRINT/SQFT — 16x20 = 320 sq ft. Diagram labels the floor 192" x 240" (= 16'0" x 20'0"). Arithmetic correct.

WALL HEIGHT 8 ft — "This is a large barn shed with 8′ tall walls" verbatim; 91 1/2" studs + 3 plates x 1 1/2" = 96". Correct.

OVERALL HEIGHT 205" — diagram reads 205" (= 17 ft 1 in, correct conversion), 202" and 261 1/2" for the roof plan, 104" sidewall, 72" x 79 1/4" door, 30" x 30" windows, 240" length, 192" width. All confirmed visually. Comment "What is the overall height of this?" → "About 16′" confirmed verbatim.

ROOF/PITCH — "I – 4 pieces of 2×6 lumber – 76 1/2″ long 16xTRUSS" confirms 16 trusses x 4 rafters; "22.5 degrees cuts to both ends" and "place the every 16″ on center" verbatim. Gusset diagram (Building-the-rafters-large-barn-shed.png) confirms 24" x 5"/5 1/4" gussets at peak + both knees and NO bottom chord/ceiling joist/collar tie — the "open gambrel arch" caveat is fair. The derived ~67.5°/22.5° slopes (~29:12 over 5:12) check out independently: tan 67.5° = 2.414 → 28.97/12; tan 22.5° = 0.414 → 4.97/12; 76.5·(sin67.5+sin22.5) ≈ 100" rise and ≈ 200" run, matching the 202" roof plan. No pitch ratio, load, or stamp is published — correct.

FOUNDATION — skid diagram (Fitting-the-skids-3.jpg) confirms 8" at BOTH edges and four 39 5/8" gaps: 8+8+(5x3.5)+(4x39.625) = 192.0" exactly. So the record's clear-span defence of 2x8 @16" o.c. is sound, NOT misleading: the 189" joists run the 16 ft direction and bear on five lengthwise 240" skids, clear span 39 5/8" (43 1/8" o.c.). No engineering error in that field. "Compact a thick layer of gravel…", "use rafter ties to secure the skids to the frame of the floor", the unanswered pier-block comment from Eric, and the PART 3 "anchor kit" line all verified.

DOORS — door IS centred: front-wall cut list "2 pieces of 2×4 lumber – 55″ long … 1 piece – 185″ long … 2 pieces of 2×6 lumber – 75″ long" ⇒ 55 + 75 + 55 = 185. All door/jamb/leaf dimensions and the quotes "The door panels are the pieces that you cut out for the door openings." and "Install a latch to lock the doors into place tightly." verified verbatim, as are "hinges" and "anchor kit" with no hardware spec.

LOFT — the record's caveat is right: the only loft mention in the whole 3-part set is one sentence in PART 2, "If you need even more storage space, you can create a loft to the top of the storage shed." No loft framing, no headroom, no stairs — commenter Ryan ford asked for a loft floor plan (no reply) and Mark Delgado's "is there a plan for stairs?" got "No".

Foundation Layout drawing dimensions the block run at 19 ft 6 in. with outer skid rows 13 ft 7-1/2 in. apart and 3 in. joist overhangs. plans.wall_framing: True timber post-and-beam: 6x6 posts on T-Rex steel connectors seated in 5 in. deep chainsaw-cut slots (edges chamfered 45 deg with a router) and locked with 1/2 in. dia. x 6 in. aluminum pins driven through drilled holes; 6x10 plate beams and 6x10 crossbeams on top; 4x6 bottom plates and 4x6 girts between posts; 4x5/4x6 diagonal knee braces at every post plus 45-deg braces in the upper wall. Window openings framed with 4x6 trimmer studs, 4x6 rough sill and 4x6 header, with a 4x6 nailer under each crossbeam. Bents at 4, 8, 12, 16 and 20 ft, 3 ft 8 in. clear bays, 6 in. end overhangs. plans.roof: Gable roof at 10/12 pitch. Rough-sawn pine 4x8 rafters, 10 ft 1-1/16 in. long overall (9 ft 0-1/16 in. to the seat), miter-cut 40 deg at the peak, 6 in. plumb heel cut, 5-5/16 in. level seat cut, 5-1/2 in. plumb tail cut; screwed to the 6x10 plate beam with two 10 in. structural screws each. 2x10 ridge beam slid in after the first two rafter pairs, rafters to ridge with two 6 in. screws. 4x6 fly rafters create a 6 in. gable overhang, fastened with 10 in. screws 12 in. apart. Deck is skipped 1x8 sheathing covered with 1/2 in. plywood; 1x6 rake board trimmed flush to the fascia plus 1x2 shadow-line trim. Aluminum drip-cap flashing, starter course, stair-step asphalt shingles with 1-1/2 in. roofing nails, overlapping ridge caps. Roof brackets and a staging plank recommended for the upper half.
plans.siding: Vertical 1x8 tongue-and-groove pine boards nailed directly to the timber frame with 2-1/2 in. galvanized nails. Start at the centre of the gable end with the two middle boards splined so tongues face out; snap a chalkline across the jagged ends, screw a straight 2x4 fence to the siding and trim to length with a circular saw set 1-1/8 in. deep. Notch around rafter tails on a tablesaw; siding is run right over the transom opening and routed out later. Finished with scrubbed-in semi-transparent stain, plus a dry-stacked thin-stone skirt to fake a rubble-rock foundation. Note: the materials list also lists 10 sheets of 1/2 in. plywood wall sheathing that the instructions never install.
plans.loft: Partial overhead loft. Three 6x6 loft joists dropped between the 6x10 crossbeams on T-Rex connectors, resting on temporary 2x4 cleats and pinned at each end; loft floor built from 1-1/2 in. thick tongue-and-groove pine planks pounded together with a rubber mallet. Loft area, headroom, extent and access (ladder or stair) are never dimensioned or drawn - there is no loft plan sheet.
plans.doors: A pair of hinged plank doors on the gable end plus a sliding barn door on a side wall. The Plank Door detail dimensions each leaf: 3/4 in. tongue-and-groove pine planks 84-3/4 in. long (6-3/4 in. typical width, 3/4 x 3/4 in. rabbets, tongue/groove edges ripped off at the outer stiles), three 3/4 in. dia. threaded rods through the planks with construction adhesive on each end, hinges at 8 in. from top and bottom and 34-3/8 in. spacing to the middle hinge, hung on a 2x4 mounting post 91 in. long that is screwed to the timber frame with 6 in. screws through counterbores plugged with 1 in. hardwood plugs. The sliding door runs on a horizontal steel track carried by five iron stand-off brackets lag-screwed to the barn, with a stay roller at the lower corner and a pine board covering the exposed PT rim joist.
plans.windows: One 30 in. dia. round gable window (circle cut through the 1x8 pine siding with a jigsaw, secured with four 2-1/2 in. screws through its perimeter flange, opening framed with 4x4s and a 4x4 diagonal brace in each corner). One transom window in the rear wall on a PVC (or cedar/redwood/PT) sill, held by a stop strip and trim-head screws. One hinged barn sash with sill (3 in. horns), side and head casings, apron, wood-dowel stops on 2x2 cleats and a barrel bolt. Materials list calls out one 24 in. x 36 in. framed window unit.

pros: Completely free with no paywall, no email gate and no watermark nag - the drawings, the full written build sequence and the entire materials list are all on the page.

Real timber-frame engineering intent: 6x6 posts, 6x10 plate beams and crossbeams, 4x6/4x5 knee braces at every post and 45-deg upper-wall bracing give far more racking resistance than a 2x4 stick-framed shed of the same size.

The steel T-Rex connector + 1/2 in. aluminum pin joinery is a legitimate shortcut to traditional mortise-and-tenon: you get timber-frame looks and shear strength without cutting joinery by hand, and the jig-and-drill sequence is spelled out step by step.

Genuinely usable hard numbers where it counts: floor frame 20 x 14 ft with 9 ft 8-3/4 in. joist bays at 16 in. o.c., foundation block run 19 ft 6 in. with rows 13 ft 7-1/2 in. apart, bents at 4/8/12/16/20 ft with 3 ft 8 in. bays, and a fully dimensioned rafter template (10 ft 1-1/16 in., 40 deg peak, 6 in. heel, 5-5/16 in. seat, 5-1/2 in. tail).

Skid-on-concrete-block foundation means no concrete pour, no forms and no excavation - the cheapest and fastest 280 sq ft base you can build, and it keeps the structure legally 'moveable' in some jurisdictions.
Bents at 4 ft on centre with 4x8 rafters over a 14 ft span means no trusses to build and no interior posts - you get a clear 14 ft span and an open cathedral volume with a usable partial loft.

Unusually complete finish detail for a free plan: skipped 1x8 sheathing under plywood, drip cap, starter course, stair-step shingling, 1x6 rake with 1x2 shadow-line trim, spline-started centre siding boards, PVC transom sill, barn sash with sill horns and barrel bolt, plug-concealed door screws, and a dry-stacked stone skirt.

Fully dimensioned plank-door detail (84-3/4 in. planks, 91 in. mounting post, 3/4 in. threaded rods, hinge layout) plus a sliding barn-door track detail - two door types most free plans skip entirely.
A matching ShedDrafts YouTube episode walks the same build, so you can watch the sequence you are reading.
cons: Not a plan set. There is no PDF, no printable sheet, no scaled elevations and no floor plan - just nine ~800 px raster images and prose. You cannot hand this to a lumberyard or a plan checker.
No overall height, ridge height, wall height or post length is published anywhere, so you cannot check it against a local height limit or order 6x6 posts without doing your own layout.

The materials list contradicts the drawings in several places. It lists 40 8-ft 2x6 studs at 16 in. o.c. plus 2x6 top and bottom plates and 10 sheets of 1/2 in. wall sheathing, none of which appear in the timber-frame drawings or the instructions (which nail 1x8 siding straight to the frame). It also lists a 2x10 ridge twice (wall framing and roof framing) and 12 concrete blocks where the text calls for three rows of five (15).
Internal dimension conflict: the materials list says 14 floor joists 9 ft 10 in. long; the Floor Frame drawing dimensions the bay at 9 ft 8-3/4 in. Set out from the drawing, not the list.

Zero engineering. No stamp, no wind/snow/seismic loads, no anchoring, uplift or shear-wall calculations, and no hold-down detail from the frame to the skids. The claim that inspectors want to see these 'technical receipts' is marketing, not certification - expect to pay an engineer if your jurisdiction reviews a 280 sq ft accessory building.

Genuinely hard for a first-timer. It requires slot-cutting 6x6s with a chainsaw attachment on a circular saw, router chamfering, two shop-made jigs, and a portable beam saw or 12 in. sliding compound miter saw to cut 4x8 rafters.

Heavy timber = heavy lifting and heavy cost. 20 ft 6x10 plate beams, 6x10 crossbeams, 6x6 posts and rough-sawn 4x8 rafters cannot be handled solo; budget for helpers or a telehandler, and expect a materials bill well above a 2x4-framed 14x20.
Rough-sawn 4x8 pine, 6x10 beams and 1-1/2 in. T&G pine loft planks are sawmill items, not big-box stock - sourcing and lead time are real project risks and no cost estimate is given.
Skids on surface-laid concrete blocks with no frost footings will heave in cold climates and the plan offers no alternative foundation for a 280 sq ft loaded structure with a loft.
The loft is drawn only as three 6x6 joists in the isometric. No loft plan, no headroom, no extent, no floor-load capacity and no stair or ladder is provided, so the loft is effectively undesigned.
The site's CDN is unreliable and will sometimes serve a completely different shed plan at this URL - a real risk if you bookmark it or print from it later.
No cut list, no sheet-goods layout diagram, no cost estimate and no build-time estimate.

- Foundation Layout confirms 19 ft 6 in. block run, 20 ft skids, 13 ft 7-1/2 in. between outer skid lines, 8-in.-wide x 16-in.-long solid-concrete block, five blocks per row x 3 rows.
- Building Section labels match: 6x6 corner post, 4x5 diagonal brace, 4x6 girt, 4x6 bottom plate, 6x10 plate beam, 6x10 crossbeam, 6x6 loft joist, 2x10 ridge beam, 4x8 roof rafter, 4x6 fly rafter, 2x6 rim joist. It really is a timber frame, not stick framing - that claim holds.

- Image: /home/ethan/woodshed/assets/img/sheddrafts-14x20-post-beam-barn.jpg is a real JPEG, 800x587, 126,667 bytes, and RMSE-compares at 0.84% against the live og:image (same photo, jpeg-recompressed webp). No fix needed.

COMPLETENESS GAPS THE RECORD SHOULD ALSO CARRY IN CONS (beyond the two materials-list contradictions it already flags, which I confirmed - 40 8-ft 2x6 studs, 2x6 top/bottom plates, and 10 sheets of 1/2 in. wall sheathing that nothing installs):
- The materials list is far more broken than the record admits: 14 joists at 9 ft 10 in. for a 14-ft-wide floor that needs ~16 at 14 ft; 12 concrete blocks where the drawing and instructions show 15; 18 rafters where 6 pairs = 12; the 2x10 ridge listed twice in two different sections; plus joist hangers, hurricane ties, post base anchors and anchor bolts that appear in no drawing or instruction. Treat the materials list as unusable, not merely "sectioned".
- There is NO post/bent layout plan and no wall elevation. Post spacing has to be reverse-engineered from the shaded doubled joists on the Floor Frame sheet. For a plan whose whole selling point is the timber frame, that is the single biggest omission.
- The "Hang The Hinged Doors" section actually describes hanging the SLIDING door (stand-off brackets, steel track, roller assemblies, stay roller). The sliding door itself is never built or dimensioned anywhere - no drawing, no plank count, no size.

PRICE - character-exact. Page HTML contains NO "$" string at all (grep for prices returns zero hits); price is injected by a ShopifyBuy buy button. I pulled the Storefront API myself (domain icreatables.myshopify.com, token 9a405159890a118f845380bfb9370da4, product id 8262671270163 taken from the page's own script) and got: title "14x20-LTL Lean To Loft Shed Plans Emailed", availableForSale true, min=max variant price 49.99 USD, single variant "Default Title". The 23 1/2" difference between the two = roof buildup at the high edge (~11" vertical for a 2x10 at 6/12 + sheathing) plus floor structure (3/4" deck + 5 1/2" joist + 5 1/2" skid = 11 3/4"), which is consistent with one dimension being floor-to-plate and the other grade-to-roof. Roof pitch 6/12 stated on page and drawn in the section ("6 / 12" triangle). Overhang 6" front/back/sides stated on page.

ROOF ORIENTATION - the record's footprint_note is right and I verified it independently rather than accepting it: section sheeting length is 16'-10"; 14 ft + two 6" overhangs = 15 ft horizontal run, x 1.118 (6/12) = 16'-9.3" ~ 16'-10". So the slope runs across the 14 ft dimension and the tall/short walls are the 20 ft walls. The straight-on rear elevation render is a plain rectangle at ~2.86 w:h (20' / 7'-7" = 2.64) and the end-wall render shows the sloped profile with 3 skid ends visible under it, both consistent.

LOFT - floor plan shows "LINE OF LOFT ABOVE" at two locations with "OPEN TO BELOW" and a 6'-9" dimension between them, so loft-at-both-ends with a 6'-9" middle opening is confirmed. Loft framing = F1.1 2x10 14'-0" QTY 12 (16" o.c. over the two ~6'-7 1/2" ends), matching "2x10 loft joists at 16 o.c." Loft headroom genuinely not dimensioned.

All four renders (front, top/aerial, rear, left-rear, end elevation) show four high windows in the tall 20 ft wall above the doors and no windows anywhere else, so "four high clerestory windows in the tall wall" is supported. Note a vendor drawing inconsistency the record did not mention: the published floor plan labels only TWO "2020 WINDOW" symbols (one at each end of the door wall, outside the 6'-9" opening), while the page text and every render show four. Also confirmed: no window line item anywhere in the materials list, so the record's "owner-supplied and unbudgeted" con is correct.

plans.style: modern-studio (single-slope / mono-pitch shed roof with clerestory window band)
plans.price: $50.99 emailed PDF (Shopify buy button on page, product 16x20-S2 Modern Shed Plans Emailed, sku modern16x20-S2). A postal-mailed version, sku modern16x20-S2-P, is listed in the same store at $56.99 but is not embedded on this page. No price appears in the page HTML — it is injected by the Shopify buy-button JS.
plans.format: instant PDF download (emailed on purchase); optional postal-mailed prints of the same 8-1/2 x 11 sheets
plans.page_count: Not stated for this plan. The vendor's plan-example page says a typical set runs sheets 1 through 8.x (title, floor plan, exterior elevations, alternate elevations, foundation, floor framing, wall framing, alternate wall framing, roof framing, section, construction details) — roughly 13 sheets — all on 8-1/2" x 11" paper, and that "Each set of shed plans is unique and may contain more or less pages."
plans.summary: iCreatables' 16x20-S2 is a 320 sq ft modern/studio shed: a single-slope 2/12 roof over 2x4 walls, 7'-7" at the low wall and 10'-1 3/4" at the tall wall, with a band of five 3410 clerestory windows under the high eave plus a 7230 and a 6030 window. The 16-ft roof span is carried on 9-1/2" I-joist rafters (page text calls them "2x10 I joists") rather than trusses, so there are no interior posts and no loft. The set includes two foundations (treated wood skids or a concrete slab) and four door-placement options, so the 6068 double-door opening can be framed on any of the four walls. The full materials list is a free public PDF on the page, which is unusually generous and lets you price the build before buying.
plans.foundation: Two options included: treated wood skids or a concrete slab. Page says "6x6 Wood skid and Concrete slab"; the free materials list instead itemizes F3 "4x6 Skid, treated 20'-0"" x 4, plus F5 gravel. Skid layout gives roughly 5'-4" spacing across the 16' width.
plans.floor_framing: 2x6 floor joists with 3/4" T&G OSB sheathing when the skid foundation is used; materials list: 16 pcs 2x6 joist at 14'-0", 2 pcs 2x6 rim joist at 20'-0", 11 sheets 3/4" full-face T&G OSB, 24 Simpson A23 clips. Rated floor load 50 psf ("the same floor load rating used in building homes"). No floor framing is needed if the slab option is used.
plans.wall_framing: 2x4 studs at 16" on center with a double top plate, "just like a home is framed"; 7/16" OSB wall sheathing (24 sheets); 2x6 headers (8'-0" x3 and 20'-0" x2). Studs come in mixed lengths — 8'-0" (54), 9'-0" (14), 10'-0" (12) and 12'-0" (2) — plus 2x4 plates in 16'-0" (8, short walls) and 20'-0" (5, long walls) and ten 8'-0" door trimmers. The mixed stud lengths are driven by the two 16' END walls, which carry the sloping top plates: because the I-joist rafters span the 16' direction, the short (7'-7") and tall (10'-1 3/4") walls are the two 20'-long walls and both have level top plates.
plans.wall_height: Short (low) wall 7'-7"; tall (high) wall 10'-1 3/4". The same page states the tall wall as 10'-2 1/2" lower down, so the two figures on the page disagree by about 3/4".
plans.overall_height: Not stated on the plan page. The vendor's "How Tall Is My Shed?" height sheet for the 16'-wide Modern Studio Shed (7'-7" and 10'-1.75" wall heights) dimensions 12'-5" at the high side and 9'-2" at the low side, measured from the bottom of the skids, with 11 3/4" of floor structure below the subfloor.
plans.roof: Single-slope shed roof, 2/12 pitch, 9-1/2" I-joist rafters spanning 16' (11 at 17'-0"), 2x4 rafter extensions, 7/16" plywood sheathing, Simpson H1 ties; no trusses. Roofing is 25-year asphalt shingles applied per the manufacturer's low-slope instructions, or metal — the materials list calls out 36" PBR low-slope metal roofing (8 pcs at 20'-0") plus ice-and-water shield over the whole 400 sf deck.
plans.siding: Page: "T1-11 siding or installing O.S.B. and other sidings like vinyl or stucco." The free materials list instead specifies W7 1x8 tongue-and-groove siding, 600 s.f., over W8 house wrap or 15 lb felt, with 1x3 and 1x7 textured-plywood trim. Page also lists 1x4 vinyl, Masonite or cement trim for corners, eaves and fascia.
plans.doors: Plans show how to frame openings for 6068 double doors, and "There are four door options to build the 16x20 shed with the double doors on any of the 4 shed walls" — wall framing sheets cover the tall wall, short wall and end walls. The free materials list lists only D1 "Optional pre-hung double door 3068, 3'-0" x 6'-8"" (verify jamb size, swing and lock openings when ordering), which conflicts with the 6068 figure on the page; the hero render shows a single narrow entry door with a small landing/step. Doors themselves are an optional buy, not detailed as shop-built.
plans.windows: From the free materials list: W11 one 7230 awning/casement/fixed window (7'-2" x 3'-0"), W12 five 3410 fixed windows (3'-4" x 1'-0") forming the clerestory band under the high eave, W13 one 6030 awning/casement/fixed window (6'-0" x 3'-0"). Windows are not included in the plan purchase; you buy them separately.
plans.loft: none — the flat 2/12 I-joist roof leaves no loft space, and no loft or storage platform is shown or mentioned
plans.skill_level: Vendor claim: "Professionally drawn with step by step instructions to show both an old pro or a first time framer how to build a shed", and the FAQ says "Our plans are designed for homeowners to build their own sheds." Realistically intermediate at this size — a 16' clear roof span on ordered I-joists, 10' tall wall and 320 sq ft of sheathing is a lot more work than the vendor's small sheds.
plans.est_material_cost: Not stated for this plan. The vendor FAQ offers only a generic rule of thumb: "Construction costs are typically around $10.00 per square foot for a basic shed" (that would be roughly $3,200 at 320 sq ft), alongside customer-reported 2016 figures for other models ($2,400 for a 12x16 gambrel, $3,000 for a 12x20). Treat as stale and low-confidence; the FAQ itself says to take the materials list to a lumber yard for a real price.
plans.permit_notes: No engineer's stamp. FAQ: "Do the plans have engineering? No, the plans do not come with an engineers stamp" — you must take them to a locally licensed structural engineer if your jurisdiction requires calcs for snow, wind or seismic. The vendor claims the plans "have implemented elements from the 'prescriptive codes' in the IRC" and "are used regularly to apply for and get building permits." Relevant here: the FAQ notes the code exempts detached accessory structures only up to 120 sq ft (some towns 200 sq ft), so at 320 sq ft a permit is essentially certain. Roof snow load is not fixed: "The roof load varies depending on your regional weather conditions. Check with your local building department or truss plant for your local snow load." Florida/high-wind buyers are told to email for a Palm Beach County-based wind document.
plans.refund_policy: No refunds. FAQ: "Due to the electronic nature of our product we do not offer refunds." Mitigation offered is the free downloadable materials list, the free plan-sample sheets and build videos. A second, cheaper plan set can be bought at half price by emailing after the first purchase.

pros: 320 sq ft of genuinely clear, unobstructed floor: the 2/12 roof is framed with 9-1/2" I-joist rafters spanning the full 16' width, so there are no interior posts, no truss webs overhead and 7'-7" to 10'-1 3/4" of usable wall.
The complete materials list is a free public PDF on the page, so you can price the whole build at a lumber yard before spending $50.99 - very few vendors expose real quantities pre-purchase.
House-grade framing spec rather than shed-grade: 2x4 studs at 16" o.c. with a double top plate, 7/16" OSB sheathing all round, 50 psf floor load, Simpson A23 clips and H1 hurricane ties itemized.
Two foundations in one set (treated skids or concrete slab) and four door-placement options, so one purchase covers most site orientations without buying a second plan.
Clerestory window band (five 3410 fixed units) plus a 7230 and a 6030 window make this a credible office/studio rather than a storage box - good daylight without wall-hogging glazing.
Cheap for the size ($50.99 instant PDF), and a second cheaper plan set is offered at half price if you also want a different building.
Vendor states the plans follow IRC prescriptive practice and are routinely used to obtain permits, and offers a Palm Beach County-based high-wind document on request.
cons: No engineer's stamp: "the plans do not come with an engineers stamp." At 320 sq ft you are far past the 120 sq ft permit exemption the vendor's own FAQ cites, so many jurisdictions will require a local structural engineer to review and stamp - an extra cost the $50.99 does not cover.

The 16' span rests on 9-1/2" I-joist rafters, an engineered product you must order from a lumber yard (11 pcs at 17'-0"); they are not a stocked big-box item everywhere, they need care in handling and blocking, and no snow-load rating is given for them - "The roof load varies depending on your regional weather conditions."

2/12 is a low slope. Asphalt shingles must be applied under the manufacturer's low-slope rules (the list calls for ice-and-water shield over the entire 400 sf deck) or you switch to PBR metal panels - either way roofing is fussier and more expensive per square than a normal gable.
No loft and no attic storage at all - the flat roof and I-joist rafters mean every square foot you get is the 320 on the floor.

The page contradicts itself and the free materials list in several places: tall wall given as both 10'-1 3/4" and 10'-2 1/2"; skids described as 6x6 on the page but 4x6 in the list; siding described as T1-11/OSB on the page but 1x8 tongue-and-groove in the list; the door is "6068 double doors" on the page but "double door 3068 3'-0" x 6'-8"" in the list, and the hero render shows a single entry door. Expect to reconcile these against the purchased sheets.

The free list itemizes 16 pcs of 2x6 floor joist at 14'-0" for a 16'-wide floor with no girder or beam line called out, so the skid/floor layout is not verifiable from the free list alone - check the foundation and floor framing sheets before ordering lumber.
Drawings are 8-1/2" x 11" only, emailed or mailed; there is no large-format permit set, which some plan examiners dislike.
No refunds of any kind, and the postal option costs $6 more for identical letter-size sheets.
Nothing about insulation, interior finish, electrical or HVAC is included, which matters if the point is a year-round office/studio.
The skid foundation is offered but is the weak option at this size and height; a permitted 16x20 with a 10' tall wall will usually want the concrete slab, which adds real cost and a concrete crew.

plans.summary: A $69.99 emailed PDF plan set for a 16x20 (320 sq ft) stick-framed shed with a 10/12 gable roof, a 5/12 shed dormer over the long wall, and a full-width attic loft with an 8'x4' opening facing the dormer windows. Framing is conventional house-style construction: 2x6 floor joists on treated 4x6 skids, 2x4 studs at 16" o.c. with double top plates and 8'-1" walls, and site-cut 2x8 rafters (the plans give cut angles so rafters are assembled on the ground). Openings are 6'-0" x 6'-8" homemade double doors on the gable end with a 6'x1' transom above, a 2'-6" x 6'-8" side door, three 2'-0" x 3'-6" single-hung windows, three 3'x1'-4" fixed dormer windows and two 12" gable vents. The full itemized materials list is published free as a downloadable PDF before purchase, which is unusual and lets you get lumberyard bids first.
plans.foundation: Primary is a wood-rail/skid foundation: four 20'-0" treated 4x6 skids on gravel (per the free materials list). The page's feature bullets claim "5 Foundations - Skid, concrete slab, poured concrete pier, concrete block pier, precast pier," but the detail list lower on the same page says only "The shed plans include plans for a wood rail foundation" - contradictory.
plans.floor_framing: 2x6 floor joists (16'-0", qty 16) with 2x6 rim joists (20'-0", qty 2) and 3/4" T&G OSB sheathing (10 sheets), 16 Simpson A23 clips. Floor load rated 50 psf.
plans.wall_framing: 2x4 at 16" on center with a double top plate, "just like a home is framed." 66 studs at 92-5/8", 2x4 plates in 16' and 20' lengths, 2x6 headers (8' and 10').
plans.wall_height: 8'-1" (framed with 92-5/8" precut studs); vendor height chart shows 7'-8 1/2" clear
plans.roof: Gable roof at 10/12 pitch with a 5/12 shed dormer. Site-built rafters from 2x8s (19 @ 12'-0"), 2x8 loft/dormer rafters (7 @ 10'), 2x10 ridge board (22'), 2x4 collar ties (11), 2x4 sub-fascia, 7/16" OSB roof sheathing (18 sheets), 18 Simpson H2.5 hurricane ties. NOT engineered trusses — rafters are cut on site from angles given in the plans. 10" overhang on sides and gable ends. 25-year asphalt shingles over 15 lb felt (~5 squares). Roof snow load 40 psf. Caveat: the page prose says the roof "is sheeted with 1/2" O.S.B." while the materials list specifies 7/16" — a vendor internal contradiction; 7/16" is the itemized quantity.
plans.siding: T1-11 (T-111) exterior plywood siding, 26 sheets of 4x8x1/2"; page says other sidings such as vinyl may be used. 1x4 and 1x6 wood/Masonite/cement trim for corners, eaves, fascia and door.
plans.loft: Full attic loft over the whole 16x20 footprint with an 8'-0" x 4'-0" opening at the front, positioned in front of the dormer windows. Loft floor is 2x8 joists (12 @ 16', 2 @ 12', 8 @ 8') with 2x8 rim joists and 3/4" T&G OSB, hung with Simpson LUS26/LUS46 hangers. The 2x8s span the full 16' width and also act as rafter ties; the page states the loft floor is rated for a lighter floor load than the 50 psf main floor. Headroom is not stated - vendor height chart shows only 7'-4 1/4" from top plate to ridge, sloping to nothing at the eaves. Access is not designed: the materials list notes "Ramp or stair materials are not shown."
plans.doors: 2'-6" x 6'-8" is right per the drawings, but the record fails to flag that the page's own spec bullet contradicts it with 2'-8".
plans.windows: Three 2036 single-hung windows 2'-0" x 3'-6" on the 20' side wall; one 6010 fixed transom 6'-0" x 1'-0" above the double doors; three 3014 fixed windows in the shed dormer (3'-0" x 1'-4" per the elevation sheet, 3'-0" x 1'-6" per the standalone materials list); two 12" x 12" premade gable vents.
plans.overall_height: Conflicting sources: the plan's own rear elevation is dimensioned 14'-0 1/4" from grade to ridge, while iCreatables' "How Tall Is My Shed" dormer chart lists 17'-1" for 16'-wide dormer sheds (on 4x6 wood rails; about 12" lower on a concrete slab). plans.summary: A 320 sq ft (16' x 20') gable storage-shed plan set from iCreatables, drawn as a conventionally framed mini-building: 2x4 walls at 16" o.c. with a double top plate and 8'-1" wall height (standard 92-5/8" studs), 2x6 floor joists with 3/4" T&G OSB over treated 6x6 skids, or a concrete slab as the alternate foundation. The 16' roof span is carried by 11 plant-manufactured, engineered common trusses at 4/12 pitch that you order from a local truss plant, with a 16" overhang all around and 25-year asphalt shingles. As drawn it has a 3068 prehung single door plus a 6068 prehung double door and one optional 5'-0" x 4'-0" window, with T1-11 siding. Delivery is an instant-download PDF (8-1/2 x 11 sheets you print at home) or mailed prints, and iCreatables publishes the complete materials list as a free public PDF before you buy.
plans.format: instant PDF download (emailed link) — or mailed printed set for $65.99; drawings sized for 8-1/2" x 11" home-printer paper
plans.page_count: Not stated for this plan. Site-wide, "a typical set" is sheets 1-8 plus sub-sheets: title, floor plan, exterior elevations (+alternates), foundation plan, floor framing, wall framing (+alternate for larger sheds), roof framing, truss details, full-size truss angle, building section, construction details — roughly 12-14 sheets.
plans.foundation: Two foundations included: (1) treated 6x6 wood skid — free materials list calls out 8 pcs of 6x6 treated skid at 10'-0" plus gravel, i.e. spliced runs giving intermediate support rows under the 16' joists; (2) concrete slab. On a slab the framed wood floor is omitted and the building sits ~12" lower.
plans.floor_framing: 2x6 floor joists (16 pcs @ 16'-0") with 2x6 rim joists (2 pcs @ 20'-0") and 3/4" (23/32") T&G OSB sheathing, 10 sheets, plus 32 Simpson A23 clips. 50 psf floor load rating ("the same floor load rating used in building homes"). Used only with the skid foundation.
plans.wall_framing: 2x4 studs at 16" on center with a double top plate, "just like a home is framed" — 58 studs @ 92-5/8", 6 short plates + 8 long plates @ 16'-0", 6 trimmers, 5 pcs 2x6 header @ 8'-0"
plans.wall_height: 8'-1" (framed with standard 92-5/8" precut studs; page notes longer studs may be substituted to raise the wall)
plans.overall_height: 12'-1" to the ridge measured from the ground with the wood-rail/framed-floor foundation, 11'-1 1/4" from the shed floor to the peak (per iCreatables' "16' WIDE GABLE STYLE SHED / 8'-1" WALL HEIGHT" height drawing). About 12" lower when built on a concrete slab.
plans.roof: Gable, 4/12 pitch, 11 manufactured/engineered common roof trusses (pitch and/or an attic space can be changed when ordering from the truss plant); 7/16" OSB roof sheathing (12 sheets), 2x4 sub-fascia, 16" overhang on all sides (reducible by cutting the rafter tails), 15 lb felt, metal drip edge, 25-year asphalt shingles (4 squares). Snow load is deliberately left to the local truss plant / building department.
plans.siding: T1-11 (T1-11 4x8 sheets, 21 pcs) — or OSB sheathing with vinyl, stucco or other finish siding. Trim is 1x4/1x6 wood, vinyl, Masonite or cement board at corners, eaves and fascia; "Z" metal flashing at horizontal siding joints.
plans.doors: One 3'-0" x 6'-8" (3068) prehung single door and one 6'-0" x 6'-8" (6068) prehung double door. The floor plan puts the 6068 double door on a 16' end wall and the 3068 door on a 20' sidewall next to the window. Plans for building the doors yourself are included if you don't want to buy prehung units.
plans.windows: One optional 5'-0" x 4'-0" window (listed as a "5040 XO Window" in the materials list), shown on the 20' sidewall
plans.loft: None as drawn — 4/12 common trusses leave no usable storage loft. The page notes the pitch "and / or adding a attic space can be changed when ordering the trusses from the truss plant," so a loft/attic is a customer-driven truss modification, not part of the plan set.
plans.skill_level: Beginner-to-intermediate per the vendor: "Professionally drawn with step by step instructions to show both an old pro or a first time framer how to build a shed." Realistically it assumes you can handle a 16' span roof and set trusses, plus lay a slab or level a 4-row skid pad.
plans.build_time: not stated (the only time claim is that buying trusses "saves you a days worth of work")
plans.permit_notes: iCreatables' 16x20 index page states: "Because of the large size the 16x20 sheds typically require a building permit... you should be sure to verify with your local building department the codes in your area during the planning stages." The license/disclaimer page adds that the plans were drawn without knowledge of your site, make no assurance of local code compliance (snow/wind/seismic/frost/soil), and recommends having a local engineer, architect or building official verify them. Snow load and truss design are explicitly punted to the local truss plant, which is actually helpful for permitting since the truss manufacturer supplies stamped/engineered truss calcs.

pros: Real house-grade framing spec rather than a hobby sketch: 2x4 walls at 16" o.c. with double top plate, 8'-1" walls from standard 92-5/8" precut studs, 50 psf floor load, 2x6 headers — easy for a building department to read and easy to insulate/finish later as an office or shop.

The 16' roof span is handled by pre-engineered trusses ordered from a truss plant local to your build site, so the roof structure comes with load-rated engineering for your snow/wind zone. That is the single biggest permit-friendliness advantage over rafter-cut DIY plans at this size, and it removes a full day of site work.

Genuinely flexible: 4/12 pitch and/or an attic space can be changed when you order the trusses, wall height can be raised with longer studs, roof overhang can be trimmed at the rafter tails, and siding can be T1-11 or OSB + vinyl/stucco.
Two complete foundation options (treated 6x6 skids over gravel, or concrete slab) so you can pick the cheaper/permit-appropriate one; slab version drops the whole 2x6 + OSB floor package.
The full materials list is published free as a PDF before you buy, so you can price the build and sanity-check the design without spending a cent — rare among paid-plan vendors.
$59.99 for 320 sq ft is cheap relative to the ~$5,000+ of materials, and iCreatables sells matched sizes (14x20-B, 16x24-B, 12x24-B) if you want to stretch or shrink the same design.
Standard off-the-shelf openings (3068 and 6068 prehung units) plus included plans to build those doors yourself if you'd rather save the money.
cons: You cannot finish the roof without a third party: the plan intentionally does not give you rafter cut lengths or a rafter option, so you must find a local truss plant, get 11 trusses designed/quoted/delivered, and coordinate lead time. If no truss supplier will do a small order near you, this plan stalls.

Skid foundation is heavier than it looks — 8 pcs of treated 6x6 at 10' (about 4 bearing rows across the 16' width, since 2x6 joists cannot span 16' unsupported) over a gravel pad that has to be flat and level across a 16x20 area. Treated 6x6 is a real cost driver; the slab alternative trades that for concrete work.

Some quantities in the FREE public materials list look light for a 16x20 roof with 16" overhangs — 12 sheets of 7/16" OSB (384 sf) and 4 squares of shingles against a roof surface closer to ~440 sf, and only 2 pcs of 16' 2x4 sub-fascia for ~45 lf of eave. Wall, floor and siding counts pencil out fine, so treat the roof lines as a starting point and re-measure off the purchased drawings before ordering.

The page's own copy is sloppy: one heading reads "16x20 Gable Shed Plans With a Overhead Door" although this plan has no overhead/garage door (that is the separate 16x20-GD product), and the drawings, images and free materials list are labeled 16x20-G while the SKU is shed16x20-B. Nothing here is a design defect, but it makes it hard to be sure which variant you are buying.
No loft, no attic storage and no interior layout as drawn — a 4/12 common truss gives you a bare 320 sq ft box with 8'-1" walls; a loft means paying for a truss redesign.

At 320 sq ft this will almost certainly need a permit, and the license explicitly disclaims code compliance (soil, frost depth, wind, seismic, egress) and recommends you pay a local engineer/official to review. Budget for permit fees and possibly stamped foundation details.

All sales final, no refunds of any kind (electronic product), and the license covers building exactly one structure. Prices are JS-injected by a Shopify buy button, so nothing on the page itself states a price.
Only one optional 5'-0" x 4'-0" window — if you want an office/studio you are designing your own fenestration and adding your own headers.

plans.summary: iCreatables' 16x20-B is a straightforward 320 sq ft gable storage shed sold as an instant-download PDF plan set for $59.99 (the on-page Shopify Buy button resolves to product "16x20-B Backyard Shed Plans Emailed" at $59.99; a postal-mailed twin exists in the store at $65.99). It is framed like a house: 8'-1" walls of 2x4 studs at 16" o.c. with a double top plate using standard 92-5/8" precut studs, 2x6 floor joists with 23/32" T&G OSB rated to 50 psf, T1-11 siding, and a 4/12 gable roof built from 11 manufactured common trusses you order from a truss plant local to your site rather than site-built rafters. Two foundations ship in the same set — treated 6x6 wood skids with a framed floor, or a 4" concrete slab on a 12" monolithic perimeter footing. The full itemized materials list is a genuinely free PDF download right on the page (captured in lumber_list below), which is unusual and lets you price the build before spending anything.
plans.foundation: Two foundation options in the one plan set: (1) 6x6 treated wood skid with a framed floor (free materials list: 8 pcs 6x6 x 10'-0" treated + gravel); (2) concrete slab. No slab thickness or footing dimension is published anywhere on the page — and the vendor FAQ warns the shed plans "include a concrete slab detail without the deeper footing and foundation required for areas that have frost." No concrete/rebar quantities on the free sheet.
plans.floor_framing: 2x6 floor joists with 3/4" (23/32" T&G OSB) floor sheathing when the skid foundation is used. Materials list: 16 pcs 2x6 x 16'-0" joists, 2 pcs 2x6 x 20'-0" rim joists, 10 sheets 23/32" T&G OSB, 32 Simpson A23 clips. Rated floor load 50 lb per sq ft, "the same floor load rating used in building homes." Note the joists are 16 ft members but 2x6 cannot clear-span 16 ft — with four 20 ft skid runs made from the eight 10 ft 6x6s, the joists bear on intermediate skids; exact skid spacing is on the purchased sheets.
plans.wall_framing: 2x4 framing at 16" on center with a double top plate, "just like a home is framed." Uses standard 92-5/8" precut studs. Materials list: 58 studs 2x4 x 92-5/8", 6 pcs 2x4 x 16' short plates, 8 pcs 2x4 x 16' long plates, 6 trimmers 2x4 x 92-5/8", 5 headers 2x6 x 8'-0".
plans.wall_height: 8'-1" (framed with standard 92-5/8" studs). Page notes longer studs may be substituted to increase wall height.
plans.overall_height: not stated
plans.roof: Gable roof at 4/12 pitch, designed for pre-engineered manufactured trusses ordered from a truss plant local to the build site — materials list calls for 11 "Common Roof Truss, manufactured, 4x12 pitch" (i.e. 24" o.c. across the 20 ft length) plus 12 sheets 7/16" OSB roof sheathing and 2 pcs 2x4 x 16' sub-fascia. 16" roof overhang on all sides (may be reduced by cutting rafter tails shorter). Roofing is 25-year asphalt shingles, 4 squares / 358 sq ft, over 15 lb felt with 10 pcs of 10 ft metal drip edge. Roof pitch and/or an attic/storage space can be changed when ordering the trusses. Snow load is not fixed by the plan — vendor says roof load varies regionally and to confirm with your building department or truss plant.
plans.siding: 1/2" T1-11 4x8 sheets (21 sheets on the materials list), with the page noting you can instead install OSB sheathing and finish with other sidings such as vinyl or stucco. Trim is 1x4 and 1x6 wood, vinyl, Masonite or cement board at corners, eaves and fascia; list shows 16 pcs 1x4 x 10' trim, 1 sheet rough-sawn plywood soffit, 4 pcs 10 ft "Z" metal flashing.
plans.windows: One optional 5'-0" x 4'-0" window ("5040 XO", qty 1 on the materials list). The page explicitly calls the window optional.
plans.doors: One 3068 pre-hung single door (3'-0" x 6'-8") and one 6068 double door (6'-0" x 6'-8"), "style per owner". Plans for building these doors yourself are included if you would rather not buy pre-hung units. No overhead/garage door despite one page heading saying otherwise.
plans.loft: none — this is a plain gable with 4/12 common trusses and no loft or ceiling joist package. The page does note that "adding a attic space can be changed when ordering the trusses from the truss plant," so a storage attic is an option you arrange with the truss plant, not something the plan details.

plans.skill_level: Aimed at DIY homeowners; no explicit skill rating is published. The page claims the plans are "Professionally drawn with step by step instructions to show both an old pro or a first time framer how to build a shed." The FAQ answer to a self-described beginner says "Our plans are designed for homeowners to build their own sheds... The plans show the cut lengths and placement of each of the boards" and points beginners to the free plan example, the free materials list and the How To Build A Shed videos/manual before buying. Realistically this is an intermediate build: 16 ft spans, crane-free but two-person truss setting, a 320 sq ft floor or slab, and pre-hung door hanging.
plans.permit_notes: iCreatables states outright that "Because of the large size the 16x20 sheds typically require a building permit" and to verify local codes during planning. Plans are drawn to prescriptive IRC (International Residential Code) requirements and the vendor says they are "regularly used to apply for building permits" and are "detailed enough to submit for Permit Approval," but they carry NO engineer's stamp: "the plans do not come with an engineers stamp." If your jurisdiction demands stamped drawings or specific snow/wind/seismic calcs, you must take the plans to an engineer licensed in your state, and the vendor recommends a solo/small-team engineer for cost. They warn the plans may need to be red-lined by the plans examiner. Roof snow load is deliberately left to the local truss plant. Florida/high-wind (Palm Beach County, 160 mph) supplementary engineering info is available free by emailing support@icreatables.com.

The reason for this is that there is no way for the product to be returned without the buyer retaining a copy of the product." pros: The itemized materials list is free on the page with no email gate or upsell — you can price the entire build at a local lumber yard for $0 before deciding to buy the $59.99 plan. Very few paid-plan vendors do this.

Roof is designed around pre-engineered manufactured trusses ordered locally, so the 16 ft span is engineered for YOUR snow and wind loads by the truss plant, and you skip a day of site-built rafter work. The vendor notes truss cost is often not much above the cost of the lumber to build them yourself.
Framed to residential convention: 2x4 at 16" o.c., double top plate, 92-5/8" precut studs, 8'-1" ceiling, 50 psf floor. Nothing exotic, everything stocked, and a plans examiner will recognize it.
Two foundations in one purchase (skid or slab) instead of forcing a choice at checkout — useful if you don't yet know whether your jurisdiction will accept a skid-on-gravel accessory building.
Real 8'-1" wall height plus a 6'-0" x 6'-8" double door makes this usable as a workshop/garage-adjacent space rather than a crouch-in garden shed.
4/12 pitch keeps overall height and shingle quantity down (4 squares / 358 sq ft), which helps with height-limit ordinances and cost.
Free downloadable example plan set and build videos let you judge drawing quality before a non-refundable purchase.
Vendor supplies free Florida/160 mph Palm Beach County supplementary engineering info on request — a real help in hurricane country.
Plans are drawn to prescriptive IRC and are explicitly marketed as permit-submittal-ready, and the vendor is candid about what they do and do not cover.
$59.99 is mid-market, and it includes a How To Build A Shed manual plus door-building plans that other vendors sell separately.
cons: No engineer's stamp. The vendor says so plainly. If your building department requires stamped drawings or snow/wind/seismic calculations — and at 320 sq ft many will require a permit — you pay a local engineer on top of the $59.99, which can easily exceed the plan price.

You are dependent on a third party for the roof: 11 trusses must be ordered from a local truss plant, which means lead time, a delivery/offload plan, and a cost the plan cannot quote. If no truss plant will sell to a homeowner in small quantity, the roof design is not directly buildable as drawn.
Absolutely no refunds — "Due to the electronic nature of our product we do not offer refunds." Evaluate the free sample set carefully first.

The free materials list is exterior-shell only. It contains no house wrap/building paper for the walls, no wall sheathing behind the T1-11 (the T1-11 is doing the bracing), no insulation, no interior finish, no electrical, no ramp, and no foundation anchors or hold-down hardware. Budget accordingly.

The concrete slab option is included in the drawings but the free materials list quantifies only the skid foundation (8 pcs 6x6x10' treated plus unquantified gravel) — no concrete yardage, rebar/mesh, or form lumber. You cannot price the slab route from the free sheet.

The page's own heading says "16x20 Gable Shed Plans With a Overhead Door Include The Following:" while the spec list and materials list show only 3068 and 6068 swinging doors. That is a vendor copy-paste error; if you want a garage door you need the separate 16x20-GD product, so confirm before ordering.
No loft or ceiling joists — 320 sq ft of floor and nothing overhead. An attic/storage truss is possible but only by renegotiating the truss order, which the plan does not detail.

Overall building height is never published, so you cannot check a local height ordinance from the listing alone; the 16" overhang on all four sides also pushes the drip line past the 16x20 footprint into your setback math.
Exact page count is not published — the vendor only says a typical set is the ~13-sheet sequence and "may contain more or less pages."
Drawings are 8-1/2 x 11 only, even for the mailed version. Convenient to print, but small for reading framing dimensions on a windy job site; there is no large-format option.

Concrete slab, 16 ft spans and setting eleven trusses put this at the upper end of a first-timer's ability despite the "first time framer" marketing; plan on a helper and likely a rented lift or many hands for the roof.
The postal-mailed version ($65.99) is a separate store item, not a checkbox on this page — easy to buy the wrong one.
