plans.http_status: 200 via Wayback Machine (snapshot redirected to /web/20061219014041id_/, content-type application/pdf, 1,085,911 bytes). The live host www.cps.gov.on.ca no longer resolves - direct curl returns 000 / exit 6, so Wayback is the only route.
plans.footprint_note: This is a parametric plan, not one fixed size. The sheet fixes three building WIDTHS (spans): 7320mm (24'), 9150mm (30'), 11590mm (38'). LENGTH is builder-chosen "in multiples of 2440mm (8') up to maximum length L, based on limits of diaphragm upper floor to resist wind, see Table 1, Sheet 10". 24x16 (two 8' bays on the narrowest span = 384 sq ft) is therefore the smallest legal build and the only configuration that lands in the user's 240-480 sq ft target - but note the plan never draws a short building; its worked example is a 38'x96' barn, and the shortest span is still 8 ft wider than the 16 ft the user asked for. Maximum lengths at 0.35 kPa wind: 48' (24' wide), 56' (30'), 64' (38') on floor fastening schedule A; 104'/120'/136' on schedule B.
plans.style: Two-storey gambrel-roof barn with a full-footprint hayloft; buildable as post/pole frame on pressure-treated 6x6s or as 2x6 stud wall on a continuous concrete foundation, clad in 29ga. prepainted steel
plans.price: Free
plans.summary: CPS Plan 8315 "Gambrel Roof Barn" is a free 10-sheet engineered drawing set from the Canada Plan Service, sealed-office work by Argue & Associates Consulting Engineers and conforming to the National Farm Building Code of Canada 1995. It covers three building widths in one document - 7320mm (24'), 9150mm (30') and 11590mm (38') - each two storeys with a 3050mm (10') ground-floor wall height and a full hayloft above, at any length in 8 ft multiples up to a wind-governed maximum given in Table 1. Its real distinguishing content is the wind engineering: the plywood loft floor is designed as a horizontal diaphragm anchored to endwall shear walls, and the plan gives factored shear values (2.56 and 5.21 kN/m for fastening schedules A and B), maximum building length versus 1/10 hourly wind force from 0.20 to 0.65 kPa, anchor-bolt counts and nail spacings, plus a step-by-step worked example. It is NOT a standalone buildable set: the gambrel braced-rafter roof frames are separate CPS plans (M-9251/2/3 for 24', M-9254/5/6 for 30', M-9260/1/2 for 38'), the sliding doors are CPS plan 9341, and there is no bill of materials, no cut list, no window schedule, no interior floor plan and no ground-floor slab detail.
includes: Sheet 1 of 10 - "Gambrel Roof Barn": perspective sketch of the finished barn, three dimensioned endwall elevations (one per span), 14 keyed notes, plus MATERIALS specification box, APPLICATION note and WARNING note

Sheet 2 - "Foundation Plans": plan views for all three spans; each drawing shows the pole-frame option on one side and the stud-wall/steel-interior-post option on the other, with interior post grids at 2440mm (8') or 3050mm (10') c/c and endwall concrete anchorage callouts

Sheet 3 - "24-ft. Span Details": full cross-section, both wall build-ups in detail circles, 25 keyed notes, footing size table keyed to max ground snow + rain (2.46 / 5.83 / 8.98 kPa) and interior post footing size table
Sheet 4 - "30-ft. Span Details": same content for the 9150mm span (snow 3.36 / 5.34 / 8.33 kPa)
Sheet 5 - "38-ft. Span Details": same content for the 11590mm span (snow 1.65 / 2.72 / 4.39 kPa)

Sheet 6 - "Endwall and Beam Details": interior steel/wood post options, welded 1/4" steel column capital, plan views of the built-up plank beam, 3/4"x12" plywood splice plates, 8" concrete infill between endwall poles, 25 keyed notes

Sheet 7 - "Wind Bracing Details": full endwall framing elevation for the 38' span, 2x6 diagonal endwall brace with clinched-nail double-shear connection, 18ga. galvanized steel stud anchor detail, removable 2x6 guard rail across the loft doorway

Sheet 8 - "Sidewall, Floor and Gambrel Arch Anchorage Details": isometric connection views for both wall systems, Table 7 (nail spacing to plywood by braced-rafter size) and Table 9 (joist hanger model by braced-rafter size)

Sheet 9 - "Diaphragm Wind Bracing Selection": plywood layout diagrams A and B, floor fastening schedule A (factored shear Vr = 2.56 kN/m) and schedule B (Vr = 5.21 kN/m), endwall shear-wall section through foundation and rebar, welded steel strap anchor detail

Sheet 10 - Table 1 "Maximum Diaphragm Floor Length" by 1/10 hourly wind force (0.20-0.65 kPa) x building width x fastening schedule, with anchor bolt counts and spacings and nail spacings, plus an 8-step "Diaphragm Wind Bracing - Selection by Example" for a 38'x96' barn at London, Ontario
pros: Genuinely free, no email or registration, and genuinely engineered - a consulting-engineering office (Argue & Associates) produced 10 full-size sheets to the National Farm Building Code of Canada 1995, with real load paths worked out end to end.

The wind engineering is far more explicit than any typical free shed plan: the loft plywood floor is designed as a horizontal diaphragm with published factored shear (2.56 kN/m schedule A, 5.21 kN/m schedule B), Table 1 gives maximum building length against 1/10 hourly wind force from 0.20 to 0.65 kPa, and it specifies anchor bolt counts, anchor spacing, and nail spacing to plywood and blocking for each case.

Footings are selected from a table against actual ground snow + rain load (e.g. 24' span: 20" round at 2.46 kPa up to 26" round at 8.98 kPa) at 120 kPa (2500 psf) assumed soil bearing, with an explicit instruction to adjust for weaker or stronger soil - real sizing, not a rule of thumb.

Three widths and any length in one document: 24', 30' or 38' span, length in 8 ft increments up to 136' in the best case. You can scale from a ~384 sq ft shop to a 100-ft building without changing plans.

Two complete wall systems drawn side by side - pole frame on PT 6x6s at 8' c/c with 2x6 girts, or 2x6 stud wall on a continuous 8" reinforced concrete wall - so you can pick by budget, site and permit climate.

Full-footprint hayloft with engineered joist sizes AND overlap lengths at the beam (e.g. 2x8x14' at 24" c/c overlapped 4' on the 24' span), plus specified bridging - a genuinely usable second floor, not a token storage shelf.

Connection-level detail that most plans skip: joist hanger model by rafter size (Simpson LB 28 / JB 28 top-flange or equal), 18ga. 1-1/2"x18" galvanized uplift straps, 3/4"x12" plywood beam splice plates with 16 nails per location, clinched-nail double-shear brace connections, welded steel strap anchors tied to the foundation rebar.

Safety content you almost never see in shed plans: emergency exit doors at both ends that must open outward, a removable 22"x36" loft exit panel at each end, and a permanently attached exit ladder with rung spacing (12" c/c), wall clearance (7") and termination height (39"-59" above grade) specified.
Metal-clad over strapping means a fast, low-maintenance, low-cost skin: 29ga. prepainted galvanized steel on 1x4 strapping at 24" c/c for both roof and walls.
The PDF is small (1.1 MB) and archives cleanly - saved locally at /home/ethan/woodshed/assets/pdf/cps-8315-24x16-gambrel-barn.pdf so the dead source domain no longer matters.
cons: Minimum width is 24 ft. There is no 16-ft-wide option anywhere in the set, so the smallest possible build is about 24x16 = 384 sq ft - wider than the user's 16x20 target and at the top of the acceptable range. If you want 16 ft wide, this plan cannot give it to you.

Not a standalone plan set. The gambrel braced-rafter frames - the entire roof structure - are separate CPS plans (M-9251/9252/9253 for 24', M-9254/9255/9256 for 30', M-9260/9261/9262 for 38'), and the 10'x10' sliding doors are CPS plan 9341. Without those companions you have no rafter geometry, no cutting angles and no door details.

No bill of materials, no quantity take-off, no cut list. Sheet 1's MATERIALS box is a specification (concrete strength, lumber grade, steel gauge), not a shopping list. Every board count, sheet count and fastener count is your own work.
No window schedule or window details at all - the Sheet 1 perspective shows sidewall windows, but nothing is dimensioned or detailed anywhere in the 10 sheets.

No ground-floor surface is specified. The sections show earth inside the perimeter; there is no concrete slab thickness, reinforcement, vapour barrier or granular base detail. Budget and design that yourself.

No stair to the loft. Access as drawn is the 6'x8' or 5'x7' sliding loading door plus an exterior emergency exit ladder. Adding an interior stair means re-cutting joists and re-checking the diaphragm you just paid for in engineering.

No insulation, vapour barrier, electrical, plumbing or interior finish is shown, and the mandatory interior 3/8" plywood shear sheathing is structural - you cannot delete or re-nail it to suit a finish without breaking the wind design.

Foundation and beam work are well beyond a normal shed. The stud-wall option needs a formed, reinforced, continuous 8" concrete wall on a 20"x8" footing to below frost; even the pole option needs continuous concrete on all four sides or 8" concrete infill between the endwall poles to anchor the shear walls. Plus a 4-to-6-ply built-up plank beam on steel HSS or 6x6 columns with a welded 1/4" steel capital.

Metric-first drawings (imperial in brackets) and the PDF has no text layer - it is AutoCAD 2000 vector outlines, so you cannot search, copy or grep any dimension. Everything must be read off the sheet by eye.

Canadian code, Canadian climate data, farm-building code. It is engineered to NFBC 1995 with NBCC 1995 Section 2.5 climatic data, and Sheet 1 explicitly makes the user responsible for verifying the criteria against local conditions. A US building department will not accept it without re-engineering and a local stamp - and a farm building code carries lower requirements than a code for human occupancy.
The archived sheets carry no signed or sealed engineer's stamp; the title block REVISED field is blank and the drawings are dated Jan. 2000, so they are 26 years out of date against current codes.

Internal inconsistency in stud spacing you must reconcile before framing: Sheets 3/4/5 note 15 say "38x140mm (2x6) sill, top plates and studs @ 610mm (2') c/c", while Sheet 7 note 5 says "Stud wall, 38x140mm (2x6) @ 1220mm (48\") c/c" with 2x4 girts at 24" c/c. These are two different wall systems presented as one.
Documented typo: Sheet 4 note 14 refers you to "Sheet X" for endwall shear-wall anchor spacing (Sheets 3 and 5 correctly say Sheet 10).

The Canada Plan Service is discontinued and cps.gov.on.ca is dead, so the companion braced-rafter and sliding-door plans are hard to obtain and there is no support, errata channel or updated revision.
Sheet 1 WARNING: the whole structure is designed assuming all doors are closed and remain intact in a severe wind. A 10'x10' sliding door left open or blown in invalidates the wind design.

plans.foundation: Two options, both drawn. (1) Continuous cast-in-place concrete: 508mm (20") wide x 200mm (8") deep continuous footing with 15M rebar dowels @ 610mm (24") c/c, supporting a 203mm (8") continuous concrete foundation wall with 15M rebar continuous top and bottom and 1/2"x10" L-anchor bolts @ 1220mm (4') c/c; wall rebar horizontal 15M @ 500mm (20") c/c and vertical 15M @ 610mm (24") c/c. (2) Pole frame: individual round or square concrete footings under 140x140mm (6x6) PT poles, sized from the per-span table against max ground snow + rain - 24' span 510mm (20") to 670mm (26") round; 30' span 540mm (21") to 690mm (27"); 38' span 580mm (23") to 700mm (28"). Interior post footings 508-750mm (20"-30") depending on 8' or 10' post spacing. Footing depth minimum 610mm (24") or to below frost depth, and at least 1/3 of the footing diameter/width thick. Sizes assume 120 kPa (2500 psf) soil bearing, adjustable if soil tests differ. Concrete min. 25 MPa at 28 days, 5% air entrained; rebar min. 400 MPa deformed; 50mm (2") cover over steel and 75mm (3") between steel and earth. CRITICAL: regardless of wall system, both endwalls need concrete on all four sides of the building, or 200mm (8") concrete infill placed between the endwall poles (rebar both ways @ 530mm/21"), to anchor the diaphragm shear walls - anchor bolt count per endwall comes from Table 1 (5 to 16 bolts). Gravel splashpad extending 610mm (2') beyond the wall.
plans.floor_framing: The "floor" in this plan is the LOFT floor, which doubles as the engineered horizontal wind diaphragm; the ground floor surface is not specified. Loft joists at 610mm (24") c/c throughout, lapped over the centre beam: 24' span - 38x184x4270mm (2x8x14') overlapped 1220mm (4') at the beam, 5-102x4.33mm (4") clinched spiral nails at each lapped end, bridging at midspan. 30' span - 38x184x3660mm (2x8x12') overlapped 990mm (39"). 38' span - 38x235x4270mm (2x10x14') overlapped 648mm (25 1/2"). Sheathing: 15.5mm (5/8") T&G softwood plywood on the 24' and 30' spans, 19mm (3/4") on the 38' span, end joints staggered 1220mm (48") at joists, 38x89mm (2x4) blocking between joists, and 38mm (2") spaced blocking the same depth as the joists nailed with 5-127x4.88mm (5") spirals through the joists. Diaphragm fastening schedule A: 76x3.1mm (3") spirals @ 150mm (6") c/c at panel ends, 300mm (12") to intermediate joists, 38mm (1 1/2") at T&G edges - factored shear Vr = 2.56 kN/m. Schedule B adds 2x4 blocking screwed under each square-edge longitudinal joint with 50x4mm (2" #8) flat socket-head wood screws @ 150mm (6") c/c into predrilled plywood - Vr = 5.21 kN/m. Design load is stored baled hay at 1.57 kN/m3 (10 lb/ft3). Support: a built-up plank beam on interior posts at 2440mm (8') or 3050mm (10') c/c, plus a 38x184x4880mm (2x8x16') continuous sill/header at the walls (2x10x16' on the 38' span).
plans.wall_framing: Two systems, both fully detailed, and both require an interior structural plywood shear skin. (A) Stud wall: 38x140mm (2x6) sill, top plates and studs. Sheets 3/4/5 note 15 give studs @ 610mm (24") c/c; Sheet 7 note 5 (the wind-bracing sheet, drawn for the 38' span) instead shows 2x6 studs @ 1220mm (48") c/c with 38x89mm (2x4) wall girts @ 610mm (24") c/c and two studs spaced 40mm (1 9/16") apart at each wall-brace location, all studs continuous sill to rafter except at door openings. Double 2x6 top plate with joints staggered at least 1800mm (6') and corners overlapped; 2x6 blocking fitted between studs and 2x4 blocking at mid-height; studs notched in way of the gambrel rafter and lag-screwed 3/8"x6" through girt and purlin into the stud. (B) Pole frame: 140x140mm (6x6) CCA PT poles @ 2440mm (8') c/c, 3660mm (12') long, on the concrete footings above, spiked with 203x8.23mm (8"x0.32") galvanized spikes into all four sides of the pole into a concrete anchor plug; 38x140mm (2x6) girts toe-nailed between poles @ 610mm (24") c/c; base band of 6-38x140x4880mm (2x6x16') PT T&G planking with ends staggered 2440mm (8') at poles and 2 spiral nails per plank per pole; 2x8x16' (or 2x10x16' on the 38' span) plate beams / joist header at the pole tops with joints staggered 8' at poles; an extra 89x140mm (4x6) pole at each sliding door jamb. Both systems: 9.5mm (3/8") unsanded sheathing softwood plywood on the INSIDE face, face grain horizontal (vertical in pole frame), all four edges nailed to framing or blocking with 64x3.25mm (2 1/2", 10ga.) galvanized commons at 150mm (6") c/c generally and 63-89mm (2 1/2"-3 1/2") at endwall shear walls per Table 1. Endwall diagonal brace: 2x6 between doubled studs at the top and doubled blocking at the bottom, nailed top and bottom with 8-127x4.88mm (5") spiral nails, 4 driven from each side and clinched to achieve double shear, with a 2x6 stiffener. Interior posts: steel HSS 102x102x3.2mm (HSS 4x4x0.125", 6.47 lb/ft) or 140x140mm (6x6) No.1 Northern grade PT poles - "DO NOT recut factory-treated bottom end". Framing lumber (other than PT) is No.1/No.2 S-P-F.
plans.wall_height: 3050mm (10') labelled on all three elevations as the sidewall/ground-floor height. Sections resolve this into 2446mm (8'-0 1/4") of studs (or pole above the sill) plus 610mm (2') of exposed concrete foundation/pole above grade.
plans.roof: Gambrel, built from site-erected braced-rafter "gambrel arch" frames at 610mm (24") c/c with a 305mm (12") overhang and 2x4 lookout rafters at 24" c/c at the gables. The frames themselves are NOT on this plan - you must obtain the companion plan for your span and load: 24' span M-9251 (light duty 2x4), M-9252 (medium duty 2x6), M-9253 (heavy duty 2x8); 30' span M-9254 (2x6), M-9255 (2x8), M-9256 (2x10); 38' span M-9260 (2x6), M-9261 (2x8), M-9262 (2x10). Covering: 0.34mm (29ga.) galvanized prepainted steel roofing, screw-fastened per the manufacturer, over 19x89mm (1x4) strapping @ 610mm (24") c/c. Each braced rafter lands on the loft sill in a single joist hanger selected by rafter size from Table 9 (2x10 - Simpson LB 28 top-flange or equal; 2x8 - Simpson JB 28 top-flange or equal; 2x6 and 2x4 - standard universal joist hanger with 2 tails hammer-bent down), with all holes nailed using 38x3.7mm (1 1/2") special concrete nails; rafters 2x6 and larger add a 38x450x1.21mm (1 1/2"x18"x18ga.) galvanized steel strap predrilled for four nails. Eave gets 50mm (2") continuous slot ventilation with a 12x12mm (1/2") galvanized hardware-cloth bird screen L-bent to 90 degrees. Sheet 1's WARNING requires all bridging and bracing to be installed as specified by the roof frame manufacturer. A cupola appears in the perspective sketch but is not detailed anywhere.
plans.siding: 0.34mm (29ga.) galvanized prepainted steel siding to ASTM-A-446 grade A, Z275 (G-90), profile "to be as intended for farm roofing/siding as appropriate", screw-fastened per the manufacturer, over 19x89mm (1x4) strapping @ 610mm (24") c/c. Behind that, the structural interior skin is 9.5mm (3/8") unsanded softwood sheathing plywood nailed on all four edges (this is the shear wall - not optional). The pole-frame version adds a base band of six 2x6x16' PT tongue-and-groove planks, rabbeted 9.5x50mm (3/8"x2") at the top plank to receive the plywood, nailed through planking and plywood into the bottom girt with 4" galvanized spirals @ 150mm (6") c/c. All nails exposed to weather, treated wood, concrete or soil must be hot-dip galvanized.
plans.loft: Full-footprint hayloft over the entire building, and its plywood floor IS the engineered wind diaphragm - it is not optional storage. Clear loft heights by span: 24' - 2440mm (8') to the collar line plus 1220mm (4') to the ridge; 30' - 2745mm (9') plus 1525mm (5'); 38' - 3660mm (12'-8") plus 1525mm (5'). Designed for stored baled hay at 1.57 kN/m3 (10 lb/ft3). Access as drawn: a sliding hayloft loading door, 1830x2440mm (6'x8') or 1525x2135mm (5'x7'), with a removable 2x6 guard rail across the doorway; plus a 550x900mm (22"x36") minimum emergency exit at each end with a panel easily removed from inside and a permanently attached exit ladder (rungs @ 305mm/12" c/c, 175mm/7" clear of the wall, terminating 1000-1500mm/39"-59" above outside grade). No interior stair is shown or dimensioned.
plans.doors: 3050x3050mm (10'x10') sliding doors at BOTH ends of the barn, per separate CPS plan 9341 ("designed for wind load and suitable for insulating"); an overhead garage door may be substituted. An access / emergency exit door at both ends, which must open outwards if installed in the sliding door (Sheet 2 shows a 762x2135mm / 30"x84" exit door option in the sliding door). Sliding hayloft loading door 1830x2440mm (6'x8') or 1525x2135mm (5'x7'). Loft emergency exit, minimum opening 550x900mm (22"x36"), removable panel from inside, both ends of barn, with permanently attached exit ladder. Pole frame gets an extra 89x140mm (4x6) pole at each sliding door jamb; stud frame gets a 38x184mm (2x8) side door jamb and 2x6 door head jamb beyond a doubled stud. Sheet 7 note 9 explicitly states jamb and head details are omitted from that sheet. Sheet 1 WARNING: the structure is designed assuming all doors are closed and remain intact in a severe wind.
plans.windows: not stated - no window schedule, sizes, counts, locations, headers or flashing details appear on any of the 10 sheets. The Sheet 1 perspective sketch shows five sidewall windows and loft-level louvres/openings, but none are dimensioned or detailed. Wall openings are your own design problem and would need checking against the shear-wall nailing schedules.
plans.overall_height: Not stated as a single figure anywhere in the set. Components given: 3050mm (10') sidewall height on the elevations, resolved in section as 610mm (2') exposed foundation/pole above grade plus 2446mm (8'-0 1/4") of stud/pole; then the loft interior at 2440mm (8') plus 1220mm (4') to the ridge on the 24' span, 2745mm (9') plus 1525mm (5') on the 30', and 3660mm (12'-8") plus 1525mm (5') on the 38'. Summing the 24' span components gives roughly 6.9-7.0 m (about 22'-23') to the ridge above grade, but that is my arithmetic, not a plan dimension. Filed under unknowns.
plans.skill_level: Advanced / experienced builder or small contractor crew, not a first-time shed builder. The work spans formed and reinforced cast-in-place concrete (or drilled pole footings plus concrete infill between endwall poles), setting and plumbing 6x6 PT poles or framing a two-storey stud wall, assembling a 4-to-6-ply built-up plank beam with plywood splice plates on steel HSS or 6x6 columns with a welded 1/4" steel column capital, erecting gambrel braced-rafter frames at height, a strictly-specified plywood diaphragm floor and shear-wall nailing schedule where fastener spacing is structural, and screw-down metric-gauge steel cladding. There is welding in the details (column capital, steel strap anchors welded to rebar). You must also do your own quantity take-off and your own metric-to-imperial conversion, and you must independently source the roof frame and door plans. The 24 ft minimum width and two-storey height also mean staging, lifting equipment and at least a small crew.
plans.materials_list_available: free-on-page, but specifications only - Sheet 1's MATERIALS box plus roughly 25 keyed notes per detail sheet give every member size, grade, spacing and fastener, so a complete take-off is derivable. There is NO quantity list, board count or cut list anywhere in the 10 sheets.
plans.permit_notes: Sheet 1 APPLICATION note: the plan conforms to the National Farm Building Code of Canada 1995 - a farm-building code, with lower requirements than a code for human occupancy - and the user must verify the stated design criteria meet all local design conditions, building regulations and special requirements, and is responsible for making all required changes. Footing selection is keyed to National Building Code of Canada 1995 Section 2.5 climatic data (max ground snow + rain, kPa) and wind selection to 1/10 hourly wind force q in kPa; the worked example uses q = 0.36 kPa for London, Ontario. Drawings are dated Jan. 2000 with the REVISED field blank, are labelled "NO SCALE", and the archived copy carries no signed or sealed engineer's stamp even though the engineering firm is named in the border. Practical read: this is credible engineering to reference and copy details from, but it is 26-year-old Canadian farm-building code work in metric, and a US (or current Canadian) building department will require re-engineering, current climatic loads and a locally licensed stamp before issuing a permit - especially if you intend habitable or commercial use rather than agricultural. Also note the endwall shear-wall anchorage and diaphragm nailing are the whole basis of the wind design, so any substitution there voids it.
other_sizes: Building width 7320mm (24') - Sheet 3 details, bays 12'+12', roof frames M-9251/9252/9253
Building width 9150mm (30') - Sheet 4 details, bays 10'+10'+10', roof frames M-9254/9255/9256
Building width 11590mm (38') - Sheet 5 details, bays 13'+12'+13', roof frames M-9260/9261/9262

Length: any multiple of 2440mm (8') up to the Table 1 maximum. At q = 0.35 kPa, schedule A allows 14.64m (48') on the 24' width, 17.08m (56') on 30', 19.52m (64') on 38'; schedule B allows 31.72m (104'), 36.60m (120') and 41.48m (136') respectively

_verification.notes:
Adversarial check of every verifiable field. Source: /tmp/8315.pdf (1,085,911 bytes, 10 pages) read visually page by page - the PDF has essentially no text layer (pdftotext yields 293 bytes total), so all verification was done by rendering at 200-500 dpi with pdftoppm and reading crops.

WHAT CHECKED OUT (a lot of this record is unusually accurate):
- Page/sheet count: 10, and every sheet's title block reads "SHEET n OF 10". Confirmed.
- Title block: PLAN 8315, "Gambrel Roof Barn", DATE JAN. 2000, DESIGNED JET, DRAWN JBA, CHECKED BEM, SCALE NO SCALE, Argue & Associates Consulting Engineers, Guelph - Canada. All confirmed.
- Sheet titles verbatim: 2 "Foundation Plans", 3 "24-ft. Span Details", 4 "30-ft. Span Details", 5 "38-ft. Span Details", 6 "Endwall and Beam Details", 7 "Wind Bracing Details", 8 "Sidewall, Floor and Gambrel Arch Anchorage Details", 9 "Diaphragm Wind Bracing Selection". All exact. (Sheet 10's title block also reads "Diaphragm Wind Bracing Selection"; the record described sheet 10 by content instead, which is fine, and its quoted "Maximum Diaphragm Floor Length" and "Diaphragm Wind Bracing - Selection by Example" are both verbatim.)
- Keyed-note counts: Sheet 1 = 14, Sheet 3 = 25, Sheet 6 = 25. All correct.
- Spans 7320 (24'), 9150 (30'), 11590 (38') confirmed on sheets 1 and 2.
- Quoted length rule verbatim on Sheet 2 note 4: "Length in multiples of 2440mm (8') up to maximum length L, based on limits of diaphragm upper floor to resist wind, see Table 1, Sheet 10".
- Snow+rain footing tables all three correct: 24' = 2.46/5.83/8.98 kPa; 30' = 3.36/5.34/8.33; 38' = 1.65/2.72/4.39. 24' round footings 510 (20") / 600 (24") / 670 (26"). Soil note verbatim: "footing sizes based on soil bearing strength 120 kPa (2500 psf); where soil tests reveal stronger or weaker soil, footing areas may be adjusted accordingly". 120 kPa = 2506 psf, so the record's parenthetical is right.
- Factored shears verbatim on Sheet 9: "Fastening Schedule A - factored shear Vr = 2.56 kN/m" and "Fastening Schedule B - factored shear Vr = 5.21 kN/m".
- Table 1 at 0.35 kPa, spot-checked cell by cell: schedule A = 14.64 m (48') at 24', 17.08 m (56') at 30', 19.52 m (64') at 38'; schedule B = 31.72 m (104') / 36.60 m (120') / 41.48 m (136'). Record's numbers are exactly right. Wind range 0.20-0.65 kPa confirmed. Anchor bolt counts (8/7/5 sched A, 16/13/10 sched B), bolt spacings and nail spacings to plywood and blocking are all present as claimed.
- Worked example verbatim: "To build a 2-story gambrel roof barn 11.59 x 29.28m (38' x 96') at London, Ontario", Steps 1-8. Confirmed 8 steps.
- Cross-referenced plan numbers confirmed both ways: Sheet 1 notes 10-12 say "see CPS plans 9251, 9252 or 9253" / "9254, 9255 or 9256" / "9260, 9261 or 9262"; Sheets 3/4/5 note 11 use the "M-" prefix (M-9251 ... M-9262). Sliding doors "see CPS plan 9341" confirmed on Sheet 1 notes 4, 6, 7.
- Sheet 6 details verbatim: note 24 "Column capital, cut and weld from 6.35mm (1/4\") steel flat bar", note 10 "Plywood splice plate 19x300mm (3/4\"x12\")", note 22 "200mm (8\") concrete infill placed between endwall poles", note 4 steel HSS 102x102x3.2 or wood 140x140 (6x6).
- Sheet 7 details verbatim: NOTE 1 "This sheet illustrates the 11590mm (38') span, with details engineered for 1/10 hourly wind force q = 0.6 kPa"; note 13 clinched "(to achieve double shear)"; note 16 "1.21x114x457mm (18ga. x 4 1/2\" x 18\") galvanized steel stud anchor"; note 18 "38x140mm (2x6) removable guard rail across doorway".
- Sheet 8: Table 7 is nail spacing by braced rafter size (100/150/200/300 mm for 2x10/2x8/2x6/2x4) and Table 9 is joist hanger requirement by braced rafter size (Simpson LB 28 / JB 28 "Top Flange" or equal). Both as described.
- Cladding: "0.34mm (29ga.) galvanized prepainted steel roofing/siding" - the record's "29ga. prepainted steel" is right.
- Code conformance verbatim: "This plan conforms to the requirements of the National Farm Building Code of Canada 1995."
- Completeness honesty: verified there is no bill of materials, no cut list, no window schedule (elevations show no windows at all - only the perspective sketch does), no interior floor plan, and no ground-floor slab detail (the cross-sections show a granular fill floor only). The record's "NOT a standalone buildable set" caveat about the roof frames being separate plans is accurate and important - without CPS 9251-9262 you cannot frame the roof at all.

DIMENSION NUANCE (verified, no correction needed): the "3050mm (10') ground-floor wall height" is real but is floor-to-loft, not framed wall height. Sheet 1 elevations dimension 3050 (10'); Sheet 3/6 details resolve it as 2446mm (8'-0 1/4") of 2x6 stud wall sitting on 610mm (2') of exposed 203mm (8") concrete foundation above the interior granular floor (2446 + 610 = 3056). Pole-frame version uses 6x6 poles 3660mm (12') long, embedded 610mm. So a builder gets ~10' clear to the loft joists but only 8' of stud wall - worth stating explicitly rather than letting "10' wall" imply 10' of framing.

PRICE: correct as "Free" / 0. No price, currency string, order form or fee appears anywhere in the 10 sheets (the only "$n" hits in the file are binary-stream artifacts, not text). It is a freely downloadable government-published PDF, so "Free" is the honest value and no number was invented.

IMAGE: /home/ethan/woodshed/assets/img/cps-8315-24x16-gambrel-barn.jpg is a real JPEG, 1000x594, grayscale, 132,497 bytes, and is a genuine crop of the Sheet 1 perspective sketch of this exact barn (cupola, gambrel roof, cutaway hayloft with baled hay, sidewall windows, gravel splashpad). No fix needed.

sqft arithmetic: 24 x 16 = 384. Correct.

corrections.reported: each drawing shows the pole-frame option on one side and the stud-wall/steel-interior-post option on the other
corrections.correct: the 30' and 38' plans show the stud wall / steel interior post option on the left side and the pole frame / wood interior post option on the right; the 24' plan shows pole frame with wood interior posts @ 3050mm (10') c/c on BOTH sides
corrections.evidence: Sheet 2 note 1 (read at 400 dpi): "7320mm (24') foundation plan; both sides show optional pole frame wall exterior and wood interior posts @ 3050mm (10') c/c". Only notes 2 and 3 (30' and 38' spans) say "left side shows optional stud wall exterior and steel interior posts @ 3050mm (10') c/c; right side shows optional pole frame wall exterior and wood interior posts @ 2440mm (8') c/c". This matters because 24' is the exact span the record recommends - the stud-wall/steel-post layout is never drawn in plan for it.

corrections.reported: length in 8 ft increments up to 136' in the best case
corrections.correct: length in 8 ft increments up to 232' in the best case
corrections.evidence: Table 1, Sheet 10 ("Maximum Diaphragm Floor Length, m (ft)"): the largest entry is 70.76 m (232') for 11.59 m (38') building width, floor fastening schedule "B", at 1/10 hourly wind force 0.20 kPa. 136' (41.48 m) is only the 38'/schedule-B value at 0.35 kPa - which the record correctly cites in footprint_note but then wrongly recycles as the absolute best case in pros.

corrections.reported: 2x8x14' at 24" c/c overlapped 4' on the 24' span
corrections.correct: 2x10x14' at 24" c/c per Sheet 2 note 9, which conflicts with Sheet 3 note 8's 2x8x14' - the plan contradicts itself on the 24' span joist depth
corrections.evidence: Sheet 3 note 8 does read "Floor joists 38x184x4270mm (2x8x14') @ 610mm (24") c/c overlapped 1220mm (4') at (7)... bridging at midspan", so the record quoted a real line. But Sheet 2 note 9, keyed to the 24' foundation plan, reads "Floor joists above, 38x235x4270mm (2x10x14') @ 610mm (24") c/c" (verified at 400 dpi). The 2x10 is the credible one: the 24' cross-section on Sheet 3 is 3660 (12') + 3660 (12') about a single centre beam, so clear span is ~12'-0", and Sheet 3 note 10 loads the loft with baled hay at 1.57 kN/m3 (10 lb/ft3) - roughly 80 psf over an 8' stack. A 2x8 No.1/No.2 S-P-F at 24" o.c. over 12'-0" at that load is grossly overstressed, and the 30' span sheet uses the same 2x8 for only a 10'-0" span. Presenting 2x8 as the engineered answer without flagging the conflict is the one claim in this record a builder could get hurt by.

unsupported_claims: summary: "sealed-office work by Argue & Associates Consulting Engineers" - no P.Eng seal, stamp or signature appears on any of the 10 sheets. The title block on every sheet has DESIGNED JET / DRAWN JBA / CHECKED BEM and a blank APPROVED column, and the firm name appears only as unstamped marginal text "Argue & Associates Consulting Engineers, Guelph - Canada". The set is engineer-authored but not sealed; calling it sealed overstates its permit standing.

footprint_note: "24x16 ... is therefore the smallest legal build and the only configuration that lands in the user's 240-480 sq ft target" - both halves are wrong on the plan's own parametrics. Length is "in multiples of 2440mm (8')", so 24'x8' (192 sq ft) is the smallest legal length, not 16'. And 30'x8' (240 sq ft), 38'x8' (304 sq ft) and 30'x16' (480 sq ft) all land inside the stated 240-480 sq ft window, so 24x16 is not the only in-target configuration.

vendor: "distributed by the Ontario Ministry of Agriculture, Food and Rural Affairs" - OMAFRA is nowhere on the document. The only attribution in the sheet margins is "Funding for this project has been provided under the Canada-Ontario Agreement for the Ice Storm Recovery Assistance Program, Annex A; Assistance for the Agricultural Sector and Rural Communities in Eastern Ontario. This program is jointly funded by the Government of Canada and Government of Ontario." The gov.on.ca host makes OMAFRA plausible but it is an outside inference, not sourced from the plan.

plans.name: 16x24 Gambrel Shed Plans (shed16x24-GB)
plans.http_status: 200 for BOTH forms. The .html URL 301-redirects (correctly) and serves the identical 16x24 gambrel page; no mis-cached foreign product content is reproducible.
plans.style: gambrel-barn (multi-pitch barn roof with storage loft)
plans.price: $59.99 emailed PDF / $65.99 postal mailed
plans.format: instant PDF download (emailed at purchase, 8.5x11 sheets) or postal-mailed prints of the identical 8.5x11 sheets for $6 more. Free How To Build A Shed eBook bundled. Materials list PDF is free on the page without buying.
plans.page_count: not stated; site says a typical set is ~13 sheets and that gambrel designs get extra sheets for roof and loft framing details
plans.foundation: Two options included: treated 4x6 wood skids on gravel (6 skids at 12 ft), or concrete slab. Slab detail is shown without a deep frost footing. On skids the floor sits about 1 ft 1.5 in above grade; a slab build is roughly 12 in lower overall.
plans.floor_framing: 2x6 joists at 16 in on center, 3/4 in T&G OSB, 50 psf floor load. List: 19 ea 2x6 at 16 ft joists, 3 ea 2x6 rim, 12 sheets OSB, 20 Simpson A23 clips.
plans.wall_framing: 2x4 at 16 in on center with double top plate, "just like a home is framed". 80 studs at 92-5/8 in, 2x6 headers, optional 2x12 header for the side door.
plans.wall_height: 8 ft 1 in
plans.overall_height: 17 ft 11 in from grade on skids (16 ft 9.5 in from the floor deck); about 12 in lower on a slab. From the site Gambrel Shed Heights section drawing, not the product page.
plans.roof: Gambrel, site-built gusseted trusses (2x6 upper and lower top chords, 2x4 collar tie, 2x4 post, 2x10 bottom chord at 16 ft doubling as loft joist, OSB gussets, 22 Simpson H2.5 ties). 13 trusses over 24 ft = 24 in on center. 7/16 in OSB sheathing; 12 in overhang front and back, 6 in sides. Pitch per the site heights drawing: 7:12 upper, 12:7 lower. Explicitly NOT engineered - the page tells you to hire a structural engineer to size the roof members and connections.
plans.siding: Textured plywood siding with 1-1/2 in battens at 12 in on center (board and batten look); 28 sheets of 4x8x1/2 in plus 100 ea 1x2 battens. Cedar shingles or horizontal lap siding may be substituted.
plans.windows: 5 ea 2626 windows (2 ft 6 in x 2 ft 6 in), a stock size orderable from any window company; 3 on one long wall, 2 on the other per the floor plan. Plus 2 ea 12x18 gable vents.
plans.doors: Double doors making a 6 ft 0 in x 6 ft 8 in opening on the 16 ft end wall (two 3068 leaves) plus one 3 ft 0 in x 6 ft 8 in single door on a long wall. Build your own with the included door plans or buy factory pre-hung.
plans.loft: Yes. The page claims "The multi pitched roof adds 300 sf. of useable loft area inside the shed." The heights drawing shows 9 ft 9 in clear width at 6 ft 3 in headroom under the collar beam. Caveat: the free materials list includes only 7 sheets of 3/4 in T&G OSB for the loft deck (about 224 sq ft), so the stock loft is a partial deck, not full 16x24 coverage - a customer build blog confirms he "extended the 2nd story floor the entire length" as a modification. No stair or ladder is shown in the materials list; loft access detail not stated.
plans.skill_level: No explicit rating. Vendor markets plans as suitable for "both an old pro or a first time framer", with cut lengths and placement for every board plus a How To Build A Shed manual. Realistically intermediate: 16 ft clear-span site-built gambrel trusses, a 384 sq ft floor and loft framing are a big step up from a small gable shed.
plans.permit_notes: Drawn to IRC prescriptive-code practice and "regularly used to apply for building permits", but with NO engineer stamp — the site is explicit: "Do the plans have engineering? No, the plans do not come with an engineers stamp." High snow/wind/seismic areas need a locally licensed engineer to review and stamp. Site notes IBC 105.2 exempts detached accessory structures under 120 sq ft, so at 384 sq ft a permit is almost certainly required. The vendor also warns on its garage-plans page that "The Larger Sheds are in a grey area of information between a house and a shed", and that its separate garage plans carry extra content (braced wall panels, hold-downs, full footing/stem-wall plans, electrical) that some departments demand at this size. No snow-load or wind-load rating is stated on this plan page.
plans.materials_list_available: free-on-page (verified - downloaded the 1-page PDF without purchase)
plans.refund_policy: No refunds: "Due to the electronic nature of our product we do not offer refunds." Free plan examples and the free materials list are offered to help you decide pre-purchase. Second set of plans at half price by emailing after the first purchase.
plans.est_material_cost: not stated for this plan. Site FAQ gives a general "around $10.00 per square foot for a basic shed" (about $3,800 at 384 sq ft) and customer-reported figures of $2,400 for a 12x16 gambrel with loft and $3,000 for a 12x20 gambrel with loft, Spring 2016.
plans.summary: iCreatables' largest gambrel barn shed: a 16x24 (384 sq ft) board-and-batten barn with 8 ft 1 in walls, a 6 ft 3 in-headroom storage loft under a two-slope gambrel roof, 5 stock 2626 windows, a 6 ft double door on the gable end and a 3 ft man door on the side. Delivered as instant-download 8.5x11 PDFs ($59.99) or mailed prints ($65.99), with two foundations (treated 4x6 skids or a concrete slab), a complete numbered materials list, home-built door plans and a bundled how-to-build eBook. The standout feature for shoppers is that the full materials list is a free PDF download on the page, so you can price the build at a lumberyard before spending a dime. The standout risk is the roof: the page itself says the 16 ft span gambrel truss is large enough that you should hire a local structural engineer to size the members and connections, and the plans carry no engineer stamp.

Wall framing plans with door and window opening framing

Door plans for building your own doors, or dimensions for factory pre-hung units
Free How To Build A Shed eBook/manual with every purchase
Companion how-to video on framing the gambrel rafter/truss for this specific 16x24 plan
pros: Free, genuinely complete materials list downloadable without purchase - you can get a real lumberyard bid before buying the $59.99 plan
384 sq ft with a 6 ft 3 in-headroom, 9 ft 9 in-wide loft is a lot of usable volume for the money; the gambrel gets loft space that a gable shed of the same footprint cannot
Residential framing standards throughout (2x4 at 16 in on center, double top plate, 50 psf floor) so it will read as code-compliant to a plans examiner
Two foundation options in one plan set: cheap treated 4x6 skids for a moveable shed, or a slab if you want a permanent floor
Two door openings including a 6 ft double door on the gable end - wide enough for a mower, ATV or garden tractor

plans.footprint_note: 240 sq ft of floor plus a partial 12 ft loft. Skids and rim joists are cut 240" (20'-0") and floor joists 141" (12'-0" overall with rim joists), so 12x20 is the exact framed footprint. The gambrel roof adds overhangs on all four sides, so the roof outline is larger than 12x20.
plans.style: Gambrel / barn-style shed with 8 ft walls, loft joists, double front doors, one side man-door and a side window
plans.price: Free (all three parts published in full on the site). An optional "PREMIUM PLANS" PDF of the same design is sold on Gumroad for $9.99.
plans.summary: A free, fully published 3-part DIY plan for a 12x20 (240 sq ft) gambrel/barn shed from MyOutdoorPlans: Part 1 covers the skid foundation, floor, four wall frames and T1-11 siding; Part 2 covers the eleven gambrel trusses, gable end panels, front/back overhangs, 3/4" roof sheathing and shingles; Part 3 covers the double front doors, a 32"x80" side door and all 1x4 trim. Each part carries its own complete cut list and shopping list plus 15-18 labeled 3D diagrams, so the free version is genuinely buildable end-to-end rather than a teaser. Framing is 2x4 studs at 24" on center on 2x8 floor joists over four 4x4 skids, with 2x4 trusses gusseted with 1/2" plywood at 24" on center. Nothing is engineer-stamped and no dimensioned elevation with an overall height is published, so it is a hobbyist plan set, not a permit package.
includes: Part 1 (this page): floor/skid framing, all four wall frames, T1-11 siding, with cut list + shopping list
Part 2 (12x20-gambrel-shed-roof-plans): gambrel truss layout, 1/2" plywood gussets, gable end panels, front/back overhangs, roof sheathing, trims, shingles
Part 3 (12x20-gambrel-shed-doors-plans): door jambs, double front doors, side door, and all exterior 1x4 trim
Per-part 'Cut & Shopping Lists' with lettered components (A through R) keyed to the diagrams
Roughly 15-18 labeled 3D diagrams per part (~49 total) plus side/front/back rendered views
Tools list and time estimate on each part
Loft joists (6 pcs 2x8 at 144") included in the Part 1 cut list
Optional paid PDF version ($9.99, Gumroad) adding cut-layout diagrams, color-coded parts and a cost estimate
pros: Truly free and truly complete: floor, walls, roof and doors are all published, each with its own cut and shopping list - no gate, no upsell required to build it
Cut lists are given as exact piece counts and lengths (e.g. '16 pieces of 2x8 - 141" long'), so you can price and buy lumber directly from the page
Skid-on-grade foundation (four 4x4 skids, 240" long) means no concrete work - the cheapest and fastest foundation for a 240 sq ft building
Gambrel roof buys real headroom over the 12 ft width and the plan already includes 2x8 loft joists, so the usable storage volume is much larger than a gable shed of the same footprint
24" on-center studs and T1-11 sheet siding keep the material count and labor low; the whole shell is 8 ft studs and full 4x8 sheets with little ripping
Only basic tools are needed - miter saw, drill, hammer, level - and the only tricky cut is the repeated 22.5 degree rafter end and birdsmouth
Buildable in the ~240-480 sq ft target range; author's time estimate is one week for the shell and roof plus one day for doors
Reader comments on the pages are answered by the author and surface real errata (e.g. the roofing quantity), which is more transparency than most free plan sites offer
cons: Trusses are NOT engineered. A reader asked directly whether the roof is engineered or rated for a 47 psf ground snow load and the author replied 'That is all there is.' If your county requires stamped trusses (common for >12 ft spans), you cannot use this roof as drawn.

No overall building height, no roof pitch/rise dimension and no dimensioned elevation drawings are published - you cannot check it against a height limit or fill out a permit application from the free pages.

The 12 ft loft joists are only 6 pieces of 2x8 over a 20 ft length (~48" on center) spanning the full 12 ft unsupported. That is far outside normal residential span/spacing practice; treat the loft as light storage only or re-size it yourself.

Studs at 24" on center is the minimum for an 8 ft wall carrying a gambrel roof, and the plan omits any wind/uplift hold-down detail beyond 'rafter ties' from frame to skid - marginal in high-wind or heavy-snow areas.

The material lists contain acknowledged inconsistencies: Part 2 lists 450 sq ft of tar paper/shingles in one place and 250 sq ft in another (author confirmed 450 is correct), and Part 3 still repeats a stray '250 sq ft of tar paper/asphalt shingles' line that does not belong to the door work. Verify quantities before ordering.

3/4" plywood is specified for both the floor AND the roof deck (13 sheets on the roof). That is much heavier and more expensive than the 7/16"-1/2" normally used on a shed roof and is a real cost driver - roughly 21 sheets of 3/4" total.
Skids on a merely 'leveled surface' with no gravel pad, footing depth or frost detail specified; on soft or sloping ground you will have to design the base yourself.

The paid PDF describes a somewhat different building than the free pages (16" on-center studs, 'double 8 ft front doors', a 4'x4' side window), so the free and premium versions are not identical - don't mix the two lists.
No cost estimate, no window schedule and no hardware list (hinge/latch sizes) on the free pages.
The site is behind Cloudflare and 403s automated fetches, so archiving or offline reading requires the Wayback Machine.

plans.build_time: Author's stated Time field: "One week" for Part 1 (floor/walls) and "One week" for Part 2 (roof), plus "One day" for Part 3 (doors & trims). The boilerplate intro paragraph also claims "you could get the job done in about a day," which contradicts the Time fields - budget the one-to-two-week figure.
plans.skill_level: Intermediate DIY. Not stated on the page; inferred from the work involved - building and standing four 8 ft walls, cutting 11 gambrel trusses with repeated 22.5 degree angles and birdsmouths, and working on a roof. Only common tools are required (miter saw, drill, hammer, level), no shop machinery.
plans.permit_notes: The plan repeatedly tells you to check local codes ("You need to read the local codes so you make sure the plans you are going to use comply with the legal requirements" and "you have to comply with a few legal regulations"), and the Gumroad listing states "It is your responsibility to make adjustments to the plans, to comply with your local building codes" with a liability disclaimer. Critically, the trusses are NOT engineered: a commenter asked whether the roof was engineered or rated for 47 psf ground snow load in order to get a county permit and the author answered "That is all there is." Another commenter notes many counties only demand engineered trusses above a 12 ft span, and warns that a gambrel's larger surface area can make the wind rating the limiting factor. There are no load ratings, no stamped drawings, no overall height and no foundation/frost detail, so expect to have an engineer review or re-detail the roof if your jurisdiction requires it for a 240 sq ft accessory building.

quotes: This step by step diy project is about 12x20 gambrel shed plans. I have designed this large storage shed with a gambrel roof, so you can organize your tools. Furthermore, if you want to set up a small hobby workshop, this project might suit your needs and be friendly with your pocket.
Smart Tip: You need to read the local codes so you make sure the plans you are going to use comply with the legal requirements.

Use 2x4 lumber for the rest of the components (plates and studs). Drill pilot holes through the plates and insert 3 1/2" screws into the studs. Place the studs every 24" on center and make sure the corners are square. You can adjust the size of the window and door openings to suit your needs.

The first step of the shed roof project is to build the rafters for the trusses. In order to get a professional result, you need to use a miter saw and to make 22.5 degree cuts to both ends of the beams. AS you can notice in the diagram, you also need to make birdsmouth cuts to the rafters that go on the top of the side walls.
Lay the rafters on a level surface. You can make a simple jog so you speed up the process. Use 1/2" plywood for the gussets and follow the instructions in the diagram for a professional result.
Fit the trusses to the top of the shed frame, placing them every 24" on center. Plumb the trusses with a spirit level and then secure them into place with rafter ties.

This large barn shed is ideal for a large property, as you can not only store a lot of items, but you can also use it as a workshop. Moreover, you can build a simple loft to the shed, so you can enhance the storage space even more.

WHAT HELD UP (verified verbatim against Wayback captures of all three parts):
- Price: CONFIRMED character-for-character. Free pages carry no price; the Get-PDF-Plans button links to myoutdoorplans.gumroad.com/l/yshbq whose ld+json says "price":9.99, "priceCurrency":"USD". price_usd 0 for the free plan is right.
- Footprint / sqft: 12x20 = 240 sq ft, arithmetic checks. A - 4 pcs 4x4 @240in SKIDS; B - 2 pcs 2x8 @240in + 16 pcs @141in FLOOR FRAME (141 + 2x1.5 rim = 144in = 12ft). Footprint note is accurate, including "overhangs to the front, back and on the sides" (verbatim on Part 2).
- Wall height: derivation is sound and honestly flagged as derived. Studs 91 1/2in (confirmed in cut list D/E/F/G and in the dimensioned side-wall diagram) + 3 plates (G = 2 pcs @240in + 1 pc @233in) = 96in = 8ft. The page never prints "8 ft".
- Overall height and roof pitch/rise: genuinely NOT published - correctly reported as unknown. I read Gambrel-rafters-12-ft.png (rafters 60in, cut angle labeled "67.5 degrees" in the drawing while the text says "22.5 degree cuts") and Gussets.jpg (only gusset sizes: 29in base, 14 1/2in, 6in, 3 3/4in). No truss height, no rise, no elevation.
- 11 trusses: CONFIRMED - Part 2 cut list "I – 4 pieces of 2×4 lumber – 60″ long 11xTRUSS", and 11 trusses at 24in o.c. over 240in is internally consistent.
- 3/4in plywood everywhere: CONFIRMED and a good catch. Part 1 shopping list "8 pieces of 3/4″ plywood – 4'x8'" (floor), Part 2 "13 pieces of 3/4″ plywood – 4'x8'" (roof) = ~21 sheets. 1/2in plywood gussets confirmed.
- Doors: front M = "2xDOOR", two 36in leaves with T1-11 36in x 87 1/2in; side O = T1-11 32in x 80in. Both confirmed. Side door + one window + double front doors also visible in the local hero image.
- 24in o.c. studs confirmed in prose ("Place the studs every 24″ on center") and by the 22 1/2in clear spacing in the diagram.
- Engineering sanity: the floor is fine and the record does not misstate it - 141in 2x8 joists span crosswise over four 240in skids spaced ~48in apart, so unsupported spans are ~4ft. The loft con is directionally correct (2x8 @144in clear span, no interior support). 450 sq ft of roofing is consistent with 13 sheets (416 sq ft) of deck.
- Completeness: the record is broadly honest that all three parts are free and buildable - each part really does carry its own Cut/Shopping list, Tools and Time. Two completeness gaps it misses: (a) the loft has cut-list lumber but zero installation steps or diagrams; (b) cut-list letters collide across parts - Part 1 uses H = LOFT JOISTS and I = SIDING, while Part 2 reuses H = SIDING and I = TRUSS/OVERHANG, and Q is never used, so "A through R" is not a clean sequence. Also Part 1 item I totals 16 T1-11 sheets while its own shopping list says 15.

plans.summary: A $6, 33-page PDF plan set for a 320 sq ft stick-built gable shed by HowToSpecialist, sold on the author's Gumroad storefront. The design is a plain 16x20 rectangle: 4x4 skids on compacted gravel, a 2x6 floor frame with a 3/4" plywood deck, 2x4 walls at 24" on center with 91 1/2" studs (about 8 ft walls), T1-11 5/8" siding, and eleven site-built 2x6 trusses at 24" o.c. with 1/2" plywood gussets that clear-span the full 16 ft so the floor is completely open. It has a roughly 6 ft wide double door under a doubled 2x6 header and two 36"x36" windows in one side wall. Crucially, the identical design is published free in three parts on howtospecialist.com (frame / gable roof / double doors) with the complete cut and shopping lists, so the $6 buys a consolidated, printable PDF rather than information you cannot otherwise get.

plans.foundation: Five 4x4 skids about 240" (20 ft) long, running the 20 ft length of the building and spaced roughly 44" apart across the 16 ft width (45 3/4" / 43 3/4" / 43 1/2" / 43 3/4"), set on a thoroughly leveled and compacted thick gravel bed; the floor frame is toenailed to the skids or locked down with rafter ties. No piers, footings, anchoring to concrete, or frost-depth detail is given.
plans.floor_framing: 2x6 floor frame — 2 rim joists 240" long plus 16 joists at 189", spaced 16" on center (14 1/2" clear) — decked with 3/4" plywood (8 sheets 48"x96" plus 4 pieces 48"x48"), screwed with 1 5/8" screws every 8" along the joists. Text says joists may be cut "from 2x6 or 2x8 lumber."
plans.wall_framing: 2x4 studs at 24" on center, studs cut 91 1/2" long; single bottom plate and double top plate; doubled 2x6 headers with 1/2" plywood sandwiched between the beams over the door and window openings. Walls are assembled flat on the finished deck, tilted up, plumbed, braced diagonally, then screwed to the deck and to each other with 3 1/2" screws.
plans.wall_height: Approximately 8 ft (2x4 studs cut 91 1/2" + 1 1/2" bottom plate + 3" double top plate = 96"). Not stated as a dimension anywhere in the text.
plans.roof: Gable roof built from 11 site-built trusses at 24" on center: 22 top-chord rafters of 2x6 at 130" and 11 bottom chords of 2x6 at 185", with 2x4 web supports (4 @ 7 1/4", 22 @ 21 1/4", 4 @ 35", 18 @ 48") and 1/2" plywood gussets screwed on with 1 5/8" screws; trusses fastened down with rafter ties. Separate 2x6 overhang ladders (8 rafters at 130" plus 36 blockings at 8") at the front and back. Sheathing is 3/4" plywood, 16 4x8-sheet equivalents. Rafters get 30-degree cuts at both ends plus birdsmouth cuts — the pitch is never given as a fraction (30 degrees works out near 7/12). Covering: 500 sq ft tar paper with 2" overlaps, drip edge, then 500 sq ft asphalt shingles. 1x8 fascia/roof trims (2 @ 263 1/4", 4 @ 132").
plans.siding: T1-11 5/8" plywood siding: 18 sheets at 48"x96" for the four walls, plus 4 pieces 32"x48" and 4 pieces 48"x59 3/4" for the gable ends. Nailed with 6-8d nails every 8" along framing. 1x4 trim (4 @ 94", 2 @ 192", 4 @ 93 3/4") plus 1x8 roof trims.
plans.doors: Double front doors. Each leaf is a 2x4 frame (two 36" rails, two 80 1/2" stiles, one 29" mid-rail) assembled with pocket holes and 2 1/2" screws, panelled with a 36"x77 1/2" piece of T1-11 and 2" brad nails. Opening is framed with 2x4 jambs (2 @ 87 1/2", 1 @ 79") under a doubled 2x6 header cut 75" long — roughly a 6 ft wide x 6'-8" tall opening. Hardware called out only as "shed hinges & latch" plus handles; no specific model or schedule.
plans.windows: Two 36" x 36" rough openings framed in one side wall (headers from 8 pieces of 2x6 at 39", plus 32 1/2" cripples, 36" and 12" blocking). Only that one side wall gets windows; the opposite side wall and the back wall are blank. The window units themselves are not specified, sized as products, or included in the shopping list, and no flashing detail is given.

pros: $6 for a 33-page PDF with a complete cut list, shopping list and tool list is about as cheap as a full 320 sq ft plan set gets.

Zero-risk evaluation: the entire design, including every material quantity, is published free in three parts on howtospecialist.com, so you can read all the steps and confirm the plan suits you before paying.
Site-built 2x6 trusses at 24" o.c. clear-span the full 16 ft width — no interior posts, so all 320 sq ft of floor is usable and the layout is free.

Genuinely simple stick framing: a plain rectangle, 2x4 walls at 24" o.c. built flat on the deck and tilted up, with no compound angles apart from the truss cuts. Realistic for a first large build with a helper.
3/4" plywood floor deck on 2x6 joists is noticeably beefier than the 1/2"-5/8" decks in many budget shed plans, and 3/4" roof sheathing is heavy-duty for a shed.
Well-lit and accessible for the size: a roughly 6 ft wide double door under a doubled 2x6 header plus two 36"x36" windows, so it works as a workshop rather than just storage.
Skid-on-gravel foundation means no concrete, no excavation and no inspector-visible footings — cheapest and fastest possible base if your site and jurisdiction allow it.
Materials are all commodity stock (2x4, 2x6, 4x4, 3/4" ply, T1-11), so no specialty orders and easy price shopping.
cons: The trusses are NOT engineered or stamped — they are shop-built 2x6 chords with 1/2" plywood gussets and 2x4 webs, with no load rating, gusset size/nailing schedule, or truss design drawing. In any snow-load region or plan-review jurisdiction you will likely be told to hire an engineer or buy manufactured trusses.

Foundation is only five 4x4 skids on compacted gravel with no piers, footings, anchors, or frost-depth detail. Spread across the 20 ft length that is roughly 5 ft between skids under a 320 sq ft building — an on-grade solution that most permit offices will not accept at this size, and one that offers no uplift or frost resistance.
Floor joist on-center spacing is never stated (16 joists over the length implies roughly 16" o.c., but you have to infer it), and no skid-to-joist span relationship is given.

Roof pitch is never expressed as a fraction — only "30 degree cuts" — so you cannot check asphalt shingle minimum-pitch requirements or compute overall height without scaling the drawings. Overall height is nowhere in the text.

Cut list and shopping list contradict each other in places: the 4x4 skids are cut at 192" (16 ft) but the shopping list says buy five 20-footers; the floor frame cut list wants 2 pieces at 192" while the shopping list buys 2 pieces at 20 ft; part 2 lists "11 pieces of 2x6 lumber - 16″" where feet are clearly meant. Re-tally quantities before ordering.

24" o.c. studs with 5/8" T1-11 as the only wall skin means no structural sheathing under the siding and no let-in or metal bracing detail beyond temporary diagonal boards — thin shear resistance for a 16x20 with a 6 ft door opening in a 16 ft wall.
"Time: One Day" per stage is unrealistic; no skill level, no estimated material cost, no weight/load figures, and no foundation sizing are provided anywhere.

No refund policy is published on the listing and this product has 0 ratings of its own (the seller shows a 4.8 average across 23 ratings on 19 products), so you are buying largely on the free web version's reputation.
You are paying for packaging: the $6 PDF appears to be the same three free articles consolidated, and the listing does not claim any added engineering, elevations, or detail beyond them.
Windows are openings only — no unit specification, sizing, flashing, or head-trim/water-management detail. Door hardware is just "shed hinges & latch."
No electrical, insulation, ventilation, gable vent, or interior finish guidance, despite being pitched as a hobby workshop.
Personal use only; no commercial or resale license.

_verification.notes:
WHAT CHECKS OUT (verified against Gumroad + the three free source articles pulled through Wayback, plus the actual plan diagrams):
- Price $6 exactly (price_cents 600, product:price:amount 6.0, schema.org price 6.0, no PWYW, no tiers). Not fabricated.
- 33 pages, 1.63 MB, single PDF, imperial, personal-use only — all verbatim from the listing.
- includes list: the listing's own bullets are "*Step by step diagrams *Step by step Instructions *Full Cut list *Full Shopping list *Full Tool List" plus "1 PDF file with full plans" and the imperial/personal-use lines. All 8 record entries are supported.
- footprint 16x20, sqft 320 (16 x 20 = 320, arithmetic correct). Front/back wall plates 192", side wall plates 240" — confirmed in cut list.
- The entire transcribed lumber_list (Part 1 cut list A–H, Part 1 shopping list, Part 2 cut list H/I/I/J) matches the source character-for-character, including the source's own oddities ("2 piece of 2×4", "18 piece – 48″", "11 pieces of 2×6 lumber – 16″"). Impressive transcription accuracy.
- wall_height arithmetic (91 1/2 + 1 1/2 + 3 = 96") is correct and honestly flagged as derived.
- Roof pitch: I verified the ~30 degrees / ~7:12 claim geometrically. Building-the-rafters-4.jpg labels the ridge cut "30 degrees / 60 degrees" and the rafter 130" with the birdsmouth 18 1/2" from the tail; 130 − 18.5 = 111.5" vs 96/cos30 = 110.9". The 185" bottom chord with 48" king post also gives atan(53.5/92.5) = 30.0 degrees. So 30 degrees is the true slope and "near 7/12" (6.93:12) is right.
- Door: front-wall bottom plate segments 2 @ 56 1/2" + 72" opening = 185", and the doubled 2x6 header at 75" = 72 + 2x1.5. So "roughly 6 ft wide" is exactly right (72"). Leaf 36" x 80 1/2" with a 36"x77 1/2" T1-11 panel — verified.
- Windows, jambs, hinges/latch quote ("shed hinges & latch"), 1x4 and 1x8 trim lengths, 500 sq ft tar paper/shingles, 16 sheets of 3/4" roof plywood, 11 trusses at 24" o.c. over 240" — all verified.
- Image: /home/ethan/woodshed/assets/img/howtospecialist-16x20-gable-shed.jpg is a real 600x419 JPEG, 126,766 bytes, and is the correct HowToSpecialist render of THIS shed (gable end with 6 ft double doors, two windows in one side wall, watermarked HowToSpecialist.com). Byte-different from but visually identical to the Gumroad og:image. No fix needed.
- The record's honesty about the free-vs-paid situation is correct and is its strongest point: Parts 1/2/3 (16x20-shed-plans, 16x20-gable-shed-roof-plans, 16x20-double-shed-doors-plans) do carry the complete cut and shopping lists, and the paid listing's own description literally opens "about free 16×20 shed plans."

ADDITIONAL COMPLETENESS GAPS THE RECORD SHOULD LIST AS CONS (not yet mentioned):
1. The 1/2" plywood truss gussets — the load path for eleven site-built trusses spanning 16 ft — appear in NO cut list and NO shopping list, in either part. Neither is gusset size, shape or fastener pattern given ("Mark the cut lines on the plywood sheets" is the whole instruction). Same for the 1/2" plywood sandwiched in the built-up headers. A buyer cannot price or cut the single most safety-critical component.
2. The Part 1 cut list is internally inconsistent with its own shopping list on both the skids (192" vs 20 ft) and the rim joists (192" vs 20 ft). Anyone cutting from the cut list alone builds a floor that is 4 ft short in one direction.
3. No engineering: no snow/wind load, no span tables, no stamp, and 2x6 rafters at 24" o.c. clear-spanning 16 ft at 30 degrees with plywood-gusseted site-built trusses would need local approval in most jurisdictions. The listing's own disclaimer pushes this entirely onto the builder.
4. Every part is labelled Time: "One Day" — three days total for a 320 sq ft building. Not credible and worth a con.
5. Window units are neither specified nor in any shopping list, and no flashing/head-flashing detail is given (record already says this — correct).
6. 3/4" plywood is specified for BOTH floor deck and roof sheathing; 3/4" roof sheathing at 24" o.c. is significant unnecessary cost/weight.

corrections.correct: Five 4x4 skids about 240" (20 ft) long, running the 20 ft length of the building and spaced roughly 44" apart across the 16 ft width (45 3/4" / 43 3/4" / 43 1/2" / 43 3/4"), set on a thoroughly leveled and compacted thick gravel bed; the floor frame is toenailed to the skids or locked down with rafter ties. No piers, footings, anchoring to concrete, or frost-depth detail is given.

With 240" skids the joists are carried every ~44", which is fine for 2x6. plans.summary: A single-storey 16x20 gable garden/storage shed sold as an instant-download PDF by Shedplans.org for $19.99 (list $34.99). Published dimensions are 15'-9" W x 20'-1 1/2" L x 11'-6" H for 320 sq ft, with clapboard siding over plywood sheathing, asphalt shingles, a pair of shop-built doors in a 5'-4" (64 in.) rough opening with a plywood ramp, two shop-built 3'-4" windows with louvered shutters, decorative lattice panels and a half-round gutter system. Unusually, the vendor publishes a free 14-step PDF of the same design, so the real structural spec is verifiable: a concrete-trench-and-brick perimeter foundation, 2x8 PT joists at ~15 in. o.c., 2x4 PT walls with 6'-11" studs, and thirty-four site-cut 2x6 rafters on a 3/4"x7 1/4" ridge board with 2x4 collar ties. The paid upgrade mainly buys the materials list, cut list, tools list, fastener list and extra blueprints, which the free edition deliberately omits.
plans.wall_height: Wall frames are 7'-2" tall as drawn: 1 1/2" bottom plate + 6'-11" studs + 1 1/2" top plate (front/back/side wall sheets all dimension 6'-11" studs). Finished siding height on the front elevation is dimensioned 6'-7".
plans.foundation: Poured-concrete trench footing with a brick bearing course, not skids: "For the foundation, dig the trenches at least 1 feet wide and 1 feet deep", "Fill the trenches to ground level with concrete and let cure", then "use standard-sized bricks and lay them across the foundation. You will need roughly 285 bricks for this step." Layout is a 20'-7 1/2" x 16'-7 1/2" perimeter of 8"-wide runs with two intermediate beams creating three ~4'-7 3/4" bays.
plans.floor_framing: Fifteen 1 1/2" x 7 1/4" (2x8) pressure-treated joists cut to 15'-9", drawn at 14 spaces of 1'-1 1/2" clear (roughly 15 in. on center), fastened with 5" wood screws; plywood floor deck. Note: the joists span the 15'-9" width but bear on the two intermediate foundation beams, so the clear span is only ~4'-8".
plans.wall_framing: 2x4 (1 1/2" x 3 1/2") plus some 3 1/2" x 3 1/2" posts, all specified as pressure-treated. Front wall: 20' top plate, two 7'-4" bottom plates, sixteen 6'-11" studs, a 5'-4" door header and three 11" cripples. Back wall: seventeen 6'-11" studs, two 20' plates, studs drawn at 1'-1 1/2" clear (~15 in. o.c.). Side walls: 15'-5" long, twelve 6'-11" studs, two 3'-4" boards for the window header and rough sill, four 2'-10 1/2" studs and four 5 1/2" cripples. Plates are screwed, not nailed: 'Connect the beams with 2x4" wood screws' - the PDF's notation is gauge x length (2.2 '8x5" wood screws' = #8 x 5"; 7.7 / 9.5 / 10.4 '6x1" wood screws' = #6 x 1" for hinges), so 2x4" means a 4-inch screw. Nails and staples do appear elsewhere: 2" galvanized nails for siding shields (7.6, 13.4), 1/2" galvanized nails for window beading (9.4), and 'an industrial stapler' for shingles (8.4).
plans.roof: Gable, site-cut stick framing (no engineered trusses): 'cut thirty four rafters 9'-5 1/2" long' from 1 1/2" x 5 1/2" (2x6) PT lumber, 'fifteen collar ties 7'-2 1/4" long' from 2x4 PT, and a ridge board of 3/4" x 7 1/4" PT board 20' long; rafters drawn at 16 spaces of 1'-1 1/2" (~15-16 in. o.c.), joined with 2x3" (3-inch) wood screws. Plywood sheathing, building paper, metal drip edge and asphalt shingles; 'You will need 400 Sq Ft of asphalt shingle roofing.' Pitch is never stated. About 5:12 is the only value consistent with the published 11'-6" overall height (94.5" half-span x 5/12 = 39.4" rise on top of a ~96" top-plate height gives ~136" vs the stated 138"), and the 9'-7" x 20'-5" roof planes then imply roughly 12" of horizontal overhang (2 x 9.583 x 20.417 = 391 sq ft, matching the 400 sq ft shingle call-out). Treat the pitch as unconfirmed and lay the rafter out yourself.
plans.siding: Exterior: "Plywood sheathing, clapboard siding, asphalt shingles"; the door step calls out 1/2" x 6" wood siding boards. Interior: "Plywood sheathing". Finishes: "Choice of paint or stain" (final step: "decorate it any way you want using your favorite paint, stain, or preservative").
plans.doors: One pair of shop-built side-hinged doors in an "extra-wide 64-inch" (5'-4") rough opening with a 6' header height. Each leaf is 9/16" plywood at 2'-7 3/4" x 5'-11 3/4" over a 2x4 PT frame, with 2 1/2" x 3/4" trim, 1/2" x 6" siding boards, three 3" hinges, 4" surface bolts and 6" door pulls. A five-frame PT plywood ramp (3'-3/4" x 5'-9" top plane, 9 1/4" rise) is included, plus two decorative 6'-7" lattice "door shutters" flanking the doors.
plans.windows: Two shop-built windows, one in each side wall: 3'-4" x 3'-4" rough opening with the sill at 2'-10 1/2", outer frame of 1 1/2" x 2 1/2" PT, inner sash of 1 1/2" x 1 1/2" PT with milled glazing recesses, real glass held by window beading and 1/2" galvanized nails, two 3" hinges and an interior lock. Four louvered/jalousie shutters (3'-3 3/4" x 1'-7 3/4", twenty-two 1'-5 3/4" jalousies) plus square louvered gable vents. Note a discrepancy: the sales page says "square windows with 3′ 9″ sides" while the drawings dimension the opening at 3'-4".
plans.loft: none stated - it is a single-storey shed with 6'-11" studs and 2x4 collar ties across the rafters, so there is no floored loft and no loft headroom given

pros: Genuinely verifiable before you pay: the vendor publishes a free 14-step / 19-page PDF of this exact design, so you can read the foundation, floor, wall, rafter and door specs (and judge the drawing quality) before spending $19.99.
Real 320 sq ft at the target size, with published overall dimensions (15'-9" x 20'-1 1/2" x 11'-6") rather than nominal-only marketing numbers.

Substantial foundation for a shed this size: 12"-wide x 12"-deep concrete trench footings plus two intermediate beams, so the 2x8 floor joists only span about 4'-8" clear. This is a far stiffer floor than the 4x4-skid designs common at this price, and it will happily take a riding mower, ATV or commercial chipper.

Roof is simple site-cut stick framing (2x6 rafters, 2x4 collar ties, 1x8 ridge) - no truss jig, no crane, no truss shop order, and 34 rafters at ~15-16 in. o.c. is a conservative, code-friendly spacing for a 15'-9" span with collar ties.
Everything is buildable from a normal lumberyard order with hand and cordless tools; no engineered lumber, LVL headers or steel.
Extra-wide 5'-4" (64 in.) double-door opening plus an integral plywood ramp, which is exactly what makes a 320 sq ft shed usable for wheeled equipment.

Package extras that most cheap plans skip: shop-built windows and doors from scratch, louvered shutters, lattice panels, gable vents and a fully detailed half-round gutter/downspout layout with part counts.
Cheap and low-risk: $19.99 instant download, 50% off a second plan, PayPal, and a money-back guarantee (30 days per the product page, 60 days per the refunds policy).

The vendor offers the same treatment in most sizes you are considering (14x20, 12x20, 12x24, 12x24 gable, 16x20 garage, 16x24, 16x24 lean-to, 14x24 garage, 20x20 garage), all at $19.99, so cross-shopping footprints is easy.

The full free edition is mirrored - in a better copy - by the parent brand: craft.camp publishes the identical 14-step PDF unencrypted, at higher image resolution, with the 'coop' typo fixed, listed openly on https://craft.camp/free/shed-plans/ with no email gate. So you can read every dimension in this design before deciding whether the $19.99 materials/cut list is worth it.
cons: Not engineered and not stamped: no snow load, wind load, ground-snow rating, anchoring detail or code reference anywhere on the page or in the PDF, and no permit guidance. For a 320 sq ft building most jurisdictions will require a permit, and many plan reviewers will want a stamped or at least load-rated roof/foundation - budget for a local engineer's review.

The material call-outs specify pressure-treated lumber for essentially everything - wall studs, rafters, collar ties, window sash, shutters, trim. That is a significant and largely unnecessary cost premium over KD SPF for framing above the deck, it is heavier and wetter to work with, and PT is a poor substrate for paint and for milling window sash.

The ridge is only a 3/4" x 7 1/4" board (a 1x8). With 34 rafters over a 15'-9" span that is a thin ridge; combined with collar ties instead of a structural ridge beam it is workable but leaves no margin, and the plans never state the roof pitch, the rafter birdsmouth/plumb-cut angles, or a bearing detail at the plates.

Roof pitch is never published. I could only infer roughly 5:12 by scaling the 9'-7" roof-plane dimension - so you cannot pre-order trusses, verify snow capacity, or check headroom without laying the rafter out yourself.

Framing is dimensioned as clear spacing (1'-1" to 1'-1 1/2" between studs/joists) rather than standard on-center layout, which works out near 15 in. o.c. That wastes sheet goods, means no plate is marked out in the usual 16 in. increments, and makes the cut counts hard to reconcile with 4x8 sheathing.

The floor depends entirely on the concrete-and-brick trench foundation being poured level and square: a laid-brick bearing course with no anchor bolts, sill sealer, or hold-down detail is a weak point for uplift and for rot at the sill.

Everything is screwed together ("connect the beams with 2x4\" wood screws", 2x3" screws for the roof) with no nailing schedule, no hardware list in the free edition, and no joist hangers or hurricane ties called out.

The free 14-step edition has no wall sheathing or siding installation step at all - it jumps from door assembly to roof sheathing - and no materials list quantities, cut list, tools list or fastener list. You are effectively required to buy the premium edition to get a buildable bill of materials.

Sloppy production: the final page of the PDF reads "Now that your coop is all done", the sales copy says the windows have "3' 9\" sides" while the drawings dimension a 3'-4" opening, and the site's own refund window is stated as both 30 and 60 days. One published customer review says "The plans are missing a critical step" and another that they are "a little hard to follow in some places".

No loft, only 6'-11" studs, and no interior partition/electrical/insulation detail - so despite the marketing claim of workshop/studio/home-office use, there is nothing in the plan about making it habitable or conditioned.
Site drainage detail is a decorative gutter run only; there is no perimeter drainage, vapour barrier, or slab option, and the design has no crawl-space ventilation detail under the raised joists.
The live site is behind a bot wall that serves a JS interstitial to non-browser clients, so the product page (and its plan preview images) can be hard to read or re-verify without a real browser.

Same design sold twice under one company: Mediage LLC also lists this exact plan through its parent brand Craftcamp as '16x20 Workshop Shed Plans Gable Roof' at the same $19.99 (https://craft.camp/p/16x20-garden-shed-plan/), and the free 14-step edition is the same document on both sites (filename SKU SHED33 matches the Shedplans.org SKU SHED33). Prefer the craft.camp free copy - unencrypted, higher resolution, typo fixed - over the AES-256 copy-blocked Shedplans one. Shedplans' own product page no longer links the free edition at all (the free-vs-premium table is HTML-commented out) and its 'Free shed plans' nav link now sends you off-site to craft.camp, so you only find the free PDF if you already know the URL.

No designer is credited anywhere, so you cannot check the design against a named professional. The About page offers only 'our team of professionals has more than 5 years of experience' and 'our designers are all certified Autodesk pros'; the PDF's metadata Author is the website itself ('Shedplans.org', or 'Craft.camp' on the mirror), created 2018-08-06 in a UTC+03:00 timezone with no individual named. Joseph Truini - the genuinely credentialed shed author the site leans on - is billed as 'Main Editor' for site articles, not as the author of this plan set, so do not read his name as an endorsement of these drawings.

plans.summary: A free, fully public three-part step-by-step build for a 320 sq ft (16x20) single-slope storage shed, framed 2x4 at 16" on center on a 2x8 floor frame over ten 4x4 skids, sheathed in 5/8" T1-11 and roofed with 2x10 rafters at 16" OC carrying 3/4" plywood, tar paper and asphalt shingles. Every part publishes its own lettered cut list plus a shopping list, tool list and time estimate on the page — no email gate, no upsell required — and each step has a color 3D SketchUp-style diagram. The roof spans the full 16 ft between the 20-ft front and back walls with no interior posts; the author explicitly tells commenters that rafter depth depends on local snow load ("You can go smaller, if you live in an area with mild winters"), so nothing here is engineered or stamped. An optional consolidated PDF of Part 1 (single cut list + shopping list) is sold through Gumroad for $9.99, but it is not needed to build from the site.
