pros: Genuinely free and complete: all three parts publish full lettered cut lists, shopping lists, tool lists and 3D step diagrams on the page — no email capture, no paywalled materials list, and the optional $9.99 PDF only re-packages what you can already read.

Cheapest 320 sq ft shell to build of the common roof styles: one flat roof plane, no trusses to cut or gussets to make, no gable ends, no ridge. Author's framing: "compared to a gable or barn shed, this lean to is easier and cheaper to build."
Setback-friendly geometry — the high wall goes against a property line or existing building with all roof runoff shedding away from it, and there is no gable overhang to encroach.
Big 8 ft double-door opening at a full 80" head height, so a mower, ATV or garden tractor fits; the doors are shop-built from 2x4 and T1-11 rather than bought.
Generous headroom for a shed: ~8 ft at the door wall rising to about 11 ft at the back, which makes wall shelving, a loft added later, or standing work under the high side easy.

Cut list quantities cross-check cleanly on the big-ticket items (16 joists and 16 rafters at 16" OC for a 20 ft length, 320 sq ft of 3/4" floor deck, 450 sq ft of shingles), which is a good sign the geometry was actually modelled.
Well-thought-out skid layout: ten 10 ft 4x4s form five continuous 20 ft skid lines under the joists, so the 189" 2x8 joists are actually supported roughly every 4 ft instead of spanning 16 ft.

Nice structural touches for a free plan — 1/2" plywood sandwiched inside the doubled 2x6 door header, double studs at all wall ends, back wall built as two manageable 10 ft sections you can stand by hand.
Proven buildable: the site hosts reader photos of this exact plan (brags/diy-16x20-lean-to-shed) and 11 comments where the author answers structural questions.
cons: Nothing is engineered. 2x10 rafters at 16" OC over a ~16 ft clear span with no interior post, purlin or beam is right at the limit of span tables for #2 SPF under snow load, and the author's own guidance is a comment-thread judgement call ("It depends on the snow load... you can go smaller"). No stamped drawings for permit review.

Derived roof pitch is only about 2:12 to 2 1/4:12, and the plan finishes it with tar paper and asphalt shingles. Most shingle manufacturers require special low-slope double-underlayment application below 4:12 and void warranties below 2:12 — plan on a metal panel or a membrane instead (one commenter says she is switching to metal).

Pitch, wall heights and overall height are never stated numerically anywhere in the three parts; you have to reverse-engineer them from the cut list, and the plan gives no rafter plumb-cut/bird's-mouth angles or rafter template dimensions — just "mark the cut lines on the 2x10 boards".

Cut list and shopping list disagree: the cut list needs ten 4x4 skids at 120" but the shopping list buys only "4 pieces of 4x4 lumber – 10'", and the 16-ft side walls list 86 1/2" studs where the front/back walls reconcile to 91 1/2". Re-verify quantities and heights before your lumber run.

A 320 sq ft structure is over the permit-exempt threshold in most US jurisdictions, and a gravel-and-skid foundation is frequently rejected for a permitted building of this size — the plan only says "alternatively, you can use posts and footings" with no footing sizes or frost depth.

3/4" plywood specified for BOTH the floor (10 sheets) and the roof deck (14 sheets) is a real cost and weight driver — that is ~24 sheets of 3/4", roughly double the cost of a conventional 7/16" OSB roof deck, and 70 lb sheets to hoist onto a low-slope roof.
No windows at all and no ventilation detail — no soffit, gable or ridge vents are drawn, which matters on a shed with a nearly flat, unvented plywood roof deck.
No insulation, no vapor barrier, no wiring, no housewrap behind the T1-11, and no ramp for the 8 ft doors — expect to design those yourself.

Fastening is screw-based throughout (3 1/2" screws through plates into studs, screws through bottom plates into the floor) with no nailing schedule or hurricane/uplift tie schedule; inspectors in high-wind areas will want more than "rafter ties".

Delivery is three separate web pages you must read in order, with no single printable document unless you buy the $9.99 Gumroad PDF, which the site itself describes as having "just 1 Cut list and 1 Shopping list" (i.e. Part 1 only).
Diagrams are the site's standard 600 px-wide SketchUp renders — low resolution for shop use, and the source site blocks direct access (Cloudflare 403), so you may need a mirror to read it at all.

In addition, compared to a gable or barn shed, this lean to is easier and cheaper to build. Make sure you check the local codes and make adjustments to the plans, if required.

pros: Genuinely free and genuinely complete for a DIYer: every assembly from skids to shingles to doors to railings is diagrammed, and the cut list plus shopping list are on the page with no email gate or paywall
Real cut list with piece-by-piece lengths (A-W groups) AND a board-count shopping list, so you can price the job at a lumberyard before starting
Gambrel roof plus 2x6 loft joists and a 3/4 in. plywood loft floor (~132 sq ft by sheet count) gives far more usable storage volume than a gable shed of the same footprint

Skid foundation (four 12 ft and four 8 ft 4x4s) means no concrete work, and the skid spacing under 141 in. joists keeps actual floor joist spans short (roughly 4 ft), so the floor framing is not overspanned
All framing is 2x4/2x6 dimensional lumber and 4x4s, cut with a miter/circular saw - no engineered beams, no crane, no ordered trusses; trusses are built flat on the ground with plywood gussets
Page explicitly tells you that you can substitute 2x6 studs if you want to insulate the walls and use it as a year-round workshop
Porch is recessed under the main roof rather than added on, so there is no secondary roof, no ledger flashing detail, and no extra roof-to-wall leak point
Cheap material palette: T1-11 siding doubles as sheathing and finish, doors are shop-built from 2x4 frames and T1-11 rather than purchased units
Optional $9.99 PDF exists if you want the whole thing offline in one file, but you are not forced into it
cons: Only about 192 sq ft is actually enclosed - the 48 sq ft porch eats into the 12x20 footprint. If you need 320 sq ft of interior space this plan does not deliver it, and you would have to redesign the stepped front wall to fill in the porch

Not engineered and not stamped: the gambrel trusses are site-built 2x4s with 1/2 in. plywood gussets and no snow, wind, or seismic rating; there is no engineer's seal, no load table, and only a generic 'read the local codes and make adjustments' disclaimer. A 240 sq ft building exceeds the common 120/200 sq ft permit-exempt thresholds, so many jurisdictions will want stamped drawings this plan cannot supply

Loft joists are 2x6 at 16 in. o.c. spanning the full 12 ft width with no interior bearing wall or mid-span support. That is beyond typical 2x6 allowable spans for anything more than very light storage - treat the loft as light storage only, or upsize the joists

Cut list has real errors. Part 2 lists the truss (item K) as only 2 pieces of 2x4 at 55-1/2 in. for a '16x TRUSS', which cannot build a gambrel truss (it needs four rafter members); the shopping list's 46 pieces of 10 ft 2x4 implies four. Roofing quantity is stated twice and contradicts itself: '500 sq ft of tar paper, 50 sq ft of asphalt shingles' and then '550 sq ft of tar paper, 250 sq ft of asphalt shingles'. Fifty sq ft of shingles is nowhere near enough for a gambrel roof this size. Expect to re-verify every quantity yourself

Part 1 cut list also has labeling/typo problems: two different groups are both tagged FRONT WALL (E and G), item F is tagged SIDE WALL, 'C' is used for both posts and decking, and there is a '2 pieces f 2x4' typo. Following the letters blindly will confuse you

Build time is inconsistent and unrealistic: Part 1 says 'One week', Part 2 says 'One day', and boilerplate in both intros claims 'you could get the job done in about a day'. Budget multiple weekends for a 240 sq ft building with 16 trusses and a loft

Foundation guidance is thin: 4x4 skids laid on grade and tied together with rafter ties, with no gravel pad, no piers or footings, no frost-depth guidance, and no leveling procedure. A 12x20 building with a loft is heavy enough that a bare-skid-on-dirt foundation will settle unevenly

No structural sheathing or bracing under the siding - 5/8 in. T1-11 nailed with 6d nails at 8 in. is the only wall skin, and the stepped front wall with a 12 ft porch opening removes shear wall length exactly where the building is weakest
Loft has no access: no ladder, stair, or hatch is designed or cut-listed, and loft headroom is never stated
Overall height, roof pitch angles beyond '22.5 degree cuts', and any material cost estimate are all absent
Both doors are site-built from 2x4 frames and T1-11 panels with no weatherstripping, threshold, or sill flashing detail; the same is true around the three windows (trim only, no flashing or WRB)
The page is behind Cloudflare and returns 403 to non-browser clients, and the plan is split across two articles, so archiving it locally takes deliberate effort

_verification.notes:
PRICE: fully confirmed character-by-character. The free page publishes no price at all (grep for '$' in both archived HTMLs returns zero hits - prices are not in the HTML). The 'GET PDF PLANS' button on Part 1 links to https://myoutdoorplans.gumroad.com/l/mVUUV, which returns 200 with "name":"12x20 Gambrel Shed with Porch and Loft Plans", "price":9.99, price_cents:999, priceCurrency "USD", og price:amount content="9.99". The Gumroad blurb also matches the record almost word for word: "1 PDF file with full plans! (plans from the blog revised and grouped in 1 PDF file with 1 Cut list, 1 Shopping list)" and "Included in the plans: Step by step diagrams / Step by step Instructions / Full Cut list / Full Shopping list / Full Tool List". So price=Free, price_usd=0 and the $9.99 PDF are all correct.

FOOTPRINT / SQFT: correct, and the derivation in footprint_note holds up under three independent cross-checks. (1) Floor sheathing D = 5 sheets 48x96 + 2 at 48x48 = 160+32 = 192 sq ft. (2) Porch decking C = 9 boards 5/8x5 1/2x144 = 49.5 sq ft; 192+49.5 = 241.5 ~ the 240 sq ft footprint. (3) The L-shape is provable from the wall schedule: BACK WALL I = 240" (20 ft); FRONT WALL comes in three pieces E=96" (8 ft), E=48" (4 ft return), G=144" (12 ft inner wall); SIDE WALLs are F=144" (12 ft) and H=96" (8 ft). Sum of wall runs = 20+12+8+4+12+8 = 64 ft, whereas a plain 12x16 rectangle would need only 56 ft. So the porch really is a 12 ft x 4 ft notch cut into the front-right corner, the shell really is L-shaped, and the porch beam confirms it (C posts list 1 pc 4x4 at 143 1/2" = 12 ft and 1 pc at 47 1/2" = 4 ft). sqft 240 = 12 x 20 checks out.

PORCH-UNDER-MAIN-ROOF claim: verified quantitatively, not just from the picture. 16 trusses at 16" o.c. = 15 x 16" = 240" = the full 20 ft length, and roof sheathing item O totals 8x(48x96) + 4x(48x48) + 8x(7.5x96) + 4x(7.5x48) = 370 sq ft, which equals 4 rafters x 55 1/2" = 222" of roof surface per truss x 20 ft = 370 sq ft. The roof therefore spans the porch. Record is right that there is no secondary porch roof.

TRUSS CON is CORRECT and I independently derived it: with 22.5-degree end cuts, four 55 1/2" members per truss give 55.5*cos(67.5) + 55.5*cos(22.5) = 21.2 + 51.3 = 72.5" of horizontal run per side, i.e. exactly the 144" (12 ft) span, and a 6 ft rise. So a truss needs four 55 1/2" rafters; item K's "2 pieces of 2x4 lumber - 55 1/2\" long 16x TRUSS" is literally half a truss. The shopping list's 46 pcs of 10 ft 2x4 (2 cuts of 55 1/2" per 120" board = 92 pieces) is consistent with 4 per truss. Both quoted roofing lines are verbatim: "500 sq ft of tar paper, 50 sq ft of asphalt shingles" (appears twice) and "550 sq ft of tar paper, 250 sq ft of asphalt shingles". Against a computed 370 sq ft of roof surface, BOTH shingle figures are short - 50 sq ft absurdly so, and even 250 sq ft is only 2/3 of what is needed. The record understates this slightly by only calling out the 50.

FLOOR SPAN PRO is CORRECT: floor frame A is 2 pcs 2x6 at 144" + 10 pcs at 141" (a 144x144 box) and 2 pcs at 96" + 7 pcs at 141" (a 96x144 box) = 240" x 144" overall. Skids B = 4 pcs 4x4 at 144" + 4 pcs at 96", running perpendicular to the 141" joists, which puts bearing at roughly 47-48" o.c. So the 141" joists are NOT overspanned, exactly as the pro says.

LOFT-JOIST CON is defensible: R = 2x6 at 16" o.c. spanning the full 144", secured to the trusses at the top plate with no interior bearing wall or strongback anywhere in the drawings. 2x6 SPF #2 at 16" o.c. is roughly 10-12 ft depending on assumed live load, so 12 ft is at or past the limit for anything above light storage. Fair as written.

OTHER PROS/CONS SPOT-CHECKED AND CONFIRMED VERBATIM ON THE PAGE: "Make sure you read the local codes and make adjustments if necessary."; "you can switch to 2x6s if you want to install insulation between the studs and use it as an workshop, even during the cold winter days."; "insert 6d nails, every 8\" along the framing."; "Cut the posts at 92 1/2\""; "Make notches to one end of the plates"; skids "laid on grade" with "Use rafter ties to secure the skids under the frame" and no pad/pier/frost guidance; Time = "One week" (Part 1) vs "One day" (Part 2) with "you could get the job done in about a day" in both intros; openings = "3 shed windows 24\"x36\"", "1 exterior door 32\"x80\"", T1-11 door panels at 32"x80" and 36"x80"; studs every 16" o.c.; 5/8" T1-11 as the only wall skin with no structural sheathing or let-in/metal bracing mentioned anywhere.

MINOR IMPRECISION not worth a correction: cons say "two different groups are both tagged FRONT WALL (E and G)" - true, but there are actually THREE FRONT WALL lines (E appears twice as a letter, plus G), and F/G are listed out of alphabetical order. The rest of that con (C used for both POSTS and DECKING, F tagged SIDE WALL, the "2 pieces f 2x4" typo) is verbatim accurate. Also note the author calls the double doors "double side doors" in the intro while the record calls them an "end wall" - both are defensible since the 12 ft walls are the gambrel ends; the rendering shows them on the gambrel end.

IMAGE: /home/ethan/woodshed/assets/img/myoutdoorplans-12x20-gambrel-barn-porch.jpg is a real JPEG, 711,724 bytes, 1255x906, and I viewed it. It is the correct SketchUp rendering: red T1-11 gambrel barn shed, double doors on the near gambrel end, and a railed porch recessed into the far front corner under the continuous main gambrel roof - which visually corroborates the footprint_note. No fix needed. (The archived page carries no og:image tag; the wp-content/uploads/2020/01/12x20-barn-shed.jpg path 404s in Wayback, but the local file is already correct so no refetch was required.)

TARGET FIT: at 240 sq ft footprint / ~192 sq ft enclosed this is at the low end of the acceptable 240-480 sq ft band and well short of the user's 320 sq ft goal. The record's first con is honest about that and should stay prominent.

plans.summary: A free, three-part DIY plan set for a 14x20 ft (280 sq ft) gambrel barn shed: Part 1 covers the skid floor, the four 2x4 stud walls and the T1-11 siding; Part 2 covers the site-built gambrel trusses, gable-end panels, overhangs, 3/4" plywood roof deck and shingles; Part 3 covers the 96"-wide double front doors, the 36" side door and the 1x4 exterior trim. Each part publishes its own lettered cut list plus a board-by-board shopping list on the page at no charge, and the plan's dimension drawing states real numbers: 168" x 240" floor, 190 3/4" overall height, 103 3/4" side-wall height, 96" x 80 3/4" double doors, 36" x 80 3/4" side door and a 30" x 30" window. The gambrel roof is built from 2x4 rafter segments cut at 22.5 degrees with shop-made 1/2" plywood gussets, 16 trusses at 16" on center — cheap, but not engineered or stamped. Foundation is the simplest possible: four 4x4x20' skids bedded on compacted gravel, with rafter ties tying the skids to the floor frame and optional ground anchors for wind.
plans.format: Three free HTML step-by-step articles with 3D SketchUp-style diagrams for every stage; cut list, shopping list and tool list printed on each page. No free PDF — the consolidated 38-page PDF is a paid Gumroad download.
plans.page_count: Free version: 3 web articles (Part 1 frame/walls/siding, Part 2 roof, Part 3 doors/trim); no PDF. Paid version: 38 pages (Gumroad "Length: 38 pages", "Size: 1.96 MB").
plans.foundation: Skid spacing IS dimensioned: 3 clear gaps of 51 1/4 in (~54 3/4 in on center) across the 168 in width, per the Fitting-the-skids-9.jpg diagram
plans.floor_framing: 2x6 floor frame: 2 rim beams 240" long plus 16 joists 165" long, joists 16" on center, assembled with 3 1/2" screws through the rim joists. Deck is 3/4" tongue-and-groove plywood (6 full 48"x96" sheets, 3 at 48"x48", 2 at 24"x96", 1 at 24"x48"), screwed with 1 5/8" screws every 8" along the joists.
plans.wall_framing: 2x4 platform-framed walls, studs 91 1/2" long placed 16" on center, single bottom plate and double top plate, 3 1/2" screws through plates into studs. Double studs with 1/2" plywood blocking spacers at both ends of each wall frame. Door headers are doubled 2x6 with a 1/2" plywood spacer glued and screwed between (2x6 at 99" for the front double-door opening).
plans.wall_height: 8 ft framed walls (91 1/2" studs + bottom plate + double top plate = 96"). The plan's dimension drawing shows 103 3/4" from the base of the shed to the top of the side wall. Siding is inset 1 1/2" below the top plate.
plans.roof: Site-built gambrel trusses: each truss uses 4 pieces of 2x4 at 66" long with 22.5-degree miters at both ends (the lower rafters also get a birdmouth-style cut to sit on the top plates), joined with 1/2" plywood gussets and 1 5/8" screws. 16 trusses total, set 16" on center and tied down with rafter ties. Gambrel end supports from 2x4 (56 1/4", 66 1/4", 76 1/4"), gable ends clad in T1-11, built-up 2x4 overhangs (8 pcs 66" + 16 blocks 6 1/2") front and back. Sheathing is 3/4" plywood; covered with 500 sq ft of tar paper and 500 sq ft of asphalt shingles plus drip edge. 1x6 roof trims cut at 67.5 degrees (miter saw set to 22.5). Trusses are NOT engineered or stamped.
plans.overall_height: 190 3/4" (15 ft 10 3/4 in) to the ridge; 103 3/4" to the top of the side wall (stated on the plan's dimension drawing)
plans.siding: T1-11 5/8" siding panels, 4'x8' sheets (17 sheets in Part 1 plus 7 more in Part 2 for the gambrel ends), nailed with 6-8d nails every 8" along the framing, sheets inset 1 1/2" below the top plate on the front and back. Exterior trim is 1x4 lumber nailed with 2" nails; gaps filled with wood putty then painted or stained. The build text also recommends cedar or another weather-resistant lumber species if budget allows.
plans.doors: Double front doors: 96" total opening width x 80 3/4" high, each leaf built from T1-11 siding with a 2x4 perimeter frame (2 pcs 2x4 at 80", 2 at 48", 1 diagonal/mid at 41" per leaf) fastened with 1 1/4" screws, hung on 2x4 jambs (2 at 80 3/4", 1 at 103") with shed hinges and a latch. Side door: 36" x 80 3/4", T1-11 panel on a 2x4 frame (2 at 36", 2 at 80", 1 at 29"), jambs 2 at 80 3/4" + 1 at 43".
plans.windows: 30 in x 30 in rough opening; window header/sill = 4 pcs of 2x6 at 33 in (the 2 pcs at 39 in are the side-DOOR header)
plans.loft: None drawn. Part 2 only suggests it in prose: "You could also frame a small loft to the barn shed. Just fit 2x6 beams to the base of the trusses and then lay 3/4" plywood sheets." No loft framing diagram, no beam span or spacing, no headroom figure, no access/ladder detail and no floor-load statement — the gambrel shape gives the volume for a loft but you would be engineering it yourself.
plans.build_time: "Time: One week" is stated in the info box of each of the three parts. Contradictory boilerplate in the Part 1 intro claims "If you have all the materials and tools required for the project, you could get the job done in about a day" — treat the schedule as unreliable; a 280 sq ft shed with 16 site-built trusses is realistically multiple weekends.
plans.skill_level: not stated (no skill rating is published; the tool list is basic — hammer, tape, framing square, level, miter saw, drill/driver, sander — but building and setting 16 gambrel trusses is intermediate work)
plans.materials_list_available: free-on-page — each of the three parts publishes a lettered cut list (A through R) and a separate board-count shopping list plus fastener/hardware list, all visible without payment or email signup
plans.permit_notes: No engineering, no stamped drawings, no load/wind/snow design criteria, no code references. The pages repeatedly push responsibility to the builder: "Remember that you need to select the location for the shed with attention and that you have to comply with a the local building regulations", "Make sure you check the local codes and make adjustments to the plans, if required", and the Gumroad listing states "It is your responsibility to make adjustments to the plans, to comply with your local building codes." At 280 sq ft this is over the permit-exempt threshold in most US jurisdictions, and the shop-made plywood-gusset trusses spanning 14 ft are the item most likely to draw a plan-review objection. The skid-on-gravel foundation is permit-friendly where a movable accessory structure is allowed but will not satisfy a jurisdiction requiring frost-depth footings.
plans.refund_policy: Not applicable to the free web plans. The optional Gumroad PDF is marked "No refunds allowed" (policy updated 2025-11-30).

The gambrel roof spans the full 14 ft with nothing but 2x4s: four 66" segments per truss mitered at 22.5 degrees and joined with 1/2" plywood gussets. That means cheap short stock (90 pcs of 2x4x6') instead of buying or trucking engineered trusses, and it is buildable flat on the deck with a miter saw.

Real published dimensions, not just diagrams: 168" x 240" floor, 190 3/4" overall height, 103 3/4" side-wall height, 96" x 80 3/4" double front doors, 36" x 80 3/4" side door, 30" x 30" window, 175" x 261 3/4" roof envelope with overhangs.
8 ft walls plus the gambrel volume makes this the most storage-per-dollar shape at this footprint, and Part 2 tells you where to hang a loft (2x6 beams on the truss bottom chords + 3/4" plywood).

Cheapest possible foundation: four 4x4x20' skids on compacted gravel, tied with rafter ties, optional ground anchors. No concrete, no forms, no frost footings, no excavation beyond stripping sod — and it keeps the building arguably movable for zoning purposes.
96" of clear double-door opening plus a separate 36" walk door means a mower, ATV or garden tractor goes in the front while you still have normal access from the side.

plans.summary: A free, illustrated step-by-step post-frame pole barn: eleven 6x6 posts set on post anchors in concrete-filled holes, 2x6 splash boards, 2x8 truss carriers lag-screwed to the posts, and 2x4 horizontal girts every 2 ft, closed in with 1/2" OSB, house wrap and the siding of your choice. The roof is thirteen site-built 2x4 king-post trusses at 24" on center with a 25-degree rafter cut, carried on 2x4 purlins at 24" OC and covered with about 270-275 sq ft of metal sheeting (or an optional 1/2" plywood deck for asphalt shingles). Both a dimensioned cut list and a whole-board shopping list are published free on the page — no email gate — but the project is split across two articles and Part 1 alone is not buildable: the trusses, sheathing, and roofing are all in Part 2. Critically, this is a shelter rather than a finished shed — no floor or slab is specified, no windows appear anywhere, and the front opening is framed but no actual door is detailed.
includes: Free step-by-step written instructions with 3D rendered diagrams for every step (Part 1: layout, posts, door framing, splash boards, truss carriers, girts)
Part 2 article covering trusses, wall OSB, purlins, roof sheets, trims and roofing
Dimensioned cut list keyed A-E (Part 1) and F-L (Part 2) with a part count and label for each member
Separate shopping list in whole board lengths (e.g. "9 pieces of 6x6 lumber - 10 ft") plus fastener and hardware callouts
Tools list and a stated build time
Post layout diagram with color-coded post positions, 3-4-5 squaring and batter-board instructions
Optional paid extra: one consolidated 33-page PDF (1.45 MB) with 1 cut list and 1 shopping list, $9.99 via Gumroad
pros: Genuinely free and genuinely complete on the lumber side: the full dimensioned cut list AND a whole-board shopping list are printed on the page with no email gate and no paywall, so you can price the whole frame at a lumberyard without doing your own takeoff.
Post-frame is the cheapest way to enclose 288 sq ft: 11 6x6 posts on anchors replace an entire perimeter foundation and floor deck, and 2x4 girts at 24" OC use far less lumber than 16" OC stud walls.

Posts stand on post anchors above the concrete rather than being buried, so no post is in contact with soil - a real longevity win over typical burying-the-post pole barn builds. The plan also gives the alternative (add 3-4 ft to post length to bury them).

Real usable headroom and clear span: 12 ft clear width, 10 ft side posts, and a pre-framed front opening roughly 8 ft wide x 8 ft tall that suits an overhead or sliding door - it will take a vehicle, tractor or long stock.
Roofing choice is designed in: purlins for direct metal sheeting, or add the optional 1/2" plywood deck (13 sheets, flagged with an asterisk) if you would rather use asphalt shingles.
The author explicitly tells you to buy engineered trusses rather than build his 2x4 truss, and defers beam sizing to local code - honest, useful advice rather than false confidence.
Simple, repetitive assembly once the posts are up: horizontal girts and purlins are far more forgiving to cut and hang than a full stud wall plus rafter set.
cons: Not a shed - it has no floor. No wood floor, no slab, no gravel floor spec, no thickness or reinforcement anywhere. The only ground prep given is "Remove the vegetation layer and make sure the surface is level." A concrete slab for 288 sq ft is a large unbudgeted cost you must design yourself.
No windows at all: none in the cut list, none in any diagram. If you want daylight you are designing and framing the openings from scratch, which on a girt wall means adding your own trimmers.

The door opening is framed but there is no door: 2x6 cripple studs and a 6x6 header are shown, but no jamb, no leaf, no track, no overhead-door rough-opening spec, no hardware. The plan says only "You can adjust the size of the opening to suit your needs."

Split across two pages and Part 1 is unbuildable alone - it stops after the girts. All trusses, wall sheathing, purlins, roofing and trims are in Part 2, and Part 2 in turn tells you to go back to Part 1 for the cut lists. Treat the two pages as one plan.

Zero engineering. The 13 site-built trusses are 2x4 with a single 28 3/4" king post and no webs spanning 12 ft; there is no snow load, no wind load, no span table, no uplift detail, no stamp. The author writes "the local codes will determine the size of the beam more accurately" - i.e. he is not telling you. A permit office will likely demand engineered trusses and a real footing/uplift detail.
No footing depth or diameter, no concrete volume, and no frost-depth guidance for the 11 post holes - a significant omission for a structure this tall and this exposed.

Harder than a skid shed despite the marketing: plumbing eleven 6x6 posts in wet concrete, bracing them, cutting post tops level at 10 ft, and lifting 13 trusses onto 10 ft carriers needs a helper, a post-hole digger and staging. The body text claims "you could get the job done in about a day" while the Time box on both pages says "One week" - trust the week, and only if you are experienced.

Editorial sloppiness undermines trust in the numbers: Part 2's opening and closing lines both call the project a "12x16 pole barn", and roofing quantity is given as 270 sq ft in the cut list but 275 sq ft in the shopping list.
No published overall height, no roof pitch expressed in x/12, and no elevation dimensions - you have to back these out of the 120"/131 1/2"/154" post lengths and the 25-degree rafter cut yourself.
The live page is behind Cloudflare and 403s to ordinary tools, so the content here came from a 2023 archived snapshot; the page may have been revised since.
The one-file PDF is a $9.99 Gumroad purchase carrying an explicit "No refunds allowed" policy, and it is only the free blog content regrouped.

quotes: This step by step diy woodworking project is about free 12x24 pole barn plans. I had a request for a medium sized pole barn built on a post frame structure, so this is my take.
The posts will be set to the footings using anchors, so the lumber is protected from the elements.
You can cover the pole barn with OSB and siding, or you can go for metal sheets.
If you want to set the posts into the ground, add 3-4' to the posts length.
Use 2x8 lumber for the beams (the local codes will determine the size of the beam more accurately).
Place the 2x4 girts every 2' on center and secure them to the posts with 3 1/2" screws.

I recommend you buy engineered trusses, as they give you a good balance between costs and benefits. They will give you instructions on the span you need to leave between them and on the thickness of the truss carriers. (Part 2)

However, I will show you my take on building the trusses by yourself. Remember to read the local codes so you can make adjustments if needed. The first step is to build the rafters for the trusses. Use 2x4 lumber and make a 25 degree cut to one end. (Part 2)
Fit the trusses to the top of the pole barn, every 2 ft on center. (Part 2)
This step is optional. If you go for metal sheets you install them directly to the purlins. However, you could fit 1/2" plywood sheets and go for asphalt shingles. (Part 2)
Remember to take a look over PART 1 of the free plans, to get access to the cut / shopping lists and to the instructions regarding the frame of the barn. (Part 2)

The article publishes no price; it ends with a Gumroad button: Get PDF Plans. That product page (myoutdoorplans.gumroad.com/l/AMUXG, title \"12x24 Pole Barn Plans\") carries / currency USD, and its attributes JSON reads {\"name\":\"Size\",\"value\":\"1.45 MB\"},{\"name\":\"Length\",\"value\":\"33 pages\"}. Its description says \"1 PDF file with full plans! (plans from the blog revised and grouped in 1 PDF file with 1 Cut list, 1 Shopping list)\". So $9.99, 33 pages, 1.45 MB, 1 cut list + 1 shopping list are all exactly right, and price_usd 0 for the web plan is right (no email gate; both lists are printed inline). FOOTPRINT/SQFT - CONFIRMED. 12x24 = 288 sq ft, and 288 = 12 x 24. Outside envelope 288\" x 144\" is provable from the cut list (B: 2 pieces 2x6 - 288\" plus 1 piece - 141\"; C: 2 pieces 2x8 - 288\" and 2 pieces - 141\"), so the footprint_note's long-wall/short-wall assignment is right and the gable/door end is indeed the 12 ft end. QUOTES - all found verbatim: \"Remove the vegetation layer and make sure the surface is level.\" / \"the local codes will determine the size of the beam more accurately\" / \"you could get the job done in about a day\" / \"One week\" (Time box on BOTH pages) / \"You can adjust the size of the opening to suit your needs\" / \"9 pieces of 6x6 lumber - 10 ft\" / \"If you want to set the posts into the ground, add 3-4' to the posts length.\" / \"I recommend you buy engineered trusses\" and \"consider buying engineered trusses\". The 12x16 con is CONFIRMED and is a good catch: Part 2's first line is \"about free 12x16 pole barn gable roof plans\" and its last line is \"This woodworking project was about 12x16 pole barn roof plans.\" ENGINEERING claims verified as internally consistent: 11 posts (8 x 120\" + 2 x 131 1/2\" + 1 x 154\"), 12 boards of 6x6 in the shopping list because a 12th 10-footer yields the 99\" 6x6 door header. The post lengths back-check the 25-degree pitch exactly (120 + 72tan25 = 153.6 ~ 154\" ridge post; 120 + 24tan25 = 131.2 ~ 131 1/2\"), and the 28 3/4\" king post matches 33.6\" rise minus a 3.86\" plumb-cut rafter depth. 25 degrees is ~5.6/12 and is never stated as a pitch, so that con is fair. 13 trusses over 24 ft at 24\" OC is right; F really is a webless king-post truss. Door opening ~96\" x 96\" is right (2 x 2x6 at 96\" trimmers, 99\" 6x6 header, 22 1/2\" splash boards each side summing to 144\"). \"No floor / no slab / no windows / no door leaf / no footing depth\" all confirmed - none appear in either cut list or either article body. ONE MORE SOURCE DEFECT the record misses (worth adding to cons): Part 1's post sequence contradicts itself. \"Installing the posts\" says to \"dig the holes and then set the anchors into place ... Let the concrete to dry out and then install the 6x6 posts\", then two sentences later says to \"use temporary braces to lock the posts into place tightly while pouring the concrete in the holes\". A builder cannot follow both; the plan never resolves whether posts go in before or after the pour. IMAGE - fine, no fix needed: /home/ethan/woodshed/assets/img/myoutdoorplans-12x24-pole-barn.jpg is JPEG 1600x805, 74149 bytes. It is the correct render - a MyOutdoorPlans-watermarked red board-and-batten 12x24 pole barn, single open front bay, no windows, shingled gable roof, matching the 600x302 article images under /wp-content/uploads/2020/02/ (same 1.987 aspect ratio; the page's og:image is only the site logo PNG, so the article render is the right choice).

plans.summary: This is a factory-built, panelized single-car garage KIT from Sheds Unlimited (Morgantown, PA), not a downloadable plan. Sheds Unlimited assembles the whole building in their shop to test fit, then disassembles, packages and ships it, so the 16×20 arrives as a floor structure, framing, wall components, exterior materials and windows with printed and video assembly instructions. It is a 5/12-pitch gable ("Workshop") shell on pressure-treated 4×4 skids with PT 2×4 floor joists 12" o.c., 5/8" plywood floor, 2×4 trusses 16" o.c., 7/16" OSB roof sheathing and 30-year architectural shingles; it has a framed 9×7 garage-door opening (the door itself is NOT included), one 3' pedestrian door and two 24×36 screened windows. At $15,303 (wood siding) or $20,235 (vinyl) for 320 sq ft it is by far the most expensive way in this comparison to get a 16×20 — and Sheds Unlimited state outright that a kit costs the same as a fully assembled building, so you save nothing by building it yourself.
includes: Floor structure (pressure-treated 4×4 skids, PT 2×4 joists 12" o.c., 5/8" plywood floor)
Framing (2×4 trusses 16" o.c.)
Wall components (pre-built panels)
Exterior materials — siding, 7/16" OSB roof sheathing, 30-yr architectural shingles, trim
(2) 24×36 windows with screens, trim and shutters
One 3 ft pedestrian door (wooden with wood siding, fiberglass with vinyl siding)
Framed 9×7 rough opening for a garage door (8×7 on 10'-wide kits)

Printed assembly instructions plus step-by-step assembly video
Per-kit list of the exact tools and fasteners you must supply

plans.foundation: Gravel pad or concrete pad — the company publishes separate "Gravel Pad Preparation" and "Concrete Foundation Preparation" guides and offers same-day professional site prep. The building itself bears on pressure-treated 4×4 skids. Concrete blocks are explicitly discouraged: "We do not recommend using concrete blocks under your building… Over time an unlevel pad can cause the building to settle which can cause doors and windows to bind." Site prep is the customer's responsibility.
plans.floor_framing: "Base made from pressure-treated 4×4 skids"; "Pressure-treated 2×4 floor joists, 12 inches on-center"; "5/8 inch plywood flooring" (spec list is generic to all sizes of this model — no beam/skid layout published for the 16' width)
plans.wall_framing: Not stated as a dimension/spacing. The page only says the walls are "built from studs and sheeting (just like your house)" and that the kit ships pre-built "wall components." No stud size, spacing, sheathing thickness or header schedule published.
plans.wall_height: not stated
plans.overall_height: Not stated for the 16'-wide version. The published "Height to Roof Peak" table stops at 15'6": 10' wide – 10'3"; 12' wide – 11'1"; 14' wide – 11'5"; 15'6" wide – 12'1". So a 16×20 is presumably about 12'1" to the peak, but the site never says so.
plans.roof: Gable / "A-frame" roof, 5/12 pitch with 4" overhang on the eaves. "2×4 trusses, 16 inches on-center", "7/16 inch OSB roof sheathing", "30yr architectural shingles". The site does NOT say the trusses are engineered or that stamped truss drawings are provided.
plans.siding: Two choices. (1) Engineered wood: LP SmartSide / Smart Panel T1-11, lowest-cost option, painted any color you choose, 5/50-year warranty, comes with wooden double doors and wooden slat shutters. (2) Double 4" Dutchlap vinyl with weathered-wood-grain texture, 50-year warranty, comes with fiberglass double doors and vinyl raised-panel shutters. Vinyl adds about $4,932 on a 16×20 ($20,235 vs $15,303).
plans.windows: "2 – 24×36 windows with screens and shutters" (elsewhere listed as "(2) 24×36 Windows w/screens & trim"). Window and door locations are customizable: "Absolutely! Only if there is not enough space in the wall to fit the windows and/or doors will we need to recommend otherwise."
plans.doors: One 3 ft single pedestrian door with no glass (wooden on wood-sided kits, fiberglass on vinyl-sided kits), plus a framed 9×7 opening for a garage door (8×7 on 10'-wide kits). Important conflict on the page: the "Standard Features" block lists a "9×7 Raised Panel garage door with no glass," but the kit description says "We do not include the garage door itself due to the difficulty of shipping garage door panels without damage." For the KIT, budget separately for the overhead door.
plans.loft: none — this model has no loft or attic trusses, and Sheds Unlimited will not sell two-story buildings as DIY kits ("These buildings require a high degree of construction experience to assemble and would be difficult to build safely in without specialized tools and equipment.")
plans.skill_level: Intermediate DIY, panelized assembly rather than stick-framing. "We recommend a minimum of 2 people to assemble our shed kits, particularly when handling heavy components such as walls and floors. For larger buildings, it can be nice to have as many as 3-4 people." No numeric skill rating is published. Requires real tools: framing/coil/roofing nail guns, circular and reciprocating saws, metal and shingle snips, two 8' stepladders.
plans.build_time: "Assembling a shed kit should take one to three days depending on the size of the building and your construction expertise." (generic to all kit sizes; a 16×20 garage is at the top of the range, so plan on 3+ days with 2-4 people)
plans.permit_notes: Customer's responsibility: "Every town has different regulations about adding an accessory structure. Contact your town or township… You will be responsible for obtaining any required permits and the fees associated with them." They suggest the wooden-floor/portable argument: "If you are purchasing a portable structure (one with a wooden floor), make sure the town understands the building is not a permanent structure. In most of cases, property taxes will not be affected if the building is not permanent and the pad is permeable." Sheds Unlimited will run the permit process for a flat $1,300, but only in DE, PA, MA, CT, MD, RI, VA and NJ. Note that at 320 sq ft this exceeds the common 200 sq ft / 120 sq ft permit exemption thresholds in most jurisdictions.

Only deposit terms are published: "we ask for a 30% deposit if the cost of the building is under $8,000.00 and 50% if the order is over $8,000.00… The balance is due on delivery." (A 16×20 is over $8,000, so 50% down.) NYC/Long Island deliveries also require 50%. No cancellation or refund language appears anywhere on the page.
other_sizes: Sibling kit lines from the same vendor: Standard Workshop Shed Kits ($2,520-$11,443), Classic Workshop Shed Kits ($3,024-$34,675), Standard MaxiBarn (gambrel) Shed Kits ($2,705-$35,559), Standard Saltbox Shed Kits ($2,705-$34,547), Standard MiniBarn Shed Kits ($2,317-$9,378)
pros: Zero design/engineering work for you — the whole 16×20 is factory-cut and pre-assembled once in their shop to verify fit, then knocked down and shipped, so the panels go together without you sizing a single stud: "Our kit manufacturing process allows us to test the fit of every single kit before it's shipped. This quality control standard ensures that there are no surprises when you receive your shed kit."
Very fast shell: "Assembling a shed kit should take one to three days" with 2 people (3-4 recommended for larger buildings) — versus weeks of weekends stick-framing from a plan set.
Exact 16×20 is a real catalog size, and the price grid is published openly for four widths (10/12/14/16) x lengths from 16 ft to 48 ft, so you can size up or down with known cost.
The garage-door rough opening (9×7) comes already framed and headered — the one piece of a garage most DIYers get wrong.

Real long-warranty exteriors included, not builder-grade: LP SmartSide engineered wood with a 5/50-year warranty or Double 4" Dutchlap vinyl with a 50-year warranty, plus 30-year architectural shingles and paint color of your choice.

Documentation is unusually good for a kit: printed step-by-step instructions, a video walkthrough, phone support during assembly, and a free 17-page sample of the instructions so you can judge the difficulty before buying.

Permit-friendly if you are in their footprint — they will run the entire permit process for a flat $1,300 in DE, PA, MA, CT, MD, RI, VA and NJ, which removes the biggest non-construction obstacle for a 320 sq ft accessory structure.
Skid-mounted wooden floor means a gravel pad is acceptable — no slab pour, no frost footings, no concrete truck, and it supports the "portable structure" argument with the township.
cons: Brutally expensive per square foot for a DIY project: $15,303 wood / $20,235 vinyl for 320 sq ft works out to roughly $48-$63/sq ft for a bare unfinished shell. A 16×20 built from a $50 plan set typically runs a fraction of that in lumber.

You get no discount for doing the labor. Verbatim: "If you purchase the kit to assemble yourself, the price of the packaged kit will be the same as a normal, assembled building." You are paying assembled-building money and then supplying your own weekend.

The 16'-wide price grid has a huge unexplained step, and it is real vendor pricing rather than a listing error. 14×20 is $8,844 but 16×20 is $15,303 — 73% more money for 12.5% more floor area, and 16×20 nearly matches 14×48 ($16,755) at less than half the area. The identical step shows up in all five of Sheds Unlimited's other kit lines and in their assembled-building grids, but no page explains it; every peak-height table stops at "15'6" wide", so the likely driver is that 16'-wide buildings exceed their one-piece road-delivery envelope. If a 16-ft width is not a hard requirement, 14×24 ($9,811, 336 sq ft) is dramatically better value for the same usable area.

The garage door itself is not in the kit: "We do not include the garage door itself due to the difficulty of shipping garage door panels without damage." Add $1,000-$2,500 plus install. Note the page contradicts itself — the "Standard Features" box lists a 9×7 raised panel door, so confirm in writing before ordering.

Floor system is a portable-shed floor, not a garage floor. PT 2×4 joists at 12" o.c. cannot span 16 ft, so the 16-wide must rely on multiple intermediate 4×4 skid lines — but no skid/beam layout is published for the 16' width, and a 5/8" plywood deck on 2×4s is a questionable surface to park a car on and to jack a car up on. If you actually want to store a vehicle, expect to want a slab instead, which this kit is not designed for.

Structural documentation is thin for permitting: the site never says the 2×4 trusses are engineered or stamped, publishes no wall stud size or spacing, no header schedule, no snow/wind load rating, and no peak height for the 16' width (the height table stops at 15'6" – 12'1"). At 320 sq ft you are over most permit-exemption thresholds, so a plan reviewer may ask for exactly the data that is missing.

Nominal 16' may not be true 16'. The company's own height table and price search list "15'6" wide" buildings, so verify whether the "16×20" is 16'0" or 15'6" before you pour a pad or plan interior layout.

Geographically locked: kits are only sold within roughly 300 miles of Morgantown, PA (PA, NJ, NY, CT, MD, DE, VA, WV). Outside the Northeast/Mid-Atlantic this product simply is not available to you, and shipping is a separate mileage-plus-permits charge that is never quoted online.

No loft and no upgrade path to one — this is a single-story gable with common 2×4 trusses, and Sheds Unlimited flatly will not sell two-story buildings as kits. If you want the attic storage that a 16×20 gambrel gives you, this is the wrong product.

Tool requirement is real and non-trivial: three separate nail guns (framing, coil, roofing), circular and reciprocating saws, metal and shingle snips, two 8' stepladders. Renting or buying that stack is an unbudgeted cost for an occasional DIYer.

Money is committed early with no published exit: 50% deposit up front on any building over $8,000 (so on a 16×20), balance on delivery, and no refund or cancellation policy appears anywhere on the page.
Nothing about the interior is included — no insulation, no electrical, no interior sheathing, no flooring, no concrete apron. Budget a second project after the shell is standing.

The page really does say both: "Standard Workshop Single-Car Garage Kits with engineered wood siding also come with: Wooden Double Doors" AND "Standard Features / With Wood Siding: Standard Wooden 3ft Single Door". summary — "by far the most expensive way in this comparison to get a 16×20". Comparative claim about other records; not checkable against this source. It is at least directionally plausible: Sheds Unlimited's own /kit-sizes/16x20-shed-kits/ page shows the garage kit as the priciest 16×20 kit they sell.

format — "Physical DIY kit shipped on a truck". Reasonable, but shipping is not included in the quoted price and the page gives no figure: "Our shipping cost is a mileage charged based off of the size and style of the building plus any shipping permits necessary." The record's est_material_cost list of buyer-supplied extras omits freight, which on a 320 sq ft kit shipped hundreds of miles is a material omission.

cons_original: Brutally expensive per square foot for a DIY project: $15,303 wood / $20,235 vinyl for 320 sq ft works out to roughly $48-$63/sq ft for a bare unfinished shell. A 16×20 built from a $50 plan set typically runs a fraction of that in lumber.

You get no discount for doing the labor. Verbatim: "If you purchase the kit to assemble yourself, the price of the packaged kit will be the same as a normal, assembled building." You are paying assembled-building money and then supplying your own weekend.

The 16'-wide price grid has a huge unexplained step. 14×20 is $8,844 but 16×20 is $15,303 — 73% more money for 14% more floor area, and 16×20 even costs more than 14×48 ($16,755 is close). If a 16-ft width is not a hard requirement, 14×24 ($9,811, 336 sq ft) is dramatically better value for the same usable area.

The garage door itself is not in the kit: "We do not include the garage door itself due to the difficulty of shipping garage door panels without damage." Add $1,000-$2,500 plus install. Note the page contradicts itself — the "Standard Features" box lists a 9×7 raised panel door, so confirm in writing before ordering.

Floor system is a portable-shed floor, not a garage floor. PT 2×4 joists at 12" o.c. cannot span 16 ft, so the 16-wide must rely on multiple intermediate 4×4 skid lines — but no skid/beam layout is published for the 16' width, and a 5/8" plywood deck on 2×4s is a questionable surface to park a car on and to jack a car up on. If you actually want to store a vehicle, expect to want a slab instead, which this kit is not designed for.

Structural documentation is thin for permitting: the site never says the 2×4 trusses are engineered or stamped, publishes no wall stud size or spacing, no header schedule, no snow/wind load rating, and no peak height for the 16' width (the height table stops at 15'6" – 12'1"). At 320 sq ft you are over most permit-exemption thresholds, so a plan reviewer may ask for exactly the data that is missing.

Nominal 16' may not be true 16'. The company's own height table and price search list "15'6" wide" buildings, so verify whether the "16×20" is 16'0" or 15'6" before you pour a pad or plan interior layout.

Geographically locked: kits are only sold within roughly 300 miles of Morgantown, PA (PA, NJ, NY, CT, MD, DE, VA, WV). Outside the Northeast/Mid-Atlantic this product simply is not available to you, and shipping is a separate mileage-plus-permits charge that is never quoted online.

No loft and no upgrade path to one — this is a single-story gable with common 2×4 trusses, and Sheds Unlimited flatly will not sell two-story buildings as kits. If you want the attic storage that a 16×20 gambrel gives you, this is the wrong product.

Tool requirement is real and non-trivial: three separate nail guns (framing, coil, roofing), circular and reciprocating saws, metal and shingle snips, two 8' stepladders. Renting or buying that stack is an unbudgeted cost for an occasional DIYer.

Money is committed early with no published exit: 50% deposit up front on any building over $8,000 (so on a 16×20), balance on delivery, and no refund or cancellation policy appears anywhere on the page.
Nothing about the interior is included — no insulation, no electrical, no interior sheathing, no flooring, no concrete apron. Budget a second project after the shell is standing.

Tool list and time estimate
Optional $9.99 Gumroad PDF: 'plans from the blog revised and grouped in 1 PDF file with 1 Cut list, 1 Shopping list'
pros: Genuinely free and genuinely complete for the shell: both the wall part and the roof part publish full cut lists AND board-length shopping lists on the page, no email wall, no gated download.
Post-frame construction is the cheapest way to get 384 sq ft enclosed - no floor system, no perimeter footing, no slab required, just 12 holes and concrete. The site's own estimate is $5,000-$8,000.
10 ft walls (posts 156" with 36" buried = 120" above grade) and a clear 16 ft truss span give real equipment/tractor headroom - far better than a stick-framed shed of the same footprint.
99" x 96" framed gable-end opening is wide enough for a tractor or a car, and the plan shows the 6x6 header and cripple framing rather than hand-waving it.
Only 12 posts and 8 ft truss spacing means very few parts and fast dry-in; one person plus a helper can raise it over a handful of weekends.
Flexible finish path: OSB + house wrap + T1-11 siding, or metal panels screwed straight to the girts, skipping OSB and siding entirely; roof can be metal or plywood + shingles.
Author is honest about the weak point - he tells you outright to consider buying engineered trusses and that local code governs post depth and beam size.
The dimension, post-layout and truss detail drawings are dimensioned, so you can verify the numbers against the cut list rather than trusting it blindly.
cons: NOT engineered and NOT stamped. No snow load, wind load, seismic or exposure category is stated anywhere. At 384 sq ft this is well past the 120-200 sq ft permit exemption most jurisdictions use, so you will need a permit and a plans examiner may reject an unstamped 16 ft truss.

Site-built trusses at 8 ft on center is aggressive for a DIY plan. Truss plate sizes/gauge are not specified (the list just says 'Truss plans, Truss plate' and 'Truss ties'), and the author himself steers you to buy engineered trusses - which means the free truss cut list is the part you should probably throw away.
2x4 purlins spanning 8 ft between trusses at 24" o.c. is marginal for snow country; no purlin span table or load basis is given.

No floor at all. There is no slab, gravel pad, or floor framing step or material in either cut list, and no vapor barrier - budget separately for concrete or gravel and expect the interior to be at grade.

No windows anywhere in the design or the cut lists, and no door: only a rough opening. No door leaf, slider track, hinges, or hardware is designed or listed, so the biggest single build decision is left entirely to you.
The plan is split across two URLs; if you only read Part 1 you get walls with no roof, and the two shopping lists must be combined by hand to buy lumber.
Concrete quantity is never stated - twelve 36" deep holes for 6x6 posts is a real amount of concrete and it is not in any list. Fastener quantities are also missing (screw sizes only, no counts).

Contradictory time estimates on the same page: the boilerplate intro says 'you could get the job done in about a day', the Time box says 'One week', and the body text says '5 to 7 weekends'. The one-day figure is copy-paste boilerplate and is nonsense for this build.
Cut-list arithmetic needs checking: side truss carriers are given as 189"/192"/190 1/2"/94 1/2" sections against a 288" side, so you have to work out the splice layout from the diagrams yourself.
Optional PDF is $9.99 with 'No refunds allowed' - fine given the free version exists, but it buys convenience only, not engineering.

plans.floor_framing: none — the plans include no floor. No joists, no slab, no gravel pad appears in any step or cut list; the renders show the barn sitting on an at-grade pad you must provide yourself.
plans.wall_framing: Post-frame: twelve 6x6 posts (8 @ 156", 2 @ 180", 1 @ 204", 36" of each in concrete) spaced roughly 8 ft on center along the 24 ft sides (86 1/4" / 90 1/2" / 86 1/4"); pressure-treated 2x6 splash boards at the base; horizontal 2x4 girts with 2x4 blockings/spacers between, girts every 2 ft on center on the side walls; 2x10 truss-carrier beams screwed to the post tops with 5 1/2" screws (front/back band beams plus spliced side carriers); 2x6 45-degree knee braces (12 @ 48") from posts to carriers.
plans.wall_height: 10 ft above grade (156" posts less 36" buried = 120"); the dimension drawing shows 122 3/4" to the eave line, and the Gumroad description confirms "10 ft walls"
plans.overall_height: 173" (14 ft 5 in) to the ridge per the dimension drawing
plans.roof: Gable, 25-degree slope (roughly 5.6:12). Site-built trusses: 2x6 rafters cut at 25 degrees, 2x6 bottom chord 192" (16 ft clear span), 2x4 W-shaped webs, metal truss plates fastened with 1 5/8" screws — 4 trusses per the cut list, set every 8 ft on center onto the 2x10 carriers with truss ties, plus 2x4 diagonal bracing and 2x4 bottom-chord ties and 2x6 blocking between trusses. 2x4 purlins every 2 ft on center. Roofing: 550 sq ft of metal panels screwed to the purlins, or optionally 1/2" plywood deck plus asphalt shingles. Overhangs adjustable; roof plan dimension 219 3/4" x 312". The author states "I recommend you buy engineered trusses."
plans.siding: 1/2" OSB wall sheets nailed to the girts with 6d nails every 8", then house wrap, then T1-11 siding sheets. Alternative offered: "go for metal sheets from the very beginning and not use OSB and siding." Trims are 2x6 front/back roof trims and 1x8 side roof trims.
plans.windows: none — no windows appear in the design, diagrams, or cut lists
plans.doors: One large framed opening in the front gable end: 99" wide x 96" high rough opening, with a 6x6 header (the 99"-long 6x6 in cut list A) and 2x6 cripple studs above. "You can adjust the size of the opening to suit your needs." No door leaf, slider track, or hardware is designed or listed.
plans.loft: none
plans.permit_notes: No engineering, no stamp, no design loads. The page repeatedly defers to local authority: "Read the local building codes, so you make sure you comply with the building codes"; "make sure you read the local building posts, to determine the depth exactly to your local front line [frost line] specifications"; "Use 2×10 lumber for the beams (the local codes will determine the size of the beam more accurately)"; "Read the local building codes and consider buying engineered trusses." At 384 sq ft with 10 ft walls this is far above the typical 120-200 sq ft permit-exempt threshold, so expect a permit; a plans examiner is likely to want engineered trusses and a stamped post-embedment/uplift detail rather than this sheet. The Gumroad listing adds an explicit liability disclaimer and "It is your responsibility to make adjustments to the plans, to comply with your local building codes."

quotes: This step by step diy woodworking project is about free 16×24 pole barn plans. I have designed this pole barn so you can build a sturdy and cheap shelter.

The first step of the project is to build the posts for the barn shed. As you can see in the diagram, you need to set the posts in concrete for about 3′ (make sure you read the local building posts, to determine the depth exactly to your local front line specifications).

I recommend you buy engineered trusses, as they give you a good balance between costs and benefits. They will give you instructions on the span you need to leave between them and on the thickness of the truss carriers.

However, I will show you my take on building the trusses by yourself. Remember to read the local codes so you can make adjustments if needed. The first step is to build the rafters for the trusses. Use 2×6 lumber and make a 25 degree cut to one end.
Fit the rest of the trusses, every 8′ on center. Plumb the trusses and then lock them to the carrier beams, using ties.
Most certainly, you won’t find 24′ long 2x10s, so you need to install the carriers in sections.
Building a 16×24 post frame pole barn will likely cost you between $5,000 and $8,000, depending on the materials and any custom features you decide to include.
You can expect to spend about 5 to 7 weekends constructing your 16×24 post frame pole barn.

Last but not least, you need to take care of the finishing touches. Wrap the barn with homewrap and then make it pretty with T1-11 siding sheets. Alternatively, you can go for metal sheets from the very beginning and not use OSB and siding.
Make sure you read PART 2 of the 16×24 pole barn project, where I show you how to build the gable roof.

plans.summary: A free two-part web tutorial for a 12 x 24 ft (288 sq ft) gable shed, built stick-frame on 4x4 skids over a gravel pad, with 2x6 floor joists at 16" OC, 2x4 walls at 16" OC, and nineteen site-built 2x4 trusses at 16" OC with 1/2" plywood gussets at a 6:12 pitch. Part 1 covers floor, skids, floor sheathing, all four wall frames and the front/back siding; Part 2 (12x24-gable-shed-roof-free-pdf-download) covers the trusses, overhangs, roof sheathing, shingles, trims, the 8'x6'8" double front doors and the 3'x6'8" side door. Overall height is 142 3/4" (about 11 ft 11 in) with an eave at 106 1/4", and the openings are a 96"x80" rough opening for the double doors, 36"x80" for the man door, and two 24"x36" windows. The step-by-step 3D SketchUp diagrams and instructions are free on the page, but as of late 2025 the on-page cut and shopping lists were replaced with an "UNLOCK PREMIUM PLANS FOR CUT & SHOPPING LISTS" upsell; the ad-free 40-page PDF with the full cut list, shopping list and tool list costs $8 on Gumroad.
includes: Free on-page step-by-step written instructions, part 1 (structure) and part 2 (roof + doors)
Color 3D SketchUp diagrams for every assembly step (floor frame, skids, each wall frame, trusses, gussets, overhangs, roof sheathing, shingle courses, door frames, jambs, trims)
A labeled dimensions drawing (144" x 288" floor, 163 1/4" x 313 1/2" over overhangs, 142 3/4" overall height, 106 1/4" eave)
Front, back and side rendered views
Tool list (miter saw, jigsaw, drill, chalk line, tape, level, roofing nailer)
Stated rough openings: 96"x80" double doors, 36"x80" side door, 24"x36" windows
Full cut list (A-H part 1, H-R part 2) plus a buy-this-many-boards shopping list - free on the page until mid-2025, now behind the premium upsell but still readable in Wayback snapshots
Paid $8 Gumroad PDF: 40 pages, ad-free, step-by-step diagrams, step-by-step instructions, full cut list, full shopping list, full tool list
pros: Only a 12 ft roof span, so the 2x4 site-built trusses at 16" OC are a genuinely reasonable, cheap, DIY-able assembly - no long-span engineering headaches and no need to buy engineered trusses (the author explicitly says you may substitute bought trusses if you prefer)

Complete build path really is covered: floor, skids, all four walls, siding, trusses, overhangs, sheathing, felt, shingles, trims, both doors and window trim. Nothing important is left as 'finish to taste'
Every step has a dimensioned 3D diagram, which is far easier for a first-timer to read than an architectural elevation set

Real cut list AND a real shopping list (e.g. 145 total 2x4x8s, 22 sheets of T1-11, 15 sheets of 1/2" roof ply, 430 sq ft of shingles) - enough to price the whole build at a lumberyard before you start
Skid foundation on 2-3" of gravel means no concrete, no footings, no forms; big cost and labor saving and often keeps the build classed as 'movable/temporary' in permit terms

Generous openings: 8 ft double front doors will take a mower, ATV or garden tractor, and the author notes you can widen the opening or substitute a garage door, and links a separate shed-ramp tutorial
Two doors and two windows make it usable as a workshop, not just dead storage
Author explicitly permits building from the plan commercially, and the paid version is only $8
cons: The on-page cut and shopping lists have been paywalled since around Oct 2025 ('UNLOCK PREMIUM PLANS FOR CUT & SHOPPING LISTS'), so a visitor today gets diagrams and prose but no material quantities without paying - the site still calls itself 'Free DIY Plans'

Not engineered and not stamped. The FAQ states plainly: 'Are your plans stamped? No. If your town asks for stamped plans, then you need to work with a local engineer.' No snow, wind or seismic load rating is given for the plywood-gusset trusses
288 sq ft is well over the 100-200 sq ft permit exemption in most US jurisdictions, so expect a permit review that these unstamped drawings may not satisfy

Ten 4x4 skids run crosswise at roughly 32" OC along the 24 ft length, which demands a large, genuinely flat, well-drained 12x24 gravel pad; any settlement over that length will rack a 24 ft building and bind the doors
Skid-on-gravel means no frost protection - marginal in cold climates for anything you want dead level long-term
The stated build time of 'One Day' per part is not credible for a 288 sq ft building with 19 trusses; budget multiple weekends and at least one helper for standing 24 ft walls and setting trusses

Cost drivers are heavy: the shopping list calls for pressure-treated 3/4" plywood for the floor (9 sheets) plus PT 2x6 joists and PT 4x4 skids, and 22 sheets of T1-11 - PT plywood and T1-11 are both expensive line items
Documentation gaps: no insulation, wiring, vapor barrier, gutter, ventilation/soffit-vent, hurricane-tie schedule, or ramp detail inside the plan; no material cost estimate is published
The plan is split across two separate articles, so you must find and read Part 2 to get the roof and doors
Site is behind Cloudflare and heavily ad-laden (commenters on the page complain they cannot find the download button); direct scripted access returns 403

plans.floor_framing: 2x6 pressure-treated joists: two 288" rim joists and 19 joists at 141" long, spaced 16" on center; joist hangers optional. Deck is 3/4" pressure-treated plywood (seven 48"x96" sheets plus four 48"x48" sheets, 9 sheets total) screwed with 1 5/8" screws every 8" along the joists.
plans.wall_framing: 2x4 studs at 16" on center, studs cut 91 1/2" long (8 ft walls). Single bottom plate, doubled top plates (288" + 281" per long wall). Double 2x6 header over the front double-door opening, with a 1/2" plywood spacer glued between the 2x6s to build out to 3 1/2"; 2x4 double headers above and below the windows; double 2x6 39" header over the side man door. Assembled flat on the finished floor deck, then stood, plumbed and screwed down with 3 1/2" screws.
plans.wall_height: Studs 91 1/2" (8 ft nominal walls). Eave height above grade 106 1/4" per the dimensions drawing.
plans.overall_height: 142 3/4" (about 11 ft 10 3/4") from grade to ridge, per the plan's dimensions drawing
plans.roof: Gable roof at 6:12 pitch. Nineteen site-built 2x4 trusses at 16" on center: two 90" rafters, a 144" bottom chord and a 28 3/4" king post per truss, joined with 1/2" plywood gussets and construction glue (metal plates offered as an alternative); the author notes bought engineered trusses may be substituted. Gable-end overhangs framed from 2x4s (four 90" pieces and ten 8 1/2" blockings). Sheathing is 1/2" plywood (15 sheets of 4x8 equivalent). Covered with 430 sq ft of tar paper stapled with 2" minimum overlaps, then 430 sq ft of three-tab asphalt shingles with a described 7-course starter offset pattern. 1x6 fascia/roof trims on all four sides.
plans.siding: 5/8" T1-11 plywood siding, 22 sheets of 4'x8' total (11 sheets in Part 1 for the front and back walls, 11 in Part 2 for the side walls, gable ends and door panels), nailed with 6d nails every 8" along the framing. 1x4 trims around the windows.
plans.doors: Front double doors in a 96" x 80" rough opening, shop-built from 2x4 frames (two 73" stiles, one 48" and one 41" rail per leaf) with T1-11 panels glued and screwed on, hung on shed hinges in 2x4 jambs (two 80" plus one 103"). Side man door in a 36" x 80" rough opening, same construction (two 73" stiles, 36" and 29" rails, 36"x80" T1-11 panel) in 2x4 jambs (two 80" plus one 36"), with latch and optional door stop; the plan notes you may substitute a standard prehung 36" door.
plans.windows: Two windows in the front wall, 24" x 36" (2 ft x 3 ft) each, framed with 2x4 double headers above and below the openings; the plan says the opening size is easy to adjust if you already own differently sized units. 1x4 trims around each window.
plans.loft: none - the trusses have a full-depth 144" bottom chord with a king post and no storage platform, walk-up or attic access is shown or dimensioned anywhere in either article
plans.skill_level: not stated
plans.build_time: Listed as "One Day" for each of the two parts (i.e. "One Day" on both Part 1 and Part 2). Treat as marketing; a 288 sq ft shed with 19 site-built trusses realistically takes several weekends with help.

plans.summary: A genuinely free, no-email-gate 22-page PDF framing set for a 12' x 24' (288 sq ft) gable cabin with a loft, drawn in SketchUp/LayOut by Michael Janzen and released under a Creative Commons Attribution-Noncommercial 3.0 US license. The set is fully dimensioned to the 1/8 inch and covers a cross section, floor framing, floor sheathing, front/back/left/right wall framing plus a 4x8-panel sheathing layout for each wall, roof framing, loft framing and sheathing, a loft-to-wall connection, a decorative eave-support detail, porch framing, an alternating-step ladder, and four 3D renderings. Framing is 2x6 studs, 2x10 floor joists, 2x10 loft joists and 2x10 rafters all at 24" o.c. on a 2x12 ridge board, over two 4x8 girders on ten concrete piers; sheathing is called out as 5/8" on the walls and 3/4" on the roof. It is a framing-geometry set only: there is no materials list, no cut list, no written instructions, no window/door schedule, no floor plan, and the cover sheet states outright that it was "not prepared by or checked by a licensed engineer and/or architect."

pros: Truly free and ungated: a direct 22-page PDF download with no email capture, no cart, and no paid upgrade; the CC BY-NC 3.0 US license explicitly lets you copy and modify it for non-commercial use.

288 sq ft lands squarely in the target range, and every plane (floor, all four walls, roof, loft, porch) is drawn and dimensioned to the 1/8 inch, so you can lay out and cut studs from the sheets without guessing.
Rare for a free plan: separate 4x8 sheathing-layout sheets for all four walls and the loft, showing exactly where panel joints fall. That kills a lot of takeoff and cut waste.

The 129 1/2" walls plus a 12:12 roof give real loft headroom - roughly 92" from loft floor to ridge at the center, versus the 4-ft crawl loft you get in a typical shed plan. Loft can be framed full-length or over just one end.
Pier-and-beam foundation (ten concrete piers at 66" o.c. under two 4x8 girders) is the cheapest and most DIY-achievable option: no slab, no concrete truck, no formwork.
24" o.c. framing throughout (studs, floor joists, loft joists, rafters) cuts stick count, nailing and labor materially versus 16" o.c.

Includes the details free plans normally omit: loft-to-wall connection, decorative timber eave/window canopy brackets, entry porch frame, and a space-saving alternating-step ladder with the sizing rule spelled out.
Rafter cut geometry is spelled out (112 1/2" rafter, 93" run, 45 deg, 7 5/8" and 4 3/4" seat/tail dims), which is the part most self-taught builders get wrong on a steep roof.
Author is honest about scope - the foundation is deliberately left to local code and the disclaimer is on the cover, not buried.
cons: No materials list, no cut list, and no written step-by-step instructions anywhere in the 22 pages. You do the entire takeoff and sequencing yourself from the drawings.

Explicitly not engineered: "These house plans were not prepared by or checked by a licensed engineer and/or architect." No snow, wind or seismic design, no shear-wall or hold-down schedule, no pier/anchorage sizing. Not a permit-ready submittal for habitable space.

Structural concern: 2x10 rafters at 12:12 bear on a 2x12 ridge BOARD (non-structural), and the loft floor sits roughly 26" BELOW the top plate, so there are no rafter or collar ties at the plate line. Outward thrust on the wall tops needs to be resolved with ties, a structural ridge beam, or engineering.

Structural concern: 2x6 studs at 24" o.c. running 129 1/2" (10'-9 1/2") exceed the 10 ft maximum in the common IRC prescriptive stud tables for bearing walls - verify with your building department or an engineer before framing.

Structural concern: 2x10 floor joists at 24" o.c. span 138" (11'-6") clear between the two 4x8 girders. That is at the edge of acceptable for a floor and will feel bouncy; 16" o.c. or a third center girder is the practical fix.
Cost driver: 5/8" wall sheathing and 3/4" roof sheathing are much thicker (heavier, pricier) than the 7/16" walls and 1/2" roof most sheds use - roughly a 40-70% jump on sheet goods.

Cost/difficulty driver: 10'-9 1/2" tall 2x6 walls are heavy to build flat and tilt up, and the 12:12 roof means staging, harnesses and cutting 9'-4" rafters at height. This is not a weekend one-person build.
No floor plan, no room layout, no elevations with finishes, no insulation, plumbing or electrical detail, and no drawing scale or scale bar. Everything is raw inches with no feet-inch conversion.

Rough openings only, no window or door schedule or sizes: 36" x 82" front door RO, an unusually narrow 19 1/2" x 82" rear door RO, two 72" x 36", four 22 1/2" x 48", one 22 1/2" x 36", and 24" x 48" in each gable. You must buy units to fit or re-frame.
Wall-height discrepancy: the vendor's own index page says "The walls are 12-feet high" while the drawings show 129 1/2" studs (10'-9 1/2"). Resolve before ordering lumber.

Permit friendliness is poor for a shed: a 288 sq ft structure with a loft, two doors, nine windows and near-11-ft walls reads as a dwelling/accessory dwelling in most jurisdictions, well past the usual 120-200 sq ft no-permit exemption.
The live tinyhousedesign.com free-plans page still links this PDF but the link now returns 404 - the file is only retrievable from the Wayback Machine. No support, no errata, no revisions since 2012.
Drafting slip: page 12 is titled "Right Wall Framing" but is actually the right wall sheathing layout.

plans.foundation: Pier and beam. Ten concrete piers in two rows of five at 66" o.c. along the 288" length, carrying two 4x8 girders set 138" apart (near the 144" outside edges). Sizes, depths, footings and anchorage are deliberately not specified - the sheet carries the note "Choose a foundation suitable to your local conditions and codes." No slab, crawlspace or skid option is drawn.
plans.floor_framing: 2x10 joists at 24" o.c. spanning 138" (11'-6") clear between the two 4x8 girders, over a 144" x 288" perimeter. Floor sheathing shown in a staggered 4x8 layout (thickness not called out in the floor sheets; only 3/4" roof and 5/8" wall sheathing are labeled in the cross section).
plans.wall_framing: 2x6 studs at 24" o.c., 129 1/2" tall (10'-9 1/2"), with 5/8" wall sheathing applied in 48"-wide panels in two 96" courses plus 7 5/8" (running continuously from below the floor framing up through the gable). Gable ends framed with balloon-style studs to 132 1/2" at the plate and a 133" gable base with a 27" ridge post area. All four walls have their own framing sheet and their own sheathing-layout sheet.
plans.wall_height: 129 1/2" studs (10 ft 9 1/2 in) per the Cross Section and all four wall-framing sheets; 132 1/2" to the top of the gable-end plate. Note the vendor's index page instead says "The walls are 12-feet high" - the drawings are the more specific source.
plans.roof: Gable, 12:12 pitch (drawn as 45 deg). Site-cut 2x10 rafters at 24" o.c. on a 2x12 ridge board; rafter length 112 1/2" over a 93" run; 3/4" roof sheathing. Eave/tail detail dims 7 5/8", 4 3/4", 5 1/2", 6 1/4" with a modest overhang. No trusses and nothing engineered - a 2x12 ridge board is not a structural ridge beam, and no collar or rafter ties are drawn at the plate line (the loft floor is about 26" below it). Renderings show standing-seam-look metal roofing but no roofing spec is given.
plans.loft: Yes - the plan's main selling point. 2x10 loft joists at 24" o.c. spanning the 133"/144" width, with the loft deck set at roughly 103 3/4" above the main floor (91" clear headroom below it on the main level). The Loft Framing sheet notes "Frame a loft on one side or a full loft," so it can run the full 24 ft or cover just one end. A 60 3/8" x 33" opening is framed for the ladder. Loft headroom: about 25 3/4" at the sidewalls rising to roughly 92" at the ridge centerline, so genuine standing room down the middle. Access is via the detailed alternating-step ladder (98 5/8" long, 76 deg, 13" treads), sized "1 inch narrower than loft opening." A dedicated "Loft Connects to Wall" 3D detail and a loft sheathing layout are included. No guardrail or edge protection is shown.
plans.doors: Two, given as rough openings only with no schedule or unit sizes: 36" wide x 82" tall in the front gable wall (under the porch canopy) and an unusually narrow 19 1/2" wide x 82" tall in the rear gable wall. Header sizes are not called out.
plans.windows: Nine rough openings, no schedule or unit sizes: right wall - three at 22 1/2" x 48"; left wall - one at 22 1/2" x 48" plus two at 72" x 36"; back wall - one at 22 1/2" x 36"; and one 24" x 48" gable opening in each of the front and back gables. Header sizes are not called out. Renderings show white double-hung and casement units with the decorative timber canopies over the large left-wall pair.
plans.siding: Not specified. The 3D renderings show a brown shingle- or lap-look siding with dark trim and timber accents, but no siding material, thickness, fastening or rainscreen detail appears anywhere in the set. Only the 5/8" structural wall sheathing is called out.
plans.overall_height: Not stated on any sheet. Derivable from the drawings: 129 1/2" wall + approximately 66 1/2" gable rise (12:12 over the 133" gable span) is about 196" (roughly 16 ft 4 in) above the subfloor, before adding the 2x10 floor joists on 4x8 girders and whatever pier height you use - so realistically about 17-18 ft to the ridge above grade.
plans.skill_level: Advanced DIY / experienced framer. The author gives no skill rating. In practice this set assumes you can do your own materials takeoff, read framing elevations without instructions, cut a 12:12 rafter with birdsmouth and tail from run/angle dimensions, safely raise 10'-9 1/2" 2x6 walls, and independently resolve the rafter-thrust, tall-stud and floor-span issues the drawings leave open. It is not appropriate as a first build.
plans.permit_notes: Not permit-ready. The cover sheet states verbatim: "These house plans were not prepared by or checked by a licensed engineer and/or architect. TinyHouseDesign.com does not represent or imply itself to be a licensed engineer and/or a licensed architect. Enjoy these free house plans but use them at your own risk." No engineer or architect stamp, no design loads (snow, wind, seismic), no shear-wall, hold-down or foundation-anchorage details, and no load calculations. The foundation is explicitly punted to you: "Choose a foundation suitable to your local conditions and codes." Because it is a 288 sq ft structure with a loft, two doors, nine windows and near-11-ft walls, most jurisdictions will treat it as habitable/accessory-dwelling construction rather than an exempt shed. Three specific items a reviewer will likely question: (1) 2x6 studs at 24" o.c. at 129 1/2" exceed the 10 ft limit in the common IRC prescriptive stud tables for bearing walls; (2) 2x10 rafters at 12:12 on a non-structural 2x12 ridge board with no rafter or collar ties at the plate line (loft floor is ~26" below the plate); (3) 2x10 floor joists at 24" o.c. over a 138" clear span. Budget for a local engineer to review or re-detail if you intend to permit it. License is Creative Commons Attribution-Noncommercial 3.0 United States, so commercial use or resale of the drawings is not permitted.
plans.refund_policy: Not applicable - the plan is free and released under Creative Commons Attribution-Noncommercial 3.0 United States (http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc/3.0/us/). No purchase, no warranty, no support; the cover sheet's "use them at your own risk" disclaimer is the only stated term.
other_sizes: The same TinyHouseDesign free-plans page offers Micro Gambrel (8' x 7'4"), 8x12 Tiny House v.1, 5x8 Tiny Market House v.1, 8x8 Tiny House v.3, 8x16 Tiny Solar House v.2, and 8x20 Solar House with Gables v.1 - all far under 200 sq ft and outside the target range.
The 12x24 Homesteader's Cabin v.2 is the only plan on the site in the 240-480 sq ft band; the index page calls it "the largest tiny house design you'll find here."
No alternate widths, lengths or roof pitches are offered for this plan - the drawings are fixed at 144" x 288" and 12:12.
A SketchUp source file is offered on the same page for the Micro Gambrel only, not for this plan.
