plans.footprint_note: The vendor markets this as "20x16": 20'-0" along the front wall (where both doors are) by 16'-0" deep. The floor plan sheet is dimensioned 20' x 16' = 320 sq ft. Same design also offered as 20x12 (240 sq ft).
plans.style: Modern clerestory / offset shed (mono-pitch) roof — two separate single-slope roof planes with a 1'-6" clerestory window band between them, four awning-style clerestory windows facing the higher opening. Vertical T1-11 plywood siding.
plans.price: $64.99 (emailed PDF download); $70.99 for the postal-mailed printed set
plans.summary: A 320 sq ft (20' x 16') modern clerestory shed plan set from iCreatables, sold as an instant-download PDF for $64.99 (or $70.99 postal mailed). The roof is two offset single-slope planes — 4/12 on the tall plane and 2/12 on the lower plane — separated by a 1'-6" clerestory band with four 2616 windows, giving a daylit interior with 12'-4" of height at the high point and 13'-2" overall from grade. Framing is conventional house-style construction: 2x6 floor joists at 16" o.c. with 3/4" T&G OSB (or a concrete slab), 2x4 walls at 16" o.c. with a double top plate, 2x8 rafters with 1/2" OSB sheathing, and two 16'-0" 1-3/4" x 11-7/8" LVL beams carrying the clerestory bearing line. Three foundation options are drawn (treated wood skid, concrete slab, treated-lumber-or-metal joists on a gravel bed), and the complete numbered materials list is published as a free PDF on the page before you buy.
includes: Complete PDF plan set, instant emailed download, drawn on 8-1/2 x 11 paper for home printing (postal-mailed option +$6)
Complete materials list broken down by part of the shed, with a code/numbering system so each part maps to a drawing (also free on the page before purchase)
Three foundation designs: treated wood skid, concrete slab, and treated lumber or metal floor joists on a gravel bed
Floor plan, exterior elevations, foundation plan, floor framing plan, wall framing plan, roof framing plan, building section (sheet 8) and construction details
Rafter birdsmouth cut template and angle dimensions
Home-built door plans in addition to the pre-hung door callouts
Step-by-step written instructions aimed at both pros and first-time framers
Free 'How To Build A Shed' eBook with every plan purchase
pros: Materials list is published free and in full on the page (2-page PDF, ~40 line items with quantities and lengths) — you can price the whole build and sanity-check the design before paying $64.99.
Genuinely daylit, modern-looking building: four 2'-6" x 1'-6" clerestory windows plus a 3020 side window make it usable as a studio/office rather than a dark storage box.

Real house-style framing spec: 2x4 walls at 16" o.c. with a double top plate, 2x6 floor joists at 16" o.c., 3/4" T&G floor, 50 psf floor load and 30 psf roof snow load — stronger than most big-box shed kits.
Structural hardware is actually specified, not hand-waved: two 16'-0" 1-3/4" x 11-7/8" LVL beams, 11 Simpson LRU26Z hangers, 27 H2.5 hurricane ties, ST30 and CS16 straps, 12 A23 clips.
Three foundation options in one set, so the same purchase works whether you pour a slab or set it on treated 4x6 skids.
No trusses to build or order — the roof is stick-framed 2x8 rafters at manageable ~10'-8" and ~11'-8" runs, and the plans give the birdsmouth template.
7'-7" lower wall height lets standard factory pre-hung doors (5068 double and 2668 single) go on any wall, which cuts both siding and door-building labor.
Vendor states the plans follow IRC prescriptive practice and are regularly used to obtain building permits.
cons: 13'-2" overall height from finished grade is tall for a backyard accessory building — many jurisdictions cap sheds around 10-12 ft, so check your height limit before buying.
At 320 sq ft this is over the permit-exempt threshold in most places (commonly 100-200 sq ft), so expect a permit, setbacks and possibly a footing inspection.
Not engineer-stamped. The FAQ is explicit that if your building department wants stamped calcs for local wind/seismic/snow you must hire a licensed engineer in your state yourself.

The 2/12 low-slope plane is the weak point in bad weather: asphalt shingles on 2/12 require a special low-slope underlayment application and the plans just tell you to check with the shingle manufacturer.

The clerestory is the hard part of the build — two roof planes at different pitches, a 1'-6" framed window band, Z-flashing where the lower roof meets the upper wall, and rafters hung off LVL beams. This is not a beginner's first shed.
Two 16'-0" LVL beams are a real cost and handling problem: heavy, expensive, special-order at most yards, and awkward to lift into place without help.

The skid foundation uses five 16'-0" treated 4x6 skids with 20'-0" 2x6 joists running over them, so it needs a large, dead-level, well-drained gravel pad across the whole footprint — not just four blocks.
Digital product with a no-refunds policy; the only pre-purchase preview is the generic plan-example page, not this specific set.
No loft is drawn even though there is 12'-4" of interior height at the high side, so the storage volume above head height is unused unless you engineer it yourself.
Sheet count, build time and an estimated material cost are all absent from the page — you cannot budget time or dollars from the listing alone.

PART 2: 16x16 gambrel roof plans - truss rafters with 22.5-degree cuts, 1/2 in plywood gussets, truss layout, gambrel end supports and end panels, overhang assemblies, 3/4 in plywood roof sheathing, tar paper and asphalt shingles, 1x6 roof trims (separate free page)

pros: Genuinely free with no email gate, no upsell and no paywall - the author explicitly rejects the idea of a paid version: "There is no $37 offer, all my plans are free and it will stay like this."

Every part publishes a real cut list AND a consolidated shopping list, so you can price the whole build before starting; PART 1 alone lists 6 4x4x16, 15 2x6x16, 11 2x4x16, 41 2x4x8, 8 sheets of 3/4 in plywood and 16 sheets of T1-11.

256 sq ft with a gambrel roof gives a lot of usable volume for the footprint, and PART 2 states a loft can be added (author's comment: fit 12 ft support beams to the bottom of the trusses, then a 3/4 in plywood floor).

Skid-on-gravel foundation means no concrete, no footings and no excavation beyond stripping sod and compacting gravel - the cheapest and fastest foundation for this size, and often the difference between "permanent structure" and "portable" in local code.
Floor joists are well supported: 6 4x4 skids run at roughly 3 ft 2 in spacing under 2x6 joists at 16 in on center, so no joist is actually asked to span 16 ft.
Site-built trusses from 2x4s with plywood gussets are all miter-saw work at one repeated angle (set the saw to 22.5 degrees) - no truss delivery, no crane, no engineered lumber.
Author answers questions in the comments with specific numbers (2 rafter ties per rafter with 1 5/8 in screws; trusses 16 ft outside to outside; how shortening base rafters lowers overall height).
cons: Not a complete standalone plan: this URL is PART 1 (floor + walls + siding) only. You must also work through PART 2 (roof) and PART 3 (doors/trims) to get a finished building, and the three cut lists must be merged by hand.

Trusses are NOT engineered - plywood gussets are specified only as "1/2 in plywood for the joints," with no gusset dimensions, no nailing/screw schedule per joint, and no snow or wind load rating. A 16 ft gambrel truss at 24 in on center is a real structural element, and nothing here is stamped.

No pressure-treated lumber is specified anywhere, yet the 4x4 skids sit directly on compacted gravel in ground contact. The page only suggests "cedar or other weather resistant lumber" generically - substitute PT for the skids and rim/floor framing yourself.

At 256 sq ft this is well over the common 100-200 sq ft permit exemption in most US jurisdictions, so a permit is likely - and the author says outright that the plans are "for informational purpose," declines custom or permit work, and one commenter reports her county refusing a permit without building plans.
No windows at all in any of the three parts - a 16x16 shed with only double doors for light and no vents. Adding openings means re-framing headers yourself.

Studs at 24 in on center with T1-11 nailed as the only sheathing means the walls rely entirely on the siding for racking resistance; no shear panels, hold-downs, hurricane ties on the walls, or anchorage of the skids to the ground are shown.

Roof material quantity is self-contradictory: PART 2's list says "450 sq ft of tar paper, 450 sq ft of asphalt shingles" and then repeats it as "250 sq ft" a few lines later. Build time is contradictory too ("One week" in the Time tab vs. "you could get the job done in about a day" in the boilerplate intro).

Steep and tall: a commenter got trusses up and said "I just can not see me having the skill to finish this with it being so high with such a steep slope." Expect scaffolding for the roof, and overall height is never published.
No overall height, no wall/roof section, no scaled elevations, no PDF download, no fastener schedule beyond generic screw sizes, and no ramp for the 6 ft doors.
Loft is discussed but not designed - no beam sizing, no span check, no headroom figure, no loft joist layout.

plans.floor_framing: 2x6 floor frame: 2 rim joists 192" long plus 13 joists 189" long, i.e. 16 in on center across the 16 ft width, all supported at roughly 3 ft 2 in intervals by the 6 4x4 skids beneath. Assembled with 3 1/2" screws through pilot holes in the rim joists. Deck is 3/4" plywood: 6 sheets 48"x96" plus 4 pieces 48"x48", fastened with 1 5/8" screws every 8" along the framing. Author confirmed in comments that 15 total 2x6x16 are needed for the floor frame.
plans.wall_framing: 2x4 stud walls, studs 24" on center, with a single bottom plate and a double top plate. Back wall: 2 plates 185" + 1 plate 192" + 9 studs 91 1/2". Side walls (x2): 2 plates 192" + 1 plate 185" + 11 studs 91 1/2" each, with doubled studs at both ends and 1/2" plywood blocking between the double studs. Front wall: 1 plate 192" + 1 plate 185" + 8 studs 91 1/2" + 2 pieces 86" + 2 pieces 56 1/2", with a double header of two 2x6 x 75" and 1/2" plywood sandwiched between the header beams. Walls are screwed down through the bottom plates into the floor with 3 1/2" screws and plumbed with a spirit level. Door opening size is explicitly adjustable ("You can adjust the size of the door opening to suit your needs").

Joints are reinforced with 1/2" plywood gussets screwed on with 1 5/8" screws. Trusses are plumbed and locked down with rafter ties (2 ties per rafter, 1 5/8" screws, per the author's comment). 2x4 gambrel end supports with 22.5-degree tops, pocket-holed and secured with 2 1/2" screws. PART 2 adds 8 more sheets for the gambrel end panels (4 pieces 48"x76 1/4" and 4 pieces 48"x96"), fastened with 1 5/8" screws. PART 3 adds 1x4 trims on all four walls, nailed with 2" nails every 8". Finish: fill holes with wood putty, sand 120-220 grit, then paint or stain.

plans.skill_level: Intermediate to advanced DIY. No skill level is stated on the page, but the build involves 16 ft floor framing, standing three full 16 ft wall sections, cutting and setting nine 16 ft site-built gambrel trusses at height, and sheathing a steep two-pitch roof. A commenter on PART 2 reports getting a few trusses up and concluding "I just can not see me having the skill to finish this with it being so high with such a steep slope," and the author's reply to a hardware question was "I wouldn't recommend you this project if you have these kind of questions."
plans.build_time: Contradictory on the page. PART 1's Time tab says "One week"; PARTS 2 and 3 each say "One day". The boilerplate paragraph repeated on all three pages also claims "If you have all the materials and tools required for the project, you could get the job done in about a day," which is not credible for a 256 sq ft gambrel building. Plan on roughly one to two weekends per part for a two-person crew.
plans.permit_notes: No permit or code guidance beyond "Select the location for the barn shed after reading the local building codes." There is no engineer's stamp, no design load, no wind/snow rating, no scaled elevations and no PDF - so this is not a submittable drawing set. The author is explicit in the comments: asked whether the drawings can be submitted for a building permit, he replied "I don't design custom plans and my plans are for informational purpose." Another commenter reports "my county is insisting on building plans before they will provide me a permit." At 256 sq ft the building is over the typical 100-200 sq ft accessory-structure exemption in most US jurisdictions, so a permit is likely required and you will probably need to have plans drawn or reviewed locally. The skid-on-gravel foundation may also fail a frost-depth or anchorage requirement in some jurisdictions.
plans.refund_policy: Not applicable - the plans are free and nothing is sold on the page. The author states "all my plans are free and it will stay like this." The site does link to a separate "Premium Plans" section, but this plan is not part of it.

plans.footprint_note_original: 16 ft x 16 ft = 256 sq ft floor. Floor frame is built exactly 16'x16' (192" rim joists); walls sit on the deck edge so the footprint is 16x16 at the deck. Roof adds "generous overhangs" front and back (PART 2 builds 2x4 overhang assemblies), so the roof plan is larger than 16x16 — the page never gives the overhang dimension. Author confirms in comments that trusses are "16 ft outside to outside."
plans.summary_original: A free, three-part step-by-step web plan for a 16x16 (256 sq ft) gambrel/barn shed on 4x4 skids, with 8 ft 2x4 walls at 24" on center, T1-11 siding, site-built gambrel trusses at 24" on center, and 6 ft wide x ~7 ft 3 in tall double front doors. PART 1 (this URL) covers the skid foundation, floor frame, all three wall frames and siding; PART 2 covers the gambrel trusses, plywood gable/end panels, overhangs and shingle roof; PART 3 covers the double doors, jambs and 1x4 trims. Each part publishes a real cut list plus a consolidated shopping list, so the whole build is quantified in lumber terms — but it is dimensioned 3D illustrations and prose only: no scaled elevations, no PDF, no foundation or truss engineering, and no windows. The author states flatly in the comments that "all my plans are free and it will stay like this" and that "my plans are for informational purpose," so this is not a permit-ready or stamped drawing set.

_verification.notes:
CONFIRMED (verbatim/arithmetic): price - no dollar figure is published anywhere on PART 1/2/3, so "Free" / price_usd 0 is correct and nothing was invented. Footprint 16x16 and sqft 256 check out (16x16=256; floor frame B = "2 pieces of 2x6 lumber - 192\" long, 13 pieces - 189\" long"; author's comment "16 ft outside to outside"). Three-part structure confirmed (PART 1 /16x16-gambrel-shed-plans/, PART 2 /16x16-barn-shed-roof-plans/, PART 3 /16x16-barn-shed-doors-plans/). Wall height 8 ft is correct as a derivation (91 1/2" studs + 1 1/2" bottom plate + 3" double top plate = 96"). Studs 24" OC verbatim ("Place the studs every 24\" on center"). Trusses 24" OC verbatim; 36 rafters / 4 per truss = 9 trusses = 192" at 24" OC, internally consistent. 22.5-degree miter verbatim ("22.5 degree cuts to both ends of the 2x4 beams") and the comment clarification about 67.5 vs 22.5 exists. 1/2" plywood gussets verbatim ("Use 1/2\" plywood for the joints"), with no gusset dimensions given - and the shopping list allots only ONE 4'x8' sheet of 1/2" plywood for ~45 gusset joints, which strengthens the record's "not engineered" con. 3/4" plywood roof sheathing, tar paper + shingles, 1x6 roof trims (8 pieces, 74") all confirmed. PART 3 confirmed: doors are "2 pieces of T1-11 siding - 36\"x87 1/2\" long" = 6 ft wide x 7 ft 3 1/2 in tall, hinges & latch, 1x4 trims on all walls. PART 1 lumber list matches exactly, character for character: 6 4x4x16, 15 2x6x16, 8 sheets 3/4" plywood, 11 2x4x16, 41 2x4x8, 2 2x6x8, 16 T1-11 4'x8'. Roofing self-contradiction CONFIRMED verbatim: PART 2 lists "450 sq ft of tar paper, 450 sq ft of asphalt shingles" (twice) and then "250 sq ft of tar paper, 250 sq ft of asphalt shingles" a few lines later; ~450 is the physically right number (2 x 147" of slope x 16 ft = ~392 sq ft plus overhangs), so 250 is the bad figure. Build-time contradiction CONFIRMED for PART 1 ("One week" in the Time tab vs "you could get the job done in about a day" in the intro); note PART 2 and PART 3 both say "One day". Commenter quote CONFIRMED verbatim on PART 2: "I just installed a few trusses and I just can not see me having the skill to finish this with it being so high with such a steep slope." Permit comment CONFIRMED on PART 1 ("my county is insisting on building plans before they will provide me a permit"). "cedar or other weather resistant lumber" and "generous overhangs" CONFIRMED verbatim; no PT lumber is specified anywhere, so that con is fair. No windows and no vents anywhere in the three parts - confirmed. No PDF for this plan. Comment counts: PART 1 = 15, PART 2 = 7, PART 3 = 0.

ENGINEERING SANITY CHECK: pros[4] is sound in substance - the 189" 2x6 joists are crossed by six 16 ft 4x4 skids at ~37-38" (189/5), so no 2x6 spans anywhere near 16 ft. Overall height, which the record correctly says is never published, works out to roughly 16 ft: with 73 1/2" rafters mitered at 22.5 deg, the lower rafters rise 73.5*sin(67.5) = 67.9" and the uppers 73.5*sin(22.5) = 28.1", total 96" of roof rise over 8 ft walls (and the half-span run also lands exactly on 96"). That independently corroborates both the "steep and tall" con and the commenter's complaint.

ADDITIONAL SOURCE INCONSISTENCY THE RECORD MISSES (candidate extra con): PART 3 keys the door jambs as 1x4 in the cut list ("M - 1 piece of 1x4 lumber - 79\" long, 2 pieces - 87 1/2\" long  JAMBS") but the step text says "Fit the 2x4 jambs around the double door opening" - the record states "2x4 door jambs" as settled fact. Likewise PART 1's front-wall header is "2 pieces of 2x6 lumber - 75\" long" while the bottom-plate segments (2 x 56 1/2" out of 192") imply a 79" rough opening, and PART 3's head jamb is 79" - the header is 4" too short to span its own opening. PART 3's shopping list is also internally broken (8 pieces of 1x4 at 96" for trims, but only "2 piece of 1x4 lumber - 8'" bought).

ARCHIVE CAVEAT: the 2024-04-17 snapshot of PART 1 carries corrupted <title>/og:/canonical metadata pointing at "Free Pole Barn Plans" on howtospecialist.com; the article body is nonetheless the genuine 16x16 gambrel content. plans.name: 16' x 24' Bonanza Barn-Style (Gambrel) Storage Building — Model EBB-1624
plans.footprint_note: Cut sheet header reads "BONANAZA 16 X 24" (sic) / MODEL EBB-1624; the drawing sheets are titled "16' X 24' BONANZA". 24' is the length (joists span the 16' width, bands run the 24' sides); the double doors are in a 16' end wall. 384 sq ft, one size up from the user's 16x20 target — the identical design is offered by the vendor in 16x12, 16x16 and 16x20 as well.
plans.style: Gambrel / barn-style storage shed ("Bonanza" line), stud-framed on wood skids, double doors in one end wall
plans.price: Free (the 13-page PDF downloads with no email gate or paywall); the same design is also sold inside Backroad Home's $29.00 "Instant Download Building Plan Set #BP-101"
plans.summary: A complete, genuinely buildable 16'x24' gambrel storage building distributed as a single free 13-page PDF: nine pages of illustrated step-by-step construction instructions with jobsite photos, a one-page quantity cut sheet ("Loading Sheet") listing every stick of lumber plus nails by the pound, and three scanned drawing sheets (floor plan + floor framing, front/side elevations, roof framing + a labeled wall/roof section). The building sits on three spliced pressure-treated 4x4 skids with 2x6 joists at 16" o.c., 2x4 walls at 24" o.c. with 65-1/2" studs (6' walls), and site-built gambrel trusses at 24" o.c. made from four 72" 2x6 segments joined with scrap 1/2" plywood gussets — 14' to the ridge. It is written by a production shed builder (Fred Strickland, "over a thousand sheds") and is full of real assembly tricks: frame and skin the walls flat on the deck then tilt them up, prefab the doors nailed to their siding sheet and cut them free after erection, use 2x6 fly rafters on the front and 2x4 on the back so shingle courses land on an even foot. What it deliberately does NOT contain is engineering: no design loads, no lumber grade, no fastener schedule, no anchoring detail, and the gambrel trusses are explicitly non-engineered ("the size of the gussets is not critical").
includes: 9 pages of illustrated step-by-step written instructions (floor, side walls, roof, end walls, roof sheathing, fly rafters, beveled overhang, roofing, trim) with ~14 jobsite photos
A one-page CUT SHEET (Loading Sheet) for MODEL EBB-1624 with quantity, size and usage for every member, plus shingles, felt, flashing, hasp and nails by the pound
A separate DOOR MATERIALS sub-list (jambs, uprights, stiles, base, corner blocks, hinges)
A dedicated 'Doors Made Easy' section with 4 photos/diagrams and a hinge-mounting jig sketch
Drawing sheet: FLOOR PLAN (24' x 16', studs @24" o.c., door dimensions) + FLOOR FRAMING (2x6 joists @16" o.c., 4x4 skids, 16" cantilevers)
Drawing sheet: FRONT ELEVATION and SIDE ELEVATION with 6' wall height and 14' overall height dimensioned
Drawing sheet: ROOF FRAMING plan (2x6 common rafters @24" o.c., three ridge lines) plus a fully labeled wall/roof section calling out every material
pros: Free and complete — no email gate, no upsell, no watermark: instructions, full quantity cut list, floor plan, floor framing, elevations, roof framing and a labeled section are all in the one PDF, even though the same design is normally sold inside a $29 bundle

The cut sheet is a true 'loading sheet': every piece with its exact cut length (189" joists, 65-1/2" studs, 72" rafters, 74" jambs) plus 20 bundles of shingles, 2 rolls of felt, 3 pcs Z-bar and 7 lb each of 12d and 6d nails — you can price the whole build at a lumberyard in one pass

Written by a production builder, so it is optimized for speed and waste, not for drawing-board elegance: build and skin the walls flat on the deck then tilt, prefab both doors nailed to their siding sheet and saw them free on site, temporary 2x4 ledger to hold the front siding while you nail it

Cheapest possible foundation — three treated 4x4 skids on the ground or on concrete blocks, shimmed level with roofing shingles. No concrete, no footings, no excavation, and a skid building often stays classed as a portable/temporary accessory structure
384 sq ft with a gambrel roof and a 14' ridge on 6' walls gives a lot of usable volume; there is plenty of room to add loft joists yourself even though the plan has none
24" o.c. studs and 24" o.c. trusses keep both the lumber count and the labor down for a building this size

Genuinely clever detail work you would not think of yourself: 2x6 fly rafters on the front gable and 2x4 on the rear so shingle courses land on an even foot, and the male/female siding lap arranged so the closed doors weather-seal against each other
Sibling free PDFs exist for the same design family (8x8 and 10x8 Bonanza gambrel, and 8x8 / 10x8 / 16x24 gable 'Organizer'), so you can cross-read them to sanity-check the method
cons: The gambrel trusses are NOT engineered. They are shop-built from four 72" 2x6 segments gusseted with whatever scrap plywood is on hand, and the text says outright that 'the size of the gussets is not critical.' No gusset nailing pattern, no snow or wind load, no species or grade. This will not pass a plan review anywhere that wants stamped trusses.

Zero engineering data of any kind: no design loads, no lumber grade, no fastener schedule beyond 'nail about every 8 inches', no uplift/anchoring detail, no bracing plan. 384 sq ft is well over the permit-exempt threshold in most jurisdictions, so you will likely need someone else to supply the structural justification.

Only three drawing sheets, hand-lettered and scanned circa 2003, and they are rotated/upside-down inside the PDF. There is no dimensioned truss layout — you are told to lay the truss out full scale on the deck between stop blocks set exactly 16' apart and eyeball the peak to a chalk line.

The floor is 2x6 joists at 16" o.c. bearing on only three 4x4 skids, with the deck cantilevered ~16" past each outer skid, and the skids themselves are spliced from two 12' pieces with 4' 2x4 scabs rather than a single 24' timber. Fine for boxes and a mower; light if you want a vehicle, a lathe, or heavy shelving loads.

Only a 60" double-door opening on a 384 sq ft building — too narrow for a car and tight for a wide mower deck or an ATV with racks. If you want a drive-through you are on your own (the text only says 'It's your building; you can do anything you want').

No windows, no vents, no loft, no ceiling, no insulation, no electrical, no ramp — it is a bare storage shell. The vendor's marketing photo shows a gable vent that appears nowhere in the cut sheet or drawings.

1/2" hardboard/Masonite panel siding is nailed directly to the studs with no separate structural sheathing and no housewrap, so the siding IS the shear bracing. No let-in bracing or alternative is specified, and hardboard siding at grade on a skid building is a long-term rot risk.

The end walls intentionally have no top or bottom plates — siding is nailed straight to floor and rafters, with studs cut and notched around the rafters in place. It works but it is confusing if you have only ever framed conventionally, and it makes the end walls fussy to square.

Distribution is fragile: backroadhome.net is 1990s-era static HTML and the PDF is only reliably reachable through the Wayback Machine. The archived bytes have a broken cross-reference table and most PDF readers refuse to open them until you repair the file (qpdf in.pdf out.pdf) — hence the locally saved repaired copy.
Nothing in the PDF states a material cost, a build time, or a skill level, so you cannot compare it on those axes without doing your own takeoff.

Pages 1-9 = illustrated step-by-step instructions with jobsite photos; page 10 = CUT SHEET / Loading Sheet plus DOOR MATERIALS; pages 11-13 = three scanned drawing sheets (elevations; floor plan + floor framing; roof framing + wall section). No text layer on the drawing sheets (scanned raster).
plans.foundation: On-grade skid foundation. Three pressure-treated 4x4 skids run the 24' length, each spliced from two 12' pieces with 4' treated 2x4 scabs. Set them on bare ground or lift the framed floor and slide concrete blocks underneath, then level with shims ("roofing shingles make great shims"), treated 2x4 blocking, or whatever is needed. No slab, no footings, no frost depth, no anchoring or tie-down detail is given.
plans.floor_framing: 2x6 pressure-treated floor joists at 16" o.c., cut 189" long, spanning the 16' width; 19 joists total over the 24' length. 2x6 treated band boards along both 24' sides (4 pcs of 12' spliced into two 24' bands), joists nailed through the bands on 16" centers. The framed deck is positioned so the joists cantilever roughly 16" past each outer skid; joists are toenailed to the skids "every other one is sufficient." Deck is 3/4" plywood — 10 sheets 4x8 plus 4 pieces 4x4 — with staggered joints. Floor is framed, then squared by equalizing the diagonals, then leveled, then decked.
plans.wall_framing: 2x4 pine studs at 24" o.c., cut 65-1/2" (26 wall studs listed). 2x4 bottom plate, top plate and double top plate (12 pcs 2x4x12'); the instructions note that buildings wider than 16' need the top plate doubled with staggered joints. Side walls are laid out and framed flat on the finished deck, the siding is nailed on while flat, then the whole panel is tilted up: nail through the siding into the band board with 6d commons from outside, then through the bottom plate into the floor with 12d from inside. The end walls are framed AFTER the trusses are set and deliberately use no top or bottom plates — end studs are cut to length and notched around the rafters (8 pcs 2x4x12', 6 pcs 2x4x10', 4 pre-cut studs).
plans.roof: Site-built gambrel trusses at 24" o.c. Each truss is four 72" 2x6 pine segments: the two upper members are cut 20 degrees at the peak and 22-1/2 degrees at the lower joint, the two lower members are cut 22-1/2 degrees at both ends. Joints are joined with scrap 1/2" plywood gussets (39 listed) nailed with 4-5 nails per member; the section sheet calls the upper slope "2 x 6 PINE RAFTERS @ 5 ON 12 PITCH @ 24\" O.C." Trusses are assembled on the deck against stop blocks set exactly to the 16' building width and land directly over the studs. Sheathing is 1/2" CDX plywood (12 sheets 4x8 + 12 pcs 2x8) with staggered joints, nailed about every 8". Underlayment 15# felt (2 rolls, optional per the text), roofing 20 bundles of 20-year 3-tab seal-tab shingles, 3 pcs Z-bar flashing. Gable ends get fly rafters — 2x6 on the front, 2x4 on the rear (specified deliberately so the shingle courses "always work out on an even foot") — cut 72-1/2" with 20 deg / 22-1/2 deg ends, toenailed flat into the end truss, plus a 2x4 beveled overhang cut at 22-1/2 degrees running the full length of the building.
plans.siding: 1/2" Masonite-type hardboard panel siding with interlocking male/female vertical edges, nailed directly to the studs (no separate structural sheathing, no housewrap): 12 pcs 4x6 for the side walls and 12 pcs 4x8 for the end walls. Siding is flushed with the top of the 2x4 top plate and hangs 2" below the bottom plate. On the end walls the siding is run up past the rafters and trimmed off from the roof afterward (router with a panel bit, circular saw, or preferably a reciprocating saw). 1x3 outside corner trim, 8 pcs at 6'. The building is delivered "finished and ready to paint" — no finish schedule.
plans.wall_height: 6' — 65-1/2" studs plus plates; dimensioned as 6' on the front elevation
plans.overall_height: 14' to the ridge, dimensioned on the front elevation sheet
plans.doors: One pair of site-built swinging doors in the 16' front end wall, 60" total opening ("8' Wide Models use 48\" door – All wider models use the 60\" door"), roughly 72" tall per the section note. Each door is a 2x4 frame — 74" uprights, 23" stiles, a 2x6 23" base, corner blocks — held with corrugated fasteners, hinged to a 74" 2x4 jamb with one pair of 4" butt hinges, then a full sheet of siding is nailed over the whole assembly and the door outline is cut through the back of the siding, leaving three 4" tabs uncut so it stays square in transit. The jamb must stand 1/4" above the door top for swing clearance. A 60" 2x4 header is set 1/2" low to act as a doorstop, plus a 69" 2x4 lintel. Closes with a 4" hasp for a padlock. The male siding lip on one leaf overlaps the female edge of the other for a weather seal.
plans.windows: None. No windows, sashes, glazing or vents appear anywhere in the cut sheet or on the three drawing sheets. (The vendor's marketing photo shows a small gable vent that is not part of the plan.)
plans.loft: none — there are no loft or ceiling joists, no loft decking and no loft access in the cut sheet or drawings. The gambrel shape plus 6' walls and a 14' ridge leaves roughly 7'-8" of clear height under the peak, so a loft is easy to add, but you would be designing it yourself.
plans.skill_level: Beginner-to-intermediate DIY, explicitly written for a first-timer ("This was the first thing I have ever built in my life"), but a 16x24 with 8-foot-tall tilt-up wall panels and 16'-span gambrel trusses realistically needs two or three people and a good chop saw. The author flags the doors as "the most complicated part of the building."

_verification.notes:
CONFIRMED, character-by-character, against the actual PDF and the vendor pages:

- 13 pages (pdfinfo). Structure exactly as claimed: pages 1-9 = illustrated instructions, page 10 = "CUT SHEET (Loading Sheet)", pages 11-13 = three scanned drawing sheets. Sheet titles read "16' X 24' BONANZA" in the title block; cut-sheet header reads "BONANAZA 16 X 24" (sic) / "MODEL EBB-1624". All verbatim.
- Footprint 16x24 = 384 sq ft. Multiplies out correctly. FLOOR PLAN sheet is dimensioned 24' x 16'; SIDE ELEVATION 24', FRONT ELEVATION 16'.
- Wall height 6' and overall height 14' are both explicitly dimensioned on the FRONT ELEVATION. Correct.
- Doors in a 16' end wall, 60" opening: floor plan string reads 24-24-20-60-18-24-24; cut sheet has a 60" header and a 69" lintel; page 6 caption reads "8' Wide Models use 48" door - All wider models use the 60" door." Section adds "DOORS @ 72" HEIGHT". The record's con about the 60" opening being too narrow for a car is fair.
- Cut-sheet numbers in the pros all check out: 19 pcs 2x6 189" floor joists, 26 pcs 2x4 65-1/2" wall studs, 52 pcs 2x6 72" rafters (26 + 26), 2 pcs 2x4 74" jambs, 20 bundles 3-tab shingles, 2 rolls 15# felt, 3 pc Z-bar flashing, 7 lbs 12d and 7 lbs 6d common nails (plus 6 lbs roof tacks, which the record omits), 39 gussets, 4" hasp, DOOR MATERIALS sub-list (jambs/uprights/stiles/base/corner blocks/hinges).
- Arithmetic cross-checks all confirm the record's reading of the geometry: 19 joists at 16" o.c. = 18 spaces = 288" = 24' length; 26 studs at 24" o.c. = 13 per 24' sidewall x 2; 52 rafter segments / 4 = 13 trusses at 24" o.c. over 24'; 39 gussets / 13 = 3 per truss.
- Three 4x4 skids running the 24' length, spliced: 6 pcs 4x4 treated 12' + 6 pcs 2x4 treated 4' "Skid Splices" = 3 x 24' skids with two scabs each. FLOOR FRAMING sheet shows 3 skids under the joists ("TREATED 4X4 SKIDS BELOW JOISTS") with 16" cantilevers dimensioned at both edges. The record's engineering read is sound: 2x6 joists at 16" o.c. span only ~6'8" clear between skids with a 16" cantilever, so the joists are fine; the honest weakness is the 4x4 skids themselves and the ground bearing, which the con names correctly.
- Verbatim quotes verified in the PDF: "The size of the gussets is not critical", "nail about every 8 inches", "It's your building; you can do anything you want", "CUT SHEET (Loading Sheet)", "BONANAZA 16 X 24", "MODEL EBB-1624", "roofing shingles make great shims", "It allows the roofing shingles to always work out on an even foot", "Be sure to use 2x6's on the front and 2x4's on the back", the temporary 2x4 ledger trick, the pre-fab-doors-nailed-to-the-siding-then-saw-them-free method, and the male/female siding lap for the door weather seal. All present.
- No windows, no vents, no loft, no ceiling, no insulation, no electrical, no ramp: grep for windows/vent/loft/insulat/electric/ramp in the PDF text returns zero hits, and none appear in the cut sheet. Con is honest.
- Vendor claims all verified on http://www.backroadhome.net/fs-ibp-16w-bonanza-barn-plans.html: "Instant Download Building Plan Set #BP-101" verbatim, "Plans are $29.00", "Designs by Fred Strickland", "Sizes Included: 16'x12', 16x16', 16'x20' and 16'x24'", link to Backyard3.com. So price_usd 0 for the PDF plus the $29.00 #BP-101 bundle reference is accurate.
- Sibling free PDFs claim is exactly right. Wayback CDX on backroadhome.net turns up FS-B88.pdf, FS-B108.pdf, FS-B1624.pdf (Bonanza gambrel) and FS-O88.pdf, FS-O108.pdf, FS-O1624.pdf (Organizer gable) — 8x8 and 10x8 Bonanza, 8x8 / 10x8 / 16x24 Organizer, precisely as stated.
- Drawings are rotated 180 degrees inside the PDF (Page rot: 0, but the scanned images are upside down). Con confirmed.

IMAGE: /home/ethan/woodshed/assets/img/backroadhome-16x24-bonanza-gambrel.jpg is a real JPEG, 471x354, 34,066 bytes, and visually correct — a built gray/lavender gambrel barn-style shed with white-trimmed double doors centered in the gable end and a shingled gambrel roof, i.e. the Bonanza design. No fix needed. (The photo shows a small gable louver above the doors that the plan does not include — cosmetic only.)

COMPLETENESS HONESTY: good overall. The record does not oversell this as an engineered plan and its cons correctly flag the missing loads, grade, anchoring and stamped trusses. Two things it should add: (1) the free download is dead at source and survives only in the Wayback Machine; (2) the trusses have no bottom chord or collar tie in the material list at all, which is the single biggest structural gap in the package and also guts the "add your own loft" pro.

BIGGEST SINGLE ERROR: the "over a thousand sheds" quote does not exist in the cited PDF (it says "literally hundreds"), and "hand-lettered" is wrong — the sheets are CAD.

plans.summary: A complete 13-page DIY plan for a 16x24 (384 sq ft) gable-roof storage building on pressure-treated 4x4 skids, by production shed builder Fred Strickland, published as an ungated PDF on BackroadHome.net and now reachable only through the Wayback Machine. Pages 1-9 are illustrated step-by-step instructions with jobsite photos (floor on skids, sidewalls framed and sided flat on the deck then tipped up, gusseted rafter pairs, end walls, roof deck, fly rafters, shingles) plus a detailed prefab-door method where each door is built flat and nailed to its siding sheet before the wall is stood up. Page 10 is a full quantity takeoff titled CUT SHEET (Loading Sheet) with every piece cut to length, including a separate door materials list and nail/felt/shingle counts. Pages 11-13 are CAD sheets: front and side elevations (16 ft wide, 6 ft to the eave, 9 ft 7 in overall), floor plan plus floor framing plan, and roof framing plan plus a wall section with material callouts. It is a genuinely buildable set rather than a single framing detail, but it carries no engineering, no design loads and no window/vent details, and the same design was sold commercially inside plan set BP-101 for $29.00.
includes: 9 pages of illustrated step-by-step building instructions with construction photos
Front and side elevations with overall height (9'-7") and eave height (6')
Floor plan with stud layout, plus floor framing plan (skids, bands, joists)
Roof framing plan showing 2x6 common rafters at 24 in o.c. and ridge line
Wall section detail with material callouts and a rafter-cutting/gusset detail
Rafter length table for 8/10/12/16 ft wide Organizer models
One-page CUT SHEET (Loading Sheet): quantities, sizes and cut lengths for the whole building
Separate DOOR MATERIALS list plus the Doors Made Easy prefab-door walkthrough
Nail, felt, shingle, Z-flashing, corner trim and hardware quantities
pros: Genuinely complete for a free file: instructions, elevations, floor plan, floor framing, roof framing, wall section and a full cut list in one PDF
Cut sheet is a real takeoff with cut lengths (joists 189 in, wall studs 63-1/2 in, rafters 104 in long point to short point), so you can price and cut without doing your own math
4x4 skid foundation means no concrete, no footings - cheap and fast, can sit on grade or be lifted onto concrete blocks and shimmed level
Clear 16 ft interior span with no posts and 384 sq ft of floor - big enough for a real workshop or mower/ATV storage
Cost-efficient framing: studs and rafters at 24 in o.c., 4x8/4x6 panel siding, most parts land on even feet, so waste is low
Low tool bar: circular saw, hammer or nailer, drill; no engineered trusses to order and no crane, since walls are framed flat on the deck and tipped up
The prefab door method (doors built flat, hinged to the jamb, nailed to a siding sheet, then cut free on site) is the strongest idea in the plan and saves real time
Sequencing advice comes from someone who states he built hundreds of these, so it reads as practical rather than theoretical
One instruction set plus the rafter table covers the 8/10/12/16 ft wide models, which makes resizing (e.g. to 16x20) straightforward
cons: No engineering: no snow or wind design loads, no stamp, no anchoring or uplift detail - hard to permit, and 384 sq ft is far above typical permit-exempt sizes

The trusses are only rafter pairs joined by a plywood gusset at the peak: 26 rafters and 13 gussets are listed, but no bottom chords, ceiling joists or collar ties, so a 16 ft span at 5:12 depends on the walls resisting rafter thrust
Internal contradictions: the wall section labels 2x4 rafters while the cut sheet and roof framing plan call 26 pcs of 2x6 at 104 in; the text says studs are 65 in while the cut sheet says 63-1/2 in
Only three drawing sheets for a 384 sq ft building - no dimensioned door/rough-opening detail, no end-wall stud elevation, no gable framing dimensions, no electrical
No windows, no vents, no ramp and no loft in the plan or cut sheet (the vendor photo shows a gable vent that is not listed anywhere)
Dated 1/2 in Masonite hardboard panel siding that deliberately hangs 2 in below the band board, close to grade - needs immediate paint and is prone to edge swelling
Only three skids under a 24 ft floor with 16 in cantilevers: demands a well-drained, carefully levelled pad and is not a frost-protected foundation
Low headroom: 6 ft to the eave and doors only 72 in tall, tight for a workshop bench wall or tall equipment

Source site is effectively dead - the live PDF URL no longer serves the file, so the archived copy (saved locally here) is the only access; the design remains copyright Fred Strickland and was sold for $29.00

plans.foundation: On-grade pressure-treated wood skids: three 24 ft long 4x4 P.T. skids (six 12 ft pieces spliced with 2x4 treated splices) set under the joists 16 in in from the joist ends so the floor cantilevers; optionally lifted onto concrete blocks and shimmed level (roofing shingles or 2x4 treated blocks suggested as shims). No slab, footings or anchors.
plans.floor_framing: 2x6 pressure-treated floor joists at 16 in o.c. (19 joists cut 189 in) spanning the 16 ft width, 2x6 P.T. band boards marked on 16 in centers, joists toenailed to the skids (every other joist called sufficient), 3/4 in CDX plywood decking with staggered joints. Clear joist span between skids works out to roughly 6 ft 8 in.
plans.wall_framing: 2x4 pine studs at 24 in o.c.; wall studs cut 63-1/2 in per the cut sheet (the text says 65 in). Side walls are framed flat on the deck with the siding nailed on, then stood up; siding runs 72 in so it laps 2 in above the top plate and 2 in below the bottom plate. Single bottom plate with doubled, staggered top plates on runs over 16 ft. End walls get no top or bottom plates - studs are nailed to the floor and notched around the rafters. Door opening uses a 60 in header plus a 69 in lintel with a 2x4 stud each side.
plans.wall_height: 6 ft to the eave per the front elevation (studs 63-1/2 in per the cut sheet, 65 in per the instruction text)
plans.overall_height: 9 ft 7 in per the front elevation
plans.roof: Gable, 5-in-12 pitch, 22-1/2 degree plumb cuts. Site-built rafter pairs (26 pcs 2x6 at 104 in long point to short point) joined by 13 plywood gussets at the peak, set 24 in o.c. directly over the studs. 1/2 in CDX plywood decking, 15 lb felt underlayment, 20-year 3-tab seal-tab shingles (16 bundles). 2x6 fly rafters on the front gable and 2x4 on the rear (deliberate, so shingle courses work out on an even foot), with a 2x4 beveled overhang board cut at 22-1/2 degrees. Note the wall section labels the rafters 2x4 while the cut sheet and framing plan call 2x6.

Siding is nailed on while the wall lies flat and is trimmed to the roof line afterwards with a reciprocating saw.

_verification.notes:
EVERYTHING ELSE CHECKS OUT, and most of it checks out unusually well.

CONFIRMED verbatim / from the source:
- Page count: pdfinfo says Pages: 13. Record's 13-page claim is exact. Pages 1-9 are instructions (the archived vendor page independently says "a nine page instruction booklet"), p10 is the cut sheet, p11-13 are CAD sheets.
- Footprint / sqft: p11 title block reads "16' X 24' ORGANIZER"; front elevation dimensioned 16', side elevation 24'; p13 FLOOR PLAN dimensioned 24' x 16'. 16 x 24 = 384 sq ft. Correct.
- Model number: p10 header reads "CUT SHEET (Loading Sheet) / ORGANIZER 16 x 24    MODEL EBO-1624". Both quoted strings verified character-for-character. (Nuance: "MODEL EBO-1624" is on the cut sheet, not in the CAD title block, which reads only "16' X 24' ORGANIZER".)
- Heights: p11 FRONT ELEVATION dimensions read 9'-7" overall and 6' to the eave. Both correct.
- Roof pitch: p12 wall section reads "2 X 4 PINE RAFTERS @ 5 ON 12 PITCH @ 24\" O.C." 5-in-12 confirmed, and it checks arithmetically - 96 in run x sqrt(1+25/144) = 104.00 in, exactly the cut sheet's "26  2x6 Pine  104\"  Rafters (Long point to short point)".
- Cut list numbers quoted in pros: joists 189", wall studs 63 1/2", rafters 104" - all three verified verbatim on p10.
- The record's two claimed internal contradictions are both real: p2 text says "the siding is cut 72\" and the studs are 65\"" vs cut sheet "63 1/2\""; p12 wall section labels "2 X 4 PINE RAFTERS" while the roof framing plan and cut sheet both call 2x6 at 104". Good catch by the extractor.
- "Rafter length table for 8/10/12/16 ft wide Organizer models" - confirmed on p6 ("Rafter Lengths: 8' Wide Models = 52\", 10' = 65\", 12' = 78\", 16' = 104\""), alongside the "Cutting the Rafters" and "Plywood Gusset" details under the heading "Organizer Wall Section Details".
- "Doors Made Easy" (p7) and the prefab-door walkthrough (p8-9, incl. cutting all but three 4-inch sections so the door travels intact) - verified verbatim.
- 26 rafters + 13 gussets and NO bottom chords, ceiling joists, collar ties or even a ridge board anywhere in the cut sheet or the roof framing plan. The con about 16 ft span at 5:12 relying on the walls to resist rafter thrust is sound and is the single most important warning in the record.
- Masonite: p12 wall section reads "1/2\" MASONITE SIDING"; p2 confirms the siding "stick up past the top of the wall 2\" and hang down past the bottom 2\"". Con verified.
- Three skids with 16 in cantilevers: p13 FLOOR FRAMING shows "TREATED 4X4 SKIDS BELOW JOISTS", "4 X 4 SKID", "2 X 6 BAND", "2 X 6 FLOOR JOISTS @ 16\" O.C." with 16" cantilever dimensions at both ends. Cut sheet's 6 pcs of 4x4 x 12' = three 24 ft skid lines. Confirmed.
- No windows, no vents, no ramp, no loft anywhere in the cut sheet - confirmed. And the vendor photo really does show a gable vent that is not in the takeoff (visible in the local image), so that con is accurate.
- No engineering: grep for snow/wind/load/design load/stamp across the extracted text returns only "Loading Sheet". Confirmed.
- Vendor attribution: archived sales page is titled "Backyard Organizer Do-It-Yourself Shed Plans from Backyard3.com" and credits "Professional builder Fred Strickland". "BackroadHome.net / Backyard3 - designs by Fred Strickland" is correct. Refund context ("sixty day money-back guarantee") also real.
- p1 says "after building literally hundreds of them", which is what the record's pro claims. (The sales page inflates this to "more than a thousand sheds" - the record wisely used the PDF's own number.)
- "no 16x20 PDF is archived" - confirmed. A CDX filter for FS-O* on backroadhome.net returns only FS-O1624.pdf, FS-O108.pdf and FS-O88.pdf.

IMAGE: /home/ethan/woodshed/assets/img/backroadhome-16x24-gable.jpg is a real JPEG (JFIF, 487x325, 42,038 bytes) showing a tan panel-sided gable shed with 60-inch double doors in the gable end, a gable vent above them, shingled 5:12 roof and gable-end overhangs, sitting on skids/blocks. It is the correct building. No fix needed.

ENGINEERING SANITY: no bad numbers found. 2x6 joists at 16 in o.c. span only about 78.5 in between skids (189 in less two 16 in cantilevers, three skids), which is well inside allowable - the record does not overstate the floor. 2x6 rafters at 24 in o.c. over a 104 in sloped length are fine as members; the real risk is thrust, which the record already flags. Cut sheet quantities cross-check internally (12 sheets of 4x6 siding = 48 lf = two 24 ft sidewalls; 12 pcs of 2x4x12' = 144 lf = bottom + top + double top plate on both sidewalls; 26 studs = 13 per 24 ft wall at 24 in o.c.).

THREE THINGS THE RECORD MISSED that belong in cons:
1. A THIRD internal contradiction on door height: the p12 wall section says "DOORS @ 72\" HEIGHT" while the p7 door detail dimensions the door uprights and jambs at 74". The record's "doors only 72 in tall" is defensible (it matches the section) but the plan disagrees with itself by 2 inches.
2. The skids are NOT continuous 24 ft timbers - the cut sheet calls "6  4x4 Treated Pine  12'  Skids" plus "6  2x4 Treated Pine  4'  Skid Splices", i.e. each 24 ft skid is two 12 ft pieces butt-spliced with scabbed 2x4s. For a foundation member that is a meaningful weakness and is not mentioned anywhere in the record.
3. Sheet-to-page mapping in the summary is inverted: p11 = elevations, p12 = roof framing plan + wall section, p13 = floor plan + floor framing plan. The record lists them as elevations / floor plan / roof framing, implying p12 is the floor plan.

MINOR: footprint_note says "the vendor's sales page listed 16x12, 16x16, 16x20 and 16x24". True for the 16 ft wide family, but the page actually advertises nineteen sizes from 8'x8' up to 16'x24' - worth stating so a reader knows the 16x20 is a real catalog size, not an extrapolation.

Bottom line: the record is substantively accurate and unusually well-sourced for a Wayback-only PDF. Three real defects (truss-count arithmetic, invented "BP-101" product code, and a false "no dimensioned door detail" con), plus a $29 vs $29.00 precision issue. Nothing that changes the recommendation - this is a genuinely complete free plan set for a 384 sq ft building and it is honest about lacking engineering.

plans.style: Single-slope lean-to / skillion storage shed on skids, T1-11 siding, metal roof, man door on the front and 8 ft double doors on one side
plans.price: $8 (Gumroad, "16x16 Lean to Shed Plans", 34-page PDF). The illustrated step-by-step article itself is free to read.
plans.summary: A free two-part illustrated tutorial from HowToSpecialist for a 16x16 (256 sq ft) lean-to storage shed built on 4x4 skids, with an $8 / 34-page PDF version sold through Gumroad. The design is 2x4 stick framing at 16" on center over 2x6 floor joists, wrapped in 5/8" T1-11 siding, with a single-slope roof of 220"-long 2x6 or 2x8 rafters at 16" on center, 1x4 purlins and 12 metal roof panels (3'x10'). It has a shop-built 36"x80" man door and two 32"x36" PVC windows on the front wall plus a shop-built 8 ft double door (two 48"x80" leaves) on one side. Overall height is 148 3/4" (12'-4 3/4") at the high side over an 86 1/2" tall wall frame, and the author states the build "will be an expensive construction 2000+ usd" and takes about one week per part.
includes: Free Part 1 web article: floor frame, skids, floor sheathing, front/back/side wall frames, wall assembly and the raised top back wall that creates the lean-to slope (Steps 1-4)
Free Part 2 web article (16x16-lean-to-shed-roof-plans): rafters, side roof supports, T1-11 siding, purlins, roof trims, metal roofing, windows, front man door and side double doors (Steps 5-9)
3D SketchUp-style step diagrams with dimension callouts on nearly every step
Overall-dimensions elevation drawing (192" x 192", 148 3/4" and 102 3/4" heights)
Free-on-page Cut & Shopping list for Part 2 (siding, rafters, purlins, roofing, trims, doors, jambs, hardware)
Tool list and a stated time estimate ('One week')
$8 Gumroad PDF: 1 file, 34 pages, 1.41 MB - step-by-step diagrams, step-by-step instructions, full cut list, full shopping list, full tool list, imperial measurements, personal use only
Reader-submitted 'Made from this plan' photos
pros: Real 256 sq ft of usable space at a genuine DIY difficulty level - all conventional 2x4/2x6 stick framing, no engineered components, no crane, no concrete slab required.

Lean-to/single-slope roof is the simplest possible roof to frame (no ridge, no trusses, no hip cuts) and the author notes it is 'the ideal choice if you want to build it near the property line' because everything drains one way.

Floor is properly supported: 2x6 joists at 16" on center bear on four 4x4 skids spaced 59 1/4" apart, so the joist clear spans are only about 5 ft - no over-spanned floor, which is a common flaw in free shed plans this size.
On-grade skid foundation over a stripped-and-gravelled pad means no footings, no concrete pour and no frost-depth excavation - by far the cheapest foundation for this footprint.

8 ft wide double doors on the side plus a separate 36"x80" man door on the front - wide enough to roll in a mower, ATV or workbench, and the two doors let you use it as a workshop without blocking access.
Two 32"x36" front windows are already framed into the plan, so it works as a hobby room / workshop rather than a windowless box.
The complete illustrated tutorial is free to read; the $8 PDF is optional convenience plus the Part 1 cut list, so you can fully evaluate the design before paying anything.

Author explicitly says the openings are adjustable ('You can adjust the size of the openings to suit your needs', 'You can play with the location for the windows') and that stud length on the top back wall sets the roof slope, so the design is easy to customise.
cons: Biggest structural concern: the rafters are single 220" (20 ft stock) 2x6 or 2x8 members at 16" on center spanning the full 16 ft wall-to-wall with NO intermediate beam, no truss and no collar ties. The author only offers 'use 2x6 or 2x8 lumber (read the local codes for best choice)' with no span table, snow load or species/grade guidance. A 16 ft clear span is beyond common 2x8 roof-rafter span tables, so this roof needs to be checked - and probably upsized or given a mid-span beam - anywhere with real snow load.

Nothing is engineered or stamped. No load calculations, no wind/seismic detail, no hold-downs or anchorage of the building to the ground - it simply sits on skids on gravel, which many jurisdictions will not accept for a 256 sq ft permitted structure.

256 sq ft is over the permit-exempt threshold in most US jurisdictions (commonly 100-200 sq ft), so this will very likely need a permit - and these drawings are unlikely to be sufficient submittal documents as-is.

The Part 1 Cut & Shopping list (skids, floor joists, floor sheets, wall plates and studs, headers) has been REMOVED from the free page and replaced with an 'UNLOCK PREMIUM PLANS FOR CUT & SHOPPING LISTS' link to the $8 Gumroad product. You can follow Part 1's diagrams but you cannot price or buy the floor and wall lumber from the free page.
The page's own text is wrong about the area - it claims '192 sq ft floor surface' for a 16x16 building (256 sq ft). Small errors like this are a warning to verify every quantity yourself.

Metal panels are screwed straight to 1x4 purlins with no solid sheathing and no underlayment or condensation control mentioned. If you want asphalt shingles instead you must add a full layer of roof sheathing that is not in the material list.
Roof slope is shallow (about 3:12, derived from 148 3/4" high side vs 102 3/4" low side - the plan never states a pitch), which limits roofing choices and is poor for heavy snow shedding.

Cost driver: 13 pieces of 20 ft 2x6/2x8 for the rafters. Twenty-foot stock is expensive, often special-order, and awkward to transport and lift solo. Add 21 sheets of 5/8" T1-11 and 12 metal panels - the author's own '2000+ usd' estimate is from a 2021 article and is optimistic at today's prices.
Doors are shop-built 2x4 frames clad in T1-11 rather than pre-hung units - cheap, but they need careful hinging and weatherstripping and they sag over time on an 8 ft double opening.

Split across two web pages with only a $8 PDF tying them together; the Part 2 URL is barely archived, so the free roof/door instructions could disappear from the live site the way the Part 1 cut list did.
No refunds allowed on the Gumroad purchase (policy updated 2026-01-11).
No loft, no insulation detail, no electrical, no ventilation/soffit detail and no interior finish guidance.

plans.format: Free two-part HTML step-by-step tutorial with 3D rendered diagrams (Part 1 = floor and walls, Part 2 = roof, siding and doors), plus an optional paid PDF sold on Gumroad (1 file, 34 pages, 1.41 MB, imperial units, personal use only)
plans.page_count: 34 pages (the paid Gumroad PDF). The free version is 2 web articles covering Steps 1-9.
plans.foundation: On-grade skid foundation: four 4x4 skids spaced 59 1/4" on center, locked to the floor frame with rafter ties and 1 1/2" structural screws (at least 2 ties per skid). Author instructs you to remove the vegetation layer, level the surface and apply a layer of gravel for drainage. No concrete, footings or anchors specified.
plans.floor_framing: 2x6 joists at 16" on center, assembled with 3 1/2" screws through the rim into the joist ends; frame is 192" x 189" and is checked square by measuring diagonals. Decked with 3/4" plywood, edges flush and no gaps, fastened with 1 5/8" screws every 8". Joists bear on the four 4x4 skids, so clear spans are about 5 ft.
plans.wall_framing: 2x4 studs at 16" on center (studs 78 1/2" long; wall frames drawn 86 1/2" overall), assembled with 3 1/2" screws through the plates. Double 2x6 headers over the door and window openings with a 1/2" plywood spacer sandwiched between, glued and screwed from both sides with 2 1/2" screws. Double studs with 1/2" plywood spacers at both ends of each wall. Walls are screwed down through the bottom plate into the floor with 3 1/2" screws and tied to each other with 2 1/2" screws. A separate 2x4 "top back wall frame" is added above the back wall to create the lean-to slope - the author notes you can change the stud length there to change the slope.

plans.roof: Single-slope lean-to roof. 13 rafters cut from 2x6 or 2x8 lumber, 220" long with birdsmouth cuts at both ends, fitted every 16" on center with rafter ties and 1 1/2" structural screws - spanning the full 16 ft with no intermediate support. 2x4 side lean-to supports (pocket-holed, 2 1/2" screws). 30 pieces of 1x4 purlins 106" long screwed to the rafters with 2 1/2" screws. 12 metal roof panels (3'x10') screwed directly to the purlins; asphalt shingles offered only as a substitution (would require adding sheathing). 1x8 roof trims front and back to hide the rafter ends, plus 1x8 side trims. Generous overhangs on all four sides (roof plan approx 212 1/4" x 217"). Slope is never stated numerically - approximately 3:12 by derivation.
plans.siding: 5/8" T1-11 siding panels - 21 sheets of 4'x8' plus cut pieces, nailed with 6-8d nails every 8" along the framing, no gaps between panels. Optional 1x4 decorative corner trims and 1x4 decorative window trims.

plans.summary: A single-sheet USDA / Cooperative Extension working drawing (title block: "SHEEP SHED", "USDA / EX. 5019 / SHEET 1 OF 1", issued by Cooperative Extension Work in Agriculture and Home Economics, State of North Dakota, North Dakota Agricultural College and USDA cooperating), still hosted free by NDSU as an image-only scanned PDF with no text layer. It draws a 16'-0" x 24'-0" post-frame shed: 4x4 posts at 6'-0" o.c. on 8"-diameter concrete piers set below frost and strapped down with 1-1/2" x 1/4" x 18" strap iron, 2x4 girts, vertical 1x12 boards with 1x3 battens, 2x4 rafters at 24" o.c. on a 1x6 ridge board at 6:12 pitch, board sheathing under "prepared roofing", and a 12" galvanized ventilator hood at the ridge. Post/eave height is 6'-0" with 7'-6" to the pair of 1x6 ties at each post; there is no floor system at all (the 1x4 T&G in the bill of materials is explicitly "(doors)"), so it is designed for an earth floor. The sheet includes perspective, plan, south elevation, cross section, a 3/4"=1'-0" section and lower-jamb plan of the counterweighted south door, a feed-rack detail, and a complete Bill of Materials — but no step-by-step instructions, no design loads, no rafter cutting detail, and no engineer's stamp.
includes: Perspective view (rendered 3/4 view of the finished shed)
PLAN at 1/4"=1'-0" with 16'-0" x 24'-0" dimensions, pier layout, door/gate locations and feed-rack layout
SOUTH ELEVATION at 1/4"=1'-0" with gable-end opening dimensions (2'-5", 4'-0", 2'-10", 4'-0", 2'-5")
CROSS SECTION at 1/2"=1'-0" with post height, tie height, pitch triangle, pier and feed-rack section
SECTION OF SOUTH DOOR at 3/4"=1'-0" plus PLAN OF LOWER JAMB (batten slot, cleat, removable 2x6 threshold, 6" hinge, sash cord)
FEED RACK detail (9'-0" long x 3'-0" wide, 1x2 slats 6" o.c.)
Full BILL OF MATERIALS: concrete, lumber cut lengths, and miscellaneous hardware including nails by the pound
Counterweighted-door hardware callouts (2" and 3" pulleys, 1/8" wire cable, 1/4" sash cord, 20 lb counterweights)
pros: Genuinely free, no email wall, no upsell, no account — a direct 98 KB PDF download from a .edu server that returns 200 today.

The Bill of Materials is complete and on the page: every lumber piece with count and exact length, plus concrete quantities, roofing squares, hinges, hasps, bolts and nails by the pound. You can price the whole build at a lumberyard from this one sheet.

384 sq ft (16x24) sits right in the target range, and post-frame construction at 6'-0" o.c. is the cheapest and fastest way to get that footprint standing — 10 posts, no continuous foundation, no floor slab, no floor joists.

Foundation demand is minimal: ten 8"-diameter concrete piers below frost, total 3 sacks cement / 9 cu ft sand / 15 cu ft gravel. That is hand-mixable in a wheelbarrow, no concrete truck, no excavator.

Roof framing is dead simple stick framing — 2x4 rafters at 24" o.c. against a 1x6 ridge board over a 16 ft span, with a 2x4 knee brace and two 1x6 ties at each post. No trusses to buy, no crane, no truss delivery.
The 6:12 gable sheds snow well and the ridge ventilator plus board-and-batten walls make it very forgiving of moisture — good for unheated storage in a cold climate.
Well-detailed where it counts for a beginner: the door section is drawn at 3/4"=1'-0" with the jamb, batten slot, cleat, strap anchor and removable threshold all called out.
Public-domain federal/extension drawing, so there is no license, no refund question, and you can print, mark up and hand it to a helper freely.
cons: This is a livestock building, not a storage shed or workshop. There is NO floor system anywhere in the drawing — the only T&G in the bill of materials is annotated "(doors)". You are building over dirt unless you design and pay for a slab or a floor frame yourself.

NOT a modern step-by-step plan set. One sheet, no written instructions, no build sequence, no cut diagrams, no rafter bird's-mouth or plumb-cut detail, no nailing schedule, no rough-opening schedule. You must already know how to lay out and cut rafters.

No engineering. There is no engineer's stamp, no code edition, no snow/wind/live-load values, and no bracing calculation. A 2x4 rafter at 24" o.c. over a 16 ft span with only a mid-height tie will not satisfy many modern inspectors, especially in a high-snow county.

Only the two side elevations you actually get are the perspective and the south elevation. There is no north/east/west elevation and no side-wall framing elevation, so the girt spacing on the 24 ft walls has to be inferred.

6'-0" post/eave height is low. Interior headroom is 7'-6" to the ties at mid-span only; along the walls you have about 6 ft. That is cramped for a workshop and rules out most shelving-plus-standing-work layouts.

Widest opening is only about 4'-0" (two ~4 ft counterweighted door leaves in the south gable end, plus a 3'-0" x 7'-0" door). Nothing here will pass a garden tractor with a deck, let alone a vehicle, without redesigning the end wall.

Hardware and materials are period-specific and partly obsolete: "prepared roofing", 4-light sash windows measured by glass size (10"x12" and 12"x16"), sash cord, strap iron, 20 lb counterweights, board roof sheathing (620 ft BM) rather than plywood or OSB. Expect to substitute and re-estimate.
Image-only scan with no OCR text layer — every dimension must be read off a hand-lettered 1950s-era blueprint, and some small callouts are near the edge of legibility even at 200 dpi.

The plan sheet is undated and there is no accompanying web page: the NDSU /aben-plans/ directory index now returns a soft 404, so there is no vendor description, revision date, or support contact behind it.
The pier layout is dimensioned only as "below frost" with no depth number, so the single most site-dependent detail is left entirely to you.

plans.footprint_note: 16'-0" x 18'-0" (288 sq ft) as dimensioned on the Fig. 2 "PLAN" view of Plan 311, the combination garage-and-shop. This is a single illustrated figure inside a 16-page extension bulletin, not a standalone dimensioned plan set. The bulletin's written sizing guidance is separate and slightly larger: "For a combination garage and shop, the floor should be at least 12x18 feet, altho 18x20 feet is better," and if the shop is part of a machine shed "one dimension will usually be 18 feet and the other will vary between 14 and 20 feet." plans.style: Stud-frame hip-roof garage/workshop on a concrete perimeter foundation with a concrete slab floor; one-fourth pitch (6-in-12) roof; clear span, no interior posts

plans.summary: "The Farm Shop," University of Minnesota Agricultural Extension Special Bulletin 190 (September 1937, by C. H. Christopherson, H. B. White and L. W. Neubauer), is a free 16-page scanned PDF that combines written construction specifications for a farm workshop with three plan figures. The in-scope building is Fig. 2, Plan 311 "Garage and Shop": a 16'-0" x 18'-0" (288 sq ft) clear-span frame building with a hip roof, shown as a front elevation, a wall/eave section carrying framing callouts, and a dimensioned floor plan with the shop layout (workbench, carpenter's and machinist's vises, post drill, tool cabinet, shelves). Framing per the figure is 2x4 studs at 2'-0" o.c. on a 2x4 sill, doubled 2x4 top plates, 2x4 rafters at 2'-0" o.c. with 2x4 lookouts at 2'-0" o.c. and roughly 18 in. of eave, and 2x6 ties at 4'-0" o.c.; the body text adds that ties and rafters "should be braced with 1x6-inch boards." Openings are a pair of 4'-0" x 7'-6" swing doors on 10-in. heavy T hinges with a concrete incline apron, a 2'-8" x 6'-8" service door, and four 6-light sash of 10x12-in. glass. The prose section specifies a concrete foundation about 18 in. into the ground, 6 in. thick at the top and 10-12 in. at the base, at least 6 in. above grade with anchor bolts for the sill and reinforcing at the corners; a concrete floor sloped 1 in. in 10 ft toward the doorway (rammed earth as a cheap alternative); board-and-batten or drop siding over building paper, boarded and optionally insulated inside if heated; a one-fourth pitch roof covered with wood shingles, galvanized iron, composition shingles or roll roofing; and a brick or tile chimney extending 3 ft above the roof if a forge or stove is used. It is a design guide plus one figure — there is no bill of materials, cut list, or rafter layout, and the framing is 1937-vintage and well below modern prescriptive code.

pros: Genuinely free, no email or account required; direct PDF download from a university digital repository and public-domain-era US extension material
Slab-on-grade with a 2x4 sill means no floor joists, beams or piers to build — the floor is the foundation, which is durable, drive-in capable and rot-proof for a workshop
16x18 ft (288 sq ft) is a clear span with no interior posts, unlike the companion Plan 208 machine shed which relies on 6x6 posts and a 3-2x10 girder
Hip roof at one-fourth pitch keeps overall height low and sheds wind well; roughly 18 in. of lookout-framed eave protects board siding
Rare among shed plans in specifying a heatable, insulatable shop: inside board sheathing, building paper, loose fill insulation, and a brick or tile chimney 3 ft above the roof for a stove or forge
Openings are sized for real equipment: 8 ft of double door (12 ft doorway recommended for large machines), a separate 2'-8" x 6'-8" service door, and a concrete incline apron so you can drive in
Four 6-light 10x12-in. sash arranged for cross ventilation with two windows over the workbench, one at each vise — daylighting is designed, not an afterthought
Complete interior shop layout (workbench, two vises, post drill, tool cabinet, shelves) is drawn to the same plan, so the space planning is usable even if you re-frame the shell to modern code
Bonus buildable: the Fig. 3 Plan 170 12-ft farm workbench is separately dimensioned
cons: This is a design guide with one figure, not a plan set: no bill of materials, no cut list, no rafter or hip-jack layout, no fastener schedule, no sheathing plan. You detail and quantify everything yourself.

1937 framing is substantially under-built by modern standards: 2x4 rafters at 2'-0" o.c. over a 16 ft span, 2x6 ties at only 4'-0" o.c., 2x4 studs at 2'-0" o.c., and a single 2x4 sill. Expect to upsize members and tighten spacing for any snow-load jurisdiction.

No engineered trusses and no truss drawing — the hip roof must be hand-cut, which is the hardest framing task in the whole building and is exactly the part the figure does not detail (no rafter lengths, plumb/seat cuts, hip or jack layout).

Permit-unfriendly as drawn: no design loads, no species/grade, no shear or uplift bracing beyond '1x6-inch boards', and the publisher itself warns the bulletin 'may not reflect current scientific knowledge or recommendations.'

Foundation and floor are the dominant cost and the hardest DIY step: a concrete perimeter wall about 18 in. deep plus a full slab plus an exterior concrete incline. Slab thickness, mix, and reinforcing schedule are never given (only 'reinforcing rods should be used at the corners' and an alternative 4x12-in. footing).
An 18-in. foundation depth is shallow for Minnesota frost; the bulletin gives no frost-depth requirement and the section simply labels the depth 'Variable'.

Specified materials are period products — wood shingles laid 4 to 4-1/2 in. to the weather, galvanized iron roofing, roll roofing, drop siding, dressed-and-matched interior boards, building paper, dry shavings or shredded flax straw insulation. No plywood/OSB, housewrap or modern underlayment guidance, so material substitution is on you.

The original blueprint sheets for Plan 311 (and Plans 208 and 170) were mail-order items from the Bulletin Department, University Farm, St. Paul, listed in Special Bulletin 111. That ordering channel no longer exists, so the printed figure in this PDF is all you get.
Scan legibility: the figure is a 1937 halftone, and several callouts (18 in. eave, 8'-6", 6'-10") are only readable when the page is rendered at high resolution and zoomed.
No cost estimate, no build time, no skill-level rating anywhere in the document.
No loft or attic storage — 2x6 ties at 4'-0" o.c. are collar/ceiling ties, not a storage floor, and no ceiling or attic access is drawn.
The written size guidance (12x18 minimum, 18x20 better) conflicts slightly with the 16x18 figure, so you must choose which to build to.

plans.foundation: Concrete perimeter foundation. Verbatim: "The foundation should be of concrete, extending about 18 inches into the ground. A footing will not be needed if the soil is uniformly hard. The foundation should be 6 inches thick at the top and 10 to 12 inches thick at the base. If a 4x12-inch footing is used, the foundation may be 6 inches thick. In either case the foundation should extend at least 6 inches above the ground level." Anchor bolts are to be embedded in the concrete to attach the sills, and reinforcing rods used at the corners "as these are the weak spots in most foundations." The Fig. 2 section shows the foundation with the depth below grade labeled "Variable" and a 6-in. exposure above grade.
plans.floor_framing: None — there is no wood floor system. The floor is a concrete slab poured inside the foundation ("Concrete Floor" on the Plan 311 plan view), sloped about 1 inch in 10 feet toward the doorway, with a "Concrete Incline" apron outside the double doors to drive machinery in. A 2x4 sill sits on the foundation and carries the studs. The bulletin allows a rammed earth floor as a cost substitute "provided it is kept several inches above the outside ground level." Floor drains are mentioned but discouraged because water freezes in the drain pipes in cold weather. Slab thickness and reinforcement are not stated.
plans.wall_framing: 2x4 studs at 2'-0" o.c. on a 2x4 sill, capped with doubled 2x4 top plates ("2 - 2\"x4\" Plates" on the Fig. 2 section). Studs are anchored via the sill and foundation anchor bolts. Walls may alternatively be non-frame: "The farm shop may be of frame construction, or it may be of fireproof materials such as brick, tile, or concrete blocks." No corner bracing, headers, or shear detail is specified for the walls.
plans.roof: Hip roof at one-fourth pitch, shown in the Fig. 2 section as a 6-in rise over a 12-in run (6:12). Text: "For a combination shop and garage or a separate shop building, the hip roof or a gable roof will be satisfactory. It should be framed with 2x4-inch rafters, 2 feet on centers, and with 2x6-inch ties, 4 feet on centers. A one-fourth pitch roof is recommended. With less pitch the roof would not drain properly, and with more pitch the cost would be greater." The section adds 2x4 lookouts at 2'-0" o.c. carrying an eave overhang dimensioned about 18 in. Ties and rafters "should be braced with 1x6-inch boards." On an extra wide building 2x6 rafters would be used. Covering options given: wood shingles (best grade, laid 4 or 4-1/2 in. to the weather), galvanized iron roofing properly coated with zinc, composition shingles, or roll roofing. No trusses, no engineering, no rafter span table, no ridge/hip member sizes.
plans.siding: "Vertical boards with battens are frequently used in frame construction. This makes an inexpensive covering which will last for years because the boards dry off quickly after a rain. Either vertical or horizontal drop siding may be used." Building paper is recommended between the studding and the boards to keep out wind. If the shop is heated, the walls should also be boarded on the inside with dressed and matched lumber, with cavity insulation "ideal" but potentially too costly unless dry shavings, shredded flax straw or similar fibrous materials are locally cheap. The Fig. 2 front elevation depicts horizontal drop siding.
plans.doors: Plan 311 figure: a pair of side-hinged double doors, each leaf 4'-0" x 7'-6" (8 ft total opening), hung on 10-in. heavy T hinges per the front elevation, opening onto the concrete incline; plus a 2'-8" x 6'-8" service door in the same wall near the corner. General text guidance: "Double doors having a total width of 8 feet and a height of 8 feet will make it possible to bring into the shop most of the farm machines. A doorway 12 feet wide would be better for bringing in the large machines for overhauling. The doors may be hinged or hung on a track." A service door is recommended on the side nearest the house, and a connecting door between machine shed and shop where applicable. Note the 8 ft door height in the text differs from the 7'-6" leaf height dimensioned on the Plan 311 figure. No door construction/member sizes are given.
plans.windows: Four windows, each a 6-light sash of 10x12-inch glass, called out on the Plan 311 figure as "6 lt. 10\"x12\"". Text: "The shop should have windows large enough to admit plenty of light for doing all kinds of repair work and arranged to provide good cross ventilation. Two windows should be provided over the workbench, one at each vise. Four windows, each consisting of six 10x12-inch lights would be sufficient for the average shop." The Plan 311 plan view shows four openings — one in the rear wall, one in the left wall, and two in the workbench wall (matching the "one at each vise" rule). No rough opening sizes, headers, or sash details are given.
plans.wall_height: 8'-6" from the floor/sill to the top of the doubled 2x4 plate, per the vertical dimension on the Fig. 2 section. A second vertical dimension of 6'-10" appears on the same section (unlabeled — most likely the window head or sill height above grade); the grade line is drawn about 6 in. below the floor.
plans.overall_height: not stated
plans.loft: not stated — no loft, attic floor, or ceiling is drawn for Plan 311. The only horizontal framing above the walls is 2x6 ties at 4'-0" o.c., which are collar/ceiling ties, not a storage floor.

plans.permit_notes: Treat this as reference material, not a permit set. There are no design loads, no lumber species or grade, no engineer's stamp, no shear wall or uplift/hold-down detail, and no plan sheet at a usable scale — only one figure. The framing as drawn (2x4 rafters at 2'-0" o.c. over a 16 ft span, 2x6 ties at 4'-0" o.c., 2x4 studs at 2'-0" o.c., single 2x4 sill, ~18 in. foundation depth) will not satisfy modern IRC prescriptive tables in a snow-load or frost region, and a 288 sq ft accessory building generally exceeds the 120-200 sq ft permit-exempt threshold in most jurisdictions, so a permit will typically be required. The University Digital Conservancy attaches its own disclaimer to the record: "This archival publication may not reflect current scientific knowledge or recommendations. Current information available from the University of Minnesota Extension: https://www.extension.umn.edu." Plan on re-sizing members to a current span table (or pairing this layout with engineered trusses) and having a local designer produce the submittal drawings.
