plans.summary: Plan 6004 is a free single-sheet 1966 Extension drawing for a 16x20 ft (320 sq ft) post-frame camp cabin with a 6-in-12 gable roof and raised wood floor, still hosted as a PDF by NDSU Extension. Everything rides on 4x4 pressure-treated poles buried 4 ft minimum in tamped earth with no concrete: 2x6 x 16 ft joists at 24 in O.C. bear on 2x6 perimeter beams plus a center 2x8 beam (two 8 ft spans) under 1 in T&G flooring, walls are 2x4 girts on the poles under a doubled 2x8 plate, and the roof is site-cut 2x6 x 11 ft 2 in rafters at 30 in O.C. on a 2x8 ridge with 2x6 collar beams at 5 ft O.C. and a 2 ft overhang. The sheet shows two 3-0 x 6-8 doors (one in each 20 ft wall), eight 28x28 window units, two 2-tier bunks and a stove, with board-and-batten or lap siding both called out and roofing left as ROOF AS DESIRED. It is a complete framing concept but one drawing only: no materials list, no instructions, no engineering stamp.
plans.foundation: Embedded-post (pole) foundation, no concrete. 4x4 x 14 ft pressure-treated poles at 4'-0" minimum depth, backfilled with TAMPED EARTH. Note 4: LENGTHS OF POLES ARE DEPENDENT ON SLOPE OF BUILDING SITE. No footing pads, piers, concrete collars, or uplift anchorage detailed.
plans.floor_framing: Floor beams are spiked to the poles with 6-20d threaded nails only. The 2x4 bearing block with 8-40d spikes is NOT part of the floor framing - it carries the doubled 2x8 TOP PLATE at the top of the wall.
plans.wall_framing: Post-frame/pole-frame. 4x4 PT poles carry floor and roof; 2x4 GIRT and 2x4 GIRT & HEADER horizontals between poles; doubled 2-2x8 PLATE with 2x4 PLATE CAP; 2x4 STUD infill in gable ends. Section says 4x4 x 14'-0" PT POLE, 10'-0" O.C., but plan dimensions space posts at 5'-0" bays on the 20 ft walls and 3'-11"/4'-1"/4'-1"/3'-11" on the 16 ft walls - the 10'-0" O.C. most likely applies to the interior center-beam pole row.
plans.wall_height: 6'-9" floor to underside of the doubled 2x8 plate; 7'-9" floor to top of the 2x4 plate cap (both dimensioned in Section A-A)
plans.overall_height: not stated
plans.roof: Gable, 6-in-12 pitch (12 run / 6 rise). Site-cut stick rafters: 2x6 x 11'-2" at 2'-6" O.C. on a 2x8 RIDGE BOARD, with 2x6 x 14'-0" COLLAR BEAM at 5'-0" O.C. and 2x6 FALSE RAFTER at the gable. 1" T&G sheathing. Eave overhang 2'-0". Design roof load 40 lbs/sq ft. NOT engineered trusses. Roofing intentionally unspecified: ROOF AS DESIRED.
plans.siding: Board and batten primary: rough-sawn 10-12 in boards with 2-3 in battens over the between-board cracks. Lap siding 10 in to weather shown as alternative. OTHER SIDING MATERIALS MAY BE USED IF DESIRED. Design based on rough-sawn Eastern hemlock. No housewrap, sheathing, or insulation layer in the wall section.
plans.windows: Eight units per the WINDOW SCHEDULE: A = 28 in x 28 in, 3 units (ganged band on the front elevation); B, C, D, E, F = 28 in x 28 in, 1 each. Sizes are approximate, units are inswinging and hinged at the top, other styles or sizes may be substituted. Section also notes WINDOW OPENING TO SUIT.
plans.doors: Two 3'-0" x 6'-8" door openings, one in each 20 ft long wall, directly opposite each other, each reached by wood steps of 2x12 STRINGER and 2x10 TREAD. Only a DOOR FRAME is detailed - leaf type, material, and hardware not specified.
plans.loft: none - single-story open room. Only overhead framing is 2x6 x 14'-0" collar beams at 5'-0" O.C. (ties, not a floored loft). Sleeping is at floor level via two 2-TIER BUNK units against one 16 ft end wall; a STOVE is dashed in near the center.

pros: Genuinely free, one click from the official NDSU Extension catalog, direct PDF, HTTP 200, no email or cart
Cheapest possible foundation: 4x4 PT poles tamped into 4 ft holes, zero concrete or forms, and it self-levels on a sloping site since pole lengths follow the site slope

Every structural member is called out with size, length and spacing (2x6 x 11'-2" rafters at 30 in O.C., 2x6 x 16'-0" joists at 24 in O.C., 2-2x8 plate, 4x4 poles), so you can price and cut straight off the section
Design loads are actually published - 40 psf roof and 40 psf floor - more than most free plans state, letting you check against local snow load
Fastening is specified: 6-20d threaded nails beam-to-pole, 8-40d spikes for the bearing block, hardened threaded framing nails required
All 2x and 4x dimension lumber plus 1 in T&G - no plywood, engineered lumber, metal connectors or crane; circular saw, post-hole digger and a helper
The 16 ft width is broken into two 8 ft joist spans by a center 2x8 beam, so 2x6 floor joists are reasonably sized rather than a stretch
Cutaway framing perspective plus the plate-pole detail make the trickiest connection visually unambiguous
Siding and roofing left open, so you can build from cheap rough-sawn stock or match an existing building
cons: No materials list and no cut list - the catalog uses an explicit ML flag for plans that have one and 6004 does not carry it, so every quantity is your own take-off
Not a construction manual: one sheet, no step-by-step instructions, no photos, no sequencing. Assumes you already know how to frame

1966 vintage and unengineered. NDSU's disclaimer says these plans are conceptual and that snow load variations and NDS changes make it imperative that professional services be used to tailor them, and that no cooperating university warranties them
Permit-hostile as-is: unsigned and unsealed, only 40 psf roof load, no wind or seismic design, no lateral bracing or shear detail, and at 320 sq ft it exceeds common 120-200 sq ft permit exemptions
Embedded 4x4 poles on tamped earth at only 4 ft depth may be under local frost depth, and modern codes generally want concrete footing pads or collars under posts
4x4 poles are small for a permanent post-frame building by current practice (6x6 or laminated columns are the norm), and PT 4x4 in direct earth contact is the main long-term rot risk
Site-cut stick rafters at 30 in O.C. with a hand-set 2x8 ridge - no engineered trusses, so you cut and raise roughly 18 rafter pairs individually
Uninsulated by design: single-layer board-and-batten walls with no sheathing, 1 in T&G roof deck, open underfloor. Any conditioned or year-round build means redesigning wall and floor assemblies
Only 6'-9" clear to the underside of the plate, below the 7 ft habitable ceiling minimum in most codes, and there is no loft despite the 16 ft width
Two 3'-0" x 6'-8" people doors and no large or double door - useless as a garage or equipment shed without redesigning a post-frame wall opening
Scanned image-only PDF: not searchable or selectable, and fine annotations approach the limit of legibility when printed small
Design is based on rough-sawn Eastern hemlock, a full-dimension species unavailable or costly in most of the country; substituting S4S softwood changes actual member depths
Drawing ambiguity: the section says 4x4 PT POLE 10'-0" O.C. while the plan dimensions posts at roughly 4-5 ft centers, so total pole count is not unambiguous

plans.name: Horse Barn, Gambrel Roof — NDSU/USDA Plan 6262 (16' x 24', two-story with hay mow)
plans.footprint_note: Both floor plans on Sheet 1 are dimensioned 16'-0" wide x 24'-0" long (384 sq ft ground floor), plus a full-length overhead hay mow of the same footprint. The 16'-0" width splits into an 11'-4" stall bay and a 4'-8" alley. Two interior layouts are offered in the same shell: a "TIE STALL FLOOR PLAN" (three 5-ft tie stalls plus 4'-2" grain room, 4'-4" tack room, 2'-6" ladder bay) and a "BOX STALL FLOOR PLAN" (two box stalls 11'-4" x 9'-10" and 11'-4" x 9'-4", plus a 4'-10" deep tack/storage area with ladder).
plans.style: Two-story (1-1/2 story) gambrel-roof barn with full overhead hay mow; stick-framed stud walls on a concrete slab/footings, board (vertical) siding shown in the perspective
plans.price: Free
plans.summary: This is a free two-sheet USDA Cooperative Farm Buildings Plan Exchange drawing hosted by NDSU Extension: plan number 6262, titled "HORSE BARN / GAMBREL ROOF", dated 10/76 (title block reads "MICH. '76"), and based on Michigan State University plan 722-C1-13. The building is 16'-0" x 24'-0" (384 sq ft) with a full-footprint hay mow overhead that the notes rate at "approximately 125 bales or 3 1/2 to 4 tons of hay." Sheet 1 gives two alternate floor plans (tie stall and box stall), a perspective, a tie-stall cross section and the operating notes; Sheet 2 gives two half end sections (one for galvanized corrugated metal roofing over 2x4 purlins, one for 1/2" plywood and asphalt shingles) plus box-stall construction details. It is a conceptual 2-sheet drawing set, NOT a complete buildable plan package: there is no bill of materials, no cut list, no rafter/gambrel cutting template, no window or door schedule, no foundation plan or wall elevations, and no snow/wind load design data — and the scan has no text layer, so nothing in it is searchable or copyable.
includes: Sheet 1 of 2: TIE STALL FLOOR PLAN (16'-0" x 24'-0", fully dimensioned)
Sheet 1 of 2: BOX STALL FLOOR PLAN (alternate interior layout, same 16x24 shell)
Sheet 1 of 2: exterior perspective rendering
Sheet 1 of 2: TIE STALL CROSS SECTION with stall divider heights, feed box, floor slopes and gravel/wood-block floor
Sheet 1 of 2: notes for ventilation, hay storage, water, lights, doors and roof options
Sheet 2 of 2: HALF END SECTION - galvanized corrugated roofing version (framing member sizes and spacings)
Sheet 2 of 2: HALF END SECTION - asphalt shingle version (framing, footing, slab, gravel fill)
Sheet 2 of 2: BOX STALL DETAILS front view (header, grille pipe/rods, angle iron, boards)
Sheet 2 of 2: BOX STALL isometric view with 6x6 posts
Graphic scale bars on both sheets
pros: Completely free, no email or account required - direct PDF download from a land-grant university server (HTTP 200, 173 KB, 2 pages).

384 sq ft with a full-length hay mow overhead, so it delivers a genuine second-story storage floor rather than a token loft: 2x10x16' joists at 24" o.c. under a 1" T&G deck, rated for ~125 bales / 3-1/2 to 4 tons.

Both sections give real member sizes and spacings you can price and check: 2x6 rafters at 24" o.c., 2x4 studs at 24" o.c., 2x4 knee braces at 8'-0" o.c., 1"x10"x5'-8" gussets at the gambrel break, 2x4x2'-3" pieces at 24" o.c.
Two roof-covering paths are drawn: 2x4 purlins with galvanized corrugated metal (cheap, no sheathing) or 1/2" plywood with asphalt shingles - so you can trade cost against appearance.
Stick-built gambrel from dimension lumber with plank gussets means no truss shop, no crane and no engineered components; a competent DIYer can build the rafter pairs on the mow deck.
Foundation and slab detail is explicit and cold-climate honest: 8" x 16" concrete footing, 3'-0" minimum depth, "extend footings to firm base below frost line," 5" concrete floor over 8" gravel fill.
Two interior layouts in the same shell, so the same envelope works as a 3-stall tie barn or a 2-box-stall barn - and stripped of stalls it is simply a 16x24 workshop/storage shell with a mow.
Public-domain government drawing: nothing restricts you from redrawing, scaling or handing it to an engineer or draftsman.
cons: NOT a complete buildable plan set. Two sheets only: no bill of materials, no cut list, no gambrel rafter cutting template, no wall elevations, no foundation plan, no door/window schedule, no framing plan for the mow floor beyond a single joist callout.

The scanned PDF has no text layer at all (pdftotext returns nothing) - every dimension has to be read off the raster image, and several small figures on the tie-stall section are near the limit of legibility.

Dated 10/76 and explicitly conceptual. NDSU's own disclaimer says these plans require "professional services... to tailor these plans to your situation" and that NDSU, MWPS, USDA and the cooperating universities "warranty these plans" not at all.

2x4 studs at 24" o.c. carrying a loaded hay mow plus a gambrel roof will not pass a modern plan review without engineering; no snow load, wind load or species/grade is stated anywhere on the sheets. Expect to pay an engineer to stamp it.
The gambrel rafter connection relies on a 1"x10"x5'-8" board scab at the break - a 1976 detail that a modern reviewer will want replaced with a designed plywood gusset or metal plate.
Foundation demands are real money: perimeter footings 3'-0" below grade, 8" of gravel fill and a 5" concrete floor. This is not a skid or pier shed - it is a poured foundation project.
The 2x10x16' mow joists at 24" o.c. span the 16' width; the interior partition helps, but as drawn this is an aggressive span for a hay-loaded floor and needs verification.

Purpose-built as a horse barn: dirt/creosoted-block stall floors, stall divisions of 2" plank doweled with 3/4" pins, pipe-and-rod stall grilles, alley sloped 1" in 4". Repurposing it as a plain shop means discarding much of the drawn content.
No cost estimate, no build time, no skill-level guidance, and no step-by-step instructions - it is a drawing, not a how-to.

Wayback-archived index pages confirm only "HORSEBARN, 16X24, 2 STORY, GAMBREL ROOF, BOXSTALL DETAILS ... 6262 ... '76 ... 2 [sheets]"; there is no companion write-up or supporting publication to fill the gaps.

plans.foundation: Concrete perimeter footing 8" thick x 16" wide with 3'-0" minimum depth to the bottom of footing, plus the note "EXTEND FOOTINGS TO FIRM BASE BELOW FROST LINE." Interior: 5" concrete floor over 8" gravel fill (box stall version, alley sloped 1" in 4"). The tie-stall cross section instead shows a floor of creosoted wood block or plank laid lengthwise of the stall over gravel fill, with the stall floor sloping 1" in 6". No foundation plan drawing is provided.
plans.floor_framing: Ground floor is not wood framed — it is a 5" concrete slab on 8" gravel fill (or creosoted wood block/plank over gravel in the tie stalls). The hay mow floor is framed with 2"x10"x16' joists at 2'-0" o.c. decked with 1" tongue-and-groove flooring, supported at the walls by 2x4 knee braces at 8'-0" o.c. Notes call for 12 air-inlet holes 3/4" in diameter drilled through the mow floor per horse, and a trap door to the mow that is closed during cold months.
plans.wall_framing: 2"x4" studs at 2'-0" (24") o.c. with "SHEATHING AND SIDING"; 2"x6" partition plate; 2"x4"x2'-3" members at 2'-0" o.c. at the mow-floor/eave level; 2"x4" knee braces at 8'-0" o.c. supporting the mow joists. Box stall framing uses 6"x6" square posts, 2"x8" header, 2"x6" boards and 2" plank. No nailing schedule, lumber grade or shear bracing is specified.
plans.wall_height: 7'-0" 2x4 stud wall dimensioned on the asphalt-shingle half end section; the same section also carries an 8'-11 1/2" vertical dimension from the concrete floor up to the 1" T&G mow floor line
plans.overall_height: about 15 ft 3 in (approx. 182 3/4 in) from the barn floor to the ridge - DERIVED, no ridge height is dimensioned on the sheet
plans.roof: Gambrel, stick-framed with 2"x6" rafters at 2'-0" o.c. spliced at the break with 1"x10"x5'-8" board gussets. Slope triangles show 12-and-7 on the steep lower segment and 7-in-12 on the shallow upper segment; lower rafter approx. 7'-8" long, upper approx. 4'-10". Two covering options are drawn on Sheet 2: "ROOF OF 2"x4" PURLINS COVERED WITH GALVANIZED CORRUGATED ROOFING" or "ROOF OF 1/2" PLYWOOD AND ASPHALT SHINGLES." Not engineered trusses — site-built rafter pairs with plank gussets and 2x4 knee braces.
plans.siding: Not specified by material or thickness — the sections say only "SHEATHING AND SIDING." The perspective rendering shows vertical board (board-and-batten style) siding over the whole building including the gambrel end wall.
plans.windows: Not scheduled or dimensioned. The perspective shows two small square sidewall windows plus a wall-mounted ventilation fan, and a pair of narrow lights in the hay door. Both floor plans dimension 3'-0" wall openings (and 2'-6"/2'-0" segments on the alley wall) but do not label them as windows.
plans.doors: Note on Sheet 1: "ALL DOORS TO OUTSIDE SHOULD BE 4 FEET WIDE. OUTSIDE DOORS TO BOX STALLS ARE OPTIONAL." Both floor plans show a 4'-0" door at the end wall of the alley; the box stall plan also shows 4'-0" and 2'-8" interior stall openings and a 3'-0" opening. A hay door in the gambrel end wall appears in the perspective but is not dimensioned. Box stall front details specify a 2"x8" header, 2"x6" boards, a grille of 1 1/2" pipe and 3/4" rods, 2"x2"x1/4" angle iron and 3/8" rods with 1/4"x1 1/2" steel.
plans.loft: Full-footprint hay mow over the entire 16' x 24' ground floor — effectively a complete second story, not a partial loft. Framed with 2"x10"x16' joists at 2'-0" o.c. and a 1" T&G floor, with the mow floor level dimensioned 8'-11 1/2" above the concrete floor. Notes: "OVERHEAD MOW PROVIDES STORAGE FOR APPROXIMATELY 125 BALES OR 3 1/2 TO 4 TONS OF HAY" and "CLOSE TRAP DOOR TO HAY MOW DURING COLD MONTHS OF YEAR." Access is by a fixed ladder shown in the end bay of both floor plans (2'-6" wide bay in the tie-stall layout). Mow headroom is not dimensioned; the gambrel shape gives near-full-height usable space in the middle with the roof closing in at the knees.

plans.permit_notes: The sheet itself warns: "NOTE: CONSULT LOCAL HEALTH AND BUILDING CODE AUTHORITIES BEFORE STARTING CONSTRUCTION." NDSU's building-plans index adds a blanket disclaimer that these plans "provide conceptual information" and that "[p]eriodic changes in the National Design Specifications for Wood Construction, changes in building materials, snow load variations and the serious impact of deviations from the plan make it imperative that professional services be utilized to tailor these plans to your situation," with no warranty from NDSU, MWPS, USDA or the cooperating land-grant universities. Practically: it is a 1976 drawing with no load data, no lumber grades and 2x4 studs at 24" o.c. under a loaded mow, so expect a plan reviewer to require engineering for a permit. It is also an agricultural building — in many jurisdictions ag buildings are exempted or reviewed differently than habitable structures, which may or may not help you.

plans.footprint_note: 16'-0" x 16'-0" outside dimension, dimensioned identically on all three alternate floor plans (Plan A, B, C) = 256 sq ft ground floor. This is BELOW the user's 320 sq ft target and only just inside the 240-480 sq ft acceptable band. The gambrel version adds a full-footprint hay mow above, so total enclosed volume is roughly double. NDSU's own catalog line reads "GENERAL BARN, 16'X16', GbR OR GaR WITH MOW, StW, CF". If you want the same design bigger, the adjacent catalog entry 5167 is a 16x30 two-story general barn.
plans.style: Small general-purpose farm barn, drawn two ways on one sheet: gable roof (7/12) with ceiling joists, or gambrel roof with a full hay mow. Board-and-batten vertical siding, swinging wood doors, gable louvers.
plans.price: Free (8-1/2 x 11 PDF download). NDSU sells an 18x24 blueprint-size copy on order at $4.00 per page (1 page).
plans.summary: A single-sheet 1946 USDA Cooperative Farm Buildings Plan Exchange drawing (EX. 5166, "GENERAL BARN," Sheet 1 of 1) that NDSU Extension republishes as a free PDF. It gives a 16'-0" x 16'-0" stud-wall barn with three interchangeable interior layouts — Plan A (implement bay with earth floor plus feed alley and stalls), Plan B (11'-6" x 10'-4" box stall plus cow stall, feed boxes and gate), Plan C (5'-6" feed & tool room on concrete plus two 10'-0" stalls) — and two roof options: a 7/12 gable framed with 2x4 rafters and 2x4 ceiling joists at 24" o.c., or a gambrel with a 2x8-joist mow floor rated on the drawing for "2-2 1/2 Tons Loose hay." Framing is fully annotated (2x4 studs 24" o.c., 8'-0" walls, 4x4 corner posts, 2x6 sill, 5/8"x14" anchor bolts, 8"x8"x12" footings carried below frost, 1x6 let-in braces, steel straps tying each gambrel rafter to the studs), plus cornice, window and louver details and a wiring-symbol legend. It is NOT a modern buildable plan set: one scanned sheet, no materials list, no cut list, no step-by-step, no engineering, and framing sizes that predate current code tables.
includes: Three alternate 16'x16' floor plans on one sheet (Plan A implements/feed alley/stalls, Plan B box stall + cow stall, Plan C feed & tool room + two stalls)

1/2 SECTION OF GAMBREL ROOF BARN with mow framing and hay capacity note

GABLE CORNICE construction detail (roof, rafters, 1x6, 1x2, 2x6, insulation, siding)
WINDOW DETAIL — 6-light tilting sash with latch, approx. 2'-5" high
Gable louver detail: 1"x3" beveled slats with 3/4" openings between
Foundation / footing detail: 8"x8"x12" concrete footing, 8" wall, below frost, 8"x8" interior piers with 5/8"x6" steel dowel

plans.foundation: Continuous perimeter foundation (concrete or concrete block, 8" wide) on an 8"x8"x12" concrete footing, with the explicit instruction "Carry foundations below frost and to good bearing soil." 5/8" x 14" anchor bolts through a 2x6 sill. Interior support in the gambrel version lands on 8"x8" piers with a 5/8"x6" steel dowel over a ~15" square footing. Floor is "Earth or Conc. floor" — Plan A and B use earth floors in the animal/implement areas, Plan C specifies a concrete floor in the feed & tool room. This is a frost-wall foundation, not a skid or floating slab: real excavation, forms and concrete are required.
plans.floor_framing: Gable version: no wood floor framing at all — earth or concrete floor on grade. Gambrel version: the mow floor is 2"x8" joists at 24" o.c. spanning to a 6"x8" girder carried on 6"x6" posts on 8"x8" piers, with a 1"x6" cleat, 1/2" insulation and a ceiling applied below.
plans.wall_framing: 2"x4" studs at 24" o.c. on a 2"x6" sill, 8'-0" wall height, 4"x4" corner posts, 2"x4" girts, 2"x4" corner braces, and 1"x6" let-in braces "Notched into outside face of studs" (the gambrel section also shows 1"x6" on the inside of the studs). Sheathed/insulated with 1" insulation board plus vaporproofing; interior partitions in D.&M. (dressed and matched) boards, doubled boards and 4'-6" high plank at horse stalls.
plans.wall_height: 8'-0" stud wall (sill to plate); roughly 7'-4" clear height is dimensioned inside the gable cross section.
plans.roof: upper slope 7-in-12 over a 3'-6" run (24" rise), lower slope 12-in-7 over a 4'-6" run (~7'-9" rise, ~60 degrees)
plans.overall_height: Gambrel version about 18 ft 6 in; gable version about 12 ft 8 in (floor to ridge) - DERIVED, no overall height is dimensioned on the sheet
plans.siding: Vertical siding with battens over 1" insulation board and vaporproofing, per the gable cross section. The gambrel perspective view is drawn with horizontal drop/lap siding, so either is implied.
plans.windows: "6 Light tilting sash" with a latch, roughly 2'-5" high, detailed in section. An "Optional window" is shown in the gable end above the plate, and the gambrel section notes "Window in opposite end." Gable/gambrel ends are vented with louvers built from 1"x3" beveled slats with 3/4" openings between.
plans.doors: Plan A shows a large 8'-0" x 7'-4" opening in one side wall for implements, closed with swinging (hinged) wood leaves — door swing arcs are drawn on the plans, no track hardware. A 2'-8" wide opening is centered in the rear wall on all three plans. The gable cross section shows a braced batten door about 3'-6" wide x 7'-4" high; the gambrel end shows a 2'-0" x 6'-0" braced door. Interior gates and stall partitions are shown on Plans A, B and C.
plans.loft: Only in the gambrel version: a full 16x16 hay mow on 2"x8" joists at 24" o.c., 7'-10" from mow floor to the underside of the ridge area, with the drawing stating "Capacity 2-2 1/2 Tons Loose hay." Access is by a ladder shown in a corner, with a hay chute down to the ground floor on Plans A, B and C. The sheet is explicit: "NOTE: Hay chutes and ladder shown for gambrel roof barn" — the gable version has ceiling joists only and no usable loft. There is no stair, and no headroom dimension at the mow floor perimeter (the gambrel geometry gives near-full-height sidewalls in the mow).

plans.skill_level: Intermediate to advanced, but for interpretation rather than construction. The building itself is simple stick framing a competent DIYer can execute; the challenge is that you get one 1946 scanned sheet with no instructions, no step order, no materials list and archaic construction (D.&M. boards, let-in 1x6 bracing, site-cut gambrel rafters, 6x8 timber girder). You must be able to read a blueprint and do your own takeoff and code upgrade.
plans.refund_policy: Not applicable — the 8-1/2 x 11 PDF is a free public download with no cart or account. (The optional $4.00/page 18x24 blueprint is prepaid by invoice; no refund terms are published.)
plans.permit_notes: Treat this as a design reference, not a permit submittal. NDSU's own framing on the hosting page: these plans "provide conceptual information that is excellent for planning purposes." The sheet is dated 1946 (NDSU catalog year "46"), carries no engineer's or architect's stamp, cites no building code, and gives no snow, wind or live-load values. Several members are undersized by modern standards: 2x4 rafters at 24" o.c. on a 7/12 gable of 16 ft span, 2x4 ceiling joists at 24" o.c. spanning toward the full 16 ft, and 2x8 mow joists at 24" o.c. carrying hay storage. A permit office today will want IRC-compliant rafter/joist sizing (or engineered trusses), a modern shear/bracing scheme in place of the 1x6 let-in braces, and load-path hardware. The frost-wall foundation and 8"x8"x12" footings are the one part that reads close to modern practice. Also note the intended use is agricultural — 256 sq ft with animal stalls, earth floors and gable louvers is an ag/accessory building, which in many jurisdictions is a different (often easier) permit track than a habitable structure.
pros: Genuinely free, no email gate, no account, instant direct PDF — and small (128 KB), so it archives locally with no friction.
Two complete roof schemes on one sheet: you can compare a simple 7/12 gable against a gambrel with a real full-footprint loft before committing.

Unusually dense framing annotation for a one-pager: stud, rafter, joist, girt, brace, post, sill, girder, footing, anchor-bolt and insulation sizes are all lettered, so it is a usable dimensional starting point.
Three alternate interior layouts included, which makes it easy to adapt to a workshop/storage split rather than the animal use it was drawn for.
Serious frost-wall foundation with 8"x8"x12" footings carried below frost — a permanent building, not a skid shed.
Gambrel loft is quantified (2 to 2-1/2 tons loose hay, 7'-10" to ridge) with a ladder and hay chute located on the plans, so the loft is a designed space and not an afterthought.
Roof pitch, cornice, louver and tilting-sash window details are all drawn, which is more than most free single-sheet plans give you.
Modest 16x16 footprint keeps material cost, foundation concrete and roof span all low; 2x4 walls at 24" o.c. is the cheapest wall you can frame.
Public-domain USDA drawing hosted by a land-grant university — stable, citable provenance, and the same PDF is still linked from NDSU's current site.
cons: 256 sq ft, not 320 — it is 20% smaller than the 16x20 the user is targeting, and there is no larger version of THIS drawing (5167 is a different 16x30 plan).
One sheet, one page. No step-by-step instructions, no build sequence, no 3D views, no photos.
NO materials list and NO cut list. NDSU's catalog does not carry the 'ML' flag for 5166 — every board length and count is your own takeoff.

1946 vintage: framing sizes will not pass a modern code check. 2x4 rafters and 2x4 ceiling joists at 24" o.c. over a 16 ft span and 2x8 mow joists at 24" o.c. under hay loads all need to be re-sized before you submit for permit.
No engineering, no stamp, no load table, no shear-wall or hardware schedule; the lateral system is 1x6 let-in bracing and a steel strap at the rafter heel.

Site-cut gambrel rafters with 1x8 collar beam and 1x8 gussets — no truss jig layout, no full-scale rafter template, no bevel angles given. Cutting these accurately is the hardest part of the build and the sheet does not help you.

Frost-wall foundation with 8"x8"x12" footings and 5/8"x14" anchor bolts is a real concrete job — excavation below frost, forms, and either block or poured wall. Far more work and cost than a gravel-pad-on-skids shed.

Designed as an animal barn: earth floors, stall partitions, feed boxes, feed alley, hay chute and gable louvers. Repurposing it as a workshop means adding a slab, deleting the stalls and reworking ventilation.
Scanned raster PDF with no text layer — not searchable, cannot be zoomed indefinitely, and the smallest interior dimension strings are near the limit of the scan.
Archaic materials: D.&M. boards, 1" insulation board, 6"x8" timber girder and 6"x6" posts are either expensive or awkward to source today.
No overall grade-to-ridge height, so you cannot check it against a local accessory-structure height limit without drawing it up yourself.

('cord', not 'card'), and title block 'USDA. | EX. 5166 | SHEET 1 OF 1'. Zero unsupported quotes.

FOOTPRINT/SQFT: verified. 16'-0\" x 16'-0\" outside on all three plans; the gambrel half-section legs (3'-6\" + 4'-6\" = 8'-0\" half-width) independently confirm 16 ft. 16 x 16 = 256 sq ft, matches sqft. Record is honest that this is below the 320 sq ft target.

CATALOG CLAIMS: all three verified against the LIVE beef list. The table row is exactly ['GENERAL BARN, 16'X16', GbR OR GaR WITH MOW, StW, CF', '5166', '46', '1'] — so the catalog line quote, the 1 page count, and the 1946 date are all supported (note: the date is NOT printed on sheet 5166 itself; the title block and margins are blank, unlike 5167 which carries 'REVISED NOV 7 1946' — the '46 comes from NDSU's catalog date column, which the page says is 'the date the plan was developed'). 5167 row = 'GENERAL BARN, 16X30, 2-STORY, GABLE OR GAMBREL ROOF', and I rendered 5167.pdf: floor plan is dimensioned 30'-0\" x 16'-0\", so the record's 16x30 side note is right. NDSU's live abbreviation key confirms GbR = gable roof and GaR = gambrel roof (counterintuitive but that is their key), so the record's name field ordering 'Gable or Gambrel' matches. The key also confirms 'ML = materials list' — and 5166's catalog line contains no ML, independently corroborating the record's 'no materials list'. The live page also confirms the vendor attribution: '4-digit numbers: USDA Cooperative Farm Buildings Plan Exchange' (5166 is 4-digit; 5-digit = Midwest Plan Service).

WALL HEIGHT / DOORS: 8'-0\" sill-to-plate dim confirmed in both the gable cross section and the gambrel half-section; the 7'-4\" on the right of the gable section runs plate-to-floor, consistent with the sill sitting on an 8\" foundation wall above the earth floor. The 3'-6\" x 7'-4\" batten door and the 2'-0\" x 6'-0\" gambrel-end door are both dimensioned as claimed. I pixel-measured Plan C's rear wall: the 2'-8\" opening's arrowheads center at 620 px vs a wall centerline of 617 px, so 'centered in the rear wall' is accurate. Plan A's implement opening does show hinged-leaf swing arcs with no track hardware, as claimed.

ENGINEERING SANITY: the mow floor (2x8 @ 24\" o.c. spanning 8'-0\" each side of a center 6x8 girder on 6x6 posts) is reasonable for the stated 2-2.5 tons of loose hay (~20 psf), so that claim is not misleading. The weak point the record understates: 2x4 rafters @ 24\" o.c. over an 8'-0\" horizontal run (~9'-3\" rafter) on a 7/12 gable, and 2x4 studs @ 24\" o.c. carrying a full hay mow in the gambrel version, are marginal-to-undersized against modern North Dakota ground snow loads. The record's 'framing sizes that predate current code tables' caveat is directionally right but soft, and neither it nor the visible fields mention NDSU's own explicit disclaimer on the hosting page: 'Periodic changes in the National Design Specifications for Wood Construction... snow load variations and the serious impact of deviations from the plans make it imperative that professional services be utilized... none of the cooperating Land-Grant Universities warranty these plans.' Recommend adding that verbatim disclaimer to cons.

COMPLETENESS: record is honest — one scanned 1940s sheet, no materials list, no cut list, no step-by-step, no truss/span engineering. Two further usability cons worth adding: (a) all three interior layouts are livestock/implement layouts (stalls, feed alley, hay chutes, box stall), so anyone wanting a 16x16 shop/storage shed must design the interior from scratch; (b) it mandates a real frost-wall foundation with 8\"x8\"x12\" footings — no skid or slab-on-grade option — which is a large jump in effort versus typical DIY shed plans.

corrections.evidence: The record transcribes the drawn pitch triangles in label order rather than as rise/run, which inverts both ratios versus standard usage. On the sheet the upper triangle is labeled 12 on the horizontal leg and 7 on the vertical leg = 7-in-12 (confirmed numerically: 3'-6" run x 7/12 = 24.5" = the drawn 24" rise). The lower triangle is labeled 7 on the horizontal leg and 12 on the vertical leg = 12 rise per 7 of run, i.e. steeper than 45 degrees (4'-6" run x 12/7 = 92.6" = the drawn 7'-10" dim). Writing the lower slope as '7/12' reads as a shallow 30-degree slope, the opposite of what is drawn; the parenthetical '(steep)' is the only thing preventing an outright wrong build.

plans.footprint_note: All three floor-plan options on the sheet are dimensioned 16'-0" x 16'-0" outside-of-frame (256 sq ft ground floor). The gambrel-roof version adds a full-width hay loft over the whole footprint, so usable floor area roughly doubles to ~512 sq ft; the gable-roof version has no loft. No other footprint is offered on this sheet. It is a 16x16, not a 16x20 — it is 64 sq ft short of the user's ideal target, and the sheet gives no guidance on lengthening it (though the post-and-girt 4x4-at-5'-4"-o.c. wall system and repeating 24" o.c. rafters would extend along the 16' length easily enough for someone comfortable improvising).
plans.style: Small square general-purpose farm barn, offered two ways from one sheet: (a) GAMBREL ROOF with a full hay loft over the whole footprint, or (b) GABLE ROOF single-storey with a 7-in-12 pitch and no loft. Vertical board-and-batten siding, battened plank doors, earth floor, slatted gable ventilation. Classic mid-century USDA "general barn" — implement bay plus one or two animal stalls plus feed/tool room.
plans.price: Free
plans.page_count: 2 PDF pages: page 1 is the drawing sheet (title block reads "SHEET 1 OF 1"), page 2 is the LSU AgCenter disclaimer. So there is exactly ONE drawing sheet.
plans.format: Scanned PDF (Adobe Acrobat 6.0.2 Paper Capture of a Heidelberg scan, created 2004-09-30, modified 2005-05-27), 105 KB, letter-size landscape pages at 792 x 612 pt, page rotation 180 degrees. The drawing sheet is a pure raster scan with NO selectable text — you cannot copy dimensions out, you have to read the image. Scan quality is good and legible at 300-400 dpi. Title block: "SCALE AS SHOWN" — floor plans at 1/4"=1'-0", Section (Gable Roof) at 1/2"=1'-0", Window Detail at 3/4"=1'-0".
plans.foundation: TWO alternatives detailed side by side in the Section (Gable Roof). (1) CONTINUOUS FOUNDATION: 8" wide poured concrete wall, 12" of exposure/depth shown at grade, sill anchored with 5/8" x 14" anchor bolts at 7'-0" o.c.; sheet note "Carry footings below frost and to good bearing soil." (2) PIER FOUNDATION: 8" x 8" concrete piers on 8" x 8" x 12" footings / 14" square footing pads, sill tied down with 3/16" x 1-1/4" x 18" strap anchors. Plans A/B/C dash in the "Location of piers where pier construction is used." Interior girder support (gambrel version, Plan B) is 8"x8" piers on 14"x14"x8" footings carrying 6"x6" posts, with a 5/8" x 6" iron dowel pinning post to pier. IMPORTANT restriction printed on the sheet: "Use continuous foundation for Gambrel Roof construction" — the cheap pier option is only sanctioned for the single-storey gable version.
plans.floor_framing: 2"x8" joists at 24" o.c. spanning 10'-6" on one side and 5'-6" on the other to an off-centre 6"x8" girder carried on one interior 6"x6" post (girder spans 11'-3" + 4'-9")
plans.wall_framing: Post-and-girt timber frame, not conventional platform framing. Gable version: 4"x4" posts at 5'-4" o.c. with 2"x4" studs and 2"x4" horizontal girts infilling between, 2"x6" sill and 2"x6" plate, blocking noted at the plate. Gambrel version: 2"x4" studs at 24" o.c. under a doubled ("Two 2"x4"") top plate — the sheet's NOTE says "(For stud spacing see Gambrel Roof Section)", i.e. 24" o.c. studs are the reference spacing. Interior: "Double board at horse stalls", "Plank at horse stalls only. Plank on inside where continuous foundation is used", "Double boards at stall 4'-6" high", stall partitions with 4"x4" posts at 5'-4" o.c.
plans.wall_height: 7'-4" sill to plate; 8'-0" earth floor to plate; door head 7'-4" above the earth floor
plans.overall_height: Not stated as a single overall figure. Derived from the dimensioned sections: GABLE version = 8'-0" wall + 4'-8" ridge rise (7-in-12 over an 8'-0" half-span) ≈ 12'-8" to the ridge. GAMBREL version = 8'-0" wall + the loft section's dimensioned 7'-5" lower-slope rise + 3'-0" upper-slope rise ≈ 18'-5" to the ridge. Treat both as scaled/derived, not printed.
plans.roof: Two roofs from one sheet, both stick-framed on site — NO engineered trusses anywhere. GABLE ROOF: 7" in 12" pitch (pitch triangle drawn "12" / "7""), 2"x4" rafters at 24" o.c. against a 1"x6" ridge board, 2"x4" collar ties at 24" o.c., plus 2"x4" ceiling ties at 4'-0" o.c. ("24" o.c. if ceiling is to be boarded"), tight sheathing then roofing. GAMBREL ROOF: two-slope gambrel, 2"x4" rafters at 24" o.c. with 1"x8" gussets/splice plates "each side" at both the ridge and the mid-slope break, break geometry set by 5'-2" + 2'-10" half-width offsets and 3'-0" / 7'-5" rises, 2"x6" at the eave heel, 45-degree cut noted at the lower rafter tail. Both: "Tight sheathing" + "Roofing" (type unspecified). GABLE CORNICE detail shows a 13" overhang built from 1"x2", 2"x6" and 1"x6" over the siding. Ridge/gable ventilation by "1"x3" beveled slats 3/4" openings between."
plans.siding: "Vertical boards & battens" (board-and-batten), called out in the section and drawn on both perspective views. In cold regions the note directs adding sheathing and waterproof paper inside or outside the studs — i.e. the base design is unsheathed board-and-batten straight to the frame.
plans.loft: Full-footprint hay loft in the GAMBREL version only (the gable version is open to the rafters and the girder is deleted — "OMIT GIRDER IF GABLE ROOF IS USED"). Loft framing 2"x8" joists at 24" o.c. on a 6"x8" girder, T&G board deck. Printed capacity: "CAPACITY 2 1/2 to 3 tons loose hay." Headroom is not printed but scales to about 10'-5" at the centreline (7'-5" + 3'-0" above the loft floor) with the gambrel shoulders giving usable height nearly to the walls — this is the main reason to pick the gambrel. Access is by a fixed ladder plus two hay chutes down into the stall/feed areas (chutes and ladder shown on Plans A, B and C but the sheet warns "Hay chutes and ladder shown for Gambrel Roof barn"). A 2'-0" x 6'-0" hay door is drawn in one gable end with a "Window in opposite end."
plans.doors: Large implement door opening 8'-0" wide x 7'-4" high (Plan A). Battened Z-braced personnel/stall door 3'-6" wide x 7'-4" high (dimensioned in the Section). Stall gates 4'-6" and 4'-9" wide, plus a 4'-9" gate at the box stall (Plan B). Loft hay door 2'-0" x 6'-0" in the gable end. All doors are site-built board-and-batten with Z-bracing; no hardware schedule or manufactured door callout.
plans.windows: Site-built tilting sash, "6 lt. 9" x 12"" (six lights of 9"x12" glass), drawn at 3/4"=1'-0" in the WINDOW DETAIL with latch and stop. One "Optional window" in the gable above the door, one window in the loft gable end opposite the hay door, plus a wall window on the perspective views. No quantity schedule and no manufactured window sizes — you glaze these yourself.
plans.permit_notes: Do not expect to permit this as-is. The sheet is unsigned and unsealed — title block says "ENGINEER U.S.D.A.", "TRACED BY H.B.M.", no date, no P.E. stamp. There is no wind load, no snow load, no seismic category, no species/grade for the lumber, and no fastener/nailing schedule. The PDF's own page 2 disclaimer is explicit: "This site makes available conceptual plans... These plans do not necessarily represent the most current technology or construction codes. They are not construction plans and do not replace the need for competent design assistance in developing safe, legal and well-functioning agricultural building system. The LSU Agriculture Center, the Mid-West Plan Service, the United States Department of Agriculture and none of the cooperating land-grant universities warranty these plans." Practically: 2x4 rafters at 24" o.c. over a 16' span and 2x8 loft joists at 24" o.c. carrying a hay load are 1940s-50s agricultural assumptions that a modern IRC/IBC reviewer will question. In many jurisdictions an agricultural exemption is the only realistic route; otherwise budget for a local engineer to re-check the roof and loft.
plans.skill_level: Not stated on the sheet. Realistically this is an advanced/experienced-DIY document rather than a beginner one: it is a single scaled architectural drawing with no written instructions, no step sequence, no cut list and no photos, and it assumes you can lay out a 4x4 post-and-girt frame, cut gambrel rafters from a scaled section, and hang site-built board doors and tilting sash from a 3/4"=1'-0" detail.

pros: Genuinely free, no email wall, no upsell, no account — a single 105 KB PDF you can archive locally forever, and it is now mirrored at /home/ethan/woodshed/assets/pdf/lsu-4401-16x16-gambrel-barn.pdf.

Extraordinary value per sheet: one page gives you TWO roof designs (7-in-12 gable and a full gambrel), THREE interior layouts, and TWO foundation systems. Very few paid 16x20 plan sets let you comparison-shop the roof and the foundation on the same drawing.

The gambrel version's full-footprint loft is dimensioned with real setting-out numbers (5'-2" + 2'-10" horizontal, 3'-0" + 7'-5" vertical), which is exactly what you need to cut gambrel rafters — many free gambrel plans hide this behind a purchase.

Short 16'-0" clear spans throughout. 2x4 rafters, 2x8 loft joists over a mid-span girder, and 4x4 posts at 5'-4" o.c. mean everything is one-person-liftable dimensional lumber from any yard; nothing needs a crane, a truss delivery, or engineered LVL.

The pier-foundation option on the gable version is about as cheap and permit-light a base as exists: 8"x8" piers on 14" square footings, no slab, earth floor. Enormous cost saving versus the 320 sq ft slab a 16x20 shop usually implies.
Post-and-girt walls with board-and-batten siding are forgiving of imprecision and cheap in rough-sawn or local lumber — a good match for someone with a sawmill connection or reclaimed stock.
Honest about its own limits: the disclaimer and the notes tell you plainly where design help is needed, rather than overselling a conceptual sheet as a construction set.

Real institutional provenance you can cite — USDA Cooperative Farm Building Plan Exchange drawing No. 44-1, hosted by LSU AgCenter and rated 4/4 by users on the original landing page, which described it as 'Plans of a 16' X 16' wood frame barn that could have either a gable or gambrel roof.'
cons: It is 16x16 (256 sq ft), NOT the 16x20 the user wants — 64 sq ft short, and the sheet offers no lengthened variant or guidance on extending it.

NOT A COMPLETE BUILDABLE PLAN SET. One sheet, 'SHEET 1 OF 1'. No step-by-step instructions, no assembly sequence, no bill of materials, no cut list, no nailing/fastener schedule, no rafter cut angles or bird's-mouth details, no door or window schedule, no electrical, no elevations other than two artist's perspectives. Its own disclaimer says 'They are not construction plans.'

No engineering. No P.E. stamp, no wind speed, no snow load, no lumber species or grade. 2x4 rafters at 24" o.c. over 16' and 2x8 loft joists at 24" o.c. under a 2.5-3 ton hay load are pre-1960 agricultural assumptions that will not survive a modern plan review without an engineer re-checking them.

Roofs are entirely site-cut stick framing with 1x8 plywoodless board gussets at the gambrel breaks — no engineered trusses, no metal plates. Cutting 8 to 12 identical gambrel rafter pairs off a scaled section is slow, error-prone work and the single biggest skill hurdle in the build.

Earth floor only. There is no slab, no wood floor, and no vapour barrier detail for the main level — so as drawn this is a barn/implement shed, not a dry workshop, gym or studio. Adding a slab is on you and it is a real cost line the plan never mentions.

The cheap pier foundation is explicitly forbidden for the gambrel version ('Use continuous foundation for Gambrel Roof construction'), so if you want the loft you are committed to a continuous concrete footing carried below frost — the expensive path.

The interior is committed to livestock: cow stall, box stall, stall partitions, feed boxes, feed alley, hay chutes. Repurposing it as a workshop means discarding most of what the three floor plans actually give you.

Raster-only scan with no selectable text and page rotation baked in. You must read dimensions off an image, and you cannot search, copy, or CAD-import anything. Some small fractions (anchor sizes, the 3/16"x1-1/4"x18" strap) are near the edge of legibility.
Windows and doors are all site-built (6-light tilting sash, Z-braced board doors) with no modern equivalents suggested — either you do joinery or you redesign those openings yourself.
The live URL is dead. This survives only in the Wayback Machine, so the vendor cannot answer questions, there are no revisions, and there is no support of any kind.
Board-and-batten with no sheathing as the base design means minimal shear bracing and, in a cold climate, a mandatory extra layer the note leaves you to specify.

plans.summary: This is USDA Cooperative Farm Building Plan Exchange drawing No. 44-1, "GENERAL BARN," a single scanned sheet (title block: "SHEET 1 OF 1") that LSU AgCenter published free as 4401GeneralBarn1.pdf and described as "Plans of a 16' X 16' wood frame barn that could have either a gable or gambrel roof." One page delivers a remarkable amount: two rendered elevations, three dimensioned 16'-0" x 16'-0" floor plans (implement bay + cow stall; box stall + girder; feed/tool room + two stalls), a full 1/2"=1'-0" gable section at a 7-in-12 pitch, a half-section of the gambrel version with its 2x8-at-24" loft carrying "2 1/2 to 3 tons loose hay," both a continuous-footing and an 8"x8"-pier foundation detail, a 13" gable cornice detail, and a 3/4"=1'-0" detail for a site-built 6-light tilting sash. Framing is post-and-girt — 4x4 posts at 5'-4" o.c. with 2x4 studs and girts, 8'-0" walls, 2x4 rafters at 24" o.c. against a 1x6 ridge, board-and-batten siding over an earth floor. Be clear-eyed about two things, though: it is a 16x16 (256 sq ft), not the 16x20 target, and it is explicitly NOT a complete buildable plan set — there is no bill of materials, no cut list, no fastener schedule, no step-by-step text, no load criteria and no engineer's stamp, and the PDF's own second page states these are "conceptual plans... They are not construction plans and do not replace the need for competent design assistance." Treat it as a free, unusually well-detailed design reference for a small gambrel barn with a real loft, useful for lifting the gambrel geometry and the two foundation details, but expect to develop the material list and have the roof and loft re-checked locally before you build or permit.
plans.wall_height_original: 8'-0" studs / girt wall from sill to plate (dimensioned "8'-0"" in both the gable section and the gambrel half-section). Door head height 7'-4".
plans.floor_framing_original: Ground floor is EARTH — labelled "Earth floor" in all three plans. There is no wood or slab floor system for the main level, and no concrete slab detail anywhere on the sheet. Loft floor (gambrel version only): 2"x8" joists at 24" o.c. spanning to a mid-span 6"x8" girder on 6"x6" posts, decked with T&G boards, with 1"x6" cleats at the girder. Sheet note for cold climates: "Add sheathing and waterproof paper either on inside or outside of wall studs and on underside of joist in cold regions."

CONFIRMED as correct (I read every callout on the sheet): footprint 16x16 — all three plans dimension 16'-0" x 16'-0" (PLAN-A 9'-6"+6'-6"; PLAN-B 10'-6"+5'-6"; PLAN-C 5'-6"+5'-0"+5'-6"); sqft 256 = 16x16 ✓; page_count 2 (p1 drawing, p2 disclaimer), "SHEET 1 OF 1" ✓; roof pitch 7 in 12 (pitch triangle "12"" / "7"" labelled "Pitch") ✓; gambrel break geometry 5'-2" + 2'-10" = 8'-0" half-span with 3'-0" upper and 7'-5" lower rises, so ~10'-5" centreline loft headroom ✓; scales 1/4"=1'-0" (PLAN-C), 1/2"=1'-0" (gable section), 3/4"=1'-0" (window detail) ✓; PDF metadata, 105 KB, no selectable text on the drawing ✓.

QUOTES VERIFIED VERBATIM on the sheet: "Carry footings below frost and to good bearing soil.", "CONTINUOUS FOUNDATION", "PIER FOUNDATION", "Location of piers where pier construction is used.", "Use continuous foundation for Gambrel Roof construction.", "Hay chutes and ladder shown for Gambrel Roof barn.", "Add sheathing and waterproof paper either on inside or outside of wall studs and on underside of joist in cold regions. (For stud spacing see Gambrel Roof Section)", "OMIT GIRDER IF GABLE ROOF IS USED", "CAPACITY 2 1/2 to 3 tons loose hay", "Earth floor" (all three plans), "IMPLEMENTS", "BOX STALL", "FEED & TOOL ROOM", "STALLS", "FEED ALLEY", "COW STALL 4'-8"", "Double board at horse stalls", "Double boards at stall 4'-6" high.", "Plank at stall 4'-6" high.", "Stall partition", "4"x4"posts 5'-4"o.c. See Plan", "2"x4"girt", "2"x4"studs", "Vertical boards & bttens" (sic — sheet abbreviates "battens" as "bttens"), "2"x4" ties 24"o.c.", "2"x4" 4'-0"o.c. (24"o.c. if ceiling is to be boarded)", "1"x6"ridge", "2"x4"rafters 24"o.c.", "Tight sheathing", "Roofing", "1"x3" beveled slats 3/4" openings between.", "Optional window", "GABLE CORNICE" with 1"x2" / 2"x6" / 1"x6" / 13", "1"x8"each side" (x2), "45°", "2"x8"Joist 24" o.c.", "T&G boards", "6"x8"girder", "6"x6"post", "1"x6"cleat", "Two 2"x4"", "2"x4"studs 24"o.c.", "Window in opposite end", "5/8"x14"anchor bolts 7'-0" o.c." (gable) and "5/8"x14"anchor bolts 7 ft o.c." (gambrel), "8"x8" piers", "8"x8"x12" footing", "14" Sq.", "3/16"x1 1/4"x18"anchors", "14"x14"x8" footing.", "5/8"x6" iron dowel", "Floor line", "Grade", "Tilting sash. 6 lt. 9"x12"", "2"x12"", "Block". One transcription slip in the record: the sheet spells it "continous foundation" (missing u) in the "Plank at horse stalls only." note.

COMPLETENESS — belongs in cons and I could not see it in the truncated record: (1) The source itself says it is not a buildable set — page 2, verbatim: "This site makes available conceptual plans... They are not construction plans and do not replace the need for competent design assistance in developing safe, legal and well-functioning agricultural building system... none of the cooperating land-grant universities warranty these plans." (2) One sheet only: no bill of materials, no cut list, no step-by-step instructions, no rafter/gambrel-rafter cut lengths or gusset templates, no door or hardware schedule, no electrical, no header sizing over the 8'-0"x7'-4" implement opening. (3) NO FLOOR: main level is earth in all three plans and there is no slab detail anywhere — this is a barn, not a shop/studio shell, and the record should say a slab is entirely the builder's problem. (4) Base wall is unsheathed board-and-batten straight to the frame; sheathing/paper is optional and only "in cold regions", so no shear-wall design and no insulation cavity as drawn. (5) Undated mid-century drawing with 4x4 posts at 5'-4" o.c. and 2x4 rafters at 24" o.c.: no snow/wind load basis, no uplift straps, no code path — nothing here will pass a modern permit review without a local engineer's stamp. (6) Target fit: 256 sq ft is 64 sq ft under the 320 sq ft ideal and the record is honest about that, but its aside that the frame "would extend along the 16' length easily enough" is unsupported by the sheet — the gambrel loft girder, hay chutes and 2x8 loft joists would all have to be re-laid out, so lengthening it is not a trivial repeat-a-bay exercise.

PRICE: verified. There is no price string of any kind in the PDF (no "$" anywhere on either page); the resource is a free public download from a land-grant extension service, so "Free" / price_usd 0 is correct and nothing was invented.

No fix needed.

The 8'-0" dimension is the inboard one: its top tick is at the plate but its lower arrow lands 8" BELOW the sill, at the earth-floor line (there is a separate small 8" dimension for that drop). plans.name: 16x28 DIY Studio Shed With Porch Plans
plans.footprint_note: 16x28 is the TOTAL roofed footprint (448 sq ft). Per the plan view, the enclosed building is only 16 ft x 18 ft (288 sq ft); the remaining 16 ft x 10 ft (160 sq ft) is the open covered porch, which the materials list labels "OPTIONAL PORCH". Build the shed without the porch and you have a 16x18. The front framing perspective is dimensioned 16 x 18, which confirms this.
plans.style: Gable-roof studio / cabin-style shed with a full-width shed-roof covered porch on one gable end; 2x6 insulatable walls, board-and-batten siding, metal roof, partial loft
plans.price: Free
plans.summary: 2x8 loft joists over roughly half the room
includes: Photo of a finished comparable structure (page hero)
Front framing perspective with rough-opening callouts and 16 x 18 dimensions
Materials List image (main structure + separate OPTIONAL PORCH list, with quantities)
Plan view / foundation layout (16' x 28' overall, 10' porch, 4x4 post spacing, edge of loft above)
Rear framing perspective with rough-opening callouts
Front elevation (gable end behind porch, steel entry door, pier footings, rakeboard)
Left side elevation (metal roofing, 1x6 board and 1x2 batten, slab foundation, casement windows)
Right side elevation (wall height dimension, 10' porch projection, doubled 2x6 beam, pressure-treated 4x4)
Back elevation (steel entry door, salvaged window, 1x4 trim)
Porch roof connection detail (wall section: 1/2" CDX sheathing, 1x2 batten, 1x6 siding, 2x4 24" o.c. porch rafters with 2x4 purlins)
Framing section detail (turned-down slab on grade, #4 rebar, 6"x6" wire mesh, insulated wall and roof cavity, soffit vent, drip edge)
pros: Genuinely free with no email gate, no cart, and no watermark-blurred sheets — all 11 drawings and the full materials list render directly on the page.

The materials list is unusually complete for a free page: concrete and gravel volumes, rebar footage, mesh area, every lumber size with piece counts, nail weights by type, and roofing square footage, with the porch broken out separately so you can price the build with or without it.

2x6 stud walls with insulation shown in both the wall and roof cavities of the framing section — this is one of the few free plans in this size class actually detailed for a conditioned studio/office rather than bare storage.
Turned-down slab-on-grade with #4 rebar and 6x6 mesh is drawn in section, so you get a real, frost-resistant, code-recognizable foundation detail instead of the usual 'set it on skids' hand-wave.
The porch is drawn as a genuinely optional add-on (separate pier footings, ledger, doubled 2x6 beam, own materials list), so the same drawings serve a simpler 16x18 = 288 sq ft build.
Rough openings are called out on both framing perspectives (36"x80" doors, 24"x60", 24"x32", 30"x56", 30"x30" windows), which is enough to order or salvage openings before framing.
Rafters at 2' o.c. with 2x4 purlins under metal roofing means no plywood roof deck and no shingles — fast, cheap, and a light load for one or two people to hoist.
Simple long rectangle with two gable-end doors and no dormers, hips or gambrel curves — the geometry is about as forgiving as a 448 sq ft building gets.
cons: 448 sq ft under roof (288 sq ft enclosed) is far over the typical 120-200 sq ft permit exemption, and the page says nothing about permits, setbacks, snow load, wind load or frost depth. Expect a permit, and expect the plan checker to want more than these sheets.
Nothing is engineered or stamped. No span tables, no load assumptions, no ridge beam sizing, no connector or hold-down schedule.

The loft is a real structural red flag: the list gives only five 2x8 x 16' joists, implying 2x8s spanning the full 16' width at roughly 2' o.c. That span is not plausible for a 2x8 floor loft under any residential load and needs to be re-sized or given a mid-span beam before you build it.

The drawings contradict each other on material thickness. The materials list calls for 23 sheets of 3/4" CDX sheathing and '1x6 battens', while the framing section and porch detail show 1/2" plywood/CDX and 1x2 battens. Reconcile before ordering — the difference is hundreds of dollars.

Doors, windows, insulation, housewrap, concrete forms for the slab, sill sealer and anchor bolts are all shown in the drawings but absent from the materials list, so the list understates the real bill considerably.

10.5 cu. yds. of concrete plus 10 cu. yds. of gravel is the dominant cost and the hardest DIY step: forming a 16x28 turned-down slab, placing rebar and mesh, and screeding a ready-mix truck load is not a solo weekend job.

No cut list, no rafter length or plumb/seat-cut angles, no roof pitch stated anywhere, and no step-by-step build sequence. You must derive the roof geometry yourself from 2x6 x 12' rafter stock and a 16' span.

The wall height on the side elevation is printed as "7'16\"", which is not a valid dimension — the single most important vertical dimension on the sheet is a typo, and no overall building height is given.
No downloadable PDF or printable sheet set: the plans exist only as web JPEGs, so there is nothing to hand a lumberyard, inspector or helper on site.

The prose is thin, SEO-generated filler ('assemble a spacious lumber shed in a few days', 'paint your shed once it is completed to make it more sturdy') and calls a 448 sq ft slab-on-grade building a few-days project, which is not credible.
The page hero is a stock photograph of a different rustic cabin, not a render of this design, so it overstates how finished the result will look.
The site funnels you toward a paid/opt-in '15-Page Detailed Shed Building Plans' download in the footer, implying the free sheets are deliberately short of instructions.

plans.foundation: Turned-down slab on grade for the main 16x18 building: 5 cu. yds. gravel base, 10.5 cu. yds. concrete, 300 sq. ft. of 6"x6" concrete reinforcing mesh, 600 ft. of #4 rebar (two bars drawn in the thickened perimeter edge). The optional porch sits on 4 concrete pier footings formed with 8" dia. x 4' tube forms (6 cubic feet of concrete) carrying pressure-treated 4x4 posts at 48" o.c.
plans.floor_framing: None for the main room — the finished floor is the concrete slab itself; there are no floor joists, no skids and no rim board. The only horizontal framing is the loft: 2x8 joists (5 pcs of 2x8 x 16'), labeled "2x8 Joists for Loft" on the framing perspective, over roughly the left third of the plan ("Edge of Loft Above"). The porch floor is not detailed at all.
plans.wall_framing: 2x6 x 8' studs (85 pcs) with a doubled 2x6 top plate and single bottom plates; 2x6 gable studs notched around the rafters; 2x6 x 10' stock serving as plates A and collar ties (16 pcs). Sheathed with CDX plywood (materials list says 3/4" x 4x8, 23 sheets; the porch-roof detail and framing section show 1/2"). Insulation batts are drawn in the stud cavities but are not specified or listed.
plans.wall_height: Side elevation is dimensioned "7'16"", which is not a valid dimension (likely a drafting typo). Studs are specified as 2x6 x 8', so plan on roughly an 8 ft wall before plates. Treat the printed value as unreliable.
plans.roof: Gable roof, site-built stick framing: 2x6 rafters at 2' o.c. (20 pcs of 2x6 x 12') bearing on a 2x8 ridge beam, with 2x6 x 5' collar ties on the rafter pairs that have no loft joists. 2x4 purlins run 24" o.c. over the rafters, and metal roofing with manufacturer-approved fasteners is applied over the purlins (342 sq. ft. for the main roof, 160 sq. ft. for the porch). Soffits are 1/2" AC exterior plywood with soffit vents; 1x8 fascia, 1x6 x 12' rake fascia, drip edge. The porch has its own shed roof: 2x6 x 16' ledger against the gable wall, doubled 2x6 x 16' beam on the 4x4 posts, 9 pcs 2x6 x 12' rafters with 2x4 purlins at 24" o.c. No roof pitch is given anywhere and there are no trusses — nothing is engineered.
plans.siding: 1x6 vertical board with 1x2 battens (board-and-batten) over CDX plywood sheathing. The materials list quantifies 36 pcs 1x6 x 14' and 104 pcs 1x6 x 8' siding boards plus 32 pcs 1x6 x 14' and 104 pcs 1x6 x 8' "battens" (the section detail calls the batten a 1x2, so the list's batten size appears to be an error). Trim is 1x4 x 8' at windows and doors. Fastened with 8d galvanized common nails (4 lbs.).
plans.windows: Casement windows called out on the side elevation; a "Salvaged Window" is labeled on the back elevation. Rough openings labeled on the framing perspectives are 24"x60" and two at 24"x32" (front framing) and 30"x56" and 30"x30" (rear framing). No window count, sizes-to-order, or schedule is given, and windows do not appear in the materials list.
plans.doors: Two steel entry doors, one on each gable end (front elevation, behind the porch, and back elevation), each with a 36"x80" rough opening. No overhead or double barn door. Doors are not included in the materials list.
plans.loft: Partial loft over roughly the left third of the 16x18 room, framed with 2x8 joists (5 pcs of 2x8 x 16') and shown on the plan view as "Edge of Loft Above". Rafter pairs outside the loft area get 2x6 x 5' collar ties. Loft depth, headroom, decking and access (ladder or stair) are not stated or drawn, and the implied 16 ft 2x8 joist span is structurally implausible as drawn.
plans.overall_height: not stated
plans.skill_level: not stated by the source. Realistically intermediate-to-advanced: you must form, reinforce and finish a 16x28 turned-down slab, derive your own rafter cuts and roof pitch from undimensioned elevations, and re-size the loft joists. Not a first-project shed.
plans.build_time: not stated. The page claims you can "assemble a spacious lumber shed in a few days", which is not credible for a 448 sq ft slab-on-grade building with a porch.

At 448 sq ft of roofed area (288 sq ft enclosed) it is well past the common 120-200 sq ft exemption threshold, so a permit is very likely, and a plan checker will probably ask for engineered roof and loft framing, load assumptions and a foundation detail keyed to local frost depth — none of which these sheets provide. ShedDrafts publishes a separate general "Shed Building Codes and Permit Guide For DIY Builders" article, but it is not specific to this plan. Treat the drawings as a design concept, not a permit submittal.

plans.summary: A completely free, ungated three-part step-by-step build for a 400 sq ft (20x20) clerestory shed/workshop: PART 1 frames the floor and walls, PART 2 the siding and the twin-slope roof, PART 3 the side door, garage door, 1x4 trims and a 2x10 entry ramp. Every part publishes its own lettered cut list, a shopping list, a tool list and a time estimate right on the page, with a colour 3D SketchUp-style diagram for each step - no email gate. The signature feature is an interior post-and-beam middle wall (two 4x4 posts 162" tall plus three 119 1/4" posts under a doubled 2x10 header 233" long) that splits the 20 ft depth into two ~9'3" clear openings, halves the rafter span to about 10 ft per side so plain 2x6 rafters at 16" o.c. work, and steps the two roof planes apart to create the clerestory band (which Part 2 says you can glaze instead of siding). Nothing is engineered or stamped, no elevation/overall-height dimension is published, and there are real internal inconsistencies (skids listed as 6x6 in the cut list but 4x4 in the shopping list; the side door is called 36"x80" in Part 1 but built as a 36"x83" panel in Part 3). An optional consolidated PDF is sold via Gumroad for $9.99 but is not needed to build.
plans.format: On-page web article (WordPress), three linked posts - Part 1 frame, Part 2 roof/siding, Part 3 doors + ramp + trims - each with ~12-18 colour 3D step diagrams, a lettered cut list, a shopping list, a tool list and a time tab. Optional consolidated PDF sold through Gumroad ($9.99, "1 PDF file with full plans... with 1 Cut list, 1 Shopping list"). No CAD, no DWG, no stamped drawings.

plans.foundation: On-grade skid foundation, no concrete required: "Level the surface with attention and then compact a thick layer of gravel. Fit the 6x6 skids and then attach the floor frame... use rafter ties to lock them together tightly." Cut list A calls for 12 pieces of 6x6 lumber 120" long (the Part 1 shopping list contradicts this with "12 pieces of 4x4 lumber - 10 ft"), which works out to six 20 ft skid runs of two butted 10 ft timbers - my reading of the layout, since the skid diagram is drawn at 120"x120". Fallback in the text: "If the local codes don't allow you to use 6x6 skids, you might have to pour footings" (no footing size, spacing, frost depth or anchor/uplift detail given). Slab alternative is offered: "If you are going to build the shed on a concrete slab, you can skip the floor plans." Post anchors (4) and post-to-beam connectors (2) are listed for the middle-wall posts only.
plans.floor_framing: 2x6 floor frame at 16" on center: two 240" rim joists, 16 joists 237" long, 4 pieces 13 3/4" and 13 pieces 14 1/2" blocking (the 2x6 blockings "are needed to provide support for the middle wall frame"), assembled with 3 1/2" screws through the rims. Deck is 3/4" plywood - ten 48"x96" sheets plus five 48"x48" pieces (13 sheets in the shopping list), screwed with 1 5/8" screws every 8"; the text specifies pressure-treated plywood "because the sheets will be exposed to moisture." The 237" joists are broken up by the skid runs beneath, so real joist span is roughly 4 ft; no joist hangers are called out (screws through the rim only).
plans.wall_framing: 2x4 stud framing at 16" on center throughout, doubled studs with 1/2" plywood spacers at wall ends, all headers built up from two 2x6s with 1/2" plywood glued between. Short side wall: 240" long x 86 1/2" studs, 18 studs, no openings. Tall side wall: 240" long x 110 1/2" studs, 15 studs, two 36" window openings (39" 2x6 headers) and one door opening. Front is built in two sections (114 3/4" plates each) - one with a 36"x36" window, one with the doubled 2x6 99" garage-door header; back is two identical 114 3/4" sections with 86 1/2" studs. Middle wall is post-and-beam: two 4x4 posts 162" long plus three 4x4 posts 119 1/4" long under a doubled 2x10 header 233" long (1/2" plywood between the 2x10s, post-to-beam connectors on top, post anchors at the floor), with sixteen 2x4 studs 33 1/4" long forming the clerestory band above. Above the lower front/back walls sit four angled "top wall" frames (J) with stepped studs from 7 1/2" up to 125 1/4" that close out under the two roof planes.
plans.roof: Clerestory / offset twin single-slope roof, site-built rafters, no trusses and no engineering. Thirty-two 2x6 rafters at 16" o.c. - sixteen 152 1/2" long for the tall side and sixteen 141 1/4" long for the short side - birdsmouthed (13 3/4" / 1 3/4" / 11 1/2" / 4 1/4" cuts dimensioned) with a "23 degree cut" at the top (roughly a 5:12 slope; no pitch ratio is ever stated). A 2x6 ledger 20 ft long is lag-screwed to the structure to carry one end; the other end lands on the wall top plates, secured "using rafter ties and 1 1/2\" structural screws". Built-up 2x6 overhangs are assembled for the front and back. Deck is 1/2" plywood (17 sheets), fascia is 1x8, covering is 600 sq ft of tar paper plus 600 sq ft of asphalt shingles with a shingle-offset sequence given and a one-line "Add flashings, as well." The two planes are offset vertically at the middle wall, and that step - the most leak-prone detail in the whole design - gets no dedicated flashing drawing.
plans.siding: 5/8" T1-11 sheet siding: six 4'x10' sheets and twenty 4'x8' sheets per the Part 2 shopping list, cut sizes fully listed (48"x94", 48"x118", 24"x94" etc.), nailed with 8d nails every 8" along the framing, sheets flush with the top of the wall frames and cut around openings. Trim is 1x4 (four 20 ft, twelve 8 ft, one 12 ft in Part 3, plus 1x4 lengths of 36"/43"/93 1/2"/117 1/2") and 1x8 for the roof fascias. Finish is filler, 120-220 grit sanding and "a few coats of paint". T1-11 also skins the 33 1/4" clerestory band above the middle wall by default.
plans.doors: Two doors. (1) An 8 ft wide garage-door opening in the front wall under a doubled 2x6 header (two pieces 99" long); Part 3's shopping list simply says "1 garage door 8 ft x 7 ft", and the renderings show a bought sectional overhead door with a ramp in front. (2) One side door in the tall side wall - Part 1's text calls it a "36\"x80\" door", while Part 3 builds a shop-made door from a 36"x83" T1-11 panel on a 2x4 frame (2 pieces 36", 1 piece 29", 2 pieces 76") with 2x4 jambs (2 pieces 83", 1 piece 43"), pocket-hole assembly, hinges, latch - "Alternatively you could buy a door and fit it to the opening." The tall side-wall diagram shows 78 1/2" trimmer studs under the 39" header, so the three sources for that opening height (78 1/2 / 80 / 83) do not agree. Part 3 also builds a ramp at the garage door: five 2x10 joists 48" long, a 2x4 cross slat, nine 1x6 slats 96" long on 2 1/2" deck screws.
plans.windows: Three windows, all 36" x 36" - Part 3's shopping list buys them as "3 pieces of 3 ft x 3 ft windows" (PVC), set in openings with 2x6 headers 39" long and finished with 1x4 trim. Two are in the tall side wall, one in the front wall section beside the garage door. The 33 1/4" clerestory band over the middle wall is sided with T1-11 as drawn, but Part 2 offers the upgrade: "Alternatively, you can install windows if you want more light inside the shed" - with no clerestory glazing sizes, headers, sill or flashing details provided, and no clerestory glass in any shopping list.
plans.loft: none - no loft, attic floor, collar ties or storage platform is drawn or listed. The clerestory geometry (two roof planes stepped over a 13'6" middle wall) is deliberately open and tall inside; the doubled 2x10 middle-wall header and its 4x4 posts are the only interior structure, and no loft-ready ceiling joists are specified.
plans.wall_height: Two different wall heights, taken from the dimensioned wall diagrams: short side wall 240" x 86 1/2" studs (about 7 ft 7 in framed with a bottom plate and double top plate) and tall side wall 240" x 110 1/2" studs (about 9 ft 7 in framed); the lower front and back wall sections also use 86 1/2" studs, with the angled "top wall" frames stacked above them. The middle wall assembly is dimensioned 162" (13 ft 6 in) tall overall on its diagram, with the 233" doubled 2x10 header at about 119 1/4" and the 33 1/4" clerestory studs above. Finished interior ceiling heights are never stated (framed stud lengths only).
plans.overall_height: not stated
plans.permit_notes: No code data, no design loads, no engineer's stamp, no permit package. The page only says "Select the location for the shed... making sure it complies with the local building codes", "If the local codes don't allow you to use 6x6 skids, you might have to pour footings" and "I recommend you to check out the local codes before starting the project so you learn how to get the job done legally." The Gumroad listing adds "It is your responsibility to make adjustments to the plans, to comply with your local building codes." Practical friction: at 400 sq ft this is far above the typical 100-200 sq ft permit-exempt threshold, so expect a permit and plan review with unstamped drawings; and it is tall - the middle wall alone is 162" (13'6") above the floor deck before rafters, so height limits matter. A commenter on this very page writes: "I am hoping to build a clerestory shed that measures 12'x16' and is 12' at the peak, as this is the max height allowed in my county." Nothing addresses snow/wind load, uplift/hold-down, egress, or the 2x10 header's span capacity.
plans.skill_level: not stated
plans.build_time: Per each page's Time tab: PART 1 "One week", PART 2 "One week", PART 3 "One day" - so roughly two-plus weekends-to-weeks of work for a small crew. Every page's boilerplate intro paragraph contradicts that with "If you have all the materials and tools required for the project, you could get the job done in about a day."

Everything else in the record checks out, including several things I expected to be fabricated:

PRICE — correct. The three web parts are free and ungated (full cut lists, shopping lists, tool lists, time tabs and all step diagrams are in the page body; no email wall). The "Get PDF Plans" button goes to gumroad.com/l/owNba → myoutdoorplans.gumroad.com/l/owNba, whose JSON-LD reads "price":9.99, "priceCurrency":"USD", product name "20x20 Clerestory Shed Plans". FOOTPRINT / SQFT — correct. 20x20 = 400 sq ft; floor deck cut list (10x 48"x96" + 5x 48"x48" = 400 sq ft) corroborates. Not a loft plan, so no loft headroom applies.

QUOTES — every quoted string verified verbatim in the archived HTML: "Level the surface with attention and then compact a thick layer of gravel. Fit the 6x6 skids and then attach the floor frame... use rafter ties to lock them together tightly."; "If the local codes don't allow you to use 6x6 skids, you might have to pour footings"; "If you are going to build the shed on a concrete slab, you can skip the floor plans."; "because the sheets will be exposed to moisture"; "are needed to provide support for the middle wall frame"; "double pitched roof" (Part 3 title); and the Gumroad string "1 PDF file with full plans! (plans from the blog revised and grouped in 1 PDF file with 1 Cut list, 1 Shopping list)".

INTERNAL-INCONSISTENCY CATCHES — all three are real and I confirmed them:
1. Skids: cut list "A – 12 pieces of 6×6 lumber – 120″ long SKIDS" vs shopping list "12 pieces of 4×4 lumber – 10 ft". Genuine contradiction.
2. Side door 36"x80" in Part 1 vs a 36"x83" T1-11 panel in Part 3 ("S – 1 piece of T1-11 siding – 36″x83″ long"). Genuine.
3. The reused "Fitting the floor skids" diagram is confirmed wrong — I pulled the full-size JPEG and it is labelled 120" x 120" with five 43 3/4" gaps (internally impossible: 5 x 43 3/4 alone exceeds 120"). This is a real trap for a builder and the record is right to flag it.

DIAGRAM DIMENSIONS VERIFIED FROM IMAGES (not just cut lists):
- Middle-wall diagram: 240" overall width, 233" doubled 2x10 header, 33 1/4" clerestory band, 162" total height, 119 1/4" posts, and two 111 1/4" clear openings — so the record's "two ~9'3\" clear openings" is right (111 1/4" = 9'3 1/4").
- Rafters: "L – 16 pieces of 2×6 lumber – 152 1/2″ long, 16 pieces – 141 1/4″" = 32 rafters, confirmed. The "23 degree cut" callout is genuinely printed on the Rafters-for-short-side diagram, so the record's "23-degree cuts dimensioned" is supported (the 152 1/2" diagram shows only inch dimensions and birdsmouths).

COMPLETENESS — honest. The three parts really do cover floor, all walls, middle wall, clerestory top walls, siding, rafters, overhangs, sheathing, fascia, roofing, side door, jambs, trims and ramp.
