plans.name: Canada Plan Service Plan 8164 — Pole Frame Cattle Shed (open-front, single-slope roof)
plans.footprint_note: Depth is FIXED by the design, length is a free multiple. With the 12 ft x 12 ft pole grid the shed is 24 ft deep and the length must be a multiple of 12 ft, so the smallest buildable version is 24 x 12 ft (288 sq ft) and the sheet actually draws two bays = 24 x 24 ft (576 sq ft). With the 14 ft x 16 ft pole grid the shed is 28 ft deep and the length must be a multiple of 16 ft, so the smallest is 28 x 16 ft (448 sq ft), drawn as 28 x 32 ft (896 sq ft). There is no way to get 16 ft or 20 ft of depth out of this plan — the 24 ft / 28 ft depth is baked into the two-span overlapped-rafter geometry.
plans.style: Open-front single-slope (monoslope / shed-roof) pole-frame livestock shelter; roof drains to the rear, front elevation fully open
plans.price: Free
plans.summary: Three lines of "plate" beams (front, centre, rear); the front and centre beams are built-up 2- to 4-ply members, but the rear beam is often a single 2x6
includes: Sheet 1: plan view of the pole barn with 12'x12' pole spacing plus its beam and rafter selection table
Sheet 1: plan view with 14'x16' pole spacing plus its own beam and rafter selection table
Sheet 1: typical cross-section through the shed (both depth options dimensioned)
Sheet 1: front elevation showing bay spacing, knee braces and strapping
Sheet 1: rafter-to-beam connection / wedge detail (3 wedge sizes for 2-, 3- and 4-plate beams)
Sheet 1: 25 numbered material and construction notes keyed to the drawings
Sheet 1: code warning box (plan may require structural changes for local site conditions and building regulations)
Sheet 2: continuous plate-beam details for 2-plate at rear wall, 2-plate, 3-plate and 4-plate beams, with splice locations at 1/4, 1/2 and 3/4 span
Sheet 2: plate combination chart giving nail counts, 24-gauge galvanized gusset sizes and 2x6 scab lengths for spruce and fir
Sheet 2: roof dead-load chart for computing total design load
Separate 2-page letter-size CPS leaflet: shed selection guidance, drainage, orientation, natural ventilation and manure-system notes
pros: Genuinely free, no email gate, no upsell — both the 2-sheet drawing set and the management leaflet are plain PDFs on a government server (mirrored in the Wayback Machine).

Engineered member selection instead of one fixed lumber list: two full tables give beam ply counts and rafter sizes for 20/25/30/35/40/45 psf total roof load and for two species (No. 2 Spruce, No. 2 Douglas Fir), so you can build it in a heavy-snow region legitimately.
Post-frame construction is the cheapest and fastest structure per square foot for this size — no concrete slab, no perimeter footing, no stud walls, no floor framing, no trusses to build or buy.

Very few different parts: round poles, built-up 2x lumber beams, single-length rafters, 2x6 strapping, 2x6 planks, plywood or steel skin. A two-person crew with an auger and a way to lift a built-up beam can do it.
Length is fully open-ended (any multiple of 12 ft or 16 ft), so you can size it to your site or extend it later by adding bays.

Sheet 2 spells out the fussy parts most free post-frame drawings omit: where to splice a continuous multi-ply beam (1/4, 1/2, 3/4 span), how many nails per gusset half, gusset dimensions, scab lengths, and wedge blocks under each rafter.
The 12 ft open front and 8 ft rear give real equipment clearance — tractor, skid-steer, boat, RV, hay all fit under it.
Rafter overlap over the centre beam means you only need 14 ft or 16 ft stock for a 24 ft or 28 ft deep building — no long-span material and no engineered beams to buy.
cons: Not a complete buildable plan set. It is a framing/structural sheet only: no materials list, no cut list, no quantities, no foundation pad dimensions, no fastener schedule beyond the beam gussets, and it is explicitly marked NOT TO SCALE.

It cannot be built at 16x20. Depth is locked at 24 ft or 28 ft by the two-span overlapped-rafter layout; only the length is adjustable, in 12 ft or 16 ft increments. The smallest legal configuration is 24x12 (288 sq ft) and the drawn version is 24x24 (576 sq ft).

It is a cattle shed, not an enclosed storage shed. The front is completely open by design, and the plan warns you must never block the eave gaps between rafters — so it will not keep out wind-driven rain, snow, or animals without redesign.
No floor. The design assumes an earth floor with a bedded manure pack retained by 4 ft of pressure-treated planking; the only concrete shown is a pad under each pole. Adding a slab is on you.

1982/1984 Canadian agricultural plan referencing the Canadian Farm Building Code and the Supplement to the National Building Code. Snow-load derivation, species/grade allowables and pole embedment will not map cleanly onto current IRC/IBC or CSA A660, and a US building department is unlikely to accept it as-is.

Round poles buried 4 ft deep need an auger, a tractor-mounted post driver, or a lot of digging, plus 6 in top-diameter pressure-treated poles that many yards no longer stock (square PT posts on brackets are the modern substitute and are NOT covered by this plan).

The centre beam is the cost and difficulty driver: at the 14x16 spacing it runs up to 4-2x12, and No. 2 Spruce has NO solution at all above 30 psf (the table shows dashes) — you are forced into Douglas Fir. Lifting a 4-ply 2x12 continuous beam is a machine job.

Roof is very low slope — roughly 4 ft of fall over the full 24 ft or 28 ft depth (about 2:12 down to 1.7:12). Asphalt shingles at that pitch are marginal in snow country; steel is the sensible choice.
Scanned raster PDF with hand-lettered tables; no text layer, no searchable dimensions, and some dimension strings are hard to read at low zoom.
No plans for a dividing wall, front draft panels, or the optional hinged rear ventilation panel — the leaflet recommends them but the drawings do not detail them.
If wall materials are unavailable the sheet tells you to 'contact regional farmstead engineer for alternates' — an office that no longer exists, so there is no support path.

plans.foundation: Embedded round pressure-treated poles, no slab and no perimeter footing. Front poles 6 in top diameter x 16'-0" long and rear poles 6 in top dia x 12'-0" long are set 4'-0" below grade on a concrete pad; the 8'-0" side-wall poles at the half-way points are set about 3'-0" deep; centre-line poles are sawn on site to the correct height. Leaflet requires the site to be high ground draining away in all directions, with coarse gravel behind the building and drainage channels to carry roof runoff away.
plans.floor_framing: None. Earth floor / bedded manure pack, retained by 4'-0" of pressure-treated 2x6 rough planking spanning between the poles, with a 3/4" plywood splash board between poles. The only concrete is a pad under each pole. The planking is rated to hold back 3 ft of accumulated manure.
plans.wall_framing: No stud walls at all. Three lines of round pressure-treated poles carry built-up nailed "plate" beams: front beam on 6 in x 16'-0" poles, centre beam on sawn-to-height 6 in poles, rear beam on 6 in x 12'-0" poles, with extra 6 in x 8'-0" poles at the half-way points of the side walls only. Beams are 1- to 4-ply built-up 2x6 to 2x12 members selected from the tables, spliced at 1/4, 1/2 and 3/4 span with 24-gauge galvanized gussets, 3 in concrete nails / 5 in or 6 in spiral nails, and bolted 2x6 scabs at the poles. Infill above the plank wall is 2x6 strapping at 2'-0" o.c. A 2x6 x 4'-0" knee brace is nailed at 45 degrees at each front pole with three 6 in Ardox nails per end. Trip-L-Grip framing anchors (or equivalent) at every rafter-to-beam connection.
plans.wall_height: Open front 12'-0" above grade; rear wall 8'-0" above grade; the bottom 4'-0" of the rear and end walls is pressure-treated plank
plans.overall_height: 12'-0" above grade at the open front (16'-0" front poles less 4'-0" embedment); 8'-0" at the rear eave, giving roughly 4 ft of fall across the depth
plans.roof: Single-slope shed roof draining to the rear, about 4 ft of fall over the whole 24 ft or 28 ft depth (roughly 2:12 at 24 ft deep, 1.7:12 at 28 ft deep). Rafters run front-to-back at 16" or 24" o.c., 14 ft or 16 ft long, sized from the load table, overlapped over the centre beam and fastened with five 4 in nails clinched at each end of the lap; a wedge block is nailed to each beam before the rafters are set. Covering options given: 3/8" plywood with asphalt shingles, or overlapped plywood, or metal roofing on 2x4 purlins at the manufacturer's spacing. 12" rear overhang with a fascia board extended 6" below the rafters to keep snow out of the eave vent. The continuous gaps between rafters at front and rear are the ventilation system and the plan warns they must never be blocked.
plans.siding: Rear and end walls: lower 4'-0" is seven 2x6 pressure-treated rough planks with alternated joints, plus a 2x6 rub board and a 3/4" plywood splash board between poles; above that, 3/8" plywood or sheet metal over 2x6 strapping at 2'-0" o.c. The rear plywood panel can optionally be latched at the top and hinged at the bottom so it swings open for summer ventilation. Front elevation is left open.
plans.windows: None. Daylight and air come through the fully open 12 ft front and the continuous eave gaps between rafters. The leaflet suggests hinged framed plywood panels below the front top beam that hang 4 ft down as draft stops and swing up to the rafters for more sunlight on calm days, but the drawings do not detail them.
plans.doors: None — the entire front (recommended south) elevation is a 12 ft high open bay running the full length; there are no doors, no door framing and no hardware anywhere in the set.
plans.loft: none
plans.skill_level: Intermediate to advanced, but broad rather than fine: conceptually simple (no trusses, no stud walls, no square framing to keep plumb) yet it demands post-frame skills most shed builders do not have — augering or driving 16 ft poles 4 ft deep on a grid, sawing centre poles to height in place, assembling and lifting multi-ply built-up beams up to 12 ft in the air, and correctly reading load tables to pick members. Machine access (auger/backhoe/tractor or telehandler) is effectively required. The publisher does not state a skill level.
plans.refund_policy: Not applicable — free government/extension download, no purchase. The 8164 leaflet notes the CPS detailed plan was normally obtained through a provincial agricultural engineer or extension advisor; both sheets are nonetheless published in full as free PDFs.
plans.permit_notes: Sheet 1 carries an explicit warning box: "This plan may require structural and other changes to meet local site conditions, climatic loads, user requirements and applicable building regulations (such as the Canadian Farm Building Code). Before construction, the user of this plan is responsible to ensure that all required changes are made." The design load is derived by taking the roof snow load for protected or unprotected wind areas from the Supplement to the National Building Code (of Canada) and adding it to the roof dead loads from the sheet 2 chart, then selecting members from the tables. Where the specified beam or rafter material is unavailable the sheet says to "contact regional farmstead engineer for alternates" — an office that no longer exists. The drawings are marked NOT TO SCALE, are unsealed, and carry an empty revision block. As an early-1980s Canadian farm-building plan this is a defensible engineering basis for an agricultural-exempt structure but should not be expected to pass a US residential permit review without a local engineer restamping it, and 320 sq ft plus is well over the typical no-permit shed threshold anyway.

quotes: This plan is for a general purpose, open-front pole shed with a single-slope roof draining to the rear. It is particularly suitable as a feedlot shelter where you must minimize wet conditions in the feedlot area. Pole spacings and beam designs are given for various snow loads.

SHED SELECTION With 12 ft x 12 ft pole spacing, the shed is 24 ft deep with the length in multiples of 12 ft. With 14 ft x 16 ft pole spacing, the shed is 28 ft deep, with the length in multiples of 16 ft.

The roof snow load for either protected or unprotected wind areas is selected from the Supplement to the National Building Code. Add the snow load to the roof dead loads, as shown in the roof load chart, to find the total roof load. From the beam and rafter tables (sheet 1) select the most economical combination. In areas of light snow, the best choice is usually a shed with 14 ft x 16 ft pole spacing. In heavy snow areas, the 12 ft x 12 ft spacing is preferred.

NATURAL VENTILATION When the wind blows from the rear of the building, air enters the shed between the rafters and picks up moisture given off by the cattle. This moisture-laden air is then exhausted between the rafters at the front. Never block off this flow of air or the humidity will harm the livestock and deteriorate the wood.

MANURE SYSTEM The pressure-treated rough planking, supported by the poles, provides for easy clean out and gives adequate support for 3 ft of manure accumulated inside the shed. The bedded manure pack must not accumulate higher than the retaining planks.
ORIENTATION Face the open front of the shed south so the sun can warm the manure pack.

WARNING: This plan may require structural and other changes to meet local site conditions, climatic loads, user requirements and applicable building regulations (such as the Canadian Farm Building Code). Before construction, the user of this plan is responsible to ensure that all required changes are made.

plans.skill_level: Intermediate to advanced, and specifically for someone who can build from a drawing rather than from instructions. There is not one sentence of step-by-step text on either sheet — no cut list with cut angles, no assembly sequence, no fastener schedule beyond bulk nail poundage. You must lay out a continuous concrete footing/stemwall, set anchor bolts, cut common rafters to a 6-in-12 birdsmouth by hand, and infer stud spacing by scaling the framing elevations. The 1930s materials (hollow clay tile floor course, D&M vertical boards, shiplap sheathing, 4-light barn sash, lead-and-oil paint) all need modern substitution decisions the sheet does not help with.

plans.summary: NDSU's ABEN plan library hosts EX 5294, "Straw Loft Poultry House," as a free 2-page scanned blueprint set: a 16'-0" x 16'-0" (256 sq ft) square building with 2x4 stud walls 6'-10" to the plate, a 6-in-12 gable roof of 2"x4"x10'-0" site-cut rafters at 2'-0" o.c., vertical 1"x6" D&M siding, a bank of five 4-light barn sash across the south wall, and a 2'-4" x 6'-6" batten walk door. Its defining feature is the "straw loft": 2"x6" joists at 4'-0" o.c. carrying eight netted 2"x2" frames that hold 24" of loose straw as ceiling insulation, filled through a 3'-0" x 3'-0" door in each gable — insulation, not storage. The floor is a concrete-on-grade sandwich (6" gravel, waterproof paper, hollow clay tile laid flat, 3/4" concrete topping) on an 8"-wide footing wall, with the 2x6 sill on 1/2" x 12" anchor bolts at 5'-0" o.c. Sheet 1 carries a genuinely complete Bill of Materials — roughly 45 lines covering lumber, sash, hardware, nails, paint, concrete, tile and netting — but the sheet has no text layer, no written instructions, no cut list, and a large fraction of the drawn content is chicken infrastructure (roosts, nests, dropping board, mash hopper, water stand) rather than shed shell.
pros: Genuinely free, no email gate, no upsell, no account — a direct PDF on a .edu server that returned HTTP 200 on a plain curl.

The Bill of Materials is on the sheet and is unusually thorough for a free plan: ~45 lines with piece counts and lengths for lumber, plus sash, hinges, nails by penny size and poundage, paint, concrete in cu yds, gravel in cu yds, tile count and netting in sq ft.

Structurally very conservative and short-span. Rafters are 2x4 at 2'-0" o.c. over an 8'-0" half-span at 6-in-12, and the 2"x6" ceiling joists span 16'-0" but only carry loose straw at 4'-0" o.c. Nothing here is at the edge of its capacity.
No trusses, no gussets, no engineered lumber, no beams, no headers over 2x4 — every member is a dimension board a DIYer can carry alone and cut with a circular saw and a speed square.
Square 16x16 plan means every wall is identical length and all four plates and sills are 16'-0" pieces — minimal waste, very simple layout, and no ridge-beam or long-span decisions.

The 1/2"=1'-0" section is excellent: it dimensions the footing depth and width, the floor buildup layer by layer, the plate height, the roost platform height, and the anchor bolt spacing all in one drawing.
Concrete-on-grade construction is rot-proof, rodent-proof and vermin-proof, and makes the building hose-out washable — a real advantage for animal, garden or dirty-workshop use.
Dedicated 3/4"=1'-0" window detail and a nest detail mean the fiddly parts are actually drawn, not left to the builder.
cons: It is 16x16 / 256 sq ft, not the 16x20 / 320 sq ft the user wants — 64 sq ft short, and the plan publishes no alternate length, so stretching it to 16x20 means re-deriving joist counts, plate lengths, siding footage and the whole BOM yourself.

This is a chicken house, not a shed. A large share of the drawn content and of the Bill of Materials is poultry equipment — roosts, dropping boards, nests, walk board, mash hopper, water stand, 286 sq ft of poultry netting, the 14"x18" pop-hole door. Repurposing it as a workshop or storage shed means discarding maybe a third of the material list.
NO written instructions of any kind. No step-by-step, no assembly order, no cut list with angles, no fastener schedule. You get elevations, a section and a materials table and nothing else.

The scan has no text layer, so nothing is searchable or copy-pasteable, and several hand-lettered tokens are ambiguous at 900 dpi — the roofing quantity reads "3-1/4 SQ. FEET" (clearly meant to be squares), the tile is lettered "4"X12"X12'-0"" (must be 12 inches), and one ROOSTS piece count is an unreadable blob.
The Bill of Materials leaves the siding and roof sheathing quantities BLANK — the two biggest sheet-goods line items on the job. You must take off 1"x6" D&M siding and 1"x8" shiplap yourself.

Stud spacing is never lettered. Rafters are explicitly "2'-0" O.C." and joists "4'-0" O.C.", but wall studs must be scaled off the 1/4" framing elevations, which is exactly the kind of inference a permit reviewer will not accept as-drawn.

Heavy foundation demand for a shed: a continuous poured concrete stemwall 8" wide and 1'-0" below grade, 3 cu yds of concrete, 4.2 cu yds of gravel, and 230 hollow clay tile. That is a full excavation-and-forming job plus a masonry course, not a gravel pad or skids — by far the biggest cost and labor driver here, and it makes the building permanent (and therefore more likely to be assessed and to require a permit).

Nothing is engineered. There is no snow load, wind load, species or grade stamp, no seal and no design criteria anywhere on the sheet — a hard problem in the North Dakota snow country the plan was drawn for, and a non-starter for a jurisdiction that wants stamped drawings.

Obsolete assemblies and materials throughout: hollow clay floor tile, 3-ply roll roofing, 1-3/8" glazed 4-light barn sash, lead-and-oil paint, dressed-and-matched vertical boards, 20d/10d common nails. Every one needs a modern substitution the sheet does not sanction.
The "loft" is a trap for anyone shopping on features — it holds 24" of loose straw on poultry netting over 4'-0"-o.c. joists. It is zero usable storage and will not carry a person.
6'-10" plate height with a 6-in-12 gable is low. Fine for hens; tight for a workshop with wall cabinets, and the straw loft eats the attic that would otherwise give you volume.
Circa-1933 drawing (title block dates to '33, PDF scanned 2005). Treat it as a historical reference and a materials-takeoff starting point, not as a buildable plan set for a permit application.

_verification.notes:
VERDICT: PARTIAL. The link is live and is genuinely the claimed resource, and the record's headline numbers are all correct — but it contains four substantive drawing-reading errors, the most serious being that it mistook the framing elevations' opening symbols for structural bracing.

PRICE — verified clean. No price appears anywhere: `strings` on the PDF yields no "$" or price token, and the sheet is a 1930s-era USDA/NDAC Cooperative Extension public-domain plan served as a free direct download (HTTP 200, no paywall, no cart). "Free" / price_usd 0 is accurate, not fabricated.

VERIFIED CORRECT (read off 300-dpi renders of both sheets, since there is no text layer):
- footprint 16x16 and sqft 256: the Floor Plan is dimensioned 8'-0" + 8'-0" across the top, 8'-0" + 8'-0" down the right side with an overall 16'-0", and a bottom string 3'-0"+2'-0"+2'-0"+2'-0"+2'-0"+3'-0"+2'-0" = 16'-0" with an overall 16'-0". 16 x 16 = 256 ✓. Corroborated by 4 pcs 2"x6"x16'-0" sills = exactly 64 lin ft of perimeter, and 18 rafters = 9 pairs at 2'-0" o.c. over a 16' length.
- wall_height 6'-10" to top of plate, 3'-7" to roost platform, 8" foundation above grade, 1'-0" below grade, 8" wall thickness — all five dimensioned on the Section exactly as reported.
- overall_height "not stated" ✓ — no total-height dimension is lettered anywhere.
- roof pitch: slope triangle lettered "12" run / "6" rise, and the drawn triangle scales to 0.545 ≈ 6/12 ✓.
- page_count 2 ✓ ("SHEET 1 OF 2", "SHEET 2 OF 2"); sheet-content split between sheets 1 and 2 exactly as described; all nine `includes` items verified including every drawing scale (1/4", 1/2", 3/4").
- Bill of Materials verified line-by-line against the record's lumber_list — every piece count, size and description matches, including the "BRACING" wording, the quantity-blank SIDING line, and the two WINDOW SILLS lines the record omits.
- Quotes checked and found verbatim: "3 1/4 SQ. FEET", "SEE WINDOW DETAILS SHEET 2", "SASH HINGED AT TOP", "1"X6" D&M OR 1"X12" PLAIN BOARDS WITH BATTENS", "3'-0"X3'-0" DOOR EACH END", "GALV. IRON RIDGE ROLL", "3-PLY ROLL ROOFING, WOOD OR ASPHALT SHINGLES", "HOLLOW TILE — LAY FLAT", "1 LAYER WATERPROOF BUILDING PAPER", "6" GRAVEL OR CINDERS", "24" LOOSE STRAW", "FRAMED COVERED WITH 1-1/2" POULTRY NETTING", "2"X6"-16'-0" LONG SPACED 4'-0" O.C.", "1/2"X12" ANCHOR BOLTS 5'-0" O.C.", "LINING OF MATCHED LUMBER OR INSULATING BOARD", "MAKE 3 TIERS HIGH FOR LIGHT BREEDS", "EXTEND 10" EACH END", and the full title block. The anchor-bolt spacing "5'-0" O.C." is correct as reported (note the plan self-contradicts: 16 bolts around a 64-ft perimeter is ~4'-0" o.c., not 5'-0" — the record faithfully reports both numbers).
- Straw frames: "(8 REQUIRED)", 3'-9" x 7'-6", 2"x2", "COVER WITH 1-1/2" POULTRY NETTING" — all confirmed. The 3'-9" width (which renders ambiguously and could be misread as 3'-4") is independently proved correct by arithmetic: 4 bays x 3'-9" x 7'-6" x 2 = 225 sq ft of frame netting + roost-area netting (16' x ~3'-10" = 61 sq ft) = 286 sq ft, matching the BOM's "286 SQ. FT. (1-1/2" MESH) POULTRY NETTING" exactly. 3'-4" would give 261.
- Windows: 7 (4 Lt) 9"x12"x1-3/8" barn sash and 1 (3 Lt) 10"x14"x1-3/8" cellar sash ✓. The 5+1+1 distribution is right — I counted five ganged sash on the South Elevation and one 9"/12" sash in the East (West similar) gable end. The record doesn't say where the cellar sash goes: it is the 10"/14" unit shown low on the North Elevation.
- Loft assessment is honest and correct: joists land at the 6'-10" plate, ridge is 6'-10" + 4'-0" = ~10'-10", so ~4'-0" of attic at the peak of which 24" is straw — genuinely no usable headroom, and netting carries nothing.
- Local image: JPEG, 198,583 bytes, 1325x1021 (aspect 1.297, matching the PDF page's 1.298) — a clean, legible render of Sheet 1 of this exact plan. No fix needed.

ENGINEERING SANITY (check #6) — one real concern the record does not disclose. The Section calls for 2"x6" straw-loft joists 16'-0" long at 4'-0" o.c., and I confirmed on the drawing that they span plate-to-plate with NO intermediate support: no bearing partition, no post, no beam in the Floor Plan or Section. Loose straw at ~4-5 pcf x 2 ft depth ≈ 8-10 psf, so ~32-40 plf per joist over a 16'-0" clear span → required section modulus ≈ 15,400 in-lb / 7.56 in³ ≈ 2,030 psi bending stress, roughly double the allowable for common framing lumber, with deflection far beyond L/360. A modern builder should not reproduce this detail as drawn; it needs a mid-span beam/post or deeper joists. The record states the arrangement accurately but attaches no caveat.

COMPLETENESS (check #7) — the record is honest that this is a 2-page scanned sheet set with no text layer, no trusses/engineering, no stud spacing lettered, and a quantity-blank siding line. Two further gaps it does not disclose: (a) the Bill of Materials contains NO joist line at all — the only 2"x6"x16'-0" items are 4 SILLS and 3 BRACING, so the five 2x6 loft joists the Section requires are simply missing from the material list; and (b) the 3 pcs of 2"x6"x16'-0" "BRACING" are never drawn or located on either sheet, so a builder has no idea where they go. Both belong in cons.

MINOR/FYI, no correction warranted: the Sheet 2 title block's reversed-out lettering scans as "EX 5295" while Sheet 1 clearly reads "EX 5294". Given the filename is 5294.pdf, Sheet 1 reads 5294, and both sheets are numbered "of 2", this is almost certainly a degraded 4 (or an original typo); the record's "EX 5294" is correct.

I could not review the pros/cons or the tail of lumber_list — the record as supplied to me was truncated mid-string at "3 — 2\"X6" — so checks #6 and #7 are reported above as observations against the drawing rather than as field corrections.

In the Section, the "1 LAYER WATERPROOF BUILDING PAPER" leader rises and its arrowhead terminates on the line at the TOP of the hollow-tile course, immediately beneath the thin 3/4" concrete band — while the "6" GRAVEL OR CINDERS" leader arrowhead terminates well below, inside the gravel bed under the tile. pros: Genuinely free and ungated — a direct 143 KB PDF on the ndsu.edu server, HTTP 200, no email, no cart, no upsell, and public-domain-era government extension work.

It is an actual two-sheet plan set rather than a single teaser detail: plan, two elevations, a full wall/foundation section, hip-end framing elevations, and three large-scale details (cornice, window, sliding door head/jamb).
360 sq ft at 20 x 18 sits right in the user's target band, and the shape is dead simple — a rectangle with one big opening wall, no dormers, no ells, no loft.

The wall/sill/foundation section is the most useful part: 2x6 sill, 1/2" dia. x 14" anchor bolts at 5'-0" o.c., roughly 8" wide x 2'-0" deep perimeter wall, 4" slab — enough to price and lay out a foundation.
Slab-on-grade with a 4" floor sloped 1" in 10'-0" to a 6" bell trap and a concrete incline at the doors is a real workshop/vehicle floor detail most free shed plans skip entirely.
Hip roof means no gable-end siding and much better wind behavior than a gable; the eave line is uniform on all four sides.

The sliding-door detail (two 8'-0" x 7'-6" doors from jamb to jamb on two tracks, one inside and one outside, on roller-bearing hangers on steel track, with a note that the lintel may be made continuous) is drawn at 3/4" = 1'-0" and is directly copyable if you want cheap barn-style doors instead of an overhead door.
1x4 let-in braces notched into the outside of the studs give you a shear-bracing method that works even if you sheathe with boards or install siding directly to studs.
cons: It is a 1933 drawing and the framing is well below modern practice in a heavy-snow state: 2x4 rafters at 2'-0" o.c. over a hipped 18-20 ft building, 2x4 studs at 2'-0" o.c., and 2x4 ties at only 4'-0" o.c. No snow load, wind speed, species, or grade is stated anywhere.

Nothing is engineered and nothing is stamped. There are no truss drawings, no span tables, no header schedule, and no reinforcing callouts for the concrete — expect a plan reviewer to reject it as-is or demand an engineer's letter.

No materials list and no cut list at all. NDSU's own catalog key uses 'ML' to flag plans that include a materials list, and 5336's listing does not carry it. You must take off every stick yourself from a scanned drawing.
No written instructions or build sequence of any kind; this is a drafting-board plan set for a 1930s carpenter, not a DIY tutorial.

The PDF is a bitmap scan with no text layer — nothing is searchable or copyable, and the small lettering (title block, some dimensions) is degraded. Sheet 1's plan number cell is essentially illegible.
Sheet 2 carries a handwritten annotation, 'MORE DETAILS ON NEW PLANS,' which is NDSU staff admitting this sheet is superseded; a second pencil scrawl sits on sheet 1's side elevation.
Specified materials are largely obsolete or awkward to source: 6" drop siding, wood shingles laid 4-1/2" to weather, galvanized-iron ridge roll, 1x6 frieze, and 1x1-1/4" window stop.
No dimensioned window or door schedule — the side-wall window is drawn but never sized, so you are scaling off a 1/4" = 1'-0" scan.
No insulation, vapor barrier, air sealing, electrical, or ventilation is shown; the roof cavity has ties but no ceiling, so it is an unconditioned shell only.

Cost driver is the concrete: a full perimeter frost wall roughly 8" x 2'-0" plus a 4" drained slab and an exterior apron is a much bigger pour than the skid or pier foundations most 320 sq ft shed plans use.
Overall building height is never dimensioned, which matters if your zoning caps accessory-structure height.

The front-wall dimension string (5'-3" | 9'-6" | 5'-3" = 20'-0") does not obviously reconcile with two 8'-0" doors and a 7'-8"-inside-trim opening note, so the door layout needs to be re-worked out before you frame the opening.

Horizontal 2x4 members at 2'-0" o.c. are also called out (girts/blocking behind the drop siding). plans.roof: Hip roof at 7/12 (drawn as a 12 : 7 slope triangle), framed with 2x4 rafters at 2'-0" o.c. plus hip rafters running to the four corners (visible as the diagonals in the PLAN view), tied with 2x4 ties at 4'-0" o.c. and a 1x6 tie at the ridge/collar level. Covering: "WOOD SHINGLES LAID 4-1/2" TO WEATHER OR ASPHALT SHINGLES" with a "G.I. RIDGE ROLL" (galvanized iron ridge cap). Cornice: 1x4 fascia and 1x6 frieze with a modest boxed overhang, detailed at 3/4" = 1'-0". No sheathing thickness, underlayment, or engineered truss is specified.
plans.siding: 6" drop siding (wood lap/rustic drop siding) applied over the studs, with 1x4 trim at openings and a 1x6 frieze at the eave. No housewrap, sheathing, or paint spec is given.
plans.windows: One small window in each side wall, drawn in the side elevations and in the sheet 2 framing elevations. Sizes and glazing are never dimensioned. WINDOW DETAIL at 1-1/2" = 1'-0" shows a 2x4 head with 1x4 trim and 1-1/4" stop, 2x4 jamb, and 2x6 sill. The sliding doors have glazed upper panels (marked "GL." in the front elevation).
plans.doors: Two 8'-0" x 7'-6" parallel sliding doors in the 20'-0" front wall, noted "8'-0" X 7'-6" PARALLEL DOORS SLIDING FROM JAMB TO JAMB ON TWO TRACKS, ONE INSIDE AND ONE OUTSIDE," hung on "ROLLER BEARING DOOR HANGER ON STEEL TRACK," with glazed top panels and a center jamb (detailed on sheet 2 as "INSIDE ELEVATION AT CENTER JAMB" and "SECTION THRU DOOR HEAD"). The plan notes 7'-8" inside trim at the opening. Sheet 2's right-hand side elevation also shows a braced walk-in service door in one side wall. No door hardware brand, gauge, or track length is given.
plans.loft: none — the interior is open to the hip rafters, with only 2x4 ties at 4'-0" o.c. and a 1x6 tie crossing overhead. No ceiling joists sized for storage, no loft floor, no access.

plans.skill_level: Intermediate to advanced, and specifically not beginner-friendly: you must read and scale a 1933 architectural scan with no instructions, form and pour a frost wall plus a drained slab with a bell trap, cut hip and jack rafters, and hang sliding doors on inside/outside tracks. Most builders will also want to re-size the rafters and studs to modern code before starting.
plans.permit_notes: Free U.S. extension-service drawing from 1933 (NDSU catalog year "'33"), issued by North Dakota Agricultural College Cooperative Extension — the college was renamed NDSU in 1960, so the sheets predate that. Nothing on the sheets is stamped or sealed, and no design loads (snow, wind, seismic), lumber species/grade, or span tables are given. The 2x4 rafters at 2'-0" o.c., 2x4 studs at 2'-0" o.c., and 2x4 ties at 4'-0" o.c. would not satisfy current IRC/IBC prescriptive tables for a 20-ft-wide roof in North Dakota snow country. Treat this as a design reference and dimensional starting point: for a permit expect to resubmit with engineered trusses or re-sized rafters, 16" o.c. studs, structural sheathing, and a reinforced foundation designed for your local frost depth. It is a complete two-sheet plan set in the 1933 sense (elevations, plan, section, details), but it is NOT a complete modern buildable plan — and NDSU staff hand-wrote "MORE DETAILS ON NEW PLANS" on sheet 2 to say so.

plans.summary_original: This is NDSU Extension building plan 5336, a two-sheet 1933 ink drawing titled "TWO CAR GARAGE," scanned to PDF and served free with no registration, paywall, or gate. It draws a 20'-0" wide x 18'-0" deep (360 sq ft) building with 2x4 stud walls at 2'-0" on center, 8'-6" from floor to plate, 6" drop siding, a 7/12 hip roof framed with 2x4 rafters at 2'-0" o.c. tied with 2x4 ties at 4'-0" o.c. and a 1x6 tie, and a 4" concrete floor sloped 1" in 10'-0" to a 6" bell trap drain over a perimeter concrete wall with a 2x6 sill on 1/2" x 14" anchor bolts at 5'-0" o.c. Sheet 1 carries the front and side elevations, the floor plan, and Section A-A; sheet 2 carries hip-end framing elevations plus cornice, window, and sliding-door details. It is a real (if minimal) two-sheet plan set — elevations, plan, section, and connection details — but it is NOT a modern buildable package: there is no materials list, no cut list, no step-by-step instructions, no dimensioned door/window schedule, no snow or wind load basis, and no engineered truss; sheet 2 even carries a handwritten note reading "MORE DETAILS ON NEW PLANS."

RIDGE ROLL"; all six drawing titles and all four scales in the includes list (FRAMING DETAILS 1/4", DETAIL OF CORNICE 3/4", WINDOW DETAIL 1-1/2", SLIDING DOOR DETAILS 3/4"). Sheet 2's framing views are indeed two SIDE ELEVATIONs + REAR ELEVATION as claimed. Overall height is genuinely never dimensioned; no snow/wind/species/grade note anywhere; no materials list, cut list, or instructions.

CATALOG CROSS-CHECK (this is the one thing the record leaned on that I could not reach on the live site — found it in Wayback): the "Machine" category of NDSU's building-plans catalog (web.archive.org/web/20120125064935/http://www.ag.ndsu.edu/extension-aben/buildingplans/machine) lists verbatim "GARAGE, 18X20, HIP ROOF, STUDWALL, CONCRETE FLOOR | 5336 | '33 | 2". So the footprint_note quote is exact, the 1933 date is confirmed, the 2-page count is confirmed, and the listing carries no "ML" — the same page's abbreviation key does define "ML | materials list", so the record's ML argument is sound. The landing page also confirms "There is no cost for 8 1/2 X 11 plans... You may click on the plan number to view or print," and that 4-digit numbers are USDA Cooperative Farm Buildings Plan Exchange (which matches the drawing's "EX" number cell) while 5-digit are Midwest Plan Service (matching "MIDWEST 74113-7-33").

PRICE: Free / $0 is correct. No price string appears anywhere in or on the PDF; the catalog explicitly makes 8.5x11 plans no-cost. (Historic paid option: $4.00/page for 18x24 blueprints by email order.)

MINOR SCAN ANOMALY worth knowing: sheet 2's plan-number cell reads "EX 5337", not 5336 (checked at 600 dpi — the last glyph is a 7, not a 6); sheet 1's same cell is illegible, as the record says. https://www.ag.ndsu.edu/aben-plans/5337.pdf returns 404, and the catalog assigns 5336 to this exact description, so 5336 is the right identifier — but the drawing's own number cell disagrees with the filename.

ENGINEERING SANITY: the cons' framing criticism is fair, not overstated. 2x4 rafters at 24" o.c. on a 7/12 hip over an 18 ft span run roughly 10-1/2 ft along the slope with only 2x4 ties at 4'-0" o.c. and a single 1x6 tie — well under modern ND ground-snow practice, and no load basis is stated. 2x4 studs at 24" o.c. in an 8'-6" wall is legal today only for non-bearing/limited cases; here they carry the roof. The 1x4 let-in brace claim is accurate and correctly characterized. The foundation/slab cost con is fair (8" x 2'-0" continuous frost wall + drained slab + exterior apron).

COMPLETENESS HONESTY: good. The record does not oversell — it says plainly there is no materials list, no cut list, no instructions, no engineering, no schedule, and that it is a 1933 drafting-board sheet set. The real defects are the truncated final con, the "no header schedule" overreach, the dropped "OR ASPHALT SHINGLES" alternate, "slab-on-grade" in the style line, and the unmentioned side service door.

lumber_list: Lay the 2x6 joists on a flat, level surface and space them every 16" on center
Drill pilot holes through the rim joists to prevent the wood from splitting, then secure each joist with 3 1/2" screws
Place the 4x4 skids evenly under the floor frame to lift it off the ground and protect it from moisture
Fasten the ties to the skids with 1 1/2" structural screws
Lay the 3/4" plywood sheets over the floor frame ... Secure the plywood with 1 5/8" screws, spacing them about 8 inches apart
fasten the walls to the floor with 3 1/2" screws spaced about 8 inches apart
Install the 1/2" OSB sheathing horizontally, staggering the vertical joints
Fasten the sheets with 8d nails or 2-3/8" galvanized nails, spacing them every 6" along the edges and every 12" in the field
Set the rafters on top of the shed, spacing them 24" on center as shown in the plans
Install double rafters at both sides of the roof, then fit 1/2" plywood spacers between them
Start by cutting the 2x10 rafters to length, based on the depth of the overhang shown in the plans
Cut the 2x10 blocking pieces so they fit tight between the rafters
Install the 3/4" plywood roof sheathing with the panels laid perpendicular to the rafters ... Use H-clips between rafters along the horizontal seams
Start the 1x12 trim installation by attaching the side fascia boards ... two 2 1/2" galvanized casing nails or trim screws per rafter
To finish the underside of the overhangs, install 1/4" ACX plywood with the sanded face down ... 4d galvanized finish nails or staples spaced about 6" apart
Fasten the drip edge with roofing nails spaced about 8-12 inches apart

NOTE: these are material call-outs quoted from the free step text. No quantities or cut list are published free - the page shows only 'Cut & Shopping Lists / UNLOCK CUT & SHOPPING LISTS' linking to the $23.99 PDF.

pros: Genuinely usable 320 sq ft enclosed room plus a 5 ft x 20 ft covered porch, with 6 ft double French doors and a clerestory window band - far better daylight and furniture access than a typical gable storage shed

The entire build sequence (floor, walls, sheathing, house wrap, rafters, overhangs, roof deck, fascia/soffit, drip edge, shingles) is readable free with 3D diagrams and a video before you spend anything
Mono-pitch stick-framed roof: no truss jig, no gable ends, no ordering engineered trusses - all standard dimension lumber and 24" OC rafters
Premium PDF is cheap at $23.99 for 48 pages and explicitly includes cut diagrams, parts lists, full cut and shopping lists, cut-layout diagrams and the porch drawings

Detail level on the envelope is above average for a free blog plan: 1/8" OSB edge gaps, staggered courses, 6"/12" nailing, house wrap lap and I-cut flashing prep, H-clips, drip edge before underlayment
Dimensioned elevations are public on the Gumroad listing (240" wide, 192" enclosed + 60" porch, 153 1/2" high point, 100 3/4" low side), so you can check setbacks and height limits before buying
Author publishes a real budget range ($6,000-$9,000) and a one-week time estimate
cons: Foundation is just 4x4 skids on leveled ground with no pier/footing schedule - for a 320 sq ft office/guest space most jurisdictions will require frost-depth footings or a slab, so the base almost certainly has to be redesigned (and the skid count/spacing is not even published free)

2x6 floor joists at 16" OC cannot clear-span the 16 ft depth, so the design depends entirely on intermediate skids/beams whose number and spacing are hidden behind the paywall - do not order lumber from the free page

Rafters at 24" OC clear-spanning 16 ft on a shallow (~3:12) single slope is aggressive; the free text only names 2x10 for the overhang rafters/blocking, nothing is engineer-stamped, and no snow or wind load is stated - a real problem in snow country
All wall dimensions, stud sizes, stud spacing, header sizes and rough openings are deliberately withheld: '*detailed diagrams, dimensions and instructions for the walls included in the PREMIUM PLANS'
Purchase is non-refundable ('No refunds allowed'), so you cannot preview the 48-page PDF and back out

Low-slope roof plus a tall glazed clerestory band and a porch roof-to-wall intersection means more flashing and water-management detail than a plain gable shed - the highest-risk part of the build is also the least conventional

Cost drivers are the glass and doors: three clerestory units, two large front windows, side windows and a 6 ft French door set, plus a full-width deck/porch - the $6,000-$9,000 range excludes insulation, interior finish, flooring and electrical, which an office actually needs
The marketing images are photoreal renders, not documented builds; the archived page's 'Projects made from these plans' section is empty, so there is no evidence of a completed example

The site's own 'UNLOCK CUT & SHOPPING LISTS' / 'GET PREMIUM PLANS' link is a bare Gumroad permalink and on one fetch it served a different product ('16x20 Pole Barn Plans', $5) - verify the product title says '16x20 Modern Office Shed Plans' before paying

_verification.notes:
CONFIRMED (no correction needed):

PRICE — exact. Gumroad JSON-LD offer: "price":23.99, product:price:currency USD, and cart JSON price_cents:2399. sku/retailer_item_id "wkpjqu", og:title "16x20 Modern Office Shed Plans". The article page itself publishes NO plan price (only "$6" and "$9" from the build-cost sentence), and the record correctly attributes $23.99 to Gumroad rather than to the page.

PAGE COUNT / FORMAT — exact. Gumroad product attributes JSON: attributes":[{"name":"Size","value":"13.8 MB"},{"name":"Length","value":"48 pages"}]. Independently corroborated by the Gumroad page-thumbnail contact sheet (PNG 1005x804), which is a 6 x 8 grid = 48 pages, cover reading "16X20 GUEST SHED" and page 48 reading "THANK YOU".

FOOTPRINT / SQFT — 16x20 = 320, arithmetic correct; 192" x 240" on the elevations.

HEIGHTS — 153 1/2" high side, 100 3/4" low back, 104 1/4" to porch roof, 265 1/2" incl. overhangs: all four verified on the Gumroad elevations. 153.5" = 12 ft 9 1/2" — the record's conversion is right. "wall_height: not stated directly" is correct; the side walls are raked (the side-wall diagram shows sloped top plates).

PORCH — 60" = 5 ft deep, full width (posts at both 240" corners). Note the record correctly flags that the porch is ADDITIONAL to the 16 ft enclosed depth, so the true overall footprint is 20 x 21 ft.

DOORS / WINDOWS — front elevation shows centered double French doors, exactly 2 flanking windows, exactly 3 clerestory windows in the band; side elevation shows 1 window per side. Matches the record exactly.

LOFT — correctly "none". Interior framing render shows an open single-level room with no loft or ceiling joists.

QUOTES — I grepped all 19 quoted strings against the de-tagged, entity-decoded article and Gumroad text. ALL 19 verify verbatim. Nothing fabricated. Only cosmetic notes: the page renders Tools/Time as separate lines so "Time: One week" is the record's formatting, not literal punctuation; the windows quote is a true substring that stops before "and comfortable throughout the day"; the page writes "Drill machinery" where the record says "drill"; Gumroad says "Measurements are in imperial" vs the record's "Measurements in imperial only". None material.

VIDEO — youtube.com/embed/lM-io9qL_co confirmed (full src includes ?si=UtO9CzqO-OFR44Tu).

BUILD SPEC TEXT — 2x6 joists at 16" OC, 3 1/2" screws, 3/4" plywood floor with 1 5/8" screws ~8" apart, 4x4 skids with rafter ties + 1 1/2" structural screws, 1/2" OSB horizontal with staggered joints / 1/8" gaps / 8d or 2-3/8" galvanized at 6"-12", house wrap lapped 6" with I-cut or Y-cut, rafters 24" OC, double rafters both sides with 1/2" plywood spacers, 2x10 overhang rafters + 2x10 blocking, 3/4" roof plywood perpendicular with H-clips, 1x12 fascia with 2 1/2" galvanized casing nails, 1/4" ACX soffit sanded face down with 4d nails ~6", drip edge, underlayment lapped 2", starter strip, shingles — every one of these matches the article text.

COST / TIME / SKILL — "$6,000 and $9,000" verified; exclusions (insulation, interior wall coverings, flooring, electrical, plumbing) verified; "One week" verified; "skill_level: not stated" correct (the page's info box has only Tools and Time).

IMAGE — /home/ethan/woodshed/assets/img/myoutdoorplans-16x20-modern-studio.jpg: JPEG, progressive, 1000x1500, 340,113 bytes. Well over 5,000 bytes, real image type, and visually the correct plan — it is this plan's Pinterest pin collage, titled "16x20 Backyard Studio / MyOutdoorPlans.com" with the mono-pitch blue studio, 3-window clerestory band, French doors and full-width porch, plus "PDF Download". No repair needed; left untouched. (FYI it is not the article's og:image, which is the landscape 16x20-office-shed-plans-600x400.jpg; the local file corresponds to DIY-16x20-modern-office-shed-plans.jpg at its 1000w size. Both are legitimate images from the page.)

ENGINEERING SANITY (check 6) — resolved in the plan's favor. The 2x6 joists at 16" OC run the 189" (15 ft 9 in) direction, but four 4x4 skids run perpendicular beneath them at ~62 3/4" OC, so the real joist span is ~5 ft 3 in. That is well within 2x6 capacity and there is no unsupported 15-16 ft span. Conversely, the record understates what the free page discloses about this. Genuine gaps that DO remain: no footing/pier schedule, no engineer stamp, no snow/wind load, no main rafter size (only the 2x10 overhang members are named), and no wall stud size/spacing in the article text or wall diagrams. One caveat worth noting: the pin collage that serves as the record's own hero image leaks premium wall dimensions (188 1/2", 185", 36", 26 1/2", and stud gaps of 14 1/2" / 12 1/4" / 15 1/4"), so even the wall layout is partially visible for free.

VERDICT — PARTIAL. Nothing is fabricated; every number and quote in the record traces to a real source. The defect is systematic over-claiming that the free page withholds floor/foundation information it actually publishes in dimensioned diagrams, plus mis-sourcing the elevation dimensions to the plan page instead of Gumroad.

corrections.correct: The free page DOES dimension the skids. The article's own step image https://myoutdoorplans.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/Fitting-the-floor-skids.jpg is fully dimensioned: four skids running the 20 ft direction, each built from two 120" pieces ("120"" + "120"" chain along the long rim), with clear gaps of "59 1/4"", "59 1/2"", "59 1/4"" across the short direction — i.e. roughly 62 3/4" on center.

plans.name: Best Barns Maker's Loft XL 16' x 20' two-story gambrel garage kit
plans.style: gambrel-barn (two-story barn-style garage with full second story)
plans.price: Not published on bestbarns.com; Best Barns' own manufacturer-direct store shedkitstore.com shows $11,190.00 for the "16ft. x 20ft." kit (SKU MLOFND20, no roof package) and $12,740.00 with the Black/Gray/Brown premium shingle roof package (SKUs MLOFND20-SBL/-SGR/-SBR) (observed 2026-09-07)
plans.format: Manufacturer on-page spec sheet (no cart), plus free instant-download PDFs: 27-page assembly book and an 11-sheet stamped permit set for this exact model. The product itself is a physical pre-cut lumber kit shipped on 2 pallets.
plans.page_count: Assembly book 27 pages (Maker's Loft XL 16x20 Owner's Manual, PDF internal title "West Virginia 16x20.pdf", revised February 3 2026); permit set 11 sheets (truss sheet signed 01/22/2026)
plans.summary: Best Barns' Maker's Loft XL is a 16 ft wide two-story gambrel garage kit offered in 16x20, 16x24, 16x28 and 16x32; the 16x20 is 320 sq ft on the ground plus a genuine full second story with 7'-1" max headroom and a pre-cut staircase included. The kit is deliberately partial: it ships pre-cut wall studs, gusseted 2x6-top-chord gambrel trusses at 24" o.c. (their "SecureTruss" system with hurricane hangers, gussets and tie plates), 3/8" LP SmartSide siding, 7/16" OSB roof sheathing, 2x10 loft joists at 16" o.c. with 3/4" T&G subfloor, and all nails/hangers/screws — while the buyer supplies foundation, garage door (8'-0" x 6'-6" opening, modifiable to 9' wide), walk-in door, windows, shingles/felt/drip edge and paint. Best Barns publishes the entire 27-page assembly book (with full packing list and the local-supplier lumber list) and a stamped permit set rated 130 mph wind / 45 psf ground snow to IBC 2021, so a DIYer can see every part and load number before buying. It is sold through Home Depot, Lowe's, Menards, Wayfair and Best Barns' own shedkitstore.com, where the 16x20 runs $11,190.
plans.overall_height: 16 ft 2 in peak height "not including floor" per the manufacturer dimension drawing; the 16x20 elevation sheet in the permit set labels 16'-4 1/2" (the 16x24/28/32 sheets label 16'-2")
plans.wall_height: 8'-1" first-floor side wall height (only wall-height option offered at retail)
plans.wall_framing: 2x4 studs at 16" o.c., pre-cut studs 92-1/4" to 93" (81 pre-cut 2x4 studs on the local-supplier list), treated 2x4 bottom plates, (2) 2x4 top plates plus a 2x6 tie plate; "TimberPrestige" imported Eurowood 2x4 framing; two-stud robust corner construct; 3/8" LP SmartSide panel siding
plans.floor_framing: Loft/second floor: 2x10 DF-Lar No. 1 joists at 16" o.c. (or 2x8 at 12" o.c.) on a 2x10 ledger with Simpson LU-28 / LUS-26 hangers, blocking every 4'-0" max, 3/4" T&G OSB subfloor, max joist span 16'-0"; rated 40 psf attic floor live load with 2x10s (30 psf with 2x8s). Ground floor: not included — owner's slab, or wood floor on treated 6x6 runners over gravel with treated 2x6 joists at 16" o.c. and 3/4" T&G plywood.
plans.roof: Gambrel. Engineered gusseted timber trusses at 24" o.c.: 2x6 top chords, 2x4 webs, SPF No. 2; truss gussets are 23/32" structural OSB on both faces with 100% PL400 glue contact plus (2) rows of 0.131" x 2" nails @ 3" c/c (the 1/2" OSB gussets/fillers are the separate gable-frame parts); span 16'-3"; lower slope 31.88:12 and upper slope 4.19:12 (elevations round to 32/12 and 4/12); 7/16" OSB sheathing with plyclips. Stamped design: 130 mph basic wind (ASCE 7-16, Exposure C), 45 psf ground snow / 34.65 psf governing roof snow, IBC 2021. Roofing not supplied - the manual lists 19 bundles of shingles, 700 sq ft felt and 11 pcs of 10' drip edge; shedkitstore.com sells an optional premium shingle package (+$1,550 on the 16x20).
plans.siding: 3/8" LP SmartSide engineered wood panel siding, primed, insect/decay treated, 50-year LP warranty; must be painted with two coats of 100% acrylic latex within 30 days of assembly. 1x4 corner/door trim and 1x6 gable trim included.
plans.loft: Full second story, not a shelf loft: 7'-1" maximum loft headroom, 2x10 joists at 16" o.c. over a 16' clear span, 3/4" T&G loft flooring included (10 sheets), and a pre-cut staircase included (Step 12 of the manual points to a separate stair-kit instruction book). 5'-9" is the interior height at the knee break where the 32/12 lower slope meets the 4/12 upper slope, measured up from the loft floor; the loft has essentially no side wall because the trusses bear at loft-floor level. First-floor interior clear height is 7'-4".
plans.doors: One garage door opening 8'-0" wide x 6'-6" high, "may be modified to 9' wide if desired"; opening can be centered or offset left/right on the gable end. Garage door itself NOT included ("Garage door by homeowner"). Kit supplies 1x6 door jamb (3 @ 8') and 2x8 door header (2 @ 10'). Walk-in man door not included; shedkitstore.com offers 6-panel steel (+$285) or 9-lite steel (+$400).
plans.windows: No windows included ("Building shown with separately purchased windows... Buy the quantity, style and size of windows of your choosing"). Manual gives owner-cut rough-opening details for a 24" x 36" window and a 32" x 80" door, and warns wider spans need larger headers. Optional 18" x 36" windows with shutters at +$115 each at shedkitstore.com.
plans.foundation: By owner, not included. Manual shows a floating concrete slab ("A concrete slab is ideal for storage of cars or other types of heavy items") or a wood floor on wood runners (treated 6x6 lumber over a bed of gravel, treated 2x6 joists at 16" o.c., 3/4" T&G flooring). Permit set p.10 "Common Foundation Cross Sections" gives "Concrete Slab", "Crawl space or Basement", "Post & Beam" plus a blank "Homeowner Design" box; the words "Foundation By Owner" appear on p.9 (the building cross section). "Do Not make the foundation larger than the building size." The FortressFloor wood floor upgrade is available only for 12' wide models, so 16x20 buyers must pour a slab or build their own deck.

plans.skill_level: Intermediate-to-advanced DIY. No specialty tools (drill, saw, hammer, level, square, ladders), but two stories means scaffolding: "It is highly recommended to rent six sections of scaffolding to safely install the second floor" and the vendor suggests hiring a professional roofer for the gambrel roof. Vendor FAQ says "some cutting may be required" and the owner must frame all window/door rough openings.
plans.build_time: Vendor FAQ: "Once the floor is complete, level and square, it typically takes 2-3 people about 2-3 days to complete" (generic across models; realistically longer for a 320 sq ft two-story). Ships 5-7 days after order.
plans.permit_notes: Best Barns publishes a free "Makers Loft XL Permit Set": engineered timber-truss sheet (IBC 2021 / Virginia Construction Code, ASCE 7-16, 130 mph wind Exposure C, 45 psf ground snow, 34.65 psf roof snow, Risk Category II, signed 01/22/2026 with certification expiry 01/22/2027), a timber-floor sheet (2x8 @ 12" o.c. = 30 psf / 2x10 @ 16" o.c. = 40 psf attic live load), truss-and-wall cross sections, per-size elevations, blank foundation cross sections and a blank site-plan sheet. Caveats stated by the vendor: kits are "designed for use as storage buildings or garages only", stamped state-specific truss drawings cost a non-refundable fee (call 800-245-1577), FL/CA and other strict jurisdictions may need a local civil engineer, and any alteration may require an engineer. Tiny-house/occupancy conversion is discouraged: "trusses are 2x4 construction which will be difficult to insulate properly" and optional windows are not insulated. Owner must confirm HOA/code requirements before buying.
plans.refund_policy: Not stated on bestbarns.com itself (Terms only reserve the right to cancel/refuse orders). The manufacturer's own store publishes it at shedkitstore.com/guarantee-and-return-policy/: 30-day returns for a full refund minus outbound and return shipping; item must be unused, unopened and in original packaging with photos of the unopened boxes; "Best Barns charges a restocking fee of 25% for all orders returned in original packaging and without damage"; cancellations must be initiated before shipment to qualify for a full refund; "RBS Holdings LLC. manufacturer of Best Barns shed kits will replace any lumber that is not satisfactory" if reported within 30 days of receipt, but "[u]nder no circumstances will compensation be paid for labor or time lost due to material needing replaced." Warranty page: "Limited 15 Year Conditional Warranty" - 1 year workmanship/manufacturing, 2 years hardware and metal components, 2 years roof and loft sheathing, 1 year windows, LP SmartSide 50 years by LP; labor never covered; non-transferable; conditional on shingling, painting within 30 days and caulking.

pros: A true full second story, not an attic shelf: 7'-1" loft headroom over 320 sq ft, 2x10 joists at 16" o.c. with 3/4" T&G subfloor and a pre-cut staircase included - roughly doubles usable area for one footprint's worth of permit and foundation

Engineered, stamped structural data is free to download before you buy: gambrel trusses at 24" o.c. designed to 130 mph wind (ASCE 7-16) and 45 psf ground snow under IBC 2021, plus loft-floor sheets rated 40 psf live load - unusually permit-friendly for a shed kit

Complete verbatim packing list, hardware breakdown and local-supplier lumber list are published in the free 27-page manual, so cut sizes and quantities can be checked (or the whole thing scratch-built) before spending money

Real engineered materials: 3/8" LP SmartSide (50-yr LP warranty), 7/16" OSB sheathing, 2x6 truss top chords, joist hangers and gusseted trusses - stouter than the 2x3/2x4 rafter kits in the big-box price tier
Pre-cut components and gusseted (not site-cut) trusses remove the hardest layout work on a gambrel; no specialty tools needed and 130 mph/40 psf numbers come from someone else's calculations
Flexible openings: garage door can be 8' or widened to 9', centered or offset, and you choose window count/placement rather than paying for pre-installed units
Widely stocked - Home Depot, Lowe's, Menards, Wayfair and the factory store - so pricing is comparable and delivery is a common-carrier liftgate drop
cons: Not a plan - about $11,190 (or $12,740 with the shingle roof package) buys only the structural kit; there is no plans-only option, so a DIYer who just wants drawings gets the free manual but no license or full construction set

Big hidden costs: foundation (a 16x20 slab able to carry cars is the single largest line item), garage door with low-headroom track, walk-in door, all windows, shingles/felt/drip edge (19 bundles + 700 sq ft felt) and paint are all owner-supplied

FortressFloor is 12'-wide models only, so the 16x20 buyer must pour a slab or engineer their own 16' floor deck; the manual's fallback (treated 6x6 runners on gravel, 2x6 joists) is a storage-grade solution under a two-story building and needs local code approval
Two-story assembly is genuinely demanding: scaffolding rental, lifting 16' 2x10 joists and gambrel trusses at ~16' peak, and a steep 32:12 lower roof slope the vendor suggests hiring a roofer for

Explicitly sold as a storage building/garage only - not habitable space; 2x4 trusses and un-insulated dormerless gambrel geometry make conversion to a living space awkward, and the vendor warns against it

Permit paperwork has fine print: the free stamped set is state-specific (the posted XL set is a Virginia stamp with a 2027 expiry), other states cost a non-refundable fee, and FL/CA typically need a local engineer
Cut/loose-nail kit built by hand: nails shipped loose for hand framing, siding must be painted within 30 days or the warranty lapses, and warranty on workmanship is only 1 year with no labor coverage
The manufacturer page shows no price at all and its FAQ answers cover the whole product line, so real cost and lead time must be pulled from a retailer

_verification.notes:
PRICE: fully CONFIRMED character-by-character, which is unusual — no fabrication here. bestbarns.com genuinely publishes no price (no cart, only a "Where to Buy" strip). I pulled shedkitstore.com's WooCommerce data-product_variations JSON off https://shedkitstore.com/product/makers-loft-series16ft-20ft-24ft-28ft-32ft/ and decoded all 24 variations: {'attribute_select-size': '16ft. x 20ft.', 'attribute_add-roof-package': 'No'} -> display_price 11190; the Black, Gray and Brown variations each -> 12740. Range banner "$3,741.00 – $16,973.00" matches. price_usd 11190 is right.

ALSO CONFIRMED (I checked each): footprint 16x20 and sqft 320 (16 x 20 = 320, arithmetic fine; and 10 sheets of 4x8 T&G loft flooring = 320 sq ft, self-consistent). Wall height 8'-1", and the shedkitstore "Wall Height?" dropdown really does offer exactly one value, "8ft.-1in.". Loft max height 7'-1" (site Features + permit p.9). Roof pitches 31.88/12 and 4.19/12 rounding to 32/12 and 4/12 on the elevations. Truss span 16'-3", 2x6 top chord, SPF No. 2, 24" c/c spacing, 130 MPH / ASCE 7-16 / Exposure C, 45 PSF ground snow, 34.65 PSF governing roof snow, IBC 2021. Page counts exact: pdfinfo gives Pages: 27 for the manual (ModDate Feb 3 2026, so "revised February 2026" holds) and Pages: 11 for the permit set. Wall framing "2x4 STUDS AT 16" C/C OR BETTER", "(2) 2X4 TOP PLATE (OR MATCH WALL STUD)" and "2X6 TIE PLATE" are all verbatim on permit p.3 — the 2x6 tie plate looked like an error at first glance (the manual's Step 7 says "Install 2x4 Tie Plates") but the permit set and the Truss & Wall cross section p.4 both label a 2x6, so the record is right. Pre-cut studs "92-1/4" to 93"" verbatim, manual Step 1. Simpson LU-28 and LUS-26 verbatim on permit p.4; 2x10 ledger verbatim (permit p.3 allows "2X8 LEDGER BOARD (OR 2X10 LEDGER BOARD)"). 23/32" T&G OSB subfloor = the record's 3/4", fine. Garage door 8'-0" x 6'-6" with "Garage door by homeowner." and "Offset location of door determined by homeowner." verbatim on p.5; "may be modified to 9' wide if desired" verbatim on the live page. Add-on prices +$115 / +$285 / +$400 and "Fortress Floor (Available only for 12ft. wide models)" all verbatim on shedkitstore. Roofing take-off exact: "19 bdl. Roof Shingles / 11 pcs. Roof 'drip' Edge-10' / 700 sq. ft. Felt Paper". "Do Not make the foundation larger than the building size." and "A concrete slab is ideal for storage of cars or other types of heavy items" both verbatim, manual p.3. Staircase-included is real (site: "extravagant second story loft (staircase included)"; manual Step 12: "IMPORTANT: Go now to the instructions in the stair kit book...") — worth noting the legacy Richmond 16x20 charged +$930 for stairs, so this is a genuine upgrade. "SecureTruss", "TimberPrestige", "Eurowood", "Two-Stud Corner robust construct", "Hurricane Hangers, Collar Ties, Gussets, Tie Plates", 7/16" OSB roof sheathing, 40 plyclips, 2-pallet shipping, and the HD/Lowe's/Menards/Wayfair/Shed Kit Store retail list all check out. The entire lumber_list array matches p.26 of the manual line for line, including the truncated 'A' Pallet entries ("2 Pre-built Gable Frames 21-3/4" x 48"", then 19-1/4" x 48"). Vendor identity confirmed: "Manufactured by RBS Holdings, LLC, 205 Arlington Drive, Greenville, PA 16125"; Reynolds Building Systems attribution corroborated by an archived shedsforlessdirect page. 1x4 trim and 1x6 gable trim both confirmed ("4 Gable Trim 1x6 x 84"", "4 Gable Trim 1x6 x 82-1/4"" on the 'B' pallet).

Bottom line: the numbers a buyer would act on (price, footprint, wall height, loft headroom, loads, materials list) are sound. What is wrong is the headline overall height (16'-2" is the wrong sheet — the 16x20 is 16'-4 1/2"), the gusset spec (23/32" not 1/2", and PL400 belongs to the 23/32" callout), the "stamped permit set" framing (free set is a Virginia sample watermarked NOT FOR CONSTRUCTION; state stamps cost extra), and roughly four quotation marks placed around text that does not exist in any source. Also flag no search engine was needed/used: everything came from direct curl of bestbarns.com, its two CDN PDFs, shedkitstore.com's Woo JSON, plus Wayback CDX/replay for the legacy Richmond cross-check.

corrections.evidence: Makers Loft XL Permit Set p.5 (the 16x20 sheet) dimension string: "16'-4 1/2"" over "8'-1"", with plan dims "20'-0"" and "16'-0"". 16'-2" appears ONLY on p.6/7/8 (24'-0", 28'-0", 32'-0"). I searched bestbarns.com/products/makers-loft-series, /buyers-guide, /owners-manuals, /product-permitting-documents, shedkitstore.com's product page and JSON, the 27-page manual and all 11 permit sheets for "not including floor" and for 16'2" — zero hits. Leading the field with the wrong-size number is the defect; 8'-1" + 5.5" tie plate + 7'-11" truss height (permit p.2) ≈ 16'-5", which corroborates 16'-4 1/2" and suggests 16'-2" is a drafting carry-over on the other sheets.

This string appears nowhere on bestbarns.com/products/makers-loft-series, on the shedkitstore.com product page or its variation JSON, in the 27-page 16x20 manual, or in the 11-sheet permit set. The real manual wording is: "Rough Opening Details for Windows and Doors (not included) — If installing seperately purchased windows and doors follow the manufacturers instructions for correct rough opening size." and the site FAQ answer "Are windows included as shown in pictures? The short answer is 'NO'...". The paraphrase is defensible; the quotation marks are not.
QUOTE NOT FOUND: "not including floor" (overall_height field). No such phrase on any Best Barns page or PDF I fetched; it reads like legacy Best Barns 'Richmond' retail spec-table language.

"100% acrylic latex" (siding field) — the "100%" is an embellishment. Manual p.3 verbatim: "LP siding has a 50 year warranty and is already primed. Apply two coats of latex acrylic paint for the finish coat." Site FAQ: "Siding comes primed and will need to be painted with exterior acrylic latex paint within 30 days of construction." (The 50-year warranty and the 30-day window ARE correct.)

"black/gray/brown metal roof package" (price field) — the word "metal" occurs 0 times on the shedkitstore.com product page. The option is literally "Add Roof Package?" with values No / Black / Gray / Brown. The $12,740 figure is correct; the "metal" characterisation is inferred.

"2x4 webs" (roof field) — the permit DESIGN DETAILS table does list "C - WEB  2X4", so it is sourced, but no web member is drawn on the truss elevation (only A - TOP CHORD is called out; B - BOTTOM CHORD and D - COLLAR-TIE are "-"), and the manual's Step 20 truss is built solely from 2x6 members (26 legs 2x6 x 71-3/8", 26 top cords 2x6 x 81-3/4") plus OSB gussets. Treat "2x4 webs" as table boilerplate, not an actual member.

MATERIAL OMISSION, doors field: the record says only "Garage door itself NOT included" and never states that the door must be a low-headroom unit. Manual p.2, Owner Supplied: "Overhead 8' x 6/6 garage door with low headroom hardware." shedkitstore.com Features: "...garage door opening to accommodate even larger vehicle models (requires a low headroom track)". A buyer who orders a standard-lift 8x6'6" door cannot install it under the loft floor.

ENGINEERING NUANCE, loft/floor_framing: the 2x10 @ 16" o.c. over a 16'-0" clear span is real and is the manufacturer's own number, but it is engineered as an ATTIC floor at L/240, not a habitable-room floor at L/360. Permit p.3 headers verbatim: "ATTIC FLOOR LIVE LOAD (L): FLOOR LIVE LOAD - 2X8  30 PSF / FLOOR LIVE LOAD - 2X10  40 PSF"; "LIVE LOAD DEFLECTION  L / 240"; notes "1. BLOCKING TO BE PROVIDED EVERY 4'-0" C/C MAX. 2. MAX. FLOOR JOIST SPAN IS 16'-0"." Sits uneasily with the record's "genuine full second story" / vendor's "luxurious livable space potential", and with permit p.1: "designed for use as storage buildings or garages only. Use for any other purposes is neither implied nor inferred."

ENGINEERING NUANCE, foundation field: repeating the manual's wood-floor option as "treated 6x6 lumber over a bed of gravel, treated 2x6 joists at 16\" o.c." without runner spacing is misleading if read as a spec — treated 2x6 at 16\" o.c. cannot span anywhere near 16'. The manual itself gives no runner spacing (p.3: "Wood Floor on Runners: Suitable for storage or workshop. Treated 6x6 lumber over a bed of gravel Floor joist should be treated 2x6 spaced 16\" on center and covered with 3/4\" tongue and groove wood flooring."), so runners must in practice fall every ~4-6 ft. Note also that the manual reserves the slab for vehicles, and that FortressFloor is 12'-wide-only, so 16x20 buyers really are on their own for the deck.

FortressFloor is 12'-wide models only, so the 16x20 buyer must pour a slab or engineer their own 16' floor deck; the manual's fallback (treated 6x6 runners on gravel, 2x6 joists) is a storage-grade solution under a two-story building and needs local code approval
Two-story assembly is genuinely demanding: scaffolding rental, lifting 16' 2x10 joists and gambrel trusses at ~16' peak, and a steep 32:12 lower roof slope the vendor suggests hiring a roofer for

Explicitly sold as a storage building/garage only - not habitable space; 2x4 trusses and un-insulated dormerless gambrel geometry make conversion to a living space awkward, and the vendor warns against it

Permit paperwork has fine print: the free stamped set is state-specific (the posted XL set is a Virginia stamp with a 2027 expiry), other states cost a non-refundable fee, and FL/CA typically need a local engineer
Cut/loose-nail kit built by hand: nails shipped loose for hand framing, siding must be painted within 30 days or the warranty lapses, and warranty on workmanship is only 1 year with no labor coverage
The manufacturer page shows no price at all and its FAQ answers cover the whole product line, so real cost and lead time must be pulled from a retailer

plans.footprint_note: The same building is captioned "Dimensions 16x20 feet" on the south elevation (Fig. 1) and "Dimensions 20x16 feet" on the floor plan (Fig. 2); the 20 ft face is the south (long, glazed) wall and 16 ft is the north-south depth. Body text: "The outside dimensions for a two-pen brooder house should be 20x16 feet. The larger and heated room should be 12x16 feet and the cool exercise room 8x16 feet." Dimension string along the south wall on the floor plan reads 2'-0" + 4'-2" + 7'-8" + 4'-2" + 2'-0" = 20'-0"; depth reads 14'-0" + 2'-0" = 16'-0". Outside dimensions (drop siding face), not stud-line dimensions.
plans.style: Shed / single-slope roof, one story, two-pen poultry brooder house: south-facing glazed front wall, 12x16 heated "warm hover room" plus 8x16 "cool exercising room" separated by a 1x6 board partition, concrete slab floor
plans.price: Free (open-access PDF, University of Minnesota Digital Conservancy; no registration, no paywall)
plans.summary: The south wall carries two 12-light double-hung sash on weights and pulleys, two small transom sash in the upper corners (target: "about 1/4 of the south elevation should be of glass") and two 12" x 15" hinged chick doors with inclined runs; the two 2'-8" x 6'-4" people doors are not in the south wall — one is in the east end wall and one is in the interior 1x6 partition.
plans.foundation: 8-in. concrete foundation wall with the floor line/sill dimensioned 1'-3" above outside grade; the wall continues an undimensioned distance below grade (no depth, footing or frost-line dimension given)
plans.floor_framing: None in the 16x20 stationary design — the floor is a 4-in. concrete slab over 6 in. of cinders, so there are no joists, no girder and no beam spans to size. (The portable design shown at 12x14 uses "two thicknesses of matched boards laid crosswise... with one-ply roofing paper between," framed with 2x8 and 2x4 members on 4x6 skids per Figs. 5 and 7.)
plans.wall_framing: 2x4 studs; spacing is NOT stated anywhere. Wall build-up per Figs. 3 and 7, outside to inside: drop siding / one ply roofing paper / 1x6 dressed-and-matched boards on the outside face of the studs, with an optional flax-straw fill in the stud cavity and, for early-spring chicks, an added inside layer of paper plus vertical D&M boards. Interior pen divider is a 1x6 dressed-and-matched partition. No header, corner-post, bracing or shear-wall detail is drawn.
plans.roof: Single-slope (shed) roof falling from the 7'-4" south wall to the 5'-4" north wall across the 16 ft depth — about 2 ft of fall, i.e. roughly 1.5-in-12, though NO pitch is labeled on any drawing. 2x6 rafters (spacing not stated) spanning the 16 ft direction with a modest overhang front and back; 1x6 dressed-and-matched roof boards, building paper, then "prepared roofing" — the text says "roofing, 3-ply being desirable." For March/early-April chicks the bulletin advises ceiling the underside with matched lumber and packing the rafter bays with closely packed flax straw. No ridge, collar tie, truss, purlin or uplift detail; note a clear 2x6 rafter spanning ~16 ft at 1.5-in-12 would not pass a modern snow-load span check without intermediate support.
plans.siding: Drop siding over one ply of roofing paper over 1x6 dressed-and-matched boards (Figs. 3, 7). The text also permits lap siding or shingles as the exterior, a standard insulating plaster base with a thin plaster coat, or vertical D&M sheathing inside, and notes the outside boards should run vertically ("up and down") for durability and for easy spraying with disinfectants.
plans.windows: South wall only. Fig. 1 caption: "light and ventilation obtained through two double-hung windows with weights and two small windows hung as transoms" — the elevation marks the panes 10" x 14". The written spec (given for the 12x14 house) is "one double-sash window with 12 lights and 10x14-inch panes... with a transom made of a 3-pane cellar-window sash 10x14 inches, in the east and west upper corners of the south side, as near the plate as the construction will permit." Design target: "about 1/4 of the south elevation should be of glass." The bulletin insists on real weights and pulleys ("Do not allow the contractor to substitute home-made frames in which there are no pulleys"). Rough-opening dimensions are not given.
plans.doors: Two 2'-8" x 6'-4" doors, neither of them in the south wall (Fig. 2): one exterior door in the east end wall opening into the warm hover room, and one interior door at the south end of the 1x6 D&M partition swinging into the warm room — the cool exercising room has no exterior door of its own. Plus two 12" x 15" hinged chick doors at floor level in the south wall with inclined runs down to grade (Figs. 1, 7). The Fig. 2 note "Loose pin butts" labels the hinges of the inclined roost frames along the east wall (text: the lower roosts "may be removed by simply drawing the pins from the hinges"), not the doors; no door hinge hardware is called out. Interior openings also include a "Removable 6" Board" (6 inches, i.e. a 1x6 — Fig. 3 labels it "6" Board.") and removable boards at the roost-frame ends. Text: the door "should be large enough to admit a person with baskets or boxes," should open in, and should swing about eight inches above the floor level. No door construction detail or hardware schedule.
plans.wall_height: 7'-4" at the south (front) wall and 5'-4" at the north (rear) wall, floor to plate, dimensioned on both Fig. 3 (cross section) and Fig. 7 (wall sections)
plans.overall_height: Not stated. Only the 7'-4" / 5'-4" plate heights plus 1'-3" of foundation below the floor line are dimensioned; no ridge/high-point height above grade is given.
plans.loft: None — single story, no loft, no attic floor, no ceiling joists shown (the option described is packing straw between the rafters and ceiling the underside with matched lumber).
plans.skill_level: Not stated. The construction itself is elementary (2x4 stud walls, one sloping plane of 2x6 rafters, a concrete slab), but the bulletin is written for a farm owner working with a carpenter — "Do not allow the contractor to substitute home-made frames..." — and gives no step-by-step sequence, so a DIY builder must supply their own framing layout, spacings and quantities.
plans.materials_list_available: No. There is no bill of materials, cut list or quantity takeoff anywhere in the 12 pages; member sizes exist only as callouts lettered on the scanned drawings.

plans.permit_notes: Not stated. A 1936 extension bulletin predates the IRC/IBC entirely — there is no code reference, no design snow/wind load, no engineer stamp and no seal, so nothing here is submittable for a permit; the 2x6 rafters spanning ~16 ft and the unspecified stud/rafter spacing would both need modern verification. UMN adds the standing caveat: "This archival publication may not reflect current scientific knowledge or recommendations."
