pros: Lands exactly on the target footprint — 16 x 20 ft / 320 sq ft — and the two-room split (12x16 + 8x16) is a ready-made precedent for a shop-plus-storage or shop-plus-cold-room layout.
Genuinely free and unencumbered: direct PDF download from a university repository, no email wall, no license fee, permanent handle for citation.

Simplest possible roof geometry: one plane of 2x6 rafters from a 7'-4" front wall to a 5'-4" rear wall — no ridge, no truss, no gambrel jig, no birdsmouth math on two pitches. Fastest framing of any style at this size.
Dimensioned floor plan actually resolves to the stated overall: 2'-0"+4'-2"+7'-8"+4'-2"+2'-0" = 20'-0", so window/pier bay layout on the long wall can be lifted straight off the sheet.
Slab-on-grade with an 8" perimeter wall and 4" concrete over 6" cinders removes the entire floor-joist/beam/skid problem and the girder span question that dogs most 16x20 wood-floor sheds.
Layered wall and roof build-ups are spelled out (sheathing / paper / drop siding, cavity fill, ceiled rafter bays), which is more construction detail than many modern free one-page shed plans give.

The daylighting rule of thumb — "about 1/4 of the south elevation should be of glass" — plus operable transoms at the plate is a solid, still-valid passive light-and-ventilation strategy for a south-facing workshop or studio.
Very low material bill by modern standards: no engineered lumber, no trusses, 2x4 walls, 2x6 rafters, board sheathing.
Public-domain-era government/extension publication, so copying and adapting the drawings is low-risk.
cons: It is a 1936 poultry brooder house, not a shed or workshop plan — much of the 12 pages is chick husbandry (hovers, roosts, litter, sunporches) rather than construction.
No bill of materials, no cut list, no quantities of any kind. You must do your own takeoff from lettered notes on scanned pencil drawings.
No stud spacing and no rafter spacing are given anywhere — the two numbers you most need to price and build the shell.

The 2x6 rafters appear to span the full ~16 ft depth at roughly 1.5-in-12 with no intermediate support. That will not survive a modern snow-load or deflection check (2x6 No.2 at 16" o.c. is nowhere near a 16 ft clear span), so a real build needs deeper rafters, closer spacing, or a mid-span beam.

Roof pitch is never labeled; the ~1.5-in-12 slope is inferred from the 7'-4"/5'-4" plate heights and is far too flat for shingles — it is a roll-roofing or modern membrane slope only, which raises long-term maintenance risk.
Rear plate height of 5'-4" makes the north half of the interior unusable at full standing height — fine for chicks, cramped for a shop or studio without raising the walls.
Zero engineering: no design loads, no code reference, no engineer's stamp, no uplift/lateral bracing, no anchor-bolt or hold-down detail. Not permit-submittable as-is.
Foundation detail is minimal — 8" wall, 1'-3" below the floor line — with no footing width, no frost depth (a real problem in Minnesota) and no reinforcement called out.
No electrical, no insulation R-values (the insulation options are sawdust, planer shavings or flax straw), no vapor barrier, no modern moisture detailing.
Scanned image PDF at ~5.4 x 8.6 in with hand-lettered notes; small dimensions and roost spacings are hard to read and nothing can be printed to scale.
Drawings are illustrative figures, not a coordinated sheet set: no framing plan, no elevation of the north/east/west walls, no door or window construction detail, no section through the partition.
UMN's own item record warns "This archival publication may not reflect current scientific knowledge or recommendations."
The only other design in the bulletin is a 12x14 portable (168 sq ft), which is outside the 240-480 sq ft range, so there are no larger variants to scale from.

plans.summary_original: A 12-page 1936 University of Minnesota Agricultural Extension bulletin (Special Bulletin 105, revised December 1936) whose lead design — the "Minnesota Model Two-Pen Stationary Brooder House" — is a 16 x 20 ft (320 sq ft) single-slope building that lands exactly on the target footprint. Three scanned pencil drawings document it: a south elevation (Fig. 1), a dimensioned floor plan (Fig. 2), and a cross section (Fig. 3); two generic wall sections (Fig. 7) add the south/north wall build-ups. Framing called out on the drawings is 2x4 studs, 2x6 rafters, 1x6 dressed-and-matched sheathing and roof boards, building paper plus "prepared roofing" (text recommends 3-ply), drop siding outside, optional flax-straw cavity and rafter-bay fill, a 1x6 D&M interior partition, a 4 in. concrete floor over 6 in. of cinders, and an 8 in. concrete foundation wall carried 1'-3" below the floor line. Wall heights are 7'-4" at the south wall and 5'-4" at the north wall, so the roof simply falls about 2 ft across the 16 ft depth (the pitch itself is never labeled). The south wall carries two 12-light double-hung sash on weights and pulleys plus two small transom sash in the upper corners — the text's target is "about 1/4 of the south elevation should be of glass" — two 2'-8" x 6'-4" people doors, and two 12" x 15" hinged chick doors with inclined runs. The bulletin also documents a smaller one-pen PORTABLE house at 12x14 ft on 4x6 skids with a double matched-board floor (168 sq ft, below the target range), and states a 12x14 house with a 52-inch hover suits 400 chicks. Most of the 12 pages are husbandry advice — brooder stoves, hovers, roosts, feeders, litter, sunporches, yard rotation — not construction sequence. There is no bill of materials, no cut list, no stud or rafter spacing, no cost, and no engineering; UMN itself flags the item: "This archival publication may not reflect current scientific knowledge or recommendations." Useful as a proportion/detail reference and as a genuinely free 16x20 shed-roof precedent, but it is not a buildable modern plan set on its own.
plans.foundation_original: Stationary version (the 16x20): 8-in. concrete foundation wall carried 1'-3" below the floor line and bearing below grade, with a 4-in. concrete floor poured over 6 in. of cinders (Fig. 3). Text: "Permanent houses are best placed on a foundation and floored with concrete" and "concrete floors should be laid above crushed rock or cinders and covered with a litter of sand or gravel." No footing width, frost depth, reinforcement, anchor bolt or sill-anchorage detail is given. The 12x14 portable alternative sits on 4x6 skids.

plans.name: 16x24 Gambrel Barn Shed Plans
plans.footprint_note: Floor plan dimensions 16 ft across the front (gable/door) wall and 24 ft along the sidewall, to the outside of the floor frame. Elevations agree: 16 ft on FRONT ELEVATION, 24 ft on SIDE ELEVATION.
plans.style: Gambrel / barn-style storage shed. Two-segment gambrel roof stick-framed from individual 2x6 rafters (not trusses), on a skid-supported wood floor. Vertical board-look siding, one pair of double doors in the 16 ft gable end.
plans.price: Free
plans.summary: A free, ad-supported set of eight JPEG drawing sheets on one ShedDrafts.com page for a 16 x 24 ft (384 sq ft) gambrel barn shed with 6 ft sidewalls and 14 ft overall height. The drawings are genuinely dimensioned and specified: 4x4 pressure-treated skids under 2x6 PT floor joists at 16 in o.c. with 3/4 in CDX plywood decking, 2x4 pine studs at 24 in o.c., 2x6 pine gambrel rafters at 24 in o.c. built from two 72 in segments per side with 22-1/2 degree joint cuts, 1/2 in CDX sheathing, 15# felt, 20-year seal-tab shingles and 1/2 in Masonite siding. Sheets are: rendering, front elevation, side elevation, floor plan, floor framing plan, roof framing plan, building section, and a 60 in double-door detail. Critically, there is no materials or cut list, no quantity takeoff, no written step-by-step instructions for this size, no PDF download, and no loft, collar-tie or rafter-joint connection detail - it is a dimensioned concept/framing set, not a complete construction document package.
includes: Rendering / photo of the finished gambrel shed (draft design sheet)
FRONT ELEVATION - 16 ft wide, 14 ft overall height, 6 ft to eave, 2x6 fly rafter called out
SIDE ELEVATION - 24 ft long, shingle coursing shown, 2x6 O.H. (overhang) called out
FLOOR PLAN - 16 x 24 ft with stud layout dimensioned along the front wall (24, 24, 20, 60, 18, 24, 24 in) and 24 in o.c. down the sidewall
FLOOR FRAMING PLAN - 2x6 joists at 16 in o.c. over three 4x4 skids, 2x6 band
ROOF FRAMING PLAN - 2x6 common rafters at 24 in o.c., three ridge/break lines labeled RIDGE, 2x4 trim
BUILDING SECTION - full material stack-up from skids to shingles with the 72 in gambrel segment lengths and 22-1/2 degree joint cuts
60 in DOOR detail sheet with member lengths (lintel, stiles, uprights, jambs, 2x6 base, corner blocks)
pros: Free to view with no email gate, no paywall and no registration - the eight drawing sheets load directly on the page.

The building section is unusually specific for a free web plan: it names species/grade-ish specs (pine studs and rafters, P.T. joists and skids), sheathing thickness, underlayment weight, shingle rating and siding material.

Roof geometry is actually solvable from the drawings: two 72 in rafter segments per side with 22-1/2 degree cuts at each joint, which checks out against the 16 ft span and the 14 ft minus 6 ft = 8 ft roof rise, so you can cut rafters from these numbers.
Stick-framed 2x6 rafters at 24 in o.c. mean no crane, no truss order and no shop - one or two people can build every roof member on site.
384 sq ft with a 6 ft wall and 8 ft of gambrel volume above gives a very large storage envelope for the footprint, and the gambrel shape sheds snow better than a low-slope shed roof.
Skid-on-gravel foundation is the cheapest and most permit-flexible base: no concrete, no excavation, and in many jurisdictions it keeps the building classed as movable.
Simple, cheap material palette (2x4 walls, Masonite siding, seal-tab shingles) keeps material cost near the floor for this size.
A same-footprint alternative exists on the site (16x24 gambrel 2-story) if you want an actual second floor rather than open attic volume.
cons: No materials list, cut list or quantity takeoff anywhere on the page - you must do your own takeoff for a 384 sq ft building, which is the single biggest gap here.
No written build instructions for this size. The prose is six generic sentences (and it even wanders off-topic, mentioning a potting shed and cedar lumber that appear nowhere in the drawings).

Rafters are NOT engineered and no gusset, plywood plate, purlin or collar-tie detail is given for the 22-1/2 degree gambrel joints. On a 16 ft span that joint is the whole structural story, and the plan simply does not show how to make it.

Floor framing looks marginal: 2x6 joists at 16 in o.c. run the 16 ft direction over only three 4x4 skids, i.e. roughly 8 ft clear spans. That is at or past typical limits for storage loading - expect bounce and plan on extra skids, piers or a beam line if you will store anything heavy.
Only three 4x4 skids under a 16 ft width is thin support for a 384 sq ft building; the gravel pad has to be very well compacted and dead level or the floor will rack.
6 ft sidewalls are low. You cannot stand upright against the walls, shelving depth is limited, and a standard 6 ft 8 in prehung door will not fit - the plan uses a 72 in (6 ft) door opening to suit.
No loft, attic floor or ceiling joists are drawn even though roughly 8 ft of roof volume exists, so the biggest advantage of a gambrel is left undetailed.
No windows are framed or dimensioned on any sheet, despite the page text and one caption referring to windows. Any glazing is on you, including headers and trimmers.
No PDF, no printable scaled sheet, no plan revision number and no scale bar - just web JPEGs at 600 px wide, which is thin for a plan-check submittal.

At 384 sq ft this is far above the common 100-200 sq ft permit exemption, so a permit set with real structural detail (and likely frost-depth footings rather than skids) will probably be required - and this document set is not close to submittal quality.
No stated skill level, build time, or cost, and no author credentials beyond a site username. Content is dated 2018 with a 2024 update.
The page pushes a third-party paid shed-plan offer via a popup and a footer Download Plans call to action, which is affiliate upsell rather than a download of this plan.

Floor joist should be treated 2x8 spaced 16" on center and covered with 3/4" tongue and groove wood flooring"). The quoted "Do Not make the foundation larger than the building size." is verbatim from this same page.

unsupported_claims: pros[5] "No specialty tools required (drill, ladder, hammer, saw, tape, square, 6' level)" — the quoted FAQ list is real, but the manual's own "Tools Required" block for this model adds a caulking gun and scaffolding, with the note "You will need to rent six sections of scaffolding to safely install the second floor material. Use safety harnesses when on the scaffolding." Presenting "no specialty tools" as a pro for a 16'-2"-tall two-story kit is contradicted by the model-specific manual.

pros[2] "...so the loft is wide open with nothing in your headroom" — the stamped truss has no bottom chord and no collar tie (verified), but it does have 2X4 WEB members and glued/nailed OSB gussets inside the loft volume, and the loft is only 7'-1" at center falling to 5'-9" at the knee (permit p.9). "Nothing in your headroom" overstates it.

pros[0]/pros[1] omit the conditions the stamped floor sheet imposes: the 40 psf rating is for "2X10 DF-LAR. NO. 1 @ 16" C/C" (Douglas Fir-Larch No.1, not the unspecified "2x10" in the local-supplier list), with "BLOCKING TO BE PROVIDED EVERY 4'-0" C/C MAX" and "MAX. FLOOR JOIST SPAN IS 16'-0"", and the live load is labeled "ATTIC FLOOR LIVE LOAD". A buyer who lets the local yard supply SPF 2x10s or skips blocking is outside the stamp.

price field's characterization of shedkitstore.com as "Best Barns' own factory store" is not stated anywhere on bestbarns.com — the Where-to-Buy section of the page under review links only to Home Depot, Lowe's, Menards and Wayfair, and the only shedkitstore.com link on the page is for a RapidShed product. The prices themselves are correct; the ownership relationship is an inference.

plans.name: 16x20 Gable Garage Workshop Shed Plans
plans.footprint_note: Nominal. The framing elevations are dimensioned 15'11" (front/rear wall) x 19'11" (side wall), i.e. outside-of-framing, so the slab is 16'0" x 20'0" and sheathing/siding/trim adds roughly another 1-1/2" to 2" per side. 317 sq ft of framed area, rounded to 320. Roof overhangs add 18" at the eaves and about 10-1/2" at the rakes, so the roofed footprint is larger than 16x20 for setback purposes.
plans.style: Single-car gable-roof garage / workshop shed on a slab. 8/12 gable roof on ordered trusses at 24" o.c. with 18" eave overhangs and boxed gable returns; 9 ft stud walls; 8 ft wide overhead garage door in one gable end with a doubled LVL header; separate 3'0" side-hinged entry door under a small 6/12 bracketed door hood; 7 awning windows; fiber-cement lap siding with shingle-panel gable ends and composite trim (Craftsman/cottage look).
plans.price: Free
plans.summary: A free, fully ungated set of 11 blueprint images plus a complete itemized materials list, published as web images (WEBP) on one ShedDrafts.com page — no cart, no email form, no watermark. It is a real single-car garage/workshop: 15'11" x 19'11" framed, 9'1-1/8" tall 2x4 walls sheathed in 1/2" OSB, an 8/12 gable roof carried on 9 ordered common trusses plus 2 dropped-top-chord gable trusses at 24" o.c. (16 ft span, 18" overhang), a 97-1/2" x 7'1" rough opening for the overhead door spanned by a doubled 1-3/4" x 9-1/2" x 9' LVL header, and a 38" x 6'10-1/2" side entry with a doubled 2x10 header. The finish spec is house-grade: 5/16" fiber-cement lap siding, 16"x4' shingle panels in the gables, composite trim throughout, 7 Marvin awning windows and a Simpson fir door. The critical gap is the bottom of the building — there is no floor plan and no foundation sheet, only treated bottom plates, foam sill sealer and a concrete edge drawn in Section E-E, so you must design and size the slab yourself.
includes: Hero photo of a finished comparable yellow gable garage/workshop (stock photograph, not a render of these drawings)

Sheet 01 - Front Elevation with keyed callouts A-H, plus Section A-A (eave: roofing, 5/8" OSB, 2x4 lookout, 2x4 subfascia, 3/4"x7-1/4" fascia, 3/8" soffit, 1"x5-1/2" trim) and Section B-B (garage door head: 1/2" OSB, doubled 9-1/2" LVL header, metal drip cap, 3/4"x4" jamb, 1/2"x1-1/2" stop)

Sheet 02 - Front Elevation Details: Section C-C (door and garage door jambs/casings in plan), Section D-D (corner trim, rip to 4-1/2"), Section E-E (1-3/4" door on a 5" aluminum sill over the concrete), Section F-F (siding/trim at the wall), Detail G (window trim: 31-1/4" x 29-1/4" outside trim, 1-1/2"x1-1/2" 10-degree bevel sill), Detail H (rake/eave build-up with 5/8"x48" OSB roof panel over truss)

Sheet 03 - Front Wall Elevation, fully dimensioned: 15'11" long, 9'1-1/8" tall, studs 16" o.c. with 12" end bays, 97-1/2" x 7'1" garage door rough opening under doubled 9-1/2" LVLs, 38" x 6'10-1/2" entry door rough opening under doubled 2x10s
Sheet 04 - Rear Wall Elevation: 15'11" x 9'1-1/8", blank wall, studs 16" o.c. with 12" end bays
Sheet 05 - Side Wall Elevation: 19'11" x 9'1-1/8", three window openings (26" wide x 24" high rough openings, 68-1/2" to sill) under doubled 2x10 headers, studs 16" o.c. with 15-1/2" end bays
Sheet 06 - Inner (Common) Truss, 9 required: 15'11" span, 52" peak height above the bottom chord, 10-1/4" tail, king post and two struts
Sheet 07 - Rear (Gable End) Truss: 48-1/2" peak height (top chord lowered 3-1/2"), studded webs, 2x4 lookout notches at 24" o.c.
Sheet 08 - Front (Gable End) Truss: studded webs with a 26" x 24" framed opening for the gable window
Sheet 09 - Small Roof (the entry-door hood): 6/12 pitch, 32" and 29-3/4" from peak, 10-1/2" projection past the wall, 2x4 nailers/subfascia, 5/8" OSB, 3/8" soffit, 1x6 fascia with 1x2 fascia trim

Sheet 10 - Door hood bracket and casing details: 4x4 top arm 25-1/4" long (19" exposed), 2x4 back 30" tall, 26-7/8" diagonal knee with 1-1/2" shoulders, plus a 24" section through the hood at the door casing
Sheet 11 - Truss Spacing layout over the 19'11" length: front and rear gable trusses with lookouts, 9 center (common) trusses, a 2x4 truss support/temporary brace, 2x4 subfascia
Sheet 12 - Shed Materials List image: complete itemized bill for wall framing, roof framing, exterior trim, brackets, roofing and hardware, with quantities
pros: Completely ungated and free: all 11 drawings and the full materials list render as plain images on the page with no cart, no email form, no account and no watermark. The whole set can be right-clicked or, as here, pulled straight from /wp-content/uploads/.

The roof over the 16 ft span is handed to a truss plant, not guessed at. The list specifies '9 - 16' span, 8/12 with 18" overhang' common trusses plus '2 - (order with top chord lowered 3-1/2")' gable-end trusses, and the spacing sheet shows 11 trusses over 19'11" (24" o.c.) tied down with 22 RT-7 rafter ties. Ordering engineered trusses is both the easiest and the most permit-friendly way to roof a 16 ft clear span.

The garage door header - exactly the detail most DIY garage plans fudge - is properly sized and drawn twice. Sheet 03 shows doubled 9-1/2" LVLs over a 97-1/2" rough opening and the materials list calls out '2 - 1-3/4" x 9-1/2" x 9' LVL beam'. The 38" side door gets doubled 2x10s. Section B-B even shows the jamb, stop and drip cap around the door track.

Real 9 ft walls: 100 studs at 2x4 x 104-5/8", single treated bottom plate, doubled top plate, and 4' x 9' x 1/2" OSB sheathing sheets so there is no horizontal sheathing seam. That gives 7'1" of headroom over the overhead door and enough wall for hanging storage or a wall cabinet run - much better than the usual 8 ft shed wall.

The materials list is unusually specific and genuinely usable: every stick by size and length, 22 sheets of wall OSB, 18 sheets of roof OSB, 100 pieces of lap siding, 30 gable shingle panels, ten separate nail weights by type, 22 RT-7 rafter ties, 6 tubes of caulk, and even model numbers for the openings (Marvin Awning CW2523, Simpson 3' x 6'8" Fir No. 6803). You can walk into a lumberyard with this.
Stud layout is dimensioned bay by bay on all three framing elevations (16" o.c. with 12" or 15-1/2" end bays), so plates can be marked directly off the sheets without any layout math.

The finish carpentry is actually drawn - six sections and two blow-up details covering the eave, rake, corner boards, water table, window casing bevel, aluminum sill at the slab, and both garage-door and entry-door casings. Most free plans in this size class stop at framing.

Slab-on-grade means no floor joists, no skids, no rim board and no rot detail to get wrong - the list starts with treated bottom plates and foam sill sealer, and Section E-E shows the door sill sitting on concrete.

Simple rectangle, one pitch, no loft, no dormer, no hips: the geometry is about as forgiving as a 320 sq ft garage gets, and the only fussy carpentry is the small 6/12 bracketed door hood, which is optional in practice.
cons: There is no floor plan and no foundation sheet. The slab exists only by implication (treated bottom plates, 2 rolls of foam sill sealer, a concrete edge in Section E-E). No slab thickness, no footing width or frost depth, no rebar or mesh, no anchor bolts or hold-downs, and zero concrete or gravel quantities in the materials list. The single most expensive and least reversible part of the build is undesigned - you supply it.

No floor plan also means no interior layout, no confirmation of where the side door and windows fall along the 20 ft walls, and no dimensioned relationship between the garage opening and the corners other than what you can back out of the front wall elevation.

The sheet set is front-heavy: there is no side elevation, no rear elevation and no building section. Nine of the eleven drawings are the front wall, the front-wall details, the trusses and the door hood.

The trusses must be bought, not built. The 'Inner (Common) Truss' drawing gives only span (15'11"), peak height (52") and tail (10-1/4") - no chord or web lumber sizes, no plate or gusset spec, no load assumption. If your area has no truss supplier or you wanted to site-build them, this plan does not let you.

Nothing is engineered or stamped by the publisher. No snow load, no wind speed, no shear wall or bracing schedule (the list just says 'Bracing 8 - 2x4 x 10' / 4 - 2x4 x 16'' with no drawing showing where it goes), and no anchorage from the frame to the slab. At 320 sq ft with an 8 ft overhead door this is far past every common 120-200 sq ft permit exemption; expect a permit and expect the plan checker to want a foundation detail and a truss package these sheets do not contain.

The overhead garage door is not in the plan at all. The list ends with 'You'll also need an overhead garage door, door hardware and exterior paint.' No track clearance dimension, no door model, no opener allowance. Gutters, insulation, drywall, electrical and any interior finish are likewise absent.

This is a house-grade, expensive finish spec, not a cheap shed: 100 pieces of 5/16" fiber-cement lap siding, 30 shingle panels, roughly 60 pieces of 16 ft composite trim board, 7 Marvin awning windows and a Simpson fir door. Materials will run several times a T1-11-and-3-tab equivalent, and no cost estimate is given anywhere.

Fiber cement plus composite trim is heavier, dustier and less forgiving than plywood siding - it needs silica PPE, shears or a dedicated blade, and the specified 2" ring-shank siding nails. Combined with 4' x 9' sheathing sheets and 16 ft trim boards, this is not a comfortable solo build.

No cut list, no step-by-step instructions, no build sequence, no build time, no skill level and no cost estimate. The only vertical geometry you are given for the roof is the 52" truss peak height; there is no overall building height anywhere on any sheet.

The prose is thin SEO filler and internally inconsistent - the same building is headed '16x20 Gable Garden Shed Assembly Plans' in one section and 'Truss Design And Roof Framing For 16x20 Carport' in another, and the body claims you can 'set up a beautiful workshop in some weekends', which is not credible for a 320 sq ft slab-on-grade garage.
No PDF and no printable sheet set - the plans exist only as web images, so there is nothing to hand a lumberyard, an inspector or a helper on site without screenshotting.

The page pushes a separate 'New 15-Page Detailed Shed Building Plans With Easy Instructions' download via a JavaScript popup, implying the free sheets are deliberately short on instructions. The popup's contents and any price are not in the page HTML, so what it actually delivers is unverifiable from the page.
plans.data_confidence: High for everything drawn on the sheets: all 12 images (11 drawings plus the materials list) were downloaded at full resolution and read directly, and the materials list was transcribed line by line including the overlap regions. Dimensions quoted (15'11", 19'11", 9'1-1/8", 97-1/2" x 7'1", 38" x 6'10-1/2", 26" x 24" window RO, 52" and 48-1/2" truss heights, 18" and 10-1/4" overhangs, 6/12 door hood) are read off the drawings. High confidence that no floor plan, foundation sheet, side/rear elevation or building section exists - the article contains exactly 12 plan images and they are all accounted for. FETCH CAVEAT worth knowing for the browsing site: the first direct request to this exact URL returned a cached copy of a completely different post (the 16x24 Gambrel Barn Shed page, ?p=10634) with a 200 status; re-requesting with a cache-buster returned the correct page, whose canonical and og:url both point back to this URL. If the page ever renders as a gambrel barn, retry. Medium/low confidence on anything the sheets omit: overall height, roof pitch of the main roof is given only as the truss order spec (8/12), stud spacing is dimensioned but never labeled "o.c.", and cost, build time, skill level, permit guidance, author and publish date are simply not published. Price is honestly "Free" - no dollar amount of any kind appears in the HTML - but no price string is published either; the "Download Plans" CTA is a JS popup whose contents are not in the HTML, so whether that upsell is free-for-email or paid could not be determined.

plans.format: Single web page with 12 embedded WEBP images: 11 blueprint drawings (front elevation with sections A-A and B-B, front elevation details with sections C-C through F-F and details G-H, front/rear/side wall framing elevations, three truss designs, small roof, bracket and casing details, truss spacing layout) plus one materials list image, and a stock hero photograph. No PDF, no CAD file, no printable sheet set, no downloadable archive.
plans.page_count: 12 plan images on one web page (11 drawings + 1 materials list image); no PDF page count exists
plans.foundation: Concrete slab on grade, but never drawn as its own sheet and never dimensioned. The evidence is indirect: the materials list starts with pressure-treated bottom plates (4 - 2x4 x 16' and 1 - 2x4 x 8', exactly the 72 ft perimeter), the hardware list includes 2 rolls of foam sill sealer, Section E-E shows the entry door on a 5" aluminum sill sitting on a concrete edge, and Section F-F shows the siding terminating above concrete. There is no slab thickness, no turned-down edge or footing dimension, no frost depth, no rebar or wire mesh, no anchor bolt or hold-down callout, and no concrete or gravel quantity anywhere in the materials list. You must design and size the foundation yourself.
plans.floor_framing: None. There are no floor joists, skids, rim boards or subfloor sheets in the plan or the materials list - the finished floor is the concrete slab itself. This removes a whole phase of work but also removes the plan's only chance to specify how the frame is anchored down.
plans.wall_framing: 2x4 platform framing. 100 studs at 2x4 x 104-5/8" spf, single pressure-treated 2x4 bottom plate, doubled 2x4 top plates (4 pcs 2x4 x 20' for the side walls and 4 pcs 2x4 x 16' for the front and rear). Studs are laid out at 16" bays with 12" end bays on the front and rear walls and 15-1/2" end bays on the side walls, with 3-1/2" corner returns shown. Headers are 5 pcs 2x10 x 8' spf doubled up over the 38" entry door and the three 26" side-wall windows; the overhead door gets 2 pcs of 1-3/4" x 9-1/2" x 9' LVL. Bracing is listed as 8 pcs 2x4 x 10' plus 4 pcs 2x4 x 16' but is not drawn on any sheet. Sheathed with 22 sheets of 4' x 9' x 1/2" OSB (full-height sheets, no horizontal seam).
plans.wall_height: 9'1-1/8" from the bottom of the treated bottom plate to the top of the doubled top plate, dimensioned identically on the front, rear and side wall elevations. This checks out exactly against the stud spec: 104-5/8" stud + 1-1/2" bottom plate + 3" of doubled top plate = 109-1/8". The 4' x 9' wall sheathing sheets confirm it.
plans.roof: 8/12 gable roof on ordered trusses. 9 common trusses at 15'11" span with a 52" peak height above the bottom chord, an 18" overhang and a 10-1/4" tail; plus 2 gable-end trusses ordered with the top chord lowered 3-1/2" (48-1/2" peak) so 9 pcs of 2x4 x 8' lookouts at 24" o.c. can run over them to carry the rake overhang. 11 trusses over the 19'11" length works out to 24" o.c., and 22 RT-7 rafter ties (two per truss) tie them to the top plate. Subfascia is 8 pcs 2x4 x 12'; temporary/permanent bracing is 1 pc 2x4 x 20' plus 2 pcs 2x4 x 10'. Deck is 18 sheets of 4' x 8' x 5/8" OSB. Roofing is 2 rolls of ice-and-water barrier, 1 roll of No. 15 paper, 48 lin. ft. of starter, 600 sq. ft. of shingles and 24 lin. ft. of cap. The eave build-up (Section A-A, Detail H) is 2x4 subfascia, 3/4" x 7-1/4" fascia with 3/4" x 3" fascia trim, 3/8" soffit and 1" x 5-1/2" trim. Separate small door hood roof: 6/12 pitch, 32" and 29-3/4" rafter runs, 10-1/2" projection, 2 pcs 2x4 x 12' with 2x4 nailers, 5/8" OSB, 3/8" soffit, 1x6 fascia and 1x2 fascia trim, carried on two site-built brackets (4x4 top arm 25-1/4" long, 2x4 back 30" tall, 26-7/8" knee brace).
plans.siding: 100 pieces of 6-1/4" x 12' x 5/16" fiber cement lap siding over the 1/2" OSB, fastened with 2" ring-shank siding nails (10 lbs specified, plus 2 lbs each of 2-1/2" and 1-1/4"). Gable ends switch to 30 pieces of 16" x 4' shingle panels with 1x3 x 16' composite shingle trim at the transition. All trim is composite board: 8 pcs 1" x 5-1/2" x 16' corner boards, 4 pcs 1x10 x 16' plus 4 pcs 1x2 x 16' water table, 7 pcs 1x8 x 16' fascia, 9 pcs 1" x 5-1/2" x 16' soffit trim, 7 pcs of 2' x 16' x 3/8" smooth soffit. Window and door casing is 1" x 3-1/2" x 16' composite (rip 5-1/2" scrap down for the remainder) with 1 pc 2x6 x 8' cedar ripped for sills. 6 tubes of exterior caulk. Paint is required but not included.
plans.windows: 7 windows, all Marvin Awning CW2523 per the materials list. Three per side wall (26" wide x 24" high rough openings under doubled 2x10 headers, sill at 68-1/2" above the plate line) and one in the front gable, framed as a 26" x 24" opening inside the front gable-end truss webbing. Detail G gives the trim: 31-1/4" x 29-1/4" outside casing of 1" x 3-1/2" composite with 3/4" x 1-1/2" stops and a 1-1/2" x 1-1/2" sill with a 10-degree bevel, plus 1 roll of window wrap flashing and 1-1/8" drip caps (ten 10 ft lengths).
plans.doors: Two openings. (1) Overhead garage door in the front gable wall: 97-1/2" wide x 7'1" high rough opening (an 8 ft x 7 ft door) spanned by two 1-3/4" x 9-1/2" x 9' LVLs, with 1x6 x 16' composite jambs, 1" x 5-1/2" plus 1x2 composite casing, a 3/4" x 4" jamb, a 1/2" x 1-1/2" stop and a metal drip cap detailed in Section B-B and Section C-C. The door itself, its hardware and any opener are explicitly NOT included ("You'll also need an overhead garage door, door hardware and exterior paint"). (2) Side-hinged entry door in the same gable wall: 1 Simpson 3'0" x 6'8" fir door, No. 6803, in a 38" x 6'10-1/2" rough opening under doubled 2x10s, on a 5" aluminum sill over the slab, sheltered by the 6/12 bracketed door hood.
plans.loft: none. No loft, no attic floor and no storage platform is drawn or listed - the common trusses have a king post and struts through the middle of the attic space, so a loft would require a different (attic/room-in-attic) truss order.
plans.overall_height: not stated. No sheet gives an overall building height. It derives to roughly 13 ft 5 in above the slab (9'1-1/8" wall + 52" truss peak height) before roof sheathing and shingles.
plans.skill_level: not stated by the source. Realistically intermediate to advanced: you must design, form, pour and finish a 16x20 slab that the plan does not detail, order and set 11 trusses over a 16 ft span, hoist doubled 9-1/2" LVLs over an 8 ft opening, handle 4x9 sheathing and 16 ft composite trim, and cut and hang 100 pieces of fiber-cement siding. Not a first shed, and not a comfortable solo job.
plans.build_time: not stated. The page only claims you can "set up a beautiful workshop in some weekends", which is not credible for a 320 sq ft slab-on-grade garage with a truss roof and fiber-cement siding.
plans.materials_list_available: free-on-page
plans.permit_notes: The page says nothing about permits, codes, loads or setbacks for this design. At 320 sq ft with an 8 ft overhead vehicle door it is well past the common 120-200 sq ft accessory-structure exemption, and a garage/vehicle use often triggers extra requirements (fire separation distance to the house or lot line, slab and anchorage detail, sometimes a driveway or impervious-surface review). What will stall a permit application here is the missing foundation sheet and the missing truss engineering: bring the truss supplier's stamped truss drawings and a locally appropriate slab/footing detail keyed to your frost depth, plus an anchorage schedule, none of which these sheets provide. Also check the roofed footprint, not 16x20 - the 18" eaves and roughly 10-1/2" rakes push the drip line past the framed rectangle for setback measurement. ShedDrafts publishes a general "Shed Building Codes and Permit Guide For DIY Builders" article but it is not specific to this plan.
plans.refund_policy: Not applicable - the resource is free, with no purchase, cart, account or email signup required to view any of the drawings or the materials list.

plans.footprint_note: Cover sheet states BUILD SIZE: 20'W x 16'D x 14'-11"H and CAPACITY: 320SF. The gable-end elevation dimensions the sided wall at 16'-3" wide and 19'-2" including roof overhangs, so the 16x20 is the framed/nominal footprint. Ridge runs the 20' direction (2x10 ridge is 23'-4" long with overhangs); rafters span the 16' direction. Add roughly 108 SF of loft above for ~428 SF of total floor area.
plans.style: Gable cabin with sleeping loft — 9:12 pitch, steel panel roof, T1-11 siding, cathedral interior. Marketed on the cover sheet as the "16X20 Redwood Cabin Plan"; laid out as habitable space (kitchen, bathroom with shower, flex/bedroom, living room) rather than a bare storage shed.
plans.summary: A 42-sheet PDF plan set for a 16x20 (320 SF) stick-framed cabin with a ~108 SF sleeping loft, sold for $99 as an instant download from Build Blueprint's Gumroad store. The shell is 2x6 walls on 2x6 floor joists over a 6-skid 4x4 foundation set on 24 galvanized pier-block post bases, with a 9:12 gable roof of 30 2x8 rafters at 24" o.c. on a 2x10 ridge, 22 Simpson Strong-Tie 18-gauge rafter ties, 3/4" plywood sheathing and steel roof panels. It is drawn as a small dwelling, not a shed: sheets cover a bathroom with shower, kitchen, two closets, plumbing and electrical layouts for both levels, and R-19 kraft-faced batts with 1/2" drywall. Nothing on the page or in the preview sheets addresses codes, permits, snow/wind loads or engineering, and the set is not stamped.

A dedicated "Bathroom and Loft" sheet and a loft floor plan sheet are included, and a separate electrical layout covers the loft level. Access is a straight wooden ladder in the interior renders, not a stair, and the loft is guarded with a metal railing. plans.skill_level: Not formally rated. The vendor says only: "This set of plans have everything you need to build the cabin, suitable for DIYer's or give it to a professional builder," and the store bio claims "detailed step-by-step instructions for all skill levels." Realistically intermediate-to-advanced for a DIYer: site-cut rafters with birdsmouth notches, a loft, built-up headers, metal roofing, and rough plumbing and electrical.
plans.est_material_cost: $7,500 — listed on the Gumroad page as a product attribute, "Cost to Build: 7500". No date, region, scope or itemized basis is given for that figure.
plans.permit_notes: not stated — neither the sales page nor any legible preview sheet mentions building codes, permits, inspections, snow or wind loads, seismic category, or an engineer's review. Nothing is stamped or sealed. Worth flagging because a 320 SF insulated structure with a bathroom, kitchen, plumbing and electrical is a dwelling/ADU in most jurisdictions, which typically means a full permit, setback review, water/septic approval and possibly stamped drawings.
plans.refund_policy: "No refunds allowed." Fine print: "Once your file is downloaded, digital products do not qualify for returns, exchanges, or cancellations. Please contact the seller about any problems with your order." (Policy last updated 2025-04-09.)
pros: Unusually complete for the price tier: 42 sheets covering cover page, materials list, four elevations, both floor plans, foundation, floor panels, exterior and interior wall framing, bathroom and loft, rafter layout and rafter cutting, roofing, siding layout, door schedule, window schedule, plumbing layout, electrical layout for both levels, and insulation & drywall.

The full materials list is legible in a free preview image on the sales page, so you can price the entire build (6 4x4 skids, 17 2x6 floor joists, 52 2x6 studs, 30 2x8 rafters, 2x10 ridge, 20 sheets T1-11, 18 sheets 3/4" ply, steel panels) before spending $99.

Roof is genuinely robust for a 16' span: 2x8 rafters at 24" o.c. at a steep 9:12 with a 2x10 ridge and 22 Simpson Strong-Tie 18-gauge rafter ties. The steep pitch sheds snow, and an explicit metal connector at the rafter-to-plate joint is rare at this price.

Designed as conditioned living space, not a shed: 2x6 walls sized for R-19 kraft-faced batts, 1/2" lightweight gypsum board, bathroom with shower and toilet, kitchen run, two closets, and plumbing plus electrical layouts for ground level and loft.
The ~108 SF loft turns a 320 SF footprint into roughly 428 SF of usable floor for very little extra material (12 2x8 joists, 4 sheets of plywood, 9 joist hangers).
Skid-and-pier foundation keeps site work cheap and DIY-scale: 6 4x4 skids on 24 galvanized post bases with 12 bags of concrete, no slab pour and no frost footings to dig.
Step-by-step numbered instructions with 3D isometric views on nearly every sheet, and sheets are set up to print at 8.5x11 so you do not need a plotter.
Instant 7.05 MB PDF download, so no shipping wait and you can reprint working copies as many times as you want.
cons: Not engineered and not stamped. No structural calculations, span-table references, snow or wind load rating, seismic category, or engineer's seal appear anywhere. For a 320 SF habitable building this will very likely not clear plan review in a jurisdiction that requires sealed drawings.

The page is completely silent on permits, codes and zoning even though the design is effectively a small dwelling with plumbing and electrical. Budget for a real building permit, setback review, and water/septic approval that the plan does not help you with.

$99 is roughly 7x to 9x the seller's other plans (their 4x8 and 12x10 lean-to sheds and arbors are $10.95 to $14.95, the 10x12 garden shed is $11.95), and no free sample sheet or partial preview PDF is offered - you buy on the strength of 8 preview images.
"No refunds allowed" - once the file is downloaded there are no returns, exchanges or cancellations, so there is no recourse if the sheets are not what you expected.
Zero ratings on this specific product (the store shows 4.4 from 27 ratings across all 10 products), so there are no build reports or buyer feedback to sanity-check the plan against.

The materials list is a shopping list, not a cut list: the DIMENSIONS column is blank on every single row. Lengths only exist on the individual framing sheets, so you cannot pre-cut or optimize lumber buys from the list alone.

The roofing section appears to double-count sheathing - 18 sheets of 3/4" plywood as "exterior roof panels (8'x4' per panel)" and then 18 sheets of 4'x8' 3/4" plywood as "roofing panels". One row is likely an error, which means the list needs checking before you order about $1,000 of plywood.

3/4" roof sheathing under a steel panel roof on 24" o.c. rafters is heavier and considerably more expensive than the 1/2" to 5/8" normally used; combined with 20 sheets of T1-11 and steel panels, sheet goods are the dominant cost driver here.

The $7,500 "Cost to Build" attribute has no date, no region and no scope breakdown, and it plainly cannot include windows, doors, a bathroom, kitchen cabinets, appliances, wiring and fixtures at current prices. Treat it as optimistic.

The main product photo is a stock winter photograph of a low-slope-roof cabin that does not match the 9:12 gable, loft window or T1-11 siding of the design in the drawings - and the renders show horizontal lap siding while the materials list specifies T1-11 panels. Expect some mismatch between marketing and the actual sheets.

Some framing details are inconsistent: built-up headers are described as "two 2x6's" with 1/2" plywood between (a 3.5"-thick assembly) even though the exterior walls are 2x6 (5.5") - you will need to think that detail through yourself.

Loft access is a straight ladder in the renders rather than a stair, and neither loft headroom nor loft floor height is published; with a 14'-11" ridge and a 7'-2" eave-line dimension, headroom in the loft is likely tight.
No stud spacing is stated in the preview (52 2x6 studs for roughly 72 linear feet of wall), so you cannot verify the wall layout or check it against local code without buying first.

plans.foundation: Not stated as a construction detail. The drawings show the walls sitting on a flat grey slab with a TREATED BOTTOM PLATE and the text says to bore pilot holes in the bottom plates "for fixing the anchor bolts", and the 6x6 porch posts land on METAL POST BASES — all of which implies a poured concrete slab, but no slab thickness, footing depth, rebar, mesh, gravel base or pier layout is drawn or dimensioned anywhere.
plans.floor_framing: None. Despite a heading reading "Large Gable Shed Blueprints To Craft Floor Frame And Wall Assembly", no floor framing exists in the plan: the "Floor Plan" sheet is a wall/post layout, and there is no joist, rim, skid, beam or decking detail. The building is drawn slab-on-grade with no wood floor.
plans.wall_framing: 2x4 studs at 16" o.c. on a treated bottom plate. Back wall 16'0" wide x 8'1-1/8" tall (studs 7'8-5/8"), no openings. Left and right side walls 7'8-1/2" long (7'5" at the plate) x 8'1-1/16" tall. The tall porch-facing "Front Wall" is 16'0" x 10'7-1/4" and carries the ridge. Gable-end short studs are cut to the rafter angle and nailed to the rafter undersides after the roof frame is up. Walls are assembled flat, tipped up, plumbed and diagonally braced.
plans.wall_height: 8'1-1/8" at the back and side walls (7'8-5/8" studs); 10'7-1/4" at the tall porch-facing ridge wall
plans.roof: Off-center single-ridge gable at 18 degrees (~3.9:12, i.e. roughly a 4/12). The ridge sits on top of the tall 10'7-1/4" front wall; 2x6 rafters at 24" o.c. run back to the 8'1" rear wall (BACK RAFTER 10'5") and forward over the porch to the 2x10 front beam (FRONT RAFTER 10'5"), all ends cut to 18 degrees with a 1/2"x1/2" notch and a 1"x2-1/8" seat. Total roof width 20'0" (2 ft overhang at each gable end). Build-up: 5/8" grooved plywood exposed underside, 1/2" OSB sheathing, No.15 felt at 3" laps, asphalt shingles with ridge caps, 1x8 fascia and 1x3 shingle molding. Stick-framed only — NO trusses, no engineered truss drawing, and no collar ties, ceiling joists or rafter ties are shown anywhere.
plans.overall_height: not stated
plans.siding: 5/8" rough plywood siding with 1x2 battens over the upper walls and 1/2" x 8" lap siding as a lower band; 1x4 window and door trim, 2x8 top trim, 1x6 post wrap on the 6x6 posts. Text calls for pressure-treated timber for beams and boards and says the plywood siding gives "a rustic look". Roof underside is finished with 5/8" grooved plywood.
plans.doors: Two. (1) A prehung exterior door in a 3'2-1/2" wide x 6'10-1/2" tall rough opening in the porch-facing wall. (2) An exterior barn-style sliding door, 74" wide x 89-1/2" tall, shop-built from a 2x2 frame with verticals at 16", plywood skin and 1x4/3/4"x3" battens, hung from an aluminum track on door hangers over the 6'0" x 7'1-3/8" opening in the right side wall. The track support is lag-screwed to the beam and a stop block is fitted at the open end of the track.
plans.windows: Three prefabricated aluminum storm windows set into stretchable U channels and nailed to 1x2 boards recessed about 1" behind the siding face, over 10-degree angled sills: two in the porch-facing wall at 2'2" wide x 4'2-1/2" tall with a 2'8" sill height, and one in the left side wall at 4'2-3/8" tall with a 2'6" sill. The back wall has no openings.

plans.permit_notes: The plan page itself contains no permit, code, wind-load, snow-load or seismic information, no engineer's stamp and no jurisdiction notes. At 256 sq ft of roofed footprint it is above the common small-accessory-structure exemption thresholds in many jurisdictions, and the 10'7" ridge wall plus a slab-mounted structure will typically draw a plan review. Also note there is no foundation detail to submit and no rafter/beam sizing justification, so a reviewer would likely ask for both. ShedDrafts links a separate general article, "Shed Building Codes and Permit Guide For DIY Builders", from the sidebar/footer, but it is not part of this plan.
plans.refund_policy: Not applicable — the drawings are free to view on the page with no purchase, cart or account. (The sidebar "Download Plans >>" button opens an email opt-in popup, "Get Your Free Plans Now", for a separate generic "New 15-Page Detailed Shed Building Plans" booklet, not a PDF of this 16x16 plan.)
pros: Genuinely free and ungated: all 18 drawings render directly on the page with no email capture, no cart and no watermark blur, and each image is individually downloadable, so you can save the whole set locally in a minute.

The framing elevations are actually dimensioned, which is unusual for a free page — back wall 16'0" x 8'1-1/8", side walls 7'8-1/2", ridge wall 10'7-1/4", 2x4 studs at 16" o.c., rough openings called out to the sixteenth. You can lay out plates straight off the sheets.

The rafter sheet gives real cutting data: 10'5" back and front rafters, an 18-degree end cut, a 1/2" x 1/2" notch and a 1" x 2-1/8" seat cut. That is the single hardest part of a stick-framed roof and it is spelled out.

Structurally forgiving where it counts: 2x6 rafters at 24" o.c. spanning only ~8 ft per slope, and the 20'0" 2x10 porch beam broken into ~5'4" bays by four 6x6 posts. No long spans to worry about, and the beam sizing is conservative for that spacing.

The porch is a large, genuinely useful covered outdoor workspace (16 ft x 8 ft, ~10 ft of headroom at the ridge wall) with 6x6 timber posts and exposed rafters — a much nicer-looking result than a plain box, and the hero photo shows the finished aesthetic honestly.

Roof and trim assembly is fully specified layer by layer: 5/8" grooved plywood soffit, 1/2" OSB, No.15 felt at 3" laps, shingles, 1x8 fascia, 1x3 shingle molding, 2x8 top trim, 1x6 post wraps, 10-degree angled sills. Nothing is left to guesswork on the finish.

The 6'0" x 7'1-3/8" sliding-door opening on the side wall is big enough for a mower, ATV or garden cart, and the door itself is a simple shop-built 2x2/plywood leaf with a published 74" x 89-1/2" size and hanger layout.

Free of the usual paywall bait-and-switch: the site's category index links dozens of comparable free plans (10x20 gable, 12x12 lean-to, 16x28 studio with porch), so it is easy to comparison-shop within one vendor.
cons: The headline size is misleading for anyone shopping by square footage. 16x16 = 256 sq ft is the ROOF; the enclosed, lockable room is only about 16 ft x 8 ft (~123-128 sq ft). If you want ~320 sq ft of shed you would have to redesign this, not just build it.

No floor and no foundation. There is not a single joist, skid, rim, pier or slab detail in the set, even though one heading promises a "floor frame". You are left to design the slab (thickness, footing depth, rebar, gravel, anchor-bolt spacing) yourself before you can start.

No materials list and no cut list of any kind — only material labels on the drawings. You cannot price this build or take a lumber order to a yard without doing a full takeoff from the elevations yourself.

Nothing is engineered or load-rated: no truss drawing, no snow/wind/seismic assumptions, no engineer's stamp, no span justification for the 2x10 porch beam or the 6x6 posts. Combined with the missing foundation detail, this is weak material for a permit application on a 256 sq ft structure.

No lateral or roof-spreading load path is drawn. The 10'7-1/4" ridge wall carries rafters pushing from both sides with no collar ties, rafter ties, ceiling joists or ridge-beam support columns shown, and the only bracing mentioned is temporary during erection. That is the plan's most serious structural gap.

The right side wall is essentially a 6 ft x 7 ft hole with only narrow stud legs either side, and the whole set relies on plywood siding for shear. On a small enclosed box this is probably fine, but no hold-downs, shearwall segments or sheathing nailing schedule are specified.

Instructions are terse one-line sentences, often loosely worded ("Install plywood siding over rafters with 8 inch on-center spacing", "Nail half inch thick OSB over the siding", door described as both prehung and sliding), with several unlabelled decorative beams to sort out. It reads like it was written from the drawings rather than from a build.

Real difficulty is higher than the sheets imply: notching four 6x6 posts 1.5" deep on both faces with a circular saw and handsaw, setting a 20 ft 2x10 beam level at ~10 ft, and hanging a 74" x 89-1/2" sliding leaf on a track are all two-person, ladder-and-bracing jobs.
No skill rating, build time, cost estimate or overall height is published anywhere on the page, and the last update was June 2024, so pricing and code references are absent rather than dated.

Cost drivers are front-loaded into the porch you may not want: four 6x6 posts with metal bases, a 20 ft 2x10 beam, 1x6 post wraps, exposed grooved-plywood soffit and 4 extra feet of roof width on each gable all buy you zero enclosed storage.

Windows are specified as prefabricated aluminum storm windows in U-channel — cheap and dated, and the plan gives no rough-opening tolerance or flashing/WRB detail, so water management at openings is entirely on you.
The site's prominent "Download Plans" call to action is not this plan: it is an email opt-in for an unrelated generic 15-page booklet, which is easy to mistake for a PDF of the 16x16.

No PDF/DWG/SketchUp link, no materials list, no cut list, no foundation or floor-framing sheet, no load/code data — materials_list_available "none" is right.

FOOTPRINT/SQFT: arithmetic checks (16 x 16 = 256) and the footprint_note's central claim is confirmed by the Floor Plan and the 3D views — only ~128 sq ft is enclosed, the front 16x8 is open porch, and the 20'0" roof width is a 2 ft overhang at each gable end (the beam runs parallel to the ridge, so the 2 ft extensions are gable-end overhangs). Note for the collection owner: at ~128 sq ft of lockable space this record sits below the brief's ~200 sq ft floor on enclosed area even though its roofed footprint qualifies; the record discloses this but still carries sqft 256.

LUMBER-LIST OMISSIONS (not fabrications, but the list is billed as "verbatim material callouts" and misses several): 5/8" OSB SHEATHING on the walls (labeled on 00-structural-design; the list mentions only 1/2" OSB for the roof), 2x6 CORNER boards (sheet 02), 2x6 RIDGE (sheet 09), and from 13-door-slice-details: 2x4 TRACK SUPPORT, 1x4 TRACK COVER, 3/8" ROUGH PLYWOOD door skin, TREATED SILL / TREATED 2X4 / SPACER BLOCK / OPEN BAR HOLDER. Also the beam is effectively doubled — the text says to notch the 6x6 posts "1.5 inch deep ... on both sides", i.e. a 2x10 each face — which the single-line "2x10 BEAM" entry hides.

SOURCE INCONSISTENCIES worth a con: (a) the step text says "Two posts made of 6x6 timber will support front of the roof" while both the Floor Plan and Posts-and-Front-Beam sheets show four — the record silently follows the drawings (correct) but the contradiction is a real gotcha; (b) the second section is headed "...To Craft Floor Frame And Wall Assembly" yet no floor frame is ever drawn or described — the plan assumes an existing slab with anchor bolts; (c) the record's gloss "5/8\" GROOVED PLYWOOD ... nailed over rafters at 8\" o.c. spacing per text" is an interpretation — the source sentence is the ambiguous "Install plywood siding over rafters with 8 inch on-center spacing."

plans.footprint_note: 16 ft x 20 ft footprint of the Best Barns "West Virginia 16x20" kit (same product now sold as Maker's Loft XL 16x20 — the 2026 manual PDF's internal document title is literally "West Virginia 16x20.pdf"). 320 sq ft ground floor plus a full 320 sq ft clear-span second-floor loft, so ~640 sq ft of usable floor area. The assembly manual warns "Do Not make the foundation larger than the building size."
plans.style: Two-story gambrel (barn-style) single-car garage / workshop with a full clear-span second-floor loft and an included interior staircase
plans.price: Free to watch (no plans sold, no paywall, no affiliate gate). The kit being built was listed at $10,179.00 on sale (retail $14,099.95) on shedsdirect.com as archived 2025-07-12.

plans.format: Single YouTube video, 33:27, 45 chapters — NOT a multi-episode playlist. The uploader has no companion series; the channel's other content is unrelated and the recommended videos on the page are from other creators (My DIY Builds, Red Bearded Builder).
plans.est_material_cost: not stated in text — the video has a dedicated "Costs" chapter at 02:08–04:22, but no dollar figures appear anywhere in the description and the auto-generated captions could not be retrieved (the archived timedtext URL is signature-expired and fresh requests return empty), so the on-camera numbers are unverifiable.
plans.foundation: By owner — not supplied in the kit. The builder designed and used an insulated frost-protected shallow foundation (FPSF) concrete slab; foundation design runs 05:15–08:53 and the description links two free FPSF engineering guides (HUD User and Home Innovation Research Labs), plus a pinned correction at 07:52 clarifying what the sub-slab insulation actually does. The kit manual offers two options: "Floating Slab — A concrete slab is ideal for storage of cars or other types of heavy items," or a wood floor on treated 6x6 runners over gravel with treated 2x6 joists 16" o.c. and 3/4" T&G decking.
plans.wall_framing: Rear wall frames 92-1/2"; side walls are two 8' (96") plus two 12' (144") frames; front door wall frame is 15'-5"
plans.floor_framing: Ground floor is the owner's slab (no kit floor system). Loft floor is 2x10 floor joists and joist headers hung in hangers (kit ships 18 2x6 joist hangers + 28 2x10 joist hangers) with 3/4" T&G loft flooring, clear-spanning the 16 ft width with no interior posts. Note the discrepancy: the retailer's marketing copy claims "3/4" Structurwood decking and 2x8 floor joists," but the 16'x20' packing list in the actual assembly manual specifies 2x10 floor joists and headers (3 @ 8', 7 @ 12', 8 @ 16').
plans.roof: 54 OSB truss gussets
plans.siding: 3/8" pre-primed LP SmartSide vertical panel siding (20 4x8 sheets from the local supplier plus pre-cut LP siding panels and 1-1/2" fillers on the pallets), with 1x4 and 1x6 trim boards and LP primed soffit panels. 50-year limited warranty, ships primed only — the manual requires two coats of latex acrylic finish paint by the owner and 6"–8" ground clearance at the bottom edge. Lumber is treated with Composibor (U.S. Borax) against fungal decay and insects. This builder additionally applied Flex Seal to the bottom of the stud walls (10:34) and the bottom of the siding panels (20:50).
plans.loft: Full-width clear-span second-floor loft over the entire 16x20 footprint with 7 ft 1 in headroom and no interior walls or posts on either floor; 3/4" T&G decking on 2x10 joists. Access is by an included stair kit (stairs, stair landing, stair walls, joist headers), which the video builds in unusual detail from 13:48 to 20:44 — roughly 7 of the 33 minutes.
plans.doors: an 8 ft wide x 6 ft 6 in high overhead garage door opening (no low-headroom track requirement is published for the XL)

pros: Genuinely a first-timer's build — the title is literal, and the value is in the beginner failure modes it surfaces on camera: a workaround for warped studs (10:01), fixing walls that leaned outward after the loft joists went in (19:07), and sealing the bottom plate and siding edge with Flex Seal (10:34, 20:50). Polished contractor videos skip exactly these.

45 timestamped chapters whose titles map 1:1 onto the manual's numbered steps ('Step 8 - Installing the siding panels'), so you can jump straight to whichever step you are stuck on rather than scrubbing.

Honest and self-correcting: the description opens with a pinned technical correction at 07:52 about what sub-slab insulation actually does, and explicitly warns 'Note that I sometimes went out of order or skipped some steps in the instructions.' That candor is rare and makes the rest more trustworthy.

Unusually strong foundation content for a shed video — it treats the slab as an engineering problem and links two free authoritative FPSF design guides (HUD and Home Innovation Research Labs) rather than hand-waving 'pour a pad'.

Because it links the exact kit SKU, the manufacturer's 27-page assembly manual with a complete verbatim packing list is freely downloadable and lines up with the video step-for-step — effectively a free plan set plus a free build-along.
Kit route is far more permit-friendly than a homemade gambrel: factory pre-cut 2x6 trusses rated 45 lb snow / 130 mph wind, and Best Barns publishes a free permit set PDF for this exact model.

Excellent space efficiency for a 320 sq ft footprint: a clear-span 16 ft loft with 7 ft 1 in headroom and no interior posts or walls on either floor gives roughly 640 sq ft usable — one 5-star owner review reports using it as a hunting cabin with a truck parked inside and a sleeper upstairs.
Devotes about 7 of its 33 minutes to the stair/loft-joist kit, the part beginners most often botch and the part most 16x20 shed videos don't have at all.
Zero cost and zero gating: no plans to buy, no email wall, no affiliate upsell.
cons: One 33-minute video for a two-story 320 sq ft building averages under 45 seconds per assembly step. This is a preview-and-pitfalls companion to the manual, not a follow-along build course — compare it to multi-hour, multi-episode series before relying on it.

The creator states outright that he went out of order and skipped steps, and the chapter list confirms it: manual Steps 2, 4, 6 and 9–12 have no chapter, and stair-kit steps appear in the order 1,2,3,4,(anchor),9,10,5,6,7,8. You cannot use the video as your sequence of record.

Nothing after the shell: no chapter covers the concrete pour itself, garage door installation, side door installation, insulation, electrical, interior finish, or painting the siding. The video stops at roofing plus one loft window, so the building is not finished on camera.

The cost numbers — the single most useful thing for a budget decision — are spoken only in the 02:08 chapter. There is no cost breakdown in the description and the auto-captions are not retrievable, so the budget is unverifiable from text.

This is essentially a one-off upload on a tiny channel (about 1,044 views as of the Feb 2024 snapshot). There is no follow-up video, no durability update, and no active comment thread to answer the questions the video raises.

Real cost is much higher than the kit sticker. On top of the kit (archived at $10,179 sale / $14,099.95 retail) you supply the slab, the 8' x 6'6" overhead door plus low-headroom track hardware, a man door, all windows, all roofing (shingles/felt/drip edge or metal), and all paint. 'Kit price' comparisons against plan-only options are misleading.
The 8 ft wide x 6 ft 6 in high garage door opening is short for a modern truck or SUV and mandates low-headroom track; widening to 9 ft is sanctioned but raising the height is not.

Second-story work is the real difficulty, not the framing. The manual itself tells you to rent six sections of scaffolding, wear harnesses, and consider hiring a professional roofer — so budget rental and possibly subcontracted labor.

Gambrel truss geometry is factory pre-cut with fixed gussets, so you cannot resize the building, change the roof pitch, or move the loft height. Zero design flexibility compared with a drawn plan set.

Retailer marketing and the actual manual disagree on the loft joists (2x8 vs 2x10). Trust the manual's packing list, and be aware the retailer page is behind Cloudflare so live pricing cannot be checked.
Overall/peak height is published nowhere I could find — a problem if you have a height restriction, since a two-story gambrel on a slab is roughly 16 ft tall.

plans.summary: A single 33-minute, 45-chapter YouTube video in which a self-described construction novice ("Ingrown Hare") assembles a Best Barns "West Virginia 16x20" kit — a two-story gambrel single-car garage with an 8'1" sidewall, a clear-span 320 sq ft second-floor loft at 7'1" headroom, and an included staircase, giving ~640 sq ft usable on a 320 sq ft footprint. It is free to watch and sells nothing; the description links the exact kit SKU (archived at $10,179 on sale, $14,099.95 retail) plus two free frost-protected-shallow-foundation engineering guides, and it opens with a pinned technical correction about sub-slab insulation. Coverage runs foundation design through wall panels, the full stair/loft-joist kit, gable walls, 2x6 gambrel truss assembly, OSB sheathing and metal roofing, but stops there — no concrete pour walkthrough, no garage door or man door install, no insulation, electrical or interior finish, and the creator warns he "sometimes went out of order or skipped some steps." Because the linked kit's 27-page Best Barns assembly manual is a free public PDF (its internal title is literally "West Virginia 16x20.pdf") with a complete verbatim packing list, this pairs into an effectively free plan-set-plus-build-along; both PDFs and the hero thumbnail are saved locally.
plans.wall_framing_original: Pre-cut 2x4 studs at ~16" o.c. in wall frames the builder assembles on site (only the gable frames ship pre-built)
plans.doors_original: No doors supplied with the kit. The gable end is framed for an 8 ft wide x 6 ft 6 in high overhead garage door that requires low-headroom track hardware; per Best Barns the opening "may be modified to 9' wide if desired" and the orientation is adjustable — centered, offset left, or offset right on the gable side. A walk-in man door is also owner-supplied; the manual provides a 32" x 80" rough-opening detail (37-1/2" door header, 80-1/2" header supports). The kit ships 3 1x6 8' door jambs and 2 2x8 10' door headers. In the thumbnail this builder installed a white sectional garage door plus a pair of glazed French doors on the eave wall — but neither door installation gets its own chapter.

plans.summary: A $97 downloadable timber frame plan set for a 16x24 single-plane shed-roof building, divided into two 12x16 bays: one bay is open to the roof with a ceiling that soars from about 17 ft at the high wall down to 13 ft at the low wall, and the other carries a second-floor loft with roughly 8 ft of headroom underneath. The frame is traditional pegged mortise-and-tenon with scarf joints in 8x8 posts, 8x10 plates and tie beams, 6x8 rafters and 4x8 braces, with a 3:12 roof and 2 ft overhangs on all four sides. You get 27 pages emailed as PDFs after purchase: a 12-page 11x17 construction set with 3D views plus post, loft and roof plans and section/detail drawings, a 13-page 11x17 piece-drawing set showing every cut on every timber keyed back to the construction set, and 2 pages of 8.5x11 timber and connector lists. pros: Genuinely free and completely un-gated - the entire cut list, shopping list and every diagram are visible on the page with no email or account.
Real quantity takeoff by lumber length (84 pieces of 2x4 8 ft, 29 sheets of T1-11, 650 sq ft of shingles, etc.), so you can price the job at a lumberyard without redrawing anything.
480 sq ft with 8 ft walls, an 8 ft double-door opening and three 3x4 windows is a legitimately usable workshop, not a garden locker.
Simple, repetitive, all-2x4/2x8 stick framing at 16 in o.c. with no compound roof geometry beyond two rafter angles - approachable technique-wise for a determined DIYer.
Truss geometry is actually dimensioned (20.5 / 69.5 degree cuts, W webs, plate placement), which many free plans omit entirely.
The author is honest about the weak point: he tells you twice to buy engineered trusses and to read local codes rather than pretending the design is code-compliant.
Skid-on-gravel foundation is the cheapest possible option and needs no concrete, which suits a rural or unpermitted site.
The two-part split keeps the drawing set readable, and Part 2 actually covers the site-built doors and exterior trim that most free plans skip.
cons: NOT an engineered plan and explicitly not stamped (the FAQ says so). For a 480 sq ft building most jurisdictions will demand engineering, so budget for a local engineer on top of materials.

The foundation is the biggest weakness: 12 pieces of 4x4 skid on a 2-4 in gravel bed carrying a 480 sq ft building, with no piers, footings, anchorage, frost depth or uplift detail. Expect to substitute a real pier or slab foundation.

2x8 floor joists run the full ~19 ft 9 in between skid runs. That is far beyond normal 2x8 floor-span capacity, and how much intermediate support you actually get depends entirely on how you lay the 12 ft skids, which the drawings only loosely show. Plan on more or larger beams.

Site-built 2x4 W-trusses spanning 20 ft with hand-placed metal plates are the whole structure and are not load-rated; following the author's own advice and buying engineered trusses adds meaningful cost to a supposedly cheap build.
1/2 in roof sheathing over 2x4 purlins at 24 in o.c. is thin for a 20 ft span roof, especially under snow load, and there is no ceiling, insulation, ventilation or soffit detail at all.

The title promises a Free PDF Download but no PDF file is linked - you get a print widget / CTRL+P, and a reader reports being upsold at $7.99. The author confirms in comments that no premium version of THIS plan exists, so there is no clean printable set to hand a builder.

Editorial sloppiness undermines confidence in the numbers: captions read 'Back wall panels - 16x18 shed' and 'Roof purlins - 16x18 storage shed', the siding text refers to 'girts' on a stud wall, and stated build time swings between one day, one week and a few weeks.

Cut-list quantities need reconciling before you buy: the truss section is written as a single truss ('1 3xTRUSS') while the shopping list implies about 13, and the 2x6 39 in header count exceeds what three window openings need.
No electrical, no ramp, no gutters, no shear or bracing schedule, and no ground anchorage on a large, high-sail-area building.

_verification.notes:
EVERYTHING ELSE CHECKED OUT. Quotes: all ten verified verbatim on the live pages - "comply with a few legal regulations", "read the local codes before building the shed and choosing its location" (Part 1), "read the local codes so you can make adjustments if needed" and "The instructions are basic" (Part 2), "you could get the job done in about a day" (both parts' boilerplate), "This is a simple project you should be able to build in a few weeks without much effort", "Time / One week" (both parts), "Use 6d nails to secure the sheets to the girts, every 8\"" (the copy-paste slip is real), and the FAQ verbatim: "Are your plans stamped?" / "No. If you need stamped plans for a building permit, you have to work with a local engineer." FAQ also confirms "I have not included a cost estimate in my plans".

Numbers all verify against the cut lists. Footprint 20x24, sqft 480 = 20x24 exactly. Rim joists 288 in (24 ft), 19 joists 237 in at 16 in o.c. (288/16=18 spaces=19 joists), 13 sheets 48x96 + 4 at 48x48 3/4 in ply. Side walls 288 in plates, front/back 240 in - so the gable ends ARE the 20 ft walls and the 8 ft double doors are in a gable end, as claimed. Studs 91 1/2 in + 3 plates = 96 in, wall height ~8 ft correct and indeed never printed. Front door header 2 pieces of 2x8 99 in, window headers 2x6 39 in (14 total = 7 doubles for 4 openings - the record's honesty note about the surplus is fair). Trusses: 240 in bottom chord + 2x 144 in rafters + W webs 2x 28 3/8 in and 2x 57 5/8 in, "1 3xTRUSS" = 13, at 24 in o.c., metal plates with 1 1/2 in nails, 4 pieces 2x4 144 in bottom-chord bracing. Pitch derivation is sound: 20.5 deg rafter cut / 69.5 deg bottom-chord cut gives tan(20.5)=0.374 -> 4.49:12, and 120 in run / cos(20.5) = 128 in + ~16 in overhang = the 144 in rafter. Purlins 28 pieces 2x4 156 in. Siding H list matches character-for-character (21 sheets + 1 at 13 3/4x48 + 4 at 21 3/4x48 + 4 at 39 3/4x48 + 4 at 48 3/4x48; shopping list 29 sheets). Doors L/M/N/O match exactly; note the O/M quantities are per leaf (48 - 2x3.5 = 41 rail; 36 - 2x3.5 = 29 rail), so the record's per-leaf reading is right. 3 PVC windows 3'x4', 650 sq ft tar paper + shingles, cut-list letters A through P all present. $5,000-$12,000 plus $1,000-$3,000 is verbatim. other_sizes all verified (16x18 gable shed link in body, category/16x24/ in Ovidiu's comment reply, category/20x24/ in the page HTML).

DIAGRAM COUNTS - slightly generous but within "about": Part 1 has 12 in-body plan images plus 1 intro render = 13, not "about 14"; Part 2 has 23 in-body plan diagrams plus 1 intro render = 24, so "about 23" is right and the "roughly 37 total" lands about right by luck.

TWO COMPLETENESS ITEMS THE RECORD MISSES (should be cons, per check 7): (a) beyond the "girts" slip, two Part 2 diagrams are recycled from a different project - files Back-wall-panels-16x18-shed and Roof-purlins-16x18-storage-shed, the latter carrying the visible on-page caption "Roof purlins - 16x18 storage shed" - so at least two roof/wall drawings are NOT renders of this 20x24 building; (b) the text says to "lock them to the carrier beams, using ties" but no carrier beam appears in any cut list - the 13 trusses land directly on a 2x4 double top plate, which is the more defensible engineering complaint about this plan than the (incorrect) joist-span one. Part 2's tool list also incongruously includes a "Post hole digger" for a skid foundation.

IMAGE: /home/ethan/woodshed/assets/img/myoutdoorplans-20x24-gable-shed.jpg is a valid JPEG, 1255x906, 1,027,889 bytes, and visually IS this shed (red T1-11 gable shed, 8 ft double doors in the gable end, two windows plus a side man-door on the long wall - which also independently confirms the 2-side + 1-front window split the record inferred). plans.summary: 'Emily' is a paid PDF plan set from Pin-Up Houses for a 23'-3" x 17'-6" (410 sq ft built-up) two-story A-frame cottage: a 303 sq ft ground floor with main room (140 sq ft), kitchen corner (33 sq ft), bathroom (43 sq ft) and hall (33 sq ft), a 54 sq ft covered porch recessed into the footprint, and a 161 sq ft second floor with two bedrooms (86 and 64 sq ft) plus 11 sq ft storage reached by a real straight stair, not a ladder. Construction is light stick framing on point/pier foundations (the cross-section shows small concrete pads with post bases; the vendor's own build photos show black steel ground screws under a deep built-up rim beam), with low knee walls and very steep site-built rafters carrying a metal roof to a 21 ft / 6.4 m ridge. The purchase bundles the plan PDF (layouts, sections, elevations, details, material variants, windows, doors), a step-by-step construction-progress sequence with per-step material callouts, a complete material and tool list, DWG files, DIY furniture plans and the 'How to build a tiny house' eBook, all dimensioned in both imperial and metric. Important: this is a habitable 2-bedroom dwelling with plumbing and a wiring layout, not a storage shed - the drawings are explicitly not engineer- or architect-checked.

Construction progress + comments (step-by-step build sequence with per-step MATERIAL LIST callouts)
Complete material list + tool list

DIY furniture plans included

Basic wiring diagram for water and sewer, plus locations of outlets, switches and light fixtures (per FAQ)
All dimensions given in both imperial (ft/in) and metric (m/mm)
Free downloadable 43-page A4 sample plan set (of a different, smaller design) to preview the format
Free technical support from the designer throughout construction (per FAQ)
pros: Genuine two-story living space in a ~410 sq ft footprint: 303 sq ft down plus a 161 sq ft loft with two real bedrooms, reached by a straight stair rather than a ladder - far more usable than a typical shed loft.
Loft has real headroom: 9'-11 3/4" / 3.0 m to the ridge, with 7'-6 1/2" / 2.3 m clear on the first floor, because the steep A-frame roof buys volume instead of tall walls.

Pier/point foundation only (concrete pads with post bases, or steel ground screws as in the vendor's build photos). No slab, no perimeter footing, no concrete truck - the cheapest and most DIY-friendly foundation type, and it tolerates a sloping or damp site.

Step-by-step 'construction progress' pages with a MATERIAL LIST callout on each step, so the takeoff is tied to the sequence you actually build in - unusually good hand-holding for a first-time builder.
Dual imperial + metric dimensioning, and DWG files are supplied so a local engineer can stamp or modify the design for a permit office.

Lifetime full-refund policy: 'we offer a lifetime warranty on purchased plans. At your request, we will give you a full refund at any time' - and specifically a full refund if your building authority rejects the plans.
Free 43-page sample set is downloadable before you buy, so you can judge drawing quality and detail level with zero risk.
Vendor offers paid custom modifications (resize, mirror, move partitions, add a balcony) with roughly a two-week turnaround, and says self-modification is fine.
Vertical board siding and a simple metal gable roof mean no valleys, no dormers and no complex flashing - the envelope is cheap and fast to weather in.
Materials are deliberately globally available (plywood, OSB, boards, battens, timbers, sheet metal, asphalt sheets, concrete) rather than region-specific.
cons: This is a house, not a shed. It has a 43 sq ft bathroom, a kitchen corner, plumbing and two loft bedrooms. If you want a 16x20 workshop or storage building, most of the $290 and most of the build effort goes into things you do not need.

Not engineered. The free sample set states verbatim: 'these plans were not prepared or checked by a licensed engineer and/or architect and building following these plans is at your own risk.' There are no engineered trusses - the roof is site-built rafter frames.

Snow load is a real limitation. FAQ: 'Our structures are designed to hold normal snow loads. If you will be building in areas where extreme snow conditions prevail, you will need to adjust the dimensions and rafter center distances.' You are on the hook for that engineering yourself.

Permit friendliness is explicitly not guaranteed: 'Building standards vary from area to area, so we cannot guarantee that they will pass everywhere.' A two-story habitable dwelling will almost certainly need a permit and likely a local engineer's review - budget for that on top of the plan price.

The published area figures on the page are internally inconsistent (518 sq ft in the prose vs 474 sq ft total / 410 sq ft built-up in the table), which is not confidence-inspiring when you are ordering lumber.
$290 for electronic delivery is expensive relative to shed-plan norms, and the printed set is $390.

No material list, cut list or page count is published before purchase for Emily specifically - the takeoff is entirely behind the paywall, and in the sample the material lists are graphical (quantity plus a drawn piece), so they are not a tidy spreadsheet you can hand to a lumberyard.
$37,850 stated build cost is a serious project, and the steep A-frame means a 21 ft / 6.4 m ridge - staging, scaffolding and roofing that pitch is dangerous and slow for a solo builder.
Framing member sizes (joist, stud, rafter dimensions and spacings) are nowhere published on the page, so you cannot sanity-check spans or price the frame before buying.
The A-frame geometry costs you usable floor area at the perimeter: the roof slopes nearly to deck level on the long walls, so wall-height storage and shelving along those sides is limited.
Vendor is EU-based (Czech Republic); printed sets ship from the EU and take one to three weeks, and detailing conventions are European rather than IRC-oriented.
