pros: Genuinely free, instant, no email or account gate — a 155 KB direct PDF download that returns HTTP 200.
432 sq ft (18x24) with 16'-6" of clear inside width and no interior posts, so it swallows a vehicle plus a real work bench; the section is a clear-span rafter/collar-tie roof.

Unusually complete for a free extension sheet: two sheets covering plan, all key elevations, cross section, both wall framing elevations, window details to the drip-cap and stop dimension, and garage-door head/jamb details.
Includes a fully worked alternate concrete-block wall section (course heights, plate bolting, filled-block lintel with reinforcing) — a rare free reference if you want masonry walls instead of studs.
Slab-on-grade foundation with the sub-base, slab thickness and anchor-bolt spacing spelled out; no floor framing to build, which keeps cost and labor down and suits shop/vehicle loads.
The 16'-0" x 8'-2" gable-end opening is genuinely truck-sized, and the head/jamb detail shows exactly how the track and doubled header go together.
Simple orthogonal box: no dormers, hips, or complex roof geometry to cut.
cons: No bill of materials, no cut list, no quantity take-off, no cost estimate, and no written step-by-step instructions — drawings only. You must do your own take-off.

1933-vintage engineering with no design criteria: 2x4 studs at 24" o.c., 2x4 rafters at 24" o.c. over an 18 ft span, and a 1x6 collar tie. Not engineered, unstamped, and undersized versus modern snow-load and bracing requirements; expect to upsize rafters (or substitute engineered trusses) and add sheathing for shear before a building department signs off.

Several specified materials are effectively obsolete or hard to source: 6" drop siding, board roof sheathing, G.I. ridge roll, 4-light sash with spring bolts, and 'right angle garage door hardware' for six sliding glazed leaves. Modern substitutions are on you.
Scanned image PDF with no text layer; some annotations (including the sill plate size in the section) are too blurry to read with certainty and there is no searchable or copyable text.

Cost drivers are front-loaded and concrete-heavy: a ~2 ft deep perimeter foundation wall plus a 4" slab over 6" of crushed rock over 432 sq ft, plus a concrete ramp. That is a lot of concrete and excavation before any lumber goes up.

The layout is an agricultural shop of its era — forge, stove with G.I. shield, masonry chimney with concrete cap, post drill — none of which a modern builder wants; the chimney in particular adds masonry work most people will delete.
No loft, ceiling, insulation, vapor barrier, ventilation, or electrical information whatsoever.
18x24 is larger than the user's 16x20 target, which pushes it over the 200 sq ft threshold that triggers permits in most jurisdictions and increases material cost roughly 35% over a 16x20.

DIMENSIONS CONFIRMED: 18'-0" (section + rear framing) x 24'-0" (side framing + plan); 432 sq ft = 18x24 arithmetic checks; 16'-6" clear inside (18'-0" less two 9" walls); 24'-0" side chain 5'-4"+3'-8"+15'-0" = 24'-0"; plan top chain 5'-0"+8'-0"+5'-0" = 18'-0"; roof pitch 6" in 12" (dimensioned triangle on both the section and the rear framing); wall height 8'-6" and window head 6'-10" (shown on BOTH the sheet 1 section and the sheet 2 rear framing, not only the framing elevation as the record says); chimney "APPR 2'-0"" above ridge (a detail the record omits); two window openings in rear framing; one window plus the service door in the side framing/elevation, with "(OPPOSITE WALL FRAMING SIMILAR — DOOR OMITTED)"; six glazed leaves in the front elevation (counted twice). ENGINEERING RED FLAGS the record does not carry (pros/cons were truncated out of what I was given, so I cannot confirm whether they are disclosed there — if not, they belong in cons):
1. 2"x4" rafters at 24" o.c. carry a ~8'-3" to 9'-0" horizontal run on this 18'-0"-wide building. Modern span tables cap 2x4 rafters at 24" o.c. around 6'-6"–7'-6" even at a 20 psf roof live load; North Dakota ground snow is roughly 40–70 psf. The 1"x6" collar tie does not reduce rafter span. This roof is over-spanned by a wide margin as drawn.
2. Now that the header reads 2 - 2"x8" (not 2x6), it is still grossly undersized: two 2x8s cannot span a 16'-0" opening in a gable end wall carrying the door track, the wall above and the gable load. Any real build needs an engineered header or intermediate posts.
3. 2"x4" studs at 24" o.c., 8'-6" tall, with NO wall sheathing — racking resistance is a single 1"x4" let-in brace per wall plus 6" drop siding. The record's wall_framing describes this accurately but does not flag it as inadequate by modern standards.
4. Foundation embedment is only ~1'-2" below grade in the primary (wood-wall) scheme — far above North Dakota frost depth (~4–5 ft). The alternate block scheme's 2'-0" below grade is still shallow.
5. The record IS honest about completeness in the right places: "drawings only", "no bill of materials, no cut list, no written instructions", "no engineered truss or load documentation", "no snow-load rating given", materials_list_available = "none". Those all check out.

plans.style: Gable-roof shed / one-car garage. Pier-and-beam on notched 6x6 posts, 2x4 stick-framed walls, site-built 2x6 gable trusses, galvanized metal roof over purlins, T1-11 painted siding, 9x7 overhead garage door plus double French doors, welded steel drive-up ramps.
plans.price: Free (watchable on YouTube; no plans, drawings or materials list are sold or given away)
plans.summary: A single 48-minute YouTube video in which Kordare designs and builds a 12x24 ft (288 sq ft) shed on a sloping, rocky site at his own house, from six drilled concrete piers up through metal roofing, T1-11 siding, gutters, a 9x7 overhead garage door and two welded steel drive-up ramps. The structure is deliberately overbuilt for a shed: doubled 2x10 beams dropped into notched 6x6 posts, 2x10 joists with two aligned rows of blocking, 8 ft walls instead of the usual 7 ft, and 13 site-built trusses cut from 2x6 rather than 2x4. He states his real numbers on camera - about $9,000 in total materials and roughly two months at four days a week, with the pier-and-beam floor system alone about $1,200 - and compares that to $8,500-$9,500 to simply buy a 12x24 prefab. The catch is that no plans, dimensioned drawings or materials list exist anywhere: dozens of comments ask for one and there is no answer, and the middle third of the video is sped-up music montage with the details explained retroactively in a closing walkthrough.
includes: Site selection and layout on a slope with roughly a 3 ft drop front to back

3D framing design walkthrough (a free online shed builder, never named), including how the built version deviates from it: 8 ft walls instead of 7, 1 ft eaves instead of none, metal instead of shingles
Six drilled concrete pier footers roughly 3 ft deep, bored with a friend's tractor auger, plus site-built forms to cast square pad tops
Anchor-bolting post bases to the pads and the mock-up-then-take-it-down layout sequence used to locate them
Cutting and notching 6x6 posts to height and leveling across the slope (two-person job)
Doubled 2x10 header/beam assembly (glued and nailed), 2x10 joists on hangers, doubled rim joist on the ramp side, two aligned rows of solid blocking
3/4 in plywood floor deck, staggered joints landing on the blocking
Prefabbing 2x4 walls in 8 ft sections inside a garage during bad weather, then standing and tying them together with a double top plate
Cutting one rafter template to build 26 rafters / 13 site-made 2x6 gable trusses with collar ties and a center strut
Setting trusses with hurricane ties pre-placed on the top plate, then purlins
Galvanized metal roofing panels and off-the-shelf ridge cap, no sheathing
T1-11 siding install (pre-primed 4x8 sheets), Z-channel flashing at the horizontal gable seam, and painting - 2 coats overall, 3 on the front
Hanging a prehung double French door including a site-built sill pan
Installing two 2 ft x 3 ft windows (his first time)
Vinyl gutter and downspout on the front elevation, piped away in black corrugated tube
Installing a 9 ft x 7 ft overhead garage door from the kit instructions
PVC corner trim and site-built shutters
Designing and welding two 1-1/2 x 4 in steel-tube ramps with 3/4 in PT plywood decking, hinged and through-bolted to the building
Diagonal 2x corner bracing lagged in to resist twisting under vehicle loads
Perimeter stone/gravel to finish and simplify mowing
Closing recap of actual total cost and calendar time, and an honest build-vs-buy comparison
NOT covered: electrical (explicitly deferred to a future video), insulation, vapor barrier, interior finish, shelving, closing the open soffits, and any concrete slab option
pros: Real, specific money and schedule stated on camera and unusually credible: about $9,000 total materials, about 2 months at roughly 4 days a week plus some evenings, and the pier-and-beam floor system broken out at about $1,200 (44:47-45:21). Almost no shed video gives you all three.

Honest build-vs-buy math: he prices a comparable 12x24 prefab at $8,500-$9,500 and then adds the site work he would still have owed (grading or a floor system) to land at $10,000-$10,500 delivered - so the DIY case is argued rather than assumed.

Structurally conservative for 288 sq ft. Doubled 2x10 beams on notched 6x6 posts, 2x10 joists with two aligned rows of blocking across the 12 ft span, 2x6 trusses where prefabs use 2x4, hurricane ties on every truss, 8 ft walls instead of 7 ft, and a doubled rim joist specifically to take vehicle ramp loads.

The best part is the part most shed content skips: building level on a slope. Roughly 3 ft of grade drop is solved with drilled piers and notched posts instead of excavation, and the full layout sequence (loosely mock up the perimeter, mark exactly where the post bases land, take it back down, then set anchor bolts) is walked through.

The metal-roof-over-purlins decision is justified out loud as a labor saver against sheathing plus felt plus shingles, and the actual panel arithmetic is given: 8 ft x 3 ft panels, about 9 across each slope, ridge cap in 10 ft sections with 3 used.

Genuinely start-to-finish through weather-tight and finished exterior - piers, floor, walls, trusses, roof, siding, paint, door, windows, gutters, garage door, trim, shutters, bracing and landscaping - not a framing-only teaser.

A solo-builder strategy that actually works: all 13 trusses and every wall section were prebuilt in 8 ft chunks inside a garage while it rained, then the whole shell went up in about two days with one helper.
The 9x7 overhead door plus the ramps make it a real vehicle building (mowers, go-kart, ATV, dirt bike), which is a meaningful functional step up from a walk-in shed at this size.

Small details worth stealing are explained rather than glossed: a site-built sill pan under the exterior door, Z-channel at the siding seam, why the 3/4 in plywood floor needed aligned blocking because it is not tongue-and-groove, and hinging the ramps so seasonal frost movement does not fight the pier-supported building.
Full English auto-captions exist, so the narration is searchable even though the video has no chapters.
cons: No plans, no dimensioned drawings, no cut list and no materials list anywhere. Nothing in the description, and the kordare.com store sitemap contains only a 50x70 garage-house plan set and car parts - no shed plans. Dozens of top-level comments ask for a materials list or blueprints; you would have to reverse-engineer every quantity from the video.

No chapters and no timestamps on a 48-minute video, and roughly 15 minutes of it (about 10:13-28:45, plus a music outro from ~47:00) is sped-up montage with no narration. Wall raising, truss setting, floor sheathing, roofing and siding are shown as B-roll and then explained retroactively in a closing walkthrough - so it is a very good design-decision video and only a mediocre step-by-step instructional one.

The trusses are homemade and not engineered or stamped, and no snow or wind load is ever calculated. Permits, setbacks and inspections are not mentioned once. At 288 sq ft this is over the permit-exempt threshold in many jurisdictions and is frequently reclassified as a garage - one commenter's New Hampshire town caps sheds at 12x16 - so this cannot serve as a permit submittal, and several commenters ask for prints 'for the inspector and permit' with no answer.

Foundation specifics you would need are missing: pier diameter, whether rebar was used, and pad dimensions are all unstated. Experienced commenters question whether 6 piers are enough under a 24 ft doubled-2x10 beam line and whether notching the 6x6 posts halves their bearing capacity. With no engineering behind it, a different frost depth or soil type leaves you guessing.

T1-11 is the only wall skin - no structural sheathing and no housewrap or weather-resistive barrier. Shear resistance depends on the siding plus two diagonal braces that were added as an afterthought at 43:41. Commenters also flag T1-11's real-world rot and re-sealing burden in wet or northern climates.

Stops short of a usable workshop: no insulation, no vapor barrier, no interior finish, and no electrical - he says he will run power 'eventually'. A commenter points out the 2x6 truss ceiling limits later insulation depth if you ever want to convert it to conditioned space.

Several execution details are contested by knowledgeable commenters and left uncorrected: soffits are still open at the end of the video (bat/critter entry), the metal roof screws are placed in the panel valleys rather than the ridges, and the purlins were all broken over the same two trusses so the roof plane is not properly tied together. Treat the choices as one competent amateur's, not vetted best practice.

The signature steel ramps are not reproducible for most viewers - they need a welder, and the big one weighs roughly 500 lb and had to be rolled into place on temporary casters. He calls them 'completely overbuilt' himself, and the plywood decking is left bare pressure-treated with no finish decided.

Not a one-person build. He credits one friend for augering the pier holes with a tractor and another for the post cuts and for standing walls and setting trusses, saying both would have been 'impossible' alone. Budget for help on those days.

The 12 ft depth is generous for storage but tight as a shop once a vehicle is inside, and there is no loft or attic floor as built - overhead storage requires adding 12 ft ceiling joists you would have to design yourself.

plans.build_time: About 2 months, "working on it 4 days a week roughly full time and then some other nights as well" (stated at 44:47). Started in February in snow-capable weather; the piers were poured about 5 days before framing began, in roughly 50-degree weather. Walls and trusses were prefabbed indoors during rain, and the entire shell (walls one day, trusses the next) went up in about two days with one helper.
plans.est_material_cost: About $9,000 total for everything, stated on camera at 44:57. The pressure-treated pier-and-beam floor system is broken out as roughly $1,200 of that budget (45:21). He prices a bought 12x24 prefab at $8,500-$9,500 (45:06) and notes that buying would still have left him owing grading or a floor system, putting the purchased option at $10,000-$10,500. No itemized breakdown or receipts are shown.
plans.materials_list_available: none
plans.foundation: Six drilled-and-poured concrete pier footers, roughly 3 ft deep, bored with a friend's tractor-mounted auger because the ground is very rocky ("would have been impossible to do by hand", 01:22). Site-built forms were then used to cast a squared, level pad surface on top of each pier. Post bases were anchor-bolted to the pads and carry notched 6x6 posts. The two middle pads were made wider because each takes two posts, so there are 6 footers but 8 posts. The whole thing sits on a hillside with about a 3 ft drop from front to back; posts were cut to length off a single high-point reference to bring everything level. Nothing touches grade - all lower framing is pressure treated and held clear of the ground. Pier diameter, pad size and rebar are not stated.
plans.floor_framing: Doubled 2x10 headers/beams running the 24 ft length, made from two 12 ft lengths per side, glued and nailed together, dropped into a 3 in double notch cut into the 6x6 posts. 2x10 floor joists at 12 ft length hung on joist hangers that were nailed to the beams before the beams were set (a deliberate solo-builder move). 2x10 rim joists sit in their own notch in the posts; the rim on the garage-door side is doubled specifically because the heavy ramp bolts through it and vehicles drive up it. Two rows of solid blocking across the 12 ft joist span, deliberately kept in a straight aligned line - he says one row would probably do, but he used two for stiffness and because the deck is not tongue-and-groove. Deck is 3/4 in plywood, 9 sheets, joints staggered and landing on the blocking so every panel edge is supported. All floor framing is pressure treated.
plans.wall_framing: 2x4 stud walls about 8 ft tall - deliberately 8 ft rather than the 7 ft typical of prefab sheds. Walls were prefabbed in 8 ft sections inside his garage and carried out; the two 12 ft end walls were also built as 8 ft plus 4 ft sections and temporarily screwed together to be moved as one. A double top plate ties the sections together and carries the roof load. Headers over the door and window openings are 2x6 "to help with some strength". Horizontal mid-height blocking rows run between studs (visible around 16:43 and questioned by commenters as over-engineering). There is no separate wall sheathing and no housewrap or WRB - the T1-11 siding is the only skin. Extra 2x4 verticals at 16 in o.c. were added in the gable ends purely to back the siding. Diagonal 2x bracing was later lagged into the two ramp-side corners with 3/8 in lags to stop the structure twisting if something heavy is driven in and braked. Main-wall stud spacing is never stated.
plans.wall_height: 8 ft (stated; he explicitly notes prefab sheds are usually 7 ft and he chose 8 ft)
plans.roof: Gable roof on 13 site-built trusses. Rafter members are 2x6 at roughly 8 ft length - he calls this out at 45:46 as an upgrade over the 2x4 trusses on a bought shed. One rafter was cut and traced to make 26 identical rafters, assembled into 13 trusses with collar ties near the peak and a center support strut. Hurricane ties were set on the top plate first so truss locations were pre-marked, then each truss was toe-nailed both sides and the ties fully nailed off afterward. No plywood sheathing at all: purlins run over the trusses at roughly 2 ft on center (spacing nudged slightly so a purlin sits just below the ridge to leave room for venting), then galvanized metal roofing panels roughly 8 ft x 3 ft, about 9 across each slope, screwed one screw per purlin per rib. Off-the-shelf ridge cap in 10 ft sections, 3 used. About 1 ft of eave and rake overhang all around, carried on flying rafters, for looks and weather protection. Soffits were still open at the end of the video. Pitch and ridge height are not stated. Commenters flag two issues: screws driven in the panel valleys rather than on the ribs, and all purlins broken over the same two trusses.
plans.siding: T1-11 grooved plywood siding in 4x8 sheets, bought pre-primed, applied directly over the studs with no sheathing or housewrap beneath. Butted tight up under the rafters on the front wall; a Z-channel flashing was installed at the horizontal seam on the gable end so water running down the upper sheet cannot get behind the lower one. Painted white - two coats overall, three on the front wall - with the grooves brushed first (he suggests a high-nap roller instead if repeating). All trim is PVC: corner boards built on sawhorses then installed, plus door and garage-door trim and site-built shutters, all in a gray he names as "Horizon Gray" for contrast. Vinyl gutter and downspout on the front elevation only, pitched roughly to the downspout and run out past the footers in black corrugated drain tube; no gutter on the back because the siding sits high off the ground there. Perimeter stone/gravel matching the house finishes the base.
plans.doors: One 9 ft wide x 7 ft high overhead sectional garage door, installed from the manufacturer's instructions (his first time); the mounting brackets happened to land on a truss so almost no extra framing was needed, but he notes framing would have to be added to fit an opener later. A site-built jamb/threshold with 3/8 in plywood shimming was made at the garage door so the seal lands correctly and rain grades out of the building. Plus one prehung double French door on the front wall, set on a site-built sill pan so any water that gets past the door drains out rather than in. Both openings are served by welded steel ramps: a small one about 6.5 ft wide x 6 ft long at the double doors (3 hinges) and a large trapezoidal one at the garage door, roughly 12 ft on one side, 5 ft on the other and about 9.5 ft deep, weighing around 500 lb (5 hinges). Ramps are 1-1/2 x 4 in steel tubing at 24 in spacing, decked in 3/4 in pressure-treated plywood, coated with roll-on Rust-Oleum, hinged to the building (so seasonal frost movement at the unfooted ground end does not fight the pier-supported shed) and through-bolted into the doubled header and doubled rim joist. A 2x10 guard rail is lagged along the high side of the big ramp every 16 in.
plans.windows: Two windows, 2 ft x 3 ft, both on the front (long) wall, set into pre-sized rough openings, shimmed off the sill and leveled. Headers over them are 2x6. Site-built PVC shutters in "Horizon Gray" flank them. This was the creator's first-ever window installation. Brand and model are not stated.
plans.loft: None as built. The 2x6 trusses use only collar ties near the peak plus a center support strut, so the volume above is open but has no floor. He discusses the trade-off explicitly at 07:27: running that web member all the way down to the top plate would make it a true 12 ft ceiling joist and allow overhead storage, so he leaves the option to add ceiling joists in a section later. No loft headroom figure and no ladder or access is shown, and a commenter notes the 2x6 ceiling depth would also constrain insulation if it were ever converted.
plans.overall_height: not stated
plans.skill_level: Intermediate DIY, but unusually forgiving to watch because the creator is transparent about being a first-timer at most of it - he says on camera this was his first time ever installing a roof, gutters, windows, an exterior door, a garage door and PVC trim (35:28, 36:57, 43:33, 46:11-46:13). Skills genuinely required: laying out and leveling piers on a slope, cutting and notching 6x6 posts, conventional 2x4 wall framing, building repeatable trusses off a template, and screwing down metal roofing from a ladder/roof. Two people are needed for the post cuts and for standing walls and setting trusses (he credits helpers "Steve" for augering the holes and "Austin" for the post cuts and shell raising, and calls both "impossible" solo); everything after the shell he did alone. The steel ramps additionally require welding and metal cutting and are optional/extra - he admits they are "completely overbuilt".
plans.permit_notes: Not addressed anywhere in the 48 minutes - no permit, setback, zoning, snow load, wind load or inspection discussion, and no engineer's stamp on the homemade trusses. Worth flagging for this size: 288 sq ft is above the permit-exempt shed threshold in many jurisdictions and is often reclassified as a garage or accessory structure (one commenter notes his New Hampshire town caps a "shed" at 12x16, and the creator himself says the building "could really be considered a one-car garage"). Multiple commenters ask for prints "for the inspector and permit" and none exist, so this resource cannot support a permit application on its own.
plans.refund_policy: Not applicable - free video, nothing is sold. The creator's store (kordare.com) sells a 50x70 garage-house plan set and automotive parts but no shed plans.

ONE ENGINEERING CLAIM I CHECKED AND CLEARED (do not add it as a con): a commenter alleges the 3 in notch "halved the load bearing capacity" of the 6x6. It is not governing — the remaining 2.5 x 5.5 in = 13.75 in^2 bearing section carries ~13,750 lb at 1,000 psi Fc, versus a middle-post reaction of only ~3,600 lb at 50 psf. The notch is fine; the 12 ft girder span is the actual problem.

corrections.field: pros[2] ("Structurally conservative for 288 sq ft") / summary ("deliberately overbuilt for a shed: doubled 2x10 beams")
corrections.reported: Structurally conservative for 288 sq ft. Doubled 2x10 beams on notched 6x6 posts ... deliberately overbuilt for a shed
corrections.correct: Structurally conservative above the deck, but the girders are the weak link: doubled 2x10 beams span a full 12 ft between piers, roughly 2x the IRC girder table span for a 2-ply 2x10 carrying 6 ft of tributary floor
corrections.evidence: Transcript 04:15-04:23: "these are 2x 10 and 12 ft long so that's how you get the 24 doubled up." 13:39-13:53 confirms only corner posts plus one middle post per side; 02:23 "I've got six Footers" and 01:51-01:57 "the uh middle two are a little wider because I'm putting two posts on those." So each doubled-2x10 girder segment spans 12 ft, carrying half the 12 ft joist span = ~6 ft tributary. IRC R502.5(1) gives a 2-2x10 girder at 12 ft building width a span of roughly 5'-9" to 6'-6" depending on species. Hand-check at 50 psf: M = 5,400 ft-lb, S = 42.8 in^3, fb = 1,514 psi vs ~875-1,050 psi allowable for #2 material; deflection = 0.44 in vs L/360 = 0.40 in. Fails bending and deflection before dead load. A commenter (@hunterh1033) asks exactly this: "Have you found the 3 posts is enough for your 24 foot span?" and gets no reply. The record's own footprint_note markets the building as a one-car garage with vehicle ramps, which makes this the single most important thing to say in cons, not a pro.

plans.name: 16x18 Timber Frame Plan (King Post, SKU 6981)
plans.http_status: 200 via WebFetch and via Wayback (2025-10-06 snapshot); direct curl returns 403 (Cloudflare/BigScoots)
plans.footprint_note: Spec tab states 16 ft wide by 18 ft long outside-of-post to outside-of-post = 288 sq ft gross; the description separately claims "The interior space is 288 square feet", though with 8x8 posts the true clear interior is roughly 266 sq ft
plans.style: Heavy timber frame, king post gable at 8:12 pitch, 3 bents / 2 bays, curved 4x8 knee braces, upper bents tying the king posts, 2 ft overhangs all around
plans.summary: A paid 34-page instant-download PDF from Timber Frame HQ for a mortise-and-tenon king post timber frame measuring 16 ft x 18 ft outside-of-post to outside-of-post (288 sq ft interior) with 2 ft overhangs on all four sides, a 9 ft 10 in plate and a 15 ft 9 in peak at 8:12 pitch. The timbers are heavy: 8x8 posts, 8x12 plates, tie beams and ridge, 4x10 rafters and 4x8 braces. The set breaks down as 23 pages of construction drawings, 7 pages of post-and-beam conversion drawings (a bolted/fastened alternative to cut joinery), 3 pages of roof-pitch options and a 1-page timber list, all formatted 8.5 x 11 for home printing, plus 3D and x-ray renderings and an interactive Sketchfab model embedded on the product page. It is frame-only: no foundation design, floor system, siding, roofing, window or door details are published, and Timber Frame HQ explicitly puts structural analysis, engineering and code compliance on the buyer.

plans.format: Instant PDF download, sized 8.5 in x 11 in (letter) for easy printing at home; interactive 3D model viewable on the product page (Sketchfab). A printed-set option is offered on some other TFHQ plans but is not shown on this product.

plans.wall_framing: Heavy timber bents: 8x8 posts with 4x8 knee braces and 8x12 tie beams and plates; plate height 9 ft 10 in. Wall infill/enclosure (stud walls, SIPs, sheathing, insulation) is not part of the plan.

plans.summary: Sheds Unlimited's Standard MaxiBarn Shed Kit is a panelized gambrel-roof barn kit built by their Lancaster County, PA crews and shipped as pre-assembled walls, floor deck and trusses for DIY erection — not a paper plan. At 16×20 (320 sq ft) it lists $14,170 with painted SmartSide engineered-wood siding or $18,484 with Double 4" Dutchlap vinyl. Framing is conventional and well documented: PT 4×4 skids, PT 2×4 joists 16" o.c., 5/8" floor, 2×4 studs 16" o.c. with a double 2×4 top plate, 2×4 trusses 16" o.c., 7/16" OSB sheathing, synthetic underlayment and 30-yr architectural shingles. The gambrel profile is explicitly marketed as loft-ready ("the extra headspace under the gambrel roof provides the option of overhead lofts"), but a loft is a paid custom option, not part of the standard kit.
plans.foundation: Customer's responsibility. Sheds Unlimited publishes separate "Gravel Pad Preparation" and "Concrete Foundation Preparation" guides and sells same-day professional site prep. The kit sits on pressure-treated 4×4 skids, so a level compacted gravel pad is the intended base; a concrete slab is also supported (a reviewer's shed was fitted to an existing slab with a stiffened floor). Concrete blocks are explicitly ruled out: "We do not recommend using concrete blocks under your building... Over time an unlevel pad can cause the building to settle which can cause doors and windows to bind."
plans.floor_framing: "Base made from pressure-treated 4×4 skids"; "Pressure-treated 2×4 floor joists, 16 inches on-center"; "5/8 inch flooring". Sibling spec sheet adds "Boxing: Pressure-treated 2x4s". Note the 2×4 joists at 16" o.c. must span the 16 ft width unless intermediate skids/beams carry them — the page does not state how many skids or the beam layout for the 16' wide model.
plans.wall_framing: "Studs: 2x4s, 16″ on-center"; "Top Plate: Double 2x4s" (from the matching assembled Standard MaxiBarn spec sheet). The kit page itself only says "our shed barn kit walls and floors are built from studs and sheeting (just like your house)". Walls arrive as pre-built, pre-sheathed, pre-painted panels; the manual has you toenail the 2×4 bottom plate into the floor joists with 3" framing nails.
plans.wall_height: not stated — the MaxiBarn is described only as having "high sidewalls" versus the low-wall MiniBarn; no numeric sidewall dimension is published for any size.
plans.overall_height: not stated for the 16' wide model. The published "Height to Roof Peak" table stops one step short: 8′ wide – 10′6″, 10′ – 10′11″, 12′ – 11′2″, 14′ – 11′10″, 15′6″ – 12′. The likely reading is that the "16×20" is built at a road-legal 15′6″ nominal width (12′ peak), but the page never says this outright.
plans.roof: Gambrel / "barn style" roof. Pitch is given only as "Barn Style Roof Pitch" — no numeric pitch is published for the MaxiBarn (by contrast the Classic Workshop page states 6/12). Structure: "2×4 trusses, 16 inches on-center", "7/16 inch OSB roof sheathing", "Roof Underlayment: Synthetic", "30yr architectural shingles", drip edge included. Trusses are factory-built and shipped complete, but nothing on the page says they are engineer-stamped. Being a "Standard" collection building it has no roof overhangs on the eaves or gables.
plans.siding: Two choices. (1) Engineered wood: LP SmartSide / Smart Panel T1-11, painted in your choice of Sherwin-Williams colors, 5/50-year warranty — the cheaper option and the basis of the $14,170 price. (2) Double 4" Dutchlap vinyl with weathered wood-grain texture, 50-year no-fade warranty, maintenance-free — $18,484 at 16×20. Corner trim and fascia included in the color of choice.
plans.doors: One set of double doors, standard. "16′ wide shed = 6ft Double Door" for both siding types. Wood-siding kits get wooden double doors with "Classic" style hinges and painted wood slat shutters; vinyl-siding kits get fiberglass double doors and vinyl raised-panel shutters. Door and window placement is customizable: "Absolutely! Only if there is not enough space in the wall to fit the windows and/or doors will we need to recommend otherwise." Note a 6 ft opening is the widest standard door even on the 16' wide building — narrow for driving in a tractor or vehicle.
plans.windows: "2 – 18×27 windows with screen and shutters". These are small; the Classic Workshop line by comparison ships 24×36 windows. Upgraded window options are available as paid add-ons.
plans.loft: Not included. The gambrel is marketed as loft-ready — "The extra headspace under the gambrel roof provides the option of overhead lofts as well" and "This design allows for the addition of an overhead loft area, meaning you can get two levels of storage in the same shed!" — and lofts appear under paid "Interior Additions". No loft dimensions, loft-floor framing spec, headroom figure, load rating or access method (ladder vs stair) is published, and loft pricing is not on this page.
plans.skill_level: Moderate DIY, two-person minimum. Manual: "Some steps in this install can be challenging, so we recommend that you have a team of at least two people for the install. We also recommend that at least one individual have some construction knowledge." Nail guns (framing, coil, roofing) are recommended to speed things up but "the entire shed can be installed with a simple hammer and nail." Because walls and trusses arrive pre-built, the hard framing layout work is already done — but the pre-built 16 ft wall panels are heavy and awkward, so realistically this needs 3+ people or equipment at that size. Sheds Unlimited flatly refuses to sell two-story buildings as kits, which frames where they draw the DIY line.
plans.build_time: not stated. No labor-hour or day estimate is published. The follow-along video is indexed in timestamps (roughly 8+ minutes of video covering unpacking through shingling) but that is video runtime, not build time.
plans.permit_notes: Buyer's responsibility: "Every town has different regulations about adding an accessory structure. Contact your town or township... You will be responsible for obtaining any required permits and the fees associated with them." Sheds Unlimited will run the whole permit process for a flat $1,300, but only in DE, PA, MA, CT, MD, RI, VA and NJ. They also coach the portable-structure angle: "If you are purchasing a portable structure (one with a wooden floor), make sure the town understands the building is not a permanent structure. In most of cases, property taxes will not be affected if the building is not permanent and the pad is permeable." Practically, 320 sq ft is over the permit-exempt threshold in most jurisdictions, and one reviewer confirms stamped plans exist and work: "The local permit process went smoothly with the plans I purchased from Sheds Unlimited." The page does not state whether such plans are included, extra, or bundled into the $1,300.

includes: Free 3D SketchUp model (.skp for SketchUp 8 and 2017-2021) of a complete 16 x 24 ft shed/garage
Framing modeled member-by-member: floor posts and beams, wall studs and blocking, plates, headers, rafters and a two-piece 2x6 ridge
Most boards are separate named components (e.g. '2x4x8', 'Floor center beams'), so you can measure or report a cut list yourself inside SketchUp
Finish surfaces: lap siding, 3/8 in sheathing, 3/4 in floor deck sheets, asphalt shingle roof (37 materials in the file)
A dynamic/animated overhead garage door, an entry door animatable with SketchyPhysics 3.2, a pair of glazed patio doors, one window and a scale human figure
Public glTF/GLB export (1.6 MB) that anyone can download and view without SketchUp or an account
USDZ and .zip versions of the same model
pros: Truly free, no email wall and no upsell; 1,638 downloads, 4,173 views and a 5.0 average from 9 ratings
Footprint is exactly the size the user wants: floor deck measures 16.0 x 24.0 ft = 384 sq ft, decked with twelve 4x8 sheets with no waste
Author says it is a shed he actually built at his home, so the layout is a real-world one rather than a paper exercise
3D beats 2D for understanding assembly: you can orbit, hide layers and section-cut every corner, the header over the garage door, the rafter-to-plate detail, etc.
Individual boards are separate named components, so a SketchUp user can generate a real quantity/cut list from the model in minutes
Openings suit workshop/garage duty: an overhead door plus a man door on the long wall and double patio doors on the end wall, unlike most 16x24 shed plans that only give you a double barn door
8 ft 6 in side walls give genuine standing headroom along the walls and room for wall storage
The shallow ~2:12 gable keeps overall height to about 11 ft 8 in, which helps with height limits and makes roof sheathing/shingling less scary than a steep pitch
A public GLB copy exists, so the design is viewable/measurable even without SketchUp or a Trimble account
cons: Not a plan set. No dimensioned drawings, no elevations, no framing schedule, no step-by-step instructions, no fastener/hardware notes, no PDF - just a 3D file you must interrogate yourself.

No materials list published. The author only offers 'a Xcel with the approximate material list' by emailing mrob1001@yahoo.com - a personal Yahoo address last active around 2013-2014, so assume it is dead.
Nothing is engineered or stamped and no snow/wind loads, code references or footing details are given; a plan-check department will almost certainly not accept this as-is for a 384 sq ft building.

Framing is drawn at nominal sizes (members measure exactly 2.0 x 4.0 in and 2.0 x 6.0 in, not 1.5 x 3.5 / 1.5 x 5.5), so every stud bay, plate length and sheathing layout taken off the model is dimensionally wrong by up to 1/2 in per member and errors accumulate over 24 ft.
Board labels are unreliable: '2x4x4'' measures 24 in, '2x6x5'-11 1/4#1' measures 48 in, '2x4x12"-6"' measures 154 in, '2x4x1'-8 1/4"' measures 12 1/2 in. You must measure, never trust the name.

Roof is structurally naive: 2x4 rafters at 24 in o.c. spanning 8 ft on a two-piece 2x6 'ridge beam' with zero collar ties, rafter ties or ceiling joists. At a ~2:12 pitch that is a thrust problem, and 2x4 rafters at 24 in o.c. will not pass in most snow regions.

Floor system is lighter than standard practice: 2x6 beams at 4 ft o.c. with 2x4 crossmembers, leaving 3/4 in decking to span about 48 in. Expect a bouncy floor; anyone parking a vehicle or a shop machine on it should re-engineer to 2x8 joists at 16 in o.c.

Foundation is 18 in long 4x4 posts sitting on grade with no concrete piers, footings or frost protection modeled - a rot and frost-heave design in most climates, and you will have to solve the foundation entirely on your own.
Wall sheathing is only 3/8 in with studs at 24 in o.c.; that is thin for shear and for fastening siding, and many jurisdictions want 16 in o.c. or braced-wall detailing for a building this size.
Doors and windows are explicitly not to scale and are other authors' borrowed components, so rough openings in the model are meaningless - you must resize them to real units you buy.
The overhead door is cut into the long load-bearing eave wall with only a doubled 2x6 header, which is marginal under rafters at 24 in o.c.
Needs SketchUp (free web version can open .skp, desktop is a paid subscription) and a free Trimble sign-in to download; anonymous download of the .skp is blocked (HTTP 401).
Last updated 2014, no comments thread and no written reviews - all 9 ratings are bare 5-star clicks, so there is no build feedback or errata to learn from.

At 384 sq ft with a garage door, this exceeds the permit-exempt threshold in most US jurisdictions (commonly 120-200 sq ft), so you will be in a permit process with a document set this model cannot supply.

pros: Genuinely free and immediately measurable: 320 sq ft of real framing geometry you can section, dimension and quantity-take-off yourself in free SketchUp — or via the public .glb, which downloads with no account at all.
The framing is conventional and inspector-shaped: 2x4 studs at 16 in OC in all four walls, single bottom plate with a lap-spliced double top plate, trusses at 24 in OC. Nothing exotic to argue about.

12:12 scissor trusses clear-span the full 16 ft with no post or bearing wall, and lift the ceiling to roughly 12 ft at the centerline — that vaulted volume is the whole reason to choose this over a rafter-and-collar-tie roof.
Slab-on-grade keeps it simple and cheap: no joist spans to verify, no rot-prone wood floor, and the slab is drawn at exactly 16x20 x 4 in so concrete volume is easy to price (about 3.95 cu yd).
12-in eave overhangs are already built into the truss tails (18 ft overall roof width), so wall tops and siding stay protected without redesign.

Openings are generously proportioned and properly framed: a 40-in rough opening with a header bottom at 7 ft 1 1/2 in, carried on a built-up double 2x10 with a 1/2-in plywood spacer on 84-in trimmers.
Metal connector plates are modeled at every truss joint, so the intended truss shape and joint locations are unambiguous when you take it to a truss plant for a quote.
cons: It is NOT a buildable plan set. There are no drawings, no cut list, no material quantities, no instructions, no sequencing and no cost estimate — and the uploader left the description, details and tags entirely blank ("description":"", "tags":[]).

Nothing is engineered. No design loads, snow/wind assumptions, lumber grades or engineer's seal, and no truss design drawings despite the plated scissor trusses. You will need sealed truss designs or a truss-plant quote to permit it.

Walls are modeled with full 96-in studs, so plate height is 100.5 in (8 ft 4.5 in). Real 92-5/8 in precut studs give 8 ft 1 1/8 in; build it as drawn and standard 8-ft sheathing/siding won't reach, so you need 9-ft sheets or filler strips and every elevation shifts.

The envelope is completely absent: no sheathing, housewrap, siding, roof deck, roofing, fascia, insulation or ventilation — and no gable-end infill framing above the top plates (the end trusses are ordinary scissor trusses, not gable-end frames), so both 16-ft ends are literally open triangles.
No windows and only one 40-in door opening in a 320 sq ft building; most owners will re-frame openings, which means redoing headers and stud layout.
No loft or attic storage at all, and the sloping scissor bottom chords make adding one later awkward — a real cost if you wanted 320 sq ft plus overhead storage.

No footing or thickened slab edge, no anchor bolts, hold-downs, hangers or fasteners are modeled, and the slab is drawn dead flush with the outside of the framing (no ledge, no slope, no vapor barrier).
Roughly 16 ft 9.5 in to the ridge above slab is tall for an accessory building — check height limits and the practicality of working at that height before committing.

plans.summary_original: SteelMaster's "Cabins" page sells a prefabricated Quonset arch shell as a DIY kit, ordered by model + width/height + length. The 320 sq ft configuration is the S-Model S16-12 at 20 ft long: $7,250 for pre-cut, pre-punched 22-gauge Galvalume Plus steel arch panels, bolts and nuts (only two bolt sizes), assembly instructions, and — notably — FREE state-stamped engineered blueprints certified for the buyer's state wind/snow/seismic loads, which is the single strongest permit-friendliness argument on the page. The shell is clear-span with 100% usable floor space and no framing lumber at all. But the price is deliberately "open-ended": both endwalls, all doors and windows, the concrete keyway foundation, and the floor are excluded and must be locally sourced or bought as add-ons, and SteelMaster provides no installation, electrical, or plumbing services. Standard 22-gauge S16-12 arches are rated for a 40 psf ground snow load; higher loads require heavier steel at higher cost. This is a fundamentally different animal from a stick-framed 16x20 shed plan: no lumber list, no cut list, no floor plan, curved interior walls, and a peak height of only 12 ft so a loft is low-clearance sleeping/storage at best.
plans.footprint_note_original: The "Cabins" page is one configurable WooCommerce product, not a single fixed building. You pick Model (A or S), Width-and-Height (12'W x 11'H, 16'W x 12'H, 17'W x 12'H, 20'W x 13'H, 20'W x 11'H) and Length (14/16/18/20/22/30 ft). 16x20 is reached as S-Model "S16-12" (16 ft wide arch, 12 ft peak) x 20 ft length = 320 sq ft nominal, SKU WC-S161220C, $7,250. The A-Model (gable-look) does not come in a 16 ft width — its narrowest cabin option is 17'W x 12'H, so a true gable 16x20 is not orderable off this page. The page does not state whether the 16 ft width is measured outside-of-arch or clear interior, so usable interior width may be slightly under 16 ft.

plans.summary: The Heartland Duluth is a built-on-site wood "garage shed" sold on heartlandsheds.com in five 16-ft-wide sizes; the 16x20 (320 sq ft, overall 16' x 20' x 12'6") is $10,519 on sale from $12,229, and that price includes delivery of all materials plus professional installation by a Heartland crew - usually completed in one day, with a 6-8 week lead time. The shell is 2x4 walls at 16" o.c. with primed LP SmartSide siding, 8' sidewalls, a 5/12 gable roof on 9 rafters at 24" o.c. with felt, drip edge and lifetime-warranty architectural shingles, an 8' W x 7' H double door, two 16"x8" vents and a standard 16' x 4' storage loft. The floor is included: LP ProStruct treated decking over joists at 12" o.c. on 4x4 pressure-treated runners, rated 52 lbs/sq ft. Published structural ratings are 30 psf roof load and 115 mph wind. Customer supplies the site (level within 6"; slab, pavers or leveled ground) and pays extra for paint ($1,584 package for the 16x20), windows, ramps, roll-up/service doors, anchors and the optional $299 permit service. Permits are the buyer's responsibility; stamped drawings are available for a fee. Warranty is 10-year limited material / 1-year labor; installed sheds cannot be returned and a 25% restocking fee applies to returns and cancellations. For someone who actually wants to DIY a 16x20, this is the price-comparison benchmark rather than a buildable plan - no drawings or cut list come with it.

plans.summary: Texas Arched Cabins sells DIY arched-shell steel kits, not wood-frame shed plans. The kit is a patented curved-steel-rib arch (ribs every 2 ft) bolted to floor plates and a ridge beam, skinned in corrugated galvalume metal, with wall insulation and all color-matched fasteners plus a step-by-step build manual. Nothing else is in the box: foundation, floor, both end caps (gable walls), doors, windows, interior finish, installation and delivery are all explicitly excluded from the kit price. Sizes are priced by linear foot per width; 16 ft wide runs $325/LF, so a 16x20 shell is $6,500 kit-only ($7,900 with the color and insulation upgrades), with delivery billed at $2/mile one-way from Cypress, Texas. Kits meet IBC minimums of 150 mph wind and 30 psf snow, drawings for permitting are available, and site-specific engineered drawings cost $850-$2,500+ and take 2-4 weeks. Lead time is 8-10 weeks from order; terms are 50% down / 50% one week before shipping, with a 15% restocking fee on cancellation (25% inside 20 days of delivery). No turnkey option and no traveling build crew since 2018 — you or a local contractor build it.
includes: Build manual (step-by-step written instructions)

Color-coordinated fasteners needed to assemble the cabin

Optional paid add-ons: roof color upgrade (+$35/LF at 16 ft wide), insulation upgrade (+$35/LF), fireplace thimble ($400), delivery ($2/mile), steel slab embeds, engineered drawings ($850+)
pros: Very cheap per square foot for a weathertight shell: $6,500 for a 320 sq ft 16x20 arch is roughly $20/sq ft of shell, and the metal skin is also the roofing and the siding — no sheathing, no housewrap, no shingles to buy.

Clear-span structure: curved steel ribs span the full 16 ft with no interior posts, headers or trusses to build, and no rafter/birdsmouth cutting. Nothing structural has to be engineered or cut by the builder.
Published wind/snow ratings — IBC minimum 150 mph wind and 30 psf snow — which is far more than a typical DIY shed plan can claim, and the company says it has been permitted in 26 named states.
Real permit path exists: drawings for permitting are available, and site/size-specific stamped engineered drawings can be bought through their engineering firm (start at $850).

Length is fully flexible in 2 ft increments up to 40 ft at a flat linear-foot rate, so you can right-size the building instead of accepting a fixed model, and pricing is transparently published as a rate table.
Fixed-price promise: 'If we give you a price or its listed on our site at time of deposit we won't ask you for more money down the road.'

Insulation for the arched walls is in the base kit (R13/R22 standard, upgradeable), and the metal comes in 23 Energy Star rated colors — the shell arrives already insulated rather than needing a separate insulation budget.
Very high headroom for the footprint: 14'3"-14'6" to the ridge on a 16 ft wide arch, enough for a storage or sleeping loft that the owner frames in.
Ribs bolt/weld together with an illustrated manual and phone support; no complex carpentry skills required for the shell itself.
Nationwide delivery to the lower 48, or customer pickup at the Cypress, TX plant on your own trailer to avoid the mileage charge.
cons: THE FLOOR IS NOT INCLUDED. The kit contains 'floor plates' (the steel plates the ribs anchor to) — not a floor system. The FAQ is explicit: 'The kit price does not include the foundation, installation, interior, end caps, delivery, or anything that is not included above.' You supply the slab or the entire wood floor/deck framing and decking yourself.

THE PRICE IS KIT-ONLY: not delivered and not assembled. Delivery is a separate $2.00/mile ONE-WAY charge from Cypress, Texas 77429 — from, say, 800 miles away that is $1,600 on top of the $6,500, which can be a quarter of the project cost. There is no delivered-and-assembled option at all: 'Do you provide turnkey Arched Cabins? A. No.' The traveling build team was discontinued at the end of 2018.

BOTH END WALLS ARE NOT INCLUDED. The two gable 'end caps' — framing, sheathing, siding, and every door and window — are 100% owner-supplied and owner-designed. On a 16x20 those two arched end walls are the hardest, most visible carpentry in the whole project (curved top plate, custom-cut studs, custom-cut siding) and the kit gives you no plan for them, only rubber trim and foam closures to seal against them.
No doors, no windows, no interior finish, no electrical, no plumbing, no loft — all owner-supplied. Budget for these separately; the shell price is not a building price.

Curved walls mean lost usable space: the 320 sq ft is a nominal footprint measured at the floor plate, and the site's own square-footage numbers carry an unexplained '**' footnote. Furniture, shelving, cabinets and wall storage do not fit against a barrel wall, which is a real penalty for a workshop or shed use.

Windows, skylights, doors or bump-outs in the arched sides are strongly discouraged — 'to keep the Arched Cabin structurally sound we don't recommend cutting into the ribs' — so daylight and access are essentially limited to the two ends unless you pay for reinforcement engineering.

Foundation demands are real and extra-cost: for a slab you must place steel embeds in the wet concrete to weld the ribs to, and the company recommends a soil sample and a custom foundation designed for your soil. That is concrete/welding work, not a gravel pad and skids.

Permitting can be the biggest hidden cost driver: engineered drawings start at $850 and 'can run $2500 or more' and take 2-4 weeks (sometimes longer with revisions). A shed-sized 320 sq ft building may not justify that; and appraisers/lenders struggle with the design — traditional mortgages 'aren't usually a good fit.'
No materials or cut list is published anywhere, and no downloadable plan set — you cannot price-shop or source the shell locally, and you cannot evaluate the design before paying.

Cancellation is expensive: 15% restocking fee any time after the deposit, rising to 25% of the total invoice within 20 days of the scheduled delivery date. 50% down is required to hold a delivery date. Credit card payments carry a 3% surcharge.
8-10 week manufacturing lead time from order, so this is not a this-weekend project.
Delivery access is restrictive: paved entry, no 4x4-required approach, driveway at least 10 ft wide with no hairpin or sharp turns, trucks and trailers up to 45 ft long.

Design is patented and licensed (U.S. Pat. Nos. 9,822,522 and D792,983); the company states it 'will actively prosecute anyone found to have replicated our design,' so you cannot copy it or build a second one.

Site data is internally inconsistent — the /cabins/ page says standard R13 insulation, R25 upgrade, 23 colors and 14'3" height for the 16 ft wide, while the FAQ says R22 standard, R39 upgrade, 35 colors and 14'6". Get the current spec in writing on your quote.
There is no published 16x20 line item; the $6,500 is arithmetic off the vendor's own linear-foot rate table, so confirm it on a written quote before budgeting.

PRICE — verified character-by-character and it is exactly right, which is unusual. The published price chart (an IMAGE, /wp-content/uploads/2024/12/pricing-chart.jpg — not greppable text, I read it visually) gives: 16 ft wide base kit $325/LF, Color Upgrade $35/LF, "Insulation upgrade to R25 (no installation)" $35/LF, "Fireplace Thimble for Flue Pipe" $400, "Delivery for kits up to 24 ft" $2.00/mile, ">24 ft" $2.50/mile. So 20 LF × $325 = $6,500 base and $6,500 + 20 × $70 = $7,900 upgraded — both correct. The vendor's own instruction sanctions the arithmetic: "Find the Arched Cabin base kit cost by multiplying the linear foot (LF) cost found in the column of the width you've chosen by the length of the cabin you want." Cross-check confirms the rate: published 16x24 = $7,800 (=24×325) and 16x32 = $10,400 (=32×325); upgraded 16x24 $9,480 and 16x32 $12,640 both back-solve to exactly $70/LF. price_usd 6500 is therefore a vendor-formula price, not a fabrication — though note 16x20 itself is NOT a listed size.

FOOTPRINT/SQFT — 16 × 20 = 320 ✓. footprint_note is accurate: the 16 ft section lists only 16x24 (384 sq ft**, 14'3" tall) and 16x32 (512 sq ft**, 14'3" tall), and the page does say "can manufacture Arched Cabin kits in even numbers up to 40 feet long" and "we DO offer custom sizes" — 20 is even, so a 16x20 is orderable. The observation that the "**" on every sq-ft figure is undefined on the page is correct (only the single "*" footnote is defined, and it covers upgrades/delivery). No page count applies (kit, not a plan set) — correctly typed kind:"kit".

QUOTES — all verbatim except cons[1] (above): "we can manufacture Arched Cabin kits in even numbers up to 40 feet long" ✓; "The kit price does not include the foundation, installation, interior, end caps, delivery, or anything that is not included above." ✓ exact; "can run $2500 or more" ✓; "If we give you a price or its listed on our site at time of deposit we won't ask you for more money down the road." ✓ exact (home page, not /cabins/).

OTHER FACTS ALL CONFIRMED: floor/foundation excluded ✓; kit-only, not delivered, not assembled ✓; delivery one-way from Cypress, Texas 77429 ✓ (FAQ: "Delivery fees are one way from our manufacturing location in Cypress, Texas 77429"); traveling build team ended "until the end of 2018" ✓; ribs "run every 2 feet" ✓; ridge beam "4″ thick" ✓; 150 mph / 30 psf IBC minimums ✓ (FAQ also notes highest recorded engineering 165 mph / 180 psf); permitted states — I counted the FAQ list and it is exactly 26 ✓; engineered drawings $850 → $2,500+, 2-4 weeks ✓; 8-10 week lead time ✓ (home page: "8-10 weeks from the date you place your order"); "a direct line to our company's build team" ✓; "step-by-step build instructions" ✓; Super Span "40 year warranty, is made from 32-50% recycled steel and comes in 23 Energy Star rated colors" ✓ (home page, verbatim); 50% down / 50% one week before ✓; 15% restocking, 25% within 20 days ✓; lower-48 delivery and customer pickup "at our manufacturing facility on an appropriate trailer" ✓; $20.31/sq ft math ✓; $2/mile × 800 mi = $1,600 ✓.

COMPLETENESS HONESTY — good. The record does not pretend this is a plan set: it says up front "not wood-frame shed plans", the floor/end caps/doors/windows/interior are called out in caps as excluded, and it notes the vendor has no floor plans of its own (FAQ: "We suggest searching the size of the floor plan you're looking for in Google Search or on Pinterest"). Worth adding: the vendor supplies NO end-cap drawings and NO floor plans at all, so a buyer needs a separate design source — the hardest carpentry (two curved-top gable walls) has zero documentation in the kit.

Net: price, footprint, sqft, exclusions, terms, ratings and nearly all quotes verify exactly. Defects are one non-included item smuggled into the includes list, one truncated quote, a color-upgrade conflation, an unflagged R25/R39 conflict, and one internally contradictory pro.

plans.name: 14x20 Shed Build (Land to House, 17-part series)
plans.footprint_note: 4 ft x 8 ft
plans.style: metal roof and primed (as-yet unpainted) fiber-cement siding
plans.price: Free
plans.summary: numbered Part 1 through Part 17 in 15 of the 17 core video descriptions (Part 7 and Part 12 omit the list)
includes: Part 1 - Foundation footers: digging to frost line, gravel drainage fill, placing and leveling solid concrete paver blocks, line level across the pad, stacking pavers on the low side (11:53)
Part 2 - Platform/floor: plastic vapor barrier, 2x8 treated frame construction, 3/4" treated plywood decking (26:06)
Part 3 - Building the 2x6 roof trusses flat on the finished platform using a screwed-down 2x4 jig template, plywood gussets with Liquid Nails (10:00)
Part 4 - Framing a basic (blank) shed wall, treated bottom plate, studs marked 16" on center, 8 ft finished wall height, standing the wall (12:33)
Part 5 - Framing the window wall: king studs, trimmers, doubled 2x4 header, cripples and sill (8:59)
Part 6 - Framing the front door wall with doubled 2x6 header over the opening (11:25)
Part 7 - Top plate lapped over wall junctions, Simpson H1 clips at 24" o.c., setting the gable-end truss then the rest, ridge board for spacing (21:10)
Part 8 - OSB wall sheathing lapped down over the treated plywood floor edge, then house wrap (18:47)
Part 9 - 7/16" OSB roof sheathing with stop blocks, staggered joints, H clips, then synthetic underlayment (14:23)
Part 10 - Front door awning / porch cover: fascia header, angled ledger, joist hangers, 4x4 support posts (16:37)
Part 11 - Metal roof panel install, screw placement discussion, ridge cap and rake trim (16:32)
Part 12 - Window install: Tyvek cutting and folding, flashing tape, stretchy sill/corner membrane, caulk on sides and top only so water can drain (10:46)
Part 13 - HardiePlank/Hardie board exterior siding, scoring 4x8 panels with an angle grinder, cutting the window opening (16:09)
Part 14 - Building custom doors from 2x4s plus a 2x6 knob stile, pocket-hole frame, hinge mortising, OSB inner skin, Hardie outer skin, knob/strike plus top and bottom latches (18:02)
Part 15 - Pressure-treated 2x8 ramp and 4 ft deep landing on joist hangers, 4x4 posts set below the frost line, tapered ripped 2x8 ramp stringers on paver blocks, plywood surface (17:52)
Part 16 - Miratec trim at doors, window and eaves; Hardie board soffit and fascia; Hardie corner strips (17:32)
Part 17 - Final walkthrough: full exterior/interior tour, features recap, things the host would change, and an on-camera total cost breakdown (13:43)
Bonus - Tongue and groove pine interior lining for the film-studio corner (9:00)
Bonus - DIY stud-mounted wall shelves with triangle brackets for the shed interior (23:54)
pros: Genuinely complete start to finish: dirt and gravel footers through final trim and walkthrough, with no jump cuts past a whole stage. Very few free shed series actually film the trim, soffit, fascia, ramp and door-building steps.

The order of operations is the real value: trusses are built on the finished platform (Part 3) before any walls go up, using the deck as a flat jig and the deck edges to set equal overhangs. That is the trick that makes site-built trusses come out consistent, and it is shown rather than described.

Structurally conservative for a shed of this size: 2x8 pressure-treated floor framing, 2x6 trusses at 24" o.c., a lapped double top plate, and Simpson H1 hurricane ties at every truss. That is a better uplift detail than most DIY sheds get and reads well to an inspector.

Foundation is the cheap, permit-friendly kind: solid concrete blocks on gravel dug to the local frost line, no concrete pour, no forms, and the leveling method (start at the high point, line level out from there, double-stack pavers on the low side) is demonstrated on visibly sloped ground.

Every framing member gets a spec on camera or in the description: treated 2x4 bottom plate, 16" o.c. studs, 8 ft walls, doubled 2x4 window header, doubled 2x6 door header, plywood gussets with adhesive plus screws, 7/16" roof OSB with H clips.
Chapter timestamps are in the descriptions for Parts 1, 2, 4, 5, 6 and 7, so you can jump straight to "Standing the wall up" or "Installing H1 clips" instead of scrubbing.

Finishes are long-life, not throwaway: house wrap, Hardie fiber-cement panel siding and Hardie soffit/fascia, Miratec rot-resistant trim, metal roofing with proper ridge cap and rake trim, and a full window flashing sequence with sill membrane and drainage-gap caulking.

The awning and the 2x8 ramp with a 4x8 landing on frost-depth 4x4 posts solve the two things people forget on a 280 sq ft shop: a dry place to cut lumber and a way to actually drive a mower or ATV inside.
17 numbered part links are hard-coded into every description, so navigation does not depend on the playlist order (which is shuffled - the Part 17 walkthrough sits at playlist position 4).
Free, ad-supported, nothing gated. The channel's own store sells only ram pumps, so there is no plan upsell pressure.
cons: No plan, no drawing, no cut list, no materials list anywhere. Nothing in any of the 19 descriptions, and the Land to House store carries only ram pump products. You must reverse-engineer quantities from the video, which for a 280 sq ft building is a real amount of work.

The critical roof dimensions are never given. Part 3 literally says "I then move the center end up until I have the pitch that I need" - no pitch, no rise, no truss span or heel height, no overall building height. You cannot check your snow or wind load, and you cannot order trusses to match.

Floor joist spacing is never stated. You know the joists are 2x8 treated and the deck is 3/4" treated plywood, and that the platform is meant to hold an ATV and a mower, but not whether joists are 16" or 24" o.c. or how many block piers carry them - which is exactly the span question a 14 ft wide floor turns on.

The trusses are shop-built on site with plywood gussets and construction adhesive - not engineered, not stamped, no gusset size or nailing schedule given. Anywhere that requires a truss submittal or an engineer's seal, this design will not pass as filmed.

Roof sheathing choice is explicitly local: the host says 7/16" OSB is "plenty strong" because "our area does not get much snow." In a real snow-load region that call, and the 24" truss spacing behind it, needs rechecking.
Total material cost is only spoken aloud in the Part 17 walkthrough - there is no figure in any description, so you have to watch it to get the number, and it cannot be cited from text.

Zero electrical, insulation, drywall or interior finish in the 17-part build. The only interior content is two bonus videos (tongue-and-groove pine on one corner, wall shelves). If you want a wired, insulated shop you are on your own past Part 17.

No permit, zoning, setback or frost-depth code guidance. Frost line is referenced as "the recommended frost line safe depth" for your area but never as an actual number, and 280 sq ft is over the permit-exempt threshold in a great many jurisdictions.

Nothing is anchored to the ground. The building sits on loose stacked concrete pavers with no ties, straps or anchor bolts shown at the foundation, which is a common inspection failure and a real uplift concern in a windy site.

Playlist ordering is confusing on the page: the finished walkthrough is the 4th thumbnail and the truss video is 3rd, so the visual order does not match the Part 1-17 sequence. Follow the numbered description links, not the playlist.

Hardie panel siding is heavy, brittle in transit, cut with an angle grinder (silica dust), and needs painting after install - a bigger cost, tool and PPE burden than the T1-11 or LP SmartSide most DIY shed builds use.
One window only for 280 sq ft, and no loft or storage platform is built anywhere in the series, so daylight and vertical storage are both left to you.

plans.foundation: Paver-block pier footers, no concrete pour. Holes dug down to the locally recommended frost-line depth, backfilled with small gravel for drainage, then solid concrete blocks ("paver stones ... solid concrete blocks made for building a shed") set on the gravel. Leveling starts at the highest point of the ground and works out with a line level; on the low side two pavers are stacked to reach height. A plastic vapor barrier goes down before the platform is framed. Pier count and grid spacing are not stated.
plans.floor_framing: 2x8 pressure-treated frame with 3/4" pressure-treated plywood decking, over a plastic vapor barrier. Explicitly built to carry ATVs and lawnmowers and to resist moisture. Joist spacing is discussed on camera ("joist spacing") but no number appears in the description.
plans.wall_framing: 2x4 stick framing at 16" on center, walls built flat on the deck and stood up. Pressure-treated 2x4 bottom plate, untreated 2x4 studs and top plate, plus a separate lapped top plate added later. Studs cut so the finished wall is 8 ft tall including bottom plate, top plate and cap plate. Assembly uses Liquid Nails plus a mix of screws and nails. Window opening: two king studs, trimmers, a doubled 2x4 header, cripples above and below, and a sill. Door opening: king studs, trimmers, a doubled 2x6 header, cripples to the top plate.
plans.wall_height: 8 ft ("I wanted the walls to be 8 foot tall. So my studs needed to be cut down to accommodate the bottom and top boards plus a top plate")
plans.overall_height: not stated
plans.roof: Gable roof on site-built 2x6 trusses at 24" on center. Trusses are assembled flat on the finished platform against a screwed-down 2x4 jig template, cut to a point at the peak, and joined with plywood gussets set in Liquid Nails with screws holding them while the adhesive cures. Top plate is lapped over the wall junctions; trusses land in Simpson Strong-Tie H1 clips at 24" o.c. on the outside of the top plate, with a ridge board maintaining spacing. Sheathing is 7/16" OSB (called "otherwise known as 1/2\"") laid with stop blocks at the eave, staggered 8 ft and 4 ft joints, and H clips between rows, then a plastic waterproof synthetic underlayment, then metal roofing panels with a purchased ridge cap and rake trim. Pitch is never stated.
plans.siding: Three layers. OSB structural wall sheathing first, run down to cover the edge of the 3/4" treated plywood floor and fastened with 2-1/2" screws; then house wrap / Tyvek for weather protection; then HardiePlank / Hardie board fiber-cement panels in 4x8 sheets attached with Torx screws, cut and notched by scoring with an angle grinder and snapping over a 2x4. Painted after install. Trim is Miratec at the doors, window and eaves; Hardie board is used for soffit and fascia and as corner strips to hide the house wrap.
plans.windows: One window, in a side wall, framed with king studs, trimmers, a doubled 2x4 header, cripples and a sill. Installed with folded and taped Tyvek, a stretchy sill/corner membrane, caulk on the two sides and top of the nail flange but deliberately not the bottom so water can drain, then screwed off and the flange covered with more membrane. Size, type and brand are not stated. The host notes it adds light and airflow and could serve as an emergency exit.
plans.doors: Shop-built pair of doors in the gable-end front wall, plus a covered entry. Each leaf is an inner frame of 2x4s with a 2x6 on the knob/strike side, joined with pocket-hole screws; hinges mortised with a chisel or router; OSB skin on the inside (its screws are what lock the frame together) and Hardie board on the outside. One leaf gets a knob and strike plate so it can be locked; the other gets top and bottom latches. Access is completed by a pressure-treated 2x8 ramp and a 4 ft deep landing framed on joist hangers off a ledger, carried on 4x4 posts set below the frost line, with tapered ripped 2x8 ramp members resting on paver blocks and plywood decking on top. A front-door awning/porch cover on 4x4 posts shelters the entry.
plans.loft: none
plans.skill_level: Beginner to intermediate DIY. The descriptions market it as beginner-friendly ("Perfect for beginners and experienced builders alike", "In this beginner-friendly tutorial"), and the framing, foundation and door work are all shown at a pace a first-timer can follow. In practice you need to be comfortable working from a ladder to set trusses and hang metal roofing on a 14 ft span, handling heavy and brittle Hardie panels, and - because there is no plan or cut list - doing your own layout, span checks and material takeoff for a 280 sq ft building.

plans.summary_original: A free 19-video YouTube playlist from Land to House LLC documenting a complete 14x20 ft (280 sq ft) tool shed / small shop built start to finish over 59 days. The core build is numbered Part 1 through Part 17 in every video description and runs roughly 4 h 22 m; the playlist adds two follow-up interior videos (tongue-and-groove pine lining for a film-studio corner, and DIY wall-mount shelves) for 4 h 55 m total. Coverage is genuinely end-to-end: paver-block footers dug to the frost line, a 2x8 pressure-treated platform with 3/4" treated plywood decking over a plastic vapor barrier, site-built 2x6 plywood-gusset trusses assembled on the deck, 2x4 walls at 16" on center framed flat and stood up, H1 hurricane ties, 7/16" OSB roof sheathing with H clips and synthetic underlayment, metal roofing with ridge cap and rake trim, house wrap plus Hardie fiber-cement siding, Miratec trim with Hardie soffit and fascia, a shop-built pair of doors, a porch awning, and a pressure-treated 2x8 ramp and landing. There is no downloadable plan, cut list, or materials list anywhere — every dimension you get is whatever the host says on camera, and the channel's store sells only ram pumps, not shed plans.

unsupported_claims: pros: "Structurally conservative for a shed of this size: 2x8 pressure-treated floor framing, 2x6 trusses at 24\" o.c., a lapped double top plate, and Simpson H1 hurricane ties at every truss. "Engineered truss drawings stamped for your individual state can be obtained upon request... A non refundable fee will be required." Marketing callout: "SecureTruss State Seal available for your state." Kits are "designed for use as storage buildings or garages only" — not habitable space; any alteration may require a civil engineer, and FL/CA have stringent extra requirements the homeowner must satisfy. You get 2x4 walls at 24" o.c. with 8'1" ceilings, a 10/12 gable roof on pre-built SecureTruss trusses with 7/16" OSB sheathing, 3/8" primed LP SmartSide siding, trim, and an 8'-wide loft with 4'3" headroom running the full length of the building on the truss bottom chords. Best Barns publishes the full 26-page assembly book with a complete parts list and a free 6-page engineered permit set (150 mph ultimate wind, 45 psf ground snow) for download without buying, so you can vet the structure and the permit paperwork before spending anything.

pros: Free, ungated engineering: a 6-page permit set with a stamped-style engineered truss sheet (150 mph ultimate wind, 45 psf ground snow / 30.65 psf roof snow), elevations, foundation cross-sections and a blank site plan is downloadable before you buy — and state-sealed truss drawings can be purchased for stubborn code offices.

Full parts list and the entire 26-page assembly book are free to download per size and door style, so you can inventory-check the kit and see exactly what the 'not included' items are before spending $6k.

Pre-built trusses, pre-built gable frames and pre-cut studs/siding remove the two hardest jobs (truss layout and a 10/12 roof) — Best Barns claims 2-3 people finish in 2-3 days once the floor is done, and no specialty tools are needed.

Genuinely tall for a shed: 8'1" first-floor walls plus a 10/12 pitch give a 13'7" peak and an 8'-wide, 4'3"-tall loft running the entire 20 ft length — far more usable than the token loft on most kits.
3/8" LP SmartSide primed engineered siding with insect/decay treatment is a step above T1-11 or OSB-and-paint, and 24" o.c. 2x4 walls with two-stud corners keep the lumber count down.
Only 12 ft wide, so trusses clear-span the whole building with no interior posts and the 4x4/2x4 PT floor system stays cheap — no beams or piers to engineer.
Free curbside shipping to the contiguous US, and defective/damaged lumber is replaced free within 30 days of delivery.
cons: Maxes out at 12 ft wide — you cannot get 16x20 from this series. 12x20 is 240 sq ft vs the 320 sq ft target, and the widest option (12x24) is still only 288 sq ft in a 12 ft-wide footprint.

Sticker price is not the build price. Add a floor (slab, or +$1,215 for the 12x20 FortressFloor), roofing (+$1,025 metal package, or buy shingles/drip edge/nails), every window (+$115 or +$145 each), a walk-in door (+$285-$400), and paint — a realistically finished 12x20 lands well north of $8,000.

No ladder, steps or stair kit is offered for the full-length loft on this listing, and the loft floor is 7/16" OSB on the 2x4 truss bottom chords rated to only 10 psf floor live load — light storage, not a workshop mezzanine or sleeping loft.
Siding must be painted with exterior acrylic latex within 30 days of construction or you risk the warranty and the panels — that is a real weekend of work on top of the build.

Buildings are licensed 'for use as storage buildings or garages only'; any alteration (adding a window opening, insulating, wiring as habitable space) may require a civil engineer, and FL/CA builds likely need a local engineer at your cost.

At 240 sq ft you are above the common 200 sq ft permit exemption, so expect a permit — and the truss sheet loads (45 psf ground snow) may not cover heavy-snow regions without buying stamped state drawings.
Returns are punishing: 25% restocking fee plus non-refundable inbound and outbound freight, and the kit must be unopened with photo proof — effectively no return once you start sorting parts.
Curbside-only delivery of ~2 pallets at roughly 1,300 lb with no help past the end of the driveway; you need several people and a plan on delivery day.

The vendor's own product page is inconsistent — the title says '16ft. - 20ft. - 24ft.' while every size is 12 ft wide, and the page's roof-package selector renders a bogus 'Clear' colour option; verify the exact SKU and inclusions with the seller before ordering.

The manual's parts list splits into 'Material Packaged on Pallet' and a 'Supplied by Local Supplier' table (42 studs, plates, 15 sheets of siding, 12 sheets of OSB). Best Barns' FAQ and return policy imply that lumber and sheathing come with the kit, but the listing never says so explicitly — confirm before assuming you do not have to buy sheet goods.
