plans.summary: SteelMaster's "One Car Garage" is a configurable Quonset-style bolt-together steel arch building kit, not a wood shed plan. The nearest size to a 16x20 shed is the S-Model 16'W x 22'L x 12'H (352 sq ft) at $7,645, priced "open-ended" — i.e. the arch shell only, with no front wall, no back wall, no doors and no accessories. The kit is 22-gauge, 80,000 PSI grade-80 steel with Galvalume Plus (AZM180/AZ65) coating, 7.5 in corrugation, pre-punched panels and a single bolt size, and it ships free with state-stamped engineered blueprints, a construction manual and a 50-year rust-perforation warranty. Buildings are designed for a standard keyway concrete slab that you pour yourself; SteelMaster provides no installation, and endwalls/doors/windows are extra-cost add-ons or must be sourced locally.
includes: 80-grade steel arch panels (22-gauge standard), 100% pre-cut with pre-punched holes and only one bolt size
AZ60/AZM180 Galvalume Plus corrosion coating on all panels
NZF30000 commercial-grade grade-2 hex bolts
LPDE industrial-strength washers
Serrated hex-head locking nuts

FREE state-stamped engineered blueprints (sealed by a licensed PE; includes slab plan with keyway dimensions or anchor-bolt data, foundation sections A-A and B-B, front/rear/side elevations, and an arch profile showing panel placement and gauge)
Construction manual (hand-delivered with the building)
Shipping/freight included, anywhere a tractor-trailer can drive
FREE garage design consultation with a state-certified building specialist
50-year warranty against rust perforation (exclusions apply)
pros: True clear span — no interior columns, beams or trusses, so all 352 sq ft is usable and the layout is fully flexible; SteelMaster markets it as "100% usable interior space".

State-stamped, PE-sealed engineered blueprints are included free and are explicitly intended for permit submission; the company says it has supplied buildings in all 50 states and designs to IBC/ASCE-7. This is the single biggest permit advantage over a generic wood shed plan.
Engineered load capacity is far beyond any DIY stick-framed shed: rated up to 300 PSF snow and 190 MPH wind when specified for the site, in 80,000 PSI grade-80 steel.

Very low skill floor for the shell: pre-punched panels, one bolt size, minimal cutting or drilling, basic hand tools plus a drill/impact gun. Multiple reviewers on the page report assembling theirs with family help.
Effectively zero maintenance and no rot or insect risk — Galvalume Plus needs no paint or sealing, and the warranty runs 50 years.
Freight is included in the listed price, which removes a large and usually unpredictable line item on steel-building quotes.
Expandable: length can be increased later in 2 ft increments by bolting on more arches, so a 16x22 can become 16x24 or 16x30 without demolition.
Fast shell erection — SteelMaster states a 3-person crew raises 6–8 arches per day, so an 11-arch 22 ft building is a 1–2 day shell.
cons: The advertised price is a shell only. "This building is priced open-ended (no front wall, no back wall, no doors, no accessories)." You must buy or build both endwalls plus any garage door, man door and window frames, so the real delivered cost is well above $7,645.

Foundation is on you and is a hard requirement: buildings are designed around a standard keyway concrete slab, and site prep, slab and installation are all listed under "Additional Costs". That is a significant concrete pour for a 16x22.
Cost per square foot ($19/sq ft for the shell alone, before slab, endwalls and doors) is far higher than a DIY wood-framed 16x20 shed built from a plan set.

The 22-gauge base price may not be legal where you live — the page warns arches "are priced in standard 22-gauge and may not meet your snow and/or wind load requirements" and heavier steel costs more.

Curved geometry costs usable space and complicates finishing: on the S-Model only the straight sidewalls are full height, and the sidewall height is not published (only 12 ft overall). Shelving, interior walls and insulation against an arched roof are all harder than in a square shed.

Not a one-person job. SteelMaster recommends 3+ people and ladders/scaffolding or a rented scissor lift; several reviewers on the page say "Definitely need four men to build" and "it does require 3 or more people".

Documentation quality is a real complaint theme in the page's own reviews — multiple buyers report the manual/schematics are vague or arrived only after delivery ("Got bldg layout and construction blueprints only after I took delivery"; one buyer says "There are absolutely NO directions for putting these together").
Nearly non-existent buyer protection after 3 days: deposits become non-refundable and "all sales are final" once the 3-day cancellation window closes, and returns are never accepted.
No published plan you can study before committing — you cannot see the blueprint set until you order, unlike a paid or free wood shed plan.
Nothing offered is exactly 16x20; the shortest length is 22 ft, and the exact price only appears after configuring the selector (the price is embedded in page metadata, not visible on load).

plans.foundation: Concrete slab. The FAQ says "A concrete slab is the most common foundation. In some situations, alternative foundations may be acceptable depending on local code and site conditions." Foundation and site prep are excluded from the price and are the buyer's cost. An optional base connector / industrial base plate is a paid accessory.
plans.floor_framing: None — no floor, joists or skids are supplied. The steel arches bolt directly to an owner-poured concrete slab (keyway or anchor-bolt attachment).
plans.wall_framing: No studs or framing members. Self-supporting cold-formed corrugated steel arch panels, 22-gauge minimum, premium 80-grade / 80,000 PSI steel, 7.5 in standard corrugation depth, in 2 ft wide arch sections. 100% of arch panels are pre-cut with pre-punched holes and use only one size bolt: grade 2 hex bolts with NZF3000 commercial-grade coating, LPDE washers and serrated hex-head locking nuts. On the S-Model the sidewalls are straight and the roof arches.
plans.roof: Arched steel roof formed by the same bolted arch panels as the walls — no trusses, rafters, purlins or sheathing, and no separate roofing material. S-Model = straight sidewalls with a rounded roofline that "deflects wind and snow"; the arch can be engineered for up to 300 PSF snow and 190 MPH wind. (If snow load is the driving concern SteelMaster recommends the X-Model's 4:12 pitch, available on this page at 22 ft width only.)
plans.siding: No separate siding. Structural panels are the exterior skin: Galvalume Plus (AZM180 / AZ65, also cited as AZ60) coated steel, gray, Energy Star rated. No painting or sealing required; 50-year warranty against rust perforation.
plans.doors: None included — the kit is sold with no front wall and no back wall. Steel endwalls, custom endwalls, overhead and canister garage doors, steel-framed openings and man/service doors are all paid add-ons (or can be locally sourced). Per the FAQ: "for smaller widths like 16 feet, a single garage door is typical, while a 20-foot-wide garage can accommodate both a garage door and a walk-in entry door."
plans.windows: None included. Steel window frames are an available add-on, but the FAQ states the windows themselves "must be sourced locally". Framed window openings must be designed into the order.
plans.loft: None supplied. SteelMaster notes the S-Model "provides overhead space for taller items or lofted area", but no loft framing, decking, headroom figure or access is included or specified — any loft would be owner-designed and owner-built inside the arch.

Since each section is 2 feet in length, a 22-foot-long garage (11 arches) can typically be assembled in one to two days, depending on the garage's width and height." Add slab cure time, endwall construction and door installation. For scale, one reviewer on the page reports 3 weeks for a much larger 40x52 Q-Model.
plans.skill_level: Low-to-moderate for the steel shell — "requiring minimal tools and limited building expertise", with pre-punched panels and one bolt size — but it is a crew job, not a solo job: 3+ people, heavy rope, drift pins and S hooks to lift arches, and ladders, scaffolding or a rented scissor lift. Required tools per the page: cordless drill driver / 3/8" variable-speed electric drill / pneumatic impact gun with bits, 20'-100' tape, level, plumb bob, chalk line, drift pins, S hooks, plus hard hats, gloves and safety glasses. Concrete slab work and garage-door hanging generally need a contractor. Several reviewers rate the assembly easier than expected; others found the instructions inadequate.
plans.permit_notes: Strong permit story. "Every building comes with complimentary state-stamped engineer-stamped drawings prepared by a licensed professional engineer. These drawings are typically required by local building departments and are suitable for permit submission, unlike generic CAD drawings that are not reviewed or approved by an engineer." Buildings are engineered to IBC and ASCE-7 and to the site's local wind, snow and seismic loads, with state-certified specialists in all 50 states. SteelMaster still puts the onus on the buyer: "final compliance depends on your specific location, so make sure to do your due diligence with your city or county to verify local zoning rules, required permits, and HOA rules if applicable." Note the base 22-gauge arch "may not meet your snow and/or wind load requirements" — a code-compliant order may require thicker (and pricier) steel. One reviewer: "having a blueprint from them to apply for building permit made that process much easier."

plans.name: 16' x 20' Standard Horse Package (open-front post-frame run-in / loafing shed) — from the Sutherlands "Building Guide: Post Frame Buildings" brochure
plans.http_status: 200 (direct curl, application/pdf, 18,610,473 bytes; no Cloudflare block, no Wayback needed)
plans.footprint_note: Brochure heading is "16' x 20' Standard Horse Package" (gross footprint 320 sq ft) but the body text says "It features approximately 280 sq. ft of enclosed area for our 16' x 20' size" — i.e. ~280 sq ft measured inside the posts/walls. Sutherlands' current (2025) Harrisonville MO price flyer sells the same building as "20x16 (2 bays)" with "10ft Wide Bays with 4x4 Post," so the geometry is 20 ft of open frontage (two 10 ft bays with one center post) x 16 ft deep. Both the brochure and the flyer say other sizes are available (30x16 3-bay, and 12x20/12x30/15x30 Livestock Shelters), so 16x20 is one point on a size ladder, not a fixed SKU.
plans.style: Post-frame (pole-built) open-front, three-sided run-in / loafing shed with a single-slope (shed) roof and steel roofing and siding. This is livestock shelter geometry, not an enclosed storage shed: no doors, windows or floor are listed.
plans.price: Not published in this brochure — the brochure carries no prices at all, only "FREE ESTIMATES on any size shed" and "stop by for a free estimate." Sutherlands' separate 2025 Harrisonville, MO price flyer (linked from sutherlands.com/post-frame-buildings) lists the same building as "Standard Horse Sheds (10ft Wide Bays with 4x4 Post) — 20x16 (2 bays) MATERIALS ONLY .......... $3,499." That $3,499 is MATERIALS ONLY: not delivered, not erected, no floor, and the flyer states "Delivery and tax based upon location. Customer is responsible for all permits" and "Pricing Subject to change with market conditions." Store-specific to Harrisonville MO.
plans.summary: The only building in it at exactly 16' x 20' is the "16' x 20' Standard Horse Package" on printed page 11 (PDF page 15); the brochure also lists several other packages inside the 240-480 sq ft target range — a 12' x 20' Storage Barn Package, the Cherokee and Cimarron Garage Packages in Standard Sizes "12' x 20' • 14' x 24' • 20' x 24' • 24' x 30'", and the 13' x 36' Traditional Loafing Shed (468 sq ft).
includes: 2 x 4 wall girts
2 x 4 roof purlins
Easy-to-build rafters (site-built rafters, NOT engineered trusses)
Treated posts (size and embedment depth not stated in the brochure; the 2025 Harrisonville flyer specifies 4x4 posts at 10 ft bay spacing for the Standard Horse Shed)
2 x 6 treated splashboard
Nails and hardware
Plans

Choice of FARMLAND (hot-dipped galvanized corrugated) or SUBURBAN (45-year limited warranty painted Metal Sales) steel roofing and siding, with color-matched roofing and siding screws — offered per the 'Available as Farmland or Suburban' banner and the Metal Sales panel page, though the 16x20 bullet list itself does not spell out roofing/siding/screws the way the 13x36 loafing shed list does
Free in-store estimate, help with sizing/placement/options, permit information and financing options; online Pole Barn Color Designer for color scheme
Installation available at select Sutherlands locations (per sutherlands.com); otherwise materials-only for DIY
pros: Cheapest published path to 320 sq ft of roofed post-frame structure that we have seen: $3,499 materials-only for the 20x16 two-bay Standard Horse Shed in Sutherlands' 2025 Harrisonville MO flyer, about $11/sq ft — a fraction of a stick-framed or precut 16x20 shed kit.

Post-frame foundation demands are minimal: embedded treated posts plus a 2x6 treated splashboard, no slab, no footings, no frost walls, no floor system. It goes up on unimproved ground with a post-hole auger, which is the single biggest cost saving versus a 16x20 on skids or a slab.

Structurally trivial to build: 10 ft bays, 2x4 girts, 2x4 purlins and site-built 'easy-to-build' rafters over a 16 ft depth. No crane, no truss setting, no sheathing, no shingles — a realistic two-person build.

Steel envelope means near-zero maintenance: SUBURBAN painted Metal Sales panels carry a 45-year limited warranty with snug-fitting sidelaps, or FARMLAND hot-dip galvanized corrugated for the cheapest rust-resistant option; color-matched screws included, colors previewable with the online Pole Barn Color Designer.

Bought through a local lumberyard rather than as a fixed online SKU: size, bay count, wall height, door openings and colors are all quotable ('OTHER OPTIONS AND SIZES AVAILABLE'; 'Sizes up to 40ft clear span and porches up to 20ft wide'), you get a free estimate, and you can walk back in for extra material mid-build.

The brochure explicitly offers an 'Engineering Wet Stamp if required' as an add-on on every post-frame item, so there is a defined route to permit-ready stamped drawings in jurisdictions that demand them.
Sutherlands offers full installation at select stores and materials-only where it doesn't, so the same package works for a DIY build or a turnkey one.

A same-family enclosed alternative is quoted from the same counter: the brochure's Suburban Post Frame garage line (engineer-designed trusses, 10'4-1/2" sidewalls, overhead + walk doors) and 3-Sided packages let you scale up to a fully enclosed post-frame shop without changing vendors.
cons: NO FLOOR IS INCLUDED. The 16x20 Standard Horse Package material list contains no skids, joists, decking or slab — the brochure photo shows bare earth. Contrast the wood-shed packages in the same brochure, which do state a floor ('Plywood floor over 4" x 4" treated skids' on the 8x8 Mini Barn; 'Wood floor over 4 x 4 skids 2" x 6" floor joist 12" o.c.' on the 12x16). A 16x20 concrete slab is entirely your cost and is not in the $3,499.

PRICE IS MATERIALS-ONLY, AND IT IS NOT ON THE TARGET PAGE. The brochure publishes no prices whatsoever. The $3,499 comes from a separate 2025 Sutherlands Harrisonville MO flyer and is labeled 'MATERIALS ONLY' with 'Delivery and tax based upon location. Customer is responsible for all permits' and 'Pricing Subject to change with market conditions' — so it is not delivered, not erected, store-specific, and stale-able.

It is an open-front, three-sided run-in shed, not a lockable building. No doors, no windows, no walk door and no overhead door appear in the package list, and the photo shows an open two-bay front with a center post. Enclosing the front (extra girts, panels, header, doors) is an unpriced change order.

Site-built rafters, not engineered trusses: the 16x20 gets 'Easy-to-build rafters' while only the bigger Suburban / Deluxe Suburban / Traditional 3-Sided packages get 'Engineer designed trusses for continuous interior space.' Nothing in the brochure gives snow, wind or roof live-load capacities for the 16 ft rafter span.

'Engineering Wet Stamp if required (not included)' — permit friendliness is conditional and costs extra. No footing depth, post embedment, concrete collar, uplift anchoring or bracing detail is published anywhere, and the flyer makes permits the customer's responsibility ('Check your local permits and building codes').

Almost no dimensions are published for this size: wall/eave heights, roof pitch, overhangs, post size and header spans are all absent for the 16x20 (the flyer adds only '10ft Wide Bays with 4x4 Post'). By comparison the brochure's 13x36 loafing shed states '8' or 10' ceilings in front' and the Suburban garage states 10'4-1/2" sidewalls. You cannot pre-check this against your code or compare it to a real plan set.

No cut list, no bill of materials, and no sample drawings. The design is generated in Sutherlands' in-house post-frame software at the counter, so you cannot price-shop the lumber list against a big-box quote or see the plans before buying.

The brochure is a 2017 document (PDF created Aug 2017) still linked as the live 'Building Guide,' and the current website/flyer product names have already moved on (Livestock Shelters, Standard Horse Sheds, Tuffy Horse Sheds, YardStar shed line). Expect brochure specs and lineup to be out of date at the counter.

Regional availability only: Sutherlands is a Midwest/Plains chain headquartered in Kansas City, packages are quoted per store, and both pricing and installation availability vary by location — outside its footprint this option simply isn't buyable.

As a workshop the layout is compromised: only ~280 sq ft is 'enclosed' per the brochure, interior girts are exposed on the inside face of the steel, and a center post stands in the middle of the 20 ft opening.

Everything reported for the 16x20 is transcribed directly from the target PDF (printed page 11 / PDF page 15) and is verbatim-checkable, and the $3,499 / 4x4 post / 10 ft bay data comes from Sutherlands' own current 2025 Harrisonville price flyer linked off sutherlands.com/post-frame-buildings. Confidence is only medium because the brochure is a marketing catalog: it publishes no drawings, no dimensions beyond nominal size, no loads, no cut list and no prices, so most engineering and cost specifics are genuinely undeterminable from the source rather than merely unfound. plans.summary: Timber Frame HQ's 16x24 King Post Plan (SKU 5322) is a $97 instant-download 33-page PDF for a two-bay, 16 ft x 24 ft (post-to-post) heavy timber frame with 2 ft overhangs on all four sides, an 8'8" tie-beam height, a 9'10" top plate and a 15'8" peak at 8/12 pitch. The set breaks down as 14 pages of construction drawings, 9 pages of detailed individual piece drawings, 3 pages of roof-pitch variations (drawings supplied for 3/12 through 12/12) and a 7-page post-and-beam conversion plan, plus a full timber list. The frame is cut from 8x stock: 8x8 posts, 8x12 tie beams (modifiable to 8x10), 8x12 or 8x10 plates and ridge, 4x10 rafters and 4x8 knee braces. It is a frame-only plan — no foundation, floor, wall enclosure, siding, window or door design is published, and Timber Frame HQ explicitly disclaims engineering, stating the buyer must obtain any structural analysis and confirm local codes.

pros: Very complete drawing package for the money: 33 pages including 9 pages of individual piece drawings, which is what actually lets a first-timer lay out mortise-and-tenon joinery.
Two-bay 16x24 frame at 384 sq ft sits right in the target size range, and the 2 ft overhangs on all four sides give real weather protection to walls and door openings.
Generous headroom: 8'8" to the tie beam and 9'10" to the top plate, so the space works as a shop or garage without feeling low.
Roof pitch is not locked in - bonus drawings cover 3/12 through 12/12, so you can match a snow load, a neighborhood aesthetic or a height restriction.

The included 7-page Post and Beam Conversion Plan is a genuine escape hatch: you can build the same geometry with bolted/fastener connections instead of cutting traditional joinery, and Timber Frame HQ sells a matching 16x24 King Post Post-and-Beam Fastener Kit ($1,197).
Flexible finishing - the same frame is sold as an open pavilion, a cabin, a garage or a shop, so you can enclose it or leave it open.
A full timber list is included, so material takeoff is done for you (the companion CNC kit quotes 2,843 board feet of #1 Douglas Fir for this exact frame, a useful cross-check).
Stated 30-day, no-reason, full-refund guarantee on individual plan purchases.
Well-trodden design: 3 published customer reviews (4/5, 5/5, 5/5) and the frame is also offered as a factory kit, so the geometry has been cut before.
cons: Frame only. No foundation design, floor framing, wall enclosure/infill, siding, roofing, window or door details are published on the page - you must design or source all of that separately.

Not engineered or stamped. The page states flatly that the purchaser is responsible for obtaining "any and all structural analysis, engineering and specifications that may be required" and for verifying all measurements, so permit offices in snow/wind/seismic jurisdictions will likely require a local engineer's review at extra cost.

Heavy timber is the real cost and logistics driver: ~2,843 board feet of 8x8, 8x12, 4x10 and 4x8 stock. An 8x12 tie beam 16+ ft long is a two-or-more-person, often machine-assisted lift - you will need a crane, telehandler or a raising crew.
Cutting 8x mortise-and-tenon joinery demands tools most shed builders do not own (large chain mortiser or heavy drill/chisel setup, beam saw, big framing chisels) and a flat deck to lay out bents.
The page bills it as "a great starting project" but that means starting-level for a timber framer, not for someone whose last project was a 2x4 shed.
Comparable frame cost is high if you do not mill your own: the CNC-cut kit version of this same frame lists at $23,750 plus shipping.
No loft or second floor is shown - the tie beams sit at 8'8" and no loft floor framing is published, so storage over the bays is not part of the design.
The full timber list is only inside the purchased PDF; the page publishes headline timber sizes but no lengths or piece counts, so you cannot price the job before buying.
License is restrictive: build once, personal use only, no modifications, no derivative works, no commercial use.
Product page lists a "Instant Download + Printed Set" purchase option but no price is published for the printed set.
Site is behind Cloudflare and blocks scripted access; you may need a normal browser to buy.

Minor nuance the record glosses: that arithmetic sums to 33 with no page left over for the timber list, so the "Full timber list" (a Description bullet) must live inside the 14 construction pages rather than being a separate sheet — contrast the sibling 16x18 plan, whose spec tab explicitly itemises "Timber List - 1 page". plans.summary: A DIY pre-cut lumber kit (not a plan) for a 12 ft wide gable garage in 16, 20 or 24 ft lengths, sold by Shed Kit Store and made by Best Barns. Walls are 2x4 framed at 24" o.c. with 8'1" sidewalls and a rough 8' x 7' garage-door opening; the kit ships with LP SmartSide primed siding, 7/16" OSB roof sheathing, pre-built-on-site "SecureTruss" 2x4 trusses with gussets, collar ties and H1 hurricane hangers, and all framing nails/screws. Deliberately incomplete by design: garage door, walk-in door, windows, shingles/metal roofing, drip edge, paint and the floor are all separate purchases, and a concrete slab or the optional $1,358 FortressFloor wood deck is required. The full 21-page illustrated owner's manual — including a complete packing list and the optional wood-floor framing detail — is a free public PDF download, so you can see exactly what you get before buying.
includes: Pre-cut 2x4 wall studs (42 pcs on the 12x20) and 2x4/2x8 wall plates, tie plates and 2x8-10' door header
Pre-cut 2x4 truss rafters (18 @ 80-1/2"), collar ties (7 @ 82"), 7/16" truss gussets (14 @ 8"x16") and 14 H1 metal truss hangers
14 pcs 4x8 LP SmartSide primed exterior siding panels plus cut gable/filler siding pieces
4 pcs 4x8 7/16" OSB roof sheathing plus cut sheathing pieces (48"x81-1/4", 48"x72", 36-1/2" sizes)
1x3 / 1x4 corner trim, gable trim, side-wall fascia, soffit panels and soffit fillers
All framing fasteners: 10d sinkers, 6d galv. and common, 16d galv., hanger nails, 100 ea. 1-1/2" exterior screws, 125 ea. 2-1/2" deck screws
'Z' flashing, metal plates, 1x6 keystone, 3/8" door jambs
21-page illustrated Assembly Book / Owner's Manual (free PDF download)
Free freight shipping to the contiguous 48 states, curbside with liftgate
Rough 8' x 7' garage door opening framed and trimmed (door itself NOT included)
pros: Real 12 ft clear span with 8'1" sidewalls — no interior posts, and tall enough to hang a garage door or work overhead; the 6/12 gable gives usable attic space even without the loft option.

Structure is genuinely engineered-ish for weather: SecureTruss 2x4 trusses with gussets, collar ties, tie plates, two-stud corners and 14 H1 hurricane hangers; Best Barns claims up to 130 mph wind on select models and 40 lb/sq ft snow on the majority of its trusses.
The complete 21-page manual with the full packing list is a free public PDF, so you can audit exactly what lumber arrives and how it goes together before spending a dollar.

Pre-cut studs, rafters and gussets remove most of the layout and cutting work — Best Barns says 2-3 people finish assembly in 2-3 days once the floor is level and square, with no specialty tools (drill, hammer, saw, level, square, ladder).
LP SmartSide engineered siding treated against insects and fungal decay, primed and ready for paint — a step above T1-11 on a typical big-box kit.
Cost control: you only buy the shell. The prep-for-vinyl version is $630 CHEAPER than standard on the 12x20 if you already plan to side it yourself.
Free shipping to the lower 48 and a documented 30-day no-cost replacement for damaged, defective or sub-standard lumber.
cons: Not 16 ft wide despite the '16ft-20ft-24ft' page title — 12 ft is the only width, so the biggest option (12x24, 288 sq ft) is still well short of the 320 sq ft the user wanted, and a 12 ft wide bay is tight for a car plus workbench.

The kit is far from turnkey: garage door, walk-in door, windows, shingles/metal roofing, drip edge, roofing nails, paint, Class 25 sealant and the floor are all extra. Realistic finished cost is well above the $3,879 shell price.
Foundation is on you — a concrete slab or the $1,358 FortressFloor wood deck (3/4" plywood, PT 2x4 joists 12" o.c. on PT 4x4 runners) is required, and the pad must be exactly 12'-0" x 20'-0".

The manual's packing list has a separate 'Material Supplied by Local Supplier' table (42 pre-cut wall studs, 4x 2x4-10' plates, 6x 2x4-12', treated plates, 2x8-10' header, 14 pcs 4x8 siding, 4 pcs OSB, nails) — verify with the seller which of those actually ship versus which you source, because it materially changes the price.

No stamped engineering, sealed drawings or load calculations are published for this specific model; wind/snow numbers are hedged ('select models', 'majority of our roof trusses'), which can be a problem for a permit office on a 240-288 sq ft structure.
Loft ('Tall') option adds $1,770 on the 12x20 and switches the roof to a steeper 10/12, and the loft is only 8' wide with 4'3" max headroom — with NO ladder or stairs included.
Siding must be painted with exterior acrylic latex within 30 days of construction or you risk the finish/warranty.
Curbside-only freight on ~2 pallets (typ. 4' x 7' x 30", ~1,300 lb) — you must move it up the driveway yourself, and returns carry a 25% restocking fee plus both-way freight.

plans.doors: Base kit frames and trims a rough 8' wide x 7' high garage door opening (2x8-10' header, 99" long) but the garage door itself must be purchased separately. Optional 8' wide x 7' high transom (carriage-style with transom windows) doors add roughly $600-$650 depending on size. Optional walk-in doors: 6-Panel Steel (hinged left or right) +$285; 9-Lite Steel (hinged left or right) +$400. Galvanized door sill included for use with the optional floor.
plans.loft: Optional on the "Tall" style only (+$1,770 on the 12x20): 8' wide loft running the full length of the building, 4'3" maximum headroom, and the roof pitch increases to 10/12. Explicitly "no ladder or steps included."
plans.skill_level: Beginner-to-intermediate DIY. Manufacturer: "No specialty tools are needed. The most common tools needed are a drill, ladder, hammer, saw, tape measure, pencil, safety glasses, square and 6' level." Also required per the manual: dust mask, screwdriver with bits, framing square, 6'-8' ladders. Kits ship with loose nails for hand framing (nail-gun nails must be bought separately) and "depending on the model and accessories ordered some cutting may be required."
plans.build_time: "Once the floor is complete, level and square, it typically takes 2-3 people about 2-3 days to complete. Individual skill and size of kit will affect these times." Ships 5-7 days after order.
plans.permit_notes: Manual's first instruction: "Always check with your local HOA or building code office for any requirements or restrictions." No stamped/sealed engineering, sealed drawings or model-specific load table is published for this model. Manufacturer-wide claims are hedged: "Select models provide a 130-mph wind load" and "The majority of our roof trusses provide a 40 lb. snow load capability per square foot. Review the specifications for each model." At 240-288 sq ft this building is above the common 200 sq ft permit-exempt threshold in many jurisdictions, and a Best Barns customer review on the manufacturer's own site mentions "still working to obtain a permit." Expect to submit the manual plus your own slab detail; there is nothing here an engineer has signed.

plans.summary:
A factory-built, fully enclosed 16 x 20 ft steel garage from Eagle Carports (SKU-FB209), 8 ft eave height, with a "vertical" A-frame roof — the strongest of Eagle's three roof styles because the panels run down the slope so water and snow shed off rather than sitting across the ribs. The frame is 14-gauge galvanized steel tube, typically 2.5" square, using Eagle's bent tubular "bow" trusses (used on their 12–24 ft wide buildings) with a peak brace, so the 16 ft width is clear-span with no interior posts. Skin is 29-gauge steel AG panel with 3/4" ribs 9" on center, Rawhide sides/ends with Barn Red roof and trim, finished with a Beckers paint system carrying a 20-year chalk-and-fade warranty. The base configuration already includes two 6' x 7' roll-up garage doors and one 36" x 80" walk-in door — Eagle labels it "2 Car."

Critically, this is not a DIY plan set or a shipped box of parts you assemble. Eagle's published process is: order through a dealer with a down payment, factory fabrication, then delivery and erection by an Eagle subcontractor crew, with the final balance "collected immediately upon installation." Installation takes "between one hour to two days"; typical lead time is 8–10 weeks. NO FLOOR AND NO FOUNDATION ARE INCLUDED — you provide a level surface (bare ground, asphalt, or a concrete pad you pour yourself), and the site must be within 3" of level or you incur cut-leg, extra-labor, or return-trip fees ($150 or 5% of the building price, whichever is higher). For someone targeting ~320 sq ft, this is the "skip the framing entirely" option: fast, weatherproof, low-maintenance, clear-span — at the cost of no plans, no DIY, a bare uninsulated shell, and a slab you still have to buy.
includes: Steel frame: 14 gauge galvanized steel, typically 2.5" square tube, with bent tubular 'bow' trusses (Eagle uses bows on 12–24 ft wide structures) plus peak brace, legs, leg braces, base rail and end-wall posts
Vertical roof: 29 gauge steel AG panel, 3/4" tall ribs 9" OC, on hat channel, Barn Red
Fully enclosed sides and ends (Sides/Ends: Color Match), Rawhide color, 29 gauge steel panel
Barn Red trim (L-trim / J-trim around openings)
Two 6' x 7' roll-up sheet-metal garage doors (shown side by side on the 16 ft gable end)
One 36" x 80" walk-in door — per Eagle's glossary, fiberglass and foam core in an aluminum frame with a 10"x10" window and a locking doorknob (no deadbolt available)
Beckers paint system with a 20 year chalk & fade warranty on painted sheet metal
Delivery and on-site erection by an Eagle subcontractor installation crew (per the site's How It Works and FAQ pages; the product page itself does not restate this)
Interactive 3D model of the building ('Open in 3D', build.eaglecarports.com)
90 day workmanship guarantee after installation
pros: Zero framing skill needed: Eagle's subcontracted crew delivers and erects the whole building, typically in "one hour to two days." No cutting, no crew of friends, no rented tools, no weekend-eating multi-month build like the DIY 16x20 plan sets it competes with.

True clear span: the bent tubular bow truss carries the full 16 ft with no interior posts or bearing wall, so all 320 sq ft is usable open floor — better than a post-frame or center-bearing stick-built shed of the same footprint.
Doors are already in the base spec — two 6' x 7' roll-ups plus a 36" x 80" walk-in — which on most DIY builds is $1,500–$3,000 of separate purchases and the fussiest part of the job.

Vertical roof is the right upgrade to take: panels run down the slope so snow and water shed instead of pooling across the ribs, and Eagle's own warranty language ties the 20-year paint coverage to having a vertical roof (buildings 31 ft+ with regular or boxed-eave roofs lose it entirely).

Heavier frame than entry-level metal carports: 14 gauge galvanized 2.5" square tube rather than the thinner 12/14 ga hybrid frames often used at this price point, and galvanizing means no rot, no repainting, no shingle replacement.
Very low maintenance and permanent-feeling for the money: warranty just asks you to keep it clean of leaves/debris and wash it roughly every 6 months.

Site-specific load engineering is part of the process — Eagle publishes a Wind & Snow Ratings tool and tells you to pull your own ASCE 7 Risk Category I wind and snow numbers and share the report with your dealer before ordering, so the building is spec'd to your actual loads rather than a generic rating.
Buying friction is low: instant-quote form, 3D configurator, dealer network, sales-tax lookup, financing and rent-to-own are all offered on-site.
Faster than a self-build even including lead time — 8 to 10 weeks from order to a finished, lockable, weathertight 320 sq ft building.
cons: NO FLOOR IS INCLUDED. The price buys frame, panels, doors and trim only. You supply the surface — bare ground, asphalt, or a concrete slab you pour and pay for separately. Nowhere on the page is a floor, slab, or slab cost mentioned or quoted. For a workshop or anything heated, budget a 4" concrete pad on top of the building price.

NO FOUNDATION IS INCLUDED EITHER. Anchoring is to whatever you provide (Eagle's glossary shows asphalt anchors 'used in asphalt installations only'); the specific anchor type shipped with this model is not stated. The FAQ requires the pad be "at least 2” wider on all sides of the frame" and the site to be within 3" of level, or you pay cut-leg fees, extra labor, or a return-trip fee of "$150 USD or %5 of the building price whichever is higher."

THE PRICE IS NOT PUBLISHED ON THE PAGE. $7,062 exists only in the page's Schema.org Offer and Google Tag Manager dataLayer; the visible page routes you to an "instant quote" lead form and a dealer. Treat $7,062 as an unconfirmed base figure, not a quote.

WHAT THE PRICE COVERS IS NEVER STATED ON THE PRODUCT PAGE. Based on Eagle's How It Works and FAQ pages (delivery and installation by subcontractor, "final balance is collected immediately upon installation") it should be a delivered-and-installed price, not kit-only — but the product page does not say so, and taxes, permits, site prep, and additional options are clearly extra.

It is NOT a DIY kit and NOT a plan set. No drawings, cut list, bill of materials, or assembly instructions are published; you cannot legally self-erect it and keep coverage, because "ANY alterations, by anyone other than Subcontractor approved by Seller, VOIDS ALL WARRANTIES on the purchased unit."

Workmanship warranty is only 90 days after installation. Only the painted sheet metal gets 20 years; no structural/frame warranty term is published, and Eagle states it "is not liable for any damages as a result of inclement weather."

Bare, uninsulated shell: no insulation, vapor barrier, interior lining, electrical, or windows in the base spec. Insulation (double bubble foil or 2" fiberglass) and windows (24"x30" or 30"x36" single-pane aluminum) are paid add-ons, and condensation dripping off bare 29 ga steel over a slab is a real workshop problem.
29 gauge steel is the thinnest common panel gauge — expect dents from hail and ladders, and screw-hole gasket maintenance over the years.

"2 Car" is generous marketing. Two 6 ft roll-up doors on a 16 ft wide end wall means two very narrow 20 ft deep bays. Realistically it is one vehicle plus workshop/storage, and an 8 ft eave with 6'x7' doors rules out tall trucks, a lift, or any loft (no loft is offered).

Permit friendliness is unaddressed. The page says nothing about permits, code compliance, engineer-sealed drawings, or a certified/engineered version. A 320 sq ft garage usually needs a permit; Eagle only publishes a 'look up your own ASCE 7 wind and snow loads and send them to your dealer' workflow, so ask a dealer explicitly whether stamped drawings are available for your jurisdiction.

Geographically limited: the site pops a modal for ZIP codes "outside our coverage area," and the install crew tows a 30–36 ft trailer, so "maneuvering into small, narrow, or steep driveways may not be possible."
No refund, cancellation, or deposit-return policy is published anywhere on the page or the warranties page — only the warranty terms.

Thin selection at this footprint: only two 16 ft wide garages are cataloged (16x20 and 16x25) out of 153 metal garages, so if you want a different door layout or eave height at 16 ft wide you are into custom-order territory.

plans.summary: A factory-direct bolt-together steel arch building kit, 16' W x 20' L x 11' H (320 sq ft), sold on sale at $3,710 (down from $5,161). This is not a wood shed and not a plan set — it is a shipped/pickup kit of continuous 22-gauge corrugated steel arch panels that form roof and walls in one, plus all fasteners, bolts, washers, screws and an instruction manual. The arch is clear-span (no interior posts) and carries a 35-year warranty. As priced it is an OPEN-ENDED shell: the product bullets say "Open End Arch Construction," and end walls, walk-in doors and windows are separately configured/priced options on the site's ZIP-gated configurator. No floor and no foundation are included — the vendor's FAQ says these buildings are installed on a concrete slab or engineered foundation, and the configurator says "For best results, buildings should be installed on a concrete footer." The sale price is strictly factory-pickup or in-North-Carolina delivery; anywhere else requires a freight quote. Buildings ship with "factory generic plans"; stamped engineered drawings for a permit are a paid add-on. Compared with a wood-framed 16x20 shed, this trades framing labor and design flexibility for a very fast bolt-up (vendor claims hours, not days), an unfinishable curved interior, and a hard dependency on a poured concrete footer.

plans.summary: An 8-page 1935 University of Minnesota Agricultural Extension bulletin that is a master index to roughly 230 numbered farm building blueprints (plan numbers run 101-333) prepared by UMN's Division of Agricultural Engineering. Each line gives a plan number, a footprint size, and a one-line program description, grouped by building type: Houses, Barns (beef, bull, feeding, general purpose, horse, sheep, plus stalls, stanchions, types of roofs, ventilation), Corn Cribs & Granaries, Farmsteads, Garages, Hog Houses, Ice Houses, Machine Sheds, Milk Houses, Potato Warehouses, Poultry Houses, Privies, Roadside Markets, Septic Tank, Shops & Garages, Silos, Smoke House, Storage Cellars, and a two-column Miscellaneous list of shop fixtures and how-to sheets. The bulletin also contains a farmstead layout diagram (FARMSTEAD-PLAN 221, nine numbered buildings), a 10-point "Essentials of a Good Farmstead" siting checklist, and the 1935 ordering terms (10 cents per blueprint). Critically, none of the actual drawings are included in this PDF or attached to the Conservancy item — it is a bibliography of plans, not a buildable plan set, and the 1935 ordering address is defunct. For a 16x20 DIY shed builder its value is (a) locating specific archival sheet numbers to chase (266 = 16x20, 311 = 16x18 shop/garage, 301 = 20x24 machine shed, 168 = 16x24 granary), (b) the roof-type and studding-height vocabulary, and (c) still-valid farmstead siting advice. UMN itself flags the document as archival and possibly out of date.

cons: INDEX ONLY - the bulletin contains no drawings, no dimensions beyond the footprint, no framing sizes, no spans, no cut list. Nothing here can be built from.

1935 vintage with no engineering content: no snow or wind loads, no anchoring, bracing or shear detail, no pressure-treated lumber, no modern code references. UMN itself states 'This archival publication may not reflect current scientific knowledge or recommendations.' Not permit-ready anywhere.
No wall heights except sporadic 'Studding 8/9/12 ft.' notes, no roof pitches, and no foundation information for any listed building

Program mismatch: the great majority of entries are working agricultural buildings (barns to 34x80, potato warehouses to 40x100, a 20x180 poultry house). Only about a dozen listed plans fall in the 240-480 sq ft range.
The single 16x20 entry (plan 266) is a poultry brooder house with a cool room; its window, vent and partition layout would need heavy rework to serve as a workshop or storage shed
OCR text layer is noisy - plan numbers appear as ']31', '?.57', 'ISS', '1<14' and similar - so several index lines have to be read from the rendered page image rather than the text layer
No cost data, no materials quantities, no sqft figures, and no modern equivalent pricing, so it cannot be compared on cost against current plan sets or kits
The Conservancy landing page 403s to scripted requests; only the direct bitstream URL fetches cleanly, which makes citing/browsing the record awkward

plans.summary: A 19-episode weekly vlog series in which one builder (Ty) puts up a 16 x 24 ft post-and-beam workshop on a homestead property on the southern Oregon coast, from grading a gravel pad through connecting power and lighting a pellet stove inside. The structural sequence is tight and self-contained in the first seven episodes: grade and compact a gravel base, set built-up 6x6 skids, frame joists and a sheathed deck, stand 4x4 posts with a top beam and horizontal nailers, frame window openings and a loft, build a site-cut rafter roof with purlins, hang vertical mahogany board-and-batten siding, screw down metal roofing and ridge cap, then stain. Later episodes cover sourcing reclaimed vintage farm windows from an Etsy vendor and installing them, painting the shop door, running electrical service to the shop, and heating it. There are no plans, no materials list and no dimensioned drawings published anywhere — the descriptions are narrative plus hashtag walls, so this is a "watch how it was sequenced" resource, not a buildable document.
includes: Site grading and a compacted gravel base pad (ep 1)
Built-up 6x6 skid foundation set on the gravel — no concrete (ep 1-2)
Floor joists and sheathed deck over the skids (ep 2)
4x4 post-and-beam wall frame with horizontal nailers/girts (ep 3)
Window rough-opening framing (ep 3)
Loft framing, started ep 3 and finished ep 4
Site-built gable rafter roof structure with purlins over the rafters (ep 4)
Vertical mahogany board-and-batten siding, boards then battens (ep 4-6)
Exposed-fastener metal roofing plus ridge cap (ep 5-6)
Exterior stain — Cabot Australian Timber Oil per hashtags (ep 7)
Sourcing and unboxing reclaimed vintage farm windows from an Etsy seller (ep 9)
Vintage farm window installation across three episodes (ep 11, 12, 13)
Shop door painting (ep 10)
Connecting electrical power to the finished workshop (ep 18)
Heating the shop — pellet stove running against plywood-lined interior walls (ep 19)
NOT included: no plans, no materials list, no cut list, no dimensioned drawings, no span or load calcs
pros: Genuinely start-to-finish for a 384 sq ft building: gravel pad, skids, deck, walls, loft, rafters, metal roof, siding, stain, windows, power and heat all appear in publish order, which is more of the arc than most shed videos show.
Skid-on-gravel foundation is the cheapest, fastest 16x24 base a solo builder can do — no concrete, no forms, no frost footings, no rebar, and no concrete delivery to a remote site.
4x4 post-and-beam walls with horizontal nailers use far less lumber and far fewer pieces than 16 in. o.c. stud walls, and can be stood one piece at a time by one person.
A loft over the 16 ft dimension is framed on camera (ep 3-4) — rare in DIY shed video series, and it is what makes this a shop-plus-storage building rather than just a shed.
Reclaimed-window sourcing is shown end to end and the vendor is actually named (Carolina Farm Decor on Etsy), a real cost lever most plan sets ignore entirely.
Episodes are a watchable 8-29 minutes, shot outdoors in daylight with the builder narrating each step; the footage is usable for understanding sequencing and order of operations.
Completely free — no paywall, no email capture, no plan upsell, no affiliate gate on the build content itself.
Uses stock-length dimensional lumber and a simple rectangle, so nothing about the design requires a lumberyard special order or a crane.
cons: No plans, no materials list and no cut list anywhere in the descriptions — you cannot order lumber or price this build from the series. This is the single biggest limitation.

The numbers you need are never published in text: wall height, overall height, roof pitch, rafter size and spacing, joist size and spacing, post spacing, header sizes, loft joist size. You would be freeze-framing and guessing.

Nothing is engineered. Rafters are site-cut (no engineered trusses, no stamped truss drawings), and a 16 ft span that also carries a loft is precisely where an owner-designed frame most needs a professional check for snow/wind load.

Built-up 6x6 skids on gravel is not an accepted permanent foundation in most permit jurisdictions at 384 sq ft; the series says nothing at all about permits, setbacks, inspections or how the building was classified.
Cost drivers here are unusual and expensive: mahogany siding and reclaimed wood windows. No dollar figures are given at any point, so the series gives you no budget baseline.

The playlist is padded — roughly 7 of the 19 episodes are unrelated homestead vlog content (asbestos abatement in the old house, a separate 12 x 16 art studio, a tractor-port, a snowstorm, harvesting a Christmas tree). The actual 16x24 build is about 12 episodes.

Vlog pacing rather than tutorial pacing: the camera frequently shows a completed step instead of the joinery or fastening detail, and there are multi-week gaps (Dec 2022 to Feb 2023) where work happened off camera.
Interior work is essentially skipped. Insulation, interior finish and flooring are never a topic; the plywood wall lining only appears incidentally behind the pellet stove in the final episode.
Very small channel (1.57K subscribers, ~2.3K playlist views), so there is no large comment thread to mine for the dimensions and details the videos omit.

Post-and-beam walls with nailers instead of studs are simple to erect but constrain later work — no continuous stud bays for standard insulation batts or easy drywall, which matters if you ever want to heat and finish the shop.

plans.summary: BarnPlans sells engineered blueprint sets for a two-story gambrel barn shell; the Barn House variant is the residential/flex-use version and starts at 16'x24' for $275. The signature feature is a clear-span, site-built engineered gambrel truss: the plans include a step-by-step jig layout so the builder assembles the trusses on the loft floor, and the result carries the roof to the side walls so the entire second floor is free of posts and load-bearing walls. What you buy is the shell only — foundation/slab through roof, including second-floor joists and stairs — with no floor plan, door/window layout, or interior finish; you design those yourself. Sets ship as 7 to 15 printed 36"x24" ("D" size) AutoCAD black-line sheets by 3-day USPS Priority Mail, not as a PDF download.

Roofing shown on the plans is wood or fiberglass shingles; the FAQ says metal roofing is a good substitute in snow country. pros: True clear-span engineered gambrel truss: the 16'-wide truss gives a 15'-5" post-free, bearing-wall-free upstairs, so every interior partition you add is non-load-bearing and the floor plan is entirely yours.

The 16x24 shell yields a genuine second floor, not a crawl-in attic — 7'-6 15/16" peak headroom with 6' of standing height starting 4'-6 1/2" in from each side wall, i.e. roughly 384 sq ft down plus a usable 384 sq ft up.

Real engineering behind it, and the site tells you against what: 2003 IBC plus CA seismic, WA snow and Hawaii hurricane criteria, with named licensed structural/professional engineers on staff — a meaningful advantage over anonymous internet shed plans when you walk into a permit office.

Trusses are designed to be site-built by the owner from dimensional lumber in a jig you assemble on the loft floor, with step-by-step layout instructions — no truss-company order, no crane-only delivery, and a large cost saving versus ordered attic trusses.
Cheap for what it is: $275 for 7-15 D-size engineered sheets, and the same set covers any length (2' increments), so you are not locked into 24'.

Detail-heavy, contractor-praised sheet set: dozens of details for foundation/slab, wall, door and window framing, second-floor joists and stairs — the page carries many testimonials from estimators, plan reviewers and construction managers about the level of detail.

Deep accessory ecosystem drawn to match the same roof geometry — 4' gambrel dormer ($75), side entry ($95), shed roof/lean-to ($85), covered deck ($95), bi-fold doors ($45), cupola ($55) — so customizing does not mean freelancing the structure.

Long track record and live human support: in business since 1997, 7,000+ plan sets sold, a large photo showcase of finished builds, and an explicit promise of phone/e-mail help "through every phase of construction."
cons: It is a SHELL plan only — no floor plan, no door/window layout, no electrical, plumbing, mechanical, insulation or interior finish. If you want to live in it you must design (and likely have drawn/approved) all of that yourself. The FAQ is blunt: "we give you the plans to build the basic 'Barn Shell' from foundation to roof including stairs and second floor."

A steel-reinforced concrete foundation and slab is mandatory — no skid, pier, or pole-barn option. That is a big cost, excavation and inspection burden for a 320-400 sq ft outbuilding, and it rules out an easily-relocatable shed.

No materials or cut list is published anywhere on the site; you must e-mail and ask for one, and it only covers the basic shell with a half loft. Nothing can be captured or priced out locally before you buy.
Paper only, shipped by mail on a Tuesday/Friday print schedule with 3-day Priority — no instant PDF download, so there is a multi-day lag and no easy reprinting or on-screen zoom.
Strictly no refunds. You cannot flip through the plan set before committing, and 'all sales are final' means the $275 is spent even if your jurisdiction rejects the approach.

The published code basis is 2003 IBC, which is several cycles old. The site does not say whether a stamped/sealed calculation package for your specific state, snow load or wind zone is included, so a plan reviewer may still send you to a local engineer.

Building your own trusses is the whole value proposition and also the whole risk: layout accuracy, plate/gusset nailing and safely standing 16' gambrel trusses on a second-floor deck is real work, and any deviation from the jig undermines the engineering.

Gambrel geometry costs you at the walls — headroom drops to 5'-5 1/4" at the pitch break and full 6' clearance does not start until 4'-6 1/2" inboard, so the outer ~4.5 ft per side of the 16'-wide loft is storage or low furniture only.

The smallest Barn House is 16x24 (384 sq ft); there is nothing between the 12x16 Minibarn and this, so a builder aiming at exactly 16x20 has to shorten the barn themselves (allowed, but the published price/sheets assume 24').

Two-story construction on a slab, plus stairs, plus site-built trusses, is materially harder and more expensive than a single-story 16x20 shed — expect $5,760-$7,680 in shell materials by the vendor's own $15-$20/sq ft footprint estimate, before doors, windows or any finish.

"Sets ship as ... printed 36\"x24\" ... black-line sheets by 3-day USPS Priority Mail, not as a PDF download." The "not as a PDF download" half is an inference. plans.summary: This is a pre-engineered DIY steel building kit, not a plan set — you buy parts, not drawings. VersaTube ships pre-cut 2"x3" 14/15-gauge galvanized steel tubing with patented "Slip-Fit" connections that need no insert tubes, plus 26 sheet-metal panels in 29 gauge, trim, anchors, hardware and printed instructions, in two separate shipments (frame from VersaTube, panels/trim direct from the sheet-metal supplier). Freight to a residence is included in the $5,872 price. The 16x21x9 model has a 3:12 gable at 11'0" peak, 9' sidewalls, trusses at 5' on center with a King brace, and is rated to 25 PSF roof / up to 41.3 PSF ground snow / up to 115 MPH wind; a 36"x80" walk-door frame kit is included and an 8'x8' garage-door frame opening is standard in one gable end. Critically, all openings are FRAMES only — the actual overhead door, walk door, windows, concrete slab and any insulation or interior finish are on you.
includes: Pre-cut 2" x 3" 14 & 15 gauge galvanized steel tube frame with patented Slip-Fit connections (no insert tubes or extra screws needed)
Roof purlins for vertical sheet metal application (no side girts required in the Frontier design)
26 sheet metal panels, 29 gauge American 5-rib profile, 36" wide: 8'6" (102") roof panels, 15'2" (182") and 6'2" (74") eave side panels
Trim, in the sheet-metal shipment
Anchors (rebar anchors for ground, or concrete wedge anchor bolts for slab/footing - selected at checkout)
Printed assembly instructions
One (1) Universal Walk Door Frame Kit - listed as 'Included in selected model'; frames a 36"W x 80"H door opening between two trusses on an eave side
One 8' x 8' garage door FRAME opening, default in the front wall (can be moved to the back wall for +$31, or the wall fully enclosed for -$31)

Choice of wall / roof / trim colors from 13 options (Ash Gray, Burnished Slate, Dark Blue, Brown, Galvalume, Light Blue, Black, Charcoal, Gray, Green, Koko Brown, Stone, Red, Tan, White) - mix-and-match beyond the 10 preset pairings carries additional fees
Freight to your residence or business ('SHIPPING INCLUDED'); frame ships in 5 business days
King truss brace
20-year limited frame warranty + product pledge; 20-year paint finish warranty on sheet metal
A model-specific assembly video: 'Frontier Garage 16x21x9 5OC 2x3' (youtube.com/watch?v=bjj2UkRSjF8)
pros: Pre-engineered and load-rated - the page publishes 25 PSF roof / up to 41.3 PSF ground snow / up to 115 MPH wind, which is far more than any free lumber shed plan gives you. No truss design or span calc on your part.
5' on-center truss spacing over a clear 16' span gives a genuinely open interior with no interior posts - hard to match in stick framing without engineered trusses or a ridge beam.
Slip-Fit tube connections mean no cutting, no notching, and no framing skill. VersaTube states the kit assembles with 'common household tools' and does not require renting special tools or equipment.
9' sidewalls with approx. 8'11-1/4" ground-to-truss-brace clearance - real headroom for a lift-free workshop, a tall truck, or overhead storage racks, which a typical 8' shed wall does not give.
Freight is included in the price, a large hidden cost with 1,100+ lb steel kits.

Very flexible foundation: 'can be anchored to almost any level surface from ground, gravel, asphalt or boat docks to concrete slab, footings, curb sections or piers to on top of stem or retaining walls'. You can skip a slab entirely and anchor into backfilled post holes with the supplied rebar anchors.
Steel + 29-ga metal skin means no rot, no repainting, no sheathing, and a 20-year frame warranty.
There is an assembly video made for this exact size/configuration ('Frontier Garage 16x21x9 5OC 2x3'), not a generic one.
Fast to erect: the FAQ says for buildings/garages this size you should get the frame up in one day and the sheet metal on the next.
Expandable later - Slip-Fit lets you add length by adding base rails and truss sections.
cons: Not a plan - $5,872 buys materials, and there is no published bill of materials, cut list, or dimensioned drawing on the page. You cannot price-shop it or source it locally, and you cannot review the design before buying.

No stamped engineering is offered on the page, and the ratings carry a hard disclaimer: 'Wind and snow ratings provided are for reference only... Conformance to local codes is the responsibility of the purchaser.' If your AHJ wants sealed drawings you must call VersaTube.

Permit trap: 'If permitting is required by your city/county, truss bracing is mandatory' - so the price you see may not be the price you can legally build, and the truss brace kit is a separate accessory line.
41.3 PSF ground snow is modest. Anywhere with real snow load you are pushed into optional extra interior truss bracing and 26-gauge metal, priced only by phone.

Openings are frames only. No overhead door, no walk door, no window units, no glazing. Budget roughly $700-1,500+ on top for an 8x8 sectional door plus a steel entry door - the page never mentions this cost.

No floor, no slab, no insulation, no vapor barrier, no interior finish. Metal-skinned steel frames sweat badly; one published customer review mentions insulation whose 'assembly orientation' was not covered in the instructions.
Uninsulated 29-ga metal over steel tube is a poor shell if you want a conditioned workshop - furring out and insulating a tube frame is much more work than filling stud bays.

Two (in practice sometimes three) separate shipments. A published customer review: 'Materials were in 3 different shipments that spanned 3 weeks. Did not like that.' Another: 'Ran out of screws. Had to buy another big bag of screws to finish.'

Warranty is conditional on speed: 'The completed frame structure with sheet metal and trim must be erected within thirty (30) days of the date of delivery to retain warranty eligibility.' That is a real constraint for a weekend-only builder.
Brutal returns: 15-day window, customer pays all return freight on a 1,100 lb palletized kit, plus a 35% restocking fee. On $5,872 that is ~$2,055 in restocking alone.
16'W x 21'L is a 336 sq ft footprint that exceeds the common 200-sq-ft permit exemption, and the 8'x8' door plus 9' walls will read as a garage, not a shed, to most zoning officials.
Hanging shelves, cabinets, or a hoist off 2x3 tubing at 5' o.c. is fussier than into wood studs.
Interior is 336 sq ft nominal but the frame is the outside dimension, so usable width is under 16'.

plans.foundation: No foundation included and none required. "Our DIY kits can be anchored to almost any level surface from ground, gravel, asphalt or boat docks to concrete slab, footings, curb sections or piers to on top of stem or retaining walls to raise the structure." Ground anchoring uses VersaTube rebar anchors centered in post holes and backfilled with concrete; slab or footing anchoring uses concrete wedge anchor bolts. Anchors are provided with the kit and the type is selected before checkout. A slab is optional (the hero render shows a concrete apron/slab).

plans.wall_framing: 2" x 3" 14 and 15 gauge galvanized domestic steel tubing, triple-coat corrosion protection, mandrel-bent. Trusses/bents at 5' on center over the 16' clear span with a "King" truss brace. Patented pre-cut Slip-Fit frame connections - "No insert tubes and extra screws are required." Frontier design uses roof purlins but "no side girts are required." Optional additional interior truss bracing for higher snow/wind loads (mandatory if you permit). plans.doors: Frame openings only - no door leaves, slabs or overhead door hardware are supplied. plans.loft: none - no loft, mezzanine or attic storage is offered or framed for. Interior clear height under the truss brace is approx. 8'11-1/4".

VERIFIED CORRECT (checked character-by-character against Wayback 20260908042358):
- PRICE $5,872 — confirmed three times in the rendered page and in the embedded JSON "unitPrice":{"value":587200,"currency":"USD"}. price_usd 5872 correct.
- 2024 comparison — the 20240301173154 snapshot really does show "Regular Price:" $5,674 / "Special Price" $5,385 with "unitPrice":{"value":538500}. 5872/5385 = +9.0%, so "~9%" is right.
- Spec table verbatim: Erected Size 16'W x 21'L x 9'H; Roof Pitch 3:12; Sheet Metal Coverage "Roof coverage is 21'2\""; Side Wall Height 9'; Peak Height 11'0"; On Center Spacing 5'; Truss Brace Description King; Ground-to-Truss Brace Clearance 8' 11-1/4"; Walk Door Opening Size 36"W x 80"H; Special Note On Frame Length "Actual frame length is 21' long with 5' on center truss spacing"; Steel Frame 2"x3" 14 & 15 gauge galvanized; Ground/Roof/Wind "41.3PSF Ground / 25PSF Roof, 115MPH Wind"; Sheet Metal Panels 26; Panel Size 8'6"(102") Roof, 15'2"(182") + 6'2"(74") Eave Side; 29 gauge; Frame Weight 1116.66 (so "1,100+ lb" is right, though that is FRAME ONLY — the metal adds more); Frame Warranty "20-year limited + product pledge"; Sheet Metal "20 year paint finish".
- Geometry checks out: 9' wall + (8' half-span x 3/12 = 2') = 11'0" peak. Roof 21'2" / 3' = 7.06 -> 7 panels/side x 2 = 14, plus 3 courses x (182"+74") x 2 eave sides = 12, total 26. Consistent.
- SQFT: 16 x 21 = 336. Correct. Slightly over the 320 sq ft target, and the record says so.
- Quotes that DO appear verbatim: "SHIPPING INCLUDED", "FRAME SHIPS IN 5 BUSINESS DAYS", "Included in selected model", "Roof purlins are included for vertical sheet metal application, but no side girts are required", "Wind and snow ratings provided are for reference only... Conformance to local codes is the responsibility of the purchaser", "If permitting is required by your city/county, truss bracing is mandatory", the one-day-frame/next-day-metal FAQ, the Slip-Fit "add additional length... by adding base rails and truss sections" FAQ, and the shipping-included FAQ. Front Wall 8'x8' +$0 / Fully Enclosed -$31 and Back Wall Fully Enclosed +$0 / 8'x8' +$31 confirmed exactly. Vendor address "50 Eastley Street, Collierville, TN 38017" and 800-810-2993 confirmed in the footer.
- VIDEO: youtube.com/watch?v=bjj2UkRSjF8 is linked from the page and oEmbed returns title exactly "Frontier Garage 16x21x9 5OC 2x3", channel VersaTube Building Systems. Model-specific, as claimed.
- IMAGE: /home/ethan/woodshed/assets/img/versatube-frontier-16x21-steel-garage.jpg is a real JPEG, 1000x1000, 328,868 bytes. I opened it: it is the correct VersaTube white gable garage render with vertical roof panels, horizontal siding and an 8x8 front opening (a truck in the bay), watermarked VersaTube. No fix needed.

THINGS THE RECORD MISSES (completeness):
1. The page is running a live promo banner: "Labor Day Sale Extended! 12% off sitewide, up to $2,000 off. No minimum purchase. Use code BBQ12 - Ends Fri, Sep 11". 12% off $5,872 is ~$5,167. The record's price field is the correct list price but does not mention that a discount code is currently on the page.
2. The configurator has an "Overhangs / No Overhangs" choice (both +$0) with the caveat "this includes framing only; you'll need to finish it with your own fascia and soffit application" — an extra DIY line item the record never mentions.
3. The configurator also has a "SELECT YOUR PLANNED EXTERIOR ROOF AND WALL SHEATHING" step (VersaFinish 24" hat channel for OSB vs. Sheet Metal variable spacing) containing the alarming strings "Important: This product is frame-only and does not include sheet metal", "We provide the additional framing for OSB, but not the OSB itself", and "Note: Thumbnails show finished structures for comparison. We provide frame-only, not exterior materials", plus "View Sheet Metal Take-Off List" / "View OSB Take-Off List" buttons. Those blocks belong to the OSB/frame-only path (and appear partly comment-wrapped), and the spec table's 26 panels / 29 gauge / sheet-metal warranty confirm the standard kit does include metal — but a buyer reading this page can reasonably be confused about whether $5,872 buys the skin, and that ambiguity deserves a con. It also partly undercuts cons[0]'s "no published bill of materials" — take-off lists are offered.
4. cons[0] "you cannot review the design before buying" is fair: dimensionsThumb = '' in the page JS, i.e. there genuinely is no dimensioned-drawing tab for this SKU.
5. Freight nuance: kits ship free, but the same FAQ says "All VersaTube parts and accessories are shipped via ground or LTL carrier, the freight is calculated at checkout and paid for by the customer" — so extra walk-door frame kits (+$93 ea) and window frame kits (+$82 ea) may carry freight. pros[4] should be scoped to the kit.
6. Engineering sanity: nothing in the record is structurally wrong. 25 PSF roof / 41.3 PSF ground snow on a 16' clear span at 5' o.c. with 2"x3" 14/15-ga tube and a King brace is plausible for a light-gauge tube system; calling 41.3 PSF ground snow "modest" is fair editorializing (it is roughly a Zone-4/5 ground snow, adequate for much of the mid-Atlantic/South but not for the Snowbelt). The "no interior posts" claim is correct for a trussed 16' span.

Net: the numbers, price, SKU, dimensions, loads, warranty and video all hold up. The failures are (a) the 13-vs-15 color count, (b) two quotes that are not from this source at all (one lifted out of context from a different VersaTube page), (c) several plausible-but-unstated spec details presented as if published (5-rib, 36" wide, printed instructions, no insert tubes), and (d) a color-surcharge claim and a truss-brace-is-an-upcharge claim that the page contradicts or does not support.

plans.name: How to build a 20x20 Garage for $3000 in 5 days (from Home Depot materials)
plans.footprint_note: Marketed as 20x20 (400 sq ft) but laid out at 01:43 as "20 ft this way 20 ft this way 19 ft right here and 19 ft right there" — i.e. 20 ft deep x 19 ft wide = ~380 sq ft. Squared by equal diagonals from 4 corner stakes and strings. Both the front and rear walls are two 109 in sections plus a center 4x4 = 221.5 in of framing (~19 ft with the side walls), while each side wall is two 10 ft sections = 20 ft. The front gable sections are 109 in wide x 13 in high above two 88 in door openings. No slab.
plans.style: Gable-roof, metal-clad two-car garage / enclosed carport with two pairs of barn-style swing doors on the gable end. Wood-framed in 2x4 with steel roofing panels used as both roof and siding. No floor, no windows.
plans.price: Free
plans.est_material_cost: $3,000 is stated as US dollars in the video (00:09, "only cost about $3,000 US"); the thumbnail says only "Total cost $3000" with no currency. The $2,600 metal figure is explicitly Canadian ("just under two grand American"), so metal is roughly 60-65% of a ~$3,000 USD total.
plans.page_count: 1 video (1 h 42 min / 6,126 seconds). This is a single one-shot build video, NOT a multi-episode series: the channel's playlists page lists only car-restoration series and no garage playlist, and the video carries no chapter markers.
plans.format: Single YouTube video, 1 h 42 min (6,126 s), published 2023-12-13, ~1.62M views. No chapters, no timestamps in the description, English auto-generated captions only. The description does list the 6 build phases in order (foundation, framing, metal strapping, doors, steel roof, finishing/door hanging) but with no times attached.
plans.foundation: Nine buried cinder blocks: one at each corner, one mid-span on each of the four sides, and one in the center to carry the ridge post. Each hole is dug "almost two cinder blocks deep" (roughly 16-18 in) because "the first like foot and a half down is mush stuff... but once you go like a foot and a half down it becomes rock hard". Blocks are set on tamped dirt (he notes sand would also work), leveled off one corner using a 10 ft 2x6 and a spirit level, left protruding slightly above grade, then backfilled and tamped. Approx. 2.5 h to dig, 2 h to level, "one day to do the foundation". No concrete, no footings below frost, no piers, no anchor bolts or hurricane straps.
plans.floor_framing: None. There is no floor at all: bare dirt inside, no joists, no sleepers, no slab. He shovels dirt back against the buried metal on the inside.
plans.wall_framing: 2x4 studs at 24 in on center, cut to 6 ft 10 in for a 7 ft finished wall height. Walls are built flat on the ground as prefabricated sections (four side sections, two 109 in rear sections, two 109 in x 13 in front header sections, plus small filler posts beside the door openings) then stood up and screwed together. Single top and bottom plates with 10 ft 2x4s for the top runs; 4x4 posts at the middle of the front and rear walls. Everything is screwed, not nailed, with #8 x 3 in construction screws; the section-to-section joints get screws through washers so the whole building can be unbolted and loaded on a trailer later. A mid-height horizontal 2x4 blocking row is added all the way around at the halfway point as a fastening line for the steel. No sheathing, no let-in bracing, no plywood corners: he states outright "once the walls are up that's where the strength comes from... any construction that's just timber like this is a little wobbly until you put the walls on", i.e. racking resistance comes entirely from the screwed-on metal skin.
plans.wall_height: 7 ft side walls (studs cut to 6 ft 10 in between plates)
plans.overall_height: not stated
plans.roof: Five 2x4 x 10 ft strapping rows per side (he planned four rows/16 boards at "2 and 1/2 ft apart", then says "I actually ended up putting five of them one 2 3 four five basically they're evenly spaced out except for that one there is a little bit closer for the cap")
plans.siding: Charcoal "Americana" steel roofing panel used vertically as siding, 3 ft net coverage per sheet (measured on camera as "exactly 3 feet from there to there"), ~7 sheets per side wall. The panel bottoms are set into a 4-5 in deep trench dug around the whole perimeter and then buried, "so it'll prevent stuff blowing underneath and it'll keep it kind of steady". Fastened with 1-1/2 in metal roofing screws with bonded rubber washers, driven in the flats on the walls (ribs on the roof), aligned with a chalk line. Trim is white to match his house: white vinyl outside corner posts and white vinyl J-channel around the door openings (chosen deliberately over metal because vinyl does not dent when hit with a shovel or wheelbarrow), 2 in x 2 in white metal angle flashing, metal drip edge over the doors, and 8 pieces of flat metal trim under the eaves. All vinyl trim is deliberately fastened loose so it can expand and contract. Cuts made with tin snips and an angle grinder cut-off disc, edges deburred with 40-grit.
plans.doors: Two 88 in wide openings in the front gable wall, each closed by a pair of outswinging barn-style doors, so 4 door leaves total. Each leaf is a 2x4 frame with 45-degree mitred corners plus a single 2x4 mid-rail, sized to 44 in minus 1/4 in wide, skinned in white "Americana" panel (5 white sheets covered all four leaves) using white 1-1/2 in screws set out with a chalk line. One leaf of each pair has its metal run 1/4 in proud so it laps the mating leaf and closes the gap. Hung on 3 in plain butt hinges bought on sale, 2 per leaf, set 8 in from the top of the wood, with small notches snipped and hammered in the metal so the hinge sits flat. Fitted solo with car jacks and shims; washers can be stacked under a hinge to fine-tune. 1x3 stops screwed around the opening so the doors close against something and cannot swing inward. Top barrel bolt on the inactive leaf plus an exterior hasp and padlock. The doors are deliberately hung high off the ground so snow does not block them, and the resulting gap is closed with strips of rubber mat screwed to the inside face. A welded hook plus a buried cinder block acts as a hold-open so wind cannot catch a door.

plans.build_time: 5 days solo. Title says "in 5 days"; on camera he says "it's only going to take you 4 to 5 days to build it start to finish" and closes with "it only took me 5 days". Roughly: day 1 foundation (2.5 h digging plus 2 h leveling), then wall sections and stand-up, perimeter trench (1 h), then metal on the walls, doors, then roof, then rafter ties. He worked alone the entire time except for the eight 16 ft rafter ties, which needed his friend Ryan to hold one end.
plans.skill_level: Beginner to intermediate, but with real judgement required because nothing is engineered. Tools shown: shovel, spirit level, circular saw, table saw (used to rip small corrections on rafter tails), angle grinder with cut-off disc, tin snips, cordless drill, chalk line, hammer, clamps, car jacks, and a welder for the door hold-open hook. Every wood connection is screwed, so no framing-nailer skill is needed. The creator states flatly: "I am not a professional. Everything I do and say is for entertainment only."

plans.permit_notes: No permit or code discussion at all beyond the disclaimer in the description: "Do everything at your own risk, don't do what I do, I am not a professional... Check your local building laws codes and regulations before building anything. every building should be strapped down, I am not responsible for anything that anybody does, this video is entirely for entertainment only." Note that he says every building should be strapped down and then does not strap this one down. As built this is very unlikely to pass an inspection in most jurisdictions: 400 sq ft usually exceeds the permit-exempt threshold, there are no frost footings, no anchorage to the foundation, no engineered header over the 88 in door openings, no lateral bracing independent of the metal skin, and 24 in o.c. 2x6 rafters on a 10 ft horizontal run with no stated design snow load. Location is Canada (he references Canadian dollars and Canadian snow), so US readers should also expect a currency and product-availability shift.
plans.summary: A 102-minute single-take YouTube build in which one man puts up a 20x20 ft (400 sq ft) two-car garage by himself in five days for about $3,000 (Canadian) using nothing but Home Depot stock: a 2x4 stick frame on nine buried cinder blocks, a structural 2x10 ridge beam over a center 4x4 post, 2x6 rafters at 24 in o.c., and charcoal "Americana" steel roofing panel used as both roof and siding, with white vinyl J-channel and corner posts as trim. It covers the whole job start to finish on camera: layout and squaring, digging and leveling the block piers, building and standing the wall sections, trenching so the siding can be buried 4 in below grade, all the flashing and trim details, building and hanging four barn-style door leaves, the roof panels and ridge cap, and the 16 ft rafter ties added at the end for snow. The build is deliberately demountable, with washers under the screws at every section joint so the whole building can be unbolted and put on a trailer. There is no written materials list anywhere: every quantity and price is spoken once on camera, and there are no chapters or timestamps to jump back to.
