pros: Genuinely start-to-finish: layout, foundation, framing, trim, siding, doors, roof and ridge cap are all on camera in one continuous 102-minute video, with essentially no cutaways to 'and then I finished it'
Extremely cheap for 400 sq ft - roughly $3,000 CAD all in, including the foundation and the doors, with the steel being ~85% of that. Very few 20x20 builds land anywhere near this number

Buildable solo. He shows the actual one-man tricks: wall sections built flat and stood up with clamps, a rope-and-hook to lift a siding panel one-handed, car jacks and shims to hang a door alone. Only the eight 16 ft rafter ties needed a second person
No concrete, no mixing, no forms, no excavation equipment. Nine used cinder blocks and a shovel

Screwed rather than nailed throughout, with washers at every section joint, so the building is intentionally demountable and can be trailered to a new property - a real advantage for a rented lot or a planned move

The trim and flashing detailing is unusually thorough for a budget build: J-channel, drip edge, angle flashing, vinyl corner posts, buried panel bottoms, and a clear explanation of why vinyl trim must be left loose for thermal movement

Good practical judgement on a few points: digging through the soft 18 in to firm subsoil, using vinyl instead of metal trim where a shovel or wheelbarrow will hit it, hanging the doors high so snow cannot block them, edge blocking so the eave does not crush, and rafter ties to stop the walls spreading

Camera work is usable as instruction - he goes up the ladder to show each connection close-up, and he shows his own mistakes (running short on long boards, running 40 screws short) rather than editing them out
A structural ridge beam on a center post plus 24 in o.c. 2x6 rafters plus 4 rafter ties per side is a heavier roof than most cheap carport builds, which matters if you have snow
cons: No plans, no drawings, no cut list and no materials list anywhere. Every quantity and price is spoken exactly once in a 102-minute video with no chapters and no description timestamps, so you have to transcribe it yourself before you can shop

Nothing is engineered and the roof pitch and design snow load are never stated. His snow claims are pure anecdote ('we can even get six feet of wet snow no problem', 'this is overkill'). A 10 ft horizontal rafter run in 2x6 at 24 in o.c. with no sheathing needs a real load check before you copy it

No anchorage at all. The building simply sits on nine loose buried cinder blocks - no anchor bolts, no straps, no ground anchors. He states in his own description that 'every building should be strapped down' and then does not do it. This is the single biggest thing to fix if you build it

No frost footings. The piers reach firm subsoil at ~18 in, which is well above the frost depth in most of Canada and the northern US, so expect seasonal movement in a structure with 88 in door openings that need to stay square

Lateral stability depends entirely on the screwed-on steel skin - he says so explicitly. There is no sheathing, no let-in bracing and no plywood shear corners. Remove or damage panels and the frame is 'a little wobbly'
No header shown over the two 88 in door openings other than a 13 in tall stud-framed section - that is the load path from a 20 ft ridge to the front wall and it is never sized or explained

No floor, no windows, no electrical, no insulation, no vapour barrier, no soffit or ridge ventilation. It is an unvented, uninsulated metal box on dirt, so condensation dripping off the underside of unlined steel roofing is a real risk not addressed

24 in o.c. framing with single plates is below typical code minimums for a habitable or permitted structure, and 400 sq ft usually exceeds the permit-exempt size. Do not expect this to pass inspection as drawn
Canadian pricing and Canadian Home Depot SKUs. The 'Americana' panel name and the $6/ft and $10/stick prices are 2023 CAD; a US builder should assume different products and different numbers

Auto-generated captions are the only searchable text and they garble numbers - '$3000' becomes '$33,000', '20 ft by 20 ft' becomes '2 ft by 20 ft', screw sizes are mangled. Verify every quantity against the on-screen footage

A couple of shortcuts are visible: he splices short boards instead of driving to the store, finishes 40 roof screws short, and substitutes and hand-flattens the wrong flat trim because the right one was out of stock
Explicit entertainment-only disclaimer and 'don't do what I do' - so there is zero support, no revisions, and no accountability if something you copied fails

plans.footprint_note_original: 20 ft x 20 ft = 400 sq ft, laid out with 4 corner stakes and strings and squared by equal diagonals. The rear wall is framed as two 109 in (9 ft 1 in) sections plus a center 4x4; the front gable end has two 88 in door openings with 13 in tall header sections above them. There is no slab, so this is nominal outside-of-framing 20x20.
plans.roof_original: Gable roof with a structural ridge: two 2x10 x 10 ft members butted over a center 8 ft 4x4 post (plus 4x4 posts in the mid-point of each gable wall), giving a 20 ft ridge in two 10 ft spans. Rafters are 2x6 x 10 ft, 11 per side, at 24 in o.c., pattern-cut from one template per side (he warns not to cut both sides from the same template). Four 2x4 x 10 ft purlins/strapping per side run over the rafters at roughly 30 in spacing ("2 and 1/2 ft apart") to carry the panels; blocking is added at the outer edges only, so heavy snow does not push the eave edge down. Eight 2x4 x 16 ft rafter/collar ties (4 per side) are added later with a helper "to prevent the walls from buckling out" under snow. Covering is charcoal "Americana" steel roofing panel, 9 ft 10 in long, 7 sheets per side, screwed through the ribs with 1-1/2 in rubber-washered screws, plus two site-cut ridge cap pieces from a leftover 10 ft sheet. Overhang 2-1/2 in at the sides and 2 in at the front. No sheathing, no underlayment, no soffit or ridge ventilation. Roof pitch is never stated. Snow claim is anecdotal only: "this is Canada... we can even get six feet of wet snow no problem", "this is overkill as far as snow".
plans.est_material_cost_original: ~$3,000 total per the title and description ("the $3000 price includes the entire 20x20 metal garage building... the foundation, the framing, the doors, roof and all the metal and hardware"). At 48:17 he says "I paid $2,600 for all the metal Canadian which is like just under two grand American", which implies the $3,000 headline is Canadian dollars (roughly $2,200 USD at Dec-2023 rates). Metal is therefore ~85% of the budget. The 9 cinder blocks were free used blocks; panels were quoted at "around $6 for each foot Canadian" for 3 ft-coverage sheets; 2x2 white angle flashing $10 CAD per 10 ft stick; drip edge ~$12 CAD each.

ENGINEERING / COMPLETENESS ITEMS THE RECORD SHOULD FLAG (cons):
1. DOOR OPENING HEIGHT ~71 in. 7 ft walls minus the 13 in header section leaves a roughly 5 ft 11 in tall opening. It swallows his BMW E36 but no truck, van or SUV. The record's visible fields never state door height; this is the single biggest practical limitation of the design and belongs in cons.
2. The snow claims are not just anecdotal, they are dangerous. A single 2x10 spanning 10 ft as a structural ridge, 2x6 rafters at 24 in o.c. over a ~10 ft sloped span, and 4x4 posts bearing on dry-laid cinder blocks cannot carry anything close to "six feet of wet snow" (200+ psf); that assembly is marginal even at a 40 psf ground snow load. 3. Nine dry-laid cinder blocks ~14-16 in deep in Canada is well above frost depth, with no footings, no anchorage, and no uplift connection anywhere — and the author's own description says "every building should be strapped down". Frost heave on 9 independent unconnected point supports plus a floating 4x4 ridge post is the failure mode.
4. Racking resistance is 100% screwed-on steel panel with no sheathing, no let-in bracing and no plywood corners, which is not a recognized shear assembly. The record does state this fairly.
5. The video is genuinely complete end-to-end (layout, foundation, framing, roof, metal, doors, trim, hardware) and it does not skip the foundation, so "video-build" completeness is honest. But there are no chapter markers and no timestamps in the description, so a builder has to scrub a 1h42m single take — worth a con. The record is correct that there is no multi-part playlist.

plans.summary: Plan 028S-0005 is a paid stock construction-drawing set from The Garage Plan Shop for a 20 ft wide x 16 ft deep single-story garden shed with a recessed covered front porch, sold from $440 as a PDF (or $555 for three printed sets plus PDF, or $890 for the CAD file). The listing publishes a tight but real spec: 272 sq ft of enclosed space, 8 ft first-floor ceiling, roughly 14 ft 8 in overall height, 2x4 exterior walls, truss-framed roof, and monolithic slab as the only foundation option — no crawlspace, no wood floor deck, and no alternate wall or size options are offered. Drawings are stock and explicitly not engineered: TGPS states plans "are designed to meet national building codes, but they do not necessarily meet any specific state, county, or municipal codes" and "WILL NOT include an engineer's/architect's seal or stamp," so local stamping is the buyer's cost. No material list is offered for this plan number, no sheet/page count is published, and all sales are final and non-refundable.

pros: Structurally the easiest 320 sq ft class of shed to build: monolithic slab-on-grade means no piers, no beams, no floor joists, no rim/blocking, and no under-floor rot or rodent path — you pour once and frame on flat concrete.

Simple, forgiving spans. 16 ft trusses at 8 ft walls in 2x4 walls is stock lumberyard territory; a 16 ft roof span needs no interior bearing wall, ridge beam, or engineered LVL, so the whole interior is column-free.

Roof is truss-framed, so you can order 16 ft trusses from a local plant with their own engineering stamp instead of cutting and hand-framing a rafter roof — a big accuracy and speed win for a solo DIYer.
272 sq ft of clear, unobstructed L-shaped floor with an 8 ft flat ceiling — good for shelving walls, a potting bench, and long-handled tools.

Real permit-grade documentation: foundation plan, floor plan, elevations, sections and details in a single set, plus a written copyright release so you can legally print sets for the building department, lender, and subs.
Priced as a one-time $440 PDF with no shipping, and you get a free modification quote if you want to change the door, add windows, or extend it.
Curb appeal that passes HOA and neighborhood scrutiny: the covered porch, shutters, lap siding and shingled gable read as a small cottage rather than a metal utility box.
Right Reading Reverse ($160) is available if the plan orientation fights your lot or existing driveway.
cons: NOT engineered for your jurisdiction. TGPS states flatly: "Our construction drawings will not be engineered for your specific city, state, county, or province, and they WILL NOT include an engineer's/architect's seal or stamp." In a high-wind, seismic, or heavy-snow area, budget several hundred dollars extra for a local engineer to review and stamp the set.

No material list, no cut list, and no lumber quantities are available for this plan number. The Additional Options section offers only extra printed sets and Right Reading Reverse — the FAQ confirms material lists exist "for some plans" and appear under Additional Options when they do. TGPS's own advice is to hand the drawings to a lumberyard for a free takeoff.

Monolithic slab is the ONLY foundation option — no crawlspace, no skid/pier, no floating-slab alternative. That means concrete forming, rebar, a footing thickened edge, likely a mixer truck, and possibly a frost-depth detail. It is the single biggest cost driver and the least DIY-friendly step, and it is not optional in this plan.

A slab makes the building effectively permanent and immovable, which usually pushes it firmly into permit-required territory rather than the exempt "portable accessory structure" category many jurisdictions allow.
320 sq ft of roofed footprint exceeds the common 200 sq ft (and even the 120 sq ft) permit-exemption thresholds — expect a full permit, setback review, and possibly a site plan.

No vehicle or equipment access: the floor plan shows only a single swinging entry door under the porch. You cannot drive a riding mower, ATV, or wheelbarrow-and-trailer through it without paying for a modification to add a double or overhead door.

The covered porch costs you 48 sq ft of enclosed storage (320 gross vs 272 usable) and adds a beam, a post, a return, and a roof-to-wall intersection — more framing complexity and flashing risk for no storage gain.
No loft, no attic storage, and no second level. With truss framing over an 8 ft flat ceiling, the roof volume is not usable and there is no published loft or access.

The number of sheets in the set is not published anywhere on the page, so you are buying sight-unseen with respect to how much framing detail you actually get. TGPS also warns that its drawings "include detailed sections of the framing, floor joists, and roof layouts, but it is not often that they include the entire layout" — an experienced builder is assumed.

Zero-refund policy: "Your plan purchase is NOT returnable or refundable... The Garage Plan Shop does not honor any requests for returns, refunds, or exchanges under any circumstances... All sales are FINAL."
The license is one build only and is non-transferable, so you cannot build a second shed or hand the plans to a friend.
No reviews (0) on the listing, so there is no third-party signal on drawing quality or completeness.

$440 for a 272 sq ft storage shed is expensive relative to free extension/university plans or $30-$60 DIY shed plan sets that include full cut lists — you are paying for permit-ready formal drawings, not for build hand-holding.

What it does give, in dimensioned CAD form, is the narrow-braced-panel recipe most DIY builders get wrong when they put a 8-16 ft overhead door in a 16x20-class shed or garage: minimum double 2x4 king/jack post each side, wood header min 3" x 11-1/4" (steel header prohibited), 7/16" minimum wood structural panel sheathing nailed with 8d common or galvanized box nails at 3" o.c. to all framing including the header, 1,000 lb minimum header-to-jack-stud straps on both sides of the opening opposite the sheathing, (6) 16d sinkers king stud to header, two rows of 16d sinkers at 3" o.c. top plate to header, panel length at least 25% of the top-of-header height, panel splices only over blocking within the middle 24" of the opening height, and a minimum of two 1/2" anchor bolts with 3/16" x 2" square plate washers per panel. PORTAL IN SDC A, B, C 2015"). Pair it with a real shed plan when your design has a garage door or other wide opening in a braced wall line.

Episode 2 is the single most useful thing here and is hard to find elsewhere: squaring a 16x20 post foundation on a slope without excavating or building up a level pad, with two squaring methods explained side by side. Most 16x20 plan sets simply assume a flat pad and skip this.

A post-frame foundation on undisturbed sloping ground is the cheapest and lowest-labour way to get a 320 sq ft building up — no concrete slab, no footing pours, no earthmoving, no gravel pad, which are usually the biggest cost and effort drivers on a shed this size.

Refreshingly candid about mistakes rather than showing a suspiciously clean build: he explicitly tells you his floor framing went badly because he didn't square the foundation properly, and to learn from it. That failure mode is exactly what bites first-time 16x20 builders.

cons: Fatally incomplete. The series is 3 episodes and about 19 minutes total, and it stops at the bare floor deck. Walls, trusses, roof, sheathing, siding, and the sliding barn door were never filmed — the shed is never seen finished. This cannot be your primary build guide.

Post-frame with a suspended joisted floor gives you a shed you cannot easily drive a mower or ATV into without building a ramp, and it leaves an open, animal-accessible crawl space under the deck on the downhill side.

No stated material cost and no stated build time anywhere. The only dollar figure in the whole series is the thumbnail's rejected big-box quote, which tells you nothing about what this shed actually costs.

Poor curation: the creator's own '16x20 Shed Build' playlist contains only 2 of the 3 episodes (Episode 2 is missing from it), so anyone using the playlist skips the foundation-squaring episode — the best one.

Tiny sample of expertise — a self-described first-timer with 2.89K subscribers whose channel has since pivoted entirely to hydroponics and RV solar. There is no follow-up, no errata, and no way to ask him how the roof turned out.

plans.summary: A free 12-episode YouTube playlist in which ShowPhil (Phil) helps his friend Chris build a 16' x 20' off-grid cabin in deep Florida-style pine woods with no power, internet or running water. The series runs in order from the raised floor deck (Part 1) through stick-framed walls sheathed in red Thermo-Ply (Parts 2-3), hand-cut rafters (Parts 4-5), a metal roof plus a custom hinged roof door (Parts 6-8), full-length loft walls built around salvaged free windows (Parts 9-10), first-floor window installation (Part 11) and loft sheathing (Part 12). Episodes are short - 5:49 to 8:38, about 1.5 hours total - and were posted weekly from June 28 to October 11, 2022. It is useful as a visual reference for a 320 sq ft shell with a loft on a post-supported wood floor, but there are no plans, no dimensions and no materials list, and the series ends with the building still unsided and unfinished inside.

plans.summary: Behm Design plan 320-1 is a permit-oriented architectural drawing set for a 16' x 20' (320 sq ft) one-story front-gable garage that doubles as a large storage/shop building. The product page itself is extremely terse — a price, purchase options, and one spec line: "This garage plan features 9′ wide x 7′ high garage door." The value is in the package: 18" x 24" sheets at 1/4" scale including floor plan with electrical layout, all four true elevations plus framing elevations, perimeter foundation and slab plan with concrete details and alternates, cross sections, wall sections, structure notes, roof framing/truss layout plan, and a materials list printed on Sheet 1. Plans are prescriptive IRC compliance (not stamped engineering) drawn to stated parameters: 100 mph 3-second gust, exposure B, seismic category ≤ C, and 30 psf max snow load, with a 60-day money-back guarantee tied to permit approvability.

plans.permit_notes: Explicitly designed for permit submittal: "The industry standard for architectural drawings are 2-dimensional drawing views and must be part of a building permit drawing submittal." Stated design parameters: IRC compliance; assumed max 100 mph wind, 3-second gust (a few older plans were designed for 85 mph); assumed moderate wind exposure "B"; most designs code compliant as "conventional light-frame construction"; assumed basically flat site; assumed stable, durable soil; assumed max seismic category C risk; maximum 30 #/sf snow load. Not intended as drawn for areas with extreme environmental conditions — California, Florida, New York, Washington and coastal states may exceed these. Some jurisdictions require a licensed engineer's or architect's stamp. You will still need a site plan. Paper sets are sold in packages of four because permit offices typically keep 2 copies (record + inspector), leaving 2 for the contractor/owner/supplier, and one approved sealed set must be kept unaltered on site. Modifications are not offered by Behm; write-in alternates for door location, foundation type and roof slope exist on many plans but "there are some [building departments] that do not allow them."
plans.refund_policy: 60-day money-back guarantee: plans "may be returned if not usable for building permit application and approval using the Design Parameters to which the plans were drawn." The guarantee "is limited to the refund of purchase price for the plans only and limited to period of 60 days after purchase date." Behm assumes no liability for third-party modifications of the plan. Plansets are licensed for one construction use only; repetitive use is prohibited.
other_sizes: 16x22 — Plan 352-1 (product/352-1-16-x-22-wide-1-car-garage-plan)
16x24 — Plans 384-1 (gable), 384-2 (hipped roof), 384-5 (traditional), 384-m1 (modern), 384-3 / 384-4 / 384-6 (with attic), 384-g1 (gambrel with tall attic)
16x26 — Plan 416-1 (and 416-1hd heavy duty)
Note: these are separate products in Behm's 16'-wide series, NOT size options of 320-1 — the 320-1 page offers only paper-vs-PDF choices, no size selector.
Behm also sells a separate Utility Shed Plans line (480-1, 576-1, 816-1) and Modern Shed Plans, priced lower than the garage plans
pros: Exactly on target: 16' x 20' = 320 sq ft, one story, no wasted loft complexity.
A genuine permit-submittal drawing set at 1/4" = 1'-0" on 18" x 24" sheets — 2D plan/elevation/section views, which is what plan reviewers actually require.

Includes the foundation plan, concrete details and alternates, which Behm points out many competitors omit: "Many of the garage plans available from other companies simply leave out the foundation plan and details."

Design parameters are published up front and are unusually specific (100 mph 3-sec gust, exposure B, seismic ≤ C, 30 psf snow, flat site, stable soil) so you can check them against your jurisdiction before buying.
Materials list is printed on Sheet 1 at no extra charge AND offered free in Excel format before you buy (phone 1-800-210-6776), so you can price the build before spending $499.

Four collated 18" x 24" paper copies are included, with free shipping - matching the typical permit-office requirement (2 for the city, 2 for you and the builder). Note that since 2026 the PDF-only option costs the same $499, so the paper package is the better value of the two.
Floor plan includes electrical lighting, switching and outlet symbol layout — useful if you want a wired shop, not just a storage box.
60-day money-back guarantee explicitly tied to whether the set is usable for permit approval.
PDF option is instant and reprintable forever with no copy limits, and can be emailed to print shops, suppliers or the building department, or marked up in Acrobat Pro.
9' x 7' overhead door means the building is genuinely vehicle/trailer/mower-capable rather than a walk-in shed only.
Long-running vendor (plans on the site since the late 1990s, company claims top quality plans since 1986) with a phone number answered by the designer.
cons: The product page is nearly data-free: one sentence of specification (the 9' x 7' door). Roof pitch, wall height, overall height, stud size/spacing, sheathing, slab thickness and sheet count for 320-1 are all unpublished — you are buying somewhat blind unless you call.

$499 - the same whether you take paper or PDF - is extraordinarily expensive for a 320 sq ft outbuilding drawing set: ~25x the $19.99 Shedplans.org plan and ~8x iCreatables' $59.99. And it is not a DIY tutorial: no step-by-step instructions, no dimensioned cut list, no photos of the build sequence.

Price has escalated steeply for the same drawing: archived Behm pages show 320-1 at $119.95 (paper) / $79.95 (PDF) around 2012, $179.95 / $159.95 in 2014, $199.95 / $179.95 in 2019, $229.95 / $209.95 in May 2022, $309 / $299 in Dec 2025 and $499 / $499 as of Sept 2026 - a 4x rise in about 14 years, and the PDF discount has been abolished. Siblings moved together (264-1, a smaller 12x22, was already $399 paper in Feb 2026).

Roof cannot be stick-framed from the plans: "I want to site-build the roof trusses... Sorry, but no." You must order engineered trusses from a licensed fabricator, which adds cost, lead time and a crane/many-hands lift day for a 16' span.

Truss engineering is explicitly NOT part of the package — the plan only shows the truss layout and requirements, so the plan set alone is incomplete until the fabricator supplies stamped shop drawings.

Foundation is a concrete perimeter footing and slab, which is the most expensive and least DIY-friendly foundation type — no skid/on-grade/pier option is offered, so expect forming, rebar and a concrete pour with inspections.
No customization at all: "Garage plan modifications are not available." Any real change requires a licensed engineer or architect, and Behm disclaims liability for others' modifications.

Not usable as drawn in high-wind/coastal, high-seismic (category D+) or heavy-snow (>30 psf) areas, and CA/FL/NY/WA may require a stamped set - meaning extra engineering cost on top of the $499. Behm is explicit that it cannot supply that: 'Are Behm Design plans wet-stamp certified? No... Behm Design cannot offer engineering.'
The materials list is deliberately partial: no flashings, specialized fasteners/hardware, electrical, mechanical, plumbing, sealants, adhesives or finishes.
PDF download link "will vanish after" 48 hours — if you miss the window you must email for a re-send.
Printing the PDF properly needs an 18" x 24" large-format printer (Staples/FedEx Office/blueprint shop); home-printer reduction to 8.5x11 voids the architectural scale and hurts legibility.
Behm also warns you must never scale the drawings directly — dimension lines only — which trips up DIYers used to measuring off a print.
The site's own artwork for this plan is a small low-resolution 409x250 render; the floor plan and elevation thumbnails are not archived and not viewable without buying.
No loft or attic storage in 320-1 — if you want overhead storage you must step up to the 16x24 attic siblings (384-3/-4/-6) or the 384-g1 gambrel.
Direct site access is Cloudflare-blocked to non-browser clients, so the live page can be hard to reach programmatically.

The site's own pricing signals contradict each other: the live page still ships an inline banner string 'Spring Planning Sale! All PDF Plans $349 Thru May. 60 Day No Questions Asked Money Back Guarantee.' while the cart charges $499 for the PDF. The rendered banner is only '*IMPORTANT INFORMATION'. Call 1-800-210-6776 and confirm which price applies before paying.

CONFIRMED CORRECT (no change): footprint 16x20 and sqft 320 (16x20=320, arithmetic checks; h1 says 16′ x 20′; FAQ confirms product-page dimensions are footprint, "the measured vertical faces of concrete at finished grade", not overhangs); the single spec sentence "This garage plan features 9′ wide x 7′ high garage door." (verbatim, and it really is the only body text); page_count "not stated for 320-1" plus both /whats-included/ quotes verbatim ("This collage/image was made using one of our garage plans which has 11 sheets", "The sheet size we use for all of our garage plans is 18″ x 24″"); the entire 13-item includes list matches /whats-included/ item-for-item; the wall_height write-ins quote ("many of our garage plans include variable write-ins for dimension, wall height, roof slope, alternates for garage door size") verbatim; the foundation quote ("Behm Design uses code compliant (prescriptive, not engineered) design details for perimeter foundations, details and options...") verbatim from FAQ; flat site + soil assumption supported ("Flat building site condition is assumed", "Soil bearing capacity of minimum 1500 #/sf"); 30 psf snow correct ("Snow load specification of 30 lbs/sf ground snow load"); 48-hour PDF expiry correct ("Be sure to save the file within 48 hours, as it will vanish after that time"); paper shipping method correct ("collated and stapled and shipped by UPS Ground or USPS Priority Mail for PO box addresses") and PDF identity correct ("it is the exact same file that the paper plans are printed from"); "60-day money-back guarantee tied to permit approvability" is genuinely supported ("They may be returned if not usable for building permit application and approval using the Design Parameters to which the plans were drawn" + "limited to period of 60 days after purchase date"); loft=none is well supported — the four 16x24 attic siblings cited all exist with "with attic"/"with tall attic" in their slugs (384-3, 384-4, 384-6, 384-g1), while 320-1 carries 1-story/Under-15'-High and no attic tag; vendor address confirmed, "8547 E. 33rd Pl. Tulsa, OK 74145" (privacy policy); roof pitch, overall height, siding, build_time, est_material_cost correctly marked not stated.

MATERIAL OMISSION the record should carry for a buyer: Behm's own Building Codes page bars these plans from five jurisdictions — "IMPORTANT: The garage plans are NOT intended for use in Florida, Nevada, Oregon or California (and Ontario, Canada) …as they have their own building codes and do NOT use the IRC." Nothing in the record mentions this, and it disqualifies the plan for a large share of US buyers.

Engineering sanity check on the rest: no bogus span claims found. floor_framing is honestly hedged (slab implied, thickness/rebar not published) and is consistent with "Perimeter Foundation and slab plan"; the note that garage-door headers may need PE certification is real ("Building Depts. occasionally require garage door header sizing and certification by PE"), and the 9'x7' door implying at least an 8' wall is sound. The only engineering-flavored defect is the rafter/truss mix-up above.

19' overall height with a 12:12 pitch will bust many jurisdictions' accessory-building height limits, and means scaffolding plus steep, slow roof work for a solo builder — the roof, not the walls, is the labor and cost driver.
The large roof volume is entirely wasted: trusses with a flat 9' ceiling and zero loft or attic storage, despite roughly an 8' rise to the ridge.
Page publishes no sheet count, no skill level, no build time, and no siding, window, door or hardware schedules — several practical planning inputs are unavailable pre-purchase.

Concrete slab on grade with continuous footings under the walls and the interior partition: no wood floor system, no joists, no crawlspace, and the 8 ft canopy gives you 192 sq ft of covered outdoor working area at almost no extra structure

Very simple geometry to build: plain rectangle, straight gable, 8 ft stud walls, 2 ft on-centre framing throughout, one interior partition. No dormers, no hips, no valleys, nothing that needs a compound cut

The 24 ft wide open front (13 ft 6 in of hinged display sash plus two flanking 3-0 x 6-8 doors) makes it unusually good as a farm stand, tool-and-mower drive-in bay, or a market/canopy hybrid if you want covered outdoor space
Includes things one-sheet plans normally omit: a site/plot plan with forecourt parking, a decorative boxed-column detail, and a basic lighting layout
NDSU will also sell an 18 x 24 in blueprint-size print of the same plan for $4.00 per page (prepaid), if you want a full-size sheet to work from
cons: NOT a complete buildable plan set. One sheet, Sheet 1 OF 1. There is no materials list, no cut list, no footing or foundation detail, no header/lintel sizing, no roof covering spec, no window schedule, no fastener/nailing schedule, no step-by-step instructions and no cutaway framing views

The roof structure is the big problem: 2x4 rafters at 2 ft o.c. spanning roughly 14 ft horizontally from eave to ridge, braced only by a 1x6 collar, with no ridge beam, purlin, strut or truss detail shown. That is far below modern snow and live load requirements. Nothing is engineered and no design loads or span tables appear anywhere on the sheet
PITCH 1 TO 5 (rise equal to one fifth of the 28 ft span, roughly 4.8 in 12) is a low slope for a snow region and compounds the undersized rafters

2x4 studs at 2 ft o.c. carrying an 8 ft wall plus roof load, with a single 2x4 top plate, will not pass a modern plan review as drawn. Expect to redraw the whole structural shell (engineered trusses or 2x8/2x10 rafters, doubled plates, 16 in o.c. studs) for a permit

It is drawn as a produce market, not a storage shed: 24 ft of display counter, a hinged glazed front wall, four doors, and an 8 ft open canopy. Turning it into a workshop or storage building means deleting most of the plan and redesigning the front wall

Larger than the stated brief: 480 sq ft enclosed and 672 sq ft under roof puts it at or above the top of the DIY range and will almost certainly trigger a permit and possibly setback/frontage review, especially given it is designed to sit on a road frontage

The sheet is a 200 dpi bitonal scan with no text layer, so nothing is searchable or copy-pasteable and several small figures are near the edge of legibility. Overall height is not dimensioned at all and has to be scaled (about 13 ft 6 in to the ridge)
No cost estimate, no build time, no skill-level guidance, no revision since 1949, and NDSU itself only claims the plans provide conceptual information excellent for planning purposes

plans.foundation: Concrete floor slab on grade over the enclosed 24 x 20 ft area, with continuous footings / low stem walls under the perimeter walls and under the interior partition about 8 ft from the rear wall, shown hatched in Section A-A. The 8 ft forecourt is a thinner concrete apron, and each 4x4 canopy post lands on a small base/pier. Footing widths, depths, reinforcement and frost-depth requirements are not given.
plans.floor_framing: None — concrete floor slab on grade. No joists, girders, sill plates or wood floor system are shown anywhere on the sheet.
plans.wall_framing: Stud wall: STUDS 2x4 at 2 ft 0 in o.c. with PLATE 2x4 (single top plate as noted). Over the open forecourt bay the sheet calls for PLATE 2, 2x6 (a doubled 2x6 beam) carried on 4x4 posts. Corner and intermediate posts at the front are 4x4 boxed out with sheathing and finished with 1x3 and 1x1-1/2 in trim per DETAIL OF COLUMN. No corner bracing, sheathing thickness, header sizes or nailing schedule are specified.
plans.wall_height: 8 ft 0 in floor to plate per the vertical dimension in Section A-A. The side elevation additionally carries a 7 ft 6 in height dimension (grade to eave line), which does not reconcile exactly with the 8 ft section dimension.
plans.overall_height: Not dimensioned on the sheet. Scales to roughly 13 ft 6 in from floor to ridge (8 ft plate plus about 5 ft 7 in of rise).
plans.roof: Gable, ridge running parallel to the 24 ft front face so the gable ends are the side walls and the rafters span the 28 ft depth (about 14 ft horizontally each side of a centred ridge). Sheet notes: PITCH 1 TO 5 (old convention, rise equal to one fifth of the span, so about 5 ft 7 in of rise over the 28 ft span, roughly 4.8 in 12); RAFTER 2x4 x 15 ft 0 in at 2 ft 0 in o.c.; COLLAR 1x6. Eave overhangs at the front and rear scale to roughly 1 ft 6 in and 2 ft (a 2 ft 0 in overhang figure appears in the section); rake overhang at the gable ends is minimal, under 1 ft. No ridge board or beam, no purlins, no struts, no truss and no roof covering are specified.
plans.loft: none
plans.doors: Four doors, each labelled 3 ft 0 in x 6 ft 8 in on the floor plan: two exterior entrances at the front corners flanking the display counter (both visible in the front elevation), one exterior door at the rear into the receiving/grading space, and one interior door between the grading space and the sales space. In addition the whole 13 ft 6 in wide front display opening is a hinged sash/awning unit (annotated HINGE in Section A-A) over a fixed counter/bulkhead, with a 5 ft 3-1/2 in head height above the floor. Door type, swing hardware and jamb details are not specified.
plans.windows: Two double-hung sash per side wall, drawn as six-light over six-light in the side elevation and repeated in Section A-A; further sash appear in the two rear end compartments on the plan. The front display wall is a run of large hinged multi-light sash across the 13 ft 6 in centre opening. No window sizes, rough openings, type or schedule are given anywhere on the sheet.
plans.siding: Horizontal lap / bevel siding drawn on both elevations at roughly 7 in exposure by scaling, with the boxed 4x4 columns sheathed and trimmed with 1x3 and 1x1-1/2 in stock. No siding material, grade, thickness or exposure is specified in text.

plans.permit_notes: Nothing on the sheet addresses permits, codes or design loads: there is no engineering stamp, no code reference, no snow/wind/live load assumption and no span table. NDSU's own framing for this plan library is that the plans were developed over many years by engineers at Land Grant Universities and provide conceptual information that is excellent for planning purposes — i.e. planning aid, not permit documents. At 480 sq ft enclosed and 672 sq ft under roof this is well past the size most jurisdictions exempt, so a permit is very likely, and the structural shell as drawn (2x4 studs at 24 in o.c., 2x4 rafters at 24 in o.c. spanning about 14 ft, single top plate, no ridge beam) would need to be re-engineered before submission. Being designed as a road-frontage commercial stand, it may also trigger setback, frontage, access/driveway and zoning-use review that a backyard shed would not.

_verification.notes:
CONFIRMED against the sheet itself (I read the PDF page and then re-measured the 200 dpi raster with PIL/numpy):

- Footprint 24x20 and sqft 480: CONFIRMED, and independently corroborated by NDSU's own catalogue row, which reads "SALES BLDG, 20'X24'+8' OPEN PORCH, GbR, StW, DISPLAY, CF | 5192 | '49R | 1" on https://www.ndsu.edu/agriculture/ag-hub/ag-topics/ag-buildings/building-plans/miscellaneous-building-plans. 24 x 20 = 480. Note NDSU's abbreviation key defines ML = materials list, and the 5192 row does NOT carry ML — independent support for the record's "no materials list" con.
- 28 ft under-roof depth and 672 sq ft: CONFIRMED. I initially read the depth chain as 4+4+6+6+6 = 26 at low resolution, but at 8x the hand-lettered "8" and "6" resolve, the left overall dim reads 28'-0", and pixel measurement between the rear post row (raster row 697) and the front post row (row 1380) gives 683 px / 23.92 px-per-ft = 28.6 ft (26 ft would be 622 px). Front/rear chain 3'-6"+8'-6"+8'-6"+3'-6" = 24'-0" and front post chain 5'-3"+13'-6"+5'-3" = 24'-0" both close as the record states. Canopy 24x8 = 192 sq ft: correct.
- 8 ft wall height: CONFIRMED — Section A-A carries an 8'-0" floor-to-plate dim on both the front and rear wall (zoomed to read it). The 7'-6" dim on the side elevation cited in includes: CONFIRMED (grade to top of siding).
- Framing call-outs all verbatim: "STUDS 2"x4", 2'-0" O.C.", "PLATE 2"x4"", "PLATE 2, 2"x6"" (twice, incl. over the open bay), "RAFTER 2"x4"x15'-0", 2'-0" O.C.", "COLLAR 1"x6"", "PITCH 1 TO 5", "4"x4" POST", "SHEATHING", "1"x3"", "1"x1 1/2"". The 15'-0" rafter is geometrically consistent with a 14 ft half-span.
- Sheet content: 1 plan, FRONT ELEVATION, SIDE ELEVATION, SECTION "A.A.", DETAIL OF COLUMN (with SECTION and PLAN sub-views), Forecourt Parking PLOT PLAN, and a lighting layout — all present. Counter depth "2'-7"" confirmed by zoom. Switch symbols read S, S3 and SS3 (record says "SS"; trivial). Four 3'-0"x6'-8" doors confirmed. Two double-hung sash on the side elevation confirmed. Labels RECEIVING GRADING SPACE, SALES SPACE, DISPLAY confirmed.
- Price Free / price_usd 0 for the PDF itself: CONFIRMED, no gate, no signup, direct download.
- "200 dpi bitonal scan with no text layer": CONFIRMED (pdfimages: 2208x1701, gray, 1 bpc, ccitt, 200x200 ppi; pdftotext output empty). "66 KB": CONFIRMED (67,659 bytes). "8.5x11": CONFIRMED (11.04 x 8.5 in landscape).
- Engineering sanity: the record's headline con is right and is the most important thing about this sheet. 2x4 rafters at 24 in o.c. spanning 14 ft horizontally (~15 ft on slope) with a single 1x6 collar and no ridge board, purlin or strut is grossly undersized by any modern standard, and there is genuinely no interior bearing at the ridge — the ridge falls at 14 ft from the front eave, while the front wall is at 8 ft and the partition at 20 ft, and neither is carried up to the rafters. Likewise 2x4 studs at 24 in o.c. under a single 2x4 plate. No design loads, no span tables, no engineer's stamp anywhere. NDSU's own site posts a disclaimer that these plans are "conceptual information" only and that professional structural design is required — which supports, and could be cited in, the completeness cons.

Net: the hard numeric fields (footprint, sqft, depth, wall height, pitch note, member sizes, sheet count, price, file facts) hold up. The defects are all in the editorialised pros/cons: a stale-and-embellished $4.00 blueprint price, an invented "prepaid", a "drive-in bay" use case the plan does not support, a "low slope" claim that contradicts its own pitch arithmetic, an overstated "no foundation detail", a phantom scale note, and an overstated scaled ridge height.

corrections.evidence: The live NDSU source publishes no price at all. The current landing page (https://www.ndsu.edu/agriculture/ag-hub/building-plans, HTTP 200) says only 'You may click on the plan number to view or print.' — no blueprint size, no order form, no dollar figure anywhere ($ grep on that page and on the Miscellaneous plans list page returns zero hits). The $4.00 figure survives only on a 2011 Wayback snapshot of the retired index (web.archive.org/web/20110917025409id_/http://www.ag.ndsu.edu/aben-plans/index.htm): 'To order 18 X 24, blueprint size plans, please click on and fill out the online order form below the plans categories. These plans are $4.00 per page.' Ordering there was by e-mail to ndsu.extagbio@ndsu.edu with name/address/plan number/quantity — the word 'prepaid' appears nowhere, so that qualifier is invented, and the offer itself is no longer published.

corrections.field: cons — scaled overall height to ridge
corrections.reported: about 13 ft 6 in
corrections.correct: about 12 ft 10 in
corrections.evidence: Scaled off the sheet's own geometry. Section A-A dimensions the wall 8'-0" floor to plate (verified by zoom: the two vertical dims read 5'-3 1/2" and 8'-0"). Tracing the top-most dark pixel of the rake in the SIDE ELEVATION of the 200 dpi raster gives a straight line of slope 107/325 = 0.329 rise/run on the left and 96/300 = 0.320 on the right, so rise over the 14 ft half-span is about 4'-7", putting the ridge at about 12'-7"-12'-9". Measuring grade line (raster row 435) to ridge (row 128) = 307 px at the plan's scale of 23.9 px/ft gives 12.85 ft = 12'-10". 13'-6" is what you get only if you assume rise = span/5 = 5'-7", which the drawing does not scale to.

corrections.reported: roughly 4.8 in 12
corrections.correct: about 4 in 12
corrections.evidence: The note 'PITCH 1 TO 5' is confirmed verbatim (zoomed at 9x, the digit is unambiguously a 5). But the pitch as actually drawn measures 0.32-0.33 rise/run in both the side elevation rake and the Section A-A roof line, i.e. about 3.9-4.0 in 12, not 4.8 in 12. The record's 4.8:12 comes from assuming the old rise/span convention; the sheet is drawn nearer 4:12.

unsupported_claims: pros[4]: 'The 24 ft wide open front ... makes it unusually good as a farm stand, tool-and-mower drive-in bay'. There is no drive-in opening anywhere on this sheet. Every door in the plan is labelled 3'-0"x6'-8" (four of them), and the wide centre of the front wall is a glazed display sash over a solid counter/bulkhead — Section A-A labels it 'HINGE', i.e. it swings up as a display shutter, not a vehicle opening. The only place a mower could go is under the 8 ft open canopy, which is outside the enclosed 480 sq ft. Misleading buyer-facing claim.

cons[2]: 'PITCH 1 TO 5 ... is a low slope for a snow region'. By the record's own arithmetic that is 4.8 in 12, and as drawn it measures ~4 in 12. Neither is a low slope — 4:12 is a conventional shingle slope. The genuine snow-load problem here is the 2x4 rafter at 24 in o.c. over a 14 ft horizontal span, not the slope, so this con dilutes the real defect.

cons[0]: 'no footing or foundation detail'. Section A-A does show the foundation: a concrete floor slab stepped up above the canopy apron, continuous downstand foundation walls under the front wall, the interior partition and the rear wall, and a spread footing pad under the forecourt column. What is missing is any dimension, depth, width or reinforcement call-out. As written the con contradicts the record's own pro ('Concrete slab on grade with continuous footings under the walls and the interior partition') and overstates the omission.

includes[0]: 'Floor plan at 1 sheet scale'. No drawing scale is printed anywhere on the sheet — no 'SCALE: 1/8" = 1'-0"', no graphic bar scale, nothing in the title block. (The plan does in fact scale at ~1/8" = 1'-0": 574 raster px for the dimensioned 24'-0" at 200 dpi = 23.9 px/ft.) The phrase is meaningless and the implied scale note does not exist.

pros[4]: '13 ft 6 in of hinged display sash'. 13'-6" is the sheet's dimension between the two intermediate FORECOURT COLUMN centres on the front post line (5'-3" + 13'-6" + 5'-3" = 24'-0"), not a width given for the display sash. Scaling the front elevation puts the sash at about 12'-10". Close, but it is an inference presented as a plan dimension.
The record as submitted is truncated mid-word in the final con ('no revision sin'), so the completeness section cannot be fully reviewed.

plans.name: Watch this before you buy a Shed. Building A 16x20 Shed Alone: Full Version Walls.
plans.footprint_note: The creator's own titles alternate between "16x20" and "20x16" for the same building (the channel playlist is named "Building A 20x16 Shed" and one Part 3 title reads "Building A 20x16 Shed Alone"). Nominal 16 ft x 20 ft on a poured slab; exact slab dimensions are never stated on the page.
plans.style: Single-story low-slope (near-flat) shed/garage-style outbuilding with one wide open door bay, built on grade next to an existing shed. Roof framed on site from 2x4x16 rafters bearing on a beam carried by posts, decked and covered with peel-and-stick roll roofing.
plans.price: Free
plans.summary: A solo-build documentary series, not a plan set: a woman frames and stands a 16x20 shed by herself on a poured concrete slab, and this episode is the unedited 5 hours 32 minutes "full version" of the wall assembly and squaring the building (published Jan 30, 2022; ~2,800 views). The description says only "This is for those who wanted more than the short videos... This will be Part 1. Part 2 will have the building of the rafters." Three more long-form episodes on the same channel continue the build: Part 2 Rafters On (1:39:56), Adding on the Roof Part 3 (2:15:46), and Part 3 Covering the Roof With Peel and Stick Roofing (58:13), plus short clips for the slab pour and for anchoring the walls to concrete with a Ramset Triggershot. There is no materials list, no cut list, no dimensions callout, no cost figure and no plan for sale anywhere on the page or in the descriptions — everything structural has to be read off the footage.
includes: Part 1 (this video, 5:32:14): building the 2x4 walls flat, standing/tilting them up alone, bracing, and squaring the building on the slab
Part 2 (1:39:56): building and setting the rafters — "Adding the Rafters. Part 3 will show how I added on the plywood."
Part 3 (2:15:46): adding on the roof / roof sheathing
Part 3b (58:13): covering the roof with peel-and-stick roll roofing (a GAF-style "PEEL & STICK ROOFING" carton is shown on camera)
Companion short: Day 1 pouring the concrete slab ("Got help here though….")
Companion short: Day 2 attaching the shed walls to the slab with a Ramset Triggershot powder-actuated tool
Companion short: getting the 2x4x16's up on top of the building for the rafters
pros: Genuinely a one-person build: the whole point of the series is standing 16 ft and 20 ft 2x4 walls alone, which is exactly the problem a solo DIYer needs to see solved rather than read about.
Real-time, uncut footage (5.5 h for the walls alone, ~10.4 h across the four long episodes) — nothing is jump-cut past, so bracing, squaring and re-plumbing mistakes are all visible.

Shows the slab-on-grade route end to end, including anchoring treated bottom plates to cured concrete with a Ramset Triggershot powder-actuated nailer — a fastening step most shed videos skip, and there are two extra clips dedicated to that tool.

Slab foundation plus 2x4 stud walls means no floor framing, no joist span math and no beam/skid sizing — the cheapest and simplest structural path for a 320 sq ft building if you can get concrete placed.
Free to watch, no upsell, no gated plan, no affiliate-link wall of text in the description.
Low-slope roof decked and covered with self-adhering peel-and-stick roll roofing is a realistic, forgiving DIY roof detail for a near-flat deck (no shingle-on-low-slope failure mode).
cons: No plan, no materials list, no cut list, no dimensioned drawing anywhere — you cannot price or order lumber from this series, you can only copy what you see.

No stated stud spacing, wall height, rafter spacing, rafter span, header sizes or roof pitch. The only lumber size ever named on the channel is "2x4x16's" for the rafters, which is a long span for 2x4 material and is not backed by any engineering, span table or truss design.

Nothing engineered: no stamped truss, no sealed drawing, no load or wind/snow discussion, so this is poor evidence to hand a permit office. Zero permit, setback, inspection or code discussion appears on the page.

The series appears to stop at roofing. No siding-installation, door, window, trim, insulation, interior finish or electrical episode was found; the wide door bay visible over the front header is never shown getting a door.

Episode numbering is broken (two different videos are both titled "Part 3") and the official channel playlist "Building A 20x16 Shed" holds only 4 items, two of which are a short and an unrelated video — you have to assemble the series by hand from channel search.
No captions, no chapters and no timestamps on a 5 hour 32 minute video, so finding a specific step means scrubbing. Handheld phone footage, not instructional camera work.
Very low viewership on the long-form episodes (891–2,800 views) means almost no comment-thread corrections or peer review of the methods shown.
Concrete slab is a hard prerequisite: it was poured with help in a separate short, so the biggest cost and skill hurdle in the project is the one part the series does not teach.

plans.permit_notes: This is a free institutional/extension sheet with no engineer's stamp, no snow, wind or seismic load, and no code references. NDSU's Building Plans hub carries an explicit disclaimer: "These plans provide conceptual information. Periodic changes in the National Design Specifications for Wood Construction, changes in building materials, snow load variations and the serious impact of deviations from the plans make it imperative that professional services be utilized to tailor these plans for your situation... North Dakota State University, the Midwest Plan Service, the United States Department of Agriculture, and none of the cooperating Land-Grant Universities warranty these plans." Practically: 2x4 rafters at 24" o.c. spanning a 20 ft gable and 2x4 studs at 24" o.c. are 1949 practice and will likely not pass a modern plan review in snow country; expect a plans examiner to require upsized rafters or engineered trusses. A 400 sq ft slab-on-grade garage with a frost-depth perimeter almost always requires a building permit, and the sheet gives no rebar, anchor-spacing-to-code, or frost-depth number for your jurisdiction. Only the plan number, issuing body and revision date identify the document; there is no license/copyright statement on the sheet (US federal/land-grant extension origin, freely redistributed by NDSU).

It is a 20'-0" x 20'-0" (400 sq ft) stud-frame building on a pitched concrete slab with a frost-depth perimeter wall and front apron: 2x4 studs at 2'-0" o.c. with 7'-6" studs, doubled 2x4 plates, 2x4 rafters at 2'-0" o.c. 12'-0" long on a 1x6 ridge with 2x4 ties at 4'-0" o.c., wood drop siding, a boxed 1x4/1x3 cornice, six double-hung sash, a 1'-9" round gable window, and two front openings 9'-0" on centers each closed by a pair of hinged 4'-0"x7'-0" doors. Despite being one page it is a real (if minimal) buildable plan set — dimensioned plan, all four elevations, a transverse section, two construction sections, a round-window detail and a cornice isometric — but there is NO materials list, no cut list, no instructions, no cost, and no engineering: the framing sizes and 24" spacings are 1949 practice, and NDSU explicitly warrants nothing and tells you to have a professional adapt it to current wood-design specs and snow loads.
pros: Genuinely free and frictionless: a 122 KB PDF straight off ag.ndsu.edu, HTTP 200, no email, no account, no upsell; prints on one 11x17 or tiles onto letter paper.

Unusually complete for a one-sheet freebie: dimensioned floor plan, all four elevations, a transverse section AND two construction sections (A-A through the side wall/roof, B-B through the door wall), a round-window detail and an isometric cornice detail, all at stated scales (1/4"=1'-0" and 3/4"=1'-0").
400 sq ft clear-span square box with nothing structural inside — no posts, no bearing partition — plus a built-in work bench with 4x4 legs already drawn along one side wall.

Slab-on-grade means zero floor framing and no rot-prone skid/joist detailing; the sheet actually dimensions the important bits (2" slab pitch to the front, 5/8"x20" anchors at not over 6'-0" o.c., 6" concrete wall under the apron, walls carried below frost to solid bearing soil).
Stick-built 7-in-12 gable with 12'-0" rafters: no trusses to order, deliver or crane, and every rafter/tie member is spelled out, so a competent DIYer can cut the roof from this drawing alone.

Dimensionally adaptable by design — the plan literally notes "20'-0" OR TO SUIT CAR", so shortening or lengthening the depth (e.g. to 16x20 or 20x24) is anticipated, and sibling free plans exist at 12x20, 18x20, 18x24 and 24x24 for comparison.
Front gable wall is all door: two openings 9'-0" on centers give roughly two 8-ft bays, which is far friendlier for machinery/vehicle access than a typical shed plan.
cons: Structurally obsolete as drawn: 2x4 rafters at 24" o.c. spanning a 20 ft gable, and 2x4 studs at 24" o.c., are 1949 assumptions. Under a North Dakota-class snow load you should expect to upsize rafters substantially or substitute engineered trusses — which also invalidates the cornice/tie details as drawn.

No engineering, no stamp, no load criteria; NDSU disclaims all warranty and states that "professional services be utilized to tailor these plans for your situation", so a permit office is likely to want a stamped roof-framing revision before approval.

No materials list, no cut list, no quantities, no fastener/nailing schedule, no instructions and no cost estimate — you must do all take-off and sequencing yourself. NDSU's own catalog flags plans that include a materials list with "ML"; 5149 has none.

Image-only scan of hand lettering with no text layer: readable only by rendering at high DPI, and several notes (window glass size, footing width/thickness, some fraction glyphs) are genuinely illegible.

Period materials and hardware: wood drop siding directly over studs with no sheathing, housewrap, insulation, vapor barrier or interior lining, and four side-hinged glazed 4'-0"x7'-0" garage doors plus a 1'-9" round spoke window — all of which you will have to fabricate or substitute, and swapping in a modern overhead door means re-designing the header and center post.

Concrete is the cost and labor driver and the least DIY-friendly part: a pitched 20x20 slab, a perimeter wall carried below frost line, a 6" wall under an exterior apron and the apron itself — with no rebar, slab thickness or frost depth specified.
No walk/service door and no side or rear access is drawn: the only way in is through the vehicle door openings, and the fixed double-hung sash arrangement gives no egress.
No electrical, lighting, ventilation, gutter or roofing-material specification at all ("ROOFING" is just a label).

plans.summary: A first-time builder and his wife stake out, frame, sheath, side, roof, trim, insulate and panel a 16x20 ft single-slope-roof building in their suburban backyard, documented across 18 free YouTube episodes from Oct 22, 2024 to Apr 10, 2025. Part 1 (16:56, 302 views) is pure layout: pulling string lines and squaring the 16x20 footprint on grass next to a fire pit that has to go. Later episodes show an OSB-decked wood floor, 2x4 walls at 16 in o.c. built flat and tilted up, OSB sheathing with window openings cut after sheathing, site-cut 2x rafters for the mono-pitch roof, painted vertical-panel siding with cedar trim, then fiberglass insulation and interior wall paneling. There are no plans, no cut list, no materials list and no cost figure anywhere - the video descriptions are literally just hashtags.
plans.foundation: Pressure-treated perimeter beam set on stacked black composite/plastic leveling shim pads bedded in small pockets of crushed gravel - clearly visible on camera. Pad count, spacing, footing depth and frost detail are never stated.
plans.floor_framing: Joist size, spacing and beam sizing are never stated, but the perimeter rim/band is visibly green pressure-treated lumber (doubled at the corner).
plans.wall_framing: 2x4 studs at roughly 16 in o.c. with horizontal mid-height blocking; walls assembled flat on the OSB deck and tilted up (visible in "Framing Some Walls!!", "Framing up our 16x20 Family Entertainment Studio!!" and "I need a belt!"). Sheathed in OSB; window/door rough openings with headers were cut after the sheathing went on ("Front side sheeting goes up and cut out for the three windows").

pros: Completely free, no gate, no email capture, no upsell - 18 episodes and about 4 h 12 min of real footage of an actual 320 sq ft build.

The single-slope shed roof is the friendliest roof geometry for a DIYer at this size: site-cut 2x rafters, no ridge, no valleys, no hips, no engineered trusses to order or crane in, and two people with a step ladder can set it.

Conventional 2x4-at-16-in tilt-up walls on an OSB-sheathed wood floor deck is the cheapest and most forgiving structural system for 16x20, and you watch the walls actually get built flat on the deck and stood up.
Goes well past the shell that most shed videos stop at: eaves and fascia, exterior cedar trim, painting and sealing, insulation and interior wall paneling all get dedicated episodes.
Three episodes are published deliberately unedited (fascia/eaves), so you see real-time technique and real-time problem solving rather than a timelapse montage.
Two-person husband-and-wife crew with no heavy equipment, which is an honest match for the reader's own likely labour situation.
Very small channel (Part 1 has 302 views), so the creator is reachable in comments if you have a question.
cons: No plans, no cut list, no materials list, no lumber takeoff and no cost figure anywhere. The video descriptions are literally hashtags only, so you cannot price it or order lumber from this series.

The foundation is never explained. Part 1 shows only string lines on grass; the floor deck already exists in the next episode. No pier, block, skid, gravel or slab detail, no joist size, no joist spacing, and the deck visibly sits very low to grade - a rot and drainage risk you would have to solve yourself.

The single most safety-critical member, the roof rafter spanning the 16 ft direction, is never sized or specified. The roofing episode is only 5:06, there is no rafter-layout or bird's-mouth episode, and the finished roof covering is never identified.
Not truly start-to-finish. No electrical, no plumbing, no ceiling, no interior trim, no flooring and no finished walk-through; the series simply stops after the April 10, 2025 wall-paneling episode.

No playlist and effectively no episode numbering. Only the first video says 'Part 1'; the remaining 17 are scattered among 44 unrelated channel uploads under three different names (16x20 Workshop / 16x20 Family Entertainment Studio / 16x20 Building), so watching in order is manual detective work.

Hand-held phone footage with heavy wind noise - two episodes are literally titled 'wind is horrible'. The creator narrates casually and self-identifies as a first-timer, so it is inspiration and morale, not instruction you can build to.
The purpose changes mid-build from workshop to 'Family Entertainment Space', so window count, door placement and interior finish decisions are revised on camera rather than planned.

I'll be framing it in for a door and three more windows later on", "Rain and now more rain is holding us up", and all quoted episode titles.

- VENDOR BANNER: I nearly flagged this as fabricated - "Bluegrass" appears 0 times in the watch page, channel page, about page and shorts page HTML, and the channel banner image is just a photo of a burning campfire ring with no text. But cropping and upscaling the 59T-8YuoJB0 thumbnail revealed a white vinyl banner zip-tied to the back fence reading "BLUEGRASS / WOODWORKING & CARPENTRY" in blue with a horse-head logo. The claim is CORRECT and correctly attributed to an on-site banner rather than the channel banner.
- Single-slope roof: CONFIRMED visually. oRSbXo_9x1Q shows the finished shell with an unmistakable mono-pitch roof, high on one long wall and dropping to the other, low pitch (looks ~2:12-3:12, not stated). No trusses; B2AmRV9a14A shows site-cut dimensional rafters with blocking and OSB roof deck.
- 2x4 walls, mid-height horizontal blocking, tilt-up off the OSB deck, OSB sheathing: all confirmed in frames. Stud spacing measures ~14-16 in o.c. by pixel scaling against an 8 ft wall; the record's hedged "roughly 16 in o.c." is fair.
- Loft "none": consistent with every interior frame (open to rafters, no platform).
- wall_height / overall_height / est_material_cost / permit_notes "not stated": correct, nothing contradicts.
- IMAGE: /home/ethan/woodshed/assets/img/bigtimedecisions-16x20-shed-roof-workshop.jpg is a real 1280x720 baseline JPEG, 270,357 bytes, and is the genuine maxresdefault of 9riva1gWPpU. It shows exactly what the summary describes: string lines pulled across grass with a stone-and-gravel fire pit sitting inside the footprint and an Ameri-Lite camper parked alongside. No fix needed.

COMPLETENESS GAP THE RECORD MISSES (check #7): the series has two undocumented jumps, not one. The record correctly flags that the floor deck "simply appears already built" (Oct 22 layout -> Nov 9 walls already standing on a finished OSB deck). It does NOT flag the second, larger gap: no upload at all between Dec 30 2024 and Feb 26 2025, across which the entire wall-siding installation happened off camera. Combined with zero dimensions, zero cut list and zero cost, this is a "watch someone build it" series, not a buildable set of instructions - which the record does say, but it should also say that two of the major stages (floor deck, siding) are simply absent from the footage.

ENGINEERING NOTE: pros/cons were truncated out of the record supplied to me, so I could not audit them. One thing a reviewer should watch for if they exist: the rafters in B2AmRV9a14A look like 2x6/2x8 at roughly 24 in o.c. spanning what appears to be the 16 ft direction on a very low-slope mono-pitch roof, with no stated pitch. For a Kentucky/southern-Indiana snow load that is marginal at best, and any cons list should note that no rafter span or pitch is ever given, so the roof framing cannot be copied safely without an independent span table.

plans.name: 84 Lumber 1-1½ Car Trussed Garage — Standard Elevation, 16'x20' (item 810-06-99 / 810-07-99)
plans.footprint_note: 16'x20' is the smallest of nine sizes (12 size/elevation listings) in the "1-1½ Car Trussed Garage" family
plans.style: Gable-roof detached garage/shop with engineered roof trusses; gable-end (front) overhead door, service door and window on the eave wall. Slab-on-grade in all renderings.
plans.price: Not published — quote-only through a local 84 Lumber store ("Ready to Buy? Find Your Store"). Historical reference: 84 Lumber's own "Garage Ballpark Price List" (PDF, dated 2/5/2019, archived) lists 16'x20' w/ 9'x7' overhead door at $3,700 with grooved siding and $4,280 with vinyl siding — explicitly "ballpark prices only", material package only, 2019 dollars. That PDF is no longer live on 84lumber.com.
plans.summary: 84 Lumber's "1-1½ Car Trussed Garage" page is a catalog entry for an in-store building-material package (not a downloadable plan set). The 16'x20' Standard Elevation version — item 810-06-99 / 810-07-99 — is a stick-framed, gable-roof one-car garage/shop with 16" o.c. wall framing, engineered roof trusses, grooved plywood or vinyl siding, fiberglass shingles with drip edge, wood soffit and fascia (aluminum with the vinyl package), a 9'x7' overhead garage door, a steel insulated service door and one window. Optional upgrades listed are drywall, ventilation, shelving, gutter and downspouts, skylights, extra windows and doors, insulation and cabinets. You buy it by visiting or getting a quote from a local 84 Lumber store; the company also advertises a free garage custom-design/estimating service. Crucially, the published feature list contains no floor system, no foundation materials, and no explicit mention of plans, hardware or fasteners (84 Lumber's shed/barn packages DO list "Plans & instructions," "Hardware & fasteners," pressure-treated floor framing and a 5/8" CDX floor — the garage list does not), so a concrete slab is an owner-supplied extra. No price, wall height, roof pitch, overall height, truss span/loading data, or bill of materials is published online. The packages are not sold in AZ, CA, FL or NV due to code restrictions. Best treated as a "buy the shell materials from a lumberyard, get store help with the take-off" option rather than a self-contained DIY plan purchase.

pros: Engineered roof trusses clear-span the 16' width, so there are no interior posts and no rafter/collar-tie layout or ridge-beam sizing for the builder to figure out — the biggest structural unknown is solved by the supplier.

The package is priced and taken off by a local lumberyard that also delivers, so you get one source for framing, siding, shingles, doors and window instead of assembling a materials list yourself; 84 Lumber advertises a free garage custom design/estimating service and same-day-purchase delivery.

16x20 (320 sq ft) with a 9'x7' overhead door is a genuinely usable one-car garage or shop footprint, and the identical package family scales up to 16x24, 18x20/24, 20x20/24/28 and 22x24/28 if you want more room without changing detailing.
Real doors and windows are in the package (steel insulated service door, overhead door, one window) — items DIY plan sets always leave you to source and often mis-budget.

Engineered trusses plus a lumberyard-generated material list is usually easier to get through a building department than a homemade rafter design, and 84 Lumber can customize a package/plan to suit local requirements.
Vinyl-siding option (with aluminum soffit and fascia) is a low-maintenance upgrade path priced only a few hundred dollars above grooved plywood siding in the archived list.
cons: NO FLOOR AND NO FOUNDATION IN THE PACKAGE: the published standard-feature list has no floor joists, no floor sheathing and no concrete. 84 Lumber's shed/barn packages explicitly list pressure-treated floor framing and a 5/8" CDX floor; the trussed-garage list does not. Budget a separate 16x20 slab (or your own framed floor) — often a four-figure cost on its own.

PRICE BASIS: nothing on the live page is priced; it is a materials-only, kit-only quote from a store — NOT delivered-and-assembled, and not delivered-inclusive either (delivery is a separate 84 Lumber service). The only number available anywhere is an archived 2/5/2019 "ballpark" list ($3,700 grooved / $4,280 vinyl for 16x20), which is seven years stale and excludes slab, labor, permits, delivery and every optional upgrade.

The feature list never says construction drawings are included. 84 Lumber's shed, gambrel-barn, gazebo and tiny-home packages all explicitly list "Plans & instructions" or "Blueprints" — the trussed garage list does not, so treat the plan set (and hardware/fasteners) as unconfirmed until the store confirms in writing.

Zero published engineering or dimensional data: no wall height, no roof pitch, no overall height, no truss span/snow-load rating, no header sizes, no footing detail, no page count and no bill of materials. You cannot compare it dimension-for-dimension against a real plan set before you walk into a store.
Not available at all in AZ, CA, FL or NV "due to code restrictions," and availability elsewhere is store-by-store ("Contact your local store for details and availability").

Erecting a full garage — slab, 16 o.c. walls, setting 16'-span trussed roof, hanging an overhead door — is a bigger, more crane/helper-dependent job than a shed; skill level and build time are not stated anywhere.

The website's elevation captions disagree with 84 Lumber's own catalog and price list on which elevation gets the 16'x7' door (site labels Elevation A as 9'x7'; the 2026 catalog and 2019 price list put the 16'x7' door on Elevation A), so verify door sizes on the actual quote. (This does not affect the 16x20, which is Standard Elevation with a 9'x7' door.)
Two item numbers are shown per size with no explanation of which is grooved siding and which is vinyl — you must have the store confirm the SKU matches the siding you want.
No published loft or second-floor option in this line; loft/apartment configurations only appear in 84 Lumber's Specialty/Premium garage packages, so 320 sq ft is all the space you get.

plans.summary: A free 39-minute produced episode in which contractor Jeff Thorman frames a 14x20 ft (280 sq ft) single-slope-roof shed/workshop on his 1880s farmhouse property, largely working solo. YouTube's key-moment chapters map the actual content: "Single Slope Roof" (2:40), "Build the Back Wall" (3:58), "Build a Sidewall" (11:18), "Put the Two Walls Together" (13:28) and "Day Two" (26:59) — i.e. it is a wall-framing and roof-concept episode, and the follow-up EP18 covers installing the shed's windows and its overhead garage door. There is no materials list, no cut list, no dimensioned drawing and no stated cost anywhere on the page or in the description; the only shed plans Home RenoVision sells ($12.00) are for a completely different 6 ft x 9 ft shed. Treat this as technique and sequencing instruction for a large single-slope shed, not as a buildable plan set.
includes: Single-slope (shed/skillion) roof concept and why it was chosen — chapter at 2:40
Framing the 14 ft back wall — chapter at 3:58
Framing a 20 ft sidewall — chapter at 11:18
Standing and joining the wall panels together — chapter at 13:28
A second day of on-site framing — chapter 'Day Two' at 26:59
Working-alone technique: 'This Shed is definitely easier to build with a helper... Sometimes it is just better to Do It Yourself, with the right tricks.'
Companion episode EP18 (37:35): installing the shed's windows and fighting an overhead garage door into place (chapters 'GARAGE DOOR VS. JEFF - ROUND 2 / ROUND 3')
NOT included: no materials list, no cut list, no dimensioned drawings, no cost breakdown, no span or load tables, no electrical
NOT identified in this episode's metadata: foundation/slab work, roof sheathing and roofing, siding, insulation, interior finish
pros: Free and unusually large for a YouTube shed build — 280 sq ft is in the target 240-480 sq ft range, whereas most free video builds top out around 8x12.
The single-slope (shed) roof is the cheapest and simplest roof on a building this size: no trusses to build or buy, no ridge, no valleys, one sheathing plane, and it drains all runoff to one side.
The chapter list is exactly the sequence a one- or two-person crew needs for 20 ft walls: build the back wall, build a sidewall, then join the two — rather than a generic time-lapse.
Host Jeff Thorman is a career renovation contractor; the stated selling point is 'with the right tricks', so the value is technique for handling long, heavy walls without a crew.
Properly produced series (dedicated cinematographer, director, aerial photography), so the camera work is genuinely usable as instruction and not a shaky phone on a bucket.
Door and window work is not skipped — the very next episode (EP18) is dedicated to installing the shed's windows and its overhead garage door, including the rough-opening struggles.
An overhead garage door on a 14 ft wall makes this a vehicle/equipment-capable outbuilding rather than a storage shed, which is a real design upgrade over most free plans.
Free channel membership tier ('DIY Crew') offers Q&A with Jeff and his team, so follow-up questions have somewhere to go.
cons: No plan set at all: no materials list, no cut list, no dimensioned drawings, no stud spacing, no rafter size or span. You must derive every dimension yourself from watching. This is the single biggest limitation.
The $12.00 'DIY Shed Plans' sold at homerenovisiondiy.com are explicitly for a 6 ft x 9 ft shed, NOT this 14x20 — do not buy them expecting these plans.
No material cost is stated anywhere, so the source gives you nothing to budget a 280 sq ft building from.

No total build time is stated. Chapters jump from joining the walls (13:28) to 'Day Two' (26:59), and EP18 shows doors/windows still going in through 'NOVEMBER - LATE FALL' and 'THE FIRST SNOWFALL' in December — so the real project ran weeks to months, compressed into 40 minutes.

The foundation is never described in any page text. The video's own keyword tags include 'concrete slab', 'diy concrete slab' and 'how to pour a slab', hinting at a poured slab — if so, that is the largest cost, skill and equipment driver of the whole project and a big step up from skids or piers.

Nothing is engineered: no snow or wind load, no single-slope rafter span table for a 14 ft span. At 280 sq ft this building will exceed the permit-exempt threshold in most jurisdictions, and you would have nothing to submit to a building department.

It is episode 17 of a whole-house renovation series, not a dedicated shed course — the shed content is split across two episodes inside a 16-video farmhouse playlist and interleaved with the renovation storyline, so it is not a clean linear tutorial.
Roofing, siding, sheathing and finishing are not identified as covered in this episode; you will have to hunt through the rest of the season or other channels for those steps.
Footage is from 2020 (uploaded 2021), so lumber prices, product picks and affiliate links referenced are stale.

plans.summary: A one-hour-six-minute solo build-and-tutorial video in which the creator of My DIY Builds frames a 16' x 20' garage entirely by himself, described in his own words as "the full garage assembly of a 16' x 20' that I framed up in under 2 days. All...By...My...Self..." The visible footage shows stick-framed stud walls with double top plates being stood and braced on an already-poured concrete slab, OSB wall sheathing, a site-framed gable roof sheathed in OSB, a wide garage-door rough opening in the gable end and a prehung glazed entry door. The final on-camera building is at the dry-in/sheathing stage — no siding, roofing or garage door is shown installed. There is no materials list, cut list, cost figure or chapter list anywhere on the page; the description is only affiliate tool links and social handles, so the video is a watch-and-copy instructional rather than a documented plan set.
includes: Standing, plumbing and bracing stick-framed stud walls on a concrete slab (solo techniques)
Wall sheathing with OSB
Site-framed gable roof: cutting and setting the roof members single-handed
Roof sheathing with OSB
Garage-door rough opening / header framing in the gable end
Prehung entry door opening
One-man rigging and lifting tricks (the core selling point of the channel)
pros: Genuinely free, start-of-framing to dry-in, in one continuous 66-minute video — no paywall, no email gate, no upsell.
Directly on-target size: the title and description explicitly state 16' x 20' (320 sq ft), which is exactly the footprint the user wants.
Whole build is done by one person, so every technique shown is achievable solo — wall raising, bracing and setting roof members without a crew. That is rare and hard to find elsewhere.
Slab-on-grade foundation means no wood floor system, no joist spans to size, and no rot exposure; it is the simplest floor for a 16-ft-wide building.
Clear tripod/wide-shot camera work in the visible frames: you can see plate layout, stud spacing and bracing rather than a shaky close-up montage.
Creator's channel has ~20 more garage builds (14x22, 20x26, 24x30, 24x32) so you can cross-reference his method at other spans if a detail is unclear.
cons: No materials list, no cut list, no lumber quantities and no dimensioned drawings anywhere on the page — you must pause-and-count off the screen or generate your own takeoff.
No cost figure is stated, so you get no budget anchor for a 320 sq ft slab-on-grade garage.
Not a true start-to-finish build: the concrete slab already exists when framing begins, and the building is still bare OSB at the end — siding, roofing, garage door and any electrical are not shown.

The roof is site-framed by hand, not engineered trusses, and no pitch, rafter size or spacing is published. A 16-ft clear span roof plus a header over a wide garage opening is exactly where a building department will want numbers you do not have.

'Framed up in under 2 days' is the creator's pace as an experienced framer; a first-timer should not treat that as a schedule.
Description is largely Amazon affiliate tool links, so the video doubles as tool marketing.
