plans.footprint_note: Stated repeatedly as "12x24 foot shed"; the plan sheet shown on the product page adds "Ensure that everything still measures 12'x24' from outside to outside," so 12x24 is the outside-of-framing dimension (288 sq ft).
plans.style: Single-storey gable-roof storage shed / backyard woodshop, double doors on one gable end
plans.price: Free (both videos); matching digital plan set sold separately for $19.00
plans.summary: A two-part YouTube build log by Keimpiece Carpentry documenting the owner-builder construction of a 12x24 ft (288 sq ft) gable shed used as a woodworking shop. Part 1 (12:01, published 2022-01-14, ~2.87M views) covers layout, the on-grade pressure-treated beam/concrete-pad foundation, floor deck, and 2x4 wall sections stood up and joined; Part 2 (9:39, published 2022-05-30, ~274K views) is the "final touches" episode covering roof, shingles, siding, trim, painting and the heavy double doors. The creator designed the whole thing in SketchUp and sells the resulting plan set for $19 at keimpiece.com; that plan set explicitly covers "foundation, framing, roof truss construction, and doors" and deliberately skips trim, soffits, siding, vents and shingles. No materials list, cut list, or dollar cost is published on the video page — the only cost claim is "I did the math and discovered I can save many thousand dollars by doing it myself."
includes: Part 1: site layout, on-grade foundation (pressure-treated beams on precast concrete pads), floor framing and deck sheathing
Part 1: 2x4 wall sections framed flat on the deck, stood up, temporarily braced, and nailed/screwed together through double joining center 2x4s
Part 1: window and door rough openings framed with headers (two window openings in the long wall, wide opening in the gable end)
Part 2: roof deck, asphalt shingles (roofing nailer used), trim and soffit work
Part 2: siding install, spray painting/finishing, window install
Part 2: hanging the double entry doors — 3 hinges per door, each door ~100 lb
Tool list in the description (track saw, framing nailer, roofing nailer, cordless sprayer) with affiliate links
Link to the paid $19 12x24 SketchUp-derived plan set covering foundation, framing, roof trusses and doors
pros: Real 288 sq ft footprint in the target size band — a genuine workshop, not a garden locker, and 12 ft of width means simple single-span 2x4 trusses instead of anything exotic.
Start-to-finish coverage across the two parts: foundation, floor, walls, trusses, roof, shingles, siding, paint and doors are all actually on camera, so nothing structurally major is hidden.
Free to watch, and the companion plan set is only $19 — cheap insurance if you want dimensioned drawings rather than pausing video frames.
The plan pages visible on the product listing are step-numbered ("Step 8 Continued") with SketchUp renders plus jobsite photos side by side, which reads well for a first-time framer.
On-grade pressure-treated beams on precast concrete pads keeps the foundation cheap and DIY-able — no slab pour, no concrete truck, and it stays movable/temporary in some jurisdictions.

Useful hard-won detail you rarely get from plan PDFs: the doors weigh ~100 lb each and needed three hinges, and the plan sheet warns to re-check 12'x24' outside-to-outside and to brace walls before they blow over.
Very high view count (2.87M on Part 1) means an active comment thread to search for gotchas.
cons: No materials list, cut list, or lumber takeoff anywhere on the video page or in the product description — you cannot price this build or make a lumberyard order from the videos alone.
No dollar figure is ever stated. "Save many thousand dollars" is the only cost claim, and 2022 lumber prices would not transfer to today anyway.
No build time stated, and the four-and-a-half-month gap between Part 1 (January 2022) and Part 2 (May 2022) suggests it was a long part-time project rather than a weekend.
Only ~21.5 minutes of runtime total for a 288 sq ft building — this is a fast-cut build montage with music, not a step-by-step tutorial. Expect to re-watch and freeze frames rather than follow along.

The paid plans explicitly do NOT cover trim, soffits, siding, vents or shingles — exactly the finish details a novice struggles with most. You get framing geometry and are on your own for the weather envelope.
Roof trusses are site-built by the owner and there is no indication they are engineered or stamped, so this will not satisfy a plan-review office that wants truss certs.
Nothing about permits, setbacks, frost depth, snow/wind loads, or anchoring is discussed — a block-on-grade foundation is a common permit sticking point for a building this size.
Wall height, overall height, roof pitch, joist and stud spacing, and header sizes are never stated on the page; you have to buy the $19 plans to get them.

The store's only stated refund policy is a boilerplate Shopify 30-day physical-goods return ("unworn or unused, with tags, and in its original packaging") with an unfilled [INSERT RETURN ADDRESS] — meaningless for an instant digital download, so treat the $19 as non-refundable.
Two videos, not an organized playlist — the parts are only linked from inside the descriptions, so ordering depends on you following those links.

plans.http_status: 200 (application/pdf, 80,531 bytes, 1 page, PDF 1.3, scanned raster image with no text layer)
plans.footprint_note: Drawn at 20 ft x 20 ft (400 sq ft), with 10 ft + 10 ft post spacing along the roost partition. A note says THIS TYPE OF HOUSE MAY BE BUILT IN ANY LENGTH TO MEET ALL REQUIREMENTS, WHEN A PARTITION IS PLACED AT 20 ft OR 30 ft INTERVALS TO AVOID DRAFTS, with a hen-capacity table running to 20 x 60. Depth stays 20 ft; only the length grows. NDSU's catalog line calls it a 20x20 CLEARSPAN SHEDROOF, but the drawing shows a 4x4 post supporting the roof at the roost partition, so it is not literally clear span.
plans.style: Open-front, single-slope (shed) roof poultry / laying house on a raised wood floor: stud-framed solid rear and end walls, south wall left open behind 1 inch mesh netting, roosts and dropping board along the low north side, nests along both end walls. Plain utility farm-building shell, no loft.
plans.price: Free
plans.summary: A single-sheet (Sheet 1 of 1) scanned Extension drawing, dated 1950 in NDSU's catalog, for a 20 x 20 ft (400 sq ft) open-front shed-roof poultry house, published free as plan Ex 5581 by NDSU Extension Agricultural & Biosystems Engineering. The sheet carries a floor plan, front (south), rear (north) and east end elevations and a cross section, with real framing callouts: 2x6 sills or floor joists on concrete piers, all studding 2x4, 2x6 rafters at 24 in o.c. 16 ft long lapped to 2x4 rafters at 24 in o.c. 8 ft long over a 2x6 beam on 4x4 posts, 1x12 or shiplap roof sheeting under composition roofing (corrugated iron allowed as an alternate). It is explicitly a poultry building, not a storage shed: the south wall is an open netted front, the north wall has two 2x7 ventilator doors and three small windows, and the interior is fitted with roosts, a dropping board, a draft baffle and nest boxes. It is a conceptual one-page sheet with NO materials list, NO cut list, no foundation reinforcing details, no nailing schedule and no load design, so it is not a complete buildable permit-ready plan set.
includes: Floor plan at graphic scale (roosts, dropping board, nests, 4x4 roof posts at 10 ft spacing)
Front elevation - South (open front with 1 inch mesh netting, five bays, hooded roof over the opening)
Rear elevation - North (two ventilator doors 2 ft x 7 ft, three small 4-light windows, poultry netting under doors and windows)
End elevation - East (3 ft x 7 ft door plus a second door labeled about 2 ft x 6 ft)
Cross section with member sizes, wall heights, roost and dropping-board layout and pier foundation
Framing callouts for sills/joists, studs, both rafter runs, roof sheeting and roofing
Hen-capacity / length table (20x20 through 20x60)
Construction notes on flooring, siding/sheeting alternatives and foundation alternatives
Graphic scale bars (1/2 in, 1/4 in, 0 to 3 ft) on each view
pros: Genuinely free, no email wall, no account, no upsell: the PDF is served directly and can be saved and printed.

Real dimensioned framing information for a 400 sq ft building, including rafter sizes, spacing and lengths, stud size, sill/joist size, sheeting and roofing - more substance than most free teaser plans.
Simple single-slope roof, hand-framed rafters, no trusses to buy or engineer; 2x6 rafters at 24 in o.c. spanning about 16 ft to an interior 2x6 beam on 4x4 posts keeps lumber sizes small and cheap.
Cheap foundation: concrete piers as drawn, with a note that concrete blocks may be substituted - no slab required, and the raised wood floor on 2x6 sills/joists is well suited to a rural site.
Scalable: the same section works at 20x30, 20x40, 20x50 or 20x60 just by extending the length, with partitions every 20 or 30 ft.
Public-domain-style Extension/USDA drawing, so there is no license or resale restriction to worry about.
cons: It is a poultry house, not a general-purpose shed: the entire south wall is an open netted front, and a lot of the sheet is roosts, dropping board, draft baffle and nest boxes. Converting it to a closed storage/workshop shed means redesigning the front wall yourself.
One sheet only, and NO materials list or cut list. NDSU's abbreviation key flags plans that have one with ML; the 5581 entry does not carry it. You must take off all quantities yourself.

1950-era design to pre-modern practice: 1x12 or shiplap board sheeting and board/car siding rather than plywood or OSB, 1 in nominal boards on the roof, no insulation, no vapor barrier, no house wrap, no hurricane/rafter ties, no nailing schedule.

No engineered load design. NDSU's own disclaimer states these plans are conceptual and that professional services are needed for structural design and code compliance because of changes in the National Design Specification, materials and snow loads. A shed roof this shallow (about 8 ft front to 6 ft rear over a 20 ft depth) is a real concern under northern snow loads and would likely need re-sizing.

Permit friendliness is poor as-drawn: no foundation reinforcing, no anchorage/uplift details, no load table, no code references, and 400 sq ft usually exceeds the permit-exempt threshold in most jurisdictions.
Scanned raster PDF, hand-lettered, no text layer, so some dimensions are hard to read and nothing is searchable or dimensionable digitally.
No electrical, no interior finish, no door/window construction details, and no window or door schedule beyond the size labels on the elevations.
Catalog calls it clearspan but the drawing shows a 4x4 post supporting the roof at the roost partition, so plan on interior posts unless you re-engineer the rafters.

plans.name: Maximum Spans: Southern Pine Joists & Rafters (2013 Edition, 46 span tables)
plans.footprint_note: varies
plans.style: Not applicable — reference span tables (floor joists, ceiling joists, rafters), not a shed style
plans.price: Free — no-cost PDF download published by SFPA on SouthernPine.com; no registration or payment seen
plans.summary: while No.2 2x10s need 12" o.c. (16'-2"), No.1 grade (16'-1" @16"), or a mid-span beam
includes: Index to Tables listing all 46 tables with their live load, dead load and deflection limit
Floor joist tables 1-7: conventional loads (30/10, 40/10, 50/10, 60/10, 40/20, 50/20, 60/20 psf), l/360
Floor joist tables 8-11: heavy live loads 75, 80, 90, 100 psf with 10 psf dead, l/360
Wet-service floor joist tables 12-14 (MC > 19%): 40, 60, 100 psf live / 10 psf dead
Ceiling joist tables 15-16: 10/5 psf and 20/10 psf, l/240
Rafter tables 17-40: snow loads, CD = 1.15, live 20-50 psf, dead 10/15/20 psf, deflection l/240 and l/180
Rafter tables 41-46: construction loads, CD = 1.25, 20 psf live, dead 10/15/20 psf, l/240 and l/180
Sizes 2x4 (ceiling joists) and 2x6 through 2x12 at 12", 16", 19.2" and 24" on center
Ten grades per table: DSS, No.1, No.2, No.3, MSR 2400f-2.0E / 1650f-1.5E / 1500f-1.6E, MEL M-14 / M-29 / M-12
Southern Pine reference design values table (Fb, Fv, Fc-perpendicular, E) by size and grade
Species span comparison graphs: Southern Pine vs Spruce-Pine-Fir vs Hem-fir (No.1/No.2 2x6 ceiling joists, 2x12 floor joists)
Design assumptions section: adjustment factors Cr, CD, CM; deflection limits; 2.0" bearing assumption; shear and compression-perp checks
Roof live-load reduction factors for 12 psf and 16 psf roof live loads (tables 17/29, 21/33, 25/37)
Three worked examples: reading table values, 14 ft living-room floor joists, and a 12x14 outdoor deck (wet-service)
Rafter conversion diagram (courtesy AWC) converting horizontal projection to sloping member length by roof slope
Nominal vs actual dry lumber size table and typical grade marks / grading-agency notes
Support requirements text: ridge beam vs ridge board rules, hangers, ceiling joists as continuous ties
"Building with Wood" / "Why Wood?" background pages and an Additional Resources list of other SFPA publications
pros: Free, code-anchored numbers: spans were computed on the same basis as AWC's code-recognized Span Tables for Joists and Rafters using SPIB design values effective June 1, 2013 — far more defensible to a plans examiner than a YouTube rule of thumb.
Covers exactly the decisions a 16x20 shed builder must make: floor joist size/grade/spacing, loft or ceiling joists, and rafter size for a given horizontal projection, at 12", 16", 19.2" and 24" o.c.
Includes heavy live-load floor tables (75, 80, 90, 100 psf) that ordinary residential tables omit — the right place to look for a workshop floor carrying machinery or a dense-storage loft.
Wet-service tables 12-14 (MC > 19%) let you size pressure-treated joists honestly for an open or ground-hugging shed floor instead of borrowing dry-service numbers.

Both snow-load (CD = 1.15) and construction-load (CD = 1.25) rafter tables, at l/240 for a finished/drywalled ceiling and l/180 for an open ceiling — you can pick the case that matches your shed instead of over-buying.
Explicitly spells out that tabulated spans are clear spans inside-to-inside of bearings, with a worked example showing you add 7" for bearing on two 2x4 walls — a very common DIY error caught.
Rafter conversion diagram turns a horizontal run into actual rafter length (its own example: 20 ft horizontal at 8:12 = 24 ft sloping), useful for cut-length and lumber-order math.
Quantifies the cost/strength trade you actually face at the lumberyard: shows how much span you gain going No.2 to No.1 to Dense Select Structural, or to MSR/MEL, at each size and spacing.
Gives the stiffness upgrade path for a bouncy shop floor: multiply the tabulated span by 0.91 for l/480 or 0.84 for l/600.
Includes the reference design values (Fb, Fv, Fc-perp, E) it used, so an engineer or a beam calculator can be reconciled against the tables.
Text-selectable 36-page PDF, small (1.25 MB), easy to keep on a phone on site; SFPA also offers a printed Pocket Span Card version of the most popular tables.
cons: Not a plan and not a kit: zero drawings, no framing layout, no cut list, no materials list, no cost estimate, no foundation, sheathing, siding, door or window information. You still need a plan set or a designer.

Southern Pine only. If your yard stocks SPF, Hem-Fir or Douglas Fir-Larch (most of the northern US and Canada), these numbers do not apply — the booklet's own comparison graphs show SPF and HF spans differ in both directions.

No header, girder, ridge beam, post or column tables. A 16x20 shed with a garage door, a loft girder or a mid-span floor beam needs SFPA's separate Headers & Beams publication or an engineer; the booklet only tells you a ridge beam is required for cathedral ceilings, not how to size it.

Simple-span, uniformly-loaded members only: explicitly excludes concentrated and partition loads, wind uplift, continuous/multi-span joists, cantilevers, and any lateral or shear-wall design — a permit reviewer in a high-wind or seismic area will want more than this.

Not engineered for your project and carries a broad disclaimer: SFPA does not grade or test lumber, does not warrant the design values, and states users have final responsibility for confirming the load assumptions. It is not a stamped or site-specific document.

You must supply the loads yourself from the governing code (roof snow, floor live load, dead load) — a beginner can easily pick the wrong table, and choosing 20 psf snow in a 50 psf ground-snow county would be dangerous.

Grade-dependent numbers require lumber you can actually verify: spans apply only to properly grade-marked material, and No.2 (the usual big-box stock) is far weaker than the DSS/MSR columns that make the long spans look easy.
Tabulated spans are capped at 26'-0" and the text warns Southern Pine is commonly available only up to 20 ft, so long-span solutions in the tables may not be purchasable locally.
Compression-perpendicular checks assume a 2.0" bearing length; ledger-hung joists on 1-1/2" bearing need an extra check the booklet does not perform.

2013 Edition, file dated 2017: still the current download on SouthernPine.com but the design values and the AWC documents behind it predate current code cycles, so cross-check against your locally adopted IRC/IBC edition.

PDF is AES-encrypted with copy disabled, so quoting or pasting table values into your own notes takes extra effort; table columns are dense and easy to misread by one row (grade columns across, spacing rows down).

Rafter tables assume rafters are properly supported at the ridge and tied at the plate (ceiling joists parallel to rafters as a continuous tie); if your shed design has no tie or ridge beam, the tabulated spans overstate what you can build.

plans.floor_framing: Not a design — but the booklet is the sizing authority for it: floor joist tables 1-14 cover 2x6 through 2x12 at 12/16/19.2/24 inch o.c., live loads 30 to 100 psf with 10 or 20 psf dead load, all at l/360 live-load deflection, plus three wet-service tables for MC>19% (pressure-treated) applications. plans.skill_level: Reference material, not instructions. Usable by a careful DIY builder but it assumes you can already determine your governing code loads (roof snow, floor live, dead), pick the right table, read grade columns, and convert outside wall dimensions to clear spans. SFPA presents its publication list as "for design-build professionals" and says the tables are "directed principally to residential construction," with users bearing "final responsibility for determining if the load and design assumptions represent actual conditions."
plans.permit_notes: Helpful for permitting but not sufficient by itself. The spans "were determined on the same basis as those in the code-recognized Span Tables for Joists and Rafters and Wood Structural Design Data, both published by the American Wood Council," using SPIB design values effective June 1, 2013 and NDS-based adjustment factors — so citing a table generally satisfies a reviewer asking how you sized joists or rafters. However: spans exclude concentrated and partition loads, exclude wind uplift, assume simple spans and 2.0\" bearing, apply only to properly grade-marked Southern Pine, and the booklet directs users to "check governing building code requirements for other applicable occupancies" and to obtain snow loads from "the governing building code." SFPA explicitly disclaims warranty of the design values and any liability. It is not stamped or site-specific, so a jurisdiction requiring engineered drawings, lateral/uplift design, or a non-Southern-Pine species will need more.

quotes: Spans in the tables are listed in feet and inches and are the maximum allowable horizontal span of the member from inside to inside face of supports.
Users of these span tables have the final responsibility for determining if the load and design assumptions represent actual conditions for their specific applications.
Spans have been limited to 26'-0" based on material availability. Southern Pine is commonly available in lengths up to 20'. Check sources of supply for longer lengths.

If each end of the joists bears completely on top of a 2x4 stud wall, the overall length of these joists will be the maximum span plus seven inches (i.e., the net width of a 2x4 stud wall is 3-1/2", times two walls equals 7").

Listed spans also do not include checks for concentrated or partition loads that may be required by building codes for specific occupancy or use categories. Uplift loads caused by wind also have not been considered.
The repetitive member factor, Cr, of 1.15 was included due to the assumption of the installation of at least three joists or rafters spaced not more than 24" on center.
A ridge board may be substituted for a ridge beam when the roof slope equals or exceeds 3 in 12, except that ridge beams are required for cathedral ceilings.
Ceiling joists are not required when properly designed ridge beams are used.
The compression perpendicular-to-grain check used to develop these span tables assumes a 2.0" bearing length. An additional check is required for shorter bearing lengths, such as for 1.5" ledgers.
Example: Given a horizontal distance of 20 feet and a roof slope of 8 in 12, the sloping distance is 24 feet.
The Southern Forest Products Association (SFPA) does not grade or test lumber, and accordingly, does not assign design values to Southern Pine lumber.

Maximum spans in these tables apply to properly identified material. Lumber must be identified by the grade mark of an agency certified by the Board of Review of the American Lumber Standard Committee (ALSC).

plans.name: Shingled Roof Carport / Pavilion Package - 16' x 20' (page H1: Shingled Roof Metal Carports)
plans.footprint_note: 16'x20' is one of sixteen published footprints (12x12 through 24x24), each offered in 8', 10', or 12' post height. 84 Lumber does not state which dimension is width vs. depth, nor which pair of walls is open - the copy only says the package builds 'an open front and back carport', so the open sides are presumably the gable ends (drive-through) and the two grooved-siding walls are the eave walls carrying the doubled 2x10 truss carriers. 16x20 = 320 sq ft of COVERED area, not 320 sq ft of enclosed lockable space.
plans.style: Post-frame (pole-built) drive-through carport / open-wall pavilion with a shingled gable roof on manufactured trusses. Not an enclosed shed: two walls sheathed in 4'x8' grooved siding, front and back left open. 84 Lumber's catalog adds 'Open wall pavilions also available.'
plans.price: Not published - material-package price is quote-only through a local 84 Lumber store ('Ready to Buy? Find Your Store'). No price is shown for the 16x20 or for any other size.
plans.summary: 84 Lumber sells this as a pre-specified building-material package (kit) for a post-frame carport with a real shingled gable roof, offered in 16'x20' among sixteen sizes and in 8', 10' or 12' post heights. Structure is 6"x6" treated posts with 2"x6" treated skirt boards and 2"x6" girts at 2' o.c., doubled 2"x10" truss carriers, and roof trusses at 2' o.c., so the short direction is clear-spanned with no interior posts. The roof is a complete house-grade assembly: 7/16" OSB with plywood clips, #15 felt, fiberglass shingles, drip edge, ridge vent, eave overhangs, aluminum soffit and fascia. Walls get 4'x8' grooved siding; hardware and fasteners are included. Critically for a shed shopper: there is NO floor, NO slab or concrete, NO doors and NO windows in the package, and the front and back are deliberately open. It is a covered parking / pavilion structure, not a lockable 320 sq ft workshop. Price is not published at all - you take the package number to a store for a quote, and that quote is for materials only, not for delivery-and-assembly. Not sold in AZ, CA, FL or NV due to code restrictions. The identical feature list appears on the live page and on page 15 of 84 Lumber's 2026 Project Idea Catalog PDF, which gives good confidence in the component list even though no drawings, spans, pitch or engineering data are published.

2"x6" treated skirt boards
2"x6" wall girts at 2' o.c.
2"x10" double truss carriers
4'x8' grooved siding (for the closed walls only)

pros: Cheapest possible way to roof 320 sq ft: post-frame with 6x6 posts and 2x6 girts at 2' o.c. skips the floor deck, the slab and the stud walls entirely - far less lumber and labor than any stick-framed 16x20 shed.

Roof trusses are supplied in the package at 2' o.c. on doubled 2x10 truss carriers, so there is no rafter layout or bird's-mouth cutting, and the 16' direction is clear-spanned - completely column-free interior.

Complete house-grade roof assembly is in the kit (7/16" OSB + plywood clips, #15 felt, fiberglass shingles, drip edge, ridge vent, eave overhangs, aluminum soffit & fascia) - it matches residential roofing rather than looking like a bolt-together metal carport, which matters in HOA/neighborhood settings.
Three post heights (8', 10', 12') on every footprint: the 12' option gives RV, boat or trailer headroom that a stick-built shed with 8' walls cannot.
Sixteen footprints from 12x12 to 24x24 (12x20, 12x24, 16x16, 16x20, 16x24, 20x20, 20x24, 24x20, 24x24 all in scope), so you can size up without changing systems.
Hardware and fasteners are included, and 84 Lumber quotes and delivers it as one package from a local store with their own fleet - far fewer supply trips than sourcing a plan-based build yourself.
Same package family can be built as an open-wall pavilion, so the structure is genuinely dual-purpose.
cons: NO FLOOR IS INCLUDED, of any kind. The published feature list has no floor joists, no floor deck and no concrete mix - compare 84 Lumber's own gazebo packages, which explicitly list 'Concrete mix / Floor framing / Floor deck'. A gravel pad or concrete slab is an entirely separate cost you must budget on top of the kit.

PRICE IS KIT-ONLY AND NOT PUBLISHED. No dollar figure appears for any size; you must get a store quote. That quote is for the material package - delivery is a separate 84 Lumber service and no installation, labor or assembly is offered anywhere on this page. Do not read it as delivered-and-assembled. (The 2016 version of this page linked a 'ballpark prices' carport PDF; that PDF is now dead and is not in the Wayback Machine, so no historical price exists either.)

It is a carport/pavilion, not a shed. Front and back are open for drive-through and only two walls get grooved siding: no doors, no windows, no insulation, nothing lockable. You cannot secure tools in it as delivered, and closing it in later means buying end walls, doors and likely extra bracing outside the package.

Foundation and post embedment are completely unspecified - no footing depth, concrete backfill, uplift anchorage or post-setting detail is published, which is exactly what a plan reviewer will demand for a 320 sq ft roof in a snow or wind zone.

No blueprints or plan set are listed in the package. 84 Lumber advertises that its shed and barn packages 'include materials and plans', but the carport feature list does not mention plans, so assume you get a material package and must confirm drawings with the store.
No truss engineering data, roof pitch, snow/wind load rating or overall height is published - so permit-friendliness is unverifiable from the source even though the trusses are factory-built.
Not available in AZ, CA, FL or NV due to code restrictions (footnote on the page).

No cut list, no quantities, no lengths and no package/SKU numbers for the carports (84 Lumber prints SKUs for its garage and pole-barn packages but not for these), so you cannot price-shop the bill of materials against a lumberyard competitor.

Setting and plumbing 6x6 posts, hanging doubled 2x10 carriers and lifting/bracing 16' trusses 8-12 ft in the air is a 2-3 person job with staging - not a solo weekend build despite the simple parts count.

plans.name: Span Tables for Joists and Rafters, 2021 Edition (AWC STJR-2021)
plans.http_status: 200 (application/pdf, 1,122,379 bytes, served brotli-compressed from CloudFront/S3; use Accept-Encoding: identity if your client mangles br)
plans.footprint_note: varies
plans.style: Not applicable - species/grade-neutral engineering reference tables, usable for any stick-framed gable, gambrel, lean-to or shed-roof building. The document depicts no building.
plans.price: Free PDF download from awc.org - no registration, no order form
plans.summary: AWC's "Span Tables for Joists and Rafters," 2021 Edition (Copyright 2020 American Wood Council; PDF ModDate 2020-10-05) is the authoritative free reference for sizing dimension-lumber joists and rafters, and it is what most published shed plans are silently derived from. 52 letter-size pages: an "Explanation of Tables" (Sections 1-9), 7 floor-joist tables at L/360 deflection (F-1 to F-7; live loads 30/40/50/60 psf over 10 or 20 psf dead), 2 ceiling-joist tables at L/240 (C-1, C-2), 24 rafter tables (R-1 to R-12 at L/240 for a drywall ceiling attached to the underside; R-13 to R-24 at L/180 for no ceiling attached; live loads 20/30/40/50 psf over 10/15/20 psf dead), Table 9.1/9.2 for required compression perpendicular to grain (Fc-perp) with bearing-length and load/spacing adjustment factors, and an 8-page Appendix A Commentary with the derivation equations, load/occupancy guide Tables A-1 to A-4, three worked examples, and a horizontal-projection-to-sloping-length conversion diagram for rafters. Floor and ceiling spans are entered by modulus of elasticity E (0.8 to 2.4 million psi) with the required Fb printed under each table; rafter spans are entered by bending design value Fb (200-3000 psi) with the required E printed under each table. Spans assume S4S PS 20-20 lumber sizes, at least three members at not more than 24 in. on center, a single simple span, uniform load, and the member fully sheathed and nailed on the top edge. To convert a table answer into a lumber order you must also open the companion free document "Design Values for Joists and Rafters" (Tables W-1/W-2), which lists Fb/E/Fc-perp by species and grade. For a 16x20 shed the practical takeaways are legible immediately: a 16 ft clear floor span at 40 psf LL + 10 psf DL needs 2x10 at 16 in. o.c. with E of at least 1.6 million psi and Fb of at least 1,255 psi (Table F-2 gives 16 ft 5 in.), while 8 ft of rafter horizontal projection (a 16 ft wide gable) is easily met by 2x6 at 24 in. o.c. with Fb of 800 psi and E of only 0.36 million psi at L/180 (Table R-13).
includes: Explanation of Tables, Sections 1-9 (scope, lumber design values, PS 20-20 lumber sizes, moisture content, span measurement, roof loads, lumber identification/grade stamp, general NDS requirements, required compression perpendicular to grain)
CEILING JOISTS, L/240: Tables C-1 (10+5 psf, drywall ceiling, no attic storage) and C-2 (20+10 psf, limited attic storage) - sizes 2x4 to 2x10
RAFTERS, L/240 (drywall ceiling attached): Tables R-1 to R-12 - 20/30/40/50 psf LL crossed with 10/15/20 psf DL, sizes 2x4 to 2x12
RAFTERS, L/180 (no drywall ceiling attached): Tables R-13 to R-24 - same load matrix, sizes 2x4 to 2x12
Table 9.1 - required Fc-perp (psi) for simple-span joists/rafters by span (2-26 ft) and bearing length (1.5, 2.0, 2.5, 3.0, 3.5 in.)
Table 9.2 - Fc-perp adjustment factors for 14 live/dead load combinations x 4 on-center spacings
Section 6 adjustment table: multipliers on tabulated span and required E for 12 psf and 16 psf roof live loads (applies to R-1, R-5, R-9, R-13, R-17, R-21)

Appendix A Commentary A.1-A.10 with derivation equations (Eq. A.1-1 to A.3.3-2), L/480 and L/600 floor adjustment factors, two-span joist guidance, 2x5 adjustment rules, repetitive-member and load-duration factors
Tables A-1 to A-4: which material/occupancy each load table is intended for (e.g. R-1 = light roof, 1 course of asphalt shingles; R-9 = heavy roof, 2 in. clay book tile)
Three worked examples (single-span floor joist, rafter with Fc-perp check, two-span floor joists over a corridor)
Conversion Diagram for Rafters - nomograph converting horizontal projection to member length for slopes 3-in-12 through 20-in-12
pros: Free, current-generation, and authoritative: published by the American Wood Council, derived from the NDS and PS 20-20, and the source most building departments already recognize - printing the relevant table page is a cheap way to justify your joist and rafter sizing on a permit application without paying an engineer.

Answers the single hardest structural question in a 16x20 shed: whether the floor can clear-span 16 ft. Table F-2 (40 psf LL + 10 psf DL, L/360) shows 2x10 at 16 in. o.c. spans 16 ft 5 in. at E = 1.6 million psi / Fb = 1,255 psi, and 2x12 at 24 in. o.c. spans 16 ft 3 in. at E = 1.2 - so you can compare a clear-span floor against a mid-span beam quantitatively instead of guessing.

Big cost lever made visible: at 24 in. o.c. instead of 16 in. o.c. the same 2x10 drops from 16 ft 5 in. to 14 ft 4 in. (F-2, E=1.6), and adding one center girder halves the span so 2x6 or 2x8 suffices. Comparing tables shows exactly how much lumber depth you buy back with a beam and piers.

Covers the whole snow-load range a shed builder actually faces - roof live loads of 20, 30, 40 and 50 psf, plus a Section 6 adjustment table for 12 and 16 psf regions - so you can size rafters for your jurisdiction rather than copying a generic plan drawn for mild climates.

Correctly separates the two rafter deflection cases most DIY plans conflate: L/180 (Tables R-13 to R-24) for an open shed with no drywall ceiling, L/240 (R-1 to R-12) if you finish the underside. Using R-13 rather than R-1 for a bare workshop legitimately buys smaller rafters.

Rafters are trivially easy at shed scale, which the tables prove: for a 16 ft wide gable (8 ft horizontal projection) Table R-13 shows 2x6 at 24 in. o.c. reaches 8 ft 2 in. at Fb = 800 psi with a required E of only 0.36 million psi - well inside No.2 SPF. Loft floors and headers, not rafters, are the real constraint.

Loft/attic sizing is covered from both directions: C-1/C-2 for a ceiling with no or limited attic storage, and F-1 (30 psf LL) for an actual attic floor or sleeping loft - useful for a 16x20 gambrel with a usable second level.

Includes the details plan sets usually omit: required compression perpendicular to grain at bearing (Tables 9.1/9.2, with the note that a two-span joist doubles the required Fc-perp at the center support), straight-line interpolation permission, L/480 and L/600 factors (0.91 / 0.84) if you want a stiffer floor than code minimum, and the repetitive-member 15 percent Fb bonus.

The horizontal-projection conversion nomograph (page A-7) plus the explicit statement that rafter span is measured on the horizontal projection prevents the most common DIY sizing error - using the rafter's cut length as the span.

Genuinely reusable across every option in a shed shortlist: it lets you audit whether a free plan's 2x6 floor joists at 16 ft are actually adequate, which is exactly the check most free shed plans never publish.
Clean 8.5x11 PDF, no paywall, printing allowed, and the companion supplement, an errata addendum, a web span calculator and a loads tutorial are all free on the same site.
cons: It is a reference document, not a plan: zero drawings, zero dimensions, no cut list, no material list, no elevations, no foundation detail, no cost or build-time estimate. You cannot build anything from this alone.

Unusable by itself - Section 2 requires the separate free companion 'Design Values for Joists and Rafters' (Tables W-1/W-2) to learn whether, say, No.2 SPF actually delivers the Fb and E the span table demands. Budget on downloading two documents, and note the September 2021 addendum that adds W-1 values for non-North-American graded lumber.
This is the 2021 edition. AWC has since published a 2024 edition (awc.org/resources/2024-span-tables/ plus a 2024 DVJR); if a plan reviewer is on a newer code cycle, cite the 2024 edition instead.

Narrow structural scope. It covers only floor joists, ceiling joists and rafters. Nothing on studs, wall plates, door and window headers, floor girders/beams, posts, piers or footings, wall or roof sheathing thickness, fastening schedules, gambrel rafter geometry, collar ties, or engineered trusses - and no wind or seismic design, only the generic Section 8 statement that 'adequate bracing and bridging to resist wind and other lateral forces shall be provided.'

No engineered trusses of any kind, and no rafter-thrust or heel-connection design. Section A.7 assumes either a properly designed ridge beam (which the document does not size) or a ridge board at 3-in-12 or steeper with ceiling joists installed parallel to the rafters as a continuous tie. If your 16x20 wants an open cathedral ceiling, you are pushed straight to a ridge beam the tables will not size for you.

All spans assume a single simple span, uniform load, at least three members at not more than 24 in. o.c., and the member fully sheathed and nailed on the top edge. Point loads (a loft post, a mini-split, a hoist) and non-uniform loads are out of scope.

Tabulated spans stop at 26 ft and the note warns to 'check sources of supply for availability of lumber in lengths greater than 20 feet' - a 20 or 24 ft clear span may be tabulated yet practically hard to buy, and the tables give no guidance on splicing or LVL substitution.

Dense two-way tables (17 to 29 columns) with the answer split between the grid and a footer row - floor and ceiling tables are entered by E with required Fb below, rafter tables are entered by Fb with required E below. Easy to read the wrong axis, and there is no beginner hand-holding beyond three examples.

Roof dead-load categories are coarse and clay-tile-flavored (light = 1 course asphalt shingles at 10 psf; heavy = 2 in. clay book tile at 20 psf). Metal roofing, which many shed builders choose, is never named; you must judge which dead load bin it falls in.

Tables A-1 to A-4 are explicitly 'a guide only and are superseded by the governing building code in the applicable jurisdiction,' and AWC disclaims all liability: 'Those using this document assume all liability from its use.' It is not a stamped or sealed engineering document.
The PDF is AES-256 encrypted with copy/text-extraction disabled (printing allowed), so pasting table values into a spreadsheet requires re-typing or a tool that ignores the permission flag.

9.1 notes: 1) Bearing width is assumed to be 1.5 in. 2) Total uniform load is assumed to be 66.67 plf. 3) Alternate Fc-perp values are possible by adjusting the tabulated values in direct proportion to the desired load. 4) See A.1.3 for 2 span floor joist requirements.

-- Appendix A.5: spans for nominal 2x5 are 82 percent of the 2x6 spans at the same spacing; E values equal the 2x6 values; Fb values are the 2x6 Fb values times 1.077
plans.floor_framing: Covered in depth for joists only. Tables F-1 through F-7 give allowable single-span floor-joist lengths for 2x6, 2x8, 2x10 and 2x12 at 12, 16, 19.2 and 24 in. o.c., all at L/360, for live loads of 30, 40, 50 and 60 psf over dead loads of 10 or 20 psf. Entered by modulus of elasticity E (0.8 to 2.4 million psi); the required bending design value Fb is printed in the footer rows and applies to all sizes in that table. plans.roof: Rafters only, in 24 tables. plans.skill_level: Intermediate to advanced. No carpentry skill needed, but you must be comfortable reading two-way engineering tables, know that floor/ceiling tables are entered by E while rafter tables are entered by Fb, and be willing to cross-reference a second document (Design Values for Joists and Rafters, Tables W-1/W-2) to convert Fb/E requirements into a species and grade you can buy. Beginners are better served by AWC's free "Tutorial for Understanding Loads and Using Span Tables" or the Span Options Calculator.
plans.permit_notes: Strong permit-support document rather than a permit submittal. The tables are calculated from the National Design Specification (NDS) and use American Softwood Lumber Standard PS 20-20 sizes, and AWC span tables are the source most residential codes and plan reviewers already recognize, so attaching the applicable table page with your species/grade/spacing circled is an inexpensive way to justify joist and rafter sizing. It is not stamped or sealed by an engineer, and AWC disclaims responsibility: "neither the American Wood Council nor its members assume any responsibility for any particular design prepared from this publication. Those using this document assume all liability from its use." Tables A-1 through A-4 are explicitly "intended as a guide only and are superseded by the governing building code in the applicable jurisdiction." Section 7 requires that lumber be identified by the grade stamp of, or certificate of inspection from, an agency recognized by the ALSC Board of Review or the Canadian Lumber Standards Accreditation Board - so ungraded or mill-run lumber falls outside these tables. Confirm your local roof snow load and floor live load before choosing a table, and check whether your jurisdiction is on a code cycle that references the newer 2024 edition.

plans.summary: Sutherlands sells this as a complete post-frame material package, not a plan you buy: a 16' x 20' three-sided horse shelter where all framing lumber, painted steel roofing/siding, screws, nails, hardware and "a set of plans" ship together from a local Sutherlands store. Standard features are treated posts set in the ground (size varies by region), a treated 2x6 splashboard, 2x4 wall girts, "easy-to-build rafters" (rafters, not trusses — unlike Sutherlands' larger pole barn and horse barn packages), 2x4 roof purlins, 8' walls, and an open front ready for stalls or gate panels that are sold separately. No price is published anywhere on the page; it is quote-only through one of ~45 participating stores across AR, CO, KS, LA, MO, MS, NM, OH, OK, TX, UT and WY, and the quote form lets you pick a materials-only or installed package plus a custom width, length and wall height (8'-20'). No itemized material list, no plan page count, no roof pitch and no post-embedment depth appear online — the page explicitly says contents vary by store and to ask a salesperson for the actual list, and that the engineering wet stamp is not included if your jurisdiction requires one.
includes: All framing material (treated posts, treated 2x6 splashboard, 2x4 wall girts, 2x4 roof purlins, rafters)
Quality painted steel roofing and siding in your choice of 18 colors plus Galvalume
Color-matched roofing and siding screws
Nails and hardware
Set of plans
Optional installed-building pricing (quote form offers "Materials Only" or "Installed Building Package")
pros: Genuinely complete material package — framing, steel, fasteners and plans arrive together from a local yard, so no cut-list shopping trip and no guessing on steel panel lengths or trim.

Post-frame construction is the cheapest way to enclose 320 sq ft: treated posts in the ground carry the roof, so there is no foundation, no slab and no floor system to build (sibling Sutherlands packages state "No concrete slab required" outright).
Only three walls and no doors or windows to frame — this is about the lowest-difficulty 320 sq ft building a DIYer can attempt, and the clear-span open front means no header work.
Rafters rather than trusses on this size means everything is stick-built on site from lumber in the pile — nothing oversized to crane or truck-deliver.
8' walls with 2x4 girts at typical 24" o.c. plus a treated splashboard is a well-proven farm-building detail; horse-safe surfaces are all wood on the inside face.
Free custom quote covers any width/length/height (8'-20' wall heights, optional 12" overhang), so you can stretch it to 16x24 or 20x24 without leaving the product line.
Regional lumberyard support: 45 participating stores, buy-in-store pickup, and Sutherlands credit financing.
cons: No price at all is published — you cannot compare cost without submitting a lead form or phoning a store, and the page warns lumber is a commodity whose price "can and do change daily".

No itemized materials or cut list online. The page explicitly says the actual list "can vary by store" and to consult a salesperson, so you cannot verify what you're getting or price-shop the pieces before committing.

"Engineering wet stamp not included (if required)" — if your county wants stamped drawings for a 320 sq ft accessory building you pay an engineer separately, and the included plans are generic, not site-specific.

Critical structural numbers are absent: roof pitch, rafter size and spacing, post size ("depends on region"), post embedment depth, girt spacing, overall height, and design snow/wind loads are all unstated on the page.

Regional only — participating stores are limited to AR, CO, KS, LA, MO, MS, NM, OH, OK, TX, UT and WY, and the quote form requires a store within 100 miles of the build site. Useless outside that footprint.
Open front means no security and no way to close the building up; stalls, gate panels and any doors are sold separately and not part of the package.
No floor, no slab, no concrete and no post-hole concrete are included, and there is no loft — usable only as a shelter/run-in, not as a workshop or storage building without extra spend.
The advertised 280 sq ft "enclosed area" vs the 16x20 (320 sq ft) headline is unreconciled, so the real interior dimension needs confirming with the salesperson before you plan stalls.
Steel-clad post frame is not permit-friendly everywhere — the page pushes code compliance entirely onto the buyer and warns "Additional material may need to be purchased to comply with local codes."

plans.name: Advanced Framing Construction Guide (APA Form No. M400A)
plans.vendor: APA – The Engineered Wood Association (Tacoma, WA)
plans.http_status: 200 (Wayback snapshot 20150327100005, application/pdf, 5,710,120 bytes, 24 pages); live https://www.apawood.org/data/sharedfiles/documents/m400.pdf = 404
plans.footprint_note: varies
plans.style: Not a building style — framing system reference ("advanced framing" / optimum value engineering, 2x6 @ 24 in. o.c. + continuous wood structural panel sheathing). Gable, hip and truss roofs are all discussed only in terms of how they drive the master framing layout.
plans.price: Free 24-page PDF download from APA. (APA states its library of 400+ publications is "available for instant PDF download or hard-copy purchase"; the hard-copy price is not stated in the document.)
plans.summary: Details are cited to the 2012 IRC, 2012 IECC and 2012 IBC (the three codes listed under "Building Codes Referenced in this Guide") plus the 2012 Wood Frame Construction Manual, which the guide lists under "Additional References" rather than as a code
plans.foundation: not stated
plans.floor_framing: Engineered wood floor joists — I-joists, structural composite lumber (SCL) and/or glulam — at 24 in. o.c., with member spans between supports maximized; engineered band joists and floor beams to increase spans between foundation elements; APA Rim Board; APA Sturd-I-Floor minimum 24 oc panels. Guide notes 24 in. o.c. joists cut joist count by about 30% vs. 16 in. o.c., that deeper/larger joists may be required, that floor vibration may need consideration, and that thicker sheathing is worth using at 24 in. o.c. for stiffness. No joist size/span table is included (it points to APA Form E710 for vibration).
plans.wall_framing: one pair of king studs and one pair of jack studs per opening (one of each per side), with jack studs omitted where an approved framing connector/header hanger or a wood structural panel box header permits a single full-height stud at each side of openings up to 48 in. wide
plans.roof: ceiling joists over insulated or conditioned spaces at 24 in. o.c. per 2012 IRC Table R802.4(1) (Ceiling Joist Spans For Common Lumber Species) where attic storage is limited and mechanical equipment is not required; rafters may likewise be spaced 24 in. o.c. but the guide cites no rafter span table for that
plans.siding: Not specified as a product. Guide notes continuous plywood/OSB sheathing acts as a withdrawal-resistant nailbase, so the common vinyl siding grades that require fastening into studs every 16 in. can be used over 24 in. o.c. framing (per siding manufacturer ICC-ES reports and APA Form TT-109), and supports brick ties, decorative trim and fiber-cement products up to 11 psf.
plans.doors: No door schedule. Framing guidance only: one pair of king studs and one pair of jack studs per opening (single full-height stud each end permitted for openings up to 48 in. wide with studs at 24 in. o.c., up to 150 mph 3-second-gust design wind, per 2012 WFCM Table 3.23D); header hangers/approved framing connectors can replace jack studs; an overall header height of 15 in. allows 6 ft 8 in. interior and exterior doors where nominal ceiling height is 8 ft or higher.
plans.windows: No window schedule. Framing guidance only: best rough-opening placement per Figure 10 using the rule "24 in. layout module + 3/4 in. + (rough opening width/2)" for 23 in. to 46-1/2 in. wide rough openings, to keep tributary load on the header at 24 in. rather than 48 in.; headers not required in non-load-bearing walls (single flat opening top plate, cripples omitted where header-to-top-plate distance is under 24 in.).
plans.loft: not stated
plans.wall_height: not stated (examples reference a "typical 8-foot wall" and nominal 8 ft ceiling heights; stud height limits are deferred to code)
plans.overall_height: not stated
plans.materials_list_available: No — there is no bill of materials, cut list or quantity takeoff. What is published is framing detail specs, connection/nailing schedules and one sheathing-vs-wind-speed table.
lumber_list: NOTE: no bill of materials or cut list is published. The following are the verbatim component and connection specifications given in the guide.
2x6 wood studs spaced 24 inches on center (vs. 2x4 wood studs spaced 16 inches on center)
Single top plates (vs. double top plates in conventional framing)
Single headers (vs. double headers and cripples in conventional framing)
Insulated three-stud corners or two-stud corner with ladder blocking
Corner stud / 2x ladder blocking at 24" o.c. or drywall clips
2x ladder blocking at 24" o.c. — Install blocking with wide face vertical for maximum backing to wall finish materials and for maximum insulation to exterior walls.
Walls continuously sheathed with plywood or oriented strand board (OSB)
Use of jack studs and cripples around openings only where required

LONGITUDINAL TOP PLATE SPLICE, prescriptive connection: 3" x 12" x 0.036" galvanized steel plate at plate splice. (12) 8d (2-1/2" x 0.113") nails each side. [Plate size and number of fasteners required is greater than prescriptive code requirements for top plate butt-joint splices; based on equivalent performance of 2012 IRC Table R602.3(1), Item 14.]

LONGITUDINAL TOP PLATE SPLICE, alternate connection (splice at stud): 2x scab, splice joint, single top plate — (8) 16d (3-1/2" x 0.135") nails each side of splice. No splitting of scab or plate permitted (2012 IRC Table R602.3(1), Item 14).
INTERSECTING WALL CONNECTION, prescriptive: 3" x 6" x 0.036" galvanized steel plate. (6) 8d (2-1/2" x 0.113") nails each side (2012 IRC Section R602.3.2).
INTERSECTING WALL CONNECTION, alternate: 2x4 or 2x6 lumber splice in lieu of metal connection plate. (2) 10d (3" x 0.128") nails each side (2012 IRC Table R602.3(1), Item 19).

Interior wall intersection: single top plate; interior wall plate tight to exterior wall plate; or interior stud set in 1/2" from exterior wall studs for continuous drywall application. Install at least one ladder block at the mid-height of the wall to restrain the adjacent stud in a straight plane.

SINGLE-PLY HEADER: single-ply load-bearing header, flush outer face of header with outer edge of studs; cavity insulation space to stud depth less single header thickness; header bottom plate to complete rough opening at header. Sizing per 2012 IRC Table R602.7.1.
LARGE OPENING SINGLE HEADERS: 3-1/8" or 3-1/2" glulam or multiple-ply SCL or lumber, jack studs as required.
APPROVED FRAMING CONNECTOR OPTION (single- or double-ply headers): header hanger or equivalent; single stud at sides of rough openings (most openings up to 48" wide).

WOOD STRUCTURAL PANEL BOX HEADER: minimum 15/32 Performance Category wood structural panel or thicker over minimum 2x4 framing; panel face shall be a single piece; 9" or 15" wide; nail pattern 3" 3" 3"; single top plate and single bottom plate continuous with no vertical joints in the wood structural panel over the opening; cripple studs on stud layout. Sanded or MDO plywood may be used on the inside surface in lieu of drywall. Per 2012 IRC Section R602.7.2, Figure R602.7.2 and Table R602.7.2.
Box header openings: single stud at sides of rough opening to 48" wide; jack stud required if span > 48".

OPENING IN NON-LOAD-BEARING WALLS: conventional headers not required; single top plate; cripple studs as required; single opening top plate (may be doubled for openings wider than 8'); use jack studs as required.
ROUGH OPENING PLACEMENT rule: 24" layout module + 3/4" + (rough opening width/2) for 23"- to 46-1/2"-wide rough openings.

Blocking: 2x horizontal blocking (installed perpendicular to the studs) can be oriented with either the edge against the sheathing/drywall or the wide face vertical against the sheathing/drywall — install with the wide face vertical for maximum backing to wall finish materials and minimal intrusion into insulatable cavity.

PERMITTED FRAMING ALIGNMENT OFFSETS - SINGLE TOP PLATES: trusses or floor joists at 24" o.c. over studs at 24" o.c., 1" maximum offset each way; rafters and ceiling joists at 24" o.c. over studs at 24" o.c., 1" maximum offset.

STACK FRAMING: APA plywood or OSB roof sheathing; roof trusses (energy heel roof trusses shown) 24" o.c.; single top plate; APA plywood or OSB wall sheathing; 2x6 studs 24" o.c. supporting one floor, roof and ceiling (height limitations per code requirements); APA Sturd-I-Floor minimum 24 oc; APA Rim Board; APA wood I-joists or SCL 24" o.c.

TABLE 1 (2012 IRC Table R602.3(3)) wind-pressure wall sheathing: 6d Common (2" x 0.113"), 1.5" penetration, 24/0 span rating, 3/8" nominal panel, 16" max stud spacing, nails 6" o.c. edges / 12" o.c. field — max wind speed 110 mph (Exp. B) / 90 (C) / 85 (D).

TABLE 1 continued: 8d Common (2-1/2" x 0.131"), 1.75" penetration, 24/16 span rating, 7/16" nominal panel, 16" max stud spacing, 6"/12" nailing — 130 mph (B) / 110 (C) / 105 (D); same nail and panel at 24" max stud spacing — 110 mph (B) / 90 (C) / 85 (D).

TABLE 1 note (c): Wood structural panels with span ratings of Wall-16 or Wall-24 shall be permitted as an alternate to panels with a 24/0 span rating. Plywood siding rated 16 o.c. or 24 o.c. shall be permitted as an alternate to panels with a 24/16 span rating.
Panel installation: space panels 1/8 inch at panel ends and edges (to limit buckling at 24" o.c. framing).

ENERGY HEEL TRUSS TO WALL: energy heel truss over plywood or OSB wall sheathing; fastening per design; optional rafter-tie or tension strap inside or over wall sheathing per manufacturer recommendation; ensure correct fastening of sheathing to top plate per shear wall, wall bracing, or combined shear and uplift requirements.

Energy heel insulation depth: roughly 10 inches for most R30 batt, loose-fill fiberglass or cellulose insulation, and roughly 12 inches for R38 (uncompressed R30 deemed to satisfy R38, uncompressed R38 deemed to satisfy R49, per 2012 IECC 402.2.1).
ENERGY STAR thermal-bridging requirements cited: insulated corners (R6 minimum), insulated headers (R3 minimum for 2x4 construction, R5 minimum for 2x6 construction).
Ladder junction material use: less than 6 feet of blocking material in a typical 8-foot wall, vs. 16 feet of stud lumber plus additional blocking for a conventional intersection.
plans.format: PDF, 24 pages, US letter (612 x 792 pt), Form No. M400A, © 2014 APA – The Engineered Wood Association. AES-encrypted for copy/change but printable and text-extractable.
plans.skill_level: Intermediate to advanced framing knowledge assumed — reads as builder/designer guidance, not a step-by-step. The guide itself warns that "if framing crews are unfamiliar with advanced framing, additional onsite supervision and quality control oversight should be planned while framers learn these new techniques," and that "some included details may require engineering by a design professional."
plans.est_material_cost: not stated — the guide repeatedly claims lower material and labor cost than conventional framing (and roughly 30% fewer floor joists at 24 in. o.c., under 6 ft of blocking vs. 16 ft of studs per wall intersection) but publishes no dollar figures.
plans.permit_notes: Permit-relevant and unusually explicit: "APA recommends that you consult your local building official early in the design phase to verify and obtain acceptance of 24-inch framing techniques in your jurisdiction." Also: "it is important that the advanced framing details are clearly specified on the architectural plans when submitted to the building department." Everything is cited to the 2012 IRC, 2012 IECC and 2012 WFCM, which makes it easy to point an inspector at a code section — but those are the 2012 editions, not current code. Buildings in high-wind regions are noted as beyond the IRC prescriptive scope and should be designed per the IBC or other engineering standards. Single top plates are allowed only under the R602.3.2 exception (tied joints + rafters/joists centered over studs within 1 in.).

pros: Free, and unusually citation-dense for a free document: nearly every recommendation is footnoted to a specific 2012 IRC / IECC / WFCM section or table, so a DIY builder can defend 24 in. o.c. framing and single top plates to a plans examiner instead of arguing from opinion.

Directly relevant to a 16x20 insulated shed/studio: 2x6 @ 24 in. o.c. with continuous plywood/OSB is the cheapest way to get a real insulation cavity, and the guide states continuously sheathed wood structural panels are code-recognized as bracing at up to 24 in. o.c. while let-in bracing and some alternative panel products are capped at 16 in. o.c.

Real, quantified material savings at this footprint: ~1/3 fewer studs than 16 in. o.c., about 30% fewer floor joists at 24 in. o.c., and wall intersections that need under 6 ft of ladder blocking instead of 16 ft of stud lumber plus blocking.

Gives you the two things needed to legally delete the double top plate: the R602.3.2 exception language and verbatim splice details (3" x 12" x 0.036" galvanized plate with 12-8d each side, or a 2x scab with 8-16d each side).

Reproduces IRC Table R602.3(3) in full, so you can pick sheathing thickness/span rating and nail spacing against your actual wind speed and exposure category (7/16 in. 24/16 panel with 8d at 6/12 covers 110 mph Exp. B at 24 in. o.c. studs) rather than guessing.

Site-built wood structural panel box headers (15/32 panel over 2x4, 9 in. or 15 in. deep) let a 4-ft-wide door or window opening land on a single stud each side with no jack studs — cheap and directly applicable to shed man doors and 4-ft windows.

Solves the vinyl-siding trap: continuous plywood/OSB sheathing is a valid nailbase between studs, so 24 in. o.c. framing does not force you off common 16-in-fastening siding (also covers brick ties, trim, fiber cement to 11 psf).

Covers the insulated-shed details most shed plans skip: energy-heel truss to wall detail, the 2012 IECC R30-deemed-R38 / R38-deemed-R49 attic trade-off with actual insulation depths (~10 in. / ~12 in.), insulated corners and headers, and air-sealing benefits of fewer members.
Offers a phased 4-step adoption path so a first-time builder can take the easy wins (2x6, 24 in. o.c.) and skip the hardest one (single top plate) without breaking the system.

Good pointer document: names the companion APA forms (F430 wall bracing, TT-109 nailable sheathing, SR-101 combined shear and uplift, Z416 nailed panel beams, X480 panel buckling, E710 floor vibration) and the 2012 WFCM for header sizing by tributary load.
cons: This is NOT a plan. Zero footprints, elevations, floor plans, cut lists, foundation details, cost estimates or step-by-step sequence. You still need a separate 16x20 plan set or design; treat M400 purely as the framing-method companion to it.

Written for houses, and it shows. The box-header spans are keyed to 28 ft and 32 ft house widths with clear-span truss roofs or interior bearing walls, and stud-height/load-path language assumes 'one floor, roof and ceiling.' Translating those tables to a 16-20 ft wide shed takes judgment — and the guide itself says 'some included details may require engineering by a design professional.'

Single top plate, the headline saving, is the highest-friction technique: it forces stack framing with a 1 in. max offset, 24 in. o.c. floor and roof members, and 'non-industry standard stud lengths which may be difficult to source.' APA flatly notes 'many builders elect to retain double top plates' — so the marquee detail may not be worth it on a one-off shed.

Permit risk is real and named: you are told to clear 24 in. o.c. framing with the building official early and to call the advanced framing details out explicitly on submitted drawings. Some jurisdictions and framers push back, and a shed permit reviewer may not know this guide.

Code vintage. Everything references the 2012 IRC / 2012 IECC / 2012 WFCM in a 2014-dated document. Section and table numbers have moved in later code cycles and wind provisions have shifted to ASCE 7-16 ultimate design wind speeds, so the Table 1 mph values and R602.7.x citations must be re-checked against your adopted code.

No sizing tables of its own for the things a shed builder actually needs: no rafter, ceiling joist, floor joist, header or stud-height spans are printed — they are all deferred to the IRC, WFCM or manufacturer literature you must obtain separately.

24 in. o.c. wall sheathing buckles between studs more readily if it gets wet during construction — the guide flags this as a serviceability issue requiring jobsite moisture management and the 1/8 in. panel gap, which is easy for a slow-moving DIY build to get wrong.

Advanced framing assumes engineered products (I-joists, SCL, glulam, energy-heel trusses, APA Rim Board, Sturd-I-Floor) that are order-in items at a lumberyard, not off-the-rack 2x lumber — a cost and lead-time driver on a small shed where the savings are modest in absolute dollars.

Fewer members means less forgiveness: the whole system depends on vertical alignment and correct nailing, and it explicitly recommends extra onsite supervision for crews new to it. A single sloppy top-plate splice or misaligned truss undoes the load path.

Sourcing is now fragile. The publisher URL 404s; only the 2015 Wayback snapshot (and the copy saved locally here) is reachable, so there may be a newer revision of M400 whose content differs and which was not available to verify.
Not a kit, so kit-specific caveats do not apply: nothing is shipped, nothing is delivered, no floor is or is not included, and there is no price to conflate.

quotes: Advanced framing with 2x6 wood studs spaced 24 inches on center, combined with wood structural panel sheathing, is one of the most cost-effective solutions for builders trying to balance increasingly stringent energy codes with structural building code requirements.
(Note that some included details may require engineering by a design professional.)
APA recommends that you consult your local building official early in the design phase to verify and obtain acceptance of 24-inch framing techniques in your jurisdiction.

When advanced framing techniques are employed — including insulated headers — the reduction in the amount of framing materials can result in up to 12 percent more insulated space within the exterior wall.

Spacing engineered wood floor joists 24 inches on center will reduce the number of joists required by about 30 percent as compared to conventional 16-inch floor joist spacing. Note that deeper or larger joists may be required.

This method requires less than 6 feet of blocking material in a typical 8-foot wall. In conventional walls, interior wall intersections include a stud at each side of an intersecting wall, requiring a total of 16 feet of stud lumber plus additional blocking material.

Single top plate construction requires that all members above the top plate are stack framed (vertically aligned with the members directly below) with a maximum alignment offset tolerance of 1 inch (Figure 11). This requirement applies to roof trusses, rafters, and second-story floor joists when single top plates are used
There is no offset limitation for placement of members bearing on double top plates when 2x6 studs at 24 inches on center are used.

4. Eliminate double top plates. Because this step requires vertical framing alignment, including 24-inch on center floor and roof framing as well as non-industry standard stud lengths which may be difficult to source, it is often the last technique builders consider. For these reasons, many builders elect to retain double top plates.

2012 IRC Table R602.7.2 allows a 15-inch-high one-sided wood structural panel box header to span 4-feet-wide openings for homes up to 28-feet wide, and 3-feet-wide or narrower openings for homes up to 32 feet wide in single-story construction with a clear-span truss roof or two-story construction with floor and roof supported by interior bearing walls.

Table 3.23D of the 2012 WFCM specifies that, for areas with up to 150 mph (3 second gust) design wind velocity, a single full-height stud is required at each end of a header above openings of up to 48-inches wide when studs are spaced 24 inches on center, subject to stud length and grade limitations.

Due to their superior structural performance, continuous sheathing with wood structural panels is code-recognized as wall bracing for studs spaced up to 24 inches on center. Most other wall bracing methods, including let-in bracing and some alternative panel products, are limited by the code to 16-inch on center framing.

Other commonly used bracing techniques prescribed by the 2012 IRC, including bracing method LIB (let-in-bracing), require a maximum stud spacing of 16 inches on center or less and are therefore incompatible with some advanced framing techniques.

The most common and cost-effective grades of vinyl siding require fastening into studs every 16 inches. However, the nailbase capabilities of a continuously sheathed wood structural panel wall allow the use of these siding products with 24-inch on center framing because the sheathing also serves as a base for fastener attachment between studs.

The potential for panel buckling between studs increases when stud spacing is widened from 16 to 24 inches on center, especially when the sheathing is subjected to moisture exposure during construction. Although this is not a structural concern, excessive buckling may cause serviceability issues.

Whatever techniques are selected, it is important that the advanced framing details are clearly specified on the architectural plans when submitted to the building department. Note that if framing crews are unfamiliar with advanced framing, additional onsite supervision and quality control oversight should be planned while framers learn these new techniques.

When energy heel (or raised heel) trusses are used to satisfy this requirement, uncompressed R30 insulation is deemed to satisfy R38 requirements and uncompressed R38 insulation is deemed to satisfy R49 attic insulation requirements.

When designing a master framing layout, start with the layout of the roof framing members, which is generally dictated by roof design and geometry, followed by the layout of the framing members below.

The 2012 IRC specifies regions that are subject to higher wind loads and thus require greater uplift and shear resistance. Buildings in these regions are beyond the scope of the prescriptive code requirements of the IRC and should be designed in accordance with the International Building Code (IBC) or other engineering standards.

plans.summary_original: APA Form M400A, "Advanced Framing Construction Guide" (© 2014, 24-page free PDF) is a reference guide, NOT a shed plan. It documents the advanced framing / optimum value engineering (OVE) system: 2x6 studs at 24 in. on center, single top plates with prescriptive splice hardware, single-ply and site-built wood structural panel box headers, two-stud or insulated three-stud (California) corners, 2x ladder-blocking junctions at interior wall intersections, minimal jack studs and cripples, engineered I-joist/SCL/glulam floors at 24 in. o.c., 24 in. o.c. rafters and ceiling joists, energy-heel trusses, and continuous plywood/OSB wall sheathing as code-recognized bracing. Every detail is cited to the 2012 IRC, 2012 IECC or 2012 Wood Frame Construction Manual, and the guide reproduces IRC Table R602.3(3) (sheathing thickness, span rating and nail spacing vs. wind speed by exposure category). For a ~16x20 DIY shed it is the document that tells you how to frame walls at 24 in. o.c. legally and efficiently — it will not tell you what to build.

plans.footprint_note: varies
plans.style: Post-frame / pole building — "wood roof trusses or rafters connected to vertical timber columns or sidewall posts," with roof purlins and wall girts carrying the cladding. Roof shape never specified (Figure 1 shows a gable cutaway). Code classification: Type VA or VB construction.
plans.price: Free — direct PDF download, no account, email capture or paywall.
plans.format: 5-page letter-size PDF, "Design for Code Acceptance" series No. 5, Copyright 2013 American Wood Council, file code 1012, Word 2010, AES-encrypted with copy/change disabled (printing allowed). Prose commentary keyed to IBC chapter/section numbers plus 4 figures. No buildable drawings.
plans.foundation: Two families described (Ch. 18 text + Figures 3, 4A, 4B), no sizes given. Embedded post: "a round hole is drilled for each post approximately four feet in the ground (or greater if required for frost protection per 1809.5)"; a pre-cast or cast-in-place round concrete pad goes in the bottom, "Pads are usually unreinforced," pad diameter sized so post load / pad area is under allowable soil bearing (IBC 1806/1807); Figure 3 labels embedment "3' - 6' Typical" plus "Collar as required by design." Anchored post: pinned to a concrete foundation with steel anchorage plates (Fig 4A), or moment connection via wet-set bracket or pre-cast concrete pier with 1/2" thru-bolt, 1/4" screw, internal steel reinforcement, hi-strength concrete, optional galvanized uplift anchor (Fig 4B). "The minimum 28 day concrete strength is 2,500 psi or 3,000 psi per Items 1 and 2 in Table 1808.8.1." No footing diameters, depths by climate, or rebar schedules.
plans.floor_framing: not stated. Figure 1 labels a "Concrete Slab (Optional)" plus a "Treated Skirt Board" and "2x8 Treated Cleats"; no wood floor system, joist size or slab thickness is discussed anywhere.
plans.wall_framing: Solid-sawn or laminated timber columns (posts) with horizontal wall girts. Figure 2 shows the two accepted arrangements: (a) girts on the exterior and interior faces of the posts, (b) girts between posts. A "Nominal 6-inch post" is referenced as the insulation cavity depth. No post size, post spacing, girt size or girt spacing is published — those are left to the designer.
plans.wall_height: not stated (only a pointer to IBC Table 503/Section 504 height limits for Type VA/VB)
plans.overall_height: not stated
plans.roof: Wood roof trusses or rafters with purlins; metal-plate-connected trusses must be designed and made per ANSI/TPI 1, and "long-span trusses require special attention to bracing and erection." Cladding: "the most common roof cladding for post-frame buildings is pre-painted corrugated steel" (IBC 1507.4); asphalt shingles over wood sheathing also common (1507.2). Steel roof panels are "commonly used as horizontal diaphragms to transfer lateral loads from the post-frame to end and interior shear walls," but a "floating" standing-seam roof "does not provide a diaphragm." Attic ventilation per IBC 1203.2; attics can be insulated to "R-40 or higher." No pitch, span, purlin size or truss spacing given.
plans.siding: "The most common exterior wall covering for post-frame buildings is pre-painted corrugated steel siding. But other materials such as exterior plywood, wood sidings, brick veneers, etc. are also common." Minimum thicknesses per IBC Table 1405.2, metal veneers per 1405.11, combustible siding and fireblocking per 1406/1406.2.3. Insulation per Figure 2: girts outside+inside the post give "total thermal resistance of R26 to R31"; girts between posts give "R19 to R21"; walls "may be easily insulated with R-30 batts."
plans.doors: not stated (no door sizes or headers anywhere; only IBC Table 705.8 exterior-opening area limits by fire separation distance are referenced)
plans.windows: not stated
plans.loft: not stated
plans.skill_level: Not a DIY build document. Written for "post-frame building designers"; you must read IBC chapters 5, 6, 7, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 18 and 23 alongside it, and it repeatedly hands sizing back to the designer (connections must be "carefully designed by the post-frame building designer, not left to the discretion of the erector"; embedment and diaphragm load-sharing require ANSI/ASAE EP 484.2, EP 486.1 or the NFBA Post-Frame Design Manual). For an owner-builder it is permit vocabulary and code background, not instructions.
plans.permit_notes: This is the document's whole purpose: "to provide guidance to post-frame building designers for meeting the requirements of the International Building Code (IBC) and to confirm that a properly designed post-frame building is in fact code compliant." It maps post-frame construction onto IBC chapters: Type VA/VB classification and Table 503 heights/areas; Table 601/602 fire-resistance (Type VB has no minimum rating); one/two/three-hour post-frame wall assemblies tested by NFBA and listed as UL Design No. V304 (BXUV.V304); one-hour roof/ceiling per Table 721.1(3) item 21-1.1; parapet exceptions in 705.11; attic ventilation 1203.2; IECC energy compliance; weather-covering thickness Table 1405.2; roofing 1507.2/1507.4; deflection Table 1604.3 (note "a" relaxes limits for corrugated metal, but purlins/girts supporting interior finishes must meet the table); uplift load path per 1604.8.1 with dead load offset per 1605.3; soils 1806, embedded posts 1807.3/1807.3.1, frost depth 1809.5, concrete strength Table 1808.8.1; preservative treatment AWPA U1 UC4B in soil and UC4A up to one foot above grade; trusses ANSI/TPI 1; ASD per 2306.1. It cites codes, it is not an approval or a stamped design — carries an explicit disclaimer that AWC "does not assume responsibility for particular designs or calculations prepared from this publication." Edition is keyed to the 2012-era IBC (2013 copyright), so section numbers may have shifted in the 2018/2021/2024 IBC.
