plans.summary: This is a March 2012 blog article on the Hansen Pole Buildings site (last modified 2026-06-11), not a shed plan. It answers a customer whose building inspector "does not like the idea of post spacing 12ft apart with double rafters" and had asked for a comparison quote using posts 8 ft on center, double 2x12 headers and single trusses every 4 ft. Hansen's answer defends its standard system — columns 12 ft on center with doubled prefabricated trusses bearing directly on the posts and 2x6 purlins hung between trusses with engineered steel hangers — citing an ice-storm post-mortem from the winter of 1996-97 in which side-by-side (not laminated) trusses failed and pulled roofs down. Useful as a structural-reasoning and permit-negotiation read for anyone considering a post-frame shed, but it contains zero drawings, dimensions, materials list or build steps.
includes: Prose article (~900 words) with one 225x202 px conceptual thumbnail image
The customer's verbatim question about 12 ft vs 8 ft post spacing
Hansen's engineering rationale for doubled trusses laminated together vs one truss on each side of the column
A first-person account of studying roof collapses after the 1996-97 ice storm
A numbered list of six claimed advantages of wide (12 ft) post spacing
A worked count example for a 48 ft long building (trusses and holes at 8 ft vs 12 ft spacing)
A statement that Hansen guarantees structural permit approval from its engineer-sealed plans given correct loading criteria
An email opt-in for a free 'Project Roadmap' planning guide (not a plan)
NO drawings, NO dimensions, NO materials or cut list, NO cost figures, NO downloadable PDF
pros: Explains a real structural trade-off clearly: doubled/laminated trusses on 12 ft columns give redundancy, whereas single trusses at 4-8 ft on headers can fail progressively ('domino effect') if one truss has a weak spot.

Grounded in a specific failure post-mortem (winter 1996-97 ice storm) rather than pure marketing, including the author's admission that his own earlier detail — one truss each side of the column with blocking — was the thing that failed.

Excellent permit-friendliness anecdote: the inspector who objected to 12 ft spacing issued the permit anyway once engineer-sealed plans were presented. Directly useful if your AHJ pushes back on wide post spacing.

Names the load-path details that actually matter in post-frame: trusses bear directly on top of the column (not nailed to the side, not on a header), purlins connect with engineered steel hangers rather than nails, and loads go into the ground through the column.
Makes the labor case for a DIYer honestly — fewer holes to dig, fewer posts to set, fewer pieces to raise — and notes wide sidewall bays let you add doors or windows later without structural headers.
Flags a genuine safety issue: standing on 2x4 purlins 16-20 ft in the air, and prefers 2x6 purlins ('50% more wood, 246% stronger').
cons: Not a buildable plan in any sense — no footprint, no elevations, no framing sections, no fastener schedule, no materials list. Anyone arriving here expecting a free 16x20 plan will get nothing constructible.

Every quantitative claim ('246% stronger', the truss nailing pattern) is asserted, not shown; the nailing pattern is explicitly withheld and 'supplied on all our plans' — i.e. gated behind buying a Hansen building.
Vendor marketing content. It exists to sell Hansen's engineered post-frame packages and to rebut a competing framing scheme, so the comparison is not neutral.

The system described is arguably overkill and awkward at shed scale: 12 ft column spacing on a 16x20 or 16x24 building leaves only one or two interior bents, and doubled trusses plus steel purlin hangers add cost and crane/lift needs a small-shed DIYer may not want.
Requires engineered trusses and engineer-sealed plans to realize the claimed permit guarantee — that means paying Hansen, not self-designing.
Foundation is embedded posts in dug holes; the article never states hole depth, diameter, concrete collar spec, or preservative treatment level, and gives no frost-depth or uplift guidance.
No pricing anywhere on the page and no published price list for the plans or kit — quotes are per-project.
Old post (2012) written by 'admin'; no engineer named, no code cycle, no load criteria (ground snow, wind speed, exposure) given, so none of it can be checked against your jurisdiction.

quotes: After talking with the building inspector he does not like the idea of post spacing 12ft apart with double rafters. Can you quote a standard setup so I can compare apple to apples, post 8ft on center with double 2x12 header and trusses every 4ft, no joist hangers needed for perlins?

While the building inspector may not "like the idea" of using post spacing 12 feet on center, it is not only a tried and true method, but it is also one which our engineers recognize as being structurally superior and will engineer seal.
Given the correct loading criteria and an engineered building, we will guarantee the ability to obtain a structural permit from our plans.

The post spacing every 8', single trusses every 4' resting upon headers is a system our engineers are not interested in risking their careers on. In the event of a single truss failure, this system will result in a domino effect and the collapse of the entire roof system.

But instead of putting the two trusses together to act as a single unit, we put one on each side of the column with blocking in between. ... With the huge loading of ice that year...the truss "weak spots" gave way - and if one truss fails, it pulls the rest of the roof down.

From then on, I started using double trusses, nailed together according to a specific nailing pattern (supplied on all our plans). Since then we've had other winters with similar ice/snow loadings, and...no more failed roofs!
By using slightly larger pieces (generally 2x6 instead of 2x4, where it takes only 50% more wood, to be 246% stronger) we are being material efficient.
Does anyone REALLY want to stand on a 2x4 roof purlin 16, 20 or more feet up in the air? When the 2x4 purlin snaps, it is a long drop to the ground.

Most building collapses come from connection failures. In our case the purlins connect to the trusses with engineered steel hangers (not just nails); the double trusses bear directly on the posts (not on the sides of the posts, or nailed onto a header).

If you think about it, if you have a 48' long building, with single trusses every 8', you have a total of 5 interior trusses. If you have double trusses every 12', you have a total of six interior trusses, but only have to dig 3 holes instead of 5. Which would you rather do?
By the way - our client DID get his building permit issued, using our plans, by the very same inspector who originally "did not like the idea".

plans.summary: This is a 2016 Hansen Pole Buildings blog post, not a shed plan. It reproduces an email from an architect asking about column spacing for a 50x70 post-frame footprint, and Hansen's reply: 12-foot column centers usually give the best value, a 48x72 footprint may be a better investment, and a quote requires eave height, location, snow/wind/seismic/soil-bearing parameters, code version, wind exposure, heated vs. unheated, and door requirements. The "free engineered plans" offer is narrow: it applies to governmental-agency projects that must go out for bid, where Hansen supplies the structural plans up front at no charge so they can be circulated to bidders. There is no 16x20-class design, no dimensions, no materials list, no cut list, no pricing, and no downloadable PDF anywhere on the page.

Described commercial path: engineered plans + materials delivered + written instructions bundled into a Hansen post-frame kit purchase
Advice to split a bid into two sections: (1) engineered plans, materials delivered and instructions provided, (2) labor to construct
Guidance that 12-foot column centers is the usual best-value spacing

They are 100% Building Code compliant." — that is the strongest permit story of any source in this category

Post-frame construction is inherently cheap and DIY-friendly at 320 sq ft scale: embedded pressure-treated columns on concrete footings mean no perimeter frost wall, no stem wall, and no floor joist system, so foundation labor and cost collapse compared to a stick-framed shed
Prefabricated engineered roof trusses on 12-ft centers mean very few truss lifts and no rafter cutting; wide clear spans come free, so a 16x20 or 20x24 shop has zero interior posts
Hansen will work directly with a client's architect or a permit office, and explicitly welcomes design professionals, which helps if a local jurisdiction demands a wet-stamped drawing
Company is long-established (LLC formed 2002, Browns Valley MN) and its blog is a large, detailed free knowledge base on post-frame detailing, eave heights, and bid processes
cons: This specific URL delivers no plan at all — no drawings, dimensions, materials list, or PDF. It is a Q&A blog post about a 50x70 commercial building. As a "16x20 shed plan" candidate it is a miss.
The "free" in the title is heavily conditional: free engineered plans are offered only where the buyer is a governmental agency and the job must be publicly bid. A private DIYer gets no free plan.

Hansen does not really sell plans standalone. Their /pole-barn-plans/ page says a plans-plus-materials-list-plus-instructions-only request "is going to cost about 25% of the value of the materials" — on a $10k package that is roughly $2,500 for paper, versus $30-$60 for a conventional shed plan PDF.

Hansen's own published size chart starts at 24x24x8 (576 sq ft, $6,000-$9,000). Nothing in the 240-480 sq ft target range is priced or catalogued, so a 16x20 is below their normal product floor and may not be economic to quote.

Vendor lock-in on materials: they warn there are "items on the pole barn plans, which are not going to be available from any other supplier" — products manufactured specifically for them. You cannot fully source a Hansen plan at a local lumberyard.
No price is obtainable without submitting a quote request, so you cannot comparison-shop from the website.
Post-frame means a bare dirt or gravel floor unless you separately pour a slab, and steel roofing/siding rather than the shingles-and-LP-siding look most backyard shed buyers want.
Digging and plumbing 5-8 deep column holes to below frost depth is the hard part of the build, and in rocky or high-water-table soil it can be worse than a simple skid or block foundation.
